Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Saṃyuttanikāye

In the Connected Discourses

Mahāvagga-aṭṭhakathā

Commentary on the Great Section

1. Maggasaṃyuttaṃ

1. The Connected Discourses on the Path

1. Avijjāvaggo

1. The Chapter on Ignorance

1-2. Avijjāsuttādivaṇṇanā

1-2. Commentary on the Discourse on Ignorance and Others

1-2. Mahāvaggassa [V 3.0153][P 3.0116][M 3.0153] paṭhame pubbaṅgamāti sahajātavasena ca upanissayavasena cāti dvīhākārehi pubbaṅgamā. Samāpattiyāti samāpajjanāya sabhāvapaṭilābhāya, uppattiyāti attho. Anvadeva ahirikaṃ anottappanti sā panesā yadetaṃ alajjanākārasaṇṭhikaṃ ahirikaṃ, abhāyanākārasaṇṭhitañca anottappaṃ, etaṃ anudeva saheva ekatova, na vinā tena uppajjatīti attho. Avijjāgatassāti avijjāya upagatassa samannāgatassa. Micchādiṭṭhīti ayāthāvadiṭṭhi aniyyānikadiṭṭhi. Pahotīti hoti uppajjati. Micchāsaṅkappādīsupi ayāthāvaaniyyānikavaseneva [V 3.0154] micchābhāvo veditabbo. Iti imāni aṭṭhapi akusaladhammasamāpattiyā micchattaaṅgāni nāma honti. Tāni pana na ekakkhaṇe sabbāni labbhanti, nānakkhaṇe labbhanti.

In the first discourse of the Great Section, as for ‘forerunner,’ it is a forerunner in two ways: by way of co-nascence and by way of decisive support. As for ‘attainment,’ the meaning is attainment, the acquisition of its own nature, and arising. As for ‘along with shamelessness and recklessness’: that ignorance which has become the forerunner of unwholesome states in the aforesaid manner—that which is shamelessness, established in the manner of not being ashamed due to not being disgusted by evil; and that which is recklessness, established in the manner of not fearing due to not being terrified of evil—arises only along with, together with, and as one with these two. It does not arise without them; this is the meaning. As for ‘one gone to ignorance,’ it means one who has gone to and is endowed with ignorance. As for ‘wrong view,’ it is a view that is not as things are, a view not leading out. As for ‘arises,’ it means it is, it arises. In wrong intention and so on too, the state of being wrong should be understood by way of not being as things are and not leading out. Thus, these eight are called the factors of wrongness for the attainment of unwholesome states. However, they are not all obtained in a single moment; they are obtained in different moments.

Kathaṃ? Yadā hi diṭṭhisampayuttacittaṃ kāyaviññattiṃ samuṭṭhāpentaṃ uppajjati, tadā micchādiṭṭhi micchāsaṅkappo micchāvāyāmo micchāsati micchāsamādhi [M 3.0154] micchākammantoti cha aṅgāni honti. Yadā diṭṭhivippayuttaṃ, tadā micchādiṭṭhivajjāni pañca. Yadā tāneva dve vacīviññattiṃ samuṭṭhāpenti, tadā micchākammantaṭṭhāne micchāvācāya saddhiṃ tāneva cha vā pañca vā. Ayaṃ ājīvo nāma kuppamāno kāyavacīdvāresuyeva aññatarasmiṃ kuppati, na manodvāre. Tasmā yadā ājīvasīsena tāneva cittāni kāyavacīviññattiyo samuṭṭhāpenti, tadā kāyakammaṃ micchājīvo nāma hoti, tathā vacīkammanti micchājīvassa vasena tāneva cha vā pañca vā. Yadā pana viññattiṃ asamuṭṭhāpetvā tāni cittāni uppajjanti[P 3.0117], tadā micchādiṭṭhimicchāsaṅkappamicchāvāyāmamicchāsatimicchāsamādhivasena pañca vā, micchāsaṅkappādivasena cattāri vā hontīti evaṃ na ekakkhaṇe sabbāni labbhanti, nānakkhaṇe labbhantīti.

How so? When a consciousness associated with wrong view arises while producing bodily intimation, then six factors are present: wrong view, wrong intention, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration, and wrong action. When it is dissociated from wrong view, then there are five factors, excluding wrong view. When those same two types of consciousness produce verbal intimation, then, in place of wrong action, along with wrong speech, those same six or five factors are present. This livelihood, when it is corrupted, is corrupted only at one of the doors of body or speech, not at the mind door. Therefore, when those same consciousnesses produce bodily or verbal intimations with livelihood as the principal factor, then bodily action is called wrong livelihood, and similarly verbal action. Thus, by way of wrong livelihood, those same six or five factors are present. But when those consciousnesses arise without producing intimation, then five factors are present by way of wrong view, wrong intention, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration; or four by way of wrong intention and so on. Thus, they are not all obtained in a single moment, but they are obtained in different moments.

Sukkapakkhe vijjāti kammassakatañāṇaṃ. Ihāpi sahajātavasena ca upanissayavasena cāti dvīhākārehi pubbaṅgamatā veditabbā. Hirottappanti hirī ca ottappañca. Tattha lajjanākārasaṇṭhitā hirī, bhāyanākārasaṇṭhitaṃ ottappaṃ. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana visuddhimagge vuttova. Vijjāgatassāti vijjāya upagatassa samannāgatassa. Viddasunoti viduno paṇḍitassa. Sammādiṭṭhīti yāthāvadiṭṭhi niyyānikadiṭṭhi. Sammākammantādīsupi eseva nayo. Iti kusaladhammasamāpattiyā imāni aṭṭhaṅgāni honti, tāni lokiyamaggakkhaṇe na ekato sabbāni labbhanti, lokuttaramaggakkhaṇe pana labbhanti. Tāni ca kho paṭhamajjhānikamagge, dutiyajjhānikādīsu pana sammāsaṅkappavajjāni satteva honti.

In the bright side, ‘knowledge’ is the knowledge of kamma as one's own property. Here too, the state of being a forerunner should be understood in two ways: by way of co-nascence and by way of decisive support. ‘Moral shame and moral dread’ means moral shame and moral dread. Therein, moral shame is established in the manner of being ashamed, and moral dread is established in the manner of being fearful. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation is as stated in the Visuddhimagga. As for ‘one gone to knowledge,’ it means one who has gone to and is endowed with knowledge. As for ‘of one who knows,’ it means of the wise, the learned. As for ‘right view,’ it is a view in accordance with reality, a view leading to liberation. The same method applies to right action and so on. Thus, for the attainment of wholesome states, these are the eight factors. They are not all obtained together at the moment of the mundane path, but they are obtained at the moment of the supramundane path. And they are obtained in the path of the first jhāna; however, in the paths of the second jhāna and so on, there are only seven, excluding right intention.

Tattha yo evaṃ vadeyya “yasmā majjhimanikāyamhi mahāsaḷāyatanikasutte (ma. ni. 3.431) ‘yā tathābhūtassa diṭṭhi, sāssa hoti sammādiṭṭhi. Yo tathābhūtassa, saṅkappo, svāssa hoti sammāsaṅkappo. Yo tathābhūtassa vāyāmo, svāssa hoti sammāvāyāmo. Yā tathābhūtassa sati, svāssa hoti [V 3.0155] sammāsati. Yo tathābhūtassa samādhi, svāssa hoti sammāsamādhi. Pubbeva kho panassa kāyakammaṃ vacīkammaṃ ājīvo ca suparisuddho’ti vuttaṃ tasmā pañcaṅgikopi lokuttaramaggo hotī”ti so vattabbo – tasmiṃyeva sutte “evamassāyaṃ ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo bhāvanāpāripūriṃ gacchatī”ti idaṃ kasmā na passasi[M 3.0155]? Yaṃ panetaṃ “pubbeva kho panassā”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ pabbajitadivasato paṭṭhāya parisuddhabhāvadassanatthaṃ. Pabbajitadivasato paṭṭhāya hi parisuddhāni kāyakammādīni lokuttaramaggakkhaṇe atiparisuddhāni hontīti ayamattho dīpito.

Herein, if someone were to say: “Because in the Mahāsaḷāyatanika Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya it is said: ‘The view of one who is thus is their right view. The intention of one who is thus is their right intention. The effort of one who is thus is their right effort. The mindfulness of one who is thus is their right mindfulness. The concentration of one who is thus is their right concentration. Moreover, their bodily action, verbal action, and livelihood are already well-purified,’ therefore, the supramundane path can also be five-factored,” they should be told: “In that very sutta, why do you not see this: ‘Thus, this Noble Eightfold Path of theirs goes to the fulfillment of development’?” And as for what is said there, “Moreover, their… are already well-purified,” that is stated to show their purity from the day of ordination onwards. For, bodily action and so on, which are purified from the day of ordination onwards, become exceedingly purified at the moment of the supramundane path—this meaning is indicated.

Yampi abhidhamme vuttaṃ “tasmiṃ kho pana samaye pañcaṅgiko maggo hotī”ti (vibha. 212), taṃ ekaṃ kiccantaraṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Yasmiñhi kāle micchākammantaṃ pahāya sammākammantaṃ pūreti, tasmiṃ kāle micchāvācā vā micchājīvo vā na hoti, diṭṭhi saṅkappo vāyāmo [P 3.0118] sati samādhīti imesuyeva pañcasu kārakaṅgesu sammākammanto pūrati. Virativasena hi sammākammanto pūrati nāma. Sammāvācāsammāājīvesupi eseva nayo. Iti imaṃ kiccantaraṃ dassetuṃ evaṃ vuttaṃ. Lokiyamaggakkhaṇe ca pañceva honti, virati pana aniyatā. Tasmā “chaaṅgiko”ti avatvā “pañcaṅgiko”tveva vuttaṃ. “Yā ca, bhikkhave, ariyacittassa anāsavacittassa ariyamaggasamaṅgino ariyamaggaṃ bhāvayato tīhi kāyaduccaritehi ārati virati paṭivirati veramaṇī akiriyā akaraṇaṃ, ayaṃ bhikkhave sammākammanto ariyo anāsavo lokuttaramaggo”ti (ma. ni. 3.139). Evaṃ pana mahācattālīsakasuttādīsu anekesu suttesu sammākammantādīnañca lokuttaramaggassa aṅgabhāvasiddhito aṭṭhaṅgikova lokuttaramaggo hotīti veditabboti. Imasmiṃ sutte ayaṃ aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo lokiyalokuttaramissakova kathito. Dutiyaṃ kosalasaṃyutte vuttameva.

And what is stated in the Abhidhamma: 'At that time, the path is five-factored' (Vibh. 212)—that was stated to show a certain distinct function. For at the time when one abandons wrong action and fulfills right action, at that time there is no wrong speech or wrong livelihood; right action is fulfilled in the presence of these five causal factors—right view, right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. For right action is indeed fulfilled by way of abstinence. This same method should be understood for right speech and right livelihood as well. Thus, this was stated to show this distinct function. And at the moment of the mundane path, only five factors are constant, whereas abstinence is inconstant. Therefore, instead of saying 'six-factored,' it was said 'five-factored.' 'And, bhikkhus, for one with a noble mind, a mind without taints, who possesses the noble path and is developing the noble path, whatever abstaining, refraining, desisting, abstinence, non-doing, and non-performance from the three kinds of bodily misconduct there is—this, bhikkhus, is right action, which is noble, without taints, and is the supramundane path' (MN 3.139). Moreover, since in many suttas, such as the Mahācattālīsaka Sutta, the status of right action and so on as factors of the supramundane path is established, it should be understood that the supramundane path is indeed eight-factored. In this sutta, this eight-factored path is taught as a mixture of the mundane and supramundane. The second is as stated in the Kosala Saṃyutta.

3. Sāriputtasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Sāriputta Sutta

3. Tatiye sakalamidaṃ bhanteti ānandatthero sāvakapāramīñāṇassa matthakaṃ appattatāya sakalampi maggabrahmacariyaṃ kalyāṇamittasannissayena labbhatīti na aññāsi, dhammasenāpati pana sāvakapāramīñāṇassa matthake ṭhitattā aññāsi, tasmā evamāha. Tenevassa bhagavā sādhu sādhūti sādhukāramadāsi.

3. In the third sutta, regarding 'All this, venerable sir': because the Elder Ānanda had not yet reached the pinnacle of the knowledge of a disciple's perfections, he did not know that the entire holy life of the path is obtained through reliance on a good spiritual friend. But the General of the Dhamma, because he was established at the pinnacle of the knowledge of a disciple's perfections, knew; therefore, he spoke thus. For that very reason, the Blessed One gave him his approval, saying, 'Good, good.'

4. Jāṇussoṇibrāhmaṇasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Jāṇussoṇi Brahmin Sutta

4. Catutthe [V 3.0156][M 3.0156] sabbasetena vaḷavābhirathenāti sakalasetena catūhi vaḷavāhi yuttarathena. So kira sabbo sacakkapañjarakubbaro rajataparikkhitto hoti. Ratho ca nāmesa duvidho hoti – yodharatho, alaṅkārarathoti. Tattha yodharatho caturassasaṇṭhāno hoti nātimahā dvinnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vā janānaṃ [P 3.0119] gahaṇasamattho. Alaṅkāraratho mahā hoti dīghato dīgho puthulato puthulo ca, tattha chattaggāhako vālabījaniggāhako tālavaṇṭaggāhakoti evaṃ aṭṭha vā dasa vā sukheneva ṭhātuṃ vā nisīdituṃ vā nipajjituṃ vā sakkonti. Ayampi alaṅkārarathoyeva.

4. In the fourth sutta, 'with an all-white chariot drawn by mares' means with a chariot yoked with four entirely white mares. It is said that the entire chariot, including its wheels, frame, and pole, was overlaid with silver. Now, a chariot is of two kinds: a war chariot and a ceremonial chariot. The war chariot is square in shape, not very large, and able to hold two or three people. The ceremonial chariot is large; it is long in length and broad in width. In it, eight or ten people—such as an umbrella-bearer, a yak-tail fan-bearer, and a palm-leaf fan-bearer—can comfortably stand, sit, or lie down. This too was a ceremonial chariot.

Setā sudaṃ assāti tā vaḷavā pakatiyā setavaṇṇāva. Setālaṅkārāti pasādhanaṃ tāsaṃ rajatamayaṃ ahosi. Seto rathoti rathopi vuttanayeneva rajataparikkhittattā tattha tattha dantakammakhacitattā ca setova. Setaparivāroti yathā aññe rathā sīhacammaparivārāpi honti, byagghacammaparivārāpi paṇḍukambalaparivārāpi honti, na evaṃ esa. Esa pana ghanadukūlena parivārito ahosi. Setā rasmiyoti rasmiyopi rajatapanāḷisuparikkhittā. Setā patodalaṭṭhīti patodalaṭṭhipi rajataparikkhittā.

Regarding 'The mares were indeed white': those mares were naturally of a white color. Regarding 'adorned with white': their adornments were made of silver. Regarding 'the white chariot': the chariot too, in the way already described, was white because it was overlaid with silver and inlaid with ivory work in various places. Regarding 'with white coverings': just as other chariots may be covered with lion skins, tiger skins, or pale woolen blankets, this one was not so. Rather, this one was covered with fine white cloth. Regarding 'white reins': the reins too were encased in silver tubes. Regarding 'the white goad': the goad too was covered with silver.

Setaṃ chattanti rathamajjhe ussāpitachattampi setameva ahosi. Setaṃ uṇhīsanti aṭṭhaṅgulavitthāro rajatamayo uṇhīsapaṭṭo seto. Setāni vatthānīti vatthānipi setāni pheṇapuñjavaṇṇāni. Tesu nivāsanaṃ pañcasatagghanakaṃ, uttarāsaṅgo sahassagghanako. Setā upāhanāti upāhanā nāma maggāruḷhassa vā honti aṭaviṃ vā pavisantassa. Ayaṃ pana rathaṃ abhiruḷho, tenassa tadanucchaviko rajatapaṭisevito pādālaṅkāro nāma esa evaṃ vuttoti veditabbo. Setāya sudaṃ vālabījaniyāti phalikamayadaṇḍāya setacamaravālabījaniyā. Na kevalañca ettakamevassa setaṃ ahosi, so pana brāhmaṇo setavilepanaṃ vilimpi, setamālaṃ piḷandhi, dasasu aṅgulīsu aṅgulimuddikā kaṇṇesu kuṇḍalānīti evamādi alaṅkāropissa rajatamayova ahosi[M 3.0157]. Parivārabrāhmaṇāpissa dasasahassamattā tatheva setavatthavilepanamālālaṅkārā ahesuṃ.

Regarding 'the white parasol': the parasol raised in the middle of the chariot was also white. Regarding 'the white turban': the turban-plate, eight finger-breadths wide and made of silver, was white. Regarding 'the white garments': the garments too were white, the color of a mass of foam. Among them, the lower garment was worth five hundred, and the upper garment was worth a thousand. Regarding 'white footwear': 'footwear' is for one who is walking on a road or entering a forest. But this one was riding in a chariot; therefore, it should be understood that what is called this was a foot ornament, suitable for the occasion and adorned with silver. Regarding 'with a white yak-tail fan': this means with a white chowrie-hair fan with a crystal handle. And not only was this much of his white; but that brahmin also anointed himself with white unguent, wore a white garland, and the rings on his ten fingers, the earrings in his ears—these and other such ornaments were also made of silver. His retinue of about ten thousand brahmins were likewise adorned with white garments, unguents, garlands, and ornaments.

Yaṃ panetaṃ sāvatthiyā niyyāyantanti vuttaṃ, tatrāyaṃ niyyāyanavibhāvanā – so kira channaṃ channaṃ [V 3.0157] māsānaṃ ekavāraṃ nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ karoti – “ito ettakehi divasehi nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ karissatī”ti puretarameva ghosanā kayirati. Taṃ sutvā ye nagarato na pakkantā, te na pakkamanti. Yepi pakkantā, tepi “puññavato sirisampattiṃ passissāmā”ti āgacchanti. Yaṃ divasaṃ brāhmaṇo nagaraṃ anuvicarati, tadā [P 3.0120] pātova nagaravīthiyo sammajjitvā vālikaṃ okiritvā lājapañcamehi pupphehi vippakiritvā puṇṇaghaṭe ṭhapetvā kadaliyo ca dhaje ca ussāpetvā sakalanagaraṃ dhūpitavāsitaṃ karonti.

As for what was said, 'He sets out from Sāvatthī,' here is the explanation of the setting out: It is said that once every six months he makes a circumambulation of the city. An announcement is made beforehand: 'In so many days from now, he will circumambulate the city.' Hearing this, those who have not left the city do not depart. And those who have left also come back, thinking, 'We shall see the glorious fortune of this meritorious one.' On the day the brahmin travels through the city, early in the morning they sweep the city streets, scatter sand, strew flowers with parched grain as the fifth, place full water pots, raise up banana trees and banners, and make the entire city fumigated and perfumed.

Brāhmaṇo pātova sīsaṃ nhāyitvā purebhattaṃ bhuñjitvā vuttanayeneva setavatthādīhi attānaṃ alaṅkaritvā pāsādā oruyha rathaṃ abhiruhati. Atha naṃ te brāhmaṇā sabbasetavatthavilepanamālālaṅkārā setacchattāni gahetvā parivārenti. Tato mahājanassa sannipātatthaṃ paṭhamaṃyeva taruṇadārakānaṃ phalāphalāni vikiranti, tadanantaraṃ māsakarūpādīni, tadanantaraṃ kahāpaṇe vikiranti. Mahājano sannipatati, ukkuṭṭhiyo ceva celukkhepā ca vattanti. Atha brāhmaṇo maṅgalikasovatthikādīsu maṅgalāni ceva suvatthiyo ca karontesu mahāsampattiyā nagaraṃ anuvicarati. Puññavantā manussā ekabhūmikādipāsāde āruyha sukapattasadisāni vātapānakavāṭāni vivaritvā olokenti. Brāhmaṇopi attano yasasirisampattiyā nagaraṃ ajjhottharanto viya dakkhiṇadvārābhimukho hoti. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

The brahmin, having bathed his head early in the morning and eaten his morning meal, adorns himself with white garments and so forth in the manner already described. Then, descending from his mansion, he mounts his chariot. At that time, those brahmins, all adorned with white garments, perfumes, and garlands, holding white parasols, surround him. Next, to gather a large crowd, they first scatter various fruits for the young children, then small coins and the like, and afterward, they scatter kahāpaṇas. The great crowd gathers, and shouts of acclamation and the tossing of cloths occur. Then, while auspicious wishes and blessings are being made, the brahmin travels around the city in great splendor. Meritorious people, ascending one-story mansions and the like, open window shutters that resemble the wings of parrots and look on. The brahmin, too, as if overwhelming the city with his fame, glory, and prosperity, heads toward the southern gate. With reference to that, this was said.

Tamenaṃ jano disvāti mahājano taṃ rathaṃ disvā. Brahmanti seṭṭhādhivacanametaṃ. Brahmaṃ vata bho yānanti seṭṭhayānasadisaṃ vata bho yānanti ayamettha attho. Imasseva kho etanti, ānanda, manussā nāma vaṇṇabhāṇakānaṃ dhanaṃ datvā attano dārikānaṃ vaṇṇagītaṃ gāyāpenti “abhirūpo hoti dassanīyo mahaddhano mahābhogo”ti, na ca tena vaṇṇabhaṇanamattena abhirūpā vā honti mahaddhanā vā, evameva mahājano [M 3.0158] brāhmaṇassa rathaṃ disvā – “brahmaṃ vata bho yāna”nti kiñcāpi evaṃ vaṇṇaṃ bhaṇati, na panetaṃ yānaṃ vaṇṇabhaṇanamatteneva brahmayānaṃ nāma hoti. Lāmakañhi etaṃ chavaṃ. Paramatthena pana imasseva kho etaṃ, ānanda, ariyassa aṭṭhaṅgikassa maggassa [P 3.0121] adhivacanaṃ. Ayañhi sabbadosavigamena seṭṭho, iminā ca ariyā nibbānaṃ yantīti brahmayānaṃ itipi, dhammabhūtattā yānattā ca dhammayānaṃ itipi, anuttarattā kilesasaṅgāmassa ca vijitattā anuttaro saṅgāmavijayo itipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati.

Regarding 'seeing him, the people': this means the great crowd, upon seeing that chariot. 'Brahma' is a designation for 'the best.' 'Truly, sirs, what a Brahma-vehicle!' means 'Truly, sirs, what a vehicle like the best of vehicles!'—this is the meaning here. Regarding 'this is for this very one': Ānanda, people give wealth to praise-singers and have them sing songs of praise for their daughters, saying, 'She is beautiful, lovely to see, of great wealth, and of great possessions!' But they do not become beautiful or wealthy by that mere act of praising. In the same way, the great crowd, upon seeing the brahmin’s chariot, although they praise it thus—'Truly, sirs, what a Brahma-vehicle!'—this vehicle does not become a 'Brahma-vehicle' by the mere act of praising. For it is inferior, a corpse. But in the ultimate sense, Ānanda, this is a designation for the Noble Eightfold Path. For this path is the best due to the removal of all faults, and because the noble ones go to Nibbāna by this path, it can be called the 'Brahma-vehicle.' Because it has become Dhamma and is a vehicle, it can be called the 'Dhamma-vehicle.' And because it is unsurpassed and because the battle with the defilements has been won, it is fit to be called 'the unsurpassed victory in battle.'

Idānissa [V 3.0158] niddosabhāvañceva saṅgāmavijayabhāvañca dassento rāgavinayapariyosānātiādimāha. Tattha rāgaṃ vinayamānā pariyosāpeti pariyosānaṃ gacchati nipphajjatīti rāgavinayapariyosānā. Esa nayo sabbattha.

Now, wishing to show its faultless nature and its victorious nature in battle, he said the words beginning with, 'culminating in the removal of lust...' Therein, 'culminating in the removal of lust' (rāgavinayapariyosānā) is so called because, while removing lust, it brings it to an end, reaches its conclusion, and is accomplished. This method is to be understood in all cases.

Yassa saddhā ca paññā cāti yassa ariyamaggayānassa saddhānusārivasena saddhā, dhammānusārivasena paññāti ime dve dhammā sadā dhuraṃ yuttā, tatramajjhattatāyuge yuttāti attho. Hirī īsāti attanā saddhiṃ adhiviṭṭhena bahiddhāsamuṭṭhānena ottappena saddhiṃ ajjhattasamuṭṭhānā hirī yassa maggarathassa īsā. Mano yottanti vipassanācittañca maggacittañca yottaṃ. Yathā hi rathassa vākādimayaṃ yottaṃ goṇe ekābaddhe karoti ekasaṅgahite, evaṃ maggarathassa lokiyavipassanācittaṃ atirekapaññāsa, lokuttaravipassanācittaṃ atirekasaṭṭhi kusaladhamme ekābaddhe ekasaṅgahe karoti. Tena vuttaṃ “mano yotta”nti. Sati ārakkhasārathīti maggasampayuttā sati ārakkhasārathi. Yathā hi rathassa ārakkho sārathi nāma yoggiyo. Dhuraṃ vāheti yojeti akkhaṃ abbhañjati rathaṃ peseti rathayuttake nibbisevane karoti, evaṃ maggarathassa sati. Ayañhi ārakkhapaccupaṭṭhānā ceva kusalākusalānañca dhammānaṃ gatiyo samanvesatīti vuttā.

Regarding 'for whom there is faith and wisdom': for which Noble Path Vehicle, faith—in the manner of a faith-follower—and wisdom—in the manner of a Dhamma-follower—these two qualities are always yoked to the pole; meaning, yoked in the yoke of equanimity (tatramajjhattatā). Regarding 'shame is the pole' (hirī īsā): shame (hirī), which arises internally, together with moral dread (ottappa), which arises externally and is established in oneself, is the pole of this path-chariot. Regarding 'the mind is the yoke-rope' (mano yottaṃ): the mind of insight and the mind of the path are the yoke-rope. For just as the yoke-rope of a chariot, made of bark-fiber and the like, binds the oxen together and brings them into one group, so too, for the path-chariot, the mundane insight-mind binds together over fifty wholesome states, and the supramundane insight-mind binds together over sixty wholesome states, into a single group. Therefore it is said, 'the mind is the yoke-rope.' Regarding 'mindfulness is the guarding charioteer' (sati ārakkhasārathi): mindfulness associated with the path is the guarding charioteer. For just as the guard of a chariot, the charioteer, yokes the draft animals, makes them bear the pole, anoints the axle, sends the chariot forth, and makes the yoked animals steady, so too is mindfulness for the path-chariot. For it is said that this mindfulness has guarding as its manifestation and investigates the courses of wholesome and unwholesome states.

Rathoti ariyaaṭṭhaṅgikamaggaratho. Sīlaparikkhāroti catupārisuddhisīlālaṅkāro. Jhānakkhoti vipassanāsampayuttānaṃ pañcannaṃ jhānaṅgānaṃ vasena jhānamayaakkho. Cakkavīriyoti vīriyacakko, kāyikacetasikasaṅkhātāni [P 3.0122] dve vīriyāni assa cakkānīti attho. Upekkhā dhurasamādhīti [M 3.0159] dhurassa samādhi, unnatonatākārassa abhāvena dvinnampi yugapadesānaṃ samatāti attho. Ayañhi tatramajjhattupekkhā cittuppādassa līnuddhaccabhāvaṃ haritvā payogamajjhatte cittaṃ ṭhapeti, tasmā imassa maggarathassa “dhurasamādhī”ti vuttā. Anicchā parivāraṇanti bāhirakarathassa sīhacammādīni viya imassāpi ariyamaggarathassa alobhasaṅkhātā anicchā parivāraṇaṃ nāma.

Regarding 'the chariot': it is the Noble Eightfold Path-chariot. Regarding 'the equipment of virtue': it has the adornment of the fourfold purity of virtue. Regarding 'the jhāna-axle': it is an axle made of jhāna, by way of the five jhāna factors associated with insight. Regarding 'the energy-wheel': it is the wheel of energy, meaning that the two energies, called bodily and mental, are its wheels. Regarding 'equanimity is the pole's stability' (upekkhā dhurasamādhi): this means the stability of the pole; the meaning is the evenness of both sides of the yoke, due to the absence of being raised or lowered. For this tatramajjhattatā-equanimity, having removed the states of sloth and restlessness from the mind's arising, establishes the mind in the middle of exertion. Therefore, for this path-chariot, it is called 'the pole's stability.' Regarding 'non-desire is the covering': just as an external chariot has coverings such as lion's skin, so too for this Noble Path-chariot, non-desire, which is known as non-greed (alobha), is called the covering.

Abyāpādoti mettā ca mettāpubbabhāgo ca. Avihiṃsāti karuṇā ca karuṇāpubbabhāgo ca. Vivekoti kāyavivekādi tividhaviveko. Yassa āvudhanti yassa ariyamaggarathe ṭhitassa kulaputtassa etaṃ pañcavidhaṃ āvudhaṃ. Yathā hi rathe ṭhito pañcahi āvudhehi sapatte vijjhati, evaṃ yogāvacaropi imasmiṃ lokiyalokuttaramaggarathe ṭhito mettāya dosaṃ vijjhati, karuṇāya vihiṃsaṃ[V 3.0159], kāyavivekena gaṇasaṅgaṇikaṃ, cittavivekena kilesasaṅgaṇikaṃ, upadhivivekena sabbākusalaṃ vijjhati. Tenassetaṃ pañcavidhaṃ “āvudha”nti vuttaṃ. Titikkhāti duruttānaṃ durāgatānaṃ vacanapathānaṃ adhivāsanakkhanti. Cammasannāhoti sannaddhacammo. Yathā hi rathe ṭhito rathiko paṭimukkacammo āgatāgate sare khamati, na naṃ te vijjhanti, evaṃ adhivāsanakkhantisamannāgato bhikkhu āgatāgate vacanapathe khamati, na naṃ te vijjhanti. Tasmā “titikkhā cammasannāho”ti vutto. Yogakkhemāya vattatīti catūhi yogehi khemāya nibbānāya vattati, nibbānābhimukho gacchatiyeva, na tiṭṭhati na bhijjatīti attho.

Non-ill will is loving-kindness and the preliminary part of loving-kindness. Non-harming is compassion and the preliminary part of compassion. Seclusion is the threefold seclusion, such as bodily seclusion and so on. 'Whose weapon' means this fivefold weapon belonging to the noble son who stands in the chariot of the noble path. Just as one standing in a chariot strikes enemies with five weapons, so too the yogi, standing in this chariot of the mundane and supramundane path, strikes hatred with loving-kindness, harm with compassion, association with a group with bodily seclusion, association with defilements with mental seclusion, and all unwholesome states with the seclusion from the substrata. Therefore, this fivefold dhamma is said to be his 'weapon.' Endurance is the patience of enduring ill-spoken, ill-come words and paths of speech. 'Leather armor' means being clad in leather. Just as a charioteer standing in a chariot, clad in leather armor, withstands incoming arrows, and they do not pierce him, so too a bhikkhu endowed with the patience of enduring withstands incoming paths of speech, and they do not pierce him. Therefore, endurance is called 'leather armor.' 'It leads to safety from the yokes' means it leads towards Nibbāna, the safety from the four yokes; it proceeds directly towards Nibbāna, neither stopping nor faltering—this is the meaning.

Etadattani sambhūtanti etaṃ maggayānaṃ attano purisakāraṃ nissāya laddhattā attani sambhūtaṃ nāma hoti. Brahmayānaṃ anuttaranti asadisaṃ seṭṭhayānaṃ. Niyyanti dhīrā lokamhāti yesaṃ etaṃ yānaṃ atthi, te dhīrā paṇḍitapurisā lokamhā niyyanti gacchanti. Aññadatthūti ekaṃsena. Jayaṃ jayanti rāgādayo sapatte jinantā jinantā.

‘This born in oneself’ means this path-vehicle is called 'born in oneself' because it is attained by relying on one's own manly effort. ‘The unsurpassed Brahma-vehicle’ means an incomparable, excellent vehicle. ‘The wise go forth from the world’ means those who possess this vehicle, the wise and discerning persons, go forth from the world. ‘Without a doubt’ means certainly. ‘They win victory’ means, conquering enemies such as lust and so forth, they are ever victorious.

5-6. Kimatthiyasuttādivaṇṇanā

5-6. Commentary on the Kimatthiya Sutta and Others

5-6. Pañcame [P 3.0123] ayamevāti evasaddo niyamattho. Tena aññaṃ maggaṃ paṭikkhipati. Imasmiṃ sutte vaṭṭadukkhañceva missakamaggo ca kathito. Chaṭṭhaṃ uttānameva.

5-6. In the fifth, the word 'eva' has the meaning of restriction. By this, it rejects another path. In this sutta, the suffering of the round of rebirth and the mixed path are spoken of. The sixth is simply clear.

7. Dutiyaaññatarabhikkhusuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Second Sutta about a Certain Bhikkhu

7. Sattame [M 3.0160] nibbānadhātuyā kho etaṃ bhikkhu adhivacananti asaṅkhatāya amatāya nibbānadhātuyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Āsavānaṃ khayo tena vuccatīti apica tena rāgādivinayena āsavānaṃ khayotipi vuccati. Āsavakkhayo nāma arahattaṃ, arahattassāpi etaṃ rāgavinayotiādi nāmamevāti dīpeti. Etadavocāti “satthārā nibbānadhātūti vadantena amataṃ nibbānaṃ kathitaṃ, maggo panassa na kathito. Taṃ kathāpessāmī”ti anusandhikusalatāya pucchanto etaṃ avoca.

7. 'This, bhikkhu, is a designation for the Nibbāna element' means this—the removal of lust, removal of hatred, removal of delusion—is a designation for the unconditioned, deathless Nibbāna element. By 'The destruction of the taints is called by that,' it is meant that indeed, by that term 'removal of lust,' etc., it is also called the destruction of the taints. Arahantship is what is called the destruction of the taints, and it is shown that this—'the removal of lust,' and so on—is also just a primary name for Arahantship. 'He said this' means: thinking, 'The Teacher, in saying "Nibbāna element," spoke of deathless Nibbāna, but the path to it was not spoken of. I will get him to speak of it,' he, being skilled in connecting the sequence of the teaching, asked and said this.

8. Vibhaṅgasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Vibhaṅga Sutta

8. Aṭṭhame [V 3.0160] katamā ca bhikkhave sammādiṭṭhīti ekena pariyāyena aṭṭhaṅgikamaggaṃ vibhajitvā puna aparena pariyāyena vibhajitukāmo idaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Tattha dukkhe ñāṇanti savanasammasanapaṭivedhapaccavekkhaṇavasena catūhākārehi uppannaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Samudayepi eseva nayo. Sesesu pana dvīsu sammasanassa abhāvā tividhameva vaṭṭati. Evametaṃ “dukkhe ñāṇa”ntiādinā catusaccakammaṭṭhānaṃ dassitaṃ.

8. In the eighth sutta, regarding the teaching 'And what, O bhikkhus, is right view?', having analyzed the Noble Eightfold Path by one method, and wishing to analyze it again by another method, He began this discourse. Therein, 'knowledge in suffering' is the knowledge that arises in four modes: by way of hearing, considering, penetration, and reviewing. In the case of the origin also, this is the same method. However, in the remaining two, due to the absence of considering, only a threefold knowledge is applicable. Thus, by this 'knowledge in suffering,' and so on, the meditation subject of the Four Truths is shown.

Tattha purimāni dve saccāni vaṭṭaṃ, pacchimāni vivaṭṭaṃ. Tesu bhikkhuno vaṭṭe kammaṭṭhānābhiniveso hoti, vivaṭṭe natthi abhiniveso. Purimāni hi dve saccāni “pañcakkhandhā dukkhaṃ, taṇhā samudayo”ti evaṃ saṅkhepena ca, “katame pañcakkhandhā rūpakkhandho”tiādinā nayena vitthārena ca ācariyasantike uggaṇhitvā vācāya punappunaṃ parivattento yogāvacaro kammaṃ karoti. Itaresu pana dvīsu saccesu – “nirodhasaccaṃ iṭṭhaṃ kantaṃ manāpaṃ, maggasaccaṃ iṭṭhaṃ kantaṃ manāpa”nti evaṃ savaneneva kammaṃ karoti. So evaṃ karonto cattāri saccāni ekapaṭivedhena paṭivijjhati, ekābhisamayena abhisameti[P 3.0124]. Dukkhaṃ pariññāpaṭivedhena paṭivijjhati, samudayaṃ pahānapaṭivedhena, nirodhaṃ sacchikiriyapaṭivedhena, maggaṃ bhāvanāpaṭivedhena paṭivijjhati. Dukkhaṃ pariññābhisamayena…pe… maggaṃ bhāvanābhisamayena abhisameti.

Therein, the first two truths are the round of existence; the latter two are that which is free from the round. Among these, for a bhikkhu, there is application of mind to the meditation subject in the round; in that which is free from the round, there is no such application of mind. For the first two truths—'the five aggregates are suffering, craving is the origin'—the yogi, having learned them from a teacher both in brief and in detail by the method beginning 'What are the five aggregates? The aggregate of form...', performs the preliminary practice by verbally reciting them again and again. But regarding the other two truths, he performs the preliminary practice merely by hearing thus: 'The truth of cessation is desirable, lovely, and pleasing; the truth of the path is desirable, lovely, and pleasing.' In doing so, he penetrates the four truths with a single penetration, and comprehends them with a single comprehension. He penetrates suffering through the penetration of full understanding, the origin through the penetration of abandoning, cessation through the penetration of realization, and the path through the penetration of development. He comprehends suffering through the comprehension of full understanding... and so on... he comprehends the path through the comprehension of development.

Evamassa pubbabhāge dvīsu saccesu uggahaparipucchāsavanadhāraṇasammasanapaṭivedho hoti, dvīsu savanapaṭivedhoyeva. Aparabhāge tīsu [M 3.0161] kiccato paṭivedho hoti, nirodhe ārammaṇapaṭivedho. Paccavekkhaṇā pana pattasaccassa hoti. Imassa bhikkhuno pubbe pariggahato – “dukkhaṃ parijānāmi, samudayaṃ pajahāmi, nirodhaṃ sacchikaromi, maggaṃ bhāvemī”ti ābhogasamannāhāramanasikārapaccavekkhaṇā natthi, pariggahato paṭṭhāya hoti. Aparabhāge pana dukkhaṃ pariññātameva hoti…pe… maggo bhāvitova hoti.

Thus, for him, in the preliminary stage, regarding the first two truths, there is penetration by way of learning, questioning, hearing, retaining, and considering; regarding the other two, there is only penetration through hearing. In the later stage, regarding three truths, there is penetration by way of function; regarding cessation, there is penetration by way of taking it as an object. Reviewing, however, occurs for one who has attained the truths. For this bhikkhu, before grasping the meditation subject, there is no reviewing, adverting, bringing to mind, or mental application such as: 'I will fully understand suffering, I will abandon the origin, I will realize cessation, I will develop the path.' This occurs only from the time of grasping onwards. However, in the later stage, suffering is indeed fully understood... and so on... the path is indeed developed.

Tattha dve saccāni duddasattā gambhīrāni, dve gambhīrattā duddasāni. Dukkhasaccañhi uppattito pākaṭaṃ, khāṇukaṇṭakapahārādīsu “aho dukkha”nti vattabbatampi āpajjati. Samudayampi [V 3.0161] khāditukāmatābhuñjitukāmatādivasena uppattito pākaṭaṃ. Lakkhaṇapaṭivedhato pana ubhayampi gambhīraṃ. Iti tāni duddasattā gambhīrāni. Itaresaṃ dvinnaṃ dassanatthāya payogo bhavaggaggahaṇatthaṃ hatthapasāraṇaṃ viya avīciphusanatthaṃ pādapasāraṇaṃ viya satadhā bhinnassa vālassa koṭiyā koṭiṃ paṭipādanaṃ viya ca hoti. Iti tāni gambhīrattā duddasāni. Evaṃ duddasattā gambhīresu gambhīrattā ca duddasesu catūsu saccesu uggahādivasena idaṃ “dukkhe ñāṇa”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Paṭivedhakkhaṇe pana ekameva taṃ ñāṇaṃ hoti.

Therein, two truths are profound because they are difficult to see, and two are difficult to see because they are profound. For the truth of suffering is evident from its arising; when struck by a stump, a thorn, and so on, one might even say, 'Ah, suffering!' The origin, too, is evident from its arising, by way of the desire to eat, the desire to enjoy, and so on. With respect to the penetration of their characteristics, however, both are profound. Thus, they are profound because they are difficult to see. As for the other two, the effort to see them is like stretching out a hand to grasp the peak of existence, like stretching out a foot to touch the Avīci hell, or like causing one tip of a hair split a hundredfold to meet the other tip. Thus, they are difficult to see because they are profound. In this way, concerning the four truths—those profound because they are difficult to see, and those difficult to see because they are profound—this was stated by way of grasping and so on: 'knowledge in suffering,' etc. At the moment of penetration, however, that knowledge is just one.

Nekkhammasaṅkappādīsu kāmapaccanīkaṭṭhena kāmato nissaṭabhāvena vā, kāmaṃ sammasantassa uppannoti vā, kāmapadaghātaṃ kāmavūpasamaṃ karonto uppannoti vā[P 3.0125], kāmavivittante uppannoti vā nekkhammasaṅkappo. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Sabbepi ca te nekkhammasaṅkappādayo kāmabyāpādavihiṃsāviramaṇasaññānaṃ nānattā pubbabhāge nānā, maggakkhaṇe pana imesu tīsu ṭhānesu uppannassa akusalasaṅkappassa padacchedato anuppattisādhanavasena maggaṅgaṃ pūrayamāno ekova kusalasaṅkappo uppajjati. Ayaṃ sammāsaṅkappo nāma.

Among thoughts of renunciation and so on, 'thought of renunciation' is so called because it is the opposite of sensual pleasures, or because it has emerged from sensuality; or it is a thought that arises for one who is contemplating sensuality; or it arises while bringing about the destruction of the basis of sensual pleasure and its subsiding; or it arises at the end of detachment from sensual pleasure. The same method applies to the remaining two terms. And all those thoughts of renunciation and so on are diverse in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of the perceptions of refraining from sensuality, ill will, and harmfulness. At the moment of the path, however, fulfilling the path factor by cutting off the basis of an unwholesome thought that would arise in these three instances and thereby effecting its non-arising, only a single wholesome thought arises. This is called Right Intention.

Musāvādā veramaṇīādayopi musāvādādīhi viramaṇasaññānaṃ nānattā pubbabhāge nānā, maggakkhaṇe pana imesu catūsu ṭhānesu uppannāya [M 3.0162] akusaladussīlyacetanāya padacchedato anuppattisādhanavasena maggaṅgaṃ pūrayamānā ekāva kusalaveramaṇī uppajjati. Ayaṃ sammāvācā nāma.

The abstinences, beginning with abstaining from false speech, are also diverse in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of the perceptions of refraining from false speech and so on. At the moment of the path, however, fulfilling the path factor by cutting off the basis of an unwholesome, immoral volition that would arise in these four instances and thereby effecting its non-arising, only a single wholesome abstinence arises. This is called Right Speech.

Pāṇātipātā veramaṇī ādayopi pāṇātipātādīhi viramaṇasaññānaṃ nānattā pubbabhāge nānā, maggakkhaṇe pana imesu tīsu ṭhānesu uppannāya akusaladussīlyacetanāya akiriyato padacchedato anuppattisādhanavasena maggaṅgaṃ pūrayamānā ekāva kusalaveramaṇī uppajjati. Ayaṃ sammākammanto nāma.

The abstinences, beginning with abstaining from taking life, are also diverse in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of the perceptions of refraining from taking life and so on. At the moment of the path, however, fulfilling the path factor by way of non-performance, by cutting off the basis, and by effecting the non-arising of an unwholesome, immoral volition that would arise in these three instances, only a single wholesome abstinence arises. This is called Right Action.

Micchāājīvanti khādanīyabhojanīyādīnaṃ atthāya pavattitaṃ kāyavacīduccaritaṃ. Pahāyāti vajjetvā. Sammāājīvenāti buddhapasatthena ājīvena. Jīvikaṃ kappetīti jīvitavuttiṃ pavatteti. Sammājīvopi kuhanādīhi viramaṇasaññānaṃ nānattā pubbabhāge nānā. Maggakkhaṇe pana imesuyeva sattasu ṭhānesu uppannāya micchājīvadussīlyacetanāya padacchedato anuppattisādhanavasena [V 3.0162] maggaṅgaṃ pūrayamānā ekāva kusalaveramaṇī uppajjati. Ayaṃ sammāājīvo nāma.

Wrong Livelihood is bodily and verbal misconduct engaged in for the sake of edibles, food, and so forth. 'Having abandoned' means having avoided. 'By right livelihood' means by a livelihood praised by the Buddha. 'He maintains his life' means he carries on his livelihood. Right Livelihood is also diverse in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of the perceptions of refraining from deceit and so on. At the moment of the path, however, fulfilling the path factor by cutting off the basis of the immoral volition of wrong livelihood that would arise in these very seven instances and thereby effecting its non-arising, only a single wholesome abstinence arises. This is called Right Livelihood.

Anuppannānanti ekasmiṃ bhave tathārūpe vā ārammaṇe attano na uppannānaṃ, parassa pana uppajjamāne disvā – “aho vata me evarūpā pāpakā dhammā na uppajjeyyu”nti evaṃ anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya. Chandanti tesaṃ akusalānaṃ anuppādakapaṭipattisādhakaṃ vīriyacchandaṃ janeti. Vāyamatīti vāyāmaṃ karoti. Vīriyaṃ ārabhatīti vīriyaṃ pavatteti. Cittaṃ paggaṇhātīti vīriyena cittaṃ paggahitaṃ karoti. Padahatīti “kāmaṃ taco ca nhāru ca aṭṭhi ca avasissatū”ti (ma. ni. 2.184) padhānaṃ pavatteti[P 3.0126]. Uppannānanti samudācāravasena attano uppannapubbānaṃ. Idāni tādise na uppādessāmīti tesaṃ pahānāya chandaṃ janeti.

As for 'of the unarisen': of those that have not yet arisen for oneself in a particular existence or in relation to an object of such a nature. But seeing them arising in another, one thinks, 'Oh, may such evil states not arise in me!' Thus, it is for the non-arising of unarisen, evil, unwholesome states. As for 'desire': one generates the will to arouse energy that accomplishes the practice for the non-arising of those unwholesome states. As for 'strives': one makes an effort. As for 'arouses energy': one sets energy in motion. As for 'exerts the mind': one makes the mind exerted by means of energy. As for 'strives': one sets in motion the chief striving with the thought, 'Willingly, let only skin, sinews, and bone remain.' As for 'of the arisen': of those that have arisen previously in oneself by way of habitual conduct. Thinking, 'Now I will not cause such states to arise,' one generates the desire for their abandonment.

Anuppannānaṃ kusalānanti apaṭiladdhānaṃ paṭhamajjhānādīnaṃ. Uppannānanti tesaṃyeva paṭiladdhānaṃ. Ṭhitiyāti punappunaṃ uppattipabandhavasena ṭhitatthaṃ. Asammosāyāti avināsatthaṃ. Bhiyyobhāvāyāti uparibhāvāya. Vepullāyāti vipulabhāvāya. Pāripūriyāti bhāvanāya paripūraṇatthaṃ. Ayampi sammāvāyāmo [M 3.0163] anuppannānaṃ akusalānaṃ anuppādanādicittanānattā pubbabhāge nānā. Maggakkhaṇe pana imesuyeva catūsu ṭhānesu kiccasādhanavasena maggaṅgaṃ pūrayamānaṃ ekameva kusalavīriyaṃ uppajjati. Ayaṃ sammāvāyāmo nāma.

'Of unarisen wholesome states' means of the first jhāna and so forth that have not yet been obtained. 'Of the arisen' means of those same states that have been obtained. 'For stability' means for the purpose of stability through an uninterrupted stream of repeated arising. 'For non-confusion' means for the purpose of non-perishing. 'For increase' means for causing growth to higher levels. 'For abundance' means for the purpose of expansion. 'For fulfillment' means for the purpose of completion through development. This right effort, too, is diverse in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of mind-moments accomplishing functions such as the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states. At the moment of the path, however, in these very four instances, a single wholesome energy arises, fulfilling the path factor by accomplishing its function. This is called right effort.

Sammāsatipi kāyādipariggāhakacittānaṃ nānattā pubbabhāge nānā, maggakkhaṇe pana imesu catūsu ṭhānesu kiccasādhanavasena maggaṅgaṃ pūrayamānā ekā sati uppajjati. Ayaṃ sammāsati nāma.

Right mindfulness, too, is diverse in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of minds apprehending the body and so forth. At the moment of the path, however, in these four foundations, a single mindfulness arises, fulfilling the path factor by accomplishing its function. This is called right mindfulness.

Jhānādīni pubbabhāgepi maggakkhaṇepi nānā, pubbabhāge samāpattivasena nānā, maggakkhaṇe nānāmaggavasena. Ekassa hi paṭhamamaggo paṭhamajjhāniko hoti, dutiyamaggādayopi paṭhamajjhānikā vā dutiyādīsu aññatarajjhānikā vā. Ekassa paṭhamamaggo dutiyādīnaṃ aññatarajjhāniko hoti, dutiyādayopi dutiyādīnaṃ aññatarajjhānikā vā paṭhamajjhānikā [V 3.0163] vā. Evaṃ cattāropi maggā jhānavasena sadisā vā asadisā vā ekaccasadisā vā honti.

The jhānas are diverse both in the preliminary stage and at the moment of the path. In the preliminary stage, they are diverse by way of attainment; at the moment of the path, they are diverse by way of the different paths. For indeed, for one person, the first path is of the first jhāna, and the second path and so on are also either of the first jhāna or of any of the second jhāna and so on. For another person, the first path is of any of the second jhāna and so on, and the second path and so on are also either of any of the second jhāna and so on, or of the first jhāna. Thus, the four paths, by way of jhāna, can be similar, dissimilar, or partly similar.

Ayaṃ panassa viseso pādakajjhānaniyamena hoti. Pādakajjhānaniyamena hi paṭhamajjhānalābhino paṭhamajjhānā vuṭṭhāya vipassantassa uppannamaggo paṭhamajjhāniko hoti, maggaṅgabojjhaṅgāni panettha paripuṇṇāneva honti. Dutiyajjhānato vuṭṭhāya vipassantassa uppanno dutiyajjhāniko hoti, maggaṅgāni panettha satta honti. Tatiyajjhānato vuṭṭhāya vipassantassa uppanno tatiyajjhāniko, maggaṅgāni panettha satta, bojjhaṅgāni cha honti. Esa nayo catutthajjhānato paṭṭhāya yāva nevasaññānāsaññāyatanā[P 3.0127].

Furthermore, this distinction of the path occurs by the principle of the foundational jhāna. For, by the principle of the foundational jhāna, for one who has obtained the first jhāna, who emerges from the first jhāna and practices insight, the path that arises is of the first jhāna; herein, the path factors and enlightenment factors are indeed complete. For one who emerges from the second jhāna and practices insight, the path that arises is of the second jhāna; herein, there are seven path factors. For one who emerges from the third jhāna and practices insight, the path that arises is of the third jhāna; herein, there are seven path factors and six enlightenment factors. This same method applies from the fourth jhāna up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Āruppe catukkapañcakajjhānaṃ uppajjati, tañca lokuttaraṃ, no lokiyanti vuttaṃ. Ettha kathanti? Etthāpi paṭhamajjhānādīsu yato vuṭṭhāya sotāpattimaggaṃ paṭilabhitvā arūpasamāpattiṃ bhāvetvā so āruppe uppanno, taṃjhānikāvassa tattha tayo maggā uppajjanti. Evaṃ pādakajjhānameva niyameti. Keci pana therā – “vipassanāya ārammaṇabhūtā khandhā niyamentī”ti vadanti[M 3.0164]. Keci “puggalajjhāsayo niyametī”ti vadanti. Keci “vuṭṭhānagāminīvipassanā niyametī”ti vadanti. Tesaṃ vādavinicchayo visuddhimagge vuṭṭhānagāminīvipassanādhikāre vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sammāsamādhīti ayaṃ pubbabhāge lokiyo, aparabhāge lokuttaro sammāsamādhīti vuccati.

In the formless realm, the fourfold and fivefold jhāna arises, and that is supramundane, not mundane, it is said. How is this? Here too, when one, having emerged from the first jhāna or one of the subsequent jhānas, having obtained the path of stream-entry, and having developed the formless attainments, is born in the formless realm, then for that person the three higher paths, which are of that same jhāna, arise there. Thus, it is the foundational jhāna alone that determines it. Some elders, however, say: 'The aggregates that have become the object of insight determine it.' Some say: 'The individual's disposition determines it.' Some say: 'The insight leading to emergence determines it.' The resolution of their views should be understood by the method stated in the Visuddhimagga in the section on insight leading to emergence. As for 'This, bhikkhus, is called right concentration': this right concentration, which is mundane in the preliminary stage and supramundane in the subsequent stage, is so called.

9. Sūkasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Explanation of the Sūka Sutta

9. Navame micchāpaṇihitanti sūkaṃ nāma uddhaggaṃ katvā ṭhapitaṃ hatthaṃ vā pādaṃ vā bhindati, tathā aṭṭhapitaṃ pana micchāpaṇihitaṃ nāma. Micchāpaṇihitāya diṭṭhiyāti micchāṭhapitāya kammassakatapaññāya. Avijjaṃ bhindissatīti catusaccapaṭicchādakaṃ avijjaṃ bhindissati. Vijjaṃ uppādessatīti arahattamaggavijjaṃ uppādessati. Micchāpaṇihitattā, bhikkhave, diṭṭhiyāti kammassakatapaññāya ceva maggabhāvanāya ca micchā ṭhapitattā, appavattitattāti attho. Imasmiṃ sutte kammassakatañāṇaṃ magganissitaṃ katvā missakamaggo kathito.

9. In the ninth, 'wrongly directed' (micchāpaṇihita) means this: a spike (sūka), when placed with its point upwards, pierces the hand or foot; but if not placed thus, it is called 'wrongly directed.' 'By a wrongly directed view' means by the wrongly established wisdom concerning kamma as one's own. 'It will shatter ignorance' means it will shatter the ignorance that conceals the four truths. 'It will give rise to knowledge' means it will give rise to the knowledge of the path to arahantship. 'Because of being wrongly directed, bhikkhus, in view' means because both the wisdom concerning kamma as one's own and the cultivation of the path are wrongly established and not put into practice. In this sutta, the mixed path is taught by making the knowledge of kamma as one's own dependent on the path.

10. Nandiyasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Nandiya Sutta

10. Dasame [V 3.0164] paribbājakoti channaparibbājako. Sesamettha uttānamevāti.

9. In the tenth, 'wanderer' refers to Channa the wanderer. The rest here is self-evident.

Avijjāvaggo paṭhamo.

10. The Chapter on Ignorance, the First.

2. Vihāravaggo

10. The Chapter on Abidings

1. Paṭhamavihārasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Discourse on the First Abiding

11. Dutiyavaggassa [P 3.0128] paṭhame icchāmahaṃ, bhikkhave, aḍḍhamāsaṃ paṭisallīyitunti ahaṃ, bhikkhave, ekaṃ aḍḍhamāsaṃ paṭisallīyituṃ nilīyituṃ ekova hutvā viharituṃ icchāmīti attho. Namhi kenaci upasaṅkamitabbo aññatra ekena piṇḍapātanīhārakenāti yo attanā payuttavācaṃ akatvā mamatthāya [M 3.0165] saddhesu kulesu paṭiyattaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ nīharitvā mayhaṃ upanāmeyya, taṃ piṇḍapātanīhārakaṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ ṭhapetvā namhi aññena kenaci bhikkhunā vā gahaṭṭhena vā upasaṅkamitabboti.

In the first sutta of the second chapter, 'I wish, bhikkhus, to go into seclusion for half a month' means: 'I, bhikkhus, wish to go into seclusion, to be hidden away, and to dwell alone for one half-month.' 'I am not to be approached by anyone except for one who brings almsfood' means that apart from one monk who, without uttering a related word himself, brings almsfood prepared in faithful families for my sake and presents it to me, I am not to be approached by any other monk or layperson.

Kasmā pana evamāhāti? Tasmiṃ kira aḍḍhamāse vinetabbo satto nāhosi. Atha satthā – “imaṃ aḍḍhamāsaṃ phalasamāpattisukheneva vītināmessāmi, iti mayhañceva sukhavihāro bhavissati, anāgate ca pacchimā janatā ‘satthāpi gaṇaṃ vihāya ekako vihāsi, kimaṅgaṃ pana maya’nti diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjissati, tadassā bhavissati dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā”ti iminā kāraṇena evamāha. Bhikkhusaṅghopi satthu vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ adāsi. So pātova gandhakuṭipariveṇasammajjanamukhodakadantakaṭṭhadānādīni sabbakiccāni tasmiṃ khaṇe katvā apagacchati.

2. But why did he speak thus? It seems that during that half-month, there was no being to be trained. Then the Teacher thought: "I will pass this half-month solely in the bliss of fruition attainment. Thus, it will be a pleasant abiding for me, and in the future, later generations will follow the example, thinking, 'Even the Teacher dwelt alone after leaving the community; how much more so should we?' That will be for their long-term welfare and happiness." For this reason, he spoke thus. The Sangha of bhikkhus, having accepted the Teacher's words, assigned one bhikkhu. That bhikkhu, rising early, would perform all duties at that time—sweeping the fragrant chamber's enclosure, providing water for washing the face and a tooth-stick, and so on—and then depart.

Yena svāhanti yena so ahaṃ. Paṭhamābhisambuddhoti abhisambuddho hutvā paṭhamaṃyeva ekūnapaññāsadivasabbhantare. Viharāmīti idaṃ atītatthe vattamānavacanaṃ. Tassa padesena vihāsinti tassa [V 3.0165] paṭhamābhisambuddhavihārassa padesena. Tattha padeso nāma khandhapadeso āyatanadhātusaccaindriyapaccayākārasatipaṭṭhānajhānanāmarūpapadeso dhammapadesoti nānāvidho. Taṃ sabbampi sandhāya – “tassa padesena vihāsi”nti āha. Bhagavā hi paṭhamabodhiyaṃ ekūnapaññāsadivasabbhantare yathā nāma pattarajjo rājā attano vibhavasāradassanatthaṃ taṃ taṃ gabbhaṃ vivarāpetvā suvaṇṇarajatamuttāmaṇiādīni ratanāni paccavekkhanto vihareyya, evameva pañcakkhandhe nippadese katvā sammasanto paccavekkhanto vihāsi[P 3.0129]. Imasmiṃ pana aḍḍhamāse tesaṃ khandhānaṃ padesaṃ vedanākkhandhameva paccavekkhanto vihāsi. Tassa “ime sattā evarūpaṃ nāma sukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedenti, evarūpaṃ dukkha”nti olokayato yāva bhavaggā pavattā sukhavedanā, yāva avīcito pavattā dukkhavedanā, sabbā sabbākārena upaṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ “micchādiṭṭhipaccayāpi vedayita”ntiādinā nayena pariggaṇhanto vihāsi.

1. 'Yena svāhaṃ' is 'yena so ahaṃ' (by which, that I). 'First fully enlightened' means having become fully enlightened right within the first forty-nine days. 'Viharāmi' (I dwell) is a present tense verb used in the sense of the past. 'I dwelt by a portion of that' means by a portion of that abiding of the first full enlightenment. Herein, 'portion' is of various kinds: the portion of aggregates, the portion of sense-bases, the portion of elements, the portion of truths, the portion of faculties, the portion of conditionality, the portion of foundations of mindfulness, the portion of jhāna, the portion of name-and-form, and the portion of phenomena. Referring to all of this, he said, 'I dwelt by a portion of that.' For the Blessed One, during the first forty-nine days at the time of his first awakening, dwelt contemplating and examining the five aggregates without remainder, just as a king who has attained sovereignty might dwell inspecting jewels such as gold, silver, pearls, and gems, having opened up his various treasuries to see the essence of his wealth. But during this half-month, he dwelt examining only a portion of those aggregates, namely, the feeling aggregate. As he observed, 'These beings experience such a kind of pleasure and such a kind of pain,' all pleasant feeling occurring up to the peak of existence and all painful feeling occurring down to Avīci became fully apparent to him in every way. Then he dwelt comprehending it by the method beginning with, 'Feeling is also conditioned by wrong view,' and so forth.

Tathā paṭhamabodhiyaṃ dvādasāyatanāni nippadesāneva katvā vihāsi, imasmiṃ pana aḍḍhamāse tesaṃ āyatanānaṃ padesaṃ vedanāvasena dhammāyatanekadesaṃ, dhātūnaṃ padesaṃ vedanāvasena dhammadhātuekadesaṃ, saccānaṃ padesaṃ vedanākkhandhavaseneva dukkhasaccekadesaṃ, paccayānaṃ padesaṃ phassapaccayā [M 3.0166] vedanāvasena paccayekadesaṃ jhānānaṃ padesaṃ vedanāvaseneva jhānaṅgekadesaṃ, nāmarūpānaṃ padesaṃ vedanāvaseneva nāmekadesaṃ paccavekkhanto vihāsi. Paṭhamabodhiyañhi ekūnapaññāsadivasabbhantare kusalādidhamme nippadese katvā anantanayāni satta pakaraṇāni paccavekkhanto vihāsi. Imasmiṃ pana aḍḍhamāse sabbadhammānaṃ padesaṃ vedanāttikameva paccavekkhanto vihāsi. Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne sā sā ca vihārasamāpatti vedanānubhāvena jātā.

Similarly, at the time of his first awakening, he dwelt having reviewed the twelve sense-bases without remainder. But during this half-month, he dwelt examining a portion of those sense-bases, that is, a part of the mind-object base by way of feeling; a portion of the elements, that is, a part of the mind-object element by way of feeling; a portion of the truths, that is, a part of the truth of suffering by way of the feeling aggregate alone; a portion of the conditions, that is, a part of dependent origination by way of feeling conditioned by contact; a portion of the jhānas, that is, a part of the jhāna factors by way of feeling alone; and a portion of name-and-form, that is, a part of name by way of feeling alone. Indeed, at the time of his first awakening, within the forty-nine days, he dwelt examining the seven treatises of infinite methods, having reviewed wholesome and other phenomena without remainder. But during this half-month, he dwelt examining only a portion of all phenomena, namely, the triad of feeling. In each respective instance, that very attainment of dwelling arose through the power of feeling.

Idāni yenākārena vihāsi, taṃ dassento micchādiṭṭhipaccayāpītiādimāha. Tattha micchādiṭṭhipaccayāpīti diṭṭhisampayuttā vedanāpi vaṭṭati. Diṭṭhiṃ upanissayaṃ katvā uppannā kusalākusalavedanāpi vaṭṭati vipākavedanāpi. Tattha micchādiṭṭhisampayuttā akusalāva hoti, diṭṭhiṃ pana upanissāya kusalāpi uppajjanti akusalāpi. Micchādiṭṭhikā hi diṭṭhiṃ upanissāya pakkhadivasesu yāgubhattādīni denti, addhikādīnaṃ vaṭṭaṃ paṭṭhapenti, catumahāpathe sālaṃ karonti, pokkharaṇiñca khaṇāpenti, devakulādīsu mālāgacchaṃ ropenti, nadīviduggādīsu setuṃ attharanti, visamaṃ samaṃ karonti, iti nesaṃ kusalavedanā uppajjati. Micchādiṭṭhiṃ pana nissāya sammādiṭṭhike akkosanti paribhāsanti, vadhabandhanādīni karonti, pāṇaṃ vadhitvā devatānaṃ [V 3.0166] upahāraṃ upaharanti[P 3.0130], iti nesaṃ akusalavedanā uppajjati. Vipākavedanā pana bhavantaragatānaṃyeva hoti.

Now, showing the manner in which he dwelt, he spoke the passage beginning, "even due to wrong view as a condition." Herein, "due to wrong view as a condition" means that feeling associated with wrong view is applicable. Feeling—whether wholesome or unwholesome—that arises having made wrong view a supporting condition is also applicable, as is resultant feeling. Among these, feeling associated with wrong view is only unwholesome. However, based on wrong view, both wholesome and unwholesome feelings arise. For those with wrong views, based on that view, give rice porridge, meals, and so forth on the observance days; they establish provisions for travelers and others; they build a hall at a crossroads; they have a pond dug; they plant flowering shrubs at shrines and the like; they lay a bridge in places difficult to cross such as rivers; they make the uneven even. Thus, for them, wholesome feeling arises. Furthermore, relying on wrong view, they revile and threaten those with right view; they perform acts of killing, binding, and so forth; having killed a living being, they make an offering to the deities. Thus, for them, unwholesome feeling arises. Resultant feeling, however, occurs only for those who have gone to another existence.

Sammādiṭṭhipaccayāti etthāpi sammādiṭṭhisampayuttā vedanāpi vaṭṭati, sammādiṭṭhiṃ upanissayaṃ katvā uppannā kusalākusalavedanāpi vipākavedanāpi. Tattha sammādiṭṭhisampayuttā kusalāva hoti, sammādiṭṭhiṃ pana upanissāya buddhapūjaṃ dīpamālaṃ mahādhammassavanaṃ appatiṭṭhite disābhāge cetiyapatiṭṭhāpananti evamādīni puññāni karonti, iti nesaṃ kusalā vedanā uppajjati. Sammādiṭṭhiṃyeva nissāya micchādiṭṭhike akkosanti paribhāsanti, attānaṃ ukkaṃsenti, paraṃ vambhenti, iti nesaṃ akusalavedanā uppajjati. Vipākavedanā pana bhavantaragatānaṃyeva hoti. Micchāsaṅkappapaccayātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Chandapaccayātiādīsu pana chandapaccayā aṭṭhalobhasahagatacittasampayuttā vedanā veditabbā, vitakkapaccayā [M 3.0167] paṭhamajjhānavedanāva. Saññā paccayā ṭhapetvā paṭhamajjhānaṃ sesā cha saññāsamāpattivedanā.

In the phrase "due to right view as a condition" also, feeling associated with right view is applicable. Feeling—whether wholesome or unwholesome—that arises having made right view a supporting condition is also applicable, as is resultant feeling. Among these, feeling associated with right view is only wholesome. Furthermore, based on right view, they perform meritorious deeds such as making offerings to the Buddha, offering rows of lamps, listening to the great Dhamma, and establishing a cetiya in a region where one has not yet been established. Thus, for them, wholesome feeling arises. Relying on their own right view, they revile and threaten those with wrong views, exalt themselves, and disparage others. Thus, for them, unwholesome feeling arises. Resultant feeling, however, occurs only for those who have gone to another existence. This same method should be applied in the passages beginning "due to wrong intention as a condition." Furthermore, in the passages beginning "due to desire as a condition," by "due to desire as a condition," feeling associated with the eight consciousnesses accompanied by greed should be understood. By "due to thought as a condition," only the feeling of the first jhāna should be understood. By "due to perception as a condition," setting aside the first jhāna, the feelings of the remaining six attainments of perception should be understood.

Chando ca avūpasantotiādīsu tiṇṇaṃ avūpasame aṭṭhalobhasahagatacittasampayuttā vedanā hoti, chandamattassa vūpasame paṭhamajjhānavedanāva. Chandavitakkānaṃ vūpasame dutiyajjhānādivedanā adhippetā, tiṇṇampi vūpasame nevasaññānāsaññāyatanavedanā. Appattassa pattiyāti arahattaphalassa pattatthāya. Atthi āyāmanti atthi vīriyaṃ. Tasmimpi ṭhāne anuppatteti tassa vīriyārambhassa vasena tassa arahattaphalassa kāraṇe anuppatte. Tappaccayāpi vedayitanti arahattassa ṭhānapaccayā vedayitaṃ. Etena catumaggasahajātā nibbattitalokuttaravedanāva gahitā.

In the passages beginning "And desire is unappeased," when the three—desire, thought, and perception—are unappeased, feeling associated with the eight consciousnesses accompanied by greed occurs. When desire alone is appeased, only the feeling of the first jhāna occurs. When desire and thought are appeased, the feelings from the second jhāna up to the base of nothingness are intended. When all three are appeased, the feeling of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is intended. 'For the attainment of the unattained' means for the purpose of attaining the fruit of Arahantship. 'There is exertion' means there is energy. 'When that state has been attained' means when the cause of that fruit of Arahantship has been attained. By 'a feeling conditioned by that' is meant a feeling that has arisen on account of that condition. By this, only the produced supramundane feeling co-arisen with the four paths is taken.

2. Dutiyavihārasuttavaṇṇanā

2. 2. Commentary on the Second Sutta on Abiding

12. Dutiye paṭisallānakāraṇaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Micchādiṭṭhivūpasamapaccayāti micchādiṭṭhivūpasamo nāma sammādiṭṭhi. Tasmā yaṃ sammādiṭṭhipaccayā vedayitaṃ vuttaṃ, tadeva micchādiṭṭhivūpasamapaccayā [P 3.0131] veditabbaṃ. Imasmiṃ pana sutte vipākavedanaṃ atidūreti maññamānā na gaṇhantīti vuttaṃ. Iminā nayena sabbattha attho veditabbo. Yassa yassa hi vūpasamapaccayāti vuccati, tassa tassa paṭipakkhadhammapaccayāva taṃ taṃ vedayitaṃ adhippetaṃ. Chandavūpasamapaccayātiādīsu [V 3.0167] pana chandavūpasamapaccayā tāva paṭhamajjhānavedanā veditabbā. Vitakkavūpasamapaccayā dutiyajjhānavedanā. Saññāpaccayā chasamāpattivedanā. Saññāvūpasamapaccayā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanavedanā. Chando ca vūpasantotiādīni vuttatthāneva.

12. In the second sutta, the reason for seclusion should be understood only in the way already stated. In the phrase "due to the appeasement of wrong view as a condition," what is called the appeasement of wrong view is right view. Therefore, that very feeling which was said to be conditioned by right view should be understood as being conditioned by the appeasement of wrong view. In this sutta, however, it is said in the commentary that they do not include resultant feeling, thinking it is "too remote." In this way, the meaning should be understood everywhere. For of whatever factor it is said "due to the appeasement of... as a condition," the respective feeling is intended as being conditioned by the opposing factor. Furthermore, in the passages beginning "due to the appeasement of desire as a condition," firstly, by "due to the appeasement of desire as a condition," the feeling of the first jhāna should be understood. By "due to the appeasement of thought as a condition," the feeling of the second jhāna should be understood. By "due to perception as a condition," the feelings of the six attainments should be understood. By "due to the appeasement of perception as a condition," the feeling of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception should be understood. The passages beginning "And desire is appeased" have the same meaning as already explained.

3-7. Sekkhasuttādivaṇṇanā

3-7. Commentary on the Sekkha Sutta and so forth.

13-17. Tatiye sekkhoti sikkhanasīlo. Kiṃ sikkhatīti? Tisso sikkhā. Sekkhāyāti tīhi phalehi catūhi ca maggehi saddhiṃ uppannāya. Sāpi hi aniṭṭhitakiccattā attano kiccaṃ sikkhatevāti sekkhā. Catutthapañcamachaṭṭhasattamāni uttānatthānevāti.

13-17. In the third sutta, 'a learner' (sekho) means one who has the nature of training. What does one train in? The three trainings. By 'of a learner' (sekkhāya) is meant the right view that has arisen together with the three fruits and the four paths. For that right view also, because its task is not yet finished, is still training in its own task; therefore, it is called 'of a learner' (sekkhā). The fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh suttas are of clear meaning.

8-10. Paṭhamakukkuṭārāmasuttādivaṇṇanā

8-10. Commentary on the First Kukkuṭārāma Sutta and so forth.

18-20. Aṭṭhame [M 3.0168] ummaṅgoti paññāummaṅgo, paññāvīmaṃsanaṃ, paññāgavesananti attho. Evañhi tvaṃ āvusoti idaṃ tassa pucchāpatiṭṭhāpanatthāya āha. Navamadasamāni uttānatthāmevāti.

In the eighth sutta, 'a tunnel' (ummaṅgo) means a tunnel of wisdom, an investigation of wisdom, a search for wisdom—this is the meaning. The phrase 'Thus indeed, friend, you...' was said for the purpose of establishing his question. The ninth and tenth suttas are of clear meaning.

Vihāravaggo dutiyo.

The Vihāra Chapter is the second.

3. Micchattavaggavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Chapter on Wrongness.

21-30. Tatiyavaggassa paṭhame micchattanti micchāsabhāvaṃ. Sammattanti sammāsabhāvaṃ. Micchāpaṭipattādhikaraṇahetūti micchāpaṭipattikaraṇahetu. Yasmā micchāpaṭipattiṃ karoti, tasmāti attho. Nārādhakoti [P 3.0132] na sampādako. Ñāyaṃ dhammanti ariyamaggadhammaṃ. Micchāñāṇīti micchāviññāṇo micchāpaccavekkhaṇo. Micchāvimuttīti ayāthāvavimutti, aniyyānikavimutti. Imesu tatiyādīsu catūsu suttesu vaṭṭavivaṭṭaṃ kathitaṃ, pacchimesu panettha dvīsu puggalo pucchito dhammo vibhatto, evaṃ dhammena puggalo dassitoti. Suppavattiyoti suppavattaniyo. Yathā icchiticchitaṃ [V 3.0168] disaṃ pavattento dhāvati, evaṃ pavattetuṃ sakkā hotīti attho. Saupanisaṃ saparikkhāranti sappaccayaṃ saparivāraṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

In the first sutta of the third chapter, 'wrongness' (micchattaṃ) means the state of being wrong. 'Rightness' (sammattaṃ) means the state of being right. 'Because of the cause which is the ground for wrong practice' means the cause for doing wrong practice. The meaning is: because one does wrong practice, therefore... 'Not an accomplisher' (nārādhako) means not one who brings to completion. 'The Dhamma that is the method' (ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ) means the Dhamma of the Noble Path. 'One of wrong knowledge' (micchāñāṇī) means one of wrong consciousness, one of wrong reflection. 'Wrong liberation' (micchāvimutti) means liberation not in accordance with reality, liberation that is not a means of escape. In these four suttas beginning with the third, the round of existence and the escape from the round are taught. Furthermore, in the last two of these, the person is questioned, the Dhamma is analyzed, and thus the person is shown by means of the Dhamma. 'Easily set rolling' (suppavattiyo) means easily able to be set in motion. The meaning is: just as one runs, setting off in whatever direction one wishes, so it is possible to set it in motion. 'With its supporting condition and requisite' (saupanisaṃ saparikkhāraṃ) means with its cause and with its retinue. The remainder is of clear meaning everywhere.

Micchattavaggo tatiyo.

The Wrongness Chapter is the third.

4. Paṭipattivaggavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Chapter on Practice.

31-40. Catutthe micchāpaṭipattinti ayāthāvapaṭipattiṃ. Micchāpaṭipannanti ayāthāvapaṭipannaṃ. Iti ekaṃ suttaṃ dhammavasena kathitaṃ, ekaṃ puggalavasena. Apārā pāranti vaṭṭato nibbānaṃ. Pāragāminoti ettha yepi pāraṅgatā, yepi gacchanti, yepi gamissanti, sabbe pāragāminotveva veditabbā.

In the fourth chapter, 'wrong practice' (micchāpaṭipattiṃ) means conduct not in accordance with reality. 'One who has practiced wrongly' (micchāpaṭipannaṃ) means one who practices conduct not in accordance with reality. Thus, one sutta is taught by way of the Dhamma, and one by way of the person. 'From the near shore to the far shore' (apārā pāraṃ) means from the round of existence to Nibbāna. Here, by 'those who go to the far shore' (pāragāmino), it should be understood that all—those who have gone to the far shore, those who are going, and those who will go—are simply 'those who go to the far shore'.

Tīramevānudhāvatīti vaṭṭameva anudhāvati, vaṭṭe vicarati. Kaṇhanti akusaladhammaṃ. Sukkanti kusaladhammaṃ. Okā anokanti vaṭṭato nibbānaṃ. Āgammāti [M 3.0169] ārabbha sandhāya paṭicca. Pariyodapeyyāti parisuddhaṃ kareyya. Cittaklesehīti cittaṃ kilissāpentehi nīvaraṇehi. Sambodhiyaṅgesūti sattasu bojjhaṅgesu.

By 'one runs along the shore' (tīram evānudhāvati) is meant: one runs along only in the round of existence, one wanders in the round. 'Dark' (kaṇhaṃ) means unwholesome Dhamma. 'Bright' (sukkaṃ) means wholesome Dhamma. 'From home to homelessness' (okā anokaṃ) means from the round of existence to Nibbāna. 'Having come to' (āgamma) means having taken as an object, having aimed at, depending on. 'One should cleanse' (pariyodapeyya) means one should make pure. 'From the defilements of the mind' (cittaklesehi) means from the hindrances that defile the mind. 'In the factors of enlightenment' (sambodhiyaṅgesu) means in the seven factors of enlightenment.

Sāmaññatthanti nibbānaṃ. Tañhi sāmaññena upagantabbato sāmaññatthoti vuccati. Brahmaññanti seṭṭhabhāvaṃ. Brahmaññatthanti nibbānaṃ brahmaññena upagantabbato. Yattha yattha pana heṭṭhā ca imesu ca tīsu suttesu “rāgakkhayo”ti āgataṃ, tattha tattha arahattampi vaṭṭatiyevāti vadanti.

'The goal of asceticism' (sāmaññatthaṃ) means Nibbāna. For since it is to be approached by means of asceticism, it is called 'the goal of asceticism.' 'The holy life' (brahmaññaṃ) means the state of excellence. 'The goal of the holy life' (brahmaññatthaṃ) means Nibbāna, because it is to be approached by means of the holy life. Furthermore, wherever in the suttas below and in these three suttas the phrase 'the destruction of lust' occurs, there the fruit of Arahantship is also fitting—so the teachers say.

Paṭipattivaggo catuttho.

The Practice Chapter is the fourth.

5. Aññatitthiyapeyyālavaggavaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the Abbreviated Section on Adherents of Other Sects.

41-48. Aññatitthiyapeyyāle [P 3.0133] addhānapariññatthanti saṃsāraddhānaṃ nibbānaṃ patvā pariññātaṃ [V 3.0169] nāma hoti. Tasmā nibbānaṃ “addhānapariññā”ti vuccati, tadatthanti attho. Anupādāparinibbānatthanti apaccayaparinibbānatthaṃ. Iti imasmiṃ peyyāle vijjāvimuttiphalena arahattaṃ kathitaṃ. Ñāṇadassanena paccavekkhaṇā, sesehi nibbānanti.

In the Abbreviated Section on Adherents of Other Sects, regarding the phrase 'for the full understanding of the course': having attained Nibbāna, the course of saṃsāra is said to be fully understood. Therefore, Nibbāna is called 'the full understanding of the course'; this is the meaning of 'for that purpose'. 'For the purpose of final Nibbāna without clinging' means for the purpose of cessation that is not a condition for renewed existence. Thus, in this abbreviated section, Arahantship is taught by means of 'the fruit of knowledge and liberation'. Reviewing is taught by means of 'knowledge and vision', and Nibbāna by means of the remaining terms.

Aññatitthiyapeyyālavaggo.

The Abbreviated Section on Adherents of Other Sects.

6. Sūriyapeyyālavaggavaṇṇanā

6. Explanation of the Abbreviated Section on the Sun.

49-62. Sūriyapeyyāle aruṇuggaṃ viya kalyāṇamittattā, kalyāṇamittatāya ṭhatvā nibbattito savipassanaariyamaggo sūriyapātubhāvo viyāti evaṃ sabbattha attho veditabbo. Sīlasampadāti catupārisuddhisīlaṃ. Chandasampadāti kusalakattukamyatāchando. Attasampadāti sampannacittatā. Diṭṭhisampadāti ñāṇasampatti. Appamādasampadāti kārāpakaappamādasampatti. Yonisomanasikārasampadāti upāyamanasikārasampatti. Puna kalyāṇamittatātiādīni sammādiṭṭhiādīnaṃ aññenapi ākārena [M 3.0170] bhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttāni. Sabbāneva cetāni suttāni pāṭiyekkaṃ puggalajjhāsayavasena vuttānīti.

In the Abbreviated Section on the Sun, the meaning should be understood everywhere thus: good friendship is like the rising of the dawn; the noble path with insight, brought forth by being established in good friendship, is like the appearance of the sun. 'Perfection of virtue' means the fourfold purity virtue. 'Perfection of aspiration' means the wholesome desire to act. 'Perfection of self' means the state of a perfected mind. 'Perfection of view' means the perfection of knowledge. 'Perfection of heedfulness' means the perfection of productive heedfulness. 'Perfection of wise attention' means the perfection of attention to the means. Furthermore, 'good friendship' and so on are stated to show the nature of right view and so on in another way. All these suttas were spoken individually according to the dispositions of individuals.

Sūriyapeyyālavaggo.

The Abbreviated Section on the Sun.

7. Ekadhammapeyyālavaggādivaṇṇanā

7. Explanation of the Abbreviated Section on a Single Quality and so forth.

63-138. Ekadhammapeyyālopi gaṅgāpeyyālopi pāṭiyekkaṃ puggalajjhāsayavaseneva tathā tathā vutte bujjhanakānaṃ ajjhāsayavasena kathito.

Both the Abbreviated Section on a Single Quality and the Abbreviated Section on the Ganges were spoken individually according to the dispositions of individuals; being taught in various ways, they were spoken according to the dispositions of those who were to awaken.

8. Appamādapeyyālavaggo

8. The Abbreviated Section on Heedfulness.

1. Tathāgatasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Tathāgata Sutta.

139. Appamādapeyyāle evameva khoti ettha yathā sabbasattānaṃ sammāsambuddho aggo, evaṃ [V 3.0170] sabbesaṃ kusaladhammānaṃ kārāpakaappamādo aggoti daṭṭhabbo. Nanu cesa lokiyova, kusaladhammā pana lokuttarāpi. Ayañca kāmāvacarova, kusaladhammā pana catubhūmakā. Kathamesa tesaṃ aggoti? Paṭilābhakaṭṭhena. Appamādena hi te paṭilabbhanti, tasmā so tesaṃ aggo. Tenetaṃ vuttaṃ sabbe te appamādamūlakātiādi.

139. In the Abbreviated Section on Heedfulness, regarding the phrase 'just so indeed': just as the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One is the foremost among all sentient beings, so too productive heedfulness is to be seen as foremost among all wholesome states. But is this heedfulness not merely mundane, whereas wholesome states are also supramundane? And is this not merely of the sense-sphere, whereas wholesome states pertain to the four planes? How then is it foremost among them? By way of being the means of their acquisition. For by means of heedfulness they are acquired; therefore, it is foremost among them. For that reason it is said, 'All these have heedfulness as their root,' and so forth.

2. Padasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Footprint Sutta.

140. Jaṅgalānanti pathavītalavāsīnaṃ. Pāṇānanti sapādakapāṇānaṃ[P 3.0134]. Padajātānīti padāni. Samodhānaṃ gacchantīti odhānaṃ upakkhepaṃ gacchanti. Aggamakkhāyatīti seṭṭhaṃ akkhāyati. Yadidaṃ mahantattenāti mahantabhāvena aggamakkhāyati, na guṇavasenāti attho.

140. 'Of those in the wilderness' means of those who move about on the surface of the earth. 'Of living beings' means of living beings with feet. 'Footprints' means footprints. 'They come together' means they attain inclusion. 'It is declared the foremost' means it is declared the best. 'Because of its greatness' means it is declared foremost by virtue of its great size, not by virtue of its qualities—this is the meaning.

3-10. Kūṭasuttādivaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Kūṭasutta and the Like.

141-148. Vassikanti sumanapupphaṃ. Imaṃ kira suttaṃ sutvā bhātiyamahārājā vīmaṃsitukāmatāya ekasmiṃ gabbhe catujātigandhehi paribhaṇḍaṃ kāretvā [M 3.0171] sugandhāni pupphāni āharāpetvā ekassa samuggassa majjhe sumanapupphamuṭṭhiṃ ṭhapetvā sesāni tassa samantato muṭṭhimuṭṭhiṃ katvā ṭhapetvā dvāraṃ pidhāya bahi nikkhanto. Athassa muhuttaṃ vītināmetvā dvāraṃ vivaritvā pavisantassa sabbapaṭhamaṃ sumanapupphagandho ghānaṃ pahari. So mahātalasmiṃyeva mahācetiyābhimukho nipajjitvā – “vassikaṃ tesaṃ agganti kathentena sukathitaṃ sammāsambuddhenā”ti cetiyaṃ vandi. Kuṭṭarājānoti khuddakarājāno. “Khuddarājāno”tipi pāṭho. Tantāvutānanti tante āvutānaṃ, tantaṃ āropetvā vāyitānanti attho. Idañca paccatte sāmivacanaṃ. Yāni kānici tantāvutāni vatthānīti ayañhettha attho. Atha vā tantāvutānaṃ vatthānaṃ yāni kānici vatthānīti evaṃ sāvasesapāṭhanayenapettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

Vassikā is the jasmine flower. It is said that King Bhātiya, having heard this discourse and wishing to test it, had a chamber prepared with four kinds of perfumes. He then had fragrant flowers brought, and placing a handful of jasmine flowers in the center of a chest, he arranged the rest in handfuls all around it. After closing the door, he went outside. After a moment had passed, as he opened the door and entered, the fragrance of the jasmine flowers was the first to strike his nose. Then, lying on the great platform facing the great stupa, he paid homage to the stupa, exclaiming: 'How well spoken by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, who declared the jasmine to be supreme among them!' Lesser kings are called 'Kuṭṭarājāno'; 'Khuddarājāno' is also a reading. 'Tantāvutāni' means 'woven in threads,' that is, 'woven by placing on a loom.' And this is a genitive case used in the sense of the nominative. The meaning here is: 'whatever garments are woven with threads.' Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as: 'any garments from those woven with threads,' in the manner of an elliptical reading. The rest is clear throughout.

Appamādavaggo aṭṭhamo.

The Chapter on Heedfulness, the Eighth.

9. Balakaraṇīyavaggo

9. The Chapter on What is to be Done with Strength

1. Balasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Bala Sutta

149. Balakaraṇīyavagge [V 3.0171] balakaraṇīyāti ūrubalabāhubalena kattabbā dhāvanalaṅghanatāpanavahanādayo kammantā. Sīle patiṭṭhāyāti catupārisuddhisīle ṭhatvā. Aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ magganti sahavipassanaṃ ariyamaggaṃ.

149. In the Chapter on What is to be Done with Strength, 'what is to be done with strength' refers to tasks such as running, jumping, heating, and carrying loads, which should be done with the strength of the thighs and arms. 'Established in virtue' means being grounded in the fourfold purity of virtue. 'The Eightfold Path' refers to the Noble Path together with insight.

2. Bījasuttavaṇṇanā
