2. Explanation of the Discourse on Seeds

150. Bījagāmabhūtagāmāti ettha pañcavidhampi bījaṃ bījagāmo nāma, tadeva paṇṇasampannaṃ nīlabhāvato paṭṭhāya bhūtagāmoti veditabbaṃ.

150. In the phrase 'seed-group and plant-group,' all five kinds of seeds are called the seed-group. That same seed, when endowed with leaves, from the state of being green onwards, should be understood as the plant-group.

3. Nāgasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Nāga Sutta

151. Balaṃ [P 3.0135] gāhentīti balaṃ gaṇhanti, gahitabalā thirasarīrā honti. Kusobbhe otarantītiādīsu ayamanupubbikathā – nāginiyo kira utusamaye [M 3.0172] patiṭṭhitagabbhā cintenti – “sace mayaṃ idha vijāyissāma, evaṃ no dārakā ūmivegañca supaṇṇassa ca pakkhanditvā āgatassa vegaṃ sahituṃ na sakkhissantī”ti tā mahāsamudde nimujjitvā sambhajjamukhadvāraṃ patvā pañca mahānadiyo pavisitvā himavantaṃ gacchanti. Tattha supaṇṇehi apakkhandanīyāsu suvaṇṇarajatamaṇiguhāsu vasamānā vijāyitvā nāgapotake gopphakādipamāṇesu udakesu otāretvā udakataraṇaṃ sikkhāpenti.

151. 'They seize strength' means they take strength; having taken strength, their bodies become firm. Regarding 'their descending into small pools and the like,' this is the sequential explanation: It is said that when the season comes, the female nāgas, being pregnant, think: 'If we give birth here, our children will not be able to withstand the force of the waves or the swooping attack of the garuḍas.' So they plunge into the great ocean, reach the mouth of the confluence, enter the five great rivers, and go to the Himavanta. There, dwelling in golden, silver, and jeweled caves where garuḍas cannot swoop down, they give birth. Then, they place the young nāgas in ankle-deep waters and the like, and teach them to swim.

Atha yadā anukkamena te nāgā gaṅgādīnaṃ nadīnaṃ orimatīrato paratīraṃ, paratīrato orimatīranti taraṇapaṭitaraṇaṃ kātuṃ sakkonti, tadā “idāni no dārakā ūmivegañca garuḷavegañca sahituṃ sakkhissantī”ti ñatvā attano ānubhāvena mahāmeghaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā sakalahimavantaṃ ekodakaṃ viya kurumānā devaṃ vassāpetvā suvaṇṇarajatādimayā nāvā māpetvā upari [V 3.0172] suvaṇṇatārakavicittaṃ samosaritagandhapupphadāmaṃ celavitānaṃ bandhitvā surabhicandanagandhapupphādīni ādāya tāhi nāvāhi pañca mahānadiyo ogāhitvā anukkamena mahāsamuddaṃ pāpuṇanti. Tattha ca vasantā dasabyāma-satabyāma-sahassabyāma-satasahassabyāma-pamāṇataṃ āpajjantā mahantattaṃ vepullattaṃ āpajjanti nāma.

Then, when those nāgas are gradually able to cross back and forth from the near shore to the far shore of rivers like the Ganges, they know, 'Now our children will be able to endure the force of the waves and the force of the Garuḷa.' Through their own power, they cause a great cloud to arise, making the entire Himavanta as if a single mass of water. They cause it to rain, create boats of gold, silver, and so on, and above they tie a cloth canopy, variegated with golden stars and hung with garlands of fragrant flowers. Taking fragrant sandalwood, perfumes, flowers, and the like, they descend the five great rivers in these boats and gradually reach the great ocean. And dwelling there, they attain a measure of ten vyāmas, a hundred vyāmas, a thousand vyāmas, and a hundred thousand vyāmas, and thus they attain greatness and immensity.

Evameva khoti ettha himavantapabbato viya catupārisuddhisīlaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, nāgapotakā viya yogāvacarā, kusobbhādayo viya ariyamaggo, mahāsamuddo viya nibbānaṃ. Yathā nāgapotakā himavante patiṭṭhāya kusobbhādīhi mahāsamuddaṃ patvā kāyamahantattaṃ āpajjanti, evaṃ yogino sīlaṃ nissāya sīle patiṭṭhāya ariyamaggena nibbānaṃ patvā arahattamaggeneva āgatesu chasu abhiññādhammesu guṇasarīramahantattaṃ pāpuṇantīti.

Just so, here, the Himavanta mountain should be seen as the fourfold purity of virtue; the young nāgas as practitioners of meditation; the small pools and so on as the Noble Path; and the great ocean as Nibbāna. Just as the young nāgas, established in the Himavanta, reach the great ocean by way of the small pools and so on and attain greatness of body, so too, practitioners of meditation, relying on virtue and established in virtue, reach Nibbāna by the Noble Path and attain greatness of the body of qualities in the six higher knowledges that come with the path of Arahantship itself.

5. Kumbhasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Kumbha Sutta

153. Kumbhoti udakaghaṭo. No paccāvamatīti na patiāvamati, na anto pavesetīti attho.

153. 'Kumbha' means a water pot. 'Does not disgorge' means it does not vomit back, it does not let enter inside again; this is the meaning.

7. Ākāsasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Ākāsa Sutta

155. Puratthimāti [M 3.0173] puratthimadisato āgatavātā. Pacchimadisādīsupi eseva nayo. Cattāropi satipaṭṭhānāti yatheva hi etesaṃ [P 3.0136] puratthimādibhedānaṃ vātānaṃ sannipāto ākāse ijjhati, evaṃ idhāpi “cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”tiādinā nayena vuttā bodhipakkhiyadhammā sahavipassanassa ariyamaggassa bhāvanāya ijjhanti, tenetaṃ vuttaṃ.

155. 'From the east' means winds coming from the eastern direction. The same method applies to the western direction and others. 'The four foundations of mindfulness'—just as the confluence of these winds from the east and other directions is accomplished in the sky, so too here, the factors of enlightenment, stated in the way beginning with 'the four foundations of mindfulness,' are accomplished by the cultivation of the Noble Path together with insight. It is for this reason that this was said.

8-9. Paṭhamameghasuttādivaṇṇanā

Commentary on the First Cloud Sutta and Others

156-157. Gimhānaṃ pacchime māseti āsāḷhamāse. Ūhatanti dvipadacatuppadānaṃ pādappahārena pathavītale uṭṭhahitvā uddhaṃ gataṃ vaṭṭivaṭṭi hutvā ākāse pakkhantaṃ. Rajojallanti paṃsurajojallaṃ.

'In the last month of summer' means in the month of Āsāḷha. 'Carried up' means that which is raised from the surface of the earth by the striking feet of bipeds and quadrupeds, having gone upwards, becoming a swirling mass, and leaping into the sky. 'Dust and filth' means fine dust and filth.

10. Nāvāsuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Nāva Sutta

158. Sāmuddikāya [V 3.0173] nāvāyātiādi heṭṭhā vāṇijakopame vitthāritameva.

158. 'A seafaring ship,' and so on—this was already explained in detail below in the simile of the merchant.

11-12. Āgantukasuttādivaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Āgantuka Sutta and So Forth

159-160. Āgantukāgāranti puññatthikehi nagaramajjhe kataṃ āgantukagharaṃ, yattha rājarājamahāmattehipi sakkā hoti nivāsaṃ upagantuṃ. Abhiññā pariññeyyāti yatheva hi tesaṃ puratthimadisādīhi āgatānaṃ khattiyādīnaṃ vāso āgantukāgāre ijjhati, evaṃ imesaṃ abhiññāpariññeyyātiādīnaṃ dhammānaṃ abhiññāparijānanādīhi sahavipassanassa ariyamaggassa bhāvanāya ijjhanti, tenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Nadīsuttaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayamevāti.

159-160. 'A guest house' means a guest house built in the middle of a city by those seeking merit, where even kings and great ministers are able to take up residence. 'To be fully understood by direct knowledge' — just as residence for those khattiyas and others who have come from the eastern direction and the like is accomplished in the guest house, so too these phenomena, such as 'to be fully understood by direct knowledge,' are accomplished by the development of the Noble Path together with insight, along with direct knowledge, full understanding, and so on. It is for this reason that this was said. The Nadī Sutta is by the same method as explained previously.

Balakaraṇīyavaggo navamo.

The Balakaraṇīya Vagga, the ninth.

10. Esanāvaggo

10. The Esanā Chapter

1. Esanāsuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Esanā Sutta

161. Esanāvagge [M 3.0174] kāmesanāti kāmānaṃ esanā gavesanā magganā patthanā. Bhavesanāti bhavānaṃ esanā. Brahmacariyesanāti micchādiṭṭhisaṅkhātassa brahmacariyassa esanā.

161. In the Esanā Vagga, 'the search for sensual pleasures' means the search, investigation, quest, and desire for sensual pleasures. 'The search for existence' means the search for states of existence. 'The search for the holy life' means the search for the holy life designated as wrong view.

2-11. Vidhāsuttādivaṇṇanā

2-11. Commentary on the Vidhā Sutta, etc.

162-171. Vidhāti mānakoṭṭhāsā mānaṭhapanā vā. Seyyohamasmīti vidhāti ahamasmi seyyoti evaṃ mānakoṭṭhāso mānaṭhapanā vā. Nīghāti dukkhā. Vacanattho panettha yassa uppajjanti, taṃ purisaṃ nīhanantīti nīghā. Sesamettha uttānamevāti.

162-171. 'Vidhā' means the divisions of conceit or the establishing of conceit. 'I am superior' is a division of conceit, or the establishing of conceit as 'I am superior.' 'Nīghā' means sufferings. The etymological meaning here is that because they strike down the person in whom they arise, they are called 'nīghā.' The rest here is clear in itself.

Esanāvaggo dasamo.

The Esanā Chapter, the tenth.

11. Oghavaggo

11. The Chapter on Floods

1-2. Oghasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-2. Commentary on the Ogha Sutta, etc.

172-173. Oghavagge [V 3.0174][P 3.0137] kāmoghoti pañcasu kāmaguṇesu chandarāgo. Bhavoghoti rūpārūpabhavesu chandarāgo. Diṭṭhoghoti dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo. Avijjoghoti catūsu saccesu aññāṇaṃ. Kāmayogādīsupi eseva nayo.

172-173. In the Chapter on Floods, the ‘flood of sensuality’ is craving and lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure. The ‘flood of existence’ is craving and lust for existence in the form and formless realms. The ‘flood of views’ is the sixty-two wrong views. The ‘flood of ignorance’ is unknowing regarding the four truths. This same method applies to the ‘yoke of sensuality,’ etc.

3-4. Upādānasuttādivaṇṇanā

3-4. Commentary on the Upādāna Sutta, etc.

174-175. Kāmupādānanti kāmaggahaṇaṃ. Diṭṭhupādānādīsupi eseva nayo. Ganthāti ganthanā ghaṭanā. Kāyaganthoti nāmakāyassa gantho ganthanaghaṭanakileso. Idaṃsaccābhinivesoti antaggāhikadiṭṭhivasena uppanno “idameva sacca”nti evaṃ abhiniveso.

174-175. ‘Grasping of sensual pleasures’ (kāmupādāna) means the grasping of sensual pleasures. This same method applies to the ‘grasping of views’ (diṭṭhupādāna), etc. ‘Knots’ (gantha) means binding, connecting. The ‘bodily knot’ (kāyagantha) is the knot of the mental body, the defilement of binding and connecting. ‘Insistence that “this alone is true”’ (idaṃsaccābhinivesa) is the insistence, arisen by way of views that grasp at extremes, that ‘this alone is true’.

5-10. Anusayasuttādivaṇṇanā

5-10. Commentary on the Anusaya Sutta, etc.

176-181. Kāmarāgānusayoti [M 3.0175] thāmagataṭṭhena kāmarāgova anusayo kāmarāgānusayo. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Orambhāgiyānīti heṭṭhākoṭṭhāsiyāni. Saṃyojanānīti bandhanāni. Uddhambhāgiyānīti uparikoṭṭhāsiyāni. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

176-181. ‘Latent tendency to sensual lust’ (kāmarāgānusaya): by reason of its persistence, sensual lust itself is a latent tendency, thus it is the ‘latent tendency to sensual lust.’ This same method applies to the remaining cases. ‘Lower fetters’ (orambhāgiyāni) means those belonging to the lower division. ‘Fetters’ (saṃyojanāni) means bonds. ‘Upper fetters’ (uddhambhāgiyāni) means those belonging to the upper division. The rest has an obvious meaning everywhere.

Oghavaggo ekādasamo.

The Chapter on Floods, the eleventh.

Maggasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Connected Discourses on the Path is concluded.

2. Bojjhaṅgasaṃyuttaṃ

2. The Connected Discourses on the Factors of Enlightenment

1. Pabbatavaggo

1. The Chapter on the Mountain

1. Himavantasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Himavanta Sutta

182. Bojjhaṅgasaṃyuttassa [V 3.0175][P 3.0138][M 3.0176] paṭhame nāgāti imepi mahāsamuddapiṭṭhe ūmiantaravāsinova, na vimānaṭṭhakanāgā. Tesaṃ himavantaṃ nissāya kāyavaḍḍhanādisabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Bojjhaṅgeti ettha bodhiyā, bodhissa vā aṅgāti bojjhaṅgā. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yā hi ayaṃ dhammasāmaggī, yāya lokiyalokuttaramaggakkhaṇe uppajjamānāya līnuddhaccapatiṭṭhānāyūhana kāmasukhattakilamathānuyogaucchedasassatābhinivesādīnaṃ anekesaṃ upaddavānaṃ paṭipakkhabhūtāya satidhammavicayavīriyapītipassaddhisamādhiupekkhāsaṅkhātāya dhammasāmaggiyā ariyasāvako bujjhatīti katvā bodhīti vuccati. Bujjhatīti kilesasantānaniddāya uṭṭhahati, cattāri vā ariyasaccāni paṭivijjhati, nibbānameva vā sacchikarotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Yathāha “satta bojjhaṅge bhāvetvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddho”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.378; dī. ni. 3.143). Tassā dhammasāmaggisaṅkhātāya bodhiyā aṅgāti bojjhaṅgā jhānaṅgamaggaṅgādayo viya. Yopesa yathāvuttappakārāya etāya dhammasāmaggiyā bujjhatīti katvā ariyasāvako bodhīti vuccati, tassa bodhissa aṅgātipi bojjhaṅgā senaṅgarathaṅgādayo viya. Tenāhu aṭṭhakathācariyā – “bujjhanakassa puggalassa aṅgāti vā bojjhaṅgā”ti.

182. In the first sutta of the Connected Discourses on the Factors of Enlightenment, the ‘nāgas’ here are those dwelling amidst the waves on the surface of the great ocean, not nāgas residing in celestial mansions. Their bodily growth and everything else dependent on the Himālaya should be understood in the manner explained previously. Here, in the word ‘bojjhaṅga,’ they are the ‘factors of enlightenment’ because they are the factors (aṅga) of awakening (bodhi) or for awakening. What is meant by this? There is a certain harmony of states (dhammasāmaggī) designated as mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity. This harmony of states arises at the moment of the mundane and supramundane paths and is the opponent to numerous troubles such as sloth, restlessness, settling down, striving, indulgence in sensual pleasure, the practice of self-mortification, and adherence to annihilationism and eternalism, etc. Because a noble disciple awakens (bujjhati) by means of this harmony of states, it is called ‘awakening’ (bodhi). ‘Awakens’ means one rises from the sleep of the continuum of defilements, or one penetrates the four noble truths, or one directly realizes Nibbāna itself. As it is said: ‘Having developed the seven factors of enlightenment, he awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.’ They are the factors of that awakening (bodhi), which is designated as the harmony of states; thus they are ‘factors of enlightenment’ (bojjhaṅga), like the factors of jhāna, factors of the path, etc. Or, because the noble disciple awakens by means of this harmony of states of the aforementioned kind, that noble disciple is called ‘awakening’ (bodhi), and the factors for that one who awakens are also the ‘factors of enlightenment,’ like the components of an army, the parts of a chariot, etc. Therefore the commentary masters said: ‘Or, they are the factors of the person who awakens; thus they are the factors of enlightenment.’

Apica “bojjhaṅgāti kenaṭṭhena bojjhaṅgā? Bodhāya saṃvattantīti bojjhaṅgā, bujjhantīti bojjhaṅgā, anubujjhantīti bojjhaṅgā, paṭibujjhantīti bojjhaṅgā, sambujjhantīti bojjhaṅgā”iccādinā (paṭi. ma. 2.17) paṭisambhidānayenāpi bojjhaṅgattho veditabbo.

Furthermore, the meaning of ‘factors of enlightenment’ should also be understood according to the method of the Paṭisambhidāmagga, which states: ‘“Factors of enlightenment” (bojjhaṅga)—in what sense are they factors of enlightenment? They conduce to awakening (bodhāya saṃvattanti), thus they are factors of enlightenment. They awaken (bujjhanti), thus they are factors of enlightenment. They awaken accordingly (anubujjhanti), thus they are factors of enlightenment. They re-awaken (paṭibujjhanti), thus they are factors of enlightenment. They fully awaken (sambujjhanti), thus they are factors of enlightenment,’ and so on.

Satisambojjhaṅgantiādīsu [V 3.0176][P 3.0139] pana pasattho sundaro ca bojjhaṅgoti sambojjhaṅgo. Satiyeva sambojjhaṅgoti satisambojjhaṅgo, taṃ satisambojjhaṅganti evaṃ sabbattha attho veditabbo. Bhāvetīti vaḍḍheti, attano [M 3.0177] cittasantāne punappunaṃ janeti, abhinibbattetīti attho. Vivekanissitantiādīni kosalasaṃyutte “sammādiṭṭhiṃ bhāveti vivekanissita”nti ettha vuttanayeneva veditabbāni.

In phrases such as ‘the enlightenment factor of mindfulness’ (satisambojjhaṅga), a ‘sambojjhaṅga’ is a praised and excellent factor of enlightenment. Mindfulness itself is the ‘sambojjhaṅga,’ thus it is the ‘satisambojjhaṅga.’ In this way, the meaning should be understood in all cases. ‘Develops’ (bhāveti) means: he makes it grow (vaḍḍheti), he generates it again and again in his own mental continuum, he brings it into being (abhinibbatteti). The phrases beginning with ‘based on seclusion’ (vivekanissita) should be understood in the way stated in the Kosala Saṃyutta, in the passage: ‘He develops right view, which is based on seclusion.’

Ayaṃ pana viseso – tattha tadaṅgavivekanissitaṃ, samucchedavivekanissitaṃ, nissaraṇavivekanissitanti, vivekattayameva vuttaṃ, bojjhaṅgabhāvanaṃ patvā pana pañcavidhavivekanissitampi eke vaṇṇayanti. Te hi na kevalaṃ balavavipassanāmaggaphalakkhaṇesu eva bojjhaṅge uddharanti vipassanāpādaka-kasiṇajjhāna-ānāpānāsubha-brahmavihārajjhānesupi uddharanti, na ca paṭisiddhā aṭṭhakathācariyehi. Tasmā tesaṃ matena etesaṃ jhānānaṃ pavattikkhaṇe kiccato eva vikkhambhanavivekanissitaṃ. Yathā ca vipassanākkhaṇe “ajjhāsayato nissaraṇavivekanissita”nti vuttaṃ, evaṃ paṭipassaddhivivekanissitampi bhāvetīti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Sesamettha heṭṭhā vuttanayameva.

This, however, is a special point. There, only three kinds of seclusion were mentioned: that based on seclusion by substitution of opposites, that based on seclusion by eradication, and that based on seclusion by escape. But when it comes to the development of the factors of enlightenment, some authorities describe it as being based on five kinds of seclusion. For they extract the factors of enlightenment not only at the moments of powerful insight, path, and fruition, but also in the jhānas that are the basis for insight, such as the kasiṇa jhānas, mindfulness of breathing, meditations on the unattractive, and the divine abodes. And this is not rejected by the commentary masters. Therefore, according to their view, at the moment of their occurrence, these jhānas are, by their function, based on seclusion by suppression. And just as it is said that at the moment of insight, it is ‘based on seclusion by escape by way of inclination,’ so too it is fitting to say that one develops that which is based on seclusion by tranquillization. The rest here is in the same way as explained below.

2. Kāyasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Kāyasutta

183. Dutiye āhāraṭṭhitikoti paccayaṭṭhitiko. Āhāraṃ paṭiccāti paccayaṃ paṭicca. Subhanimittanti subhampi subhanimittaṃ, subhassa ārammaṇampi subhanimittaṃ. Ayonisomanasikāroti anupāyamanasikāro uppathamanasikāro anicce “nicca”nti vā, dukkhe “sukha”nti, anattani “attā”ti vā, asubhe “subha”nti vā, manasikāro. Taṃ tasmiṃ subhārammaṇe bahulaṃ pavattayato kāmacchando uppajjati. Tena vuttaṃ “atthi, bhikkhave, subhanimitta”ntiādi. Evaṃ sabbanīvaraṇesu yojanā veditabbā.

183. In the second sutta, `āhāraṭṭhitika` (sustained by nutriment) means sustained by conditions. `Āhāraṃ paṭicca` (dependent on nutriment) means dependent on conditions. `Subhanimitta` (beautiful sign): the beautiful itself is a beautiful sign, and the object of the beautiful is also a beautiful sign. `Ayonisomanasikāra` (unwise attention) means attention that is not the right approach (`anupāyamanasikāra`), attention that is a wrong path (`uppathamanasikāra`); that is, attention to the impermanent as 'permanent,' to suffering as 'pleasant,' to non-self as 'self,' or to the foul as 'beautiful.' For one who frequently directs the mind towards that beautiful object, sensual desire arises. Therefore it is said: 'There is, bhikkhus, a beautiful sign,' and so on. In this way, the application should be understood for all the hindrances.

Paṭighanimittantiādīsu pana paṭighopi paṭighanimittaṃ paṭighārammaṇampi. Aratīti ukkaṇṭhitā. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “tattha katamā arati? Pantesu vā senāsanesu aññataraññataresu vā [P 3.0140] adhikusalesu dhammesu arati aratitā anabhirati anabhiramanā ukkaṇṭhitā paritassitā, ayaṃ vuccati aratī”ti (vibha. 856).

Furthermore, in the case of 'the sign of resistance' and so on, resistance itself is a sign of resistance, and so is the object of resistance. `Arati` (discontent) means disaffection. With reference to this, it is said: 'Therein, what is discontent? Regarding remote lodgings or certain exceedingly wholesome states, there is discontent, the state of being discontented, lack of enjoyment, lack of delight, disaffection, distress—this is called discontent' (Vibh. 856).

Tandīti [V 3.0177] atisītādipaccayā uppannaṃ āgantukakāyālasiyaṃ. Yasmiṃ uppanne “atisītaṃ atiuṇhaṃ aticchātosmi atidhātosmi atidūramaggaṃ gatosmī”ti vadati, yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “tattha katamā tandi[M 3.0178], yā tandī tandiyanā tandimanakatā ālasyaṃ ālasyāyanā ālasyāyitattaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati tandī”ti (vibha. 857).

`Tandī` (sloth) is adventitious bodily laziness that has arisen from conditions such as excessive cold. When it has arisen, one says: 'It is too cold, it is too hot, I am too hungry, I am too thirsty, I have walked too far.' With reference to this, it is said: 'Therein, what is sloth? That which is sloth, slothfulness, the state of having a slothful mind, laziness, the state of being lazy, the condition of being lazy—this is called sloth' (Vibh. 857).

Vijambhitāti kilesavasena kāyavinamanā. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “tattha katamā vijambhitā? Yā kāyassa jambhanā vijambhanā ānamanā vinamanā sannamanā paṇamanā byādhiyakaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati vijambhitā”ti (vibha. 858).

`Vijambhitā` (stretching) is the contortion of the body due to the power of defilements. With reference to this, it is said: 'Therein, what is stretching? That which is the body's yawning, stretching, bending forward, bending backward, stooping, arching, the state of being afflicted—this is called stretching' (Vibh. 858).

Bhattasammadoti bhattapariḷāho. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “tattha katamo bhattasammado? Yā bhuttāvissa bhattamucchā bhattakilamatho bhattapariḷāho kāyaduṭṭhullaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati bhattasammado”ti (vibha. 859).

`Bhattasammada` (drowsiness from food) is the distress from food. With reference to this, it is said: 'Therein, what is drowsiness from food? For one who has eaten, it is the stupor from food, the weariness from food, the distress from food, the bodily unwieldiness—this is called drowsiness from food' (Vibh. 859).

Cetaso ca līnattanti cittassa līyanākāro, yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “tattha katamaṃ cetaso līnattaṃ? Yā cittassa akalyatā akammaññatā olīyanā sallīyanā līnaṃ līyanā līyitattaṃ thinaṃ thiyanā thiyitattaṃ cittassa, idaṃ vuccati cetaso līnatta”nti (vibha. 860).

`Cetaso līnatta` (sluggishness of mind) is the characteristic of the mind's sinking. With reference to this, it is said: 'Therein, what is sluggishness of mind? That which is the mind's unhealthiness, unworkability, sinking down, shrinking back, inertia, the characteristic of being inert, the state of being inert, torpor, the characteristic of torpor, the state of torpor of the mind—this is called sluggishness of mind' (Vibh. 860).

Cetaso avūpasamoti yathā nāma vītaccikopi aṅgāro neva tāva sannisīdati patāpaṃ karotiyeva, yathā ca pattapacanaṭṭhāne neva tāva sannisīdati patāpaṃ karotiyeva, evaṃ cittassa avūpasantākāro, atthato panetaṃ uddhaccakukkuccameva hoti.

`Cetaso avūpasamo` (the mind's lack of pacification) is like an ember that, even when its flames have gone out, has not yet cooled down but continues to give off heat; and like a cooking hearth that has not yet cooled down but continues to give off heat. In the same way, this is the unpacified state of the mind. In essence, this is just restlessness and remorse.

Vicikicchaṭṭhānīyā dhammāti vicikicchāya ārammaṇadhammā. Ayonisomanasikāro sabbattha vuttanayova. Evamettha kāmacchando vicikicchāti ime dve dhammā ārammaṇena [P 3.0141] kathitā, byāpādo ārammaṇena ca upanissayena ca, sesā sahajātena ca upanissayena cāti.

`Vicikicchaṭṭhānīyā dhammā` (states that are grounds for doubt) are the object-states for doubt. `Ayonisomanasikāra` (unwise attention) is to be understood in the way already stated everywhere. Thus, herein, these two states—sensual desire and doubt—are explained by way of an object. Ill will is explained by way of an object and by decisive support. The remaining states are explained by way of conascence and by decisive support.

Satisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammāti satiyā ārammaṇadhammā sattatiṃsa bodhipakkhiyā ca nava lokuttaradhammā [V 3.0178] ca. Tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāroti tattha upāyamanasikārassa punappunaṃ karaṇaṃ.

`Satisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā` (states that are grounds for the enlightenment factor of mindfulness) are the object-states for mindfulness: the thirty-seven requisites of enlightenment and the nine supramundane states. Therein, `yonisomanasikārabahulīkāra` (the frequent practice of wise attention) means the repeated application of attention that is the right approach.

Kusalākusalā dhammātiādīsu kusalāti kosallasambhūtā anavajjasukhavipākā. Akusalāti akosallasambhūtā sāvajjadukkhavipākā. Sāvajjāti akusalā. Anavajjāti kusalā. Hīnapaṇītakaṇhasukkesupi eseva nayo. Sappaṭibhāgāti kaṇhasukkāyeva. Kaṇhā hi kaṇhavipākadānato[M 3.0179], sukkā ca sukkavipākadānato sappaṭibhāgā nāma, sadisavipākakoṭṭhāsāti attho. Paṭipakkhabhūtassa vā bhāgassa atthitāya sappaṭibhāgā. Kaṇhānañhi sukkā paṭipakkhabhāgā, sukkānañca kaṇhā paṭipakkhabhāgāti evampi sappaṭibhāgā. Sappaṭibāhitaṭṭhena vā sappaṭibhāgā. Akusalañhi kusalaṃ paṭibāhitvā attano vipākaṃ deti, kusalañca akusalaṃ paṭibāhitvāti evampi kaṇhasukkā sappaṭibhāgā.

Regarding 'wholesome and unwholesome states' and so on: 'wholesome' (`kusala`) means born of skill, blameless, and having a pleasant result. 'Unwholesome' (`akusala`) means born of unskill, blameworthy, and having a painful result. 'Blameworthy' means unwholesome. 'Blameless' means wholesome. This same method applies to the terms inferior and superior, dark and bright. `Sappaṭibhāga` (corresponding) refers to the dark and bright states themselves. Dark states are called 'corresponding' because they give a dark result, and bright states because they give a bright result; the meaning is that they have portions of result similar to themselves. Alternatively, they are 'corresponding' because of the existence of an opposing part. For the opposing part of dark states is the bright states, and the opposing part of the bright states is the dark states; in this way, too, they are 'corresponding.' Or, they are 'corresponding' in the sense of being mutually obstructive. For an unwholesome state obstructs a wholesome one and gives its own result, and a wholesome state obstructs an unwholesome one; in this way, too, the dark and bright states are 'corresponding.'

Ārambhadhātūti paṭhamārambhavīriyaṃ. Nikkamadhātūti kosajjato nikkhantattā tato balavataraṃ. Parakkamadhātūti paraṃ paraṃ ṭhānaṃ akkamanatāya tatopi balavataranti tīhipi padehi vīriyameva kathitaṃ.

`Ārambhadhātu` (the element of initiative) is the initial arousal of energy. `Nikkhamadhātu` (the element of exertion) is stronger than that, because of having departed from laziness. `Parakkamadhātu` (the element of striving) is stronger still, because of its advancing to higher and higher states. Thus, by these three terms, it is energy itself that is described.

Pītisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyāti pītiyā ārammaṇadhammā. Kāyapassaddhīti tiṇṇaṃ khandhānaṃ darathapassaddhi. Cittapassaddhīti viññāṇakkhandhassa darathapassaddhi. Samathanimittanti samathopi samathanimittaṃ, ārammaṇampi. Abyagganimittanti tasseva vevacanaṃ.

`Pītisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā` (states that are grounds for the enlightenment factor of joy) are the object-states for joy. `Kāyapassaddhi` (bodily tranquility) is the calming of distress in the three aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations. `Cittapassaddhi` (mental tranquility) is the calming of distress in the consciousness aggregate. `Samathanimitta` (the sign of serenity): serenity itself is a sign of serenity, and its object is also a sign of serenity. `Abyagganimitta` (the sign of non-distraction) is a synonym for that very thing.

Upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyāti upekkhāya ārammaṇadhammā, atthato pana majjhattākāro upekkhāṭṭhānīyā dhammoti veditabbo. Evamettha satidhammavicayaupekkhāsambojjhaṅgā ārammaṇena kathitā, sesā ārammaṇenapi upanissayenapi.

`Upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā` (states that are grounds for the enlightenment factor of equanimity) are the object-states for equanimity. In terms of meaning, however, states characterized by neutrality are to be understood as the grounds for equanimity. Thus, herein, the enlightenment factors of mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, and equanimity are explained by way of an object, while the remaining factors are explained by way of an object and by decisive support.

3. Sīlasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Discourse on Virtue

184. Tatiye sīlasampannāti ettha khīṇāsavassa lokiyalokuttarasīlaṃ kathitaṃ, tena sampannāti attho. Samādhipaññāsupi [P 3.0142] eseva nayo. Vimutti pana phalavimuttiyeva. Vimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ [V 3.0179] paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ. Evamettha sīlādayo tayo lokiyalokuttarā, vimutti lokuttarāva, vimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ lokiyameva.

184. In the third sutta, regarding 'endowed with virtue' (sīlasampannā), here the virtue of one whose taints are destroyed is spoken of as both mundane and supramundane; hence, the meaning is 'endowed with that'. The same method applies to concentration and wisdom. But liberation should be understood as only the liberation of fruition. The knowledge and vision of liberation is the reviewing knowledge. Thus, herein, the three beginning with virtue are both mundane and supramundane; liberation is solely supramundane; and the knowledge and vision of liberation is only mundane.

Dassanampāhanti dassanampi ahaṃ. Taṃ panetaṃ dassanaṃ – cakkhudassanaṃ, ñāṇadassananti duvidhaṃ. Tattha pasannehi cakkhūhi ariyānaṃ dassanaṃ olokanaṃ cakkhudassanaṃ nāma. Ariyehi pana diṭṭhassa lakkhaṇassa dassanaṃ, paṭividdhassa ca paṭivijjhanaṃ jhānena vā vipassanāya vā maggaphalehi vā ñāṇadassanaṃ nāma. Imasmiṃ panettha cakkhudassanaṃ adhippetaṃ. Ariyānañhi pasannehi cakkhūhi olokanampi [M 3.0180] bahukārameva. Savananti “asuko nāma khīṇāsavo asukasmiṃ nāma raṭṭhe vā janapade vā gāme vā nigame vā vihāre vā leṇe vā vasatī”ti kathentānaṃ sotena savanaṃ, etampi bahukārameva. Upasaṅkamananti “dānaṃ vā dassāmi, pañhaṃ vā pucchissāmi, dhammaṃ vā sossāmi, sakkāraṃ vā karissāmī”ti evarūpena cittena ariyānaṃ upasaṅkamanaṃ. Payirupāsananti pañhāpayirupāsanaṃ. Ariyānaṃ guṇe sutvā te upasaṅkamitvā nimantetvā dānaṃ datvā “kiṃ, bhante, kusala”ntiādinā nayena pañhapucchananti attho.

Regarding 'dassanampāhaṃ' (seeing, I say), it means: I declare that seeing, too, is of great benefit. Now, that seeing is twofold: seeing with the eye and seeing with knowledge. Therein, seeing the noble ones, looking at them with clear eyes, is called 'seeing with the eye'. But the seeing of a characteristic seen by the noble ones, and the penetration of what has been penetrated, whether by jhāna, by insight, or by the paths and fruits, is called 'seeing with knowledge'. Herein, however, seeing with the eye is intended. For indeed, looking upon the noble ones with clear eyes is of great benefit. Regarding 'hearing' (savanaṃ): it is hearing with the ear the words of those who say, 'A certain one whose taints are destroyed, by such and such a name, dwells in such and such a country, or district, or village, or town, or monastery, or cave.' This too is of great benefit. Regarding 'approaching' (upasaṅkamanaṃ): it is approaching the noble ones with a mind of this sort: 'I will give a gift, or I will ask a question, or I will listen to the Dhamma, or I will pay respect.' Regarding 'attending upon' (payirupāsanaṃ): it is attending upon by questioning. The meaning is: having heard the virtues of the noble ones, one approaches them, invites them, gives a gift, and then asks a question by the method beginning with, 'What, venerable sir, is skillful?'

Anussatinti rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānesu nisinnassa “idāni ariyā leṇaguhamaṇḍapādīsu jhānavipassanāmaggaphalasukhehi vītināmentī”ti anussaraṇaṃ. Yo vā tesaṃ santike ovādo laddho hoti, taṃ āvajjitvā “imasmiṃ ṭhāne sīlaṃ kathitaṃ, imasmiṃ samādhi, imasmiṃ vipassanā, imasmiṃ maggo, imasmiṃ phala”nti evaṃ anussaraṇaṃ. Anupabbajjanti ariyesu cittaṃ pasādetvā gharā nikkhamma tesaṃ santike pabbajjaṃ. Ariyānañhi santike cittaṃ pasādetvā tesaṃyeva santike pabbajitvā tesaṃyeva ovādānusāsaniṃ paccāsīsamānassa caratopi pabbajjā anupabbajjā nāma. Ariyesu pasādena aññattha pabbajitvā ariyānaṃ santike ovādānusāsaniṃ paccāsīsamānassa carato pabbajjāpi anupabbajjā nāma. Aññesu pana pasādena aññesaṃyeva santike pabbajitvā aññesaṃyeva ovādānusāsaniṃ paccāsīsamānassa carato pabbajjā anupabbajjā nāma na hoti.

Regarding 'recollection' (anussati): it is the recollecting of one who is seated in places for the night and places for the day, thinking: 'Now the noble ones are passing the time in caves, grottoes, pavilions, and so on, with the bliss of jhāna, insight, path, and fruit.' Or, whatever instruction has been received in their presence, reflecting on it thus: 'In this place, virtue was taught; in this place, concentration; in this place, insight; in this place, the path; in this place, the fruit'—this is recollection. Regarding 'going forth after' (anupabbajjā): it is, having placed faith in the noble ones, leaving the home and going forth in their presence. For one who, having placed faith in the noble ones, has gone forth in their very presence and practices while aspiring for their instruction and admonition, this going forth is called 'going forth after'. Even for one who, with faith in the noble ones, has gone forth elsewhere but practices while aspiring for the instruction and admonition of the noble ones, this going forth is also called 'going forth after'. But for one who, with faith in others, has gone forth in the very presence of those others and practices while aspiring for the instruction and admonition of those others, this going forth is not called 'going forth after'.

Evaṃ pabbajitesu pana mahākassapattherassa tāva anupabbajjaṃ pabbajitā satasahassamattā ahesuṃ, tathā [P 3.0143] therasseva saddhivihārikassa ca candaguttattherassa, tassāpi saddhivihārikassa sūriyaguttattherassa, tassāpi saddhivihārikassa assaguttattherassa, tassāpi saddhivihārikassa yonakadhammarakkhitattherassa[V 3.0180], tassa pana saddhivihāriko asokarañño kaniṭṭhabhātā tissatthero nāma ahosi, tassa anupabbajjaṃ pabbajitā aḍḍhateyyakoṭisaṅkhā ahesuṃ. Mahindattherassa anupabbajitānaṃ gaṇanaparicchedo natthi. Yāvajjadivasā laṅkādīpe satthari pasādena pabbajantā mahindattherasseva pabbajjaṃ anupabbajanti nāma.

Now, among those who had thus gone forth, first, those who went forth after the Elder Mahākassapa were about one hundred thousand. Likewise for his co-resident pupil, the Elder Candagutta; and for his co-resident pupil, the Elder Sūriyagutta; and for his co-resident pupil, the Elder Assagutta; and for his co-resident pupil, the Elder Yonaka Dhammarakkhita. Now, his co-resident pupil was the Elder Tissa by name, the younger brother of King Asoka. Those who went forth after him were twenty-five million in number. There is no counting or limit to those who went forth after the Elder Mahinda. Even to this day, those who go forth in the island of Laṅkā with faith in the Teacher are said to go forth after the going forth of the Elder Mahinda himself.

Taṃ [M 3.0181] dhammanti taṃ tesaṃ ovādānusāsanīdhammaṃ. Anussaratīti sarati. Anuvitakketīti vitakkāhataṃ karoti. Āraddho hotīti paripuṇṇo hoti. Pavicinatītiādi sabbaṃ tattha ñāṇacāravaseneva vuttaṃ. Atha vā pavicinatīti tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ vicinati. Pavicaratīti tattha ñāṇaṃ carāpeti. Parivīmaṃsamāpajjatīti vīmaṃsanaṃ olokanaṃ gavesanaṃ āpajjati.

Regarding 'that Dhamma': it means that Dhamma of their instruction and admonition. 'Recollects' means remembers. 'Reflects upon' means makes it an object of thought. 'Is accomplished' means is perfected. 'Investigates', and so on—all this is said by way of the range of knowledge. Alternatively, 'investigates' means one discerns the characteristics of those various Dhammas. 'Moves about' means one causes knowledge to range there. 'Engages in examination' means one arrives at investigation, observation, and searching.

Satta phalā sattānisaṃsāti ubhayampetaṃ atthato ekaṃ. Diṭṭheva dhamme paṭikacca aññaṃ ārādhetīti arahattaṃ ārādhento imasmiṃyeva attabhāve ārādheti, tañca kho paṭikacca, asampatteyeva maraṇakāleti attho. Atha maraṇakāleti atha maraṇassa āsannakāle.

Regarding 'seven fruits, seven benefits': both of these are one in meaning. Regarding 'in this very life, beforehand, one attains knowledge': it means that one who is attaining Arahantship attains it in this very existence, and that too, beforehand, meaning before the time of death has arrived. Regarding 'then at the time of death': it means then at the time near death.

Antarāparinibbāyīti yo āyuvemajjhaṃ anatikkamitvā parinibbāyati, so tividho hoti. Kappasahassāyukesu tāva avihesu nibbattitvā eko nibbattadivaseyeva arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. No ce nibbattadivase pāpuṇāti, paṭhamassa pana kappasatassa matthake pāpuṇāti. Ayameko antarāparinibbāyī. Aparo evaṃ asakkonto dvinnaṃ kappasatānaṃ matthake pāpuṇāti, ayaṃ dutiyo. Aparo evampi asakkonto catunnaṃ kappasatānaṃ matthake pāpuṇāti, ayaṃ tatiyo antarāparinibbāyī.

Regarding 'one who attains parinibbāna in the interval': it is one who attains parinibbāna without going beyond the middle of the lifespan. Such a one is of three kinds. First, having been reborn in the Aviha realm, where the lifespan is a thousand great eons, one person attains Arahantship on the very day of rebirth. If they do not attain it on the day of rebirth, they attain it at the completion of the first hundred great eons. This is one 'interval-parinibbāna attainer'. Another, being unable to do so thus, attains it at the completion of two hundred great eons; this is the second. Another, being unable even thus, attains it at the completion of four hundred great eons; this is the third 'interval-parinibbāna attainer'.

Pañcamaṃ pana kappasataṃ atikkamitvā arahattaṃ patto upahaccaparinibbāyī nāma hoti. Atappādīsupi eseva nayo. Yattha katthaci uppanno pana sasaṅkhārena sappayogena arahattaṃ [P 3.0144] patto sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī nāma, asaṅkhārena appayogena patto asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī nāma. Avihādīsupi nibbatto tattha yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā uparūpari nibbattitvā akaniṭṭhaṃ patto uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī nāma.

But one who, having passed the fifth hundred great eons, has attained Arahantship is called an 'upahacca-parinibbāyī' (one who attains parinibbāna upon reaching the latter part of the lifespan). In the Atappa realm and so on, this is the same method. Furthermore, one who is born somewhere or other and attains Arahantship with formation and with effort is called a 'sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī' (one who attains parinibbāna with prompting). One who attains it without formation and without effort is called an 'asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī' (one who attains parinibbāna without prompting). One who is reborn in the Aviha realm and so on, having stayed there for the full lifespan, is reborn higher and higher, and reaches the Akaniṭṭha realm, is called an 'uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī' (one with an upward stream, heading for Akaniṭṭha).

Imasmiṃ [V 3.0181] pana ṭhāne aṭṭhacattārīsa anāgāmino kathetabbā. Avihesu hi tayo antarāparinibbāyī, eko upahaccaparinibbāyī, eko uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmīti pañca honti. Te asaṅkhāraparinibbāyino pañca, sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyino pañcāti dasa honti, tathā atappādīsu. Akaniṭṭhesu pana uddhaṃsoto natthi, tasmā tattha cattāro sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī, cattāro asaṅkhāraparinibbāyīti aṭṭhāti evaṃ aṭṭhacattālīsa honti. Tesaṃ uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī sabbajeṭṭho ceva hoti [M 3.0182] sabbakaniṭṭho ca. Kathaṃ? So hi soḷasakappasahassāyukattā āyunā sabbesaṃ jeṭṭho, sabbapacchā arahattaṃ pāpuṇīti sabbesaṃ kaniṭṭho. Imasmiṃ sutte apubbaṃ acarimaṃ ekacittakkhaṇikā nānālakkhaṇā arahattamaggassa pubbabhāgavipassanā bojjhaṅgā kathitā.

Furthermore, in this place, forty-eight non-returners should be spoken of. In the Aviha realm, there are three who attain final Nibbāna in the interval (antarāparinibbāyin), one who attains final Nibbāna upon landing (upahaccaparinibbāyin), and one who is bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm, heading upstream (uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmin); thus there are five. These are five who attain final Nibbāna without exertion (asaṅkhāraparinibbāyin) and five who attain final Nibbāna with exertion (sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyin), making ten. Likewise in the Atappa and other such realms. However, in the Akaniṭṭha realm, there is no one who is heading upstream. Therefore, in that realm, there are four who attain final Nibbāna with exertion and four who attain final Nibbāna without exertion; thus there are eight. In this way, there are forty-eight. Among them, the one who is bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm, heading upstream, is both the eldest of all and the youngest of all. How so? Because his lifespan is sixteen thousand eons, he is the eldest of all in terms of age; and because he attains Arahantship after all others, he is the youngest of all. In this sutta are taught the enlightenment factors which are the preliminary insight for the path to Arahantship, being neither precedent nor subsequent, occurring in a single mind-moment, and having various characteristics.

4. Vatthasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Discourse on Cloth

185. Catutthe satisambojjhaṅgo iti ce me hotīti satisambojjhaṅgoti evaṃ ce mayhaṃ hoti. Appamāṇoti me hotīti appamāṇoti evaṃ me hoti. Susamāraddhoti suparipuṇṇo. Tiṭṭhatīti ettha aṭṭhahākārehi satisambojjhaṅgo tiṭṭhati – uppādaṃ anāvajjitattā anuppādaṃ āvajjitattā satisambojjhaṅgo tiṭṭhati, pavattaṃ, appavattaṃ, nimittaṃ, animittaṃ saṅkhāre anāvajjitattā, visaṅkhāraṃ āvajjitattā satisambojjhaṅgo tiṭṭhatīti. Imehi aṭṭhahākārehi tiṭṭhatīti thero jānāti, vuttākāraviparīteheva aṭṭhahākārehi cavantaṃ cavatīti pajānāti. Sesabojjhaṅgesupi eseva nayo.

4. In the fourth sutta, the phrase 'If the enlightenment factor of mindfulness is present in me' means 'If it occurs to me thus: "the enlightenment factor of mindfulness"'. The phrase 'It is immeasurable for me' means 'It occurs to me thus: "It is immeasurable"'. 'Well established' means 'well perfected'. As for 'it endures', here the enlightenment factor of mindfulness endures in eight ways: by not adverting to arising and by adverting to non-arising; by not adverting to occurrence and by adverting to non-occurrence; by not adverting to a sign and by adverting to the signless; by not adverting to formations and by adverting to the unformed. The Elder knows that it endures through these eight ways, and he understands that it ceases through the eight ways that are the reverse of those stated. This same method applies to the remaining enlightenment factors.

Iti imasmiṃ sutte therassa phalabojjhaṅgā kathitā. Yadā hi thero satisambojjhaṅgaṃ sīsaṃ katvā phalasamāpattiṃ samāpajjati, tadā itare cha tadanvayā honti. Yadā dhammavicayādīsu aññataraṃ, tadāpi sesā tadanvayā hontīti evaṃ phalasamāpattiyaṃ attano ciṇṇavasitaṃ dassento thero imaṃ suttaṃ kathesīti.

185. Thus, in this sutta, the Elder's enlightenment factors of fruition are described. For when the Elder, having made the enlightenment factor of mindfulness foremost, enters into the attainment of fruition, the other six follow in accordance with it. When he makes any one of the factors beginning with investigation-of-dhammas foremost, then also the remaining ones follow in accordance with it. In this way, the Elder taught this sutta, wishing to show his practiced mastery in the attainment of fruition.

5. Bhikkhusuttavaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the Bhikkhu Sutta

186. Pañcame [P 3.0145] bodhāya saṃvattantīti bujjhanatthāya saṃvattanti. Kiṃ bujjhanatthāya? Maggena [V 3.0182] asaṅkhataṃ nibbānaṃ, paccavekkhaṇāya katakiccataṃ, maggena vā kilesaniddāto pabujjhanatthāya, phalena pabujjhanabhāvatthāyātipi vuttaṃ hoti. Tenevettha nibbānasacchikiriyā kilesapahānapaccavekkhaṇāti sabbaṃ dassitaṃ.

In the fifth sutta, 'they conduce to awakening' means they conduce for the purpose of knowing. For what purpose of knowing? They conduce for the purpose of knowing the unconditioned Nibbāna by means of the path; for the purpose of knowing, by means of reflection, that the task has been completed. Or alternatively, by the path, they conduce for the purpose of awakening from the sleep of the defilements; and by the fruit, for the purpose of the state of realizing Nibbāna—thus it is also said. Therefore, herein, the realization of Nibbāna, the abandoning of defilements, and reflection—thus all is shown.

6-7. Kuṇḍaliyasuttādivaṇṇanā

6-7. Commentary on the Kuṇḍaliya Sutta and Others

187-188. Chaṭṭhe [M 3.0183] ārāmanissayīti ārāmaṃ nissāya vasanabhāvena ārāmanissayī. Parisāvacaroti parisāya avacaro. Parisaṃ nāma bālāpi, paṇḍitāpi osaranti, yo pana parappavādaṃ madditvā attano vādaṃ dīpetuṃ sakkoti, ayaṃ parisāvacaro nāma. Ārāmena ārāmanti ārāmeneva ārāmaṃ anucaṅkamāmi, na bāhirenāti attho. Uyyānena uyyānanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Aññena vā ārāmena pavisitvā aññaṃ ārāmaṃ, aññena uyyānena aññaṃ uyyānanti ayamettha attho. Itivādappamokkhānisaṃsanti “evaṃ pucchā hoti, evaṃ vissajjanaṃ, evaṃ gahaṇaṃ, evaṃ nibbeṭhana”nti iminā nayena itivādo hoti itivādappamokkhoti etaṃ ānisaṃsaṃ. Upārambhānisaṃsanti “ayaṃ pucchāya doso, ayaṃ vissajjane”ti evaṃ vādadosānisaṃsaṃ.

5. In the sixth sutta, 'one who depends on a monastery' means one is so called because of the habit of living depending on a monastery. 'One who frequents assemblies' means one who enters and moves about in an assembly. Both fools and the wise gather in an assembly, but one who is able to crush another's argument and illuminate their own doctrine is called 'one who frequents assemblies'. 'From monastery to monastery' means 'I wander from one monastery to another only by way of a monastery, not outside'—this is the meaning. In 'from park to park' also, this same method applies. Or alternatively, 'having entered by one monastery, I wander to another monastery; by one park, to another park'—this is the meaning here. 'The benefit of being released from such-and-such a debate' means this benefit: 'In this way there is a question, in this way an answer, in this way a grasping, in this way a disentangling'—by this method there is a debate, and release from that debate. 'The benefit of reproach' means the benefit of finding faults in an argument, thus: 'This is a fault in the question; this is a fault in the answer.'

Kathaṃ bhāvito ca, kuṇḍaliya, indriyasaṃvaroti satthā “ettakaṃ ṭhānaṃ paribbājakena pucchitaṃ, idāni pucchituṃ na sakkotī”ti ñatvā “na tāva ayaṃ desanā yathānusandhiṃ gatā. Idāni naṃ yathānusandhiṃ pāpessāmī”ti sayameva pucchanto imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Tattha manāpaṃ nābhijjhatīti iṭṭhārammaṇaṃ nābhijjhāyati. Nābhihaṃsatīti na sāmisāya tuṭṭhiyā abhihaṃsati. Tassa ṭhito ca kāyo hoti, ṭhitaṃ cittaṃ ajjhattanti tassa nāmakāyo ca cittañca gocarajjhatte ṭhitaṃ hoti. Susaṇṭhitanti kammaṭṭhānavasena suṭṭhu saṇṭhitaṃ. Suvimuttanti kammaṭṭhānavimuttiyā suvimuttaṃ. Amanāpanti aniṭṭhārammaṇaṃ. Na maṅku hotīti tasmiṃ na maṅku hoti. Appatiṭṭhitacittoti kilesavasena [P 3.0146] aṭṭhitacitto. Adīnamānasoti domanassavasena adīnacitto. Abyāpannacetasoti dosavasena apūticitto.

‘And how, Kuṇḍaliya, is restraint of the senses developed?’ The Teacher, knowing, ‘The wanderer has asked this much; now he is not able to ask more,’ and thinking, ‘This teaching has not yet reached its proper sequence; now I shall lead it to its proper sequence,’ began this discourse by questioning himself. Therein, ‘does not covet the pleasing’ means one does not crave a desirable object. ‘Does not delight in it’ means one does not delight with a satisfaction connected with the flesh. ‘His body is steady, and his mind is inwardly established’ means his mental body and his mind are established within the meditation object. ‘Well-established’ means well-established by the power of the meditation subject. ‘Well-liberated’ means well-liberated from its counterpart through the practice of the meditation subject. ‘The displeasing’ means an undesirable object. ‘He is not downcast’ means he is not downcast on that account. ‘His mind is not unestablished’ means his mind is not unsettled by the power of defilements. ‘His mind is not dejected’ means his mind is not dejected by the power of displeasure. ‘His mind is without ill will’ means his mind is not corrupted by the power of aversion.

Evaṃ bhāvito kho, kuṇḍaliya, indriyasaṃvaro evaṃ bahulīkato tīṇi sucaritāni paripūretīti ettha evaṃ sucaritapūraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ – imesu tāva chasu dvāresu aṭṭhārasa duccaritāni [V 3.0183] honti. Kathaṃ? Cakkhudvāre tāva [M 3.0184] iṭṭhārammaṇe āpāthagate kāyaṅgavācaṅgāni acopetvā tasmiṃ ārammaṇe lobhaṃ uppādentassa manoduccaritaṃ hoti. Lobhasahagatena cittena “aho vatidaṃ iṭṭhaṃ kantaṃ manāpa”nti bhaṇantassa vacīduccaritaṃ, tadeva hatthena parāmasantassa kāyaduccaritaṃ. Sesadvāresupi eseva nayo.

‘Thus, Kuṇḍaliya, when sense restraint is developed and cultivated in this way, it fulfills the three kinds of good conduct.’ Here, this fulfillment of good conduct should be understood as follows: Regarding these six doors, there are eighteen kinds of misconduct. How? At the eye-door, when a desirable object comes into range, for one who, without moving the limbs of the body and speech, gives rise to greed for that object, there is mental misconduct. For one who speaks with a mind accompanied by greed, saying, ‘Oh, how desirable, lovely, and pleasing!’ there is verbal misconduct. For one who touches that same object with the hand, there is bodily misconduct. The same method applies to the remaining sense doors.

Ayaṃ pana viseso – sotadvārasmiñhi saddārammaṇassa vatthubhūtaṃ saṅkhapaṇavāditūriyabhaṇḍaṃ anāmāsaṃ āmasantassa, ghānadvāre gandhārammaṇassa vatthubhūtaṃ gandhamālādiṃ, jivhādvāre rasārammaṇassa vatthubhūtaṃ macchamaṃsādiṃ, kāyadvāre phoṭṭhabbārammaṇassa vatthubhūtaṃ vatthatūlakapāvārādiṃ, manodvāre paññattivasena dhammārammaṇabhūtaṃ sappitelamadhuphāṇitādiṃ āmasantassa kāyaduccaritaṃ veditabbaṃ. Saṅkhepato panettha chasu dvāresu kāyavītikkamo kāyaduccaritaṃ, vacīvītikkamo vacīduccaritaṃ, manovītikkamo manoduccaritanti tīṇeva duccaritāni honti.

This, however, is the distinction: for one who touches what is not to be touched—at the ear-door, the material basis of the sound-object, such as conch shells, small drums, and other musical instruments; at the nose-door, the material basis of the smell-object, such as perfumes and garlands; at the tongue-door, the material basis of the taste-object, such as fish and meat; at the body-door, the material basis of the tangible-object, such as cloth, cotton, and cloaks; at the mind-door, the material basis of the mind-object by way of concept, such as ghee, oil, honey, and molasses—this is to be understood as bodily misconduct. In brief, herein at the six doors, transgression by way of the body is bodily misconduct; transgression by way of speech is verbal misconduct; transgression by way of mind is mental misconduct—thus there are only three kinds of misconduct.

Ayaṃ pana bhikkhu attano bhāvanāpaṭisaṅkhāne ṭhito imāni duccaritāni sucaritaṃ katvā vipariṇāmeti. Kathaṃ? Cakkhudvāre tāva iṭṭhārammaṇe āpāthagate kāyaṅgavācaṅgāni acāletvā rūpārammaṇaṃ vipassanaṃ paṭṭhāpayato manosucaritaṃ hoti, vipassanāsahagatena cittena khayadhammaṃ vayadhammanti bhaṇantassa vacīsucaritaṃ, “anāmāsabhaṇḍaṃ eta”nti anāmasantassa kāyasucaritaṃ. Sesadvāresupi eseva nayo. Evaṃ imāni vitthārato aṭṭhārasa sucaritāni honti. Saṅkhepato [P 3.0147] panetthāpi chasu dvāresu kāyasaṃvaro kāyasucaritaṃ, vacīsaṃvaro vacīsucaritaṃ, manosaṃvaro manosucaritanti tīṇeva sucaritāni honti. Evaṃ indriyasaṃvaro tīṇi sucaritāni paripūretīti veditabbo. Ettāvatā sīlānurakkhitaṃ indriyasaṃvarasīlaṃ kathitaṃ.

This monk, however, established in reflection on his own development, transforms these occasions for misconduct into good conduct. How? At the eye-door, when a desirable object comes into range, without stirring his bodily or verbal faculties, he establishes insight regarding the form-object—this is mental good conduct. With a mind accompanied by insight, saying, ‘It is of the nature to decay, of the nature to vanish,’ is verbal good conduct. By not touching it, thinking, ‘This is an item not to be touched,’ is bodily good conduct. The same method applies to the remaining sense doors. Thus, in detail, there are these eighteen kinds of good conduct. In brief, however, here too, in the six doors, restraint of the body is bodily good conduct, restraint of speech is verbal good conduct, and restraint of mind is mental good conduct—thus there are only three kinds of good conduct. Thus, it is to be understood that sense restraint fulfills these three kinds of good conduct. To this extent, the virtue of sense restraint, guarded by morality, has been taught.

Kāyaduccaritaṃ pahāyātiādīsu tividhaṃ kāyaduccaritaṃ, catubbidhaṃ vacīduccaritaṃ, tividhaṃ manoduccaritaṃ. Tassa paṭipakkhavasena kāyasucaritādīni veditabbāni. Ettāvatā kāyasaṃvaravacīsaṃvarehi pātimokkhasīlaṃ, manosaṃvarena tīṇi sīlānīti catupārisuddhisīlaṃ kathitaṃ hoti. Sakale pana imasmiṃ sutte sucaritamūlakā satipaṭṭhānā lokuttaramissakā, sattannaṃ bojjhaṅgānaṃ [M 3.0185] mūlabhūtā satipaṭṭhānā pubbabhāgā, tepi satipaṭṭhānamūlakā bojjhaṅgā pubbabhāgāva. Vijjāvimuttimūlakā pana lokuttarāva kathitāti veditabbā. Sattamaṃ uttānameva.

In the Pali text beginning with ‘having abandoned bodily misconduct,’ there is threefold bodily misconduct, fourfold verbal misconduct, and threefold mental misconduct. By way of their counterparts, bodily good conduct and so forth should be known. By this much, through bodily and verbal restraint, the Pātimokkha virtue is taught; through mental restraint, the three virtues are taught. Thus, the fourfold virtue of purification is said to be taught. However, in this entire sutta, the foundations of mindfulness rooted in good conduct are mixed with the supramundane. The foundations of mindfulness, which are the root of the seven enlightenment factors, are of the preliminary part. Those enlightenment factors rooted in the foundations of mindfulness are also only of the preliminary part. However, the enlightenment factors that are the root of knowledge and liberation are taught as only supramundane. Thus it should be known. The seventh sutta has only a clear meaning.

8. Upavānasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Upavāṇa Sutta

189. Aṭṭhame [V 3.0184] paccattanti attanāva. Yonisomanasikārāti yoniso manasikārena. Ārabbhamānovāti kurumānoyeva. Suvimuttanti kammaṭṭhānavimuttiyā suṭṭhu vimuttaṃ. Aṭṭhiṃkatvāti atthaṃ karitvā, atthiko hutvāti vuttaṃ hoti.

189. In the eighth sutta, ‘paccattaṃ’ means ‘by oneself indeed.’ ‘Yonisomanasikārā’ means ‘by wise attention.’ ‘Ārabbhamāno’ means ‘one who is undertaking indeed.’ ‘Suvimuttaṃ’ means ‘well liberated through attention to the meditation subject.’ ‘Aṭṭhiṃkatvā’ is said to mean: having made it a supreme benefit, having become one who possesses that benefit.

9. Paṭhamauppannasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the First Uppanna Sutta

190. Navame nāññatra tathāgatassa pātubhāvāti tathāgatassa pātubhāvaṃ vinā na aññasmiṃ kāle uppajjantīti attho.

190. In the ninth sutta, ‘nāññatra tathāgatassa pātubhāvā’ means: they do not arise at another time without the appearance of the Tathāgata. This is the meaning.

10. Dutiyauppannasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Second Uppanna Sutta

191. Dasame nāññatra sugatavinayāti sugatovādaṃ vinā na uppajjantīti.

191. In the tenth sutta, ‘nāññatra sugatavinayā’ means: they do not arise without the teaching of the Sugata.

Pabbatavaggo.

The Mountain Chapter

2. Gilānavaggo

2. The Chapter on the Sick

1-3. Pāṇasuttādivaṇṇanā

1–3. Commentary on the Pāṇa Sutta and so forth

192-194. Dutiyavaggassa paṭhame cattāro iriyāpathe kappentīti yesaṃ cattāro iriyāpathā atthi, tesaṃyeva vasenetaṃ [P 3.0148] vuttaṃ. Sīlaṃ nissāyāti catupārisuddhisīlaṃ nissayaṃ katvā. Satta bojjhaṅgeti sahavipassanake maggabojjhaṅge. Dutiyatatiyāni uttānatthāneva.

In the first sutta of the second chapter, the phrase ‘cattāro iriyāpathe kappenti’ is said with reference to only those beings who possess the four postures. ‘Sīlaṃ nissāya’ means: having made the fourfold virtue of purification a support. ‘Satta bojjhaṅge’ means: the path-factors of enlightenment together with insight. The second and third suttas have only a clear meaning.

4-10. Paṭhamagilānasuttādivaṇṇanā

4–10. Commentary on the First Gilāna Sutta and so forth

195-201. Catutthe [V 3.0185] tathā pahīno cāyasmato mahākassapassa so ābādho ahosīti therassa kira imaṃ bojjhaṅgabhāvanaṃ sādhukaṃ [M 3.0186] suṇantassa etadahosi “mayhaṃ pabbajitadivasato sattame divase saccāni paṭivijjhantassa ime bojjhaṅgā pātubhūtā”ti. Athassa “niyyānikaṃ vata satthusāsana”nti cintayato lohitaṃ pasīdi, upādārūpaṃ visuddhaṃ ahosi, pokkharapatte patitaudakabindu viya sarīrato rogo vinivattitvā gato. Tena vuttaṃ “tathā pahīno cāyasmato mahākassapassa so ābādho ahosī”ti. Pañcamachaṭṭhesupi eseva nayo. Imesaṃ pana tiṇṇampi janānaṃ pabbatapāde pupphitavisarukkhavātasamphassena uppanno mandasītajaro ābādhoti veditabbo. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

In the fourth [sutta], regarding the phrase 'tathā pahīno cāyasmato mahākassapassa so ābādho ahosi' ('thus that illness of the Venerable Mahākassapa was abandoned'): It is said that while the Elder was carefully listening to this development of the enlightenment factors, this thought occurred to him: 'For me, on the seventh day from the day of going forth, while I was penetrating the truths, these enlightenment factors appeared.' Then, as he was thinking, 'Indeed, the Teacher’s Dispensation leads out [of saṃsāra]!,' his blood cleared, his derived matter became pure, and the illness, having receded from his body, departed like a drop of water placed on a lotus leaf. For that reason, it was said: 'tathā pahīno cāyasmato mahākassapassa so ābādho ahosi.' In the fifth and sixth [suttas] as well, this is the same method. However, for these three persons, it should be known that the illness was a mild, cold fever that arose from contact with wind from a flowering poisonous tree at the foot of the mountain. The rest is clear everywhere.

Gilānavaggo.

The Chapter on the Sick.

3. Udāyivaggo

3. The Udāyi Chapter.

1-2. Bodhāyasuttādivaṇṇanā

1–2. Commentary on the Bodhāya Sutta and so forth.

202-203. Tatiyavaggassa paṭhame kittāvatā nu kho, bhante, bojjhaṅgāti vuccantīti bhante, kittakena nu kho bujjhanakaaṅgā nāma vuccantīti pucchati. Bodhāya saṃvattantīti bujjhanatthāya saṃvattanti. Imasmiṃ sutte missakabojjhaṅgā kathitā. Dutiye dhammaparicchedo kathito.

In the first [sutta] of the third chapter, the question 'kittāvatā nu kho, bhante, bojjhaṅgāti vuccanti?' is asked, meaning 'Venerable sir, for what reason are they called factors of awakening?' 'Bodhāya saṃvattanti' means 'they conduce to awakening.' In this sutta, mixed factors of awakening are taught. In the second [sutta], the division of the Dhamma is taught.

3-5. Ṭhāniyasuttādivaṇṇanā

3–5. Commentary on the Ṭhāniya Sutta and so forth.

204-206. Tatiye [P 3.0149] kāmarāgaṭṭhāniyānanti kāmarāgassa kāraṇabhūtānaṃ ārammaṇadhammānaṃ. Byāpādaṭṭhāniyādīsupi eseva nayo. Sakalañhi idaṃ suttaṃ ārammaṇeneva kathitaṃ. Paṭhamavaggassa [V 3.0186] dutiyasutte vuttaparicchedopettha labbhateva. Catutthe missakabojjhaṅgā kathitā. Pañcame aparihāniye dhammeti aparihānikare sabhāvadhamme.

In the third [sutta], 'kāmarāgaṭṭhāniyānaṃ' means 'of the object-dharmas that are the cause of sensual lust.' This same method should be known in regard to 'byāpādaṭṭhāniya' and so forth. For this entire sutta is taught only in terms of objects. The definition taught in the second sutta of the first chapter is indeed obtained here. In the fourth [sutta], the mixed factors of awakening are taught. In the fifth [sutta], 'aparihāniye dhamme' means 'the seven dhammas that cause non-decline.'

6-7. Taṇhakkhayasuttādivaṇṇanā

6-7. Commentary on the Taṇhakkhaya Sutta, etc.

207-208. Chaṭṭhe etadavocāti “imissaṃ parisati nisinno udāyitthero nāma anusandhikusalo bhikkhu atthi, so maṃ pucchissatīti bhagavatā [M 3.0187] osāpitadesanaṃ ñatvā desanānusandhiṃ ghaṭessāmī”ti pucchanto etaṃ avoca. Vipulantiādi sabbaṃ subhāvitattaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Subhāvito hi satisambojjhaṅgo vipulo ca mahaggato ca appamāṇo ca abyāpajjo ca nāma hoti. So hi patthaṭattā vipulo, mahantabhāvaṃ gatattā mahaggato, vaḍḍhipamāṇattā appamāṇo, nīvaraṇānaṃ dūrībhāvena byāpādarahitattā abyāpajjho nāma hoti. Taṇhāya pahānā kammaṃ pahīyatīti yaṃ taṇhāmūlakaṃ kammaṃ uppajjeyya, taṃ taṇhāpahānena pahīyati. Kammassa pahānā dukkhanti yampi kammamūlakaṃ vaṭṭadukkhaṃ uppajjeyya, taṃ kammapahānena pahīyati. Taṇhakkhayādayo taṇhādīnaṃyeva khayā, atthato panetehi nibbānaṃ kathitanti veditabbaṃ. Sattamaṃ uttānameva.

In the sixth [sutta], regarding 'etadavoca': The Blessed One anticipated, 'There is a monk in this assembly named Elder Udāyi, skilled in making connections; he will ask me.' Knowing that the Blessed One had thus concluded the discourse, Udāyi, wishing to ask with the intention 'I will make the connection for the discourse,' said this. All of this beginning with 'extensive' is said with reference to the state of being well-cultivated. For a well-cultivated mindfulness-factor-of-awakening is called extensive, come to a sublime state, immeasurable, and free from ill will. For that mindfulness-factor-of-awakening, because it has become widespread through the fulfillment of development, is called 'extensive'; because it has reached a state of greatness, it is called 'come to a sublime state'; because it has a measure of great growth, it is called 'immeasurable'; because of the hindrances being far away and being free from ill will, it is called 'free from ill will'. 'Taṇhāya pahānā kammaṃ pahīyati' means: whatever kamma having craving as its root might arise, that kamma is abandoned by the abandoning of craving. 'Kammassa pahānā dukkhaṃ' means: whatever suffering of the round having kamma as its root might arise, that suffering of the round is abandoned by the abandoning of kamma. The terms 'destruction of craving' and so on refer to the destruction of craving and so on themselves; however, it should be known that in terms of meaning, Nibbāna is taught by these terms. The seventh [sutta] is self-explanatory.

8. Nibbedhabhāgiyasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Nibbedhabhāgiya Sutta

209. Aṭṭhame [P 3.0150] nibbedhabhāgiyanti nibbijjhanakoṭṭhāsiyaṃ. Satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāvitenāti satisambojjhaṅgena bhāvitena, satisambojjhaṅgaṃ vā bhāvetvā ṭhitena, evamettha maggabojjhaṅgā missakā. Tehi bhāvitaṃ, te vā bhāvetvā ṭhitaṃ cittaṃ nibbattitalokuttarameva. Tampi pana magganissitaṃ katvā missakameva kathetuṃ vaṭṭati.

In the eighth, ‘pertaining to penetration’ (nibbedhabhāgiya) means a constituent of piercing. ‘Developed by the mindfulness factor of awakening’ (satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāvitena) means: developed by the mindfulness factor of awakening, or by the mind that remains established having developed the mindfulness factor of awakening. Thus, here the path factors of awakening are taught as mingled. The fruition-mind, perfumed by them, or established having developed them, is accomplished as purely supramundane. However, even that fruition-mind, because it is immediate to and dependent on the path, it is fitting to speak of it only as mingled.

9. Ekadhammasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the One-Quality Sutta

210. Navame saṃyojanavinibandhāti saṃyojanasaṅkhātā vinibandhā. Ajjhosānāti pariniṭṭhapetvā gahaṇā.

In the ninth, ‘fetter-bonds’ (saṃyojanavinibandhā) means the bonds that are called fetters. ‘Clinging’ (ajjhosāna) means grasping after having brought to consummation.

10. Udāyisuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Udāyi Sutta

211. Dasame [V 3.0187] abahukatoti akatabahumāno. Ukkujjāvakujjanti ettha ukkujjaṃ vuccati udayo, avakujjaṃ vayoti udayabbayavasena parivattento sammasantoti dīpeti. Dhammo ca me, bhante, abhisamitoti vipassanādhammo abhisamāgato. Maggoti vipassanāmaggova. Sace hi thero tasmiṃ samaye sotāpanno, upari tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ atthāya, sace [M 3.0188] anāgāmī, arahattamaggassa atthāya ayaṃ vipassanā veditabbā. Tathā tathā viharantanti tena tenākārena viharantaṃ. Tathattāyāti tathābhāvāya. Khīṇā jātītiādīhi tathattāyāti adhippetaṃ tathābhāvaṃ dasseti. Paccavekkhaṇatthāya upanīyatīti hi ettha adhippāyo, taṃ dassento evamāha. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

In the tenth, ‘not esteemed’ (abahukato) means one for whom much esteem is not made. ‘Upright and inverted’ (ukkujjāvakujja)—here, ‘upright’ is said to be arising, and ‘inverted’ is said to be passing away. Thus, it indicates one contemplating by revolving it according to arising and passing away—as impermanent, as suffering, and as not-self. ‘And, venerable sir, the Dhamma has been directly known by me’ (dhammo ca me, bhante, abhisamito) means the Dhamma of insight has been directly known. ‘Path’ (maggo) refers to the path of insight itself. For if the elder was a stream-enterer at that time, this insight should be understood as for the sake of the higher three paths; if a non-returner, for the sake of the path of arahantship. ‘Dwelling in such and such ways’ (tathā tathā viharantaṃ) means dwelling in those respective ways with the abiding of insight. ‘For suchness’ (tathattāya) means for that state of being, that is, for the sake of the reviewing knowledge which is the state of being one whose cankers are destroyed. By ‘destroyed is birth’ and so on, with the phrase ‘for suchness,’ he shows the intended reviewing knowledge of that state of being. For the intention here is that it is presented for the sake of reviewing knowledge; showing this, he spoke thus. The rest is clear everywhere.

Udāyivaggo.

8. The Udāyi Chapter.

4. Nīvaraṇavaggo

209. The Hindrances Chapter.

3-4. Upakkilesasuttādivaṇṇanā

3-4. Commentary on the Upakkilesa Sutta, etc.

214-215. Catutthavaggassa tatiye na ca pabhassaranti na ca pabhāvantaṃ. Pabhaṅgu cāti pabhijjanasabhāvaṃ. Ayoti kāḷalohaṃ. Ṭhapetvā idha vuttāni cattāri avasesaṃ lohaṃ nāma. Sajjhūti rajataṃ. Cittassāti catubhūmakacittassa. Lokiyassa tāva upakkileso hotu[P 3.0151], lokuttarassa kathaṃ hotīti? Uppajjituṃ appadānena. Yadaggena hi uppajjituṃ na denti, tadaggeneva te lokiyassāpi lokuttarassāpi upakkilesā nāma honti. Pabhaṅgu cāti ārammaṇe cuṇṇavicuṇṇabhāvūpagamanena bhijjanasabhāvaṃ. Anāvaraṇā anīvaraṇāti kusaladhamme na āvarantīti anāvaraṇā, na nīvaranti na paṭicchādentīti anīvaraṇā. Cetaso anupakkilesāti catubhūmakacittassa anupakkilesā.

9. In the third sutta of the fourth chapter, ‘not radiant’ (na ca pabhassaranti) means not shining. ‘And fragile’ (pabhaṅgu ca) means of a nature to break. ‘Iron’ (ayo) means black iron. Except for the four mentioned here, the remainder is called ‘metal.’ ‘Silver’ (sajjhu) means silver. ‘Of the mind’ (cittassa) means of the wholesome mind of the four planes. ‘For the mundane, let it be a defilement; how can it be for the supramundane?’ By not giving an opportunity for it to arise. For in whatever respect they do not give an opportunity to arise, in that very respect they are called defilements for both the mundane and the supramundane. ‘And fragile’ (pabhaṅgu ca) means of a nature to be destroyed by reaching a state of being crushed to powder in the object. ‘Unobstructing, unhindering’ (anāvaraṇā anīvaraṇā) means they do not obstruct wholesome qualities, therefore they are ‘unobstructing’; they do not hinder, do not conceal, therefore they are ‘unhindering.’ ‘Not defilements of the mind’ (cetaso anupakkilesā) means they are not defilements of the wholesome mind of the four planes.

8. Āvaraṇanīvaraṇasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the Discourse on Obstructions and Hindrances

219. Aṭṭhame [V 3.0188] paññāya dubbalīkaraṇāti paññāya mandabhāvakarā. Nīvaraṇānañhi abhiṇhuppāde sati antarantarā uppajjamānā paññā dubbalā hoti mandā avisadā.

219. In the eighth [sutta], 'weakening wisdom' means making wisdom feeble. For when hindrances frequently arise, wisdom that arises intermittently becomes weak, dull, and unclear.

Pañca nīvaraṇā tasmiṃ samaye na honti. Sattabojjhaṅgā tasmiṃ samaye bhāvanāpāripūriṃ gacchantīti ariyasāvakassa hi sappāyadhammassavanaṃ suṇantassa [M 3.0189] pañca nīvaraṇā dūre honti. So sace tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ sakkoti, evamassa satta bojjhaṅgā bhāvanāpāripūriṃ gacchanti. No ce sakkoti, tato vuṭṭhāya rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānaṃ gato tameva pītiṃ avijahanto pañca nīvaraṇe vikkhambhetvā visesaṃ nibbattessati. Tattha asakkontopi yāva sattadivasabbhantarā tameva pītiṃ avijahanto nīvaraṇe vikkhambhetvā visesaṃ nibbattessatīti idaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Dhammassavanavasena sakiṃ pītipāmojjapakkhiyā paṭiladdhabojjhaṅgā hi kammārāmatādīni āgamma nassanti, tathārūpaṃ pana utusappāyādiṃ labhitvā puna uppajjantāpi tasmiṃ samaye bhāvanāpāripūriṃ gacchanti icceva vuccati.

At that time, the five hindrances are not present. The seven factors of enlightenment reach full development. For when a noble disciple listens to the Dhamma that is beneficial, the five hindrances are far away. If he is able to realize a special attainment right there, then his seven factors of enlightenment reach full development. If he is not able, then rising from that place and going to a secluded place for the night or day, not abandoning that joy, he will suppress the five hindrances and realize a special attainment. Even if he is unable there, within seven days, not abandoning that joy, he will suppress the hindrances and realize a special attainment. This is what is meant by this. For the factors of enlightenment gained once through the power of hearing the Dhamma, having joy and gladness as their support, may be lost on account of delighting in work and such things. But when favorable conditions like a suitable climate are obtained and they arise again, at that time they are said to reach full development.

9. Rukkhasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Explanation of the Tree Discourse

220. Navame ajjhāruhāti abhiruhanakā. Kacchakoti aṭṭhikacchako. Kapitthanoti makkaṭathanasadisaphalo vijātapilakkho.

220. In the ninth [sutta], 'ajjhāruhā' means those that grow by climbing over. 'Kacchako' means the aṭṭhikacchaka plant. 'Kapitthano' means the vijātapilakkho, a fig tree with fruit resembling a monkey's breast that grows on another tree of a different species.

10. Nīvaraṇasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Hindrance Discourse

221. Dasame [P 3.0152] andhakaraṇāti andhabhāvakaraṇā. Acakkhukaraṇāti paññācakkhussa akaraṇā. Paññānirodhikāti paññāya nirodhanā. Vighātapakkhiyāti dukkhapakkhikā. Anibbānasaṃvattanikāti nibbānatthāya asaṃvattanikā. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthameva. Sakalepi imasmiṃ vagge missakabojjhaṅgāva kathitāti.

221. In the tenth [sutta], 'blinding' means causing the state of being blind. 'Depriving of sight' means not creating the eye of wisdom. 'Destructive to wisdom' means causing the cessation of wisdom. 'Inclined to harm' means being on the side of suffering. 'Not conducive to Nibbāna' means not leading to the goal of Nibbāna. The rest has an obvious meaning throughout. In this entire chapter, only mixed factors of enlightenment have been taught.

Nīvaraṇavaggo.

The Chapter on the Hindrances.

5. Cakkavattivaggo

5. The Chapter on the Wheel-Turning Monarch

1. Vidhāsuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Vidhā Discourse

222. Pañcamavaggassa [V 3.0189] paṭhame tisso vidhāti tayo mānakoṭṭhāsā, mānoyeva vā. Tathā tathā vidahanato hi mānova vidhāti vuccati.

222. In the first [discourse] of the fifth chapter, 'three vidhā' means three portions of conceit, or simply conceit itself. Indeed, because it arranges itself in various ways, conceit itself is called 'vidhā'.

2. Cakkavattisuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Cakkavatti Sutta

223. Dutiye [M 3.0190] rañño, bhikkhave, cakkavattissāti ettha attano sirisampattiyā rājati, catūhi vā saṅgahavatthūhi lokaṃ rañjetīti rājā, tassa rañño. “Pavattatu bhavaṃ cakkaratana”nti puññānubhāvena abbhuggatāya vācāya codento cakkaṃ vattetīti cakkavattī, tassa cakkavattissa. Pātubhāvāti pātubhāvena. Sattannanti gaṇanaparicchedo. Ratanānanti paricchinnaatthadassanaṃ. Vacanattho panettha ratijananaṭṭhena ratanaṃ. Apica –

223. In the second discourse, regarding the phrase 'of a king, a wheel-turning monarch': here, one who shines by the perfection of his own glory, or who delights the world with the four bases of sympathy, is a king (rājā). Of that king. One who, urging with a voice uplifted through the power of merit, saying, 'May the noble wheel-treasure turn,' makes the wheel turn, is a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavattī). Of that wheel-turning monarch. 'From the manifestation' (pātubhāvā) means by the manifestation (pātubhāvena). 'Of seven' (sattannaṃ) is a numerical delimitation. 'Of treasures' (ratanānaṃ) indicates the specified meaning. Here, the etymological meaning is: it is a treasure (ratana) in the sense that it generates delight (rati). Moreover—

“Cittīkataṃ mahagghañca, atulaṃ dullabhadassanaṃ;

Anomasattaparibhogaṃ, ratanaṃ tena vuccatī”ti.

“Because it is esteemed, of great price, incomparable, difficult to see, and fit for the use of a being who is not inferior, for that reason it is called a treasure.”

Cakkaratanassa ca nibbattakālato paṭṭhāya aññaṃ devaṭṭhānaṃ nāma na hoti, sabbeva gandhapupphādīhi tasseva pūjañca abhivādanādīni ca karontīti cittīkataṭṭhena ratanaṃ. Cakkaratanassa ca “ettakaṃ nāma dhanaṃ agghatī”ti aggho natthi, iti mahagghaṭṭhenāpi ratanaṃ. Cakkaratanañca aññehi loke vijjamānaratanehi asadisanti atulaṭṭhena ratanaṃ. Yasmā pana yasmiṃ kappe buddhā uppajjanti[P 3.0153], tasmiṃyeva cakkavattino, buddhā ca kadāci karahaci uppajjanti, tasmā dullabhadassanaṭṭhena ratanaṃ. Tadetaṃ jātirūpakulaissariyādīhi anomassa uḷārasattasseva uppajjati, na aññassāti anomasattaparibhogaṭṭhenāpi ratanaṃ. Yathā ca cakkaratanaṃ, evaṃ sesānipīti. Tena vuttaṃ –

From the time of the wheel-treasure's arising, there is no other place of worship for deities; everyone makes offerings of perfumes, flowers, and so on, and performs acts of veneration to it alone. Thus, it is a treasure in the sense of being esteemed. And for the wheel-treasure, there is no price such that one could say, 'It is worth this much wealth.' Thus, it is also a treasure in the sense of being of great price. And the wheel-treasure is dissimilar to other existing treasures in the world. Thus, it is a treasure in the sense of being incomparable. Furthermore, since wheel-turning monarchs arise only in an aeon in which Buddhas arise, and Buddhas arise only on rare occasions, it is therefore a treasure in the sense of being difficult to see. This treasure arises only for a great being who is not inferior in terms of birth, appearance, family, sovereignty, and so on; it does not arise for another. Thus, it is also a treasure in the sense of being for the use of a being who is not inferior. And as it is with the wheel-treasure, so it is with the remaining treasures. Therefore, it was said:

“Cittīkataṃ [V 3.0190] mahagghañca, atulaṃ dullabhadassanaṃ;

Anomasattaparibhogaṃ, ratanaṃ tena vuccatī”ti.

“Because it is esteemed, of great price, incomparable, difficult to see, and fit for the use of a being who is not inferior, for that reason it is called a treasure.”

Pātubhāvo hotīti nibbatti hoti. Tatrāyaṃ yojanā – cakkavattissa pātubhāvā sattannaṃ ratanānaṃ pātubhāvoti ayuttaṃ. Uppannañhi cakkaṃ vattetvā so cakkavattī nāma hotīti nāyuttaṃ. Kasmā? Cakkavattananiyamāpekkhatāya. Yo hi niyamena cakkaṃ vattessati, so paṭisandhito pabhuti “cakkavatti pātubhūto”ti vattabbataṃ āpajjati. Laddhanāmassa ca purisassa mūluppattivacanatopi yuttamevetaṃ. Yo hi esa cakkavattīti [M 3.0191] laddhanāmo sattaviseso, tassa paṭisandhisaṅkhāto pātubhāvoti ayamettha attho. Tassa hi pātubhāvā ratanāni pātubhavanti. Pātubhūtehi pana tehi saddhiṃ paripakke puññasambhāre so saṃyujjati, tadā lokassa tesu pātubhāvacittaṃ uppajjati. Bahulavacanato cāpi yuttamevetaṃ. Yadā hi lokassa tesu pātubhāvasaññā uppajjati, tadā ekameva paṭhamaṃ, pacchā itarāni cha pātubhavantīti bahulavacanato cāpi etaṃ yuttaṃ. Pātubhāvassa ca atthabhedatopi yuttamevetaṃ. Na kevalañhi pātubhūtameva pātubhāvo, pātubhāvayatīti pātubhāvo. Ayaṃ pātubhāvassa atthabhedo. Yasmā yo so puññasambhāro rājānaṃ cakkavattiṃ paṭisandhivasena pātubhāvayati, tasmā rañño cakkavattissa pātubhāvā. Na kevalañhi cakkavattiyeva, imāni pana satta ratanānipi pātubhavantīti ayamettha attho. Yatheva hi so puññasambhāro rañño janakahetu, evaṃ ratanānampi pariyāyena upanissayahetūti yuttamevetaṃ “rañño, bhikkhave, cakkavattissa pātubhāvā sattannaṃ ratanānaṃ pātubhāvo hotī”ti.

‘The manifestation occurs’ means arising occurs. Herein, this is the construction: ‘From the manifestation of the wheel-turning monarch, the manifestation of the seven treasures occurs.’ This is unsuitable. For is he not called a ‘wheel-turning monarch’ only after making the arisen wheel turn? This is not unsuitable. Why? Because of the dependence on the certainty of turning the wheel. For whoever will with certainty turn the wheel, he, from his rebirth-linking onwards, attains the state of being fit to be called ‘a wheel-turning monarch has manifested.’ And this is also suitable from the perspective of stating the root-arising of a person who has acquired the name. For that specific being who has acquired the name ‘wheel-turning monarch,’ his manifestation is what is called rebirth-linking; this is the meaning here. For from his manifestation, the treasures manifest. But he becomes united with them only when his store of merit has matured along with those manifested treasures; it is then that the thought ‘they have manifested’ arises in the world regarding them. And this is also suitable on account of the plural expression. For when the perception of their manifestation arises in the world, only one manifests first, and afterwards the other six manifest; thus, this is also suitable on account of the plural expression. And this is also suitable because of the different meanings of ‘manifestation.’ For ‘manifestation’ is not merely that which has manifested; ‘it causes to manifest’ (pātubhāvayati), therefore it is ‘manifestation’ (pātubhāvo). This is the difference in meaning of ‘manifestation.’ Because that store of merit causes the king, the wheel-turning monarch, to manifest by way of rebirth-linking, therefore from the manifestation of the king, the wheel-turning monarch, not only does the wheel-turning monarch himself manifest, but also these seven treasures manifest; this is the meaning here. For just as that store of merit is the generating cause for the king, so too it is, indirectly, a support-condition for the treasures. Therefore, this statement, ‘Monks, from the manifestation of the king, the wheel-turning monarch, the manifestation of the seven treasures occurs,’ is indeed suitable.

Idāni [P 3.0154] tesaṃ ratanānaṃ sarūpavasena dassanatthaṃ katamesaṃ sattannaṃ cakkaratanassātiādimāha. Tattha cakkaratanassātiādīsu ayaṃ saṅkhepādhippāyo – dvisahassadīpaparivārānaṃ catunnaṃ mahādīpānaṃ sirivibhavaṃ gahetvā dātuṃ samatthassa cakkaratanassa pātubhāvo hoti, tathā purebhattameva sāgarapariyantaṃ pathaviṃ anupariyāyanasamatthassa vehāsaṅgamassa hatthiratanassa, tādisasseva assaratanassa, caturaṅgasamannāgatepi andhakāre yojanappamāṇaṃ andhakāraṃ vidhamitvā ālokadassanasamatthassa maṇiratanassa, chabbidhaṃ dosaṃ vivajjetvā manāpacārino itthiratanassa, yojanappamāṇe padese antopathavigatānaṃ nidhīnaṃ dassanasamatthassa gahapatiratanassa, aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbattitvā sakalarajjānusāsanasamatthassa jeṭṭhaputtasaṅkhātassa pariṇāyakaratanassa ca pātubhāvo hotīti[V 3.0191]. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthārato pana tesaṃ cakkaratanādīnaṃ pātubhāvavidhānaṃ mahāsudassanādīsu suttesu āgatameva. Atthopissa tesaṃ vaṇṇanāya saṃvaṇṇitoyeva.
