Now, to show those treasures by way of their intrinsic nature, the passage beginning, 'Of which seven? The wheel-treasure...' was spoken. Therein, regarding 'the wheel-treasure' and so on, this is the meaning in brief: The manifestation of the wheel-treasure occurs, which is capable of taking the glorious power of the four great continents with their two thousand surrounding islands and bestowing it. Likewise, the manifestation of the elephant-treasure, which travels through the sky and is capable of journeying around the earth to the ocean's edge before the morning meal; of the horse-treasure, which is of the same kind; of the jewel-treasure, which is capable of dispelling darkness over a distance of one yojana and revealing light even in a darkness endowed with four factors; of the woman-treasure, who has pleasing conduct and is devoid of the six faults; of the householder-treasure, who is capable of seeing treasures hidden within the earth in an area of one yojana; and of the counselor-treasure, known as the eldest son, who, having been born in the womb of the chief queen, is capable of governing the entire kingdom. This is the summary here. But the detailed account of the manifestation of these treasures, beginning with the wheel-treasure, is found in the suttas such as the Mahāsudassana Sutta. And its meaning is fully explained in the commentary on them.

Satisambojjhaṅgaratanassātiādīsu [M 3.0192] sarikkhakatā evaṃ veditabbā – yatheva hi cakkavattino cakkaratanaṃ sabbaratanānaṃ purecaraṃ, evaṃ satisambojjhaṅgaratanaṃ sabbesaṃ catubhūmakadhammānaṃ purecaranti, purecaraṇaṭṭhena cakkavattirañño cakkaratanasadisaṃ hoti. Cakkavattino ca ratanesu mahākāyūpapannaṃ accuggataṃ vipulaṃ mahantaṃ hatthiratanaṃ, idampi dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgaratanaṃ mahantaṃ dhammakāyūpapannaṃ accuggataṃ vipulaṃ mahantanti hatthiratanasadisaṃ hoti. Cakkavattino assaratanaṃ sīghaṃ lahu javaṃ, idampi vīriyasambojjhaṅgaratanaṃ sīghaṃ lahu javanti imāya sīghalahujavatāya assaratanasadisaṃ hoti. Cakkavattino maṇiratanaṃ andhakāraṃ vidhamati, ālokaṃ dasseti, idampi pītisambojjhaṅgaratanaṃ tāya ekantakusalattā kilesandhakāraṃ vidhamati, sahajātapaccayādivasena ñāṇālokaṃ dassetīti iminā andhakāravidhamanaālokadassanabhāvena maṇiratanasadisaṃ hoti.

In the phrases beginning with 'the gem of the enlightenment factor of mindfulness,' the similarity should be understood thus: Indeed, just as the wheel-gem of a wheel-turning monarch precedes all other gems, so too the gem of the enlightenment factor of mindfulness precedes all phenomena of the four planes. Due to its nature of preceding, it is similar to the wheel-gem of a wheel-turning monarch. Among the gems of a wheel-turning monarch, the elephant-gem is endowed with a great body, is lofty, vast, and great. This gem of the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena is also endowed with a great body of Dhamma, is lofty, vast, and great; thus, it is similar to the elephant-gem. The horse-gem of a wheel-turning monarch is swift, light, and quick. This gem of the enlightenment factor of energy is also swift, light, and quick; due to this swiftness, lightness, and quickness, it is similar to the horse-gem. The jewel-gem of a wheel-turning monarch dispels darkness and shows light. This gem of the enlightenment factor of joy, due to its being exclusively wholesome, also dispels the darkness of defilements and, by way of co-nascent conditions and so forth, shows the light of knowledge. Thus, by this nature of dispelling darkness and showing light, it is similar to the jewel-gem.

Cakkavattino itthiratanaṃ kāyacittadarathaṃ [P 3.0155] paṭipassambheti, pariḷāhaṃ vūpasameti. Idampi passaddhisambojjhaṅgaratanaṃ kāyacittadarathaṃ paṭipassambheti, pariḷāhaṃ vūpasametīti itthiratanasadisaṃ hoti. Cakkavattino gahapatiratanaṃ icchiticchitakkhaṇe dhanadānena vikkhepaṃ pacchinditvā cittaṃ ekaggaṃ karoti, idampi samādhisambojjhaṅgaratanaṃ yathicchitādivasena appanaṃ sampādeti, vikkhepaṃ pacchinditvā cittaṃ ekaggaṃ karotīti gahapatiratanasadisaṃ hoti. Cakkavattino ca pariṇāyakaratanaṃ sabbatthakiccasampādanena appossukkataṃ karoti. Idampi upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaratanaṃ cittuppādaṃ līnuddhaccato mocetvā payogamajjhatte ṭhapayamānaṃ appossukkataṃ karotīti pariṇāyakaratanasadisaṃ hoti. Iti imasmiṃ sutte catubhūmako sabbasaṅgāhikadhammaparicchedo kathitoti veditabbo.

The queen-gem of a wheel-turning monarch allays the distress of body and mind and appeases the burning fever. This gem of the enlightenment factor of tranquility also allays the distress of body and mind and appeases the burning fever; thus, it is similar to the queen-gem. The householder-gem of a wheel-turning monarch, at every desired moment, by presenting wealth, cuts off distraction and makes the mind one-pointed. This gem of the enlightenment factor of concentration also, by way of what is desired, accomplishes absorption, cuts off distraction, and makes the mind one-pointed; thus, it is similar to the householder-gem. And the counselor-gem of a wheel-turning monarch, by accomplishing duties in all matters, brings about a state of being free from concern. This gem of the enlightenment factor of equanimity, by freeing the mind-arising from sloth and restlessness and establishing it in balanced effort, also brings about a state of being free from concern; thus, it is similar to the counselor-gem. Thus, it should be understood that in this sutta, the all-encompassing section of Dhamma pertaining to the four planes is taught.

4-10. Duppaññasuttādivaṇṇanā

4-10. Commentary on the Discourses beginning with the Unwise Person, and so forth.

225-231. Catutthe eḷamūgoti mukhena vācaṃ nicchāretuṃ sakkontopi dosehi mūgo asampannavacano. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

In the fourth sutta, 'eḷamūga' means that although one is able to utter speech with the mouth, due to faults one is like a mute, with imperfect speech. The remainder everywhere has a clear meaning.

Cakkavattivaggo.

The Chapter on the Wheel-Turning Monarch.

6. Sākacchavaggo

6. The Chapter on Discourse

1. Āhārasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Discourse on Nutriment

232. Chaṭṭhavaggassa [V 3.0192][M 3.0193] paṭhame ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā satisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāyātiādīsu ayaṃ purimanayato viseso. Na kevalañhi satisambojjhaṅgādīnaṃ ete vuttappakārāva uppādāya, uppannānaṃ vā bhāvanāya pāripūriyā paccayā honti, aññepi pana evaṃ veditabbā. Aparepi hi cattāro dhammā satisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti satisampajaññaṃ muṭṭhassatipuggalaparivajjanatā upaṭṭhitassatipuggalasevanatā tadadhimuttatāti. Abhikkantādīsu hi sattasu ṭhānesu satisampajaññena, bhattanikkhittakākasadise muṭṭhassatipuggale parivajjanena, tissadattattheraabhayattherādisadise upaṭṭhitassatipuggale sevanena, ṭhānanisajjādīsu satisamuṭṭhāpanatthaṃ ninnapoṇapabbhāracittatāya [P 3.0156] ca satisambojjhaṅgo uppajjati. Evaṃ catūhi kāraṇehi uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūrī hoti.

1. In the first discourse of the sixth chapter, regarding 'this is a nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of mindfulness,' and so forth, this is a distinction from the previous method. For not only do these aforementioned kinds serve as conditions for the arising of the enlightenment factor of mindfulness and so forth, or for the development and fulfillment of those already arisen, but others too should be understood in this way. Furthermore, four other phenomena conduce to the arising of the enlightenment factor of mindfulness: mindfulness and clear comprehension; avoiding a person of lapsed mindfulness; associating with a person of established mindfulness; and inclination towards that. Indeed, the enlightenment factor of mindfulness arises in the seven instances of going forward and so forth, through mindfulness and clear comprehension; by avoiding a person of lapsed mindfulness, who is like a crow that has laid aside its food; by associating with a person of established mindfulness, like the Elders Tissadatta and Abhaya; and by having a mind inclined, sloping, and gravitating towards arousing mindfulness in standing, sitting, and so forth. For this factor which has thus arisen through four causes, the fulfillment of its development occurs through the path of arahantship.

Satta dhammā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti – paripucchakatā vatthuvisadakiriyā indriyasamattapaṭipādanā duppaññapuggalaparivajjanā paññavantapuggalasevanā gambhīrañāṇacariyapaccavekkhaṇā tadadhimuttatāti. Tattha paripucchakatāti khandhadhātuāyatanaindriyabalabojjhaṅgamaggaṅgajhānaṅgasamathavipassanānaṃ atthasannissitaparipucchābahulatā.

232. Seven phenomena conduce to the arising of the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena: being one who questions, clarifying the basis, balancing the faculties, avoiding unwise persons, associating with wise persons, reflecting on the sphere of profound knowledge, and inclination towards that. Herein, 'being one who questions' means being one who frequently asks questions related to the meaning of the aggregates, elements, sense bases, faculties, powers, enlightenment factors, path factors, jhāna factors, serenity, and insight.

Vatthuvisadakiriyāti ajjhattikabāhirānaṃ vatthūnaṃ visadabhāvakaraṇaṃ. Yadā hissa kesanakhalomāni dīghāni honti, sarīraṃ vā ussannadosañceva sedamalamakkhitañca, tadā ajjhattikavatthu avisadaṃ hoti aparisuddhaṃ. Yadā pana cīvaraṃ jiṇṇaṃ kiliṭṭhaṃ duggandhaṃ hoti, senāsanaṃ vā uklāpaṃ, tadā bāhiravatthu avisadaṃ hoti aparisuddhaṃ. Tasmā kesādichedanena uddhaṃvirecanaadhovirecanādīhi sarīrasallahukabhāvakaraṇena ucchādananahāpanena ca ajjhattikavatthu visadaṃ kātabbaṃ. Sūcikammadhovanarajanaparibhaṇḍakaraṇādīhi bāhiravatthu visadaṃ kātabbaṃ. Etasmiñhi ajjhattikabāhire vatthumhi avisade uppannesu cittacetasikesu ñāṇampi avisadaṃ aparisuddhaṃ hoti aparisuddhāni dīpakapallakavaṭṭitelāni nissāya uppannadīpasikhāya obhāso [V 3.0193][M 3.0194] viya. Visade pana ajjhattikabāhire vatthumhi uppannesu cittacetasikesu ñāṇampi visadaṃ hoti parisuddhāni dīpakapallakavaṭṭitelāni nissāya uppannadīpasikhāya obhāso viya. Tena vuttaṃ – “vatthuvisadakiriyā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattatī”ti.

Clarifying the basis means making the internal and external bases clear. For when one's hair, nails, and body hair are long, or when the body is afflicted with excessive humors and smeared with sweat and grime, then the internal basis becomes unclear and impure. Likewise, when the robe is worn out, soiled, and foul-smelling, or the dwelling is squalid, then the external basis becomes unclear and impure. Therefore, the internal basis should be made clear by cutting the hair and so forth, by upward and downward purging and so forth, by making the body light, and by rubbing with powder and bathing. The external basis should be made clear by sewing, washing, dyeing, mending, and so forth. For when these internal and external bases are unclear, the mind, mental factors, and knowledge that arise are also unclear and impure, like the light of a lamp flame that arises dependent on an impure lamp bowl, wick, and oil. But when the internal and external bases are clear, the mind, mental factors, and knowledge that arise are also clear and pure, like the light of a lamp flame that arises dependent on a pure lamp bowl, wick, and oil. Hence it is said: 'Clarifying the basis conduces to the arising of the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena.'

Indriyasamattapaṭipādanā nāma saddhādīnaṃ indriyānaṃ samabhāvakaraṇaṃ. Sace hissa saddhindriyaṃ balavaṃ hoti, itarāni mandāni, tato vīriyindriyaṃ paggahakiccaṃ, satindriyaṃ upaṭṭhānakiccaṃ, samādhindriyaṃ avikkhepakiccaṃ, paññindriyaṃ dassanakiccaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti[P 3.0157]. Tasmā taṃ dhammasabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena vā, yathā vā manasikaroto balavaṃ jātaṃ, tathā amanasikaraṇena hāpetabbaṃ. Vakkalittheravatthu cettha nidassanaṃ. Sace pana vīriyindriyaṃ balavaṃ hoti, atha neva saddhindriyaṃ adhimokkhakiccaṃ kātuṃ sakkoti, na itarāni itarakiccabhedaṃ. Tasmā taṃ passaddhādibhāvanāya hāpetabbaṃ. Tatthāpi soṇattherassa vatthu dassetabbaṃ. Evaṃ sesesupi ekassa balavabhāve sati itaresaṃ attano kiccesu asamatthatā veditabbā.

Balancing the faculties means making the faculties of faith and the others equal in function. If, for a yogi, the faculty of faith is strong while the others are weak, then the faculty of energy cannot perform its function of exertion, the faculty of mindfulness its function of establishing, the faculty of concentration its function of non-distraction, nor the faculty of wisdom its function of seeing. Therefore, that faith faculty should be diminished by reflecting on the nature of phenomena, or by not attending in the way that it became strong. The story of Elder Vakkali is an example here. If, however, the faculty of energy is strong, then the faculty of faith cannot perform its function of conviction, nor can the others perform their respective functions. Therefore, that energy faculty should be diminished by developing tranquility and so forth. There too, the story of Elder Soṇa should be shown. Thus, in the remaining cases too, when one is strong, the inability of the others to perform their own functions should be understood.

Visesato panettha saddhāpaññānaṃ samādhivīriyānañca samataṃ pasaṃsanti. Balavasaddho hi mandapañño mudhappasanno hoti, avatthusmiṃ pasīdati. Balavapañño pana mandasaddho kerāṭikapakkhaṃ bhajati, bhesajjasamuṭṭhito viya rogo atekiccho hoti. Cittuppādamatteneva kusalaṃ hotīti atidhāvitvā dānādīni akaronto niraye uppajjati. Ubhinnaṃ samatāya vatthusmiṃyeva pasīdati. Balavasamādhiṃ pana mandavīriyaṃ samādhissa kosajjapakkhattā kosajjaṃ abhibhavati. Balavavīriyaṃ mandasamādhiṃ vīriyassa uddhaccapakkhattā uddhaccaṃ abhibhavati. Samādhi pana vīriyena saṃyojito kosajje patituṃ na labhati, vīriyaṃ samādhinā saṃyojitaṃ uddhacce patituṃ na labhati. Tasmā tadubhayaṃ samaṃ kātabbaṃ. Ubhayasamatāya hi appanā hoti.

Here, in particular, the teachers praise the balance between faith and wisdom, and between concentration and energy. For one strong in faith but weak in wisdom is blindly devout and places faith in what is not a proper object. One strong in wisdom but weak in faith, however, tends towards cunning, becoming incurable like a disease caused by medicine. Thinking, 'Merit arises merely from the arising of a thought,' one overshoots the mark and, by not performing acts of giving and so forth, is reborn in hell. But through the balance of both, one has faith only in a proper object. Furthermore, one strong in concentration but weak in energy is overcome by sloth, because concentration is allied with sloth. One strong in energy but weak in concentration is overcome by agitation, because energy is allied with agitation. But concentration, when yoked with energy, cannot fall into sloth; and energy, when yoked with concentration, cannot fall into agitation. Therefore, those two pairs should be made equal. For through the balance of both, absorption occurs.

Api ca samādhikammikassa balavatīpi saddhā vaṭṭati. Evaṃ saddahanto okappento appanaṃ pāpuṇissati. Samādhipaññāsu pana samādhikammikassa ekaggatā balavatī vaṭṭati. Evañhi so appanaṃ pāpuṇāti. Vipassanākammikassa paññā balavatī vaṭṭati. Evañhi so lakkhaṇapaṭivedhaṃ pāpuṇāti. Ubhinnaṃ [M 3.0195] pana samatāyapi appanā hotiyeva. Sati pana sabbattha balavatī vaṭṭati. Sati hi cittaṃ uddhaccapakkhikānaṃ saddhāvīriyapaññānaṃ vasena uddhaccapātato[V 3.0194], kosajjapakkhikena ca samādhinā kosajjapātato rakkhati. Tasmā sā loṇadhūpanaṃ viya sabbabyañjanesu, sabbakammikaamacco viya ca sabbarājakiccesu sabbattha icchitabbā. Tenāha “sati ca pana sabbatthikā vuttā bhagavatā. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Cittañhi satipaṭisaraṇaṃ, ārakkhapaccupaṭṭhānā ca sati, na vinā satiyā cittassa paggahaniggaho hotī”ti.

Moreover, for one engaged in developing serenity, even strong faith is suitable. Thus, by believing and committing, one will reach absorption. Among concentration and wisdom, however, for one engaged in developing serenity, strong one-pointedness is suitable. For in this way, one reaches absorption. For one engaged in developing insight, strong wisdom is suitable. For in this way, one reaches the penetration of the characteristics. However, through the equality of both, absorption certainly occurs. But mindfulness, being strong, is suitable in all circumstances. For mindfulness protects the mind from falling into agitation by means of faith, energy, and wisdom, which are on the side of agitation, and from falling into sloth by means of concentration, which is on the side of sloth. Therefore, it should be desired everywhere, like roasted salt in all curries, and like an all-accomplishing minister in all royal affairs. For that reason, it was said: 'Mindfulness, however, has been declared by the Blessed One to be necessary in all circumstances. For what reason? Because the mind has mindfulness for its resort, and mindfulness has protection as its manifestation; without mindfulness, there is no uplifting and restraining of the mind.'

Duppaññapuggalaparivajjanā [P 3.0158] nāma khandhādibhede anogāḷhapaññānaṃ dummedhapuggalānaṃ ārakā parivajjanaṃ. Paññavantapuggalasevanā nāma samapaññāsalakkhaṇapariggāhikāya udayabbayapaññāya samannāgatapuggalasevanā. Gambhīrañāṇacariyapaccavekkhaṇā nāma gambhīresu khandhādīsu pavattāya gambhīrapaññāya pabhedapaccavekkhaṇā. Tadadhimuttatā nāma ṭhānanisajjādīsu dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgasamuṭṭhāpanatthaṃ ninnapoṇapabbhāracittatā. Evaṃ uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūrī hoti.

'Avoidance of unwise persons' means the distant avoidance of dull-witted persons whose wisdom has not penetrated into the aggregates and so forth. 'Association with wise persons' means associating with a person endowed with the wisdom of arising and passing away, which comprehends the fifty equal characteristics. 'Reflection on the sphere of profound knowledge' means the examination of distinctions with profound wisdom that occurs in relation to the profound aggregates and so forth. 'Inclination towards that' means the state of having a mind that is inclined, sloping, and leaning towards it for the purpose of arousing the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor in postures such as standing, sitting, and so on. For this factor, thus arisen, the perfection of its development occurs through the path of Arahantship.

Ekādasa dhammā vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti – apāyabhayapaccavekkhaṇatā, ānisaṃsadassāvitā, gamanavīthipaccavekkhaṇatā, piṇḍapātāpacāyanatā, dāyajjamahattapaccavekkhaṇatā, satthumahattapaccavekkhaṇatā, jātimahattapaccavekkhaṇatā, sabrahmacārimahattapaccavekkhaṇatā, kusītapuggalaparivajjanatā, āraddhavīriyapuggalasevanatā, tadadhimuttatāti.

Eleven things conduce to the arising of the energy enlightenment factor: the state of frequently reflecting on the fear of the planes of misery, the state of frequently seeing the benefit of energy, the state of frequently reflecting on the path to be travelled, the state of frequently reflecting on the veneration of alms-food, the state of frequently reflecting on the greatness of the heritage, the state of frequently reflecting on the greatness of the Teacher, the state of frequently reflecting on the greatness of one's birth, the state of frequently reflecting on the greatness of one's companions in the holy life, the state of frequently avoiding lazy persons, the state of frequently associating with persons of aroused energy, and the state of having a mind inclined towards that.

Tattha “nirayesu pañcavidhabandhanakammakāraṇato paṭṭhāya mahādukkhaṃ anubhavanakālepi, tiracchānayoniyaṃ jālakhipanakumīnādīhi gahitakālepi, pājanakaṇṭakādippahāratunnassa pana sakaṭavahanādikālepi, pettivisaye anekānipi vassasahassāni ekaṃ buddhantarampi khuppipāsāhi āturībhūtakālepi, kālakañcikaasuresu saṭṭhihatthaasītihatthappamāṇena aṭṭhicammamatteneva attabhāvena vātātapādidukkhānubhavanakālepi na sakkā vīriyasambojjhaṅgaṃ uppādetuṃ. Ayameva te bhikkhu kālo”ti evaṃ apāyabhayaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi vīriyasambojjhaṅgo uppajjati.

Among these: For one reflecting thus on the fear of the planes of misery—'Even at the time of experiencing great suffering in the hells, beginning from the performance of the five-fold binding; even at the time of being caught by nets, fish-traps, and so on in the animal realm; and even at the time of pulling carts and so on, being struck and prodded with goads, thorns, and the like; even at the time of being afflicted by hunger and thirst in the realm of the petas for many thousands of years, even for one Buddha-interval; even at the time of experiencing suffering from wind, sun, and so on among the Kālakañcika asuras with a body of merely bone and skin measuring sixty or eighty cubits, it is not possible to arouse the energy enlightenment factor. This, O bhikkhu, is your very time'—the energy enlightenment factor arises.

“Na sakkā kusītena navalokuttaradhammaṃ laddhuṃ, āraddhavīriyeneva [P 3.0159] sakkā ayamānisaṃso vīriyassā”ti evaṃ ānisaṃsadassāvinopi uppajjati. “Sabbabuddha-paccekabuddha-mahāsāvakeheva [M 3.0196] gatamaggo [V 3.0195] te gantabbo. So ca na sakkā kusītena gantu”nti evaṃ gamanavīthiṃ paccavekkhantassāpi uppajjati.

For one who sees the benefit, it also arises thus: 'It is not possible for a lazy person to obtain the nine supramundane states; it is possible only for one with aroused energy. This is the benefit of energy.' For one who reflects on the path to be travelled, it also arises thus: 'The path travelled by all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and great disciples must be travelled by you. And that cannot be travelled by a lazy person.'

“Ye taṃ piṇḍapātādīhi upaṭṭhahanti, ime te manussā neva ñātakā, na dāsakammakarā, nāpi ‘taṃ nissāya jīvissāmā’ti te paṇītāni piṇḍapātādīni denti. Atha kho attano kārānaṃ mahapphalataṃ paccāsīsamānā denti. Satthārāpi “ayaṃ ime paccaye paribhuñjitvā kāyadaḷhibahulo sukhaṃ viharissatī”ti na evaṃ sampassatā tuyhaṃ paccayā anuññātā, atha kho “ayaṃ ime paribhuñjamānova samaṇadhammaṃ katvā vaṭṭadukkhato muccissatī’ti te paccayā anuññātā, so dāni tvaṃ kusīto viharanto na taṃ piṇḍaṃ apacāyissasi, āraddhavīriyasseva hi piṇḍapātāpacāyanaṃ nāma hotī”ti evaṃ piṇḍapātāpacāyanaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi uppajjati mahāmittattherassa viya.

For one reflecting on the veneration of alms-food, it also arises thus: 'Those who attend on you with alms-food and other requisites—these people are neither your relatives, nor your slaves or workers; nor do they give you choice alms-food and other requisites thinking, "We will live in dependence on him." Rather, they give, hoping for the great fruitfulness of their own deeds. The Teacher, too, did not permit the requisites for you seeing thus: "Having consumed these requisites, this one will abound in physical strength and dwell happily." Rather, the requisites were permitted for you with the thought: "While consuming these, this one will perform the duties of an ascetic and be freed from the suffering of the round of existence." Now you, dwelling lazily, will not show veneration for that alms-food. For it is only for one with aroused energy that there is what is called veneration for alms-food.' Thus it arises, as it did for the Elder Mahāmitta.

Thero kira kassakaleṇe nāma paṭivasati. Tasseva gocaragāme ekā mahāupāsikā theraṃ puttaṃ katvā paṭijaggati. Sā ekadivasaṃ araññaṃ gacchantī dhītaraṃ āha – “amma, asukasmiṃ ṭhāne purāṇataṇḍulā, asukasmiṃ khīraṃ, asukasmiṃ sappi, asukasmiṃ phāṇitaṃ, tava bhātikassa ayyamittassa āgatakāle bhattaṃ pacitvā khīrasappiphāṇitehi saddhiṃ dehi, tvañca bhuñjeyyāsi, ahaṃ pana hiyyo pakkaṃ pārivāsikabhattaṃ kañjiyena bhuttāmhī”ti. “Divā kiṃ bhuñjissasi, ammā”ti? “Sākapaṇṇaṃ pakkhipitvā kaṇataṇḍulehi ambilayāguṃ pacitvā ṭhapehi, ammā”ti.

The Elder, it is said, was dwelling in what is called the Farmer's Cave. In his alms-resort village, a great female lay supporter, having made the Elder her son, looked after him. One day, as she was going to the forest, she said to her daughter: 'Dear, in such-and-such a place there is old rice, in such-and-such a place milk, in such-and-such a place ghee, and in such-and-such a place molasses. When your brother, the noble Mitta, comes, cook a meal and give it to him together with the milk, ghee, and molasses. You should eat as well. As for me, I have eaten the stale meal cooked yesterday with rice-gruel.' 'What will you eat during the day, mother?' 'Having added a vegetable leaf, cook and set aside sour gruel with broken rice, dear.'

Thero cīvaraṃ pārupitvā pattaṃ nīharantova taṃ saddaṃ sutvā attānaṃ ovadi “mahāupāsikā kira kañjiyena pārivāsikabhattaṃ bhuñjitvā divāpi kaṇapaṇṇambilayāguṃ bhuñjissati, tuyhaṃ atthāya pana purāṇataṇḍulādīni ācikkhati, taṃ nissāya kho panesā neva khettaṃ na vatthuṃ na bhattaṃ na vatthaṃ paccāsīsati, tisso pana sampattiyo patthayamānā deti, tvaṃ etissā tā sampattiyo dātuṃ sakkhissasi[P 3.0160], na sakkhissasīti, ayaṃ kho pana piṇḍapāto tayā sarāgena sadosena samohena na sakkā gaṇhitu”nti pattaṃ thavikāya pakkhipitvā gaṇṭhikaṃ muñcitvā nivattitvā kassakaleṇameva gantvā pattaṃ heṭṭhāmañce, cīvaraṃ cīvaravaṃse ṭhapetvā “arahattaṃ [M 3.0197] apāpuṇitvā na nikkhamissāmī”ti vīriyaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā nisīdi[V 3.0196]. Dīgharattaṃ appamatto hutvā nivutthabhikkhu vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā purebhattameva arahattaṃ patvā vikasamānamiva padumaṃ mahākhīṇāsavo sitaṃ karontova nikkhami. Leṇadvāre rukkhamhi adhivatthā devatā –

The Elder, having put on his robe and just as he was taking out his bowl, heard that sound and admonished himself: 'It seems the great laywoman, having eaten rice left over from the previous night with sour rice-gruel, will eat even during the day a sour gruel of broken rice and greens. Yet for your sake, she speaks of old rice and so on. Indeed, depending on you, she longs for neither field, nor land, nor food, nor cloth; rather, desiring the three attainments, she gives. Will you be able to give her those attainments, or will you not? Indeed, this alms-food cannot be received by you with lust, with hate, with delusion.' Having put the bowl back into its bag and untied his belt, he turned back and went right to the farmer's cave. Having placed the bowl under the bed and the robe on the robe-rack, he sat down, making a firm resolution of energy: 'I will not leave without attaining Arahantship.' That monk, having been diligent for a long time and having dwelt in meditation, developed insight and attained Arahantship just before the mealtime. Like a blossoming lotus, the great one whose cankers were destroyed came out smiling. A deity dwelling in a tree at the cave's entrance said:

“Namo te purisājañña, namo te purisuttama;

Yassa te āsavā khīṇā, dakkhiṇeyyosi mārisā”ti. –

"Homage to you, O thoroughbred of men! Homage to you, O supreme among men! You whose cankers are destroyed, O venerable sir, are worthy of offerings."

Udānaṃ udānetvā “bhante, piṇḍāya paviṭṭhānaṃ tumhādisānaṃ arahantānaṃ bhikkhaṃ datvā mahallakitthiyo dukkhā muccissantī”ti āha. Thero uṭṭhahitvā dvāraṃ vivaritvā kālaṃ olokento “pātoyevā”ti ñatvā pattacīvaraṃ ādāya gāmaṃ pāvisi.

Having uttered a solemn utterance, she said: "Venerable sir, by giving alms to Arahants such as yourself who have entered for alms-food, elderly women will be freed from suffering." The Elder opened the door, and observing the time, knew, "It is still early morning." Taking his bowl and robe, he entered the village.

Dārikāpi bhattaṃ sampādetvā “idāni me bhātā āgamissati, idāni āgamissatī”ti dvāraṃ olokayamānā nisīdi. Sā there gharadvāraṃ sampatte pattaṃ gahetvā sappiphāṇitayojitassa khīrapiṇḍapātassa pūretvā hatthe ṭhapesi. Thero “sukhaṃ hotū”ti anumodanaṃ katvā pakkāmi. Sāpi taṃ olokayamānāva aṭṭhāsi. Therassa hi tadā ativiya parisuddho chavivaṇṇo ahosi, vippasannāni indriyāni, mukhaṃ bandhanā muttatālapakkaṃ viya ativiya virocittha.

The young girl, having prepared the meal, sat looking towards the door, thinking, "Now my brother will come, now he will come." When the Elder arrived at the house door, she took his bowl, filled it with milk-rice mixed with ghee and molasses, and placed it in his hands. The Elder, having given the blessing, "May you be happy," departed. She, too, stood just looking at him. For at that time, the Elder’s skin complexion was exceedingly pure, his faculties were exceptionally serene, and his face shone exceedingly, like a ripe palmyra fruit freed from its stalk.

Mahāupāsikā araññato āgantvā “kiṃ, amma, bhātiko te āgato”ti pucchi. Sā sabbaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Upāsikā “ajja me puttassa pabbajitakiccaṃ matthakaṃ patta”nti ñatvā “abhiramati te, amma, bhātā buddhasāsane, na ukkaṇṭhatī”ti āha.

The great laywoman, having come from the forest, asked, "Well, my dear, has your brother come?" The daughter related the entire event. The laywoman, knowing, "Today the task of my son who has gone forth has reached its culmination," said, "My dear, your brother delights in the Buddha's Dispensation; he is not discontented."

“Mahantaṃ kho panetaṃ satthudāyajjaṃ, yadidaṃ satta ariyadhanāni nāma, taṃ na sakkā kusītena gahetuṃ. Yathā hi vippaṭipannaṃ puttaṃ mātāpitaro ‘ayaṃ amhākaṃ aputto’ti paribāhiraṃ karonti, so tesaṃ accayena dāyajjaṃ na labhati, evaṃ kusītopi idaṃ ariyadhanadāyajjaṃ na labhati[P 3.0161], āraddhavīriyova labhatī”ti dāyajjamahattaṃ paccavekkhatopi uppajjati.

"Furthermore, this inheritance from the Teacher is great—namely, the seven noble treasures. It cannot be obtained by one who is lazy. For just as parents make an outsider of a misbehaving son, saying, 'This is not our son,' and he does not receive the inheritance upon their passing away, so too, one who is lazy does not obtain this inheritance of the noble treasures. Only one with aroused energy obtains it." Thus, when one reflects on the greatness of the inheritance, the enlightenment factor of energy also arises.

“Mahā [M 3.0198] kho pana te satthā, satthuno hi te mātukucchismiṃ paṭisandhiggahaṇakālepi abhinikkhamanepi [V 3.0197] abhisambodhiyampi dhammacakkappavattana-yamakapāṭihāriya-devorohana-āyusaṅkhāravossajjanesupi parinibbānakālepi dasasahassilokadhātu akampittha. Yuttaṃ nu kho te evarūpassa satthu sāsane pabbajitvā kusītena bhavitu”nti evaṃ satthumahattaṃ paccavekkhatopi uppajjati.

"Furthermore, your Teacher is great. For at the time of your Teacher's conception in his mother’s womb, at his great renunciation, at his full enlightenment, at the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the twin miracle, the descent from the deva world, the relinquishing of the life-force, and also at the time of his final Parinibbāna, the ten-thousandfold world system quaked. Is it truly fitting for you, having gone forth in the Dispensation of such a Teacher, to be lazy?" Thus, when one reflects on the greatness of the Teacher, the enlightenment factor of energy also arises.

“Jātiyāpi tvaṃ idāni na lāmakajātiko, asambhinnāya mahāsammatapaveṇiyā āgataukkākarājavaṃse jātosi, suddhodanamahārājassa ca mahāmāyādeviyā ca nattā, rāhulabhaddassa kaniṭṭho, tayā nāma evarūpena jinaputtena hutvā na yuttaṃ kusītena viharitu”nti evaṃ jātimahattaṃ paccavekkhatopi uppajjati.

"Now, by birth, you are not of low birth. You are born in the Okkāka royal lineage, which comes from the unbroken line of Mahāsammata. You are the grandson of King Suddhodana and Queen Mahāmāyā, and the younger brother of the Venerable Rāhula. For one such as you, being a son of the Conqueror, it is not fitting to live lazily." Thus, when one reflects on the greatness of one's birth, the enlightenment factor of energy also arises.

“Sāriputtamoggallānā ceva asīti mahāsāvakā ca vīriyeneva lokuttaradhammaṃ paṭivijjhiṃsu. Tvaṃ pana etesaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ maggaṃ paṭipajjasi, na paṭipajjasī”ti evaṃ sabrahmacārimahattaṃ paccavekkhatopi uppajjati.

"Sāriputta and Moggallāna, and the eighty great disciples, penetrated the supramundane Dhamma through energy alone. As for you, are you following the path of these companions in the holy life, or are you not?" Thus, when one reflects on the greatness of one's companions in the holy life, the enlightenment factor of energy also arises.

Kucchiṃ pūretvā ṭhitaajagarasadise vissaṭṭhakāyikacetasikavīriye kusītapuggale parivajjentassāpi, āraddhavīriye pahitatte puggale sevantassāpi ṭhānanisajjādīsu vīriyuppādanatthaṃ ninnapoṇapabbhāracittassāpi uppajjati. Evaṃ uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūrī hoti.

The enlightenment factor of energy also arises for one who avoids lazy persons—who are like pythons lying with their bellies full, having abandoned physical and mental energy; for one who associates with persons of aroused energy and resolute mind; and for one whose mind is inclined, sloping, and tending towards the arising of energy in postures such as standing and sitting. And for this factor, when it has thus arisen, the perfection of its development occurs through the path of Arahantship.

Ekādasa dhammā pītisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti – buddhānussati dhammo, saṅgho, sīlaṃ, cāgo, devatānussati, upasamānussati, lūkhapuggalaparivajjanatā, siniddhapuggalasevanatā, pasādanīyasuttantapaccavekkhaṇatā, tadadhimuttatāti.

Eleven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of rapture: recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dhamma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of virtue, recollection of generosity, recollection of the devas, recollection of peace, avoiding coarse individuals, associating with refined individuals, reflecting on inspiring discourses, and being inclined towards that [rapture].

Buddhaguṇe anussarantassāpi hi yāva upacārā sakalasarīraṃ pharamāno pītisambojjhaṅgo uppajjati, dhammasaṅghaguṇe anussarantassāpi, dīgharattaṃ akhaṇḍaṃ katvā rakkhitaṃ catupārisuddhisīlaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi, gihino dasasīlapañcasīlāni [P 3.0162] paccavekkhantassāpi, dubbhikkhabhayādīsu paṇītaṃ bhojanaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ datvā “evaṃ nāma adamhā”ti cāgaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi, gihinopi evarūpe kāle sīlavantānaṃ dinnadānaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi, yehi [V 3.0198] guṇehi samannāgatā devattaṃ pattā, tathārūpānaṃ attani atthitaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi, samāpattiyā vikkhambhitā kilesā saṭṭhipi sattatipi vassāni [M 3.0199] na samudācarantīti paccavekkhantassāpi, cetiyadassanabodhidassanatheradassanesu asakkaccakiriyāya saṃsūcitalūkhabhāve buddhādīsu pasādasinehābhāvena gadrabhapiṭṭharajasadise lūkhapuggale parivajjentassāpi, buddhādīsu pasādabahule muducitte siniddhapuggale sevantassāpi, ratanattayaguṇaparidīpake pasādanīye suttante paccavekkhantassāpi, ṭhānanisajjādīsu pītiuppādanatthaṃ ninnapoṇapabbhāracittassāpi uppajjati. Evaṃ uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūrī hoti.

Indeed, for one who recollects the virtues of the Buddha, the enlightenment factor of joy arises, suffusing the entire body up to access concentration. It also arises for one who recollects the virtues of the Dhamma and the Saṅgha; for one who reviews the fourfold purity of moral virtue, kept unbroken for a long time; for a householder who reviews the ten or five precepts; for one who reflects on generosity after giving excellent food to fellow practitioners during times of famine, fear, and so on, thinking, “Such a gift we have given”; for a householder who reflects on a gift given to virtuous ones at such a time; for one who reflects on the presence in oneself of such qualities by which, being endowed with them, beings attain the state of a deva; for one who reflects that defilements suppressed by meditative attainment do not arise even for sixty or seventy years; for one who avoids coarse individuals—like the dust on a donkey's back, whose coarseness is indicated by irreverent actions when seeing a shrine, a Bodhi tree, or an elder, due to a lack of faith and affection toward the Buddha and others; for one who associates with gentle individuals of affectionate and devoted heart toward the Buddha and others; for one who reflects on inspiring discourses that elucidate the qualities of the Three Jewels; and for one whose mind is inclined towards the arousal of joy in standing, sitting, and other postures. For one in whom it has thus arisen, the culmination of its development occurs through the path of Arahantship.

Satta dhammā passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti – paṇītabhojanasevanatā, utusukhasevanatā, iriyāpathasukhasevanatā, majjhattapayogatā, sāraddhakāyapuggalaparivajjanatā, passaddhakāya-puggalasevanatā, tadadhimuttatāti.

Seven things lead to the arising of the tranquility enlightenment factor: consuming excellent food, dwelling in a pleasant climate, adopting comfortable postures, balanced application, avoiding individuals with agitated bodies, associating with individuals with tranquil bodies, and being inclined towards that tranquility.

Paṇītañhi siniddhaṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjantassāpi, sītuṇhesu utūsu ṭhānādīsu ca iriyāpathesu sappāyaṃ utuñca iriyāpathañca sevantassāpi passaddhi uppajjati. Yo pana mahāpurisajātiko sabbautuiriyāpathakkhamova hoti, na taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Yassa sabhāgavisabhāgatā atthi, tasseva visabhāge utuiriyāpathe vajjetvā sabhāge sevantassa uppajjati. Majjhattapayogo vuccati attano ca parassa ca kammassakatapaccavekkhaṇā. Iminā majjhattapayogena uppajjati. Yo leḍḍudaṇḍādīhi paraṃ viheṭhayamānova vicarati, evarūpaṃ sāraddhakāyapuggalaṃ parivajjentassāpi, saṃyatapādapāṇiṃ passaddhakāyaṃ puggalaṃ sevantassāpi, ṭhānanisajjādīsu passaddhiuppādanatthāya ninnapoṇapabbhāracittassāpi uppajjati. Evaṃ uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūrī hoti.

Indeed, tranquility arises for one who eats excellent and smooth food, and for one who cultivates a suitable climate among the hot and cold seasons and a suitable posture among those of standing and so on. However, this is not said with reference to one of the lineage of great beings who is able to endure all climates and postures. For one for whom there is suitability and unsuitability, tranquility arises by avoiding unsuitable climates and postures and cultivating suitable ones. Reflecting on one's own and others' ownership of kamma is called 'balanced application.' Through this balanced application, tranquility arises. It also arises for one who avoids an individual with an agitated body, who wanders about harming others with clods of earth, sticks, and so on; for one who associates with a person of tranquil body with restrained feet and hands; and for one whose mind is inclined, bent, and sloped for the purpose of arousing tranquility in the postures of standing, sitting, and so on. For one in whom it has thus arisen, the culmination of its development occurs through the path of Arahantship.

Dasa dhammā [P 3.0163] samādhisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti – vatthuvisadakiriyatā, indriyasamattapaṭipādanatā, nimittakusalatā, samaye cittassa paggaṇhanatā, samaye cittassa niggaṇhanatā, samaye sampahaṃsanatā, samaye ajjhupekkhanatā, asamāhitapuggalaparivajjanatā, samāhitapuggalasevanatā, tadadhimuttatāti. Tattha vatthuvisadakiriyatā ca indriyasamattapaṭipādanatā ca vuttanayeneva veditabbā.

Eleven things lead to the arising of the concentration enlightenment factor: making the basis clear, maintaining balanced faculties, skillfulness with the sign, uplifting the mind at the proper time, restraining the mind at the proper time, gladdening the mind at the proper time, regarding the mind with equanimity at the proper time, avoiding unconcentrated individuals, associating with concentrated individuals, reflecting on jhāna and the liberations, and being inclined towards that concentration. Among these, making the basis clear and maintaining balanced faculties should be understood as previously explained.

Nimittakusalatā [V 3.0199][M 3.0200] nāma kasiṇanimittassa uggahaṇakusalatā. Samaye cittassa paggaṇhanatāti yasmiṃ samaye atisithilavīriyatādīhi līnaṃ cittaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ samaye dhammavicayavīriyapītisambojjhaṅgasamuṭṭhāpanena tassa paggaṇhanaṃ. Samaye cittassa niggaṇhanatāti yasmiṃ samaye accāraddhavīriyatādīhi uddhataṃ cittaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ samaye passaddhisamādhiupekkhāsambojjhaṅgasamuṭṭhāpanena tassa niggaṇhanaṃ. Samaye sampahaṃsanatāti yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ paññāpayogamandatāya vā upasamasukhānaṃ vigamena vā nirassādaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ samaye aṭṭhasaṃvegavatthupaccavekkhaṇena saṃvejeti. Aṭṭha saṃvegavatthūni nāma jātijarābyādhimaraṇāni cattāri, apāyadukkhaṃ pañcamaṃ, atīte vaṭṭamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ, anāgate vaṭṭamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ, paccuppanne āhārapariyeṭṭhimūlakaṃ dukkhanti. Ratanattayaguṇānussaraṇena ca pasādaṃ janeti, ayaṃ vuccati “samaye sampahaṃsanatā”ti.

Skill in the sign means skill in grasping the kasiṇa-sign. Uplifting the mind at the proper time: When the mind becomes lax due to excessive slackness of energy and the like, at that time, it is uplifted by arousing the enlightenment factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, and joy. Restraining the mind at the proper time: When the mind becomes agitated due to excessively exerted energy and the like, at that time, it is restrained by arousing the enlightenment factors of tranquility, concentration, and equanimity. Gladdening the mind at the proper time: When the mind is without relish due to weakness in the application of wisdom or the absence of the happiness of calm, at that time, one should arouse a sense of spiritual urgency by reflecting on the eight grounds for such. The eight grounds for spiritual urgency are: birth, aging, sickness, and death—these four; the suffering of the states of deprivation as the fifth; suffering rooted in the past round of existence; suffering rooted in the future round of existence; and suffering in the present rooted in the search for food. And by recollecting the qualities of the Three Jewels, one generates faith. This is called 'gladdening the mind at the proper time'.

Samaye ajjhupekkhanatā nāma yasmiṃ samaye sammāpaṭipattiṃ āgamma alīnaṃ anuddhataṃ anirassādaṃ ārammaṇe samappavattaṃ samathavīthipaṭipannaṃ cittaṃ hoti, tadāssa paggahaniggahasampahaṃsanesu na byāpāraṃ āpajjati sārathi [P 3.0164] viya samappavattesu assesu. Ayaṃ vuccati “samaye ajjhupekkhanatā”ti. Asamāhitapuggalaparivajjanatā nāma upacāraṃ vā appanaṃ vā appattānaṃ vikkhittacittānaṃ puggalānaṃ ārakā parivajjanaṃ. Samāhitapuggalasevanatā nāma upacārena vā appanāya vā samāhitacittānaṃ sevanā bhajanā payirupāsanā. Tadadhimuttatā nāma ṭhānanisajjādīsu samādhiuppādanatthameva ninnapoṇapabbhāracittatā. Evañhi paṭipajjato esa uppajjati. Evaṃ uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūrī hoti.

Regarding the mind with equanimity at the proper time means: when the mind, relying on right practice, is neither lax nor agitated, is not without relish, and proceeds evenly on its object, having entered the path of tranquility—then one does not apply effort in lifting up, restraining, or gladdening, just as a charioteer does not with evenly moving horses. This is called 'regarding the mind with equanimity at the proper time.' Avoiding unconcentrated individuals means avoiding from afar those individuals whose minds are scattered, who have not attained either access concentration or absorption. Associating with concentrated individuals means associating with, keeping company with, and attending upon those whose minds are composed through access concentration or absorption. Being inclined toward that means having a mind bent, inclined, and tending solely for the purpose of arousing concentration in postures such as standing and sitting. For one who practices thus, this concentration enlightenment factor arises. For one in whom it has thus arisen, the culmination of its development occurs through the path of Arahantship.

Pañca dhammā upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti – sattamajjhattatā, saṅkhāramajjhattatā, sattasaṅkhārakelāyanapuggalaparivajjanatā, sattasaṅkhāramajjhattapuggalasevanatā, tadadhimuttatāti. Tattha dvīhākārehi sattamajjhattataṃ samuṭṭhāpeti – “tvaṃ attanova kammena āgantvā attanova kammena gamissasi, esopi attano kammena āgantvā attanova kammena gamissati, tvaṃ kaṃ kelāyasī”ti evaṃ kammassakatapaccavekkhaṇena ca – “paramatthato sattoyeva natthi, so tvaṃ kaṃ kelāyasī”ti evaṃ nissattapaccavekkhaṇena ca. Dvīhevākārehi saṅkhāramajjhattataṃ samuṭṭhāpeti – “idaṃ [M 3.0201] cīvaraṃ anupubbena vaṇṇavikāratañceva jiṇṇabhāvañca upagantvā pādapuñchanacoḷakaṃ hutvā yaṭṭhikoṭiyā chaḍḍanīyaṃ bhavissati, sace panassa sāmiko bhaveyya[V 3.0200], nāyaṃ evaṃ vinassituṃ dadeyyā”ti evaṃ assāmikabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena ca, “anaddhaniyaṃ idaṃ tāvakālika”nti evaṃ tāvakālikabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena ca. Yathā ca cīvare, evaṃ pattādīsupi yojanā kātabbā.

Five things conduce to the arising of the equanimity enlightenment factor: impartiality towards beings, impartiality towards formations, avoiding individuals who are attached to beings and formations, associating with individuals who are impartial towards beings and formations, and being inclined towards that. Herein, impartiality towards beings is aroused in two ways: by reflecting on ownership of kamma—‘You have come by your own kamma and will go by your own kamma; this person too has come by their own kamma and will go by their own kamma. Whom do you cherish?’—and by reflecting on the absence of a being—‘Ultimately, there is no being; so whom do you cherish?’ Impartiality towards formations is aroused in two ways: by reflecting on the absence of ownership—‘This robe, through gradual change in color and aging, will eventually become a foot-wiping rag and be discarded with the tip of a stick. If it had an owner, they would not allow it to perish like this’—and by reflecting on its temporary nature—‘This is not long-lasting; it is only temporary.’ The same application should be made to the bowl and other requisites.

Sattasaṅkhārakelāyanapuggalaparivajjanatāti ettha yo puggalo gihi vā attano puttadhītādike, pabbajito vā attano antevāsikasamānupajjhāyakādike mamāyati, sahatthāva nesaṃ kesacchedana-sūcikamma-cīvaradhovana-rajana-pattapacanādīni karoti, muhuttampi apassanto “asuko sāmaṇero kuhiṃ, asuko daharo kuhi”nti bhantamigo viya ito [P 3.0165] cito ca āloketi, aññena kesacchedanādīnaṃ atthāya “muhuttaṃ tāva asukaṃ pesethā”ti yāciyamānopi “amhepi taṃ attano kammaṃ na kārema, tumhe naṃ gahetvā kilamessathā”ti na deti, ayaṃ sattakelāyano nāma. Yo pana cīvarapattathālakakattarayaṭṭhiādīni mamāyati, aññassa hatthena parāmasitumpi na deti, tāvakālikaṃ yācitopi “mayampi imaṃ dhanāyantā na paribhuñjāma, tumhākaṃ kiṃ dassāmā”ti vadati, ayaṃ saṅkhārakelāyano nāma. Yo pana tesu dvīsupi vatthūsu majjhatto udāsino, ayaṃ sattasaṅkhāramajjhatto nāma. Iti ayaṃ upekkhāsambojjhaṅgo evarūpaṃ sattasaṅkhārakelāyanapuggalaṃ ārakā parivajjentassāpi, sattasaṅkhāramajjhattapuggalaṃ sevantassāpi, ṭhānanisajjādīsu taduppādanatthaṃ ninnapoṇapabbhāracittassāpi uppajjati. Evaṃ uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūrī hoti.

Avoiding individuals who are attached to beings and formations: Herein, a person, whether a householder or a renunciant, who cherishes their own children and the like, or their own pupils, those with the same preceptor, and the like; who personally performs tasks such as cutting their hair, needlework, washing and dyeing robes, and baking bowls with their own hands; who, not seeing them even for a moment, looks here and there like an agitated deer, thinking, ‘Where is the novice so-and-so? Where is the young one so-and-so?’; and who, even when asked by another for the purpose of cutting hair and so on, ‘Please send so-and-so for just a moment,’ does not give them, saying, ‘We ourselves would not make them do our own work; you will tire them out by taking them’—this person is called one who is attached to beings. Furthermore, one who cherishes robes, bowls, cups, staffs, and the like; who does not allow another to even touch them with their hand; and who, even when asked for them temporarily, says, ‘We ourselves, treasuring this, do not use it. Why should we give it to you?’—this person is called one who is attached to formations. But one who is neutral and indifferent in both these matters is called one who is impartial towards beings and formations. Thus, this equanimity enlightenment factor arises for one who avoids from afar such a person attached to beings and formations, for one who associates with a person impartial towards beings and formations, and for one whose mind, in postures such as standing and sitting, is bent, inclined, and sloped towards arousing it. For one in whom it has thus arisen, its development is fulfilled by the path of arahantship.

Asubhanimittanti uddhumātakādibhedā dasa asubhārammaṇā dhammā. Yonisomanasikārabahulīkāroti ettha pana yonisomanasikāro nāma upāyamanasikāro, pathamanasikāro, uppādakamanasikāro. Apica cha dhammā kāmacchandassa pahānāya saṃvattanti – asubhanimittassa uggaho, asubhabhāvanānuyogo, indriyesu guttadvāratā, bhojane mattaññutā, kalyāṇamittatā, sappāyakathāti.

The sign of foulness: These are the ten states that are foul objects, distinguished as the bloated corpse and so on. Abundant systematic attention: Herein, systematic attention is called attention to the means, attention to the path, and generative attention. Furthermore, six things conduce to the abandoning of sensual desire: grasping the sign of foulness, devotion to the development of foulness, guarding the sense faculties, moderation in food, good friendship, and suitable talk.

Dasavidhañhi asubhanimittaṃ uggaṇhantassāpi kāmacchando pahīyati, bhāventassāpi, indriyesu guttadvārassāpi, catunnaṃ pañcannaṃ ālopānaṃ okāse [M 3.0202] sati udakaṃ pivitvā yāpanasīlatāya bhojane mattaññunopi. Tenetaṃ vuttaṃ –

Indeed, sensual desire is abandoned for one who grasps the ten kinds of sign of foulness, for one who develops it, for one who has guarded sense faculties, and for one who is moderate in food, who sustains themself by drinking water while still having capacity for four or five mouthfuls. Therefore it was said:

“Cattāro [V 3.0201] pañca ālope, abhutvā udakaṃ pive;

Alaṃ phāsuvihārāya, pahitattassa bhikkhuno”ti. (theragā. 983);

“Leaving four or five mouthfuls uneaten, one should drink water; this is enough for the comfortable abiding of a monk with a mind set on the goal.”

Asubhakammikatissattherasadise asubhabhāvanārate kalyāṇamitte sevantassāpi kāmacchando pahīyati, ṭhānanisajjādīsu dasaasubhanimittāya-sappāyakathāyapi pahīyati. Tena vuttaṃ “cha dhammā kāmacchandassa pahānāya saṃvattantī”ti[P 3.0166]. Imehi pana chahi dhammehi pahīnassa kāmacchandassa arahattamaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti.

Sensual desire is abandoned for one who associates with good friends who delight in the development of foulness, like the Elder Tissa, the practitioner of foulness meditation. It is also abandoned by suitable talk on the ten signs of foulness in postures such as standing and sitting. Therefore it was said, “Six things conduce to the abandoning of sensual desire.” For one whose sensual desire has been abandoned through these six things, its non-arising in the future occurs through the path of arahantship.

Mettā cetovimuttīti ettha mettāti vutte appanāpi upacāropi vaṭṭati, cetovimuttīti appanāyeva. Yonisomanasikāro vuttalakkhaṇova. Apica cha dhammā byāpādassa pahānāya saṃvattanti – mettānimittassa uggaho, mettābhāvanānuyogo, kammassakatāpaccavekkhaṇatā, paṭisaṅkhānabahulatā, kalyāṇamittatā, sappāyakathāti.

Loving-kindness, liberation of mind: Herein, when ‘loving-kindness’ is said, both absorption and access concentration are applicable; when ‘liberation of mind’ is said, only absorption is applicable. Systematic attention has the characteristics already stated. Furthermore, six things conduce to the abandoning of ill will: grasping the sign of loving-kindness, devotion to the development of loving-kindness, reflection on kamma as one's own property, frequent reflection, good friendship, and suitable talk.

Odissakaanodissakadisāpharaṇānañhi aññataravasena mettaṃ uggaṇhantassāpi byāpādo pahīyati, tathā odhisoanodhisodisāpharaṇavasena mettaṃ bhāventassāpi. “Tvaṃ etassa kuddho kiṃ karissasi? Kimassa sīlādīni nāsetuṃ sakkhissasi? Nanu tvaṃ attano kammena āgantvā attano kammeneva gamissasi? Parassa kujjhanaṃ nāma vītaccikaṅgāratattaayasalākagūthādīni gahetvā paraṃ paharitukāmatāsadisaṃ hoti. Esopi tava kuddho kiṃ karissati? Kiṃ te sīlādīni vināsetuṃ sakkhissati? Esa attano kammena āgantvā attano kammeneva gamissati? Appaṭicchitapaheṇakaṃ viya paṭivātaṃ khittarajomuṭṭhi viya ca etassevesa kodho matthake patissatī”ti evaṃ attano ca parassa ca kammassakataṃ paccavekkhatopi, ubhayakammassakataṃ paccavekkhitvā paṭisaṅkhāne ṭhitassāpi, assaguttattherasadise mettābhāvanārate kalyāṇamitte sevantassāpi byāpādo pahīyati, ṭhānanisajjādīsu mettānissitasappāyakathāyapi pahīyati. Tena vuttaṃ “cha dhammā byāpādassa pahānāya saṃvattantī”ti[M 3.0203]. Imehi pana chahi dhammehi pahīnassa byāpādassa anāgāmimaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti.

For one who learns loving-kindness in any way—whether by specified or unspecified pervasion of the directions—ill will is abandoned; and similarly, for one who develops loving-kindness by way of specified, unspecified, and directional pervasion. “If you are angry with this person, what can you do? Can you destroy their virtue and so on? Will you not come by your own kamma and go by your own kamma alone? To be angry at another is like taking up flameless embers, a red-hot iron rod, excrement, and so on, with the desire to strike another. And what will this person, being angry at you, do? Can they destroy your virtue and so on? They have come by their own kamma and will go by their own kamma alone. Like an unaccepted gift, or like a handful of dust thrown against the wind, this anger will fall upon their own head.” Thus, for one who reflects on their own and others’ ownership of kamma; for one who, having reflected on the ownership of kamma of both, is established in contemplation; and for one who associates with virtuous friends like the Elder Assagutta who delight in the development of loving-kindness, ill will is abandoned. It is also abandoned through suitable talk based on loving-kindness while standing, sitting, and so on. Therefore it is said: “Six things lead to the abandoning of ill will.” For ill will that has been abandoned by these six things, its non-arising in the future occurs through the path of the non-returner.

Atthi bhikkhave aratītiādi vuttatthameva. Api ca cha dhammā thinamiddhassa pahānāya saṃvattanti [V 3.0202] – atibhojane nimittaggāho, iriyāpathasamparivattanatā, ālokasaññāmanasikāro, abbhokāsavāso, kalyāṇamittatā, sappāyakathāti.

The phrase 'Atthi, bhikkhave, arati...' and so on, has a meaning that has already been explained. Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of sloth and torpor: grasping the sign in overeating, changing of posture, attention to the perception of light, dwelling in the open, good friendship, and suitable conversation.

Āharahatthakaṃ, bhuttavamitakaṃ, tatravaṭṭakaṃ, alaṃsāṭakaṃ, kākamāsakabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhāne nisinnassa [P 3.0167] hi samaṇadhammaṃ karoto thinamiddhaṃ mahāhatthī viya ottharantaṃ āgacchati, catupañcaālopaokāsaṃ pana ṭhapetvā pānīyaṃ pivitvā yāpanasīlassa bhikkhuno taṃ na hotīti evaṃ atibhojane nimittaṃ gaṇhantassapi thinamiddhaṃ pahīyati. Yasmiṃ iriyāpathe thinamiddhaṃ okkamati, tato aññaṃ parivattentassāpi, rattiṃ candālokadīpālokaukkāloke divā sūriyālokaṃ manasikarontassāpi, abbhokāse vasantassāpi, mahākassapattherasadise pahīnathinamiddhe kalyāṇamitte sevantassāpi thinamiddhaṃ pahīyati, ṭhānanisajjādīsu dhutaṅganissitasappāyakathāyapi pahīyati. Tena vuttaṃ “cha dhammā thinamiddhassa pahānāya saṃvattantī”ti. Imehi pana chahi dhammehi pahīnassa thinamiddhassa arahattamaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti.

For one who, having eaten until they must be pulled up by the hand, until they vomit, until they roll about on the spot like a python, until their robes fall off unawares, or until their mouth is so full a crow could peck from it, then sits in a place of solitude by night or by day to practice the ascetic’s duties, sloth and torpor come upon them, overwhelming them like a great elephant. But for a monk who has the habit of maintaining himself by leaving space for four or five mouthfuls and drinking water, this does not happen. Thus, for one who grasps the sign in overeating, sloth and torpor are abandoned. For one who changes from whatever posture in which sloth and torpor overcome them to another; for one who attends to the light of the moon, a lamp, or a torch at night, and to the light of the sun by day; for one who dwells in the open; and for one who associates with virtuous friends like the Elder Mahākassapa who have abandoned sloth and torpor—sloth and torpor are abandoned. It is also abandoned through suitable talk based on the ascetic practices while standing, sitting, and so on. Therefore, it is said: “Six things lead to the abandoning of sloth and torpor.” For sloth and torpor that have been abandoned by these six things, their non-arising in the future occurs through the path of Arahantship.

Atthi bhikkhave cetaso vūpasamotiādīni vuttatthāneva. Apica cha dhammā uddhaccakukkuccassa pahānāya saṃvattanti – bahussutatā, paripucchakatā, vinaye pakataññutā, vuddhasevitatā, kalyāṇamittatā, sappāyakathāti.

The phrases beginning with 'Atthi, bhikkhave, cetaso vūpasamo...' have a meaning that has already been explained. Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of restlessness and remorse: being very learned, being one who questions, proficiency in the Vinaya, associating with elders, good friendship, and suitable conversation.

Bāhusaccenapi hi ekaṃ vā dve vā tayo vā cattāro vā pañca vā nikāye pāḷivasena ca atthavasena ca uggaṇhantassāpi uddhaccakukkuccaṃ pahīyati, kappiyākappiyaparipucchābahulassāpi, vinayapaññattiyaṃ ciṇṇavasībhāvatāya pakataññunopi, vuddhe mahallakatthere upasaṅkamantassāpi, upālittherasadise vinayadhare kalyāṇamitte sevantassāpi, uddhaccakukkuccaṃ pahīyati, ṭhānanisajjādīsu kappiyākappiyanissitasappāyakathāyapi pahīyati. Tena vuttaṃ “cha dhammā uddhaccakukkuccassa pahānāya saṃvattantī”ti. Imehi [M 3.0204] pana chahi dhammehi pahīne uddhaccakukkucce uddhaccassa arahattamaggena, kukkuccassa anāgāmimaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hotīti.

Through great learning, for one who learns one, two, three, four, or five Nikāyas by way of both the Pāli text and its meaning, restlessness and remorse are abandoned. For one who frequently inquires about what is allowable and what is not; for one who is proficient through mastery of the Vinaya regulations; for one who approaches elder and senior monks; and for one who associates with virtuous friends who are bearers of the Vinaya, like the Elder Upāli, restlessness and remorse are abandoned. It is also abandoned through suitable talk based on what is allowable and not allowable while standing, sitting, and so on. Therefore, it is said: “Six things lead to the abandoning of restlessness and remorse.” When restlessness and remorse have been abandoned by these six things, the non-arising of restlessness in the future occurs through the path of Arahantship, and that of remorse through the path of the non-returner.

Kusalākusalā dhammātiādīnipi vuttatthāneva. Apica cha dhammā vicikicchāya pahānāya saṃvattanti [V 3.0203] – bahussutatā, paripucchakatā, vinaye pakataññutā, adhimokkhabahulatā, kalyāṇamittatā, sappāyakathāti.

The phrases beginning with 'Kusalākusalā dhammā...' also have a meaning that has already been explained. Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of doubt: being very learned, being one who questions, proficiency in the Vinaya, abundance of conviction, good friendship, and suitable conversation.

Bāhusaccenapi hi ekaṃ vā…pe… pañca vā nikāye pāḷivasena ca atthavasena ca uggaṇhantassāpi vicikicchā pahīyati, tīṇi ratanāni ārabbha paripucchābahulassāpi[P 3.0168], vinaye ciṇṇavasībhāvassāpi, tīsu ratanesu okappaniyasaddhāsaṅkhātaadhimokkhabahulassāpi, saddhādhimutte vakkalittherasadise kalyāṇamitte sevantassāpi vicikicchā pahīyati, ṭhānanisajjādīsu tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ guṇanissitasappāyakathāyapi pahīyati. Tena vuttaṃ “cha dhammā vicikicchāya pahānāya saṃvattantī”ti. Imehi pana chahi dhammehi pahīnāya vicikicchāya sotāpattimaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti. Iti bhagavā imasmiṃ sutte desanaṃ tīhi bhavehi nivattetvā arahattena kūṭaṃ gaṇhi. Desanāpariyosāne pañcasatā bhikkhū arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu.

Through great learning, for one who learns one… up to… five Nikāyas by way of both the Pāli text and its meaning, doubt is abandoned. For one who frequently inquires concerning the Three Jewels; for one who has mastery of the Vinaya; for one who has an abundance of conviction, known as unwavering faith in the Three Jewels; and for one who associates with virtuous friends who are resolved in faith, like the Elder Vakkali, doubt is abandoned. It is also abandoned through suitable talk based on the qualities of the Three Jewels while standing, sitting, and so on. Therefore, it is said: “Six things lead to the abandoning of doubt.” For doubt that has been abandoned by these six things, its non-arising in the future occurs through the path of stream-entry. Thus the Blessed One, in this discourse, brought the teaching to its pinnacle with Arahantship, having turned it away from the three planes of existence. At the conclusion of the teaching, five hundred monks attained Arahantship.

2. Pariyāyasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Discourse on the Method.

233. Dutiye sambahulāti vinayapariyāyena tayo janā sambahulāti vuccanti, tato paraṃ saṅgho. Suttantapariyāyena tayo tayo eva, tato uddhaṃ sambahulā. Idha suttantapariyāyena sambahulāti veditabbā. Piṇḍāya pavisiṃsūti piṇḍāya paviṭṭhā. Te pana na tāva paviṭṭhā, “pavisissāmā”ti nikkhantattā pana pavisiṃsūti vuttā. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā “gāmaṃ gamissāmī”ti nikkhantapuriso taṃ gāmaṃ apattopi “kahaṃ itthannāmo”ti vutte “gāmaṃ gato”ti vuccati, evaṃ. Paribbājakānaṃ ārāmoti jetavanassa avidūre aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ ārāmo atthi, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Samaṇo āvusoti āvuso tumhākaṃ satthā samaṇo gotamo.

233. In the second Sutta, regarding 'several' (sambahulā): According to the Vinaya method, three persons are called 'several'; beyond that is the Saṅgha. According to the Suttanta method, three persons are just called 'three'; above that number, they are called 'several'. Here, it should be understood as 'several' according to the Suttanta method. 'They entered for alms' (piṇḍāya pavisiṃsu) means they entered for alms. However, they had not yet entered, but because they had set out with the intention 'we will enter,' it is said 'they entered.' How so? Just as a man who sets out saying, 'I will go to the village,' even if he has not yet reached that village, when asked, 'Where is so-and-so?' it is said, 'He has gone to the village'—so it is here. 'The park of the wanderers' (paribbājakānaṃ ārāma): Not far from Jetavana, there was a park belonging to the wanderers of other sects; this was said referring to that. 'The ascetic, friends' (samaṇo āvuso) means: 'Friends, your teacher is the ascetic Gotama.'

Mayampi kho āvuso sāvakānaṃ evaṃ dhammaṃ desemāti titthiyānaṃ samaye “pañca nīvaraṇā pahātabbā, satta bojjhaṅgā bhāvetabbā”ti etaṃ natthi[M 3.0205]. Te pana ārāmaṃ gantvā parisapariyante ṭhatvā aññaṃ olokento viya aññavihitakā viya hutvā bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ suṇanti. Tato “samaṇo gotamo ‘idaṃ pajahatha idaṃ bhāvethā’ti vadatī”ti sallakkhetvā attano ārāmaṃ gantvā ārāmamajjhe āsanaṃ paññāpetvā upaṭṭhāyakaupaṭṭhāyikāhi parivutā [P 3.0169] sīsaṃ ukkhipitvā kāyaṃ [V 3.0204] unnāmetvā attano sayambhūñāṇena paṭividdhākāraṃ dassentā – “pañca nīvaraṇā nāma pahātabbā, satta bojjhaṅgā nāma bhāvetabbā”ti kathenti.

Regarding the statement, 'Friends, we too teach the Dhamma to our disciples in this way': In the doctrine of the sectarians, this teaching, 'The five hindrances are to be abandoned, the seven factors of enlightenment are to be developed,' does not exist. However, they go to the park, stand at the edge of the assembly, and, acting as if looking at something else or as if occupied with something else, they listen to the Blessed One's teaching of the Dhamma. Then, having noted, 'The ascetic Gotama says, "Abandon this, develop this,"' they return to their own park. In the middle of the park, they prepare a seat and, surrounded by their male and female lay supporters, they raise their heads, lift up their bodies, and, displaying the manner of something penetrated by their own self-realized knowledge, they declare: 'What are called the five hindrances are to be abandoned; what are called the seven factors of enlightenment are to be developed.'

Idha no āvusoti ettha idhāti imasmiṃ paññāpane. Ko visesoti kiṃ adhikaṃ? Ko adhippayāsoti ko adhikappayogo? Kiṃ nānākaraṇanti kiṃ nānattaṃ? Dhammadesanāya vā dhammadesananti yadidaṃ samaṇassa vā gotamassa dhammadesanāya saddhiṃ amhākaṃ dhammadesanaṃ, amhākaṃ vā dhammadesanāya saddhiṃ samaṇassa gotamassa dhammadesanaṃ ārabbha nānākaraṇaṃ vucceyya, taṃ kinnāmāti vadanti. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo.

'In this, friends' (idha no āvuso): Here, 'in this' refers to this declaration. 'What is the distinction?' (ko viseso) means: what is the extra factor? 'What is the special exertion?' (ko adhippayāso) means: what is the extra application? 'What is the differentiation?' (kiṃ nānākaraṇaṃ) means: what is the difference? 'In the teaching of the Dhamma or the teaching of the Dhamma' (dhammadesanāya vā dhammadesanaṃ): This refers to when they say, 'Regarding the teaching of the Dhamma of the ascetic Gotama together with our teaching of the Dhamma, or our teaching of the Dhamma together with the teaching of the Dhamma of the ascetic Gotama, should a differentiation be mentioned, what is that differentiation called?' The same method should be understood for the second phrase as well.

Neva abhinandiṃsūti “evameva”nti na sampaṭicchiṃsu. Nappaṭikkosiṃsūti “nayidaṃ eva”nti na paṭisedhiṃsu. Kiṃ pana te pahontā evaṃ akaṃsu, udāhu appahontāti? Pahontā. Na hi te ettakaṃ kathaṃ kathetuṃ na sakkonti “āvuso tumhākaṃ samaye pañca nīvaraṇā pahātabbā nāma natthi, satta bojjhaṅgā bhāvetabbā nāma natthī”ti. Evaṃ pana tesaṃ ahosi – “atthi no etaṃ kathāpābhataṃ, mayaṃ etaṃ satthu ārocessāma, atha no satthā madhuradhammadesanaṃ desessatī”ti.

'They neither rejoiced' (neva abhinandiṃsu) means they did not accept it, saying, 'It is just so.' 'Nor did they scorn' (nappaṭikkosiṃsu) means they did not reject it, saying, 'This is not so.' Now, did they do so being able, or being unable? They were able. For it is not that they were unable to say this much: 'Friends, in your doctrine, there are no such things as five hindrances to be abandoned, nor are there such things as seven factors of enlightenment to be developed.' Rather, it occurred to them thus: 'We have this presentation of a topic; we will report this to the Teacher, and then the Teacher will give us a sweet teaching on the Dhamma.'

Pariyāyoti kāraṇaṃ. Na ceva sampāyissantīti sampādetvā kathetuṃ na sakkhissanti. Uttariñca vighātanti asampāyanato uttarimpi dukkhaṃ āpajjissanti. Sampādetvā kathetuṃ asakkontānañhi dukkhaṃ uppajjati. Yathā taṃ, bhikkhave, avisayasminti ettha tanti nipātamattaṃ, yathāti kāraṇavacanaṃ, yasmā avisaye pañho pucchitoti attho. Sadevaketi saha devehi sadevake. Samārakādīsupi eseva nayo. Evaṃ tīṇi ṭhānāni loke pakkhipitvā dve pajāyāti, pañcahipi sattalokameva pariyādiyitvā etasmiṃ sadevakādibhede loke [M 3.0206] devaṃ vā manussaṃ vā na samanupassāmīti dīpeti. Ito vā pana sutvāti ito vā pana mama sāsanato sutvā. Ito sutvā hi tathāgato tathāgatasāvakopi ārādheyya, paritoseyya, aññathā ārādhanā nāma natthīti dasseti.

'Method' (pariyāya) means reason. 'They will not succeed' (na ceva sampāyissanti) means they will not be able to speak having accomplished it. 'And further trouble' (uttariñca vighātaṃ) means that from not succeeding, they will fall into even further suffering. For suffering arises for those who are unable to speak having accomplished it. In 'Just as, monks, it is not their domain' (yathā taṃ, bhikkhave, avisayasmiṃ), the word 'taṃ' is a mere particle. 'Yathā' is a word indicating reason; the meaning is: 'because the question was asked in what is not their domain.' 'With its devas' (sadevake) means together with the devas. The same method applies to 'with its Māra,' and so on. Thus, having included the three abodes [of devas, Māra, and Brahmā] in 'the world,' and the two [ascetics and brahmins] in 'progeny,' and having thereby encompassed the entire world of beings with these five terms, he shows: 'In this world with its devas, etc., I do not see...' 'Or having heard from here' (ito vā pana sutvā) means having heard from this, my Dispensation. For having heard from here, a Tathāgata or a disciple of a Tathāgata could satisfy and please; otherwise, there is no such thing as satisfying. This is what he shows.

Idāni attano tesaṃ pañhānaṃ veyyākaraṇena cittārādhanaṃ dassento [P 3.0170] katamo ca bhikkhave pariyāyotiādimāha. Tattha ajjhattaṃ kāmacchandoti attano pañcakkhandhe ārabbha uppannachandarāgo[V 3.0205]. Bahiddhā kāmacchandoti paresaṃ pañcakkhandhe ārabbha uppannachandarāgo. Uddesaṃ gacchatīti gaṇanaṃ gacchati. Ajjhattaṃ byāpādoti attano hatthapādādīsu uppannapaṭigho. Bahiddhā byāpādoti paresaṃ tesu uppannapaṭigho. Ajjhattaṃ dhammesu vicikicchāti attano khandhesu vimati. Bahiddhā dhammesu vicikicchāti bahiddhā aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu mahāvicikicchā. Ajjhattaṃ dhammesu satīti ajjhattike saṅkhāre paṭiggaṇhantassa uppannā sati. Bahiddhā dhammesu satīti bahiddhā saṅkhāre pariggaṇhantassa uppannā sati. Dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgepi eseva nayo.

Now, showing how the mind is pleased by his own explanation of those questions, he said, 'And what, monks, is the method?' and so on. Therein, 'internal sensual desire' (ajjhattaṃ kāmacchanda) is desire and lust that has arisen concerning one's own five aggregates. 'External sensual desire' (bahiddhā kāmacchanda) is desire and lust that has arisen concerning the five aggregates of others. 'It is included in the summary' (uddesaṃ gacchati) means it goes into the enumeration. 'Internal ill will' (ajjhattaṃ byāpāda) is aversion that has arisen regarding one's own hands, feet, and so on. 'External ill will' (bahiddhā byāpāda) is aversion that has arisen regarding those of others. 'Doubt about internal states' (ajjhattaṃ dhammesu vicikicchā) is uncertainty regarding one's own aggregates. 'Doubt about external states' (bahiddhā dhammesu vicikicchā) is great doubt regarding the eight external bases. 'Mindfulness of internal states' (ajjhattaṃ dhammesu sati) is mindfulness that has arisen for one comprehending internal formations. 'Mindfulness of external states' (bahiddhā dhammesu sati) is mindfulness that has arisen for one comprehending external formations. The same method should be understood for the enlightenment factor of investigation-of-states as well.

Kāyikanti caṅkamaṃ adhiṭṭhahantassa uppannavīriyaṃ. Cetasikanti – “na tāvāhaṃ imaṃ pallaṅkaṃ bhindissāmi, yāva me anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimuccissatī”ti evaṃ kāyapayogaṃ vinā uppannavīriyaṃ. Kāyappassaddhīti tiṇṇaṃ khandhānaṃ darathapassaddhi. Cittappassaddhīti viññāṇakkhandhassa darathapassaddhi. Upekkhāsambojjhaṅge satisambojjhaṅgasadisova vinicchayo.

'Bodily' (kāyikaṃ) refers to the energy that arises in one undertaking walking meditation. 'Mental' (cetasikaṃ) refers to the energy that arises without bodily exertion, with the thought: 'I will not break this cross-legged posture until my mind is liberated from the taints without clinging.' 'Tranquility of body' (kāyappassaddhi) is the calming of the distress of the three mental aggregates. 'Tranquility of mind' (cittappassaddhi) is the calming of the distress of the consciousness aggregate. Regarding the enlightenment factor of equanimity, the determination is just like that for the enlightenment factor of mindfulness.

Imasmiṃ sutte missakasambojjhaṅgā kathitā. Etesu hi ajjhattadhammesu sati, pavicayo, upekkhāti ime attano khandhārammaṇattā lokiyāva honti, tathā maggaṃ apattaṃ kāyikavīriyaṃ. Avitakkaavicārā pana pītisamādhī kiñcāpi rūpāvacarā honti, rūpāvacare pana bojjhaṅgā na labbhantīti lokuttarāva honti. Ye ca therā brahmavihāravipassanāpādakajjhānādīsu bojjhaṅge uddharanti, tesaṃ matena rūpāvacarāpi arūpāvacarāpi honti. Bojjhaṅgesu hi arūpāvacare pītiyeva ekantena na labbhati, sesā cha missakāva hontīti. Desanāpariyosāne keci bhikkhū sotāpannā jātā, keci sakadāgāmī, keci anāgāmī, keci arahantoti.

In this Sutta, mixed factors of awakening are discussed. For among these, mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, and equanimity, regarding internal phenomena, are only mundane because they take one's own aggregates as their object; similarly, bodily energy that has not reached the path. Rapture and concentration, which are without thought and investigation, although they are form-sphere states, are only supramundane, since factors of awakening are not obtained in the form sphere. Those elders who extract factors of awakening from the divine abidings, insight, the jhānas that are their basis, and so on, hold that they are also form-sphere and formless-sphere states. For among the factors of awakening, in the formless sphere, rapture alone is entirely unobtainable, while the remaining six are only mixed. At the end of the discourse, some bhikkhus became stream-enterers, some once-returners, some non-returners, and some arahants.

3. Aggisuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Fire Sutta

234. Tatiye [M 3.0207][P 3.0171] satiñca khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, sabbatthikaṃ vadāmīti loṇadhūpanaṃ viya sabbakammikāmaccaṃ viya ca sabbattha icchitabbaṃ vadāmīti attho. Yathā hi loṇadhūpanaṃ sabbabyañjanesupi nivisati, yathā ca sabbakammiko amacco yodhakammampi karoti mantakammampi paṭihārakammampīti sabbakiccāni sādheti, evaṃ uddhatassa cittassa niggaṇhanaṃ, līnassa paggaṇhananti sabbametaṃ satiyā ijjhati, na sakkā vinā satiyā etaṃ sampādetuṃ, tasmā evamāha. Imasmiṃ sutte pubbabhāgavipassanā bojjhaṅgāva kathitā.

234. In the third sutta, the meaning of 'Bhikkhus, I declare mindfulness to be for every situation' is: I declare it is to be desired everywhere, like roasted salt and like a versatile minister. For just as roasted salt pervades all curries, and just as a versatile minister performs the duties of a warrior, the duties of a counselor, and the duties of a doorkeeper, thus accomplishing all tasks, so too the restraining of a scattered mind and the uplifting of a sluggish mind—all this is accomplished by mindfulness. It is not possible to accomplish this without mindfulness. Therefore, he spoke thus. In this sutta, only the factors of awakening of preliminary insight are taught.

4. Mettāsahagatasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Sutta Accompanied by Loving-Kindness

235. Catutthe [V 3.0206] mettāsahagatena cetasātiādi sabbaṃ sabbākārena visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.240-241) vitthāritameva. Mayampi kho, āvuso, sāvakānaṃ evaṃ dhammaṃ desemāti idampi te purimanayeneva satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā vadanti. Titthiyānañhi samaye pañcanīvaraṇappahānaṃ vā mettādibrahmavihārabhāvanā vā natthi. Kiṃ gatikā hotīti kiṃ nipphatti hoti. Kiṃ paramāti kiṃ uttamā. Kiṃ phalāti kiṃ ānisaṃsā. Kiṃ pariyosānāti kiṃ niṭṭhā. Mettāsahagatanti mettāya sahagataṃ saṃsaṭṭhaṃ sampayuttaṃ. Eseva nayo sabbattha. Vivekanissitādīni vuttatthāneva.

235. In the fourth sutta, 'with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness,' etc.—all this is already explained in detail in every way in the Visuddhimagga. 'Indeed, friends, we too teach the Dhamma to disciples in this way'—this too they say, having heard the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, in the same way as before. For in the doctrine of the sectarians, there is no abandoning of the five hindrances or development of the divine abidings such as loving-kindness. 'What is its destination?' means 'What is its completion?' 'What is its highest point?' means 'What is its supreme?' 'What is its fruit?' means 'What is its benefit?' 'What is its conclusion?' means 'What is its end?' 'Accompanied by loving-kindness' means accompanied by, connected with, and associated with loving-kindness. This same method is to be understood everywhere. 'Based on seclusion,' etc., have the meaning already stated.

Appaṭikūlanti duvidhaṃ appaṭikūlaṃ – sattaappaṭikūlañca, saṅkhāraappaṭikūlañca. Tasmiṃ appaṭikūle iṭṭhe vatthusminti attho. Paṭikūlasaññīti aniṭṭhasaññī. Kathaṃ panettha evaṃ viharati? Asubhapharaṇaṃ vā aniccanti manasikāraṃ vā karonto. Vuttañhetaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ “kathaṃ appaṭikūle paṭikūlasaññī viharati. Iṭṭhasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ asubhāya vā pharati, aniccato vā upasaṃharatī”ti. Paṭikūle pana aniṭṭhe vatthusmiṃ mettāpharaṇaṃ vā dhātumanasikāraṃ vā karonto appaṭikūlasaññī viharati nāma. Yathāha “kathaṃ paṭikūle appaṭikūlasaññī viharati. Aniṭṭhasmiṃ [P 3.0172] vatthusmiṃ mettāya vā pharati, dhātuto vā upasaṃharatī”ti (paṭi. ma. 2.17). Ubhayamissakapadesupi eseva nayo. Appaṭikūlappaṭikūlesu hi tadeva asubhapharaṇaṃ vā aniccanti manasikāraṃ [M 3.0208] vā karonto paṭikūlasaññī viharati nāma. Paṭikūlāpaṭikūlesu ca tadeva mettāpharaṇaṃ vā dhātumanasikāraṃ vā karonto appaṭikūlasaññī viharati nāma. “Cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā neva sumano hotī”tiādinā (paṭi. ma. 2.17) nayena vuttaṃ pana chaḷaṅgupekkhaṃ pavattayamāno “appaṭikūle ca paṭikūle ca tadubhayaṃ abhinivajjetvā upekkhako tattha viharati sato sampajāno”ti veditabbo.

‘Non-repulsive’ is twofold: non-repulsive beings and non-repulsive formations. In that non-repulsive, the meaning is: in a desirable object. ‘Perceiving the repulsive’ means perceiving the undesirable. But how does one dwell thus here? By making a pervasion of foulness or by attending to it as impermanent. For this was said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: ‘How does one dwell perceiving the repulsive in the non-repulsive? In a desirable object, one pervades with foulness or attends to it as impermanent.’ On the other hand, in a repulsive, undesirable object, one who makes a pervasion of loving-kindness or attends to the elements is said to dwell perceiving the non-repulsive. As it is said: ‘How does one dwell perceiving the non-repulsive in the repulsive? In an undesirable object, one pervades with loving-kindness or attends to it as elements.’ The same method applies to cases involving a mixture of both. For in the non-repulsive and repulsive, one who makes that same pervasion of foulness or attends to it as impermanent is said to dwell perceiving the repulsive. And in the repulsive and non-repulsive, one who makes that same pervasion of loving-kindness or attends to the elements is said to dwell perceiving the non-repulsive. But one who is developing the six-factored equanimity spoken of in the way of ‘Having seen a form with the eye, one is neither gladdened...’ should be understood thus: ‘Having avoided both the non-repulsive and the repulsive, one dwells there equanimous, mindful, and fully aware.’

Ettāvatā ca imassa bhikkhuno mettāya tikacatukkajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā tadeva pādakaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pattassa saha vipassanāya maggasambojjhaṅgānaṃ ariyiddhiyā ca dassitattā desanā vinivaṭṭetabbā siyā. Idaṃ pana mettājhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā saṅkhāre sammasantopi yo arahattaṃ pāpuṇituṃ na sakkoti, yasmā tassa arahattaparamā mettā na hoti. Yaṃparamā pana hoti, taṃ dassetabbaṃ. Tasmā tassa dassanatthaṃ ayaṃ desanā āraddhā. Parato [V 3.0207] sabbaso vā pana rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamātiādīsupi iminā nayena puna desanārambhapayojanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Thus far, for this bhikkhu who has produced the jhānas of the triad and tetrad through loving-kindness, and having made that the basis, has developed insight and attained arahantship—since the path-factors-of-awakening and noble power, together with insight, have been shown, the discourse should have been concluded. However, for one who, though making this loving-kindness jhāna the basis and contemplating the formations, is unable to attain arahantship, it is because for him loving-kindness does not have arahantship as its highest point. But whatever its highest point is, that should be shown. Therefore, this discourse was begun in order to show that.
