Further on, in passages such as 'with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form,' etc., the reason for beginning the discourse again should be understood in this same way.

Subhaparamanti subhaniṭṭhaṃ, subhakoṭikaṃ, subhanipphattiṃ. Idhapaññassāti idheva paññā assa, nayimaṃ lokaṃ atikkamatīti idhapañño, tassa idhapaññassa, lokiyapaññassāti attho. Uttarivimuttiṃ appaṭivijjhatoti lokuttaradhammaṃ appaṭivijjhantassa. Yo pana paṭivijjhituṃ sakkoti, tassa arahattaparamāva mettā hotīti attho. Karuṇādīsupi eseva nayo.

'Having the beautiful as its highest point' means having the beautiful as its end, as its peak, as its completion. 'Of one with wisdom here' means: his wisdom is only here, it does not transcend this world, thus he is 'one with wisdom here'; the meaning is, of one with worldly wisdom. 'Not penetrating the higher liberation' means not penetrating the supramundane Dhamma. But for one who is able to penetrate, his loving-kindness has only arahantship as its highest point—this is the meaning. In the case of compassion and so on, this same method should be understood.

Kasmā panetāsaṃ mettādīnaṃ subhaparamāditā vuttā bhagavatāti? Sabhāgavasena tassa tassa upanissayattā. Mettāvihārissa [P 3.0173] hi sattā appaṭikūlā honti, athassa appaṭikūlaparicayā appaṭikūlesu parisuddhavaṇṇesu nīlādīsu cittaṃ upasaṃharato appakasireneva tattha cittaṃ pakkhandati. Iti mettā subhavimokkhassa upanissayo hoti, na tato paraṃ, tasmā subhaparamāti vuttā.

Why then did the Blessed One declare that these states—loving-kindness and the like—are 'culminating in the beautiful' and so on? Because, by way of correspondence, they are a proximate cause for each respective state. Indeed, for one who abides in loving-kindness, beings are non-repulsive. Then, for one who is familiar with the non-repulsive, when directing the mind to pure colors that are non-repulsive, such as blue and so on, the mind plunges into them with ease. Thus, loving-kindness is a proximate cause for the beautiful liberation, and not for what is beyond that. Therefore, it is said to be 'culminating in the beautiful.'

Karuṇāvihārissa uṇhābhighātādirūpanimittaṃ sattadukkhaṃ samanupassantassa karuṇāya pavattisambhavato rūpe ādīnavo parividito hoti[M 3.0209], athassa parividitarūpādīnavattā pathavīkasiṇādīsu aññataraṃ ugghāṭetvā rūpanissaraṇe ākāse cittaṃ upasaṃharato appakasireneva tattha cittaṃ pakkhandati. Iti karuṇā ākāsānañcāyatanassa upanissayo hoti, na tato paraṃ, tasmā ākāsānañcāyatanaparamāti vuttā.

For one who abides in compassion, while contemplating the suffering of beings that has form as its cause—such as affliction by heat—the danger in form becomes thoroughly known, due to the possibility of compassion arising. Then, for one for whom the danger in form is thoroughly known, upon setting aside one of the kasiṇas such as the earth kasiṇa and directing the mind to space, the escape from form, the mind plunges into it with ease. Thus, compassion is a proximate cause for the base of infinite space, and not for what is beyond that. Therefore, it is said to be 'culminating in the base of infinite space.'

Muditāvihārissa pana tena tena pāmojjakāraṇena uppannapāmojjasattānaṃ viññāṇaṃ samanupassantassa muditāya pavattisambhavato viññāṇaggahaṇaparicitaṃ hoti, athassa anukkamādhigataṃ ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ atikkamma ākāsanimittagocare viññāṇe cittaṃ upasaṃharato appakasireneva tattha cittaṃ pakkhandati. Iti muditā viññāṇañcāyatanassa upanissayo hoti, na tato paraṃ, tasmā viññāṇañcāyatanaparamāti vuttā.

Furthermore, for one who abides in sympathetic joy, while contemplating the consciousness of beings in whom gladness has arisen due to this and that cause for rejoicing, one becomes familiar with grasping consciousness, due to the possibility of sympathetic joy arising. Then, for such a one, having transcended the base of infinite space that was attained in sequence, when directing the mind to the consciousness that has the sign of space as its object, the mind plunges into it with ease. Thus, sympathetic joy is a proximate cause for the base of infinite consciousness, and not for what is beyond that. Therefore, it is said to be 'culminating in the base of infinite consciousness.'

Upekkhāvihārissa pana “sattā sukhitā vā hontu, dukkhato vā vimuccantu, sampattasukhato vā mā vigacchantū”ti ābhogābhāvato sukhadukkhādiparamatthagāhavimukhasambhavato avijjamānaggahaṇadukkhacittaṃ [V 3.0208] hoti. Athassa paramatthagāhato vimukhabhāvaparicitacittassa paramatthato avijjamānaggahaṇadukkhacittassa ca anukkamādhigataṃ viññāṇāñcāyatanaṃ samatikkammasambhavato avijjamāne paramatthabhūtassa viññāṇassa [P 3.0174] abhāve cittaṃ upasaṃharato appakasireneva tattha cittaṃ pakkhandati. Iti upekkhā ākiñcaññāyatanassa upanissayo hoti, na tato paraṃ, tasmā ākiñcaññāyatanaparamāti vuttā. Desanāpariyosāne pañcasatā bhikkhū arahattaṃ pattāti.

Furthermore, for one who abides in equanimity, because of the absence of advertence such as, 'May beings be happy, or be freed from suffering, or not be separated from the happiness they have attained,' and because it is possible to be turned away from grasping ultimate realities such as pleasure and pain, the mind becomes skilled in grasping what is non-existent. Then, for one whose mind is familiar with being turned away from grasping ultimate reality and whose mind is skilled in grasping what is ultimately non-existent, because it is possible to transcend the base of infinite consciousness attained in sequence, when directing the mind to the absence of the ultimately real consciousness, which is now non-existent, the mind plunges into it with ease. Thus, equanimity is a proximate cause for the base of nothingness, and not for what is beyond that. Therefore, it is said to be 'culminating in the base of nothingness.' At the end of the discourse, five hundred bhikkhus attained arahantship.

5. Saṅgāravasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Saṅgārava Sutta

236. Pañcame pagevāti paṭhamaññeva. Kāmarāgapariyuṭṭhitenāti kāmarāgagahitena. Kāmarāgaparetenāti kāmarāgānugatena. Nissaraṇanti tividhaṃ kāmarāgassa nissaraṇaṃ vikkhambhananissaraṇaṃ tadaṅganissaraṇaṃ samucchedanissaraṇanti[M 3.0210]. Tattha asubhe paṭhamajjhānaṃ vikkhambhananissaraṇaṃ nāma, vipassanā tadaṅganissaraṇaṃ nāma, arahattamaggo samucchedanissaraṇaṃ nāma. Taṃ tividhampi nappajānātīti attho. Attatthampītiādīsu arahattasaṅkhāto attano attho attattho nāma, paccayadāyakānaṃ attho parattho nāma, sveva duvidhopi ubhayattho nāma. Iminā nayena sabbavāresu attho veditabbo.

236. In the fifth sutta, 'from the very first' (pageva) means 'from the very beginning' (paṭhamaññeva). 'Overcome by sensual desire' (kāmarāgapariyuṭṭhitena) means 'seized by sensual desire' (kāmarāgagahitena). 'Overwhelmed by sensual desire' (kāmarāgaparetena) means 'followed along by sensual desire' (kāmarāgānugatena). 'Escape' (nissaraṇaṃ) refers to the threefold escape from sensual desire: escape by suppression (vikkhambhananissaraṇa), escape by substitution of opposites (tadaṅganissaraṇa), and escape by eradication (samucchedanissaraṇa). Herein, the first jhāna based on the impure is called escape by suppression; insight (vipassanā) is called escape by substitution of opposites; and the path of Arahantship (arahattamaggo) is called escape by eradication. The meaning is that one does not know even these three kinds of escape. In the phrase 'for one's own benefit' (attatthampi), etc., one's own benefit (attattho) is called the benefit for oneself which is reckoned as the fruit of Arahantship; the benefit of those who give requisites (paccayadāyakānaṃ attho) is called the benefit of others (parattho); and that very benefit, being of two kinds (sveva duvidhopi), is called the benefit of both (ubhayattho). By this method, the meaning should be understood in all instances.

Ayaṃ pana viseso – byāpādassa nissaraṇantiādīsu hi dveva nissaraṇāni vikkhambhananissaraṇañca samucchedanissaraṇañca. Tattha byāpādassa tāva mettāya paṭhamajjhānaṃ vikkhambhananissaraṇaṃ, anāgāmimaggo samucchedanissaraṇaṃ. Thinamiddhassa ālokasaññā vikkhambhananissaraṇaṃ, arahattamaggo samucchedanissaraṇaṃ. Uddhaccakukkuccassa yo koci samatho vikkhambhananissaraṇaṃ, uddhaccassa panettha arahattamaggo, kukkuccassa anāgāmimaggo samucchedanissaraṇaṃ. Vicikicchāya dhammavavatthānaṃ vikkhambhananissaraṇaṃ, paṭhamamaggo samucchedanissaraṇaṃ.

However, this is the distinction: in the phrases beginning with 'escape from ill-will' (byāpādassa nissaraṇaṃ), etc., there are indeed only two kinds of escape: escape by suppression and escape by eradication. Herein, for ill-will, the first jhāna of loving-kindness (mettāpaṭhamajjhānaṃ) is escape by suppression, and the path of the non-returner (anāgāmimaggo) is escape by eradication. For sloth and torpor, the perception of light (ālokasaññā) is escape by suppression, and the path of Arahantship (arahattamaggo) is escape by eradication. For restlessness and remorse, any kind of serenity (yo koci samatho) is escape by suppression; herein, for restlessness (uddhaccassa), the path of Arahantship is escape by eradication, and for remorse (kukkuccassa), the path of the non-returner is escape by eradication. For doubt, the determination of phenomena (dhammavavatthānaṃ) is escape by suppression, and the path of stream-entry (paṭhamamaggo) is escape by eradication.

Yā panettha seyyathāpi brāhmaṇa udapatto saṃsaṭṭho lākhāya vātiādikā upamā vuttā, tāsu udapattoti udakabharitā pāti. Saṃsaṭṭhoti vaṇṇabhedakaraṇavasena saṃsaṭṭho. Pakkuthitoti kuthito. Usmudakajātoti usumajāto. Sevālapaṇakapariyonaddhoti tilabījakādibhedena [P 3.0175] sevālena vā nīlamaṇḍūkapiṭṭhivaṇṇena vā udakapiṭṭhiṃ chādetvā nibbattapaṇakena pariyonaddho. Vāteritoti vātena [V 3.0209] erito kampito. Āviloti appasanno. Luḷitoti asannisinno. Kalalībhūtoti kaddamībhūto. Andhakāre nikkhittoti koṭṭhantarādibhede anālokaṭṭhāne ṭhapito. Imasmiṃ sutte bhagavā tīhi bhavehi desanaṃ nivattetvā arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi, brāhmaṇo pana saraṇamatte patiṭṭhito.

As for the similes spoken herein, such as 'Just as, brahmin, a bowl of water mixed with lac...' (seyyathāpi brāhmaṇa udapatto saṃsaṭṭho lākhāya vā), etc., among them, 'a bowl of water' (udapatto) means 'a bowl filled with water' (udakabharitā pāti). 'Mixed' (saṃsaṭṭho) means 'mixed by way of causing a change of color' (vaṇṇabhedakaraṇavasena saṃsaṭṭho). 'Boiling' (pakkuthito) means 'boiling' (kuthito). 'Giving off steam' (usmudakajāto) means 'having produced steam' (usumajāto). 'Covered over by moss and water-plants' (sevālapaṇakapariyonaddho) means 'covered over by moss (sevāla) of various kinds, such as that resembling sesame seeds, or by water-plants (paṇaka) that have formed covering the water's surface, having the color of a dark frog's back'. 'Stirred by the wind' (vāterito) means 'stirred and shaken by the wind' (vātena erito kampito). 'Turbid' (āvilo) means 'not clear' (appasanno). 'Agitated' (luḷito) means 'not settled down' (asannisinno). 'Having become muddy' (kalalībhūto) means 'having become like mud' (kaddamībhūto). 'Placed in darkness' (andhakāre nikkhitto) means 'placed in a location without light, such as inside a room or a well' (koṭṭhantarādibhede anālokaṭṭhāne ṭhapito). In this sutta, the Blessed One, after delivering the teaching by means of the three truths, concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of the fruit of Arahantship; the brahmin, however, was established merely in taking refuge.

6. Abhayasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Abhaya Sutta

237. Chaṭṭhe aññāṇāya adassanāyāti aññāṇatthāya adassanatthāya. Taggha bhagavā nīvaraṇāti ekaṃsena bhagavā nīvaraṇā. Kāyakilamathoti [M 3.0211] kāyadaratho. Cittakilamathoti cittadaratho. Sopi me paṭippassaddhoti tassa kira satthu santike sītalaṃ utusappāyaṭṭhānaṃ pavisitvā nisinnassa kāyadaratho paṭipassambhi, tasmiṃ paṭipassaddhe tadanvayeneva cittadarathopi. Apica maggenevassa etaṃ ubhayampi passaddhanti veditabbaṃ.

237. In the sixth sutta, 'for not-knowing, for not-seeing' means 'for the purpose of not-knowing, for the purpose of not-seeing'. 'Indeed, Blessed One, a hindrance' means 'assuredly, Blessed One, a hindrance'. 'Bodily fatigue' means 'bodily vexation'. 'Mental fatigue' means 'mental vexation'. 'That too was calmed in me' means: for him, it is said, having entered and sat down in a cool, seasonably suitable place in the Teacher's presence, the bodily vexation was calmed; when that was calmed, in consequence of that, the mental vexation was also calmed. It should be understood thus. Furthermore, it should be known that for him, both of these were calmed by the path itself.

7. Ānāpānavaggo

7. The Chapter on Mindfulness of Breathing

1. Aṭṭhikamahapphalasuttādivaṇṇanā

1. The Explanation of the Sutta on the Great Fruit of the Perception of Bones, etc.

238. Sattamādīsu aṭṭhikasaññāti aṭṭhikaṃ aṭṭhikanti bhāventassa uppannasaññā. Taṃ panetaṃ bhāvayato yāva nimittaṃ na uppajjati, tāva chavipi cammampi upaṭṭhāti. Nimitte pana uppanne chavicammāni neva upaṭṭhahanti, saṅkhavaṇṇo suddhaaṭṭhikasaṅghāṭova upaṭṭhāti hatthikkhandhagataṃ dhammikatissarājānaṃ olokentassa sāmaṇerassa viya, paṭimagge hasamānaṃ itthiṃ olokentassa cetiyapabbatavāsino tissattherassa viya cāti. Vatthūni visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.15) vitthāritāni. Sati vā upādiseseti gahaṇasese upādānasese vijjamānamhi.

238. In the seventh sutta and so on, the 'perception of bones' is the perception that arises in one who develops the thought, 'Bones, bones.' For one who cultivates this, as long as the sign does not arise, the outer skin and inner skin still appear. But when the sign has arisen, the outer and inner skins do not appear; only a mere heap of pure bones, the color of a conch shell, appears, like for the novice looking at King Dhammika Tissa mounted on an elephant's neck, and like for the elder Tissa, a resident of Cetiyapabbata, looking at a laughing woman on the road ahead. The stories are elaborated in the Visuddhimagga. 'Or with remaining substrate' means: when there is a remaining residue of grasping, a residue of clinging.

2-10. Puḷavakasuttādivaṇṇanā

2-10. The Explanation of the Sutta on the Worm-Infested, etc.

239-247. Puḷavakasaññāti puḷavaṃ puḷavanti bhāventassa uppannasaññā. Vinīlakasaññādīsupi [V 3.0210] eseva nayo. Vinicchayakathā [P 3.0176] panettha saddhiṃ bhāvanānayena visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.102) vuttā. Mettādayo tikacatukkajjhānavasena veditabbā, upekkhā catutthajjhānavaseneva.

The 'perception of a worm-infested corpse' is the perception that arises in one who develops the thought, 'Worm-infested, worm-infested.' This same method should be known for the perception of the livid and so on. The definitive explanation here, along with the method of development, is stated in the Visuddhimagga. Loving-kindness and so on should be known by way of the three-fold and four-fold jhānas; equanimity, by way of the fourth jhāna only.

8. Nirodhavaggo

8. The Chapter on Cessation

1-10. Asubhasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-10. The Explanation of the Sutta on the Foul, etc.

248-257. Asubhasaññāti asubhe paṭhamajjhānasaññā. Maraṇasaññāti “avassaṃ maritabbaṃ, maraṇapaṭibaddhaṃ me jīvita”nti abhiṇhaṃ paccavekkhantassa uppannasaññā[M 3.0212]. Āhāre paṭikūlasaññāti odanakummāsādimhi ajjhoharaṇīye paṭikūlasaññā. Sabbaloke anabhiratisaññāti sakalalokasmiṃ anabhiratiṃ uppādentassa uppannasaññā. Pahānasaññāvirāgasaññāti dve pubbabhāgā. Nirodhasaññā missakā. Evametāni aṭṭhikasaññādīni vīsati kammaṭṭhānāni niddiṭṭhāni. Tesaṃ navasu appanā honti, ekādasa upacārajjhānikā. Sesā panettha vinicchayakathā visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.294) āgatāva. Gaṅgāpeyyālādayo maggasaṃyutte vuttanayeneva veditabbā.

The 'perception of foulness' is the first-jhāna perception in a foul object. The 'perception of death' is the perception that arises in one who frequently reflects, 'I must certainly die; my life is bound to death.' The 'perception of the repulsiveness of food' is the perception of repulsiveness toward swallowable food such as rice, barley-cakes, and so on. The 'perception of non-delight in the whole world' is the perception that arises in one who generates non-delight in the entire world. The perception of abandoning and the perception of dispassion are two preliminary stages. The perception of cessation is mixed. Thus, these twenty meditation subjects, beginning with the perception of bones, have been pointed out. Among them, nine are of absorption; eleven are of access concentration. The remaining definitive explanation here has already come in the Visuddhimagga. The Ganges-repetition series and so on should be understood in the same way as stated in the Magga Saṃyutta.

Bojjhaṅgasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Bojjhaṅga Saṃyutta is concluded.

3. Satipaṭṭhānasaṃyuttaṃ

3. The Connected Discourses on the Foundations of Mindfulness

1. Ambapālivaggo

1. The Ambapāli Chapter

1. Ambapālisuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Ambapāli Sutta

367. Satipaṭṭhānasaṃyuttassa [V 3.0211][P 3.0177][M 3.0213] paṭhame ambapālivaneti ambapāliyā nāma rūpūpajīviniyā ropite ambavane. Taṃ kira tassā uyyānaṃ ahosi. Sā satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pasannacittā tattha vihāraṃ kāretvā tathāgatassa niyyātesi. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Ekāyanvāyanti ekāyano ayaṃ. Tattha ekāyanoti ekamaggo. Maggassa hi –

367. In the first sutta of the Satipaṭṭhāna Saṃyutta, the phrase 'in Ambapāli's grove' refers to the mango grove planted by the courtesan named Ambapāli, who made a living by her beauty. It is said that this was her park. Having heard the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, with a serene mind, she had a monastery built there, which she dedicated to the Tathāgata. This was said in reference to that. The words should be divided as `ekāyano ayaṃ`. Therein, `ekāyano` means a single path. For of the path—

“Maggo pantho patho pajjo, añjasaṃ vaṭumāyanaṃ;

Nāvā uttarasetū ca, kullo ca bhisi saṅkamo”ti. (cūḷani. pārāyanatthutigāthāniddeso 101) –

'Path, road, way, footpath, direct way, track, passage; boat, bridge, raft, float, and footbridge.' (Cūḷaniddesa, Pārāyanatthutigāthāniddeso 101) –

Bahūni nāmāni. Svāyaṃ idha ayananāmena vutto. Tasmā ekāyanvāyaṃ, bhikkhave, maggoti ettha ekamaggo. Ayaṃ, bhikkhave, maggo, na dvedhāpathabhūtoti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Maggoti kenaṭṭhena maggo? Nibbānagamanaṭṭhena, nibbānatthikehi magganīyaṭṭhena ca.

There are many names. Here, it is spoken of by the name `ayana` (path). Therefore, in the phrase 'This, monks, is the one-way path,' the meaning should be understood thus: 'This, monks, is a single path; it is not a forked path.' In what sense is it a path (`magga`)? In the sense that it goes (`gamana`) to Nibbāna, and in the sense that it is to be sought (`magganīya`) by those who desire Nibbāna.

Sattānaṃ visuddhiyāti rāgādīhi malehi abhijjhāvisamalobhādīhi ca upakkilesehi saṃkiliṭṭhacittānaṃ sattānaṃ visuddhatthāya. Sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāyāti sokassa ca paridevassa ca samatikkamāya, pahānāyāti attho. Dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāyāti kāyikadukkhassa ca cetasikadomanassassa cāti imesaṃ dvinnaṃ atthaṅgamāya, nirodhāyāti attho. Ñāyassa adhigamāyāti ñāyo vuccati ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo, tassa adhigamāya pattiyāti vuttaṃ [V 3.0212] hoti. Ayañhi pubbabhāge lokiyo satipaṭṭhānamaggo bhāvito lokuttaramaggassa adhigamāya saṃvattati[P 3.0178]. Tenāha “ñāyassa adhigamāyā”ti. Nibbānassa sacchikiriyāyāti taṇhāvānavirahitattā nibbānanti laddhanāmassa amatassa sacchikiriyāya, attapaccakkhāyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Ayañhi maggo bhāvito anupubbena nibbānasacchikiriyaṃ sādheti. Tenāha “nibbānassa sacchikiriyāyā”ti.

For the purification of beings: for the special purification of beings whose minds are defiled by stains such as lust, and by defilements such as covetousness, unrighteous greed, and so on. For the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation: for the overcoming, that is, for the abandoning of both sorrow and lamentation. This is the meaning. For the disappearance of pain and grief: for the disappearance, that is, for the cessation of these two—bodily pain and mental grief. This is the meaning. For the attainment of the right way: the Noble Eightfold Path is called the 'right way' (`ñāya`). It is said for its attainment, for its reaching. For this mundane path of mindfulness in the preliminary stage, when developed, leads to the attainment of the supramundane path. Therefore, he said, 'for the attainment of the right way.' For the realization of Nibbāna: it is said for the realization, for the personal direct experience, of the Deathless, which has obtained the name Nibbāna because it is devoid of the 'weaving' (`vāna`) of craving (`taṇhā`). For this path, when developed, gradually accomplishes the realization of Nibbāna. Therefore, he said, 'for the realization of Nibbāna.'

Evaṃ [M 3.0214] bhagavatā sattahi padehi ekāyanamaggassa vaṇṇo bhāsito, so kasmāti ce? Bhikkhūnaṃ ussāhajananatthaṃ. Vaṇṇabhāsanañhi sutvā te bhikkhū – “ayaṃ kira maggo hadayasantāpabhūtaṃ sokaṃ, vācāvippalāpabhūtaṃ paridevaṃ, kāyikaasātabhūtaṃ dukkhaṃ, cetasikaasātabhūtaṃ domanassanti cattāro upaddave harati. Visuddhiṃ, ñāyaṃ, nibbānanti tayo visese āvahatī”ti ussāhajātā imaṃ desanaṃ uggahetabbaṃ pariyāpuṇitabbaṃ, dhāretabbaṃ, imañca maggaṃ bhāvetabbaṃ maññissanti. Iti tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ussāhajananatthaṃ vaṇṇaṃ abhāsi kambalavāṇijādayo kambalādīnaṃ vaṇṇaṃ viya.

Thus, the Blessed One spoke the praise of the one-way path with seven phrases. If it is asked why, it was for the purpose of inspiring diligence in the monks. For having heard this praise, those monks—thinking, 'This path, it is said, removes four calamities: sorrow, which is the heart's burning; lamentation, which is verbal raving; pain, which is bodily displeasure; and grief, which is mental displeasure. It brings three special qualities: purity, the right way, and Nibbāna'—will become diligent and think that this teaching should be learned, mastered, and borne in mind, and that this path should be developed. Thus, for the purpose of inspiring diligence in those monks, he spoke this praise, just as merchants of blankets and the like praise their blankets.

Yadidanti nipāto, ye imeti ayamassa attho. Cattāroti gaṇanaparicchedo. Tena “na tato heṭṭhā, na uddha”nti satipaṭṭhānaparicchedaṃ dīpeti. Satipaṭṭhānāti tayo satipaṭṭhānā satigocaropi, tidhā paṭipannesu sāvakesu satthuno paṭighānunayavītivattatāpi, satipi. “Catunnaṃ, bhikkhave, satipaṭṭhānānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca desessāmi taṃ suṇātha. Ko ca, bhikkhave, kāyassa samudayo? Āharasamudayā kāyasamudayo”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 5.408) hi satigocaro satipaṭṭhānanti vutto. Tathā “kāyo upaṭṭhānaṃ, no sati, sati upaṭṭhānañceva sati cā”tiādīsupi (paṭi. ma. 2.35). Tassa attho – patiṭṭhāti asminti paṭṭhānaṃ. Kā patiṭṭhāti? Sati. Satiyā paṭṭhānaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ. Padhānaṃ ṭhānanti vā paṭṭhānaṃ. Satiyā paṭṭhānaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ hatthiṭṭhānaassaṭṭhānādīni viya.

The word `yadidaṃ` is a particle; its meaning is `ye ime` (which are these). The word `cattāro` is a numerical delimiter. By this, it indicates the delimitation of the foundations of mindfulness: 'not fewer than that, not more than that.' As for 'foundations of mindfulness' (`satipaṭṭhāna`), there are three kinds: (1) the object of mindfulness (`satigocara`); (2) the Teacher's transcendence of aversion and fondness towards disciples practicing in three ways; and (3) mindfulness (`sati`) itself. For in texts such as, 'Monks, I will teach you the arising and passing away of the four foundations of mindfulness... What, monks, is the arising of the body? The body arises from the arising of nutriment' (SN 47.42), the object of mindfulness is called `satipaṭṭhāna`. Similarly in texts such as, 'The body is the establishment, not mindfulness; mindfulness is both the establishment and mindfulness' (Paṭisambhidāmagga 2.93). The meaning of that term is: 'it is established (`patiṭṭhāti`) in this'; therefore, it is an 'establishment' (`paṭṭhāna`). What is established? Mindfulness. The establishment of mindfulness is `satipaṭṭhāna`. Alternatively, it is a 'principal' (`padhāna`) 'place' (`ṭhāna`); therefore, it is `paṭṭhāna`. The principal place of mindfulness is `satipaṭṭhāna`, like an elephant's station (`hatthiṭṭhāna`), a horse's station (`assaṭṭhāna`), and so on.

“Tayo satipaṭṭhānā, yadariyo sevati, yadariyo sevamāno satthā gaṇamanusāsitumarahatī”ti (ma. ni. 3.311) ettha tidhā paṭipannesu sāvakesu satthuno paṭighānunayavītivattatā satipaṭṭhānanti vuttā. Tassattho – paṭṭhapetabbato [P 3.0179] paṭṭhānaṃ, pavattayitabbatoti attho. Kena paṭṭhapetabboti? Satiyā. Satiyā paṭṭhānaṃ satipaṭṭhānanti.

'There are three foundations of mindfulness, which the noble one cultivates, and by cultivating which the Teacher, a noble one, is worthy to instruct the group.' (MN 137) Here, the Teacher's transcendence of aversion and fondness towards disciples who practice in three ways is called `satipaṭṭhāna`. Its meaning is: it is an 'establishment' (`paṭṭhāna`) because it is to be established (`paṭṭhapetabba`), that is, it is to be set in motion. By what is it to be established? By mindfulness (`satiyā`). The establishment by mindfulness is `satipaṭṭhāna`.

“Cattāro [V 3.0213] satipaṭṭhānā bhāvitā bahulīkatā satta bojjhaṅge paripūrentī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.147; saṃ. ni. 5.989) pana satiyeva satipaṭṭhānanti vuttā. Tassattho – patiṭṭhātīti paṭṭhānaṃ, upaṭṭhāti okkanditvā pakkhanditvā pavattatīti attho. Satiyeva [M 3.0215] paṭṭhānaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ. Atha vā saraṇaṭṭhena sati, upaṭṭhānaṭṭhena paṭṭhānaṃ, iti sati ca sā paṭṭhānañcātipi satipaṭṭhānaṃ. Idamidha adhippetaṃ.

Furthermore, in passages such as, 'The four foundations of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment' (e.g., SN 47.40), mindfulness (`sati`) itself is called `satipaṭṭhāna`. The meaning of this is: it is an 'establishment' (`paṭṭhāna`) because it is established (`patiṭṭhāti`); that is, it is present (`upaṭṭhāti`), having entered and plunged in, it proceeds. Mindfulness itself is the establishment, `satipaṭṭhāna`. Alternatively, it is `sati` in the sense of remembering, and `paṭṭhāna` in the sense of being present; thus, since it is both `sati` and `paṭṭhāna`, it is also called `satipaṭṭhāna`. This is what is intended here.

Yadi evaṃ kasmā “satipaṭṭhānā”ti bahuvacanaṃ katanti? Satīnaṃ bahuttā. Ārammaṇabhedena hi bahukā satiyo. Atha “maggo”ti kasmā ekavacananti? Magganaṭṭhena ekattā. Catassopi hi etā satiyo magganaṭṭhena ekattaṃ gacchanti. Vutañhetaṃ “maggoti kenaṭṭhena maggo? Nibbānamagganaṭṭhena, nibbānatthikehi magganīyaṭṭhena cā”ti. Catassopi cetā aparabhāge kāyādīsu ārammaṇesu kiccaṃ sādhayamānā nibbānaṃ gacchanti, ādito paṭṭhāya ca nibbānatthikehi maggiyantīti tasmā catassopi eko maggoti vuttā. Evañca sati vacanānusandhinā sānusandhikāva desanā hoti.

If this is so, why is 'satipaṭṭhānā' in the plural? Because of the multiplicity of mindfulnesses. Indeed, there are many mindfulnesses due to the diversity of their objects. Then why is 'maggo' (path) in the singular? Because of its unity in the sense of proceeding to Nibbāna. For these four mindfulnesses attain unity in the sense of proceeding. And this was stated: 'In what sense is it a path? In the sense of proceeding to Nibbāna, and in the sense of being sought by those who desire Nibbāna.' And these four, in the later stage, while accomplishing their function in regard to objects such as the body, proceed to Nibbāna; and from the beginning they are sought by those who desire Nibbāna. Therefore, although they are four, they are called one path. And this being so, the teaching is coherent through the connection of the words.

Katame cattāroti kathetukamyatāpucchā. Kāyeti rūpakāye. Kāyānupassīti kāyaṃ anupassanasīlo, kāyaṃ vā anupassamāno. Ayañhi bhikkhu imaṃ kāyaṃ aniccānupassanādīnaṃ sattannaṃ anupassanānaṃ vasena aniccato anupassati, no niccato, dukkhato anupassati, no sukhato, anattato anupassati, no attato, nibbindati, no nandati, virajjati, no rajjati, nirodheti, no samudeti, paṭinissajjati, no ādiyati. So taṃ aniccato anupassanto niccasaññaṃ pajahati, dukkhato anupassanto sukhasaññaṃ pajahati[P 3.0180], anattato anupassanto attasaññaṃ pajahati, nibbindanto nandiṃ pajahati, virajjanto rāgaṃ pajahati, nirodhento samudayaṃ pajahati, paṭinissajjanto ādānaṃ pajahatīti veditabbo.

'What are the four?' This is a question asked from a desire to explain. 'In the body' means in the physical body. 'One who contemplates the body' means one who is of the nature of contemplating the body, or one who is contemplating the body. For this bhikkhu, by way of the seven contemplations beginning with the contemplation of impermanence, contemplates this body as impermanent, not as permanent; he contemplates it as suffering, not as pleasure; he contemplates it as non-self, not as self; he becomes disenchanted, he does not delight; he becomes dispassionate, he is not impassioned; he causes cessation, he does not cause origination; he relinquishes, he does not take up. Contemplating it as impermanent, he abandons the perception of permanence. Contemplating it as suffering, he abandons the perception of pleasure. Contemplating it as non-self, he abandons the perception of self. Becoming disenchanted, he abandons delight. Becoming dispassionate, he abandons passion. Causing cessation, he abandons origination. Relinquishing, he abandons grasping. Thus it should be understood.

Viharatīti irīyati. Ātāpīti tīsu bhavesu kilese ātapatīti ātāpo, vīriyassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Ātāpo assa atthīti ātāpī. Sampajānoti sampajaññasaṅkhātena ñāṇena samannāgato. Satimāti kāyapariggāhikāya satiyā samannāgato. Ayaṃ pana yasmā satiyā ārammaṇaṃ pariggahetvā paññāya anupassati. Na hi sativirahitassa anupassanā nāma [V 3.0214] atthi, tenevāha “satiñca khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, sabbatthikaṃ vadāmī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.234). Tasmā ettha “kāye kāyānupassī viharatī”ti ettāvatā kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā yasmā anātāpino [M 3.0216] antosaṅkhepo antarāyakaro hoti, asampajāno upāyapariggahe anupāyaparivajjane ca sammuyhati, muṭṭhassati upāyāpariccāge anupāyāpariggahe ca asamattho hoti, tenassa taṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ na sampajjati. Tasmā yesaṃ dhammānaṃ ānubhāvena taṃ sampajjati, tesaṃ dassanatthaṃ “ātāpī sampajāno satimā”ti idaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

'He dwells' means he comports himself. 'Ardent' (ātāpī): because it torments the defilements in the three existences, it is called 'ātāpa' (ardor); this is a name for energy (vīriya). One who possesses this ardor is 'ātāpī'. 'Clearly comprehending' means endowed with the knowledge called clear comprehension. 'Mindful' means endowed with the mindfulness that takes up the body. Moreover, it is because one, having taken up the object with mindfulness, contemplates it with wisdom. For one devoid of mindfulness, there is indeed no such thing as contemplation. Therefore, He said: 'Mindfulness, O bhikkhus, I say is beneficial everywhere.' Thus, by this much, 'he dwells contemplating the body in the body,' the establishment of mindfulness as contemplation of the body is stated. Alternatively, because for one who is not ardent, inner contraction is an obstacle; one who is not clearly comprehending becomes bewildered in taking up the means and in avoiding what is not the means; and one with lapsed mindfulness is incapable of not abandoning the means and of not taking up what is not the means. Because of that, for that person the meditation subject does not succeed. Therefore, to show those qualities by whose power it succeeds, this was said: 'ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful.' Thus it should be understood.

Iti kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ sampayogaṅgañjassa dassetvā idāni pahānaṅgaṃ dassetuṃ vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassanti vuttaṃ. Tattha vineyyāti tadaṅgavinayena vā vikkhambhanavinayena vā vinayitvā. Loketi tasmiṃyeva kāye. Kāyo hi idha lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena lokoti adhippeto. Yasmā panassa na kāyamatteyeva abhijjhādomanassaṃ pahīyati, vedanādīsupi pahīyati eva. Tasmā “pañcapi upādānakkhandhā loko”ti vibhaṅge (vibha. 362) vuttaṃ. Lokasaṅkhātattā vā tesaṃ dhammānaṃ atthuddhāranayenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Yaṃ panāha “tattha katamo loko, sveva kāyo loko”ti, ayamevettha attho. Tasmiṃ loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ vineyyāti evaṃ sambandho daṭṭhabbo.

Thus, having shown the establishment of mindfulness as contemplation of the body and its associated factors, now, to show the factor of abandoning, it is said: 'having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world.' Therein, 'having subdued' means having subdued either by subduing for the moment or by subduing through suppression. 'In the world' means in that very body. For here, the body, in the sense of crumbling and dissolving, is intended as 'world.' However, since for this one covetousness and displeasure are not abandoned merely in regard to the body—they are indeed abandoned in regard to feelings and so on as well—therefore, in the Vibhaṅga it is said: 'The five aggregates subject to clinging are the world.' Or, because those dhammas are designated as 'world,' this is said by the method of extracting the meaning. But as to what was said: 'Therein, what is the world? That very body is the world'—this is the meaning intended here. The connection should be seen thus: 'having subdued covetousness and displeasure in that world.'

Vedanāsūti ettha tisso vedanā, tā ca lokiyā eva, cittampi lokiyaṃ, tathā dhammā. Yathā pana vedanā [P 3.0181] anupassitabbā, tathā anupassanto esa vedanānupassīti veditabbo. Esa nayo cittadhammesu. Kathañca vedanā anupassitabbāti? Sukhā tāva vedanā dukkhato, dukkhā sallato, adukkhamasukhā aniccato. Yathāha –

'In feelings': Herein, three feelings are intended, and they are only mundane. The mind is also mundane, and likewise the dhammas. And as feelings are to be contemplated, so one who contemplates in that way is to be understood as 'one who contemplates feelings.' This is the method for the mind and for dhammas. And how are feelings to be contemplated? Firstly, a pleasant feeling is to be contemplated as suffering, a painful feeling as a dart, and a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as impermanent. As it was said:

“Yo sukhaṃ dukkhato adda, dukkhamaddakkhi sallato;

Adukkhamasukhaṃ santaṃ, addakkhi naṃ aniccato;

Sa ve sammaddaso bhikkhu, upasanto carissatī”ti.

'He who saw the pleasant as suffering, and saw the painful as a dart; who saw the peaceful neither-painful-nor-pleasant as impermanent—that bhikkhu, truly seeing rightly, being at peace, will fare on.'

Sabbā eva cetā dukkhātipi anupassitabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ “yaṃkiñci vedayitaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ dukkhasminti vadāmī”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.259). Sukhadukkhatopi ca anupassitabbā, yathāha [V 3.0215][M 3.0217] – “sukhā kho, āvuso visākha, vedanā ṭhitisukhā vipariṇāmadukkhā”ti (ma. ni. 1.465) sabbaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Apica aniccādisattaanupassanāvasenapi anupassitabbā.

And all these feelings should also be contemplated as suffering. For this was stated: 'Whatever is felt, all that, I say, is within suffering.' And a pleasant feeling, too, should be contemplated as suffering, as it was said: 'A pleasant feeling, friend Visākha, is pleasant in its presence and suffering in its change.' The entire passage should be elaborated. Moreover, they are to be contemplated also by way of the seven contemplations beginning with impermanence.

Cittadhammesupi cittaṃ tāva ārammaṇādhipatisahajātabhūmikammavipākakiriyādinānattabhedānaṃ aniccādianupassanānaṃ sarāgādīnañca bhedānaṃ vasena anupassitabbaṃ. Dhammā salakkhaṇasāmaññalakkhaṇānaṃ suññatadhammassa aniccādisattaanupassanānaṃ “santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ kāmacchanda”ntiādīnañca pabhedānaṃ vasena anupassitabbā. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana dīghamajjhimaṭṭhakathāsu (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.373 ādayo; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.105 ādayo) satipaṭṭhānavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

In the case of mind and dhammas too: firstly, the mind is to be contemplated by way of the diversity of objects, dominance, co-nascence, planes, kamma, result, function, etc.; and by way of the contemplations beginning with impermanence; and by way of the distinctions such as 'with lust,' etc. Dhammas are to be contemplated by way of their individual and general characteristics; of the dhamma of emptiness; of the seven contemplations beginning with impermanence; and of the classifications such as 'there being sensual desire internally,' etc. The remainder is just as has been explained. This is the summary here. The detailed explanation, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the exposition on the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta in the commentaries on the Dīgha and Majjhima Nikāyas.

2. Satisuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Sati Sutta

368. Dutiye satoti kāyādianupassanāsatiyā samannāgato. Sampajānoti catusampajaññapaññāya samannāgato. Abhikkante paṭikkanteti ettha abhikkantaṃ vuccati gamanaṃ, paṭikkantaṃ nivattanaṃ, tadubhayampi catūsu iriyāpathesu labbhati. Gamane tāva purato kāyaṃ abhiharanto abhikkamati [P 3.0182] nāma, paṭinivattanto paṭikkamati nāma. Ṭhānepi ṭhitakova kāyaṃ purato onamanto abhikkamati nāma, pacchato apanāmento paṭikkamati nāma. Nisajjāyapi nisinnakova āsanassa purimaaṅgābhimukho saṃsaranto abhikkamati nāma, pacchimaaṅgappadesaṃ paccāsaṃsaranto paṭikkamati nāma. Nipajjanepi eseva nayo.

368. In the second sutta, 'mindful' means endowed with the mindfulness that contemplates the body and so on. 'Clearly comprehending' means endowed with the wisdom of the fourfold clear comprehension. In the phrase 'in going forward, in returning,' 'going forward' is said to be advancing, and 'returning' is turning back. Both of these are found in the four postures. First, in walking, one who carries the body forward is said to 'go forward'; one who turns back is said to 'return.' In standing, too, one who, while standing, bends the body forward is said to 'go forward'; one who draws it back is said to 'return.' In sitting, too, one who, while seated, moves towards the front part of the seat is said to 'go forward'; one who moves back towards the rear part is said to 'return.' In lying down, this is the method.

Sampajānakārī hotīti sampajaññena sabbakiccakārī, sampajaññasseva vā kārī. So hi abhikkantādīsu sampajaññaṃ karoteva, na katthaci sampajaññavirahito hoti.

As for 'he acts with clear comprehension,' it means he is one who performs all his duties with clear comprehension, or one who practices clear comprehension itself. Indeed, in going forward and so on, he truly practices clear comprehension; he is not devoid of clear comprehension in any posture.

Tattha sātthakasampajaññaṃ, sappāyasampajaññaṃ, gocarasampajaññaṃ, asammohasampajaññanti catubbidhaṃ sampajaññaṃ. Tattha abhikkamanacitte uppanne cittavaseneva agantvā “kiṃ nu me ettha gatena attho atthi, natthī”ti atthānatthaṃ pariggaṇhitvā atthapariggaṇhanaṃ sātthakasampajaññaṃ. Tattha ca atthoti cetiyadassanabodhidassanasaṅghadassanatheradassanaasubhadassanādivasena dhammato vaḍḍhi[M 3.0218]. Cetiyaṃ [V 3.0216] disvāpi hi buddhārammaṇaṃ, saṅghadassanena saṅghārammaṇaṃ pītiṃ uppādetvā tadeva khayato sammasanto arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Mahāvihārasmiñhi dakkhiṇadvāre ṭhatvā mahācetiyaṃ olokentā tiṃsasahassabhikkhū arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu, tathā pacchimadvāre uttaradvāre pācīnadvāre ca, tathā pañhamaṇḍapaṭṭhāne abhayavāpipāḷiyaṃ, thūpārāmadvāre nagarassa dakkhiṇadvāre anurādhavāpipāḷiyaṃ.

Therein, clear comprehension is fourfold: clear comprehension of purpose, clear comprehension of suitability, clear comprehension of resort, and clear comprehension of non-delusion. Among these, when a thought to go forward arises, instead of going merely by the power of that thought, one reflects, 'Is there a purpose for me in going there, or is there not?' Having thus considered what is purposeful and what is not, the grasping of the purpose is clear comprehension of purpose. And herein, 'purpose' means growth in the Dhamma by means of seeing a cetiya, seeing a Bodhi tree, seeing the Saṅgha, seeing elders, seeing a repulsive object, and so on. For by seeing a cetiya and arousing joy with the Buddha as its object, or by seeing the Saṅgha and arousing joy with the Saṅgha as its object, and then contemplating that very joy in terms of its decay and cessation, one attains arahantship. Indeed, at the Mahāvihāra, thirty thousand bhikkhus, while standing at the southern gate and gazing at the Mahācetiya, attained arahantship. Likewise at the western gate, the northern gate, and the eastern gate; and likewise at the place of the Question Pavilion, on the bank of the Abhaya pond, at the gate of the Thūpārāma, at the southern gate of the city, and on the bank of the Anurādha pond.

Mahāariyavaṃsabhāṇakatthero panāha “kiṃ tumhe vadatha, mahācetiyassa samantā kucchivedikāya heṭṭhimabhāgato paṭṭhāya paññāyanaṭṭhāne yattha yattha dve pādā sakkā honti samaṃ patiṭṭhāpetuṃ, tattha tattha ekapaduddhāre tiṃsatiṃsa bhikkhusahassāni arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsūti sakkā vatu”nti[P 3.0183]. Aparo pana mahāthero āha – “mahācetiyatale ākiṇṇavālikāya bahutarā bhikkhū arahattaṃ pattā”ti. There disvā tesaṃ ovāde patiṭṭhāya asubhaṃ disvā tattha paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ uppādetvā tadeva khayato sammasanto arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Tasmā etesaṃ dassanaṃ sātthaṃ. Keci pana – “āmisatopi vaḍḍhi atthoyeva, taṃ nissāya brahmacariyānuggahāya paṭipannattā”ti vadanti.

But the Elder Mahāariyavaṃsabhāṇaka said: 'What do you say? It can be said that all around the Mahācetiya, starting from the lower part of the central railing, in each and every visible spot where two feet could be placed evenly, thirty thousand bhikkhus attained arahantship in the space of a single footstep.' Another great elder, however, said: 'More bhikkhus than the grains of sand scattered on the terrace of the Mahācetiya have attained arahantship.' By seeing the elders and becoming established in their instruction, and by seeing a repulsive object and producing the first jhāna therein, then by contemplating that very jhāna in terms of its cessation, one attains arahantship. Therefore, seeing these is purposeful. Some, however, say: 'Growth comes even from material requisites, because one practices for the support of the holy life depending on them.'

Tasmiṃ pana gamane sappāyāsappāyaṃ pariggaṇhitvā sappāyapariggaṇhanaṃ sappāyasampajaññaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ? Cetiyadassanaṃ tāva sātthaṃ. Sace pana cetiyassa mahāpūjāya dasadvādasayojanantare parisā sannipatanti, attano vibhavānurūpā itthiyopi purisāpi alaṅkatapaṭiyattā cittakammarūpakāni viya sañcaranti. Tatra cassa iṭṭhe ārammaṇe lobho, aniṭṭhe paṭigho, asamapekkhane moho uppajjati, kāyasaṃsagge kāyasaṃsaggāpattiṃ āpajjati, jīvitabrahmacariyānaṃ vā antarāyo ca hoti. Evaṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ asappāyaṃ hoti, vuttappakāraantarāyābhāve sappāyaṃ. Saṅghadassanampi sātthaṃ. Sace pana antogāme mahāmaṇḍapaṃ kāretvā sabbarattiṃ dhammassavanaṃ kārentesu manussesu vuttappakāreneva janasannipāto ceva antarāyo ca hoti, evaṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ asappāyaṃ, antarāyābhāve sappāyaṃ. Mahāparivārānaṃ therānaṃ dassanepi eseva nayo.

Furthermore, in that going, having discerned what is suitable and unsuitable, the grasping of what is suitable is clear comprehension of suitability. How is this? To begin with, seeing a cetiya is purposeful. But if, during a great festival at the cetiya, a crowd gathers from ten or twelve yojanas around, and women and men, adorned according to their means, move about like painted figures; and if there, in the presence of a desirable object, greed arises for that bhikkhu, or in the presence of an undesirable object, aversion arises, or in the case of inappropriate attention, delusion arises; or if through bodily contact he commits an offense of bodily contact, or there is a danger to his life or his holy life—in such a case, that place is unsuitable. In the absence of the dangers described, it is suitable. Seeing the Saṅgha is also purposeful. But if, in a village, people have a great pavilion built and hold a Dhamma listening for the whole night, and there is a gathering of people and danger in the way described, then that place is unsuitable. In the absence of danger, it is suitable. This same method applies to seeing elders with large retinues.

Asubhadassanampi [M 3.0219] sātthaṃ. Tadatthadīpanatthañca idaṃ vatthu – eko kira daharabhikkhu sāmaṇeraṃ gahetvā dantakaṭṭhatthāya gato. Sāmaṇero maggā okkamitvā purato gacchanto asubhaṃ disvā paṭhamajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā tadeva pādakaṃ katvā saṅkhāre sammasanto tīṇi phalāni sacchikatvā uparimaggatthāya kammaṭṭhānaṃ pariggahetvā aṭṭhāsi. Daharo taṃ apassanto “sāmaṇerā”ti pakkosi[V 3.0217]. So – “mayā pabbajitadivasato paṭṭhāya bhikkhunā saddhiṃ dve kathā nāma na kathitapubbā, aññasmimpi divase uparivisesaṃ nibbattessāmī”ti cintetvā “kiṃ, bhante,”ti paṭivacanaṃ adāsi. “Ehī”ti vutte ekavacaneneva āgantvā – “bhante, iminā tāva maggena gantvā mayā ṭhitokāse muhuttaṃ puratthābhimukhā hutvā olokethā”ti āha. So tathā katvā tena pattavisesameva pāpuṇi. Evaṃ ekaṃ asubhaṃ [P 3.0184] dvinnaṃ janānaṃ atthāya jātaṃ. Evaṃ sātthampi panetaṃ purisassa mātugāmāsubhaṃ asappāyaṃ, mātugāmassa ca purisāsubhaṃ, sabhāgameva sappāyanti evaṃ sappāyapariggaṇhanaṃ sappāyasampajaññaṃ.

Seeing a repulsive object is also purposeful. And to illustrate this point, there is this story: A certain young bhikkhu, it is said, took a sāmaṇera and went for a tooth-stick. The sāmaṇera, stepping off the path and going ahead, saw a repulsive object and produced the first jhāna. Making that the basis, he contemplated the formations and realized the three fruits. Then, for the sake of the highest path, he took up his meditation subject and stood still. The young bhikkhu, not seeing him, called out, 'Sāmaṇera!' The sāmaṇera thought, 'From the day I went forth, I have never spoken two sentences with a bhikkhu. I will produce a higher attainment on another day,' and he replied, 'What is it, venerable sir?' When told, 'Come,' he came, speaking only a single word, and said, 'Venerable sir, please first go by this path to the place where I was standing, and for a moment, having faced east, look.' The young bhikkhu did so and attained the very same distinction that the sāmaṇera had. Thus, one repulsive object was for the benefit of two people. However, although it is purposeful in this way, for a man, the repulsive object of a woman is unsuitable, and for a woman, the repulsive object of a man is unsuitable. Only a repulsive object of the same kind is suitable. Thus, the grasping of what is suitable is clear comprehension of suitability.

Evaṃ pariggahitasātthasappāyassa pana aṭṭhatiṃsakammaṭṭhānesu attano cittarucikaṃ kammaṭṭhānasaṅkhātaṃ gocaraṃ uggahetvā bhikkhācāragocare taṃ gahetvāva gamanaṃ gocarasampajaññaṃ nāma.

Furthermore, for one who has thus comprehended what is purposeful and suitable, having thoroughly learned, from among the thirty-eight meditation subjects, the resort known as a meditation subject that is pleasing to one's own mind, the act of going to the resort for alms-gathering while taking that very subject along is called 'clear comprehension of the resort'.

Tassāvibhāvatthaṃ idaṃ catukkaṃ veditabbaṃ – idhekacco bhikkhu harati na paccāharati, ekacco paccāharati na harati, ekacco pana neva harati na paccāharati, ekacco harati ca paccāharati ca.

To make this evident, this tetrad should be understood: Here, a certain bhikkhu carries it forth but does not carry it back. Another carries it back but does not carry it forth. Another, however, neither carries it forth nor carries it back. And another both carries it forth and carries it back.

Tattha yo bhikkhu divasaṃ caṅkamena nisajjāya ca āvaraṇīyehi dhammehi cittaṃ parisodhetvā tathā rattiyā paṭhamaṃ yāmaṃ majjhimayāme seyyaṃ kappetvā, pacchimayāmepi nisajjācaṅkamehi vītināmetvā, pageva cetiyaṅgaṇabodhiyaṅgaṇavattaṃ katvā bodhirukkhe udakaṃ āsiñcitvā pānīyaṃ paribhojanīyaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā ācariyupajjhāyavattādīni samādāya vattati. So sarīraparikammaṃ katvā senāsanaṃ pavisitvā dve tayo pallaṅke usumaṃ gāhāpento kammaṭṭhānamanuyuñjitvā bhikkhācāravelāya uṭṭhahitvā kammaṭṭhānasīseneva pattacīvaramādāya senāsanato nikkhamitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikarontova cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ gantvā sace buddhānussatikammaṭṭhānaṃ hoti, taṃ avissajjetvāva cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ pavisati. Aññaṃ ce kammaṭṭhānaṃ hoti, sopānapādamūle ṭhatvā hatthena gahitabhaṇḍaṃ viya taṃ ṭhapetvā buddhārammaṇaṃ [M 3.0220] pītiṃ gahetvā cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ āruyha mahantaṃ cetiyaṃ ce, tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā catūsu ṭhānesu vanditabbaṃ, khuddakaṃ ce, tatheva padakkhiṇaṃ katvā aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu vanditabbaṃ. Cetiyaṃ vanditvā bodhiyaṅgaṇaṃ pattenāpi buddhassa bhagavato sammukhā viya nipaccakāraṃ dassetvā [P 3.0185] bodhi vanditabbā. So evaṃ cetiyañca bodhiñca vanditvā paṭisāmitaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā paṭisāmitabhaṇḍakaṃ hatthena gaṇhanto viya nikkhittakammaṭṭhānaṃ [V 3.0218] gahetvā gāmasamīpe kammaṭṭhānasīseneva cīvaraṃ pārupitvā gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisati.

Therein, a monk who, during the day, purifies his mind from obstructive states through walking and sitting, and likewise passes the first watch of the night, arranges his rest in the middle watch, and passes the last watch with sitting and walking; who, very early, performs the duties of the cetiya-courtyard and the Bodhi-courtyard, sprinkles water on the Bodhi tree, prepares drinking water and water for use, and fulfills his duties towards teachers and preceptors. He, having attended to his bodily needs, enters his dwelling, and while generating warmth for two or three cross-legged sittings, applies himself to his meditation subject. At the time for the alms-round, he rises, takes his bowl and robe with his meditation subject foremost, leaves his dwelling, and while attending to his meditation subject, goes to the cetiya-courtyard. If his meditation subject is the recollection of the Buddha, he enters the cetiya-courtyard without abandoning it. If it is another meditation subject, standing at the foot of the stairs, he sets it aside like an object held in the hand, takes up joy with the Buddha as its object, and ascends to the cetiya-courtyard. If it is a large cetiya, he should circumambulate it three times to the right and pay homage at four places; if it is a small one, he should circumambulate it in the same way and pay homage at eight places. Having paid homage to the cetiya, upon reaching the Bodhi-courtyard, he should pay homage to the Bodhi tree, showing reverence as if in the presence of the Buddha, the Blessed One. He, having thus paid homage to the cetiya and the Bodhi tree, goes to the place where it was set aside and takes up the laid-down meditation subject as if taking a stored item with the hand. Near the village, with his meditation subject foremost, he puts on his robe and enters the village for alms.

Atha naṃ manussā disvā “ayyo no āgato”ti paccuggantvā pattaṃ gahetvā āsanasālāya vā gehe vā nisīdāpetvā yāguṃ datvā yāva bhattaṃ na niṭṭhāti, tāva pāde dhovitvā makkhetvā purato nisīditvā pañhaṃ vā pucchanti, dhammaṃ vā sotukāmā honti. Sacepi na kathāpenti, janasaṅgahaṇatthaṃ dhammakathā nāma kātabbāyevāti aṭṭhakathācariyā vadanti. Dhammakathā hi kammaṭṭhānavinimuttā nāma natthi, tasmā kammaṭṭhānasīseneva dhammaṃ kathetvā kammaṭṭhānasīseneva āhāraṃ paribhuñjitvā anumodanaṃ katvā nivattiyamānehipi manussehi anugatova gāmato nikkhamitvā tattha te nivattetvā maggaṃ paṭipajjati.

Then, people, seeing him, say, 'Our noble one has come,' go out to meet him, take his bowl, have him seated in a rest hall or in a house, and give him rice-gruel. Until the meal is finished, they wash and anoint his feet, sit before him, and either ask questions or are desirous of hearing the Dhamma. Even if they do not ask him to speak, the commentary teachers say that a Dhamma talk should indeed be given for the sake of benefiting the people. For there is no Dhamma talk, indeed, that is separate from a meditation subject. Therefore, having given a Dhamma talk with the meditation subject foremost, having consumed the food with the meditation subject foremost, and having given the anumodanā, he leaves the village, followed by the people, and having sent them back from a certain point, he proceeds on his way.

Atha naṃ puretaraṃ nikkhamitvā bahigāme katabhattakiccā sāmaṇeradaharabhikkhū disvā paccuggantvā pattacīvaramassa gaṇhanti. Porāṇakabhikkhū kira na “amhākaṃ upajjhāyo ācariyo”ti mukhaṃ oloketvā vattaṃ karonti, sampattaparicchedeneva karonti. Te taṃ pucchanti – “bhante, ete manussā tumhākaṃ kiṃ honti, mātipakkhato sambandhā pitipakkhato”ti? Kiṃ disvā pucchathāti? Tumhesu etesaṃ pemaṃ bahumānanti. “Āvuso, yaṃ mātāpitūhipi dukkarataraṃ, taṃ ete amhākaṃ karonti, pattacīvarampi no etesaṃ santakameva, etesaṃ ānubhāvena neva bhaye bhayaṃ, na chātake chātakaṃ jānāma, edisā nāma amhākaṃ upakārino natthī”ti tesaṃ guṇe kathayanto gacchati. Ayaṃ vuccati harati na paccāharatīti.

Then, novice monks and junior monks, who had gone out earlier and finished their meal duties outside the village, see him, go out to meet him, and take his bowl and robe. It is said that the ancient monks do not perform their duties by looking at his face and thinking, 'He is our preceptor, our teacher'; they perform them simply according to the circumstances of the meeting. They ask him: 'Venerable sir, what are these people to you? Are they related on your mother's side or your father's side?' 'Seeing what do you ask?' '(Seeing) their affection and great respect for you.' 'Friends, what is very difficult even for mothers and fathers to do, that they do for us. Our bowl and robe are also their property. Through their power, we do not know fear in the midst of danger, nor hunger in the midst of famine. We have no benefactors like these.' Thus, speaking of their virtues, he goes on. This one is called: 'He carries it forth, but does not carry it back.'

Yassa pana pageva vuttappakāraṃ vattapaṭipattiṃ karontassa kammajatejo pajjalati, anupādiṇṇakaṃ muñcitvā upādiṇṇakaṃ gaṇhāti, sarīrato sedā muccanti, kammaṭṭhānavīthiṃ nārohati, so pageva pattacīvaramādāya vegasāva cetiyaṃ [M 3.0221] vanditvā gorūpānaṃ nikkhamanavelāyameva gāmaṃ yāgubhikkhāya pavisitvā yāguṃ labhitvā āsanasālaṃ gantvā pivati. Athassa dvittikkhattuṃ ajjhoharaṇamatteneva [P 3.0186] kammajatejo upādiṇṇakaṃ muñcitvā anupādiṇṇakaṃ gaṇhāti, ghaṭasatena nhāto viya tejodhātupariḷāhanibbānaṃ patvā kammaṭṭhānasīsena yāguṃ paribhuñjitvā pattañca mukhañca dhovitvā antarābhatte kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikatvā avasesaṭṭhāne piṇḍāya caritvā kammaṭṭhānasīsena āhāraṃ paribhuñjitvā tato paṭṭhāya poṅkhānupoṅkhaṃ upaṭṭhahamānaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ [V 3.0219] gahetvāva āgacchati. Ayaṃ vuccati paccāharati na haratīti. Edisā ca bhikkhū yāguṃ pivitvā vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā buddhasāsane arahattaṃ pattā nāma gaṇanapathaṃ vītivattā. Sīhaḷadīpeyeva tesu tesu gāmesu āsanasālāyaṃ na taṃ āsanamatthi, yattha yāguṃ pivitvā arahattaṃ pattā bhikkhū natthīti.

But for another monk, while performing the practice of duties in the manner described very early in the morning, the digestive fire blazes, it releases external matter and seizes the internal matter of the body, sweat is released from his body, and the meditation subject does not enter the path of progress. He, very early, taking his bowl and robe, quickly venerates the cetiya, and at the very time the cattle are going out, enters the village for alms-gruel. Having received gruel, he goes to the rest hall and drinks it. Then, for him, with just two or three swallows, the digestive fire releases the internal matter and seizes the external matter. Having reached the quenching of the burning of the fire element as if bathed with a hundred pots of water, he consumes the gruel with the meditation subject foremost, washes his bowl and mouth, and in the interval before the main meal, attends to his meditation subject. Having gone for alms in the remaining places, he consumes the food with the meditation subject foremost, and from then on, taking up the meditation subject which arises in continuous succession, he returns. This one is called: 'He carries it back, but does not carry it forth.' And such monks, having drunk gruel and undertaken insight meditation, who have attained Arahantship in the Buddha's Dispensation, are indeed beyond counting. In the island of Sri Lanka alone, in any given village, there is no seat in the rest hall where a monk has not attained Arahantship after drinking gruel.

Yo pana pamādavihārī hoti nikkhittadhuro, sabbavattāni bhinditvā pañcavidhacetovinibandhabaddhacitto viharanto “kammaṭṭhānaṃ nāma atthī”tipi saññaṃ akatvā gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisitvā ananulomikena gihisaṃsaggena saṃsaṭṭho caritvā ca bhuñjitvā ca tuccho nikkhamati. Ayaṃ vuccati neva harati na paccāharatīti.

Furthermore, whatever bhikkhu lives heedlessly, having laid down the burden of diligence and broken all observances, dwells with a mind bound by the five kinds of mental bondage. Not even making the perception that “there is such a thing as a meditation subject,” he enters a village for alms, associates improperly with householders, wanders about, eats, and then departs empty. This one is called ‘one who neither takes away nor brings back.’”

Yo panāyaṃ harati ca paccāharati cāti vutto, so gatapaccāgatikavattavasena veditabbo. Attakāmā hi kulaputtā sāsane pabbajitvā dasapi vīsampi tiṃsampi cattālīsampi paññāsampi satampi ekato vasantā katikavattaṃ katvā viharanti “āvuso, tumhe na iṇaṭṭā, na bhayaṭṭā, na jīvikāpakatā pabbajitā, dukkhā muccitukāmā panettha pabbajitā, tasmā gamane uppannakilesaṃ gamaneyeva niggaṇhatha, ṭhāne, nisajjāya, sayane uppannakilesaṃ sayaneyeva niggaṇhathā”ti. Te evaṃ katikavattaṃ katvā bhikkhācāraṃ gacchantā aḍḍhausabhausabhaaḍḍhagāvutagāvutantaresu pāsāṇā honti, tāya saññāya kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikarontāva gacchanti. Sace kassaci gamane kileso uppajjati, tattheva naṃ niggaṇhāti. Tathā asakkonto tiṭṭhati. Athassa pacchato āgacchantopi tiṭṭhati, so “ayaṃ bhikkhu tuyhaṃ uppannavitakkaṃ jānāti, ananucchavikaṃ te eta”nti attānaṃ paṭicodetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā tattheva ariyabhūmiṃ [P 3.0187] okkamati, tathā [M 3.0222] asakkonto nisīdatīti so eva nayo. Ariyabhūmiṃ okkamituṃ asakkontopi, taṃ kilesaṃ vikkhambhetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikarontova gacchati, na kammaṭṭhānavippayuttena cittena pādaṃ uddharati. Uddharati ce, paṭinivattitvā purimapadesaṃyeva eti ālindakavāsī mahāphussadevatthero viya.

As for the one who is said to ‘take away and bring back,’ he should be known by way of the observance of going and returning. For sons of good families, desiring their own welfare, having gone forth in the Dispensation, dwell together in groups of ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or a hundred, having made an agreement and dwelling thus: ‘Venerable sirs, you have not gone forth because you were oppressed by debt, nor oppressed by fear, nor oppressed by the need for a livelihood; rather, desiring to be freed from suffering, you have gone forth here. Therefore, when a defilement arises in the posture of walking, you must restrain it right there in the posture of walking; when a defilement arises in the postures of standing, sitting, or lying down, you must restrain it in that very posture.’ Having made such an agreement, when they go on alms-round, there are rocks at intervals of half an usabha, an usabha, half a gāvuta, and a gāvuta; using these as a sign, they go while attending to their meditation subject. If a defilement arises in anyone while walking, he restrains it right there. Being unable to do so, he stands still. Then the one coming behind him also stands still. That bhikkhu, thinking, ‘This bhikkhu knows the thought that has arisen in you; this action of yours is improper,’ reproves himself, develops insight, and right there enters the noble stage. Being unable to do so, he sits down; this is the same method. Even if unable to enter the noble stage, having suppressed that defilement, he goes while attending to his meditation subject. He does not lift his foot with a mind disconnected from the meditation subject. If he does lift it, he turns back and returns to the very same previous spot, like the Elder Mahāphussatthera, the dweller in Ālindaka.

So kira ekūnavīsati vassāni gatapaccāgatikavattaṃ pūrento eva vihāsi. Manussāpi sudaṃ antarāmagge kasantā ca vapantā ca maddantā ca kammāni ca karontā theraṃ tathā gacchantaṃ disvā – “ayaṃ thero punappunaṃ nivattitvā gacchati, kiṃ nu kho maggamūḷho, udāhu kiñci pamuṭṭho”ti [V 3.0220] samullapanti. So taṃ anādiyitvā kammaṭṭhānayuttacitteneva samaṇadhammaṃ karonto vīsativassabbhantare arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Arahattappattadivase cassa caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ adhivatthā devatā aṅgulīhi dīpaṃ ujjāletvā aṭṭhāsi. Cattāropi mahārājāno sakko ca devānamindo brahmā ca sahampati upaṭṭhānaṃ āgamaṃsu. Tañca obhāsaṃ disvā vanavāsīmahātissatthero taṃ dutiyadivase pucchi – “rattibhāge āyasmato santike obhāso ahosi, kiṃ so obhāso”ti? Thero vikkhepaṃ karonto “obhāso nāma dīpobhāsopi hoti, maṇiobhāsopī”ti evamādimāha. Tato “paṭicchādetha tumhe”ti nibaddho āmāti paṭijānitvā ārocesi.

It is said that for nineteen years he dwelt fulfilling only the observance of going and returning. And people, while plowing, sowing, threshing, and doing their work along the road, seeing the elder going thus, would converse among themselves: ‘This elder goes back and forth again and again. Is he lost on the path, or perhaps has he forgotten something?’ He, not taking that to heart, practicing the recluse's duties with a mind connected only to his meditation subject, attained Arahantship within twenty years. On the day he attained Arahantship, a deity dwelling at the end of his walking path lit a lamp with her fingers and stood there. The Four Great Kings, Sakka, king of the devas, and Brahmā Sahampati also came to attend upon him. Seeing that radiance, the Elder Mahātissa, the forest-dweller, asked him on the second day: ‘Venerable sir, during the night there was a radiance in your presence. What was that radiance?’ The elder, creating a diversion, said things such as: ‘Radiance, so-called, can be the light of a lamp, or it can be the radiance of a gem.’ Then, being pressed with, ‘You are concealing it,’ he acknowledged it and related what had happened.

Kāḷavallimaṇḍapavāsīmahānāgatthero viya ca. Sopi kira gatapaccāgatikavattaṃ pūrento paṭhamaṃ tāva “bhagavato mahāpadhānaṃ pūjessāmī”ti satta vassāni ṭhānacaṅkamameva adhiṭṭhāsi. Puna soḷasa vassāni gatapaccāgatikavattaṃ pūretvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. So kammaṭṭhānayutteneva cittena pādaṃ uddharanto vippayuttena uddhaṭe paṭinivattanto gāmasamīpaṃ gantvā “gāvī nu pabbajito nū”ti āsaṅkanīyapadese ṭhatvā cīvaraṃ pārupitvā kacchakarakato udakena pattaṃ dhovitvā [P 3.0188] udakagaṇḍūsaṃ karoti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? “Mā me bhikkhaṃ dātuṃ vā vandituṃ vā āgate manusse ‘dīghāyukā hothā’ti vacanamattenāpi kammaṭṭhānavikkhepo ahosī”ti “ajja, bhante, katimī”ti divasaṃ vā bhikkhugaṇanaṃ vā pañhaṃ vā pucchito [M 3.0223] pana udakaṃ gilitvā āroceti. Sace divasādipucchakā na honti, nikkhamanavelāyaṃ gāmadvāre niṭṭhubhitvā yāti.

And like the Elder Mahānāga, the dweller in Kāḷavallimaṇḍapa. It is said that he too, while fulfilling the observance of going and returning, first resolved for seven years to practice only standing and walking, thinking, ‘I will pay homage to the Blessed One’s great striving.’ Again, after fulfilling the observance of going and returning for sixteen years, he attained Arahantship. He, lifting his foot only with a mind connected to his meditation subject, would turn back when it was lifted with a disconnected mind. Having gone near a village, he would stand in a place of uncertainty where one might wonder, ‘Is it a cow or a monk?’, don his robe, wash his bowl with water from his water strainer, and take a mouthful of water. For what reason? Thinking, ‘May there not be a distraction from my meditation subject even by the mere words “May you live long!” to people who have come to give alms or to pay homage.’ But if asked about the day, such as, ‘Venerable sir, what is the date today?’, or about the number of bhikkhus, or some other question, he would swallow the water and then inform them. If there were no people asking about the day and so on, at the time of departure, he would spit it out at the village gate and go.

Kalambatitthavihāre vassūpagatā paññāsa bhikkhū viya ca. Te kira āsāḷhipuṇṇamiyaṃ katikavattaṃ akaṃsu – “arahattaṃ apatvā aññamaññaṃ nālapissāmā”ti. Gāmañca piṇḍāya pavisantā udakagaṇḍūsaṃ katvā pavisiṃsu. Divasādīsu pucchitesu vuttanayeneva paṭipajjiṃsu. Tattha manussā niṭṭhubhanaṃ disvā jāniṃsu – “ajjeko āgato, ajja dve”ti. Evañca cintesuṃ – “kiṃ nu kho ete amheheva saddhiṃ na sallapanti, udāhu aññamaññampi. Yadi aññamaññaṃ na sallapanti, addhā vivādajātā bhavissanti. Etha ne aññamaññaṃ khamāpessāmā”ti sabbe vihāraṃ gantvā paññāsāya bhikkhūsu dvepi bhikkhū ekokāse nāddasaṃsu. Tato yo tesu cakkhumā puriso, so āha – “na bho kalahakārakānaṃ okāso īdiso hoti, susammaṭṭhaṃ cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ bodhiyaṅgaṇaṃ, sunikkhittā sammajjaniyo, supaṭṭhitaṃ pānīyaṃ paribhojanīya”nti[V 3.0221]. Te tatova nivattā. Tepi bhikkhū antotemāseyeva arahattaṃ patvā mahāpavāraṇāyaṃ visuddhipavāraṇaṃ pavāresuṃ.

And like the fifty monks who spent the rains retreat at Kalambatittha Monastery. It is said that on the full-moon day of Āsāḷha, they made a resolution: 'Until we attain Arahantship, we will not speak to one another.' When entering the village for alms, they entered having taken a mouthful of water. If asked about the day or other matters, they behaved in the manner already described. There, the people, seeing the spittle, knew: 'Today one has come; today two have come.' And they thought: 'Do these monks not speak only with us, or do they also not speak with one another? If they do not speak with one another, surely a dispute has arisen. Come, let us reconcile them.' They all went to the monastery but did not see even two of the fifty monks together in one place. Then a wise man among them said: 'Sirs, the place of those who quarrel is not like this; the stupa courtyard and the Bodhi tree courtyard are well-swept, the brooms are well-placed, and drinking water and water for use are properly set out.' They turned back from that very place. Those monks, having attained Arahantship within the three months, performed the Pavāraṇā of purity on the day of the great Pavāraṇā.

Evaṃ kāḷavallimaṇḍapavāsī mahānāgatthero viya, kalambatitthavihāre vassūpagatā bhikkhū viya ca kammaṭṭhānayutteneva cittena pādaṃ uddharanto gāmasamīpaṃ gantvā udakagaṇḍūsaṃ katvā vīthiyo sallakkhetvā yattha surāsoṇḍadhuttādayo kalahakārakā caṇḍahatthiassādayo vā natthi, taṃ vīthiṃ paṭipajjati. Tattha ca piṇḍāya caramāno na turitaturito viya javena gacchati. Na hi javena piṇḍapātikadhutaṅgaṃ nāma kiñci atthi. Visamabhūmibhāgapattaṃ pana udakasakaṭaṃ viya niccalo hutvā gacchati. Anugharaṃ paviṭṭho ca dātukāmaṃ vā adātukāmaṃ vā sallakkhetuṃ tadanurūpaṃ kālaṃ āgamento bhikkhaṃ gahetvā [P 3.0189] antogāme vā bahigāme vā vihārameva vā āgantvā yathāphāsuke patirūpe okāse nisīditvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikaronto āhāre paṭikūlasaññaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā akkhabbhañjanavaṇalepanaputtamaṃsūpamāvasena paccavekkhanto aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgataṃ āhāraṃ āhāreti, neva davāya na madāya na maṇḍanāya na vibhūsanāya…pe… bhuttāvī ca udakakiccaṃ katvā muhuttaṃ bhattakilamathaṃ paṭipassambhetvā yathā purebhattaṃ[M 3.0224], evaṃ pacchābhattaṃ purimayāmaṃ pacchimayāmañca kammaṭṭhānameva manasikaroti. Ayaṃ vuccati harati ca paccāharati cāti.

Thus, like the great elder Mahānāga who dwelt at Kāḷavallimaṇḍapa, and like the monks who entered the rains-residence at Kalambatittha Vihāra, with a mind engaged only in the meditation subject, lifting his foot, he goes to the vicinity of the village. Having taken a mouthful of water and observed the streets, he proceeds along a street where there are no drunkards, gamblers, and the like, quarrelsome people, or fierce elephants, horses, and the like. And there, while wandering for alms, he does not go with speed as if in a great hurry. For there is no ascetic practice whatsoever called 'the swift alms-round.' But, like a water-cart that has reached an uneven part of the ground, he goes having become steady. And having entered house by house, waiting for a suitable time to observe whether they wish to give or do not wish to give, he takes the alms. Having come back either within the village, or outside the village, or to the monastery itself, and having sat down in a suitable, comfortable place, attending to his meditation subject, he establishes the perception of foulness in regard to food. Reflecting by way of the similes of anointing an axle, dressing a wound, and a son's flesh, he partakes of the food endowed with eight factors: not for sport, not for intoxication, not for adornment, not for beautification… And having eaten, having done what is to be done with water, and having for a moment allayed the fatigue from the meal, just as before the meal, so also after the meal, during the first watch and the last watch, he attends only to his meditation subject. This one is called: 'He carries and carries back.'

Imaṃ pana haraṇapaccāharaṇasaṅkhātaṃ gatapaccāgatikavattaṃ pūrento yadi upanissayasampanno hoti, paṭhamavaye eva arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. No ce paṭhamavaye pāpuṇāti, atha majjhimavaye pāpuṇāti. No ce majjhimavaye pāpuṇāti, atha pacchimavaye pāpuṇāti, no ce pacchimavaye pāpuṇāti, atha maraṇasamaye. No ce maraṇasamaye pāpuṇāti, atha devaputto hutvā. No ce devaputto hutvā pāpuṇāti, anuppanne buddhe nibbatto paccekabodhiṃ sacchikaroti. No ce paccekabodhiṃ sacchikaroti, atha buddhānaṃ sammukhībhāve khippābhiñño vā hoti, seyyathāpi thero bāhiyo dārucīriyo mahāpañño vā, seyyathāpi thero sāriputto, mahiddhiko vā, seyyathāpi thero mahāmoggallāno, dhutavādo vā, seyyathāpi thero mahākassapo, dibbacakkhuko vā, seyyathāpi thero anuruddho, vinayadharo vā, seyyathāpi thero upāli, dhammakathiko vā, seyyathāpi thero puṇṇo mantāṇiputto, āraññiko vā, seyyathāpi thero revato, bahussuto vā, seyyathāpi thero [V 3.0222] ānando, sikkhākāmo vā, seyyathāpi thero rāhulo buddhaputtoti. Iti imasmiṃ catukke yvāyaṃ harati paccāharati ca, tassa gocarasampajaññaṃ sikhāpattaṃ hoti.

Furthermore, one who fulfills this practice of going and returning, known as 'carrying and carrying back,' if he is endowed with supporting conditions, attains Arahantship in the first age itself. If he does not attain it in the first age, then he attains it in the middle age. If he does not attain it in the middle age, then he attains it in the last age. If he does not attain it in the last age, then at the time of death. If he does not attain it at the time of death, then having become a deva. If, having become a deva, he does not attain it, being reborn when a Buddha has not arisen, he realizes the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha. If he does not realize the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha, then in the presence of Buddhas he becomes one of swift insight, like the elder Bāhiya Dārucīriya; or greatly wise, like the elder Sāriputta; or of great psychic power, like the elder Mahāmoggallāna; or an exponent of the ascetic practices, like the elder Mahākassapa; or possessing the divine eye, like the elder Anuruddha; or a master of the Vinaya, like the elder Upāli; or a preacher of the Dhamma, like the elder Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta; or a forest-dweller, like the elder Revata; or highly learned, like the elder Ānanda; or one devoted to the training, like the elder Rāhula, the Buddha's son. Thus, in this tetrad, for this one who 'carries and carries back,' the clear comprehension of resort reaches its peak.

Abhikkamādīsu pana asammuyhanaṃ asammohasampajaññaṃ. Taṃ evaṃ veditabbaṃ – idha bhikkhu abhikkamanto vā paṭikkamanto vā yathā andhaputhujjanā abhikkamādīsu – “attā abhikkamati, attanā abhikkamo nibbattito”ti vā “ahaṃ abhikkamāmi, mayā abhikkamo nibbattito”ti vā sammuyhanti, tathā asammuyhanto abhikkamāmīti citte uppajjamāne teneva cittena saddhiṃ cittasamuṭṭhānā vāyodhātu [P 3.0190] viññattiṃ janayamānā uppajjati, iti cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāravasena ayaṃ kāyasammato aṭṭhisaṅghāṭo abhikkamati. Tassevaṃ abhikkamato ekekapāduddharaṇe pathavīdhātu āpodhātūti dve dhātuyo omattā honti mandā, itarā dve adhimattā honti balavatiyo, tathā atiharaṇavītiharaṇesu, vossajjane tejodhātu vāyodhātūti dve dhātuyo omattā honti [M 3.0225] mandā, itarā dve adhimattā honti balavatiyo, tathā sannikkhepanasannirumbhanesu.

Furthermore, in advancing and so on, non-delusion is the clear comprehension of non-delusion. This should be understood thus: Here a monk, when advancing or retreating, does not become deluded in the way that blind worldlings become deluded in advancing and so on, thinking: 'A self advances, the advance is produced by a self,' or 'I advance, the advance is produced by me.' Not being deluded thus, when the thought 'I am advancing' arises, together with that very thought, the mind-originated wind element arises, generating bodily intimation. Thus, by the force of the oscillation of the wind element which is the mind's action, this collection of bones conventionally known as 'body' advances. For him thus advancing, in the lifting of each single foot, the two elements—the earth element and the water element—are of lesser measure and are weak; the other two are of greater measure and are strong. Likewise in stretching forward and moving sideways. In releasing the foot, the two elements—the fire element and the wind element—are of lesser measure and are weak; the other two are of greater measure and are strong. Likewise in placing the foot down and in stopping.

Tattha uddharaṇe pavattā rūpārūpadhammā atiharaṇaṃ na pāpuṇanti, tathā atiharaṇe pavattā vītiharaṇaṃ, vītiharaṇe pavattā vossajjanaṃ, vossajjane pavattā sannikkhepanaṃ, sannikkhepane pavattā sannirumbhanaṃ na pāpuṇanti, tattha tattheva pabbapabbaṃ sandhisandhi odhiodhi hutvā tattakapāle pakkhittatilāni viya taṭataṭāyantā bhijjanti. Tattha ko eko abhikkamati, kassa vā ekassa abhikkamanaṃ? Paramatthato hi dhātūnaṃyeva gamanaṃ, dhātūnaṃ ṭhānaṃ, dhātūnaṃ nisajjā, dhātūnaṃ sayanaṃ. Tasmiṃ tasmiñhi koṭṭhāse saddhiṃ rūpena –

Therein, the material and immaterial phenomena that have arisen at the moment of lifting the foot do not reach the moment of bringing it forward. Similarly, phenomena that have arisen at the moment of bringing it forward do not reach the moment of moving it sideways; phenomena that have arisen at the moment of moving it sideways do not reach the moment of releasing it; phenomena that have arisen at the moment of releasing it do not reach the moment of placing it down; and phenomena that have arisen at the moment of placing it down do not reach the moment of stopping. In each and every one of those moments, having become section by section, joint by joint, part by part, they break up like sesame seeds thrown onto a hot pan, as if making a crackling sound. Therein, what one goes forward? Or to what one does the going forward belong? Indeed, in the ultimate sense, it is only the going of the elements, the standing of the elements, the sitting of the elements, the lying down of the elements. For in each of those portions, together with matter—

“Aññaṃ uppajjate cittaṃ, aññaṃ cittaṃ nirujjhati;

Avīcimanusambandho, nadīsotova vattatī”ti. –

“Another mind arises, another mind ceases; an unbroken, continuous connection proceeds like the current of a river.”

Evaṃ abhikkamādīsu asammuyhanaṃ asammohasampajaññaṃ nāmāti.

Thus, non-bewilderment in going forward and so on is called clear comprehension of non-delusion.

Niṭṭhito “abhikkante paṭikkante sampajānakārī hotī”tipadassa attho.

The meaning of the phrase “one acts with clear comprehension in going forward and returning” is concluded.

Ālokite [V 3.0223] vilokiteti ettha pana ālokitaṃ nāma purato pekkhanaṃ, vilokitaṃ nāma anudisāpekkhanaṃ. Aññānipi heṭṭhā upari pacchato anupekkhanavasena olokitaullokitāpalokitāni nāma honti. Tāni idha na gahitāni, sāruppavasena pana imāneva dve gahitāni. Iminā vā mukhena sabbānipi tāni gahitānevāti.

Here, in the phrase 'in looking ahead, in looking around,' ālokita means looking forward, and vilokita means looking from side to side. There are also others, namely olokita, ullokita, and apalokita, by way of looking down, up, and behind. Those are not taken here, but on account of suitability, only these two are taken. Or, by this introductory method, all of them are indeed taken.

Tattha “ālokessāmī”ti citte uppanne cittavaseneva anoloketvā atthapariggaṇhanaṃ sātthakasampajaññaṃ. Taṃ āyasmantaṃ nandaṃ kāyasakkhiṃ katvā veditabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

Therein, when the thought 'I will look' arises, the grasping of the purpose without looking, merely by the power of the mind, is the clear comprehension of purposefulness. This should be understood by making the Venerable Nanda a bodily witness. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Sace, bhikkhave, nandassa puratthimā disā āloketabbā hoti, sabbaṃ cetasā samannāharitvā nando puratthimaṃ disaṃ āloketi ‘evaṃ [P 3.0191] me puratthimaṃ disaṃ ālokayato nābhijjhādomanassā [M 3.0226] pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāsavissantī’ti. Itiha tattha sampajāno hoti. Sace, bhikkhave, nandassa pacchimā disā, uttarā disā, dakkhiṇā disā, uddhaṃ, adho, anudisā āloketabbā hoti, sabbaṃ cetasā samannāharitvā nando anudisaṃ āloketi ‘evaṃ me anudisaṃ ālokayato’…pe… sampajāno hotī”ti (a. ni. 8.9).

“Monks, if Nanda is to look at the eastern direction, having fully comprehended everything with his mind, Nanda looks at the eastern direction, thinking: ‘As I am looking at the eastern direction in this way, evil, unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure will not flow in.’ Thus, he is clearly comprehending in that matter. Monks, if Nanda is to look at the western direction, the northern direction, the southern direction, upwards, downwards, or the intermediate directions, having fully comprehended everything with his mind, Nanda looks at the intermediate direction, thinking: ‘As I am looking at the intermediate direction in this way…’ …he is clearly comprehending.”

Apica idhāpi pubbe vuttacetiyadassanādivaseneva sātthakatā ca sappāyatā ca veditabbā. Kammaṭṭhānassa pana avijahanameva gocarasampajaññaṃ, tasmā khandhadhātuāyatanakammaṭṭhānikehi attano kamaṭṭhānavaseneva kasiṇādikammaṭṭhānikehi vā pana kammaṭṭhānasīseneva ālokanavilokanaṃ kātabbaṃ.

Moreover, here too, purposefulness and suitability should be understood in the same way as previously stated regarding seeing a cetiya and so on. The non-abandonment of the meditation subject itself is clear comprehension of the domain. Therefore, for those whose meditation subject pertains to the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, looking ahead and looking around should be done only in accordance with their own meditation subject. Or, for those whose meditation subject pertains to the kasiṇas and so on, it should be done only with the meditation subject as the primary focus.

“Abbhantare attā nāma āloketā vā viloketā vā natthi, ‘ālokessāmī’ti pana citte uppajjamāne teneva cittena saddhiṃ cittasamuṭṭhānā vāyodhātu viññattiṃ janayamānā uppajjati. Iti cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāravasena heṭṭhimaṃ akkhidalaṃ adho sīdati, uparimaṃ uddhaṃ laṅgheti, koci yantakena vivaranto nāma natthi, tato cakkhuviññāṇaṃ dassanakiccaṃ sādhentaṃ uppajjatī”ti evaṃ pajānanaṃ panettha asammohasampajaññaṃ nāma.

“Internally, there is no self called a looker-ahead or a looker-around. But when the thought ‘I will look’ arises, together with that very mind, the mind-originated wind element arises, generating intimation. Thus, by the power of the expansion of the wind element which is the action of the mind, the lower eyelid sinks down and the upper eyelid rises up. There is no one who opens it with a machine. Then, eye-consciousness arises, accomplishing the function of seeing.” Thus, clearly knowing in this way is called clear comprehension of non-delusion.

Apica [V 3.0224] mūlapariññāāgantukatāvakālikabhāvavasenapettha asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ. Mūlapariññāvasena tāva –

Furthermore, clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood here by way of comprehensively knowing the root, the state of being adventitious, and the state of being temporary. Firstly, by way of comprehensively knowing the root:

“Bhavaṅgāvajjanañceva, dassanaṃ sampaṭicchanaṃ;

Santīraṇaṃ voṭṭhabbanaṃ, javanaṃ bhavati sattamaṃ”.
