“Life-continuum and also adverting, seeing, receiving, investigating, determining; impulsion is the seventh.”

Tattha bhavaṅgaṃ upapattibhavassa aṅgakiccaṃ sādhayamānaṃ pavattati, taṃ āvaṭṭetvā kiriyamanodhātu āvajjanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā, tannirodhā cakkhuviññāṇaṃ dassanakiccaṃ sādhayamānaṃ, tannirodhā vipākamanodhātu sampaṭicchanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā, tannirodhā vipākamanoviññāṇadhātu santīraṇakiccaṃ sādhayamānā, tannirodhā kiriyamanoviññāṇadhātu voṭṭhabbanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā, tannirodhā sattakkhattuṃ javanaṃ javati. Tattha paṭhamajavanepi “ayaṃ [M 3.0227] itthī, ayaṃ puriso”ti rajjanadussanamuyhanavasena [P 3.0192] ālokitavilokitaṃ na hoti, dutiyajavanepi…pe… sattamajavanepi. Etesu pana yuddhamaṇḍale yodhesu viya heṭṭhupariyavasena bhijjitvā patitesu “ayaṃ itthī, ayaṃ puriso”ti rajjanādivasena ālokitavilokitaṃ hoti. Evaṃ tāvettha mūlapariññāvasena asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Therein, the life-continuum proceeds, accomplishing the function of being a factor of rebirth-existence. Turning that aside, the functional mind-element proceeds, accomplishing the function of adverting. Upon its cessation, eye-consciousness proceeds, accomplishing the function of seeing. Upon its cessation, the resultant mind-element proceeds, accomplishing the function of receiving. Upon its cessation, the resultant mind-consciousness-element proceeds, accomplishing the function of investigating. Upon its cessation, the functional mind-consciousness-element proceeds, accomplishing the function of determining. Upon its cessation, impulsion runs for seven moments. Therein, even in the first impulsion moment, looking ahead and looking around by way of lust, aversion, and delusion as ‘This is a woman, this is a man’ does not occur; nor in the second impulsion moment… nor in the seventh impulsion moment. But when these, like soldiers on a battlefield, have broken up and fallen, then looking ahead and looking around by way of lust and so on as ‘This is a woman, this is a man’ occurs. Thus, firstly, clear comprehension of non-delusion should be known here by way of comprehensively knowing the root.

Cakkhudvāre pana rūpe āpāthamāgate bhavaṅgacalanato uddhaṃ sakakiccanipphādanavasena āvajjanādīsu uppajjitvā niruddhesu avasāne javanaṃ uppajjati, taṃ pubbe uppannānaṃ āvajjanādīnaṃ gehabhūte cakkhudvāre āgantukapuriso viya hoti. Tassa yathā paragehe kiñci yācituṃ paviṭṭhassa āgantukapurisassa gehasāmikesu tuṇhīmāsinesu āṇākaraṇaṃ na yuttaṃ, evaṃ āvajjanādīnaṃ gehabhūte cakkhudvāre āvajjanādīsupi arajjantesu adussantesu amuyhantesu ca rajjanadussanamuyhanaṃ ayuttanti evaṃ āgantukabhāvavasena asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

When a form-object comes into range at the eye-door, after the vibration of the life-continuum, the minds beginning with adverting arise and cease by way of accomplishing their respective functions, and at the end, impulsion arises. That impulsion is like a visitor in the eye-door, which is the house of the previously arisen adverting and so on. Just as it is not suitable for a visitor who has entered another's house to ask for something to exercise authority while the owners of the house are sitting silently, so too, in the eye-door, which is the house of the adverting and so on, while the adverting and so on are not lusting, not being averse, and not being deluded, it is not suitable for that impulsion to lust, be averse, or be deluded. Thus, clear comprehension of non-delusion should be known by way of the state of being a visitor.

Yāni panetāni cakkhudvāre voṭṭhabbanapariyosānāni cittāni uppajjanti, tāni saddhiṃ sampayuttadhammehi tattha tattheva bhijjanti, aññamaññaṃ na passanti, ittarāni tāvakālikāni honti. Tattha yathā ekasmiṃ ghare sabbesu mānusakesu matesu avasesassa ekassa taṅkhaṇaṃyeva maraṇadhammassa na yuttā naccagītādīsu abhirati nāma, evameva ekadvāre sasampayuttesu āvajjanādīsu tattha tattheva matesu avasesassa taṅkhaṇaṃyeva maraṇadhammassa javanassāpi rajjanadussanamuyhanavasena [V 3.0225] abhirati nāma na yuttāti evaṃ tāvakālikabhāvavasena asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, those minds that arise at the eye-door, culminating in determining, perish right there and then, together with their associated mental factors. They do not see one another; they are of short duration and have a momentary existence. Herein, it is like in a house where all the people have died, it is not fitting for the one remaining, who is of a nature to die at that very moment, to take delight in dancing, singing, and so on. In the same way, at a single door, when the adverting and other minds, together with their associated factors, have ceased right there and then, it is not fitting for the remaining javana, which is of a nature to perish at that very moment, to take delight by way of lust, aversion, and delusion. Thus, the clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood by way of their transient nature.

Apica khandhāyatanadhātupaccayapaccavekkhaṇavasenapetaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ettha hi cakkhu ceva rūpā ca rūpakkhandho, dassanaṃ viññāṇakkhandho, taṃsampayuttā vedanā vedanākkhandho, saññā saññākkhandho, phassādikā saṅkhārā saṅkhārakkhandho, evametesaṃ pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ samavāye ālokanavilokanaṃ paññāyati. Tattha ko eko āloketi, ko viloketi? Tathā cakkhu cakkhāyatanaṃ, rūpaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ, dassanaṃ manāyatanaṃ, vedanādayo sampayuttadhammā dhammāyatanaṃ, evametesaṃ catunnaṃ āyatanānaṃ [P 3.0193] samavāye ālokanavilokanaṃ paññāyati. Tattha ko eko āloketi, ko [M 3.0228] viloketi? Tathā cakkhu cakkhudhātu, rūpaṃ rūpadhātu, dassanaṃ cakkhuviññāṇadhātu, taṃsampayuttā vedanādayo dhammā dhammadhātu, evametesaṃ catunnaṃ dhātūnaṃ samavāye ālokanavilokanaṃ paññāyati. Tattha ko eko āloketi, ko viloketi? Tathā cakkhu nissayapaccayo, rūpaṃ ārammaṇapaccayo, āvajjanaṃ anantarasamanantarūpanissayanatthivigatapaccayo, āloko upanissayapaccayo, vedanādayo sahajātapaccayo. Evametesaṃ paccayānaṃ samavāye ālokanavilokanaṃ paññāyati. Tattha ko eko āloketi, ko viloketīti evamettha khandhāyatanadhātupaccayapaccavekkhaṇavasenapi asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Moreover, this clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood by way of reflecting on the aggregates, sense bases, elements, and conditions. Herein, the eye and forms are the form aggregate; seeing is the consciousness aggregate; the feeling associated with it is the feeling aggregate; perception is the perception aggregate; formations beginning with contact are the formations aggregate. Thus, in the combination of these five aggregates, looking and observing is discerned. Therein, what single thing looks? What observes? Similarly, the eye is the eye-base, form is the form-base, seeing is the mind-base, and feeling and other associated factors are the dhamma-base. Thus, in the combination of these four sense bases, looking and observing is discerned. Therein, what single thing looks? What observes? Likewise, the eye is the eye-element, form is the form-element, seeing is the eye-consciousness-element, and the feeling and other associated factors are the dhamma-element. Thus, in the combination of these four elements, looking and observing is discerned. Therein, what single thing looks? What observes? Further, the eye is the dependence condition; form is the object condition; adverting is the proximity, contiguity, support, absence, and disappearance condition; light is the support condition; and feeling and other factors are the co-nascence condition. Thus, in the combination of these conditions, looking and observing is discerned. Therein, what single thing looks? What observes? Thus, herein, the clear comprehension of non-delusion should also be understood by way of reflecting on the aggregates, sense bases, elements, and conditions.

Samiñjite pasāriteti pabbānaṃ samiñjanapasāraṇe. Tattha cittavaseneva samiñjanapasāraṇaṃ akatvā hatthapādānaṃ samiñjanapasāraṇapaccayā atthānatthaṃ pariggaṇhitvā atthapariggaṇhanaṃ sātthakasampajaññaṃ. Tattha hatthapāde aticiraṃ samiñjitvā vā pasāretvā vā ṭhitassa khaṇe khaṇe vedanā uppajjanti, cittaṃ ekaggaṃ na labhati, kammaṭṭhānaṃ paripatati, visesaṃ nādhigacchati. Kāle samiñjantassa kāle pasārentassa pana tā vedanā nuppajjanti, cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti, kammaṭṭhānaṃ phātiṃ gacchati, visesamadhigacchatīti evaṃ atthānatthapariggaṇhanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

'In bending and stretching' means the bending and stretching of the joints. Therein, not bending and stretching merely by the power of the mind, but having discerned the benefit and harm from the bending and stretching of the hands and feet—this discernment of benefit is the clear comprehension of purpose. For one who remains with hands and feet bent or stretched for too long, feelings arise from moment to moment, the mind does not attain one-pointedness, the meditation subject falls away, and one does not attain any special state. But for one who bends at the proper time and stretches at the proper time, those feelings do not arise, the mind becomes one-pointed, the meditation subject prospers, and one attains a special state. Thus should the discernment of benefit and harm be understood.

Atthe pana satipi sappāyāsappāyaṃ pariggaṇhitvā sappāyapariggaṇhanaṃ sappāyasampajaññaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ nayo – mahācetiyaṅgaṇe kira daharabhikkhū sajjhāyaṃ gaṇhanti. Tesaṃ piṭṭhipasse daharabhikkhuniyo dhammaṃ suṇanti. Tattheko daharo hatthaṃ pasārento kāyasaṃsaggaṃ patvā teneva kāraṇena [V 3.0226] gihī jāto. Aparo bhikkhu pādaṃ pasārento aggimhi pasāresi, aṭṭhiṃ āhacca pādo jhāyi. Aparo vammike pasāresi, so āsīvisena daṭṭho. Aparo cīvarakuṭidaṇḍake pasāresi, taṃ maṇisappo ḍaṃsi. Tasmā evarūpe asappāye apasāretvā sappāye pasāretabbaṃ. Idamettha sappāyasampajaññaṃ.

Furthermore, even when there is a purpose, having discerned what is suitable and unsuitable, the discernment of what is suitable is the clear comprehension of suitability. Herein, this is the method: It is said that in the courtyard of the Great Cetiya, young monks were undertaking recitation. Behind them, young nuns were listening to the Dhamma. Therein, one young monk, stretching out his hand, made physical contact and for that very reason became dissatisfied and became a layman. Another monk, stretching out his foot, stretched it into a fire; the foot was burnt, reaching the bone. Another stretched it into an anthill and was bitten by a venomous snake. Another stretched it onto the robe-rack in a hut, and a maṇisappa snake bit him. Therefore, one should not stretch in such an unsuitable place, but should stretch in a suitable place. This, herein, is the clear comprehension of suitability.

Gocarasampajaññaṃ [P 3.0194] pana mahātheravatthunā dīpetabbaṃ – mahāthero kira divāṭṭhāne nisinno antevāsikehi saddhiṃ kathayamāno sahasā hatthaṃ [M 3.0229] samiñjitvā puna yathāṭhāne ṭhapetvā saṇikaṃ samiñjesi. Taṃ antevāsikā pucchiṃsu – “kasmā, bhante, sahasā hatthaṃ samiñjitvā puna yathāṭhāne ṭhapetvā saṇikaṃ samiñjitthā”ti. Yato paṭṭhāyāhaṃ, āvuso, kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikātuṃ āraddho, na me kammaṭṭhānaṃ muñcitvā hattho samiñjitapubbo, idāni pana tumhehi saddhiṃ kathayamānena kammaṭṭhānaṃ muñcitvā samiñjito, tasmā puna yathāṭhāne ṭhapetvā samiñjesinti. Sādhu, bhante, bhikkhunā nāma evarūpena bhavitabbanti. Evametthāpi kammaṭṭhānāvijahanameva gocarasampajaññanti veditabbaṃ.

The clear comprehension of the resort, furthermore, should be explained by the story of the great elder. It is said that a great elder, sitting in his day-quarters and conversing with his pupils, suddenly bent his hand, then placed it back in its original position and bent it again slowly. His pupils asked him: 'Venerable sir, why, having suddenly bent your hand, did you then place it back in its original position and bend it again slowly?' 'Friends, from the time I began to apply my mind to the meditation subject, my hand has never before been bent having let go of the meditation subject. But just now, while conversing with you, it was bent having let go of the meditation subject. Therefore, I placed it back in its original position and bent it again.' 'Excellent, venerable sir! A monk should indeed be of such a nature.' Thus, herein also, the non-abandonment of the meditation subject itself is the clear comprehension of the resort; so it should be understood.

Abbhantare attā nāma koci samiñjanto vā pasārento vā natthi, vuttappakāracittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphārena pana suttākaḍḍhanavasena dāruyantassa hatthapādalaḷanaṃ viya samiñjanapasāraṇaṃ hotīti parijānanaṃ panettha asammohasampajaññanti veditabbaṃ.

Internally, there is no so-called self that bends or stretches. However, bending and stretching occurs due to the impulse of the wind element born of mind-activity of the aforesaid kind, just like the movement of the hands and feet of a wooden puppet by way of the pulling of strings. The thorough understanding of this, herein, should be understood as the clear comprehension of non-delusion.

Saṅghāṭipattacīvaradhāraṇeti ettha saṅghāṭicīvarānaṃ nivāsanapārupanavasena, pattassa bhikkhāpaṭiggahaṇādivasena paribhogo dhāraṇaṃ nāma. Tattha saṅghāṭicīvaradhāraṇe tāva nivāsetvā pārupitvā ca piṇḍāya carato āmisalābho, “sītassa paṭighātāyā”tiādinā nayena bhagavatā vuttappakāroyeva ca attho attho nāma. Tassa vasena sātthakasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Herein, regarding 'the bearing of the saṅghāṭi, bowl, and robes': the use of the saṅghāṭi and robes by way of wearing and covering, and of the bowl by way of receiving alms-food and so forth, is called 'bearing'. Therein, with regard to the bearing of the saṅghāṭi and robes, firstly, for a monk who goes for alms-food having worn and covered himself with them, the acquisition of material requisites is one purpose; and the benefit of the kind spoken by the Blessed One by the method beginning with 'for the warding off of cold' is also a purpose. These are called 'purpose'. By means of these, the clear comprehension of purpose should be understood.

Uṇhapakatikassa pana dubbalassa ca cīvaraṃ sukhumaṃ sappāyaṃ, sītālukassa ghanaṃ dupaṭṭaṃ. Viparītaṃ asappāyaṃ. Yassa kassaci jiṇṇaṃ asappāyameva. Aggaḷādidānena hissa taṃ palibodhakaraṃ hoti. Tathā paṭṭuṇṇadukūlādibhedaṃ lobhanīyacīvaraṃ. Tādisañhi araññe ekakassa nivāsantarāyakaraṃ[P 3.0195], jīvitantarāyakarañcāpi hoti. Nippariyāyena pana yaṃ nimittakammādimicchājīvavasena uppannaṃ, yañcassa sevamānassa akusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, kusalā dhammā parihāyanti[V 3.0227], taṃ asappāyaṃ. Viparītaṃ sappāyaṃ, tassa vasenettha sappāyasampajaññaṃ, kammaṭṭhānāvijahanavaseneva ca gocarasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, for one of a hot constitution and for one who is weak, a thin robe is suitable; for one who is sensitive to cold, a thick, double-layered robe is suitable. The opposite is unsuitable. For anyone whatsoever, a worn-out robe is unsuitable, for by having to apply patches and so forth, it becomes an impediment for him. Likewise, a desirable robe of varieties such as silk from Paṭṭuṇṇa, fine linen, and so forth, is unsuitable. For such a robe is an obstacle to the dwelling of one who is alone in the forest, and it can also be an obstacle to life. Unconditionally, a robe that is produced by means of wrong livelihood such as hinting and so forth, and a robe which, for one using it, causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decline—that is unsuitable. The opposite is suitable. By means of that, the clear comprehension of suitability should be understood here. And by means of not abandoning the meditation subject, the clear comprehension of domain should be understood.

Abbhantare attā nāma koci cīvaraṃ pārupanto natthi, vuttappakāracittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāreneva pana cīvarapārupanaṃ hoti. Tattha cīvarampi [M 3.0230] acetanaṃ, kāyopi acetano. Cīvaraṃ na jānāti “mayā kāyo pārupito”ti. Kāyopi na jānāti “ahaṃ cīvarena pārupito”ti. Dhātuyova dhātusamūhaṃ paṭicchādenti paṭapilotikāya potthakarūpapaṭicchādane viya. Tasmā neva sundaraṃ cīvaraṃ labhitvā somanassaṃ kātabbaṃ, na asundaraṃ labhitvā domanassaṃ. Nāgavammikacetiyarukkhādīsu hi keci mālāgandhadhūmavatthādīhi sakkāraṃ karonti, keci gūthamuttakaddamadaṇḍasatthapahārādīhi asakkāraṃ. Na tehi nāgavammikarukkhādayo somanassaṃ vā karonti domanassaṃ vā. Evamevaṃ neva sundaraṃ cīvaraṃ labhitvā somanassaṃ kātabbaṃ, na asundaraṃ labhitvā domanassanti evaṃ pavattapaṭisaṅkhānavasenettha asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Internally, there is no 'self' whatsoever that puts on the robe. Rather, the putting on of the robe occurs only by the diffusion of the wind element produced by the action of mind of the aforesaid kind. Therein, the robe is insentient, and the body is also insentient. The robe does not know, 'The body is covered by me.' The body also does not know, 'I am covered by the robe.' The elements themselves cover the aggregate of elements, just as a worn-out cloth covers a wooden figure. Therefore, having obtained a beautiful robe, gladness should not be felt; having obtained an unattractive one, sadness should not be felt. For, at Nāga dwellings, anthills, shrines, trees, and so forth, some make offerings with garlands, perfumes, incense, cloth, etc., while others show disrespect with feces, urine, mud, sticks, weapon-strikes, etc. Because of these, the Nāga dwellings, trees, and so forth do not become gladdened or saddened. In the very same way, having obtained a beautiful robe, gladness should not be felt; having obtained an unattractive one, sadness should not be felt. Thus, by means of reflection that proceeds in this way, the clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood here.

Pattadhāraṇepi pattaṃ sahasāva aggahetvā – “imaṃ gahetvā piṇḍāya caramāno bhikkhaṃ labhissāmī”ti evaṃ pattaggahaṇapaccayā paṭilabhitabbaatthavasena sātthakasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ. Kisadubbalasarīrassa pana garupatto asappāyo. Yassa kassaci catupañcagaṇṭhikāhato dubbisodhanīyo asappāyova. Duddhotapatto hi na vaṭṭati, taṃ dhovantasseva cassa palibodho hoti. Maṇivaṇṇapatto pana lobhanīyo cīvare vuttanayeneva asappāyo. Nimittakammādivasena laddho, pana yañcassa sevamānassa akusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, kusalā dhammā parihāyanti, ayaṃ ekantaasappāyova. Viparīto sappāyo. Tassa vasenettha sappāyasampajaññaṃ, kammaṭṭhānāvijahanavaseneva ca gocarasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Also in the bearing of the bowl, not taking the bowl hastily, but reflecting, 'Taking this and going for alms, I will get alms-food'—thus, by means of the purpose to be obtained because of taking the bowl, the clear comprehension of purpose should be understood. Furthermore, for one with a lean and weak body, a heavy bowl is unsuitable. For anyone whatsoever, a bowl that is patched four or five times and is difficult to clean is unsuitable. For a bowl that is difficult to wash is not allowable, as it becomes an impediment for him just when he is washing it. A bowl the color of a gem is desirable and is unsuitable in the same way as stated for the robe. Furthermore, a bowl obtained by means of hinting and so forth, and a bowl which, for one using it, causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decline—this is entirely unsuitable. The opposite is suitable. By means of that, the clear comprehension of suitability should be understood here. And by means of not abandoning the meditation subject, the clear comprehension of domain should be understood.

Abbhantare attā nāma koci pattaṃ gaṇhanto natthi, vuttappakāracittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāreneva pattaggahaṇaṃ [P 3.0196] nāma hoti. Tattha pattopi acetano, hatthāpi acetanā. Patto na jānāti “ahaṃ hatthehi gahito”ti. Hatthāpi na jānanti “patto amhehi gahito”ti. Dhātuyova dhātusamūhaṃ gaṇhanti, saṇḍāsena aggivaṇṇapattaggahaṇe viyāti evaṃ pavattapaṭisaṅkhānavasenettha asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Internally, there is no one called 'self' who takes the bowl; the taking of the bowl occurs only by the diffusion of the wind element produced by the action of mind of the aforesaid kind. Therein, the bowl is insentient, and the hands are also insentient. The bowl does not know, 'I am taken by the hands.' The hands also do not know, 'The bowl is taken by us.' The elements themselves take the aggregate of elements, just as a fire-colored vessel is taken with tongs. Thus, by means of reflection that proceeds in this way, the clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood here.

Apica [V 3.0228] yathā chinnahatthapāde vaṇamukhehi paggharitapubbalohitakimikule nīlamakkhikasamparikiṇṇe anāthasālāya anāthamanusse disvā dayālukā purisā tesaṃ vaṇapaṭṭacoḷakāni ceva kapālādīhi bhesajjāni ca upanāmenti. Tattha coḷakānipi kesañci saṇhāni, kesañci thūlāni pāpuṇanti, bhesajjakapālānipi kesañci susaṇṭhānāni, kesañci [M 3.0231] dussaṇṭhānāni pāpuṇanti, na te tattha sumanā vā dummanā vā honti. Vaṇapaṭicchādanamatteneva hi coḷakena bhesajjapaṭiggahamatteneva ca kapālakena tesaṃ attho. Evameva yo bhikkhu vaṇacoḷakaṃ viya cīvaraṃ, bhesajjakapālakaṃ viya ca pattaṃ, kapāle bhesajjamiva ca patte laddhabhikkhaṃ sallakkheti. Ayaṃ saṅghāṭipattacīvaradhāraṇe asammohasampajaññena uttamasampajānakārīti veditabbo.

Furthermore, it is as when compassionate men, seeing helpless people in a hall for the helpless—with hands and feet cut off, with pus, blood, and swarms of worms oozing from the openings of their wounds, and covered with bluebottles—bring to them strips of cloth for their wounds and medicines in potsherds and so forth. Therein, some receive fine strips of cloth, while others receive coarse ones; some receive well-formed medicine potsherds, while others receive ill-formed ones. Yet they are neither gladdened nor saddened by this. For their purpose is met with a strip of cloth merely for covering the wound, and with a potsherd merely for receiving the medicine. In the very same way is the monk who regards the robe like a bandage for a wound, the bowl like a medicine potsherd, and the alms-food obtained in the bowl like medicine in a potsherd. This one should be known as a supreme practitioner of clear comprehension, with the clear comprehension of non-delusion in the bearing of the double-layered robe, bowl, and robes.

Asitādīsu asiteti piṇḍapātabhojane. Pīteti yāguādipāne. Khāyiteti piṭṭhakhajjakādikhādane. Sāyiteti madhuphāṇitādisāyane. Tattha “neva davāyā”tiādinā nayena vutto aṭṭhavidhopi attho attho nāma, tassa vasena sātthakasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Regarding 'eaten' and so forth: 'Eaten' refers to the eating of alms-food. 'Drunk' refers to the drinking of gruel and so forth. 'Chewed' refers to the eating of flour-cakes, hard foods, and so forth. 'Savored' refers to the savoring of honey, molasses, and so forth. Therein, the eightfold purpose spoken of by the method beginning with 'not for amusement' is called 'purpose'. By means of that, the clear comprehension of purpose should be understood.

Lūkhapaṇītatittamadhurādīsu pana yena bhojanena yassa aphāsu hoti, taṃ tassa asappāyaṃ. Yaṃ pana nimittakammādivasena paṭiladdhaṃ, yañcassa bhuñjato akusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, kusalā dhammā parihāyanti, taṃ ekantaasappāyameva. Viparītaṃ sappāyaṃ. Tassa vasenettha sappāyasampajaññaṃ, kammaṭṭhānāvijahanavaseneva ca gocarasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, among coarse, refined, bitter, sweet, and other kinds of food, whatever food causes discomfort to a certain monk, that is unsuitable for him. Indeed, whatever food is obtained by means of hinting and so on, and that food which, when being eaten by a monk, causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decline—that is entirely unsuitable. The opposite is suitable. By means of that, the clear comprehension of suitability should be understood herein. And, by means of not abandoning the meditation subject, the clear comprehension of domain should be understood.

Abbhantare attā nāma koci bhuñjako natthi, vuttappakāracittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāreneva pattapaṭiggahaṇaṃ nāma hoti, cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāreneva [P 3.0197] hatthassa patte otāraṇaṃ nāma hoti, cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāreneva ālopakaraṇaṃ ālopuddharaṇaṃ mukhavivaraṇañca hoti. Na koci kuñcikāya na yantakena hanukaṭṭhīni vivarati, cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāreneva ālopassa mukhe ṭhapanaṃ uparidantānaṃ musalakiccasādhanaṃ heṭṭhādantānaṃ udukkhalakiccasādhanaṃ jivhāya hatthakiccasādhanañca hoti. Iti naṃ tattha aggajivhāya tanukakheḷo, mūlajivhāya bahalakheḷo makkheti. Taṃ heṭṭhādantaudukkhale jivhāhatthaparivattitaṃ kheḷaudakatemitaṃ uparidantamusalasañcuṇṇitaṃ koci kaṭacchunā vā dabbiyā vā anto pavesento nāma natthi, vāyodhātuyāva pavisati. Paviṭṭhaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ koci palālasantharaṃ katvā dhārento nāma natthi, vāyodhātuvaseneva [V 3.0229] tiṭṭhati. Ṭhitaṃ ṭhitaṃ koci uddhanaṃ katvā aggiṃ jāletvā pacanto nāma natthi, tejodhātuyāva paccati. Pakkaṃ pakkaṃ koci daṇḍakena vā yaṭṭhiyā vā bahi nīharako nāma natthi, vāyodhātuyeva nīharati. Iti vāyodhātu atiharati ca vītiharati ca [M 3.0232] dhāreti ca parivatteti ca sañcuṇṇeti ca visoseti ca nīharati ca; pathavīdhātu dhāreti ca parivatteti ca sañcuṇṇeti ca visoseti ca; āpodhātu sineheti ca allattañca anupāleti; tejodhātu antopaviṭṭhaṃ paripāceti; ākāsadhātu añjaso hoti; viññāṇadhātu tattha tattha sammāpayogamanvāya ābhujatīti evaṃ pavattapaṭisaṅkhānavasenettha asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Internally, there is no eater called 'self'; the receiving of the bowl occurs only through the diffusion of the wind element produced by a functional consciousness of the aforesaid kind. The lowering of the hand into the bowl occurs only through the diffusion of the wind element produced by a functional consciousness. The making of a morsel, the lifting of the morsel, and the opening of the mouth occur only through the diffusion of the wind element produced by a functional consciousness. No one opens the jawbones with a key or a machine; it is only through the diffusion of the wind element produced by a functional consciousness that the placing of the morsel in the mouth, the upper teeth's performing of the pestle's function, the lower teeth's performing of the mortar's function, and the tongue's performing of the hand's function occur. Thus, it is smeared there with thin saliva by the tip of the tongue and with thick saliva by the root of the tongue. That food, turned about by the tongue-hand in the lower-teeth-mortar, moistened by the water of saliva, and ground up by the upper-teeth-pestle, is not made to enter inside by anyone with a spoon or a ladle; it enters only by means of the wind element. Having entered, it is not held by anyone having made a straw matting; it stays only by the power of the wind element. Having stayed, it is not cooked by anyone having made a hearth and lit a fire; it is digested only by the fire element. Having been digested, it is not expelled by anyone with a stick or a rod; it is the wind element itself that expels it. Thus, the wind element conveys it towards, conveys it through, holds it, turns it about, grinds it up, dries it out, and expels it. The earth element holds it, turns it about, grinds it up, and dries it out. The water element moistens it and maintains its wetness. The fire element digests what has entered within. The space element provides an opening. The consciousness element, depending on the right application in each case, comprehends. In this way, the clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood herein by means of reflection on this process.

Apica gamanato, pariyesanato, paribhogato, āsayato, nidhānato, aparipakkato, paripakkato, phalato, nissandato, sammakkhanatoti evaṃ dasavidhaṃ paṭikūlabhāvaṃ paccavekkhaṇatopettha asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ. Vitthārakathā panettha visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.294 ādayo) āhārapaṭikūlasaññāniddesato gahetabbā.

Furthermore, the clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood herein also by reflecting on the state of repulsiveness in ten ways: by way of going, seeking, consuming, the receptacle, storing, being undigested, being digested, the result, the outflow, and being smeared. The detailed explanation on this should be taken from the exposition on the perception of the repulsiveness in food in the Visuddhimagga.

Uccārapassāvakammeti uccārassa ca passāvassa ca karaṇe. Tattha pattakāle uccārapassāvaṃ akarontassa sakalasarīrato sedā muccanti, akkhīni bhamanti, cittaṃ na ekaggaṃ hoti, aññe ca rogā uppajjanti. Karontassa pana sabbaṃ taṃ na hotīti ayamettha attho. Tassa vasena [P 3.0198] sātthakasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ. Aṭṭhāne uccārapassāvaṃ karontassa pana āpatti hoti, ayaso vaḍḍhati, jīvitantarāyopi hoti. Patirūpe ṭhāne karontassa sabbaṃ taṃ na hotīti idamettha sappāyaṃ. Tassa vasena sappāyasampajaññaṃ, kammaṭṭhānāvijahanavasena ca gocarasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

'The act of defecation and urination' means in the doing of defecation and urination. Therein, for one who does not defecate or urinate at the proper time, sweat is released from the entire body, the eyes spin, the mind does not become concentrated, and other diseases arise. But for one who does so, none of that happens. This is the purpose herein. By means of that, the clear comprehension of purposefulness should be understood. Furthermore, for one who defecates or urinates in an unsuitable place, there is an offense, disrepute increases, and there can even be danger to life. For one who does so in a suitable place, none of that happens. This is the suitability herein. By means of that, the clear comprehension of suitability should be understood, and by means of not abandoning the meditation subject, the clear comprehension of the resort should be understood.

Abbhantare attā nāma koci uccārapassāvakammaṃ karonto natthi, cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāreneva pana uccārapassāvakammaṃ hoti. Yathā pana pakke gaṇḍe gaṇḍabhedena pubbalohitaṃ akāmatāya nikkhamati, yathā ca atibharitā udakabhājanā udakaṃ akāmatāya nikkhamati, evaṃ pakkāsayamuttavatthīsu sannicitā uccārapassāvā vāyuvegasamuppīḷitā akāmatāyapi nikkhamanti. So panāyaṃ evaṃ nikkhamanto uccārapassāvo neva tassa bhikkhuno attano hoti na parassa, kevalaṃ sarīranissandova hoti. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā udakatumbato [V 3.0230] purāṇaudakaṃ chaḍḍentassa neva taṃ attano hoti na paresaṃ, kevalaṃ paṭijagganamattameva hoti. Evaṃ pavattapaṭisaṅkhānavasenettha asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Internally, there is no one called 'self' performing the act of defecation and urination; rather, the act of defecation and urination occurs only through the diffusion of the wind element produced by a functional consciousness. Just as pus and blood exit from a ripe boil when it is lanced, against one's will, and just as water spills from an overfilled water vessel, against one's will, so too the feces and urine accumulated in the rectum and bladder, being compressed by the force of the wind element, are expelled even against one's will. This feces and urine thus expelled belongs neither to that monk himself nor to another; it is merely a bodily outflow. How so? It is like old water being discarded from a water gourd: it belongs neither to oneself nor to others; it is merely a matter of cleaning. Thus, by means of reflection on this process, the clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood herein.

Gatādīsu [M 3.0233] gateti gamane. Ṭhiteti ṭhāne. Nisinneti nisajjāya. Sutteti sayane. Jāgarite ti jāgaraṇe. Bhāsiteti kathane. Tuṇhībhāveti akathane. Ettha ca yo ciraṃ gantvā vā caṅkamitvā vā aparabhāge ṭhito iti paṭisañcikkhati “caṅkamanakāle [P 3.0199] pavattā rūpārūpadhammā ettheva niruddhā”ti, ayaṃ gate sampajānakārī nāma.

Regarding 'gone' and so on: 'gone' means in the context of going; 'stood' in the context of standing; 'sat' in the context of sitting; 'asleep' in the context of sleeping; 'awake' in the context of being awake; 'spoken' in the context of speaking; 'being silent' in the context of not speaking. And herein, a monk who, after having gone or walked back and forth for a long time, stands and then reflects thus: 'The corporeal and incorporeal phenomena that occurred during the time of walking back and forth have ceased right here'—this one is called one who acts with clear comprehension in regard to going.

Yo sajjhāyaṃ vā karonto pañhaṃ vā vissajjento kammaṭṭhānaṃ vā manasikaronto ciraṃ ṭhatvā aparabhāge nisinno iti paṭisañcikkhati “ṭhitakāle pavattā rūpārūpadhammā ettheva niruddhā”ti, ayaṃ ṭhite sampajānakārī nāma.

A monk who, while making recitation, answering a question, or applying the mind to a meditation subject, stands for a long time and afterwards, being seated, reflects thus: 'The corporeal and incorporeal phenomena that occurred during the time of standing have ceased right here'—this one is called one who acts with clear comprehension in regard to standing.

Yo sajjhāyādikaraṇavaseneva ciraṃ nisīditvā aparabhāge nipanno iti paṭisañcikkhati – “nisinnakāle pavattā rūpārūpadhammā ettheva niruddhā”ti, ayaṃ nisinne sampajānakārī nāma.

A monk who, having sat for a long time for the purpose of recitation and so on, afterwards lies down and reflects thus: 'The corporeal and incorporeal phenomena that occurred during the time of sitting have ceased right here'—this one is called one who acts with clear comprehension in regard to sitting.

Yo pana nipannakova sajjhāyaṃ karonto kammaṭṭhānaṃ vā manasikaronto niddaṃ okkamitvā aparabhāge uṭṭhāya iti paṭisañcikkhati – “sayanakāle pavattā rūpārūpadhammā ettheva niruddhā”ti, ayaṃ sutte ca jāgarite ca sampajānakārī nāma. Kiriyamayacittānañhi appavattaṃ suttaṃ nāma, pavattaṃ jāgaritaṃ nāmāti.

Furthermore, a monk who, while lying down, is reciting or attending to a meditation subject, falls asleep, and upon arising later reflects thus: 'The corporeal and incorporeal phenomena that occurred at the time of lying down have ceased right here'—this one is called one who acts with clear comprehension in sleeping and in waking. Indeed, the non-occurrence of functional consciousness is called sleep, and its occurrence is called wakefulness.

Yo pana bhāsamāno – “ayaṃ saddo nāma oṭṭhe ca paṭicca dante ca jivhañca tāluñca paṭicca cittassa ca tadanurūpaṃ payogaṃ paṭicca jāyatī”ti sato sampajāno bhāsati, ciraṃ vā pana kālaṃ sajjhāyaṃ katvā dhammaṃ vā kathetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ vā parivattetvā pañhaṃ vā vissajjetvā aparabhāge tuṇhībhūto iti paṭisañcikkhati “bhāsitakāle uppannā rūpārūpadhammā ettheva niruddhā”ti ayaṃ bhāsite sampajānakārī nāma.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu who, while speaking, speaks mindfully and with clear comprehension, reflecting: 'This sound arises dependent on the lips, the teeth, the tongue, and the palate, and dependent on the mind and an appropriate effort corresponding to it'; or who, having recited for a long time, or taught the Dhamma, or reviewed a meditation subject, or answered a question, then, being silent, reflects thus: 'The material and immaterial phenomena that arose at the time of speaking have ceased right here'—this one is called one who acts with clear comprehension regarding speaking.

Yo tuṇhībhūto ciraṃ dhammaṃ vā kammaṭṭhānaṃ vā manasikatvā aparabhāge iti paṭisañcikkhati [V 3.0231] – “tuṇhībhūtakāle pavattā rūpārūpadhammā ettheva niruddhā”ti. Upādārūpapavattiyā sati bhāsati nāma, asati tuṇhī bhavati nāmāti, ayaṃ tuṇhībhāve sampajānakārī nāmāti. Evamettha asammohasampajaññaṃ tassa vasena sampajānakāritā veditabbā. Imasmiṃ sutte satipaṭṭhānamissakasampajaññaṃ pubbabhāgaṃ kathitaṃ.

A bhikkhu who, being silent, attends to the Dhamma or a meditation subject for a long time and later reflects thus: 'The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred at the time of being silent have ceased right here.' When there is an occurrence of derived materiality, it is called speaking; when there is not, it is called being silent. This one is called one who acts with clear comprehension regarding silence. Thus, here, the state of acting with clear comprehension should be understood by means of clear comprehension free from delusion. In this discourse, the preliminary-part clear comprehension mixed with the foundations of mindfulness has been explained.

3. Bhikkhusuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Bhikkhu Sutta

369. Tatiye [M 3.0234] evameva panidhekacceti so kira bhikkhu kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathāpetvā ito cito ca āhiṇḍati, kāyavivekaṃ nānuyuñjati. Tena naṃ bhagavā niggaṇhanto evamāha. Tasmāti yasmā saṃkhittena desanaṃ yācasi, tasmā. Diṭṭhīti kammassakatādiṭṭhi.

369. In the third discourse, regarding 'evameva panidhekacce': it is said that bhikkhu, having had a meditation subject explained, wanders here and there and does not apply himself to bodily seclusion. For that reason, the Blessed One, wishing to rebuke him, spoke thus. 'Tasmā' means: because you request a teaching in brief, therefore. 'Diṭṭhi' means the view of kamma as one's own property.

4. Sālasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Sāla Sutta

370. Catutthe [P 3.0200] dhammavinayoti dhammoti vā vinayoti vā ubhayametaṃ satthusāsanasseva nāmaṃ. Samādapetabbāti gaṇhāpetabbā. Ekodibhūtāti khaṇikasamādhinā ekaggabhūtā. Samāhitā ekaggacittāti upacārappanāvasena sammā ṭhapitacittā ca ekaggacittā ca. Imasmiṃ sutte navakabhikkhūhi ceva khīṇāsavehi ca bhāvitasatipaṭṭhānā pubbabhāgā, sattahi sekhehi bhāvitā missakā.

370. In the fourth discourse, 'dhammavinayo': both 'Dhamma' and 'Vinaya' are names for the Teacher’s Dispensation itself. 'Samādapetabbā' means they should be made to grasp. 'Ekodibhūtā' means become one-pointed through momentary concentration. 'Samāhitā ekaggacittā' means having the mind well-established and one-pointed by means of access and absorption concentration. In this discourse, for new bhikkhus and for those whose taints are destroyed, the developed foundations of mindfulness are the preliminary part; for the seven trainees, those developed are mixed.

6. Sakuṇagghisuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Sakuṇagghi Sutta

372. Chaṭṭhe sakuṇagghīti sakuṇaṃ hanatīti sakuṇagghi, senassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sahasā ajjhapattāti lobhasāhasena pattā. Alakkhikāti nissirikā. Appapuññāti parittapuññā. Sacejja mayanti sace ajja mayaṃ. Naṅgalakaṭṭhakaraṇanti naṅgalena kasikaraṇaṃ, adhunā kaṭṭhaṃ khettaṭṭhānanti attho. Leḍḍuṭṭhānanti leḍḍūnaṃ ṭhānaṃ. Saṃvadamānāti sammā vadamānā, attano balassa suṭṭhu vaṇṇaṃ vadamānāti attho. Mahantaṃ leḍḍuṃ abhiruhitvāti uddhanasaṇṭhānena ṭhitesu tīsu leḍḍūsu “ito sene āgacchante ito nikkhamissāmi, ito āgacchante ito”ti sallakkhetvā tesu ekaṃ leḍḍuṃ abhiruhitvā aṭṭhāsi avadamāno. Sannayhāti khurappaṃ sannayhamāno viya sannayhitvā [V 3.0232] suṭṭhu ṭhapetvā. Bahuāgato kho myāyanti “mayhaṃ atthāya ayaṃ bahutaṃ ṭhānaṃ āgato, appaṃ avasiṭṭhaṃ, idāni maṃ gaṇhissatī”ti ñatvā dāruguḷo viya vinivattitvā tasseva leḍḍussa antare paccupādi, paṭipanno paviṭṭhoti attho. Uraṃ paccatāḷesīti “ekappahāreneva [P 3.0201] lāpassa sīsaṃ chinditvā gahessāmī”ti [M 3.0235] pakkhandattā vegaṃ sandhāretuṃ asakkonto tasmiṃ leḍḍusmiṃ uraṃ patāḷesi. Tāvadevassa hadayamaṃsaṃ phāliyittha. Atha lāpo “diṭṭhā vata sattuno piṭṭhī”ti haṭṭhatuṭṭho tassa hadaye aparāparaṃ caṅkami.

372. In the sixth sutta, sakuṇagghi means one who harms birds; therefore, it is called sakuṇagghi. This is a designation for a hawk (sena). Sahasā ajjhapattā means it came upon with greedy violence. Alakkhikā means without splendor. Appapuññā means of little merit. Sacejja mayanti means 'if today we.' Naṅgalakaṭṭhakaraṇanti means a place for plowing with a plow; the meaning is a plowed field. Leḍḍuṭṭhānanti means a place of clods. Saṃvadamānāti means speaking well; the meaning is proclaiming the quality of its own strength. Mahantaṃ leḍḍuṃ abhiruhitvāti means: among three clods standing in the shape of a tripod stove, having noted, 'If the hawk comes from this direction, I will exit from this direction; if it comes from that direction, I will exit from that one,' it climbed onto one of those clods and stood there, speaking defiantly. Sannayhāti means having braced itself well, like one fitting a sharp-bladed arrow, and having positioned itself well. Bahuāgato kho myāyanti means: knowing, 'For my sake, this one has come a great distance; little remains. Now it will seize me,' it turned back as if it were a wooden ball and entered the space within that very clod; the meaning is it entered and went in. Uraṃ paccatāḷesīti means: thinking, 'I will seize the quail after cutting off its head with a single strike,' and because of rushing forward, being unable to check its momentum, it struck its chest against that clod. At that very moment, its heart-flesh burst. Then the quail, pleased and delighted, thinking, 'Ah, the back of the enemy is seen!', walked back and forth upon its heart.

7. Makkaṭasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Makkaṭa Sutta

373. Sattame duggāti duggamā. Cārīti sañcāro. Lepaṃ oḍḍentīti vaṭarukkhakhīrādīhi yojetvā lepaṃ karonti, taṃ makkaṭānaṃ dhuvagamanaṭṭhānanti sallakkhetvā rukkhasākhādīsu ṭhapenti. Pañcoḍḍitoti pañcasu ṭhānesu kājadaṇḍakaṃ pavesetvā gahetabbā kājasikkā viya oḍḍito. Thunaṃ setīti thunanto sayati.

373. In the seventh sutta, duggā means difficult to traverse. Cārīti means movement. Lepaṃ oḍḍentīti means having combined it with banyan sap and so on, they make a sticky paste; recognizing a place as one regularly visited by monkeys, they place it on tree branches and so on. Pañcoḍḍitoti means being caught in five places, like a carrying-net that is held by inserting a carrying-pole. Thunaṃ setīti means it lies groaning.

8. Sūdasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Sūda Sutta

374. Aṭṭhame sūdoti bhattakārako. Nānaccayehīti nānācayehi, nānāvidhehīti attho. Ayameva vā pāṭho. Ambilaggehīti ambilakoṭṭhāsehi. Eseva nayo sabbattha. Abhiharatīti gahaṇatthāya hatthaṃ pasāreti. Bahuṃ gaṇhātīti ekaggahaṇena bahuṃ gaṇhantopi punappunaṃ gaṇhantopi bahuṃ gaṇhateva. Abhihārānanti sataṃ vā sahassaṃ vā ukkhipitvā abhihaṭānaṃ dāyānaṃ. Upakkilesāti pañca nīvaraṇā. Nimittaṃ na uggaṇhātīti “imaṃ me kammaṭṭhānaṃ anulomaṃ vā gotrabhuṃ vā āhacca ṭhita”nti na jānāti, attano cittassa nimittaṃ gaṇhituṃ na sakkoti. Imasmiṃ sutte pubbabhāgavipassanā satipaṭṭhānāva kathitā.

374. In the eighth sutta, sūdo means a cook. Nānaccayehīti means with various kinds; the meaning is with diverse types. Or this latter reading is the original text itself. Ambilaggehīti means with sour portions. This same method should be understood in all such passages. Abhiharatīti means he extends his hand for the purpose of taking. Bahuṃ gaṇhātīti means whether taking much in a single grasp, or taking again and again, he indeed takes much. Abhihārānanti means of rewards brought forth to be given, having lifted up a hundred or a thousand. Upakkilesāti means the five hindrances. Nimittaṃ na uggaṇhātīti means he does not know, 'This meditation subject of mine has reached and is established in conformity knowledge or change-of-lineage knowledge,' and he is unable to grasp the sign of his own mind. In this sutta, only the foundations of mindfulness that are insight belonging to the preliminary part have been taught.

9. Gilānasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Gilāna Sutta

375. Navame beḷuvagāmaketi vesāliyā samīpe evaṃnāmako pādagāmo atthi, tasmiṃ. Yathāmittantiādīsu mittāti mittāva. Sandiṭṭhāti tattha tattha saṅgamma diṭṭhamattā nātidaḷhamittā[V 3.0233]. Sambhattāti suṭṭhu bhattā sinehavanto daḷhamittā. Yesaṃ yattha yattha evarūpā bhikkhū atthi, te tattha tattha vassaṃ upethāti attho. Kasmā evamāha? Tesaṃ phāsuvihāratthāya. Tesaṃ [P 3.0202] kira beḷuvagāmake senāsanaṃ nappahoti, bhikkhāpi [M 3.0236] mandā. Samantā vesāliyā pana bahūni senāsanāni, bhikkhāpi sulabhā. Tasmā evamāha.

375. In the ninth: beḷuvagāmake means there is a suburban village of that name near Vesālī; in that place. In the passage beginning yathāmittanti: mittāti means simply friends. Sandiṭṭhāti means those merely seen from meeting here and there, not very firm friends. Sambhattāti means well-devoted, affectionate, firm friends. The meaning is: wherever bhikkhus have such friends, they should spend the rains retreat in that place. Why did He say this? For the sake of their comfortable dwelling. It is said that in Beḷuvagāmaka, their lodging was not sufficient and alms-food was scarce. But around Vesālī, there were many lodgings and alms-food was easy to obtain. Therefore, He said this.

Atha kasmā “yathāsukhaṃ gacchathā”ti na vissajjesi? Tesaṃ anukampāya. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “ahaṃ dasamāsamattaṃ ṭhatvā parinibbāyissāmi. Sace ime dūraṃ gacchissanti, maṃ parinibbānakāle daṭṭhuṃ na sakkhissanti. Atha nesaṃ ‘satthā parinibbāyanto amhākaṃ satimattampi na adāsi. Sace jāneyyāma, na evaṃ dūre vaseyyāmā’ti vippaṭisāro bhaveyya. Vesāliyā samantā pana vassaṃ vasantā māsassa aṭṭha vāre āgantvā dhammaṃ suṇissanti, sugatovādaṃ labhissantī”ti na vissajjesi.

Then why did He not dismiss them, saying, “Go as you please”? Out of compassion for them. It is said that this thought occurred to Him: “I will attain parinibbāna after staying for about ten months. If these monks go far away, they will not be able to see me at the time of my parinibbāna. Then they might have regret, thinking: ‘The Teacher, while attaining parinibbāna, did not give us even a reminder. If we had known, we would not have stayed so far away.’ But if they spend the rains retreat around Vesālī, they will come eight times a month to listen to the Dhamma and receive the Sugata’s instruction.” For this reason, He did not dismiss them.

Kharoti pharuso. Ābādhoti visabhāgarogo. Bāḷhāti balavatiyo. Māraṇantikāti maraṇantaṃ maraṇasantikaṃ pāpanasamatthā. Sato sampajāno adhivāsesīti satiṃ sūpaṭṭhitaṃ katvā ñāṇena paricchinditvā adhivāsesi. Avihaññamānoti vedanānuvattanavasena aparāparaṃ parivattanaṃ akaronto apīḷiyamāno adukkhiyamāno ca adhivāsesi. Anāmantetvāti ajānāpetvā. Anapaloketvāti ajānāpetvāva ovādānusāsaniṃ adatvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Vīriyenāti pubbabhāgavīriyena ceva phalasamāpattivīriyena ca. Paṭipaṇāmetvāti vikkhambhetvā. Jīvitasaṅkhāranti ettha jīvitampi jīvitasaṅkhāro. Yena jīvitaṃ saṅkharīyati chijjamānaṃ ghaṭetvā ṭhapīyati, so phalasamāpattidhammopi jīvitasaṅkhāro. So idha adhippeto. Adhiṭṭhāyāti adhiṭṭhahitvā pavattetvā jīvitaṭhapanasamatthaṃ phalasamāpattiṃ samāpajjeyyanti ayamettha saṅkhepattho.

Kharo means harsh. Ābādho means an incompatible illness. Bāḷhā means strong. Māraṇantikā means capable of bringing one to the end of life, to the vicinity of death. Sato sampajāno adhivāsesi means having made mindfulness well-established and having discerned with knowledge, He endured. Avihaññamāno means He endured without tossing and turning from side to side due to the succession of feelings, not being oppressed or pained. Anāmantetvā means without informing. Anapaloketvā means without having given notice by way of a final exhortation and instruction; this is what is meant. Vīriyena means by both the energy of the preliminary part and the energy of the fruition attainment. Paṭipaṇāmetvā means having suppressed. Regarding jīvitasaṅkhāra: here, life itself is a life-formation. Also, that principle of fruition attainment by which life is constructed and established so that it is not cut off is a life-formation. It is this latter one that is intended here. Adhiṭṭhāya means: having resolved and brought it about, thinking, 'May I attain the fruition attainment that is capable of establishing life.' This is the brief meaning here.

Kiṃ pana bhagavā ito pubbe phalasamāpattiṃ na samāpajjatīti? Samāpajjati. Sā pana khaṇikasamāpatti. Khaṇikasamāpatti ca antosamāpattiyaṃyeva vedanaṃ vikkhambheti, samāpattito vuṭṭhitamattassa kaṭṭhapātena vā kaṭhalapātena vā chinnasevālo viya udakaṃ, puna sarīraṃ vedanā ajjhottharati. Yā pana rūpasattakaṃ arūpasattakañca niggumbaṃ nijjaṭaṃ katvā mahāvipassanāvasena samāpannā samāpatti[P 3.0203], sā suṭṭhu vikkhambheti. Yathā nāma purisena pokkharaṇiṃ ogāhetvā hatthehi ca pādehi ca suṭṭhu apabyuḷhasevālo [M 3.0237] cirena udakaṃ ottharati, evameva [V 3.0234] tato vuṭṭhitassa cirena vedanā uppajjati. Iti bhagavā taṃdivasaṃ mahābodhipallaṅke abhinavaṃ vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapento viya rūpasattakaṃ arūpasattakañca niggumbaṃ nijjaṭaṃ katvā cuddasahākārehi sannetvā mahāvipassanāya vedanaṃ vikkhambhetvā “dasamāse mā uppajjitthā”ti samāpattiṃ samāpajji, samāpattivikkhambhitā vedanā dasa māse na uppajjiyeva.

But did the Blessed One not enter fruition attainment before this? He did. However, that was a momentary attainment. A momentary attainment suppresses feeling only while within the attainment; for one who has just emerged from the attainment, feeling overwhelms the body again, like water covering moss that has been parted by the fall of a piece of wood or a potsherd. But the attainment entered by the power of great insight—having made the meditation on the sevenfold material group and the sevenfold immaterial group free of bushes and tangles—suppresses it well. Just as when a man has descended into a pond and thoroughly cleared away the moss with his hands and feet, the water covers it again only after a long time, so too for one who has emerged from that attainment, feeling arises only after a long time. Thus, on that day, the Blessed One, as if establishing new insight on the seat of great awakening, made the meditation on the sevenfold material group and the sevenfold immaterial group free of bushes and tangles, made it cohesive with the fourteen modes, suppressed the feeling with great insight, and entered the attainment with the resolution, 'May it not arise for ten months.' The feeling, suppressed by the attainment, did not arise at all for ten months.

Gilānā vuṭṭhitoti gilāno hutvā puna vuṭṭhito. Madhurakajāto viyāti sañjātagarubhāvo sañjātathaddhabhāvo sūle uttāsitapuriso viya. Na pakkhāyantīti na pakāsanti, nānākārato na upaṭṭhahanti. Dhammāpi maṃ nappaṭibhantīti satipaṭṭhānadhammā mayhaṃ pākaṭā na hontīti dīpeti. Tantidhammā pana therassa suppaguṇā. Na udāharatīti pacchimaovādaṃ na deti, taṃ sandhāya vadati.

Gilānā vuṭṭhito means having been ill, he has recovered. Madhurakajāto viya means a state of heaviness and stiffness has arisen, like a man impaled on a stake. Na pakkhāyanti means they do not appear clearly, they do not present themselves in various ways. Dhammāpi maṃ nappaṭibhanti indicates: 'The principles of the foundations of mindfulness are not clear to me.' The textual teachings, however, were well-mastered by the Elder. Na udāharati means he does not yet give the final exhortation; he speaks with reference to that.

Anantaraṃ abāhiranti dhammavasena vā puggalavasena vā ubhayaṃ akatvā. “Ettakaṃ dhammaṃ parassa na desessāmī”ti hi cintento dhammaṃ abbhantaraṃ karoti nāma, “ettakaṃ parassa desessāmī”ti cintento bāhiraṃ karoti nāma. “Imassa puggalassa desessāmī”ti cintento pana puggalaṃ abbhantaraṃ karoti nāma, “imassa na desessāmī”ti cintento puggalaṃ bāhiraṃ karoti nāma. Evaṃ akatvā desitoti attho. Ācariyamuṭṭhīti yathā bāhirakānaṃ ācariyamuṭṭhi nāma hoti, daharakāle kassaci akathetvā pacchimakāle maraṇamañce nipannā piyamanāpassa antevāsikassa kathenti, evaṃ tathāgatassa “idaṃ mahallakakāle pacchimaṭhāne kathessāmī”ti muṭṭhiṃ katvā pariharitvā ṭhapitaṃ kiñci natthīti [P 3.0204] dasseti.

Anantaraṃ abāhiraṃ means without making a distinction between internal and external, either with respect to the Dhamma or with respect to persons. For one who thinks, 'I will not teach this much Dhamma to another,' is said to make the Dhamma internal. One who thinks, 'I will teach this much to another,' is said to make it external. Likewise, one who thinks, 'I will teach this person,' is said to make the person internal. One who thinks, 'I will not teach this person,' is said to make the person external. The meaning is that the Dhamma was taught without making any such distinction. As for ācariyamuṭṭhi (the teacher's fist): just as teachers outside the Dispensation have what is called a 'teacher's fist'—not telling anyone when they are young, but telling a dear and beloved resident pupil when they are in their final time, lying on their deathbed—in the same way, this shows that the Tathāgata has no teaching whatsoever that he has kept preserved by making a 'fist' of it, thinking, 'I will teach this when I am old, in the final time.'

Ahaṃ bhikkhusaṅghanti ahameva bhikkhusaṅghaṃ pariharissāmīti vā, mamuddesikoti ahaṃ uddisitabbaṭṭhena uddeso assāti mamuddesiko, mameva uddissitvā maṃ paccāsīsamāno bhikkhusaṅgho hotu mama accayena mā vā ahosi, yaṃ vā taṃ vā hotūti iti vā pana yassa assāti attho. Na evaṃ hotīti bodhipallaṅkeyeva issāmaccherānaṃ vigatattā [M 3.0238] evaṃ na hoti. Sa kinti so kiṃ. Āsītikoti asītisaṃvacchariko, idaṃ pacchimavayaṃ anuppattabhāvadīpanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Veṭhamissakenāti bāhabandhacakkabandhādinā paṭisaṅkharaṇena veṭhamissakena. Maññeti jarasakaṭaṃ viya veṭhamissakena maññe yāpeti, arahattaphalaveṭhanena catuiriyāpathakappanaṃ tathāgatassa hotīti dasseti.

As for 'I will maintain the Saṅgha of bhikkhus,' [this means] 'I alone will maintain the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.' As for 'the Saṅgha has me as its designated leader,' [this means] 'I am the one to be designated for it,' thus 'the Saṅgha has me as its designated leader.' Or, 'Let the Saṅgha of bhikkhus exist, designating only me and looking to me for support. After my passing, let it not be, or let it be whatever it may be.' Or, for whomever this might be. This is the meaning. As for 'It is not so,' [this means] because envy and stinginess were eliminated at the Bodhi-seat, it is not so. As for 'He, what?' [it means] 'What about him?' As for 'eighty years old,' [it means] one who is eighty years of age; this was said to show the state of having reached the final age. As for 'with repairs,' [it means] with repairs, by means of restoration with things like arm-bands and wheel-bands. As for 'I think,' [it means] like an old cart, I think he maintains himself with repairs. It shows that for the Tathāgata, the maintenance of the four postures occurs by means of the repair that is the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship.

Idāni [V 3.0235] tamatthaṃ pakāsento yasmiṃ ānanda samayetiādimāha. Tattha sabbanimittānanti rūpanimittādīnaṃ. Ekaccānaṃ vedanānanti lokiyānaṃ vedanānaṃ. Tasmātihānandāti yasmā iminā phalasamāpattivihārena phāsu hoti, tasmā tumhepi tadatthāya evaṃ viharathāti dasseti. Attadīpāti mahāsamuddagatā dīpaṃ viya attānaṃ dīpaṃ patiṭṭhaṃ katvā viharatha. Attasaraṇāti attagatikāva hotha, mā aññagatikā. Dhammadīpadhammasaraṇapadesupi eseva nayo. Ettha ca dhammoti navavidho lokuttaradhammo veditabbo. Tamataggeti tamaagge, majjhe ta-kāro padasandhivasena vutto. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ime aggatamāti tamataggāti[P 3.0205]. Evaṃ sabbaṃ tamasotaṃ chinditvā ativiya agge uttamabhāve ete, ānanda, mama bhikkhū bhavissanti, tesaṃ agge bhavissanti. Ye keci sikkhākāmā, sabbesaṃ tesaṃ catusatipaṭṭhānagocarāva bhikkhū agge bhavissantīti arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ gaṇhīti.

Now, explaining that meaning, he begins with 'At that time, Ānanda...' Herein, 'all signs' refers to signs such as form. 'Some feelings' refers to worldly feelings. As for 'Therefore, Ānanda,' this means: because by this abiding in the attainment of fruition there is comfort, therefore, you too should dwell thus for that purpose; this is shown. As for 'be an island unto yourselves,' this means: like an island in the great ocean, having made the supramundane Dhamma, which is called 'self,' your island and support, you should dwell. As for 'be your own refuge,' this means: be ones who have the supramundane Dhamma, which is called 'self,' as your resort; do not have another resort. In the phrases 'the Dhamma as an island' and 'the Dhamma as a refuge' too, this same method should be understood. And here, by 'Dhamma,' the ninefold supramundane Dhamma should be understood. As for 'tamatagge,' the word division is 'tama-agge'; the 'ta' in the middle is spoken due to euphonic conjunction. This is what is said: 'These are the highest of the high' (aggatamā), thus they are called tamataggā. Thus, having cut through the entire stream of darkness, these bhikkhus of mine, Ānanda, will be in a state of supreme excellence. They will be at the summit. Whoever is eager for the training—among all of them, these bhikkhus whose pasture is the four foundations of mindfulness will be at the summit. He takes up the teaching with the pinnacle that is Arahantship.

10. Bhikkhunupassayasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Discourse at the Bhikkhunīs' Residence

376. Dasame tenupasaṅkamīti tasmiṃ upassaye kammaṭṭhānakammikā bhikkhuniyo atthi, tāsaṃ ussukkāpetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathessāmīti upasaṅkami. Uḷāraṃ pubbenāparaṃ visesanti pubbavisesato aparaṃ uḷāravisesaṃ. Tattha mahābhūtapariggaho pubbaviseso, upādārūpapariggaho aparaviseso nāma. Tathā sakalarūpapariggaho pubbaviseso, arūpapariggaho aparaviseso nāma. Rūpārūpapariggaho pubbaviseso, paccayapariggaho [M 3.0239] aparaviseso nāma sappaccayanāmarūpadassanaṃ pubbaviseso, tilakkhaṇāropanaṃ aparaviseso nāma. Evaṃ pubbenāparaṃ uḷāravisesaṃ jānātīti attho.

376. In the tenth sutta, as for 'he approached,' this means: in that residence there are bhikkhunīs who practice meditation; thinking, 'Having inspired them to strive, I will teach the meditation subject,' he approached. As for 'a sublime distinction of the latter from the former,' this means: a sublime distinction of the latter from the former distinction. Therein, the comprehension of the great elements is the former distinction; the comprehension of derived matter is called the latter distinction. Likewise, the comprehension of all matter is the former distinction; the comprehension of the immaterial is called the latter distinction. The comprehension of matter and the immaterial is the former distinction; the comprehension of conditions is called the latter distinction. Seeing name-and-form with its conditions is the former distinction; the application of the three characteristics is called the latter distinction. Thus, the meaning is that he knows the sublime distinction of the latter from the former.

Kāyārammaṇoti yaṃ kāyaṃ anupassati, tameva ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppajjati kilesapariḷāho. Bahiddhā vā cittaṃ vikkhipatīti bahiddhā vā puthuttārammaṇe cittuppādo vikkhipati. Kismiñcideva pasādanīye nimitte cittaṃ paṇidahitabbanti evaṃ kilesapariḷāhe ca līnatte ca bahiddhāvikkhepe ca uppanne kilesānurañjitena na vattitabbaṃ, kismiñcideva pasādanīye pasādāvahe buddhādīsu aññatarasmiṃ ṭhāne kammaṭṭhānacittaṃ ṭhapetabbaṃ. Cittaṃ samādhiyatīti ārammaṇe sammā ādhiyati suṭṭhu ṭhapitaṃ ṭhapiyati. Paṭisaṃharāmīti pasādanīyaṭṭhānato paṭisaṃharāmi, mūlakammaṭṭhānābhimukhaṃyeva naṃ karomīti attho. So paṭisaṃharati cevāti mūlakammaṭṭhānābhimukhañca [V 3.0236][P 3.0206] peseti. Na ca vitakketi na ca vicāretīti kilesavitakkaṃ na vitakketi, kilesavicāraṃ na vicāreti. Avitakkomhi avicāroti kilesavitakkavicārehi avitakkāvicāro. Ajjhattaṃ satimā sukhamasmīti gocarajjhatte pavattāya satiyā “satimāhamasmi sukhito cā”ti pajānāti.

As for 'the body as object,' this means: whatever body one contemplates, having made that very body the object, the fever of defilements arises. As for 'or the mind is scattered externally,' this means: or the arising of consciousness is scattered externally on various objects. As for 'one should direct the mind to some pleasing sign,' this means: thus, when the fever of defilements, sluggishness, and external distraction have arisen, one should not act with a mind stained by defilements; the meditation mind should be placed on some basis or other that inspires confidence and pleasure, such as the Buddha. As for 'the mind becomes concentrated,' this means: it is rightly placed on the object; having been well placed, it is established. As for 'I withdraw,' this means: I withdraw it from the confidence-inspiring place; I make it face only the original meditation subject. This is the meaning. As for 'he both withdraws it,' this means: he directs it toward the original meditation subject. As for 'he does not apply thought and does not sustain thought,' this means: he does not apply thought connected with defilements, he does not sustain thought connected with defilements. As for 'I am without applied thought, without sustained thought,' this means: without applied and sustained thought connected with defilements. As for 'internally mindful, I am happy,' this means: with mindfulness occurring internally within its domain, he knows: 'I am mindful, and I am happy.'

Evaṃ kho, ānanda, paṇidhāya bhāvanā hotīti evaṃ, ānanda, ṭhapetvā bhāvanā hoti. Imassa hi bhikkhuno yathā nāma purisassa mahantaṃ ucchubhāraṃ ukkhipitvā yantasālaṃ nentassa kilantakilantakāle bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapetvā ucchukhaṇḍaṃ khāditvā puna ukkhipitvā gamanaṃ hoti; evameva arahattaṃ pāpuṇituṃ uggahitakammaṭṭhānassa kāyapariḷāhādīsu uppannesu taṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ ṭhapetvā buddhaguṇādianussaraṇena cittaṃ pasādetvā kammaniyaṃ katvā bhāvanā pavattā, tasmā “paṇidhāya bhāvanā hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Tassa pana purisassa ucchubhāraṃ yantasālaṃ netvā pīḷetvā rasapānaṃ viya imassa bhikkhuno kammaṭṭhānaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā arahattaṃ pattassa phalasamāpattisukhānubhavanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

As for 'Thus, Ānanda, development is by directing,' this means: thus, Ānanda, development occurs by setting aside. For this bhikkhu, it is just as a man carrying a large bundle of sugarcane to a sugar-press, when he becomes tired, sets it down on the ground, chews a piece of sugarcane, and then picks it up again to continue; even so, for one who has taken up a meditation subject to attain Arahantship, when bodily fever and so on arise, development proceeds by setting aside that meditation subject, gladdening the mind and making it workable through recollection of the qualities of the Buddha and so on. Therefore, it is said, 'development is by directing.' And just as that man, after taking the sugarcane bundle to the press and crushing it, drinks the juice, so too for this bhikkhu who has brought the meditation subject to its culmination and attained Arahantship, the experience of the bliss of the attainment of fruition should be understood.

Bahiddhāti mūlakammaṭṭhānaṃ pahāya bahi aññasmiṃ ārammaṇe. Appaṇidhāyāti aṭṭhapetvā. Atha pacchā pure asaṃkhittaṃ vimuttaṃ appaṇihitanti pajānātīti ettha kammaṭṭhānavasena vā sarīravasena vā desanāvasena vā attho veditabbo.

As for 'externally,' this means: having abandoned the original meditation subject, externally on another object. As for 'not directing,' this means: not placing the mind. Then, in the passage 'Then one understands that afterwards and before it is undistracted, liberated, and undirected,' the meaning should be understood by way of the meditation subject, or by way of the body, or by way of the teaching.

Tattha [M 3.0240] kammaṭṭhāne tāva kammaṭṭhānassa abhiniveso pure nāma, arahattaṃ pacchā nāma. Tattha yo bhikkhu mūlakammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā kilesapariḷāhassa vā līnattassa vā bahiddhāvikkhepassa vā uppajjituṃ okāsaṃ adento sudantagoṇe yojetvā sārento viya caturassacchidde sutacchitaṃ caturassaghaṭikaṃ pakkhipanto viya vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā atiṭṭhanto alagganto arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, so puresaṅkhātassa kammaṭṭhānābhinivesassa pacchāsaṅkhātassa arahattassa ca vasena pacchā pure asaṃkhittaṃ vimuttaṃ appaṇihitanti pajānāti nāma.

Here, with regard to a meditation subject, firstly, the application to the meditation subject is called 'before,' and Arahantship is called 'after.' In this context, a monk who, having taken up a fundamental meditation subject and not giving an opportunity for the arising of the torment of defilements, or of sluggishness, or of external distraction—like a charioteer who, having yoked well-trained oxen, drives them, or like one inserting a well-smoothed square peg into a square hole—establishes insight and, not halting, not clinging, attains Arahantship; that monk, by means of the application to the meditation subject designated as 'before' and of Arahantship designated as 'after,' knows thus: 'After and before, my mind is undistracted, liberated, and undirected.'

Sarīre pana pādaṅgulīnaṃ aggapabbāni pure nāma, sīsakaṭāhaṃ pacchā nāma. Tattha yo bhikkhu pādaṅgulīnaṃ aggapabbaaṭṭhikesu [P 3.0207] abhinivisitvā byābhaṅgiyā yavakalāpaṃ mocento viya vaṇṇasaṇṭhānadisokāsaparicchedavasena aṭṭhīni pariggaṇhanto antarā kilesapariḷāhādīnaṃ uppattiṃ [V 3.0237] vāretvā yāva sīsakaṭāhā bhāvanaṃ pāpeti, so puresaṅkhātānaṃ aggapādaṅgulipabbānaṃ pacchāsaṅkhātassa sīsakaṭāhassa ca vasena pacchā pure asaṃkhittaṃ vimuttaṃ appaṇihitanti pajānāti nāma.

Furthermore, in the body, the tip-joints of the toes are called 'before,' and the skull is called 'after.' In this context, a monk who, having applied his mind to the bones of the tip-joints of the toes—like one loosening a sheaf of barley with a carrying-pole—and comprehending the bones by way of color, shape, direction, location, and demarcation, having prevented the arising of the torment of defilements and so on in between, causes his meditation to reach as far as the skull; that monk, by means of the tip-joints of the toes designated as 'before' and of the skull designated as 'after,' knows thus: 'After and before, my mind is undistracted, liberated, and without aspiration.'

Desanāyapi dvattiṃsākāradesanāya kesā pure nāma, matthaluṅgaṃ pacchā nāma. Tattha yo bhikkhu kesesu abhinivisitvā vaṇṇasaṇṭhānadisokāsavasena kesādayo pariggaṇhanto antarā kilesapariḷāhādīnaṃ uppattiṃ vāretvā yāva matthaluṅgā bhāvanaṃ pāpeti. So puresaṅkhātānaṃ kesānaṃ pacchāsaṅkhātassa matthaluṅgassa ca vasena pacchā pure asaṃkhittaṃ vimuttaṃ appaṇihitanti pajānāti nāma.

Also in the teaching, in the teaching on the thirty-two parts, the hairs of the head are called 'before,' and the brain is called 'after.' In this context, a monk who, having applied his mind to the hairs of the head and comprehending the hairs of the head and so on by way of color, shape, direction, and location, having prevented the arising of the torment of defilements and so on in between, causes his meditation to reach as far as the brain; that monk, by means of the hairs of the head designated as 'before' and of the brain designated as 'after,' knows thus: 'After and before, my mind is undistracted, liberated, and without aspiration.'

Evaṃ kho, ānanda, appaṇidhāya bhāvanā hotīti evaṃ, ānanda, aṭṭhapetvā bhāvanā hoti. Imassa hi bhikkhuno yathā nāma purisassa guḷabhāraṃ labhitvā attano gāmaṃ atiharantassa antarā aṭṭhapetvāva uccaṅge pakkhittāni guḷakhaṇḍādīni khādanīyāni khādantassa attano gāmeyeva otaraṇaṃ hoti, evameva arahattaṃ pāpuṇituṃ āraddhabhāvanassa kāyapariḷāhādīnaṃ uppattiṃ vāretvā kammaṭṭhānabhāvanā pavattā, tasmā “appaṇidhāya bhāvanā”ti vuttā. Tassa pana purisassa taṃ guḷabhāraṃ attano gāmaṃ netvā ñātīhi saddhiṃ paribhogo viya imassa bhikkhuno [M 3.0241] kammaṭṭhānaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā arahattaṃ pattassa phalasamāpattisukhānubhavanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Imasmiṃ sutte pubbabhāgavipassanā kathitā. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

'Thus, Ānanda, the development is without setting down' means: thus, Ānanda, the development occurs without interruption. For this monk, it is just as a man who, having obtained a load of molasses and carrying it to his own village, without setting it down along the way, while eating edibles such as lumps of molasses placed in his lap, sets it down only in his own village. In the very same way, for this monk who has undertaken the development of meditation to attain Arahantship, the development of the meditation subject proceeds, having prevented the arising of bodily torment and the like. Therefore, it is called 'development without setting down.' And just as that man, having brought the load of molasses to his own village, enjoys it with his relatives, so it should be understood is the experience of the bliss of the attainment of fruition for this monk who has brought his meditation subject to its culmination and attained Arahantship. In this sutta, the insight that is the preliminary part is taught. The rest is clear everywhere.

Ambapālivaggo paṭhamo.

The Ambapālī Chapter is the first.

2. Nālandavaggo

2. The Nālandā Chapter

2. Nālandasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Nālandā Sutta

378. Dutiyavaggassa dutiye nālandāyanti nālandāti evaṃnāmake nagare, taṃ nagaraṃ gocaragāmaṃ katvā. Pāvārikambavaneti dussapāvārikaseṭṭhino ambavane. Taṃ [P 3.0208] kira tassa uyyānaṃ [V 3.0238] ahosi. So bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ sutvā bhagavati pasanno tasmiṃ uyyāne kuṭileṇamaṇḍapādipaṭimaṇḍitaṃ bhagavato vihāraṃ katvā niyyātesi. So vihāro jīvakambavanaṃ viya pāvārikambavanantveva saṅkhaṃ gato. Tasmiṃ pāvārikambavane viharatīti attho.

2. In the second sutta of the second chapter, 'at Nālandā' means in the city named Nālandā. 'In Pāvārika’s mango grove' means in the mango grove of the cloth merchant Pāvārika. It is said that this was his park. Having heard the Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One, he became confident in the Blessed One and had a monastery built for the Blessed One in that park, adorned with huts, caves, pavilions, and so on, and then offered it. That monastery became known as Pāvārika’s mango grove, just like Jīvaka’s mango grove. The meaning is that he dwelled in Pāvārika’s mango grove.

Evaṃpasannoti evaṃ uppannasaddho, evaṃ saddahāmīti attho. Bhiyyobhiññataroti bhiyyataro abhiññāto bhiyyatarābhiyyo vā, uttaritarañāṇoti attho. Sambodhiyanti sabbaññutaññāṇe arahattamaggañāṇe vā arahattamaggeneva hi buddhaguṇā nippadesā gahitā honti, dvepi aggasāvakā arahattamaggeneva sāvakapāramīñāṇaṃ paṭilabhanti, paccekabuddhā paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ, buddhā sabbaññutaññāṇañceva sakale ca buddhaguṇe. Sabbampi nesaṃ arahattamaggeneva ijjhati. Tasmā arahattamaggañāṇaṃ sambodhi nāma hoti. Tena uttaritaro ca bhagavatā natthi. Tenāha “bhagavatā bhiyyobhiññataro, yadidaṃ sambodhiya”nti.

378. 'Thus with faith' means thus with arisen faith; the meaning is 'thus I have faith.' 'More greatly distinguished' means more greatly known, or even more greatly superior; the meaning is 'superior knowledge.' 'Regarding enlightenment' refers to the knowledge of omniscience or the knowledge of the path of arahantship. For the qualities of the Buddha are apprehended without remainder through just the path of arahantship; both chief disciples attain the knowledge of the perfection of disciples through just the path of arahantship; Paccekabuddhas, the knowledge of individual enlightenment; and Buddhas, the knowledge of omniscience and all the qualities of a Buddha. All of this is accomplished for them through just the path of arahantship. Therefore, the knowledge of the path of arahantship is called enlightenment. And in that regard, there is no one superior to the Blessed One. Hence he said: '...more greatly distinguished than the Blessed One, namely, with regard to perfect enlightenment.'

Uḷārāti seṭṭhā. Ayañhi uḷārasaddo “uḷārāni khādanīyāni khādantī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.366) madhure āgacchati. “Uḷārāya khalu bhavaṃ vacchāyano samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ pasaṃsāya pasaṃsatī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.288) seṭṭhe. “Appamāṇo uḷāro [M 3.0242] obhāso”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.32; ma. ni. 3.201) vipule. Svāyamidha seṭṭhe āgato. Tena vuttaṃ “uḷārāti seṭṭhā”ti. Āsabhīti usabhassa vācāsadisī acalā asampavedhī. Ekaṃso gahitoti anussavena vā ācariyaparamparāya vā itikirāya vā piṭakasampadānena vā ākāraparivitakkena vā diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā vā takkahetu vā nayahetu vā akathetvā paccakkhato ñāṇena paṭivijjhitvā viya ekaṃso gahito, sanniṭṭhānakathāva kathitāti attho. Sīhanādoti seṭṭhanādo, vane unnādayantena sīhena viya uttamanādo naditoti attho.

'Excellent' means supreme. For this word 'excellent' appears in contexts like 'eating excellent delicacies' (MN 1.366) in the sense of sweetness. In phrases like 'Venerable Vacchāyana praises the ascetic Gotama with excellent praise' (MN 1.288), it means supreme. In expressions like 'immeasurable, excellent radiance' (DN 2.32; MN 3.201), it means vast. Here, it appears in the sense of supreme. Therefore, it is said, 'excellent means supreme.' 'Āsabhī' means like the word of a bull, unwavering and unshakeable. 'Taken up with certainty' means not spoken based on hearsay, tradition, mere report, handing down of the Piṭaka, reasoning from aspects, acceptance of a view through pondering, logic, or method, but as if directly penetrated with knowledge; the meaning is that a statement of firm conviction has been spoken. 'Lion’s roar' means the supreme roar; the meaning is the utterance of the highest sound, like a lion roaring in the forest.

Kiṃ [P 3.0209] nu te sāriputtāti imaṃ desanaṃ kasmā ārabhi? Anuyogadāpanatthaṃ. Ekacco hi sīhanādaṃ naditvā attano sīhanāde anuyogaṃ dātuṃ na sakkoti, nighaṃsanaṃ na khamati, silese patitamakkaṭo viya hoti. Yathā dhamamānaṃ aparisuddhaṃ lohaṃ jhāyitvā aṅgāro hoti, evaṃ jhāmaṅgāro viya hoti. Eko sīhanāde anuyogaṃ dāpiyamāno dātuṃ sakkoti, nighaṃsanaṃ khamati[V 3.0239], dhamamānaṃ niddosajātarūpaṃ viya adhikataraṃ sobhati, tādiso thero. Tena naṃ bhagavā “anuyogakkhamo aya”nti ñatvā sīhanāde anuyogadāpanatthaṃ imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi.

'Why, Sāriputta?'—why did he begin this discourse? For the purpose of prompting a cross-examination. For some, having roared a lion’s roar, cannot respond to a cross-examination of their own lion’s roar, cannot endure scrutiny, and are like a monkey fallen onto birdlime. Just as impure metal, when smelted, burns and becomes charcoal, so they are like burnt embers. But one who, when a cross-examination is made regarding their lion’s roar, can respond, endures scrutiny, and shines even more—like purified gold when smelted—such is the Elder. Knowing that 'this one is capable of withstanding cross-examination,' the Blessed One began this discourse for the purpose of prompting a cross-examination regarding his lion’s roar.

Tattha sabbe teti sabbe te tayā. Evaṃsīlāti maggasīlena phalasīlena lokiyalokuttarasīlena evaṃsīlā. Evaṃdhammāti ettha samādhipakkhā dhammā adhippetā, maggasamādhinā phalasamādhinā lokiyalokuttarena samādhinā evaṃsamādhīti attho. Evaṃpaññāti maggapaññādivaseneva evaṃpaññā. Evaṃvihārinoti ettha pana heṭṭhā samādhipakkhānaṃ dhammānaṃ gahitattā vihāro gahitopi puna kasmā gahitameva gaṇhatīti ce. Therena idaṃ gahitameva. Idañhi nirodhasamāpattidīpanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tasmā evaṃ nirodhasamāpattivihārino te bhagavanto ahesunti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

Herein, 'all those' means all those [known] by you. 'Of such virtue' means endowed with the virtue of the path, the virtue of the fruit, mundane virtue, and supramundane virtue—thus of such virtue. 'Of such qualities' here refers to qualities associated with concentration, namely, concentration of the path, concentration of the fruit, mundane concentration, and supramundane concentration—thus of such concentration. 'Of such wisdom' means wisdom of the path and so forth—thus of such wisdom. 'Dwelling thus'—here, since the qualities associated with concentration have already been mentioned previously, why is 'dwelling' mentioned again? The Elder rightly included this. For this was stated to indicate the attainment of cessation. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: 'those Blessed Ones were ones who dwelt thus in the attainment of cessation.'

Evaṃvimuttāti ettha vikkhambhanavimutti, tadaṅgavimutti, samucchedavimutti, paṭipassaddhivimutti, nissaraṇavimuttīti pañcavidhā vimutti. Tattha aṭṭha samāpattiyo sayaṃ vikkhambhitehi nīvaraṇādīhi vimuttattā vikkhambhanavimuttīti saṅkhaṃ gacchanti. Aniccānupassanādikā [M 3.0243] satta anupassanā sayaṃ tassa tassa paccanīkavasena pariccattāhi niccasaññādīhi vimuttattā tadaṅgavimuttīti saṅkhaṃ gacchanti. Cattāro ariyamaggā sayaṃ samucchinnehi kilesehi vimuttattā samucchedavimuttīti saṅkhaṃ gacchanti. Cattāri sāmaññaphalāni maggānubhāvena kilesānaṃ paṭipassaddhante uppannattā paṭipassaddhivimuttīti saṅkhaṃ gacchanti. Nibbānaṃ sabbakilesehi nissaṭattā apagatattā dūre ṭhitattā nissaraṇavimuttīti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ. Iti imāsaṃ pañcannaṃ vimuttīnaṃ vasena evaṃ vimuttāti ettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

'Thus liberated'—herein, liberation is fivefold: liberation by suppression, liberation by substitution of opposites, liberation by cutting off, liberation by tranquillization, and liberation by escape. Among these, the eight attainments are called liberation by suppression because they are liberated from the hindrances and so forth, which are suppressed by them. The seven contemplations, such as the contemplation of impermanence, are called liberation by substitution of opposites because they are liberated from perceptions such as that of permanence, which are abandoned by them as the specific opposites. The four noble paths are called liberation by cutting off because they are liberated from the defilements which have been cut off by them. The four fruits of recluseship are called liberation by tranquillization because they arise when the defilements have been tranquillized through the power of the paths. Nibbāna is called liberation by escape because it has escaped from all defilements, is far removed, and stands at a distance. Thus, the meaning here should be understood as 'thus liberated' in terms of these five kinds of liberation.

Kiṃ [P 3.0210] pana te sāriputta ye te bhavissantīti atītā tāva niruddhā apaṇṇattikabhāvaṃ gatā dīpasikhā viya nibbutā, evaṃ niruddhe apaṇṇattikabhāvaṃ gate tvaṃ kathaṃ jānissasi, anāgatabuddhānaṃ pana guṇā kiṃ tayā attano cittena paricchinditvā viditāti pucchanto evamāha.

Regarding 'What then, Sāriputta, of those who will be?': He spoke thus, asking, 'The past Buddhas, for their part, have ceased, have gone to a state beyond designation, are extinguished like the flame of a lamp. Since they have thus ceased and gone to a state beyond designation, how will you know them? Furthermore, are the qualities of future Buddhas known by you, having been encompassed by your own mind?'

Kiṃ pana tyāhaṃ sāriputta etarahīti anāgatāpi buddhā ajātā anibbattā anuppannā, te kathaṃ jānissasi. Tesañhi jānanaṃ apade ākāse padadassanaṃ viya hoti. Idāni mayā saddhiṃ [V 3.0240] ekavihāre vasasi, ekato bhikkhāya carasi, dhammadesanākāle dakkhiṇapasse nisīdasi, kiṃ pana mayhaṃ guṇā attano cetasā paricchinditvā viditā tayāti anuyuñjanto evamāha. Thero pana pucchitapucchite “no hetaṃ bhante”ti paṭikkhipati.

“And what of me, Sāriputta, at the present time?” Thus he spoke, investigating: “Future Buddhas are yet unborn, unproduced, unarisen. How will you know them? For knowing them is indeed like seeing a footprint in the trackless sky. Now you dwell with me in the same monastery, go for alms together, and sit on my right side at the time of the Dhamma teaching. But have my qualities been known by you, having encompassed them with your own mind?” The Elder, however, whenever questioned, rejected it, saying, “No, venerable sir.”

Therassa ca viditampi atthi, aviditampi. Kiṃ so attano viditaṭṭhāne paṭikkhepaṃ karoti, aviditaṭṭhāneti? Viditaṭṭhāne na karoti, aviditaṭṭhāneyeva karoti. Thero kira anuyoge āraddhe evaṃ aññāsi “nāyaṃ anuyogo sāvakapāramīñāṇe, sabbaññutaññāṇe pana ayaṃ anuyogo”ti attano sāvakapāramīñāṇe paṭikkhepaṃ akatvāva aviditaṭṭhāne sabbaññutaññāṇe paṭikkhepaṃ karoti. Tena idampi dīpeti – bhagavā mayhaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannānaṃ buddhānaṃ sīlasamādhipaññāvimuttikāraṇajānanasamatthaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ natthīti.

For the Elder, there is both what is known and what is not known. Does he make a rejection in the sphere of what he knows, or in the sphere of what he does not know? He does not make a rejection in the sphere of what he knows; he makes it only in the sphere of what he does not know. It is said that when the investigation began, the Elder understood thus: ‘This investigation is not concerned with the knowledge of a disciple’s perfection, but rather this investigation is concerned with the knowledge of omniscience.’ Thus, without making a rejection in the sphere of his own knowledge of a disciple’s perfection, he makes a rejection in the sphere of what he does not know, that is, in the knowledge of omniscience. By that, he also reveals this: ‘O Blessed One, I do not have the knowledge of omniscience that is capable of knowing the causes—namely virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation—of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.’”

Etthāti etesu atītādibhedesu buddhesu. Atha kiñcarahīti atha kasmā evaṃ ñāṇe asati tayā evaṃ kathitanti vadati. Dhammanvayoti dhammassa paccakkhato ñāṇassa anuyogaṃ anugantvā uppannaṃ anumānañāṇaṃ nayaggāho [M 3.0244] vidito, sāvakapāramīñāṇe ṭhatvāva iminā ākārena jānāmi bhagavāti vadati.
