Therassa hi nayaggāho appamāṇo apariyanto. Yathā ca sabbaññutaññāṇassa pamāṇaṃ vā pariyanto vā natthi, evaṃ dhammasenāpatino nayaggāhassa. Tena so – “iminā evaṃvidho iminā evaṃvidho, iminā anuttaro iminā anuttaro satthā”ti jānāti. Therassa hi nayaggāho sabbaññutaññāṇagatiko eva.

“Herein” means among these Buddhas distinguished as past, and so on. “But why so?” means: he asks, “Then why, when such knowledge is absent, was this spoken by you?” “Conformity with the Dhamma” means: the inferential knowledge that arises by following the application of the knowledge that directly perceives the Dhamma—this grasp of the method is known to me. He says, “O Blessed One, standing only in the knowledge of a disciple’s perfection, I know by this very mode.” Indeed, the Elder’s grasp of the method is immeasurable and boundless. And just as there is no measure or limit to the knowledge of omniscience, so too is there none for the grasp of the method of the General of the Dhamma. Therefore, he knows: “By this reason, the Teacher is of such a nature; by this reason, he is of such a nature. By this reason, he is unsurpassed; by this reason, he is unsurpassed.” For the Elder’s grasp of the method indeed has a course similar to that of the knowledge of omniscience.

Idāni [P 3.0211] taṃ nayaggāhaṃ pākaṭaṃ kātuṃ upamaṃ dassento seyyathāpi bhantetiādimāha. Tattha yasmā majjhimadese nagarassa uddhāpapākārādīni thirāni vā hontu dubbalāni vā, sabbaso vā pana mā hontu, corānaṃ āsaṅkā na hoti. Tasmā taṃ aggahetvā paccantimaṃ nagaranti āha. Daḷhuddhāpanti thiramūlapākāraṃ. Daḷhapākāratoraṇanti thirapākārañceva thirapiṭṭhasaṅghāṭañca. Ekadvāranti kasmā āha? Bahudvāre hi nagare bahūhi paṇḍitadovārikehi bhavitabbaṃ, ekadvāreva eko vaṭṭati. Therassa ca paññāya sadiso añño natthi, tasmā attano paṇḍitabhāvassa opammatthaṃ ekaṃyeva dovārikaṃ dassetuṃ “ekadvāra”nti āha.

Now, to make that grasp of the method clear, wishing to present an analogy, he spoke the words beginning with, “Just as, venerable sir.” Therein, because in the middle country, whether a city’s ramparts, surrounding walls, and so forth are strong or weak, or even if they do not exist at all, there is no apprehension of thieves. Therefore, setting that aside, he spoke of a “border city.” “With strong ramparts” means with a firm foundation for the surrounding wall. “With strong surrounding walls and gateways” means both a strong surrounding wall and a strong door-panel assembly. Why did he say “with a single gate”? Because in a city with many gates, there must be many wise gatekeepers, but in a city with a single gate, one is sufficient. And there is no other equal to the Elder in wisdom; therefore, for the purpose of an analogy for his own state of being wise, and to indicate only one gatekeeper, he said “with a single gate.”

Paṇḍitoti paṇḍiccena samannāgato. Byattoti veyyattiyena samannāgato visadañāṇo. Medhāvīti [V 3.0241] ṭhānuppattikapaññāsaṅkhātāya medhāya samannāgato. Anupariyāyapathanti anupariyāyanāmakaṃ pākāramaggaṃ. Pākārasandhinti dvinnaṃ iṭṭhakānaṃ apagataṭṭhānaṃ. Pākāravivaranti pākārassa chinnaṭṭhānaṃ. Cetaso upakkileseti pañcanīvaraṇā cittaṃ upakkilissanti kiliṭṭhaṃ karonti upatāpenti viheṭhenti, tasmā “cetaso upakkilesā”ti vuccanti. Paññāya dubbalīkaraṇeti nīvaraṇā uppajjamānā anuppannāya paññāya uppajjituṃ na denti, tasmā “paññāya dubbalīkaraṇā”ti vuccanti. Supatiṭṭhitacittāti catūsu satipaṭṭhānesu suṭṭhu ṭhapitacittā hutvā. Satta bojjhaṅge yathābhūtanti satta bojjhaṅge yathāsabhāvena bhāvetvā. Anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhinti arahattaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ paṭivijjhiṃsūti dasseti.

‘Wise’ means endowed with wisdom. ‘Accomplished’ means endowed with skillfulness and clear knowledge. ‘Intelligent’ means endowed with intelligence, which is known as ready wit. ‘The path for going around’ means the path along the wall called ‘the path for going around.’ ‘The joint of the wall’ is the place where two bricks are separated. ‘The breach in the wall’ is a broken place in the wall. ‘Defilements of the mind’: the five hindrances defile the mind, make it impure, afflict it, and torment it; therefore, they are called ‘defilements of the mind.’ ‘Weakening of wisdom’: the hindrances, when arising, do not allow unarisen wisdom to arise; therefore, they are called ‘that which causes the weakening of wisdom.’ ‘With well-established minds’ means having minds well-placed in the four foundations of mindfulness. ‘The seven factors of enlightenment as they really are’ means having developed the seven factors of enlightenment according to their true nature. ‘Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment’ shows that they have penetrated Arahantship and the knowledge of omniscience.

Apicettha satipaṭṭhānāti vipassanā, bojjhaṅgā maggo, anuttarasammāsambodhi arahattaṃ. Satipaṭṭhānāti vā vipassanā, bojjhaṅgāmissakā, sammāsambodhi [M 3.0245] arahattameva. Dīghabhāṇakamahāsīvatthero panāha “satipaṭṭhāne vipassanaṃ gahetvā bojjhaṅge maggo ca sabbaññutaññāṇañcāti [P 3.0212] gahite sundaro pañho bhaveyya, na panevaṃ gahita”nti. Iti thero sabbabuddhānaṃ nīvaraṇappahāne satipaṭṭhānabhāvanāya sambodhiyañca majjhe bhinnasuvaṇṇarajatānaṃ viya nānattābhāvaṃ dasseti.

Furthermore, herein, ‘foundations of mindfulness’ is insight; ‘factors of enlightenment’ is the path; ‘unsurpassed perfect enlightenment’ is Arahantship. Or, ‘foundations of mindfulness’ is insight; ‘factors of enlightenment’ are mixed; ‘perfect enlightenment’ is Arahantship itself. However, the Elder Mahāsīva, the reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya, said: “If, having taken ‘foundations of mindfulness’ as insight, one were to take ‘factors of enlightenment’ as both the path and the knowledge of omniscience, the question would be excellent. But it was not taken thus by the ancients.” In this way, the Elder shows that among all Buddhas—in the abandoning of the hindrances, in the development of the foundations of mindfulness, and in enlightenment—there is no difference, just as there is no difference between gold and silver that have been broken in the middle.

Idha ṭhatvā upamā saṃsandetabbā – āyasmā hi sāriputto paccantanagaraṃ dassesi, pākāraṃ dassesi, anupariyāyapathaṃ dassesi, dvāraṃ dassesi, paṇḍitadovārikaṃ dassesi, nagaraṃ pavisanakanikkhamanake oḷārike pāṇe dassesi, dovārikassa tesaṃ pāṇānaṃ pākaṭabhāvaṃ dassesi. Tattha kiṃ kena sadisanti ce? Nagaraṃ viya hi nibbānaṃ, pākāro viya sīlaṃ, anupariyāyapatho viya hirī, dvāraṃ viya ariyamaggo, paṇḍitadovāriko viya dhammasenāpati, nagaraṃ pavisanakanikkhamanakā oḷārikapāṇā viya atītānāgatapaccuppannā buddhā, dovārikassa tesaṃ pāṇānaṃ pākaṭabhāvo viya āyasmato sāriputtassa atītānāgatapaccuppannānaṃ buddhānaṃ sīlasamathādīhi pākaṭabhāvo. Ettāvatā therena bhagavato – “evamahaṃ sāvakapāramīñāṇe ṭhatvā dhammanvayena nayaggāhena jānāmī”ti attano sīhanādassa anuyogo dinno hoti.

At this point, the simile should be connected. For the Venerable Sāriputta showed the border city, he showed the rampart, he showed the circumambulatory path, he showed the gate, he showed the wise gatekeeper, he showed the conspicuous beings entering and leaving the city, and he showed that those beings were manifest to the gatekeeper. Therein, if it is asked what is similar to what: Nibbāna is like the city, virtue is like the rampart, moral shame is like the circumambulatory path, the Noble Path is like the gate, the General of the Dhamma is like the wise gatekeeper; the past, future, and present Buddhas are like the conspicuous beings entering and leaving the city; and just as those beings are manifest to the gatekeeper, so too are the past, future, and present Buddhas manifest to the Venerable Sāriputta through their virtue, serenity, and so on. To this extent, the Elder has answered the inquiry concerning his lion's roar for the Blessed One, stating: 'Thus I, standing in the knowledge of a disciple's perfection, know through conformity with the Dhamma and by way of inference.'

Tasmāti yasmā “na kho metaṃ, bhante, atītānāgatapaccuppannesu arahantesu sammāsambuddhesu [V 3.0242] cetopariyañāṇaṃ atthi, apica dhammanvayo vidito”ti vadati, tasmā. Abhikkhaṇaṃ bhāseyyāsīti punappunaṃ bhāseyyāsi, “pubbaṇhe me kathita”nti mā majjhanhikādīsu na kathayittha, “ajja vā me kathita”nti mā paradivasādīsu na kathayitthāti attho. Sā pahīyissatīti “sāriputtasadisopi nāma ñāṇajavanasampanno sāvako buddhānaṃ cittācāraṃ jānituṃ na sakkoti, evaṃ appameyyā tathāgatā”ti cintentānaṃ yā tathāgate kaṅkhā vā vimati vā, sā pahīyissatīti.

‘Therefore’ means: because you say, ‘Venerable sir, I do not have the knowledge of penetrating the minds of the past, future, and present Arahants, the Fully Enlightened Ones, but the conformity with the Dhamma is known to me,’ therefore. ‘You should speak repeatedly’ means you should speak again and again. Do not refrain from speaking at midday and so on, thinking, ‘I have spoken in the morning’; or do not refrain from speaking on subsequent days and so on, thinking, ‘I have spoken today’—this is the meaning. ‘That will be abandoned’ means: for those who think, ‘Even a disciple like Sāriputta, endowed with swiftness of knowledge, is unable to know the mental conduct of the Buddhas; so immeasurable are the Tathāgatas,’ whatever doubt or uncertainty they have regarding the Tathāgata, that will be abandoned.

3. Cundasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Cunda Sutta

379. Tatiye magadhesūti evaṃnāmake janapade. Nālakagāmaketi rājagahassa avidūre attano kulasantake evaṃnāmake gāme. Cundo samaṇuddesoti [M 3.0246] ayaṃ thero dhammasenāpatissa [P 3.0213] kaniṭṭhabhātiko, taṃ bhikkhū anupasampannakāle “cundo samaṇuddeso”ti samudācaritvā therakālepi tatheva samudācariṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ “cundo samaṇuddeso”ti. Upaṭṭhāko hotīti mukhodakadantakaṭṭhadānena ceva pariveṇasammajjana-piṭṭhiparikammakaraṇa-pattacīvaraggahaṇena ca upaṭṭhānakaro hoti. Parinibbāyīti anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbuto. Katarasmiṃ kāleti? Bhagavato parinibbānasaṃvacchare.

379. In the third sutta: ‘in Magadha’ means in the country so named. ‘In the village of Nālaka’ means in the village so named, his own family property, not far from Rājagaha. ‘Cunda the novice’ means: this elder was the younger brother of the General of the Dhamma. The monks, having addressed him as ‘Cunda the novice’ during the time he was not yet fully ordained, continued to address him in the same way even when he was an elder. For that reason, it is said, ‘Cunda the novice.’ ‘He was an attendant’ means: he was one who performed service by giving water for the face and tooth-sticks, and by sweeping the monastic compound, massaging the back, and taking the bowl and robes. ‘He attained Parinibbāna’ means: he was fully extinguished with the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining. At what time? In the year of the Blessed One's Parinibbāna.

Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā – bhagavā kira vutthavasso veḷuvagāmakā nikkhamitvā “sāvatthiṃ gamissāmī”ti āgatamaggeneva paṭinivattanto anupubbena sāvatthiṃ patvā jetavanaṃ pāvisi. Dhammasenāpati bhagavato vattaṃ dassetvā divāṭṭhānaṃ gato, so tattha antevāsikesu vattaṃ dassetvā paṭikkantesu divāṭṭhānaṃ sammajjitvā cammakhaṇḍaṃ paññāpetvā pāde pakkhāletvā pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā phalasamāpattiṃ pāvisi. Athassa yathā paricchedena tato vuṭṭhitassa ayaṃ parivitakko udapādi “buddhā nu kho paṭhamaṃ parinibbāyanti, udāhu aggasāvakāti, tato “aggasāvakā paṭhama”nti ñatvā attano āyusaṅkhāraṃ olokesi. So “sattāhameva me āyusaṅkhārā pavattissantī”ti ñatvā “kattha parinibbāyissāmī”ti cintesi.

Herein, this is the sequential account: The Blessed One, it is said, having completed the rains-residence, departed from the village of Veḷuva. Intending, ‘I will go to Sāvatthī,’ he returned by the very path on which he had come, and arriving in Sāvatthī in due course, he entered Jetavana. The General of the Dhamma, having performed his duties for the Blessed One, went to his daytime resting place. There, after his resident pupils had performed their duties and departed, he swept the daytime resting place, prepared a piece of hide, washed his feet, sat with his legs crossed, and entered the attainment of fruition. Then, as he emerged from that state after a set duration, this reflection arose in him: ‘Do the Buddhas, I wonder, attain Parinibbāna first, or do the chief disciples?’ Then, knowing, ‘The chief disciples attain it first,’ he examined his own life-principle. Realizing, ‘My life-principle will continue for only seven days,’ he considered, ‘Where shall I attain Parinibbāna?’

Tato “rāhulo tāvatiṃsesu parinibbuto, aññāsikoṇḍaññatthero chaddantadahe, ahaṃ kattha parinibbāyissāmī”ti punappunaṃ cintento mātaraṃ ārabbha satiṃ uppādesi – “mayhaṃ mātā sattannaṃ [V 3.0243] arahantānaṃ mātā hutvāpi buddhadhammasaṅghesu appasannā, atthi nu kho tassā upanissayo, natthi nu kho”ti. Sotāpattimaggassa upanissayaṃ disvā “kassa desanāya abhisamayo bhavissatī”ti olokento “mameva dhammadesanāya bhavissati, na aññassa. Sace kho panāhaṃ appossukko bhaveyyaṃ, bhavissanti me vattāro – “sāriputtatthero avasesajanānampi avassayo hoti. Tathā hissa samacittasuttantadesanādivase (a. ni. 2.33-37) koṭisatasahassadevatā arahattaṃ pattā, tayo magge paṭividdhadevatānaṃ gaṇanā natthi, aññesu ca ṭhānesu anekā abhisamayā [M 3.0247] dissanti, there ca cittaṃ pasādetvā sagge nibbattāneva asīti kulasahassāni, so dāni sakamātumicchādassanamattampi harituṃ [P 3.0214] nāsakkhī”ti. Tasmā mātaraṃ micchādassanā mocetvā jātovarakeyeva parinibbāyissāmī”ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā “ajjeva bhagavantaṃ anujānāpetvā nikkhamissāmī”ti cundattheraṃ āmantesi – “āvuso, cunda, amhākaṃ pañcasatāya bhikkhuparisāya saññaṃ dehi. ‘Gaṇhathāvuso pattacīvarāni, dhammasenāpati nālakagāmaṃ gantukāmo’”ti. Thero tathā akāsi.

Then, while considering again and again, 'Rāhula attained Parinibbāna in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, the Elder Aññātakoṇḍañña in the Chaddanta Lake; where shall I attain Parinibbāna?' he established mindfulness with regard to his mother: 'My mother, despite being the mother of seven Arahants, lacks confidence in the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha. Does she, I wonder, have a supporting condition, or does she not?' Seeing the supporting condition for the path of stream-entry, and examining, 'Through whose teaching will her realization occur?' he saw, 'It will occur through my own teaching, not another’s. If, however, I were to be unconcerned, there will be those who say of me: “The Elder Sāriputta is a refuge even for other people. For indeed, on the day he taught the Samacittasuttanta, a hundred thousand koṭis of devas attained Arahantship; the number of devas who penetrated the three lower paths is countless; and in other instances, many realizations are seen. Moreover, eighty thousand families were reborn in heaven simply by generating confidence in the Elder. Yet now he was unable to remove even his own mother's wrong view.”' Therefore, having made the resolution, 'I will free my mother from wrong view and attain Parinibbāna in the very chamber where I was born,' he addressed the Elder Cunda, thinking, 'Today itself, having gained the Blessed One's permission, I will depart.' 'Friend Cunda, give the signal to our assembly of five hundred monks: “Friends, take your bowls and robes. The General of the Dhamma wishes to go to the village of Nālaka.”' The Elder did so.

Bhikkhū senāsanaṃ saṃsāmetvā pattacīvaramādāya therassa santikaṃ agamaṃsu. Thero senāsanaṃ saṃsāmetvā divāṭṭhānaṃ sammajjitvā divāṭṭhānadvāre ṭhatvā divāṭṭhānaṃ oloketvā “idaṃ dāni pacchimadassanaṃ, puna āgamanaṃ natthī”ti pañcasatabhikkhūhi parivuto bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā bhagavantaṃ etadavoca “anujānātu me bhante bhagavā, anujānātu sugato. Parinibbānakālo me, ossaṭṭho me āyusaṅkhāro”ti. Buddhā pana yasmā “parinibbāhī”ti vutte maraṇavaṇṇaṃ saṃvaṇṇentīti, “mā parinibbāhī”ti vutte vaṭṭassa guṇaṃ kathentīti micchādiṭṭhikā dosaṃ āropessanti, tasmā tadubhayampi na vadanti. Tena naṃ bhagavā – “kattha parinibbāyissasi sāriputtā”ti vatvā – “atthi, bhante, magadhesu nālakagāme jātovarako, tatthāhaṃ parinibbāyissāmī”ti vutte – “yassa dāni tvaṃ, sāriputta, kālaṃ maññasi, idāni pana te jeṭṭhakaniṭṭhabhātikānaṃ tādisassa bhikkhuno dassanaṃ dullabhaṃ bhavissati, desehi nesaṃ dhamma”nti āha.

The monks, having put away their lodgings and taken their bowls and robes, went to the Elder. The Elder, having put away his lodging, swept the day-abode, stood at the door of the day-abode, looked at the day-abode, and said, 'This is now the last sight; there will be no coming again.' Surrounded by five hundred monks, he approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and said this to the Blessed One: 'Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One permit me; may the Sugata permit me. The time for my Parinibbāna has come; I have relinquished the life-formation.' However, the Buddhas, because those with wrong views would find fault—arguing that if it were said, 'Attain Parinibbāna,' they would be praising the virtues of death, and if it were said, 'Do not attain Parinibbāna,' they would be speaking of the virtues of the round of existence—therefore do not say either of these two things. For that reason, the Blessed One said to him, 'Where will you attain Parinibbāna, Sāriputta?' When it was said, 'Venerable Sir, in Magadha, in the village of Nālaka, there is my birth chamber; there I will attain Parinibbāna,' the Blessed One said, 'Now, Sāriputta, you yourself know the right time. However, for your brother monks, senior and junior, the sight of such a monk as you will now be rare. Teach them the Dhamma.'

Thero – “satthā mayhaṃ iddhivikubbanapubbaṅgamaṃ dhammadesanaṃ paccāsīsatī”ti ñatvā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā tālappamāṇaṃ ākāsaṃ abbhuggantvā oruyha dasabalassa pāde vandi, puna dvitālappamāṇaṃ abbhuggantvā oruyha dasabalassa pāde vandi, etenupāyena sattatālappamāṇaṃ abbhuggantvā [V 3.0244] anekāni pāṭihāriyasatāni dassento dhammakathaṃ [P 3.0215] ārabhi. Dissamānenapi kāyena katheti, adissamānenapi. Uparimena vā heṭṭhimena vā upaḍḍhakāyena katheti adissamānenapi dissamānenapi, kālena candavaṇṇaṃ dasseti, kālena sūriyavaṇṇaṃ, kālena pabbatavaṇṇaṃ, kālena samuddavaṇṇaṃ, kālena cakkavattirājā hoti, kālena vessavaṇamahārājā, kālena sakko [M 3.0248] devarājā, kālena mahābrahmāti evaṃ anekāni pāṭihāriyasatāni dassento dhammakathaṃ kathesi. Sakalanagaraṃ sannipati. Thero oruyha dasabalassa pāde vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ satthā āha – “ko nāmo ayaṃ sāriputta dhammapariyāyo”ti. Sīhavikīḷito nāma, bhanteti. Taggha, sāriputta, sīhavikīḷito taggha, sāriputta, sīhavikīḷitoti.

The Elder, knowing, 'The Teacher desires from me a Dhamma discourse preceded by a display of various psychic powers,' paid homage to the Blessed One, rose into the sky to the height of a palm tree, descended, and paid homage at the feet of the Ten-Powered One. Again, he rose to the height of two palm trees, descended, and paid homage at the feet of the Ten-Powered One. In this way, rising up to the height of seven palm trees and displaying many hundreds of miracles, he began the Dhamma talk. He taught with a visible body and also with an invisible one. He taught with the upper or lower half of his body, sometimes invisible and sometimes visible. At times he displayed the appearance of the moon, at times the appearance of the sun, at times the appearance of a mountain, at times the appearance of the ocean. At times he became a wheel-turning monarch, at times Vessavaṇa the Great King, at times Sakka, king of the devas, at times Mahābrahmā. Thus displaying many hundreds of miracles, he gave the Dhamma talk. The entire city gathered. The Elder descended, paid homage at the feet of the Ten-Powered One, and stood. Then the Teacher said to him, 'Sāriputta, what is the name of this Dhamma discourse?' 'Venerable Sir, it is named the Sīhavikīḷita, the Lion's Play.' 'Indeed, Sāriputta, it is the Sīhavikīḷita; indeed, Sāriputta, it is the Sīhavikīḷita.'

Thero alattakavaṇṇe hatthe pasāretvā satthu suvaṇṇakacchapasadise pāde gopphakesu gahetvā – “bhante, imesaṃ pādānaṃ vandanatthāya kappasatasahassādhikaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ pāramiyo pūritā, so me manoratho matthakaṃ patto, ito dāni paṭṭhāya paṭisandhivasena na puna ekaṭṭhāne sannipāto samāgamo atthi, chinno esa vissāso, anekehi buddhasatasahassehi paviṭṭhaṃ ajaraṃ amaraṃ khemaṃ sukhaṃ sītalaṃ abhayaṃ nibbānapuraṃ pavisissāmi, sace me kiñci kāyikaṃ vā vācasikaṃ vā na rocetha, khamatha taṃ bhagavā, gamanakālo mayha”nti. Khamāmi te, sāriputta, na kho pana te kiñci kāyikaṃ vā vācasikaṃ vā mayhaṃ aruccanakaṃ atthi, yassa dāni tvaṃ, sāriputta, kālaṃ maññasīti.

The Elder, stretching forth his hands, which had the color of fresh lac, took hold of the Teacher’s feet, which resembled golden tortoises, at the ankles and said: 'Venerable Sir, for the sake of venerating these feet, I have fulfilled the perfections for one asaṅkhyeyya and more than one hundred thousand kappas. That wish of my heart has reached its culmination. From this time onwards, by way of rebirth-linking, there will be no more gathering or meeting in one place. This intimacy is severed. I shall enter the ageless, deathless, secure, blissful, cool, and fearless city of Nibbāna, which has been entered by many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas. If there is any bodily or verbal action of mine that was not pleasing to you, may the Blessed One forgive it. It is the time for my departure.' 'I forgive you, Sāriputta. Indeed, there is no bodily or verbal action of yours that is displeasing to me. Now, Sāriputta, you yourself know the right time.'

Iti bhagavatā anuññātasamanantaraṃ satthu pāde vanditvā uṭṭhitamatte āyasmante sāriputte sinerucakkavāḷahimavantaparibhaṇḍapabbate dhārayamānāpi – “ajja imaṃ guṇarāsiṃ dhāretuṃ na sakkomī”ti vadantī viya ekappahāreneva viravamānā mahāpathavī yāva udakapariyantā akampi, ākāse devadundubhiyo phaliṃsu, mahāmegho uṭṭhahitvā pokkharavassaṃ vassi.

Thus, immediately after being permitted by the Blessed One, at the very moment the Venerable Sāriputta rose after paying homage at the Teacher’s feet, the great earth—though supporting the Sineru, Cakkavāḷa, Himavanta, and Paribhaṇḍa mountains—trembled down to its water boundary, resounding at once as if saying, 'Today I am not able to support this mass of virtues!' In the sky, divine drums burst forth, and a great cloud, having arisen, poured down a rain of lotuses.

Satthā – “dhammasenāpatiṃ paṭipādessāmī”ti dhammāsanā [P 3.0216] vuṭṭhāya gandhakuṭiabhimukho gantvā maṇiphalake aṭṭhāsi. Thero tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā catūsu ṭhānesu vanditvā – “bhagavā ito kappasatasahassādhikassa asaṅkhyeyyassa upari anomadassīsammāsambuddhassa pādamūle nipajjitvā tumhākaṃ dassanaṃ patthesiṃ, sā me patthanā samiddhā, diṭṭhā tumhe, taṃ paṭhamadassanaṃ, idaṃ pacchimadassanaṃ. Puna tumhākaṃ dassanaṃ natthī”ti vatvā dasanakhasamodhānasamujjalaṃ [V 3.0245] añjaliṃ paggayha yāva dassanavisayā abhimukhova paṭikkamitvā [M 3.0249] vanditvā pakkāmi. Puna mahāpathavī dhāretuṃ asakkontī udakapariyantaṃ katvā akampi.

The Teacher, thinking, 'I will receive the final homage of the General of the Dhamma,' rose from the Dhamma seat, went towards the Fragrant Chamber, and stood on the jeweled slab. The Elder circumambulated him to the right three times, paid homage in four places, and said: 'Blessed One, one asaṅkhyeyya and more than one hundred thousand kappas ago, having prostrated myself at the feet of the Anomadassī Sammāsambuddha, I aspired to see you. That aspiration of mine has been fulfilled; I have seen you. That was the first seeing; this is the last seeing. There will be no more seeing of you.' Having spoken thus, he raised his añjali, shining with the radiance of his ten assembled fingernails, and retreated backwards while still facing the Buddha as far as he could be seen. Then, where he passed from sight, he paid homage and departed. Again the great earth, unable to bear it, trembled down to its water boundary.

Bhagavā parivāretvā ṭhite bhikkhū āha – “anugacchatha, bhikkhave, tumhākaṃ jeṭṭhabhātika”nti. Tasmiṃ khaṇe catassopi parisā sammāsambuddhaṃ ekakaṃyeva jetavane ohāya niravasesā nikkhamiṃsu. Sāvatthinagaravāsinopi – “sāriputtatthero kira sammāsambuddhaṃ āpucchitvā parinibbāyitukāmo nikkhanto, passissāma na”nti nagaradvārāni nirokāsāni karontā nikkhamitvā gandhamālādihatthā kese vikiritvā – “idāni mayaṃ kahaṃ mahāpañño nisinno, kahaṃ dhammasenāpati nisinno”ti pucchantā – “kassa santikaṃ gamissāma, kassa hatthe satthāraṃ ṭhapetvā thero pakkanto”tiādinā nayena paridevantā rodantā theraṃ anubandhiṃsu.

The Blessed One said to the monks who stood surrounding him: “Accompany, monks, your elder brother.” At that moment, all four assemblies, leaving the Fully Enlightened One alone in Jetavana, departed without exception. The residents of Sāvatthi also, thinking, “It is said that the Elder Sāriputta, having taken leave of the Fully Enlightened One, has departed, wishing to attain Parinibbāna; we shall see him,” went out, making the city gates impassably crowded. With perfumes, garlands, and other such things in hand, and with their hair dishevelled, they followed the Elder, asking, “Where now is the one of great wisdom seated? Where is the General of the Dhamma seated?” and lamenting and weeping in this and other ways, saying, “To whose presence shall we go? In whose hands has the Elder left the Teacher and departed?”

Thero mahāpaññāya ṭhitattā – “sabbesaṃ anatikkamanīyo esa maggo”ti mahājanaṃ ovaditvā – “tumhepi, āvuso, tiṭṭhatha, mā dasabale pamādaṃ āpajjitthā”ti bhikkhusaṅghampi nivattetvā attano parisāyeva saddhiṃ pakkāmi. Yepi manussā – “pubbe ayyo paccāgamanacārikaṃ carati, idaṃ idāni gamanaṃ na puna paccāgamanāyā”ti paridevantā anubandhiṃsuyeva. Tepi – “appamattā, āvuso, hotha, evaṃbhāvino nāma saṅkhārā”ti nivattesi.

The Elder, being established in great wisdom, advised the great crowd, saying: “This path is one that cannot be transgressed by any being.” Having also turned back the community of monks, advising them, “You too, friends, stay behind; do not be heedless towards the One of Ten Powers,” he departed with only his own retinue. And those people who lamented, “Formerly, the noble one would travel on a journey from which he would return, but this departure now is not for the purpose of returning again,” indeed continued to follow him. Them also he turned back, advising, “Be heedful, friends; conditioned things are indeed of such a nature, having this as their end.”

Atha kho āyasmā sāriputto sabbattha ekarattivāsena antarāmagge sattāhaṃ manussānaṃ [P 3.0217] saṅgahaṃ karonto sāyaṃ nālakagāmaṃ patvā gāmadvāre nigrodharukkhamūle aṭṭhāsi. Atha uparevato nāma therassa bhāgineyyo bahigāmaṃ gacchanto theraṃ disvā upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. Thero taṃ āha – “atthi gehe te ayyikā”ti. Āma bhanteti. Gaccha amhākaṃ idhāgatabhāvaṃ ārocehi. “Kasmā āgato”ti ca vutte – “ajja kira ekadivasaṃ antogāme vasissati, jātovarakaṃ paṭijaggatha, pañcannañca kira bhikkhusatānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ jānāthā”ti. So gantvā – “ayyike mayhaṃ mātulo āgato”ti āha. Idāni kuhinti? Gāmadvāreti. Ekakova, aññopi koci atthīti? Atthi pañcasatā bhikkhūti. Kiṃkāraṇā āgatoti? So taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Brāhmaṇī – “kiṃ nu kho ettakānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ paṭijaggāpeti[M 3.0250], daharakāle pabbajitvā mahallakakāle gihī hotukāmo”ti cintentī jātovarakaṃ paṭijaggāpetvā pañcasatānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ kāretvā daṇḍadīpikā jāletvā therassa pāhesi.

Then the Venerable Sāriputta, giving aid to the people for seven days along the way by staying one night in each place, reached the village of Nālaka in the evening and stood at the village gate at the foot of a banyan tree. Then the Elder's nephew, named Uparevata, going outside the village, saw the Elder, approached him, paid homage, and stood there. The Elder said to him: “Is your grandmother at home?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Go and announce the fact of our arrival here. And when asked, ‘Why has he come?’, say this: ‘It is said he will stay inside the village for one day today. Prepare the birth chamber, and also prepare a dwelling place for five hundred monks.’” He went and said: “Grandmother, my maternal uncle has arrived.” “Where is he now?” “At the village gate.” “Is he alone, or is there someone else?” “There are five hundred monks.” “For what reason has he come?” He told her that matter. The brahmin woman, thinking, “Why does he have a dwelling place prepared for so many? Having gone forth in his youth, does he wish to become a layman in his old age?”, had the birth chamber prepared, made a dwelling place for the five hundred monks, had torches lit, and sent them to the Elder.

Thero [V 3.0246] bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ pāsādaṃ āruyha jātovarakaṃ pavisitvā nisīdi, nisīditvā “tumhākaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gacchathā”ti bhikkhū uyyojesi. Tesu gatamattesuyeva therassa kharo ābādho uppajji, lohitapakkhandikā māraṇantikā vedanā vattanti. Ekaṃ bhājanaṃ pavisati, ekaṃ nikkhamati. Brāhmaṇī – “mama puttassa pavatti mayhaṃ na ruccatī”ti attano vasanagabbhadvāraṃ nissāya aṭṭhāsi.

The Elder, together with the monks, ascended the mansion, entered the birth chamber, and sat down. Having sat down, he dismissed the monks, saying, “Go to your dwelling places.” As soon as they had gone, a severe illness arose in the Elder; deadly pains of a bloody flux occurred. One vessel was brought in, another was taken out. The brahmin woman, thinking, “This condition of my son does not please me,” stood leaning against the door of her own living chamber.

Cattāro mahārājāno “dhammasenāpati kuhiṃ viharatī”ti olokentā nālakagāme jātovarake parinibbānamañce nipanno, pacchimadassanaṃ gamissāmā”ti āgamma vanditvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Ke tumheti? Mahārājāno bhanteti. Kasmā āgatatthāti? Gilānupaṭṭhākā bhavissāmāti. “Hotu, atthi gilānupaṭṭhāko, gacchatha tumhe”ti uyyojesi. Tesaṃ gatāvasāne teneva nayena sakko devānamindo. Tasmiṃ gate mahābrahmā ca āgamiṃsu. Tepi tatheva thero uyyojesi.

The Four Great Kings, looking to see, “Where is the General of the Dhamma dwelling?”, saw that he was lying on the couch of Parinibbāna in the birth chamber in the village of Nālaka. Thinking, “We will go for a final sight,” they came, paid homage, and stood there. “Who are you?” “Venerable sir, we are the Great Kings.” “For what reason have you come?” “We shall be attendants to the sick.” “Let it be. There is an attendant for the sick. You may go,” he said, and sent them away. After they had gone, Sakka, the king of the devas, came in the same way. When he had gone, the Mahābrahmās also came. The Elder sent them away in the same way as well.

Brāhmaṇī devatānaṃ āgamanañca gamanañca disvā “ke nu kho ete mama puttaṃ vanditvā gacchantī”ti therassa [P 3.0218] gabbhadvāraṃ gantvā “tāta, cunda, kā pavattī”ti pucchi. So taṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhitvā “mahāupāsikā, bhante, āgatā”ti āha. Thero “kasmā avelāya āgatā”ti pucchi. Sā “tuyhaṃ, tāta, dassanatthāyā”ti vatvā “tāta, paṭhamaṃ ke āgatā”ti pucchi. Cattāro mahārājāno upāsiketi. Tāta, tvaṃ catūhi mahārājehi mahantataroti? Ārāmikasadisā ete upāsike, amhākaṃ satthu paṭisandhiggahaṇato paṭṭhāya khaggahatthā hutvā ārakkhaṃ akaṃsūti. Tesaṃ tāta gatāvasāne ko āgatoti? Sakko devānamindoti. Devarājatopi tvaṃ tāta mahantataroti? Bhaṇḍaggāhakasāmaṇerasadiso esa upāsike, amhākaṃ satthu tāvatiṃsato otaraṇakāle pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā otiṇṇoti. Tassa tāta gatāvasāne jotayamāno viya ko āgatoti? Upāsike, tuyhaṃ bhagavā ca satthā ca mahābrahmā nāma esoti. Mayhaṃ bhagavato [M 3.0251] mahābrahmatopi tvaṃ, tāta, mahantataroti? Āma upāsike, ete nāma kira amhākaṃ satthu jātadivase cattāro mahābrahmāno mahāpurisaṃ suvaṇṇajālena paṭiggaṇhiṃsūti.

The brahmin woman, seeing the coming and going of the deities and thinking, “Who indeed are these who pay homage to my son and then depart?”, went to the door of the Elder’s chamber and asked, “Dear Cunda, what is the matter?” He explained the situation and then said, “Venerable sir, the great laywoman has come.” The Elder asked, “Why has she come at this untimely hour?” She replied, “To see you, dear one,” and then asked, “Dear one, who came first?” “The Four Great Kings, O laywoman.” “Dear one, are you greater than the Four Great Kings?” “They are like monastery attendants, O laywoman. From the time of our Teacher’s conception, they stood guard with swords in hand.” “After they had gone, dear one, who came?” “Sakka, the king of the devas.” “Dear one, are you greater even than the king of the devas?” “He is like a novice who carries the requisites, O laywoman. When our Teacher was descending from Tāvatiṃsa, he descended holding the bowl and robes.” “After he had gone, dear one, who came, as if blazing?” “O laywoman, this one is named Mahābrahmā, who is your lord and teacher.” “Dear one, are you greater even than Mahābrahmā, my lord?” “Yes, O laywoman. Indeed, it is said that on the day of our Teacher’s birth, four such Mahābrahmās received the Great Being with a golden net.”

Atha brāhmaṇiyā – “puttassa tāva me ayaṃ ānubhāvo, kīdiso vata mayhaṃ puttassa bhagavato [V 3.0247] satthu ānubhāvo bhavissatī”ti cintayantiyā sahasā pañcavaṇṇā pīti uppajjitvā sakalasarīraṃ phari. Thero – “uppannaṃ me mātu pītisomanassaṃ, ayaṃ dāni kālo dhammadesanāyā”ti cintetvā “kiṃ cintesi mahāupāsike”ti āha. Sā “puttassa tāva me ayaṃ guṇo, satthu panassa kīdiso bhavissatīti idaṃ, tāta, cintemī”ti āha. Mahāupāsike, mayhaṃ satthujātakkhaṇe mahābhinikkhamane sambodhiyaṃ dhammacakkappavattane ca dasasahassilokadhātu kampittha. Sīlena samādhinā paññāya vimuttiyā vimuttiñāṇadassanena samo nāma natthi, itipi so bhagavāti vitthāretvā buddhaguṇapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ dhammadesanaṃ kathesi.

Then, as the brahmin woman was thinking, “Such is the power of my son—what then must be the power of my son’s teacher, the Blessed One?”, suddenly, five-fold rapture arose and suffused her entire body. The Elder, thinking, “Joy and gladness have arisen in my mother—now is the time for a Dhamma discourse,” asked, “What are you thinking about, great laywoman?” She replied, “Dear son, I was thinking, ‘Such is the quality of my son—what then must be that of his teacher?’” “Great laywoman, at the moment of my Teacher’s birth, his Great Renunciation, his enlightenment, and the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the ten-thousandfold world-system shook. There is none equal to him in morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. For this reason too, he is the Blessed One.” And elaborating thus, he delivered a Dhamma discourse connected with the virtues of the Buddha.

Brāhmaṇī piyaputtassa dhammadesanāpariyosāne sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya puttaṃ āha – “tāta upatissa, kasmā evamakāsi, evarūpaṃ nāma amataṃ mayhaṃ ettakaṃ kālaṃ na adāsī”ti. Thero – “dinnaṃ dāni me mātu rūpasāriyā [P 3.0219] brāhmaṇiyā posāvanikamūlaṃ, ettakena vaṭṭissatī”ti cintetvā – “gaccha mahāupasike”ti brāhmaṇiṃ uyyojetvā – “cunda kā velā”ti āha. Balavapaccūsakālo, bhanteti. Bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sannipātehīti. Sannipatito bhante bhikkhusaṅghoti. “Maṃ ukkhipitvā nisīdāpehi cundā”ti ukkhipitvā nisīdāpesi.

The brahmin woman, having been established in the fruit of stream-entry at the conclusion of her beloved son's Dhamma discourse, said to her son: “Dear Upatissa, why did you act thus? Why for so long a time did you not give me this deathless state?” The Elder, reflecting, “I have now repaid the debt for my upbringing to my mother, the brahmin woman Rūpasārī; this will be sufficient,” dismissed the brahmin woman, saying, “Go, great laywoman.” Then he asked, “Cunda, what time is it?” “It is the time of late dawn, Venerable Sir.” “Assemble the community of monks.” “The community of monks has assembled, Venerable Sir.” “Cunda, lift me up and seat me.” He lifted him up and seated him.

Thero bhikkhū āmantesi – “āvuso catucattālīsaṃ vo vassāni mayā saddhiṃ vicarantānaṃ yaṃ me kāyikaṃ vā vācasikaṃ vā na rocetha, taṃ khamatha āvuso”ti. Ettakaṃ, bhante, amhākaṃ chāyā viya tumhe amuñcitvā vicarantānaṃ aruccanakaṃ nāma natthi, tumhe pana amhākaṃ khamathāti. Atha thero mahācīvaraṃ saṅkaḍḍhitvā mukhaṃ pidhāya dakkhiṇena passena nipanno satthā viya nava anupubbasamāpattiyo anulomapaṭilomato samāpajjitvā puna paṭhamajjhānaṃ ādiṃ katvā yāva catutthajjhānā samāpajji[M 3.0252]. Tato vuṭṭhāya anantaraṃyeva mahāpathaviṃ unnādento anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyi.

The Elder addressed the monks: “Friends, for the forty-four years that you have wandered with me, if there was any bodily or verbal action of mine that you did not approve of, please forgive it, friends.” “Venerable sir,” they replied, “for all this time, as we wandered without leaving you, like a shadow, there has been nothing at all displeasing in you. Rather, may you forgive us.” Then the Elder, pulling up his great robe, covered his face and lay down on his right side like the Teacher. He entered the nine successive attainments in forward and reverse order, and then again, beginning with the first jhāna, he entered up to the fourth jhāna. Rising from that, he immediately attained parinibbāna with the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining, causing the great earth to resound.

Upāsikā – “kiṃ nu kho me putto, na kiñci kathetī”ti uṭṭhāya piṭṭhipāde parimajjantī parinibbutabhāvaṃ ñatvā mahāsaddaṃ kurumānā pādesu nipatitvā – “tāta mayaṃ ito pubbe tava guṇaṃ na jānimhā, idāni pana taṃ ādiṃ katvā anekasate anekasahasse anekasatasahasse bhikkhū imasmiṃ nivesane nisīdāpetvā bhojetuṃ na labhimhā, cīvarehi acchādetuṃ na labhimhā, vihārasataṃ vihārasahassaṃ kāretuṃ na labhimhā”ti yāva aruṇuggamanā paridevi[V 3.0248]. Aruṇe uggatamatteyeva suvaṇṇakāre pakkosāpetvā suvaṇṇagabbhaṃ vivarāpetvā suvaṇṇaghaṭiyo mahātulāya tulāpetvā – “pañca kūṭāgārasatāni pañca agghikasatāni karothā”ti dāpeti.

The laywoman, thinking, “What is this? My son says nothing,” rose, and while rubbing the tops of his feet, she realized he had attained parinibbāna. Letting out a great cry, she fell at his feet and lamented until sunrise: “Dear son, before this, we did not know your virtues. Now, with you as the foremost, we did not get the chance to seat and feed hundreds, thousands, and hundreds of thousands of monks in this house, nor to clothe them with robes, nor to have a hundred or a thousand monasteries built.” As soon as the sun rose, she had goldsmiths summoned, had the golden treasury opened, had golden jars weighed out on a large scale, and gave the instruction: “Make five hundred gabled pavilions and five hundred pyres.”

Sakkopi devarājā vissakammadevaputtaṃ āmantetvā – “tāta dhammasenāpati parinibbuto, pañca kūṭāgārasatāni pañca agghikasatāni ca māpehī”ti āha. Iti upāsikāya kāritāni ca vissakammena nimmitāni ca sabbānipi dvesahassāni ahesuṃ. Tato nagaramajjhe sāramayaṃ mahāmaṇḍapaṃ kāretvā maṇḍapamajjhe mahākūṭāgāraṃ ṭhapetvā [P 3.0220] sesāni parivārasaṅkhepena ṭhapetvā sādhukīḷikaṃ ārabhiṃsu. Devānaṃ antare manussā, manussānaṃ antare devā ahesuṃ.

Sakka, king of the devas, also summoned the devaputta Vissakamma and said, “Dear one, the General of the Dhamma has attained parinibbāna. Create five hundred gabled pavilions and five hundred pyres.” Thus, those caused to be made by the laywoman and those created by Vissakamma totaled two thousand in all. Then, in the middle of the city, they had a great pavilion of heartwood made, placed a great gabled pavilion in the center of it, and arranged the rest as a retinue. They began a reverential festival. Among the devas were humans, and among the humans were devas.

Revatī nāma ekā therassa upaṭṭhāyikā – “ahaṃ therassa pūjaṃ karissāmī”ti suvaṇṇapupphānaṃ tayo kumbhe kāresi. “Therassa pūjaṃ karissāmī”ti sakko devarājā aḍḍhateyyakoṭināṭakehi parivārito otari. “Sakko otaratī”ti mahājano pacchāmukho paṭikkami. Tattha sāpi upāsikā paṭikkamamānā garubhārattā ekamantaṃ apasakkituṃ asakkontī manussānaṃ antare pati. Manussā apassantā taṃ madditvā agamiṃsu. Sā tattheva kālaṃ katvā tāvatiṃsabhavane kanakavimāne nibbatti. Nibbattakkhaṇeyevassā ratanakkhandho viya tigāvutappamāṇo attabhāvo ahosi saṭṭhisakaṭapūrappamāṇaalaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitā accharāsahassaparivāritā. Athassā dibbaṃ sabbakāyikādāsaṃ purato ṭhapayiṃsu[M 3.0253]. Sā attano sirisampattiṃ disvā – “uḷārā ayaṃ sampatti, kiṃ nu kho me kammaṃ kata”nti cintayamānā addasa – “mayā sāriputtattherassa parinibbutaṭṭhāne tīhi suvaṇṇapupphakumbhehi pūjā katā, mahājano maṃ madditvā gato, sāhaṃ tattha kālaṃ katvā idhūpapannā, theraṃ nissāya laddhaṃ idāni puññavipākaṃ manussānaṃ kathessāmī”ti saha vimāneneva otari.

A female attendant of the Elder named Revatī thought, “I will make an offering to the Elder,” and had three pots of golden flowers made. Thinking, “I will make an offering to the Elder,” Sakka, king of the devas, descended, surrounded by two and a half crores of celestial dancers. Thinking, “Sakka is descending,” the great crowd turned back and retreated. Therein, that laywoman, while retreating, was unable to step aside due to a heavy burden and fell among the people. Not seeing her, the people trampled her and went on. She died right there and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven in a golden celestial mansion. At the very moment of her rebirth, her body became like a mass of jewels, three gāvutas in size, adorned with ornaments amounting to sixty cartloads, and she was surrounded by a thousand celestial nymphs. Then, a divine full-length mirror was placed before her. Seeing her own glorious fortune, she wondered, “This fortune is magnificent. What deed, I wonder, have I done?” Reflecting, she saw: “I made an offering with three pots of golden flowers at the place where the Elder Sāriputta attained parinibbāna. The great crowd trampled me and went on. I died there and have been reborn here. I will now declare to the people the fruit of the merit I have gained on account of the Elder.” With that, she descended together with her celestial mansion.

Mahājano dūratova disvā – “kiṃ nu kho dve sūriyā uṭṭhitā”ti? Olokento – “vimāne āgacchante kūṭāgārasaṇṭhānaṃ paññāyati, nāyaṃ sūriyo, vimānametaṃ eka”nti āha. Tampi vimānaṃ tāvadeva āgantvā therassa dārucitakamatthake vehāsaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Devadhītā vimānaṃ ākāseyeva ṭhapetvā pathaviṃ otari. Mahājano – “kā tvaṃ, ayye”ti? Pucchi. “Na maṃ tumhe jānātha, revatī nāmāhaṃ, tīhi suvaṇṇapupphakumbhehi theraṃ pūjaṃ katvā manussehi madditā [V 3.0249] kālaṃ katvā tāvatiṃsabhavane nibbattā, passatha me sirisampattiṃ, tumhepi dāni dānāni detha, puññāni karothā”ti kusalakiriyāya vaṇṇaṃ kathetvā therassa citakaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā vanditvā attano devaṭṭhānaṃyeva gatā.

The great crowd, seeing it from afar, wondered, 'What is this, I wonder? Have two suns risen?' Observing, they said, 'As the celestial mansion approaches, the form of a gabled house appears. This is not the sun; it is a celestial mansion.' That mansion, having arrived at that very moment, stood in the sky above the Elder's wooden pyre. The celestial maiden, having placed the mansion in the sky, descended to the earth. The great crowd asked, 'Who are you, venerable lady?' She replied, 'Do you not know me? I am named Revatī. Having made an offering to the Elder with three pots of golden flowers, I was trampled by the people, died, and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Behold my glorious fortune! You too should now give gifts and make merit.' Thus, having spoken in praise of wholesome actions, she circumambulated the Elder’s pyre, paid homage, and returned to her own divine abode.

Mahājanopi [P 3.0221] sattāhaṃ sādhukīḷikaṃ kīḷitvā sabbagandhehi citakaṃ akāsi, citakā ekūnaratanasatikā ahosi. Therassa sarīraṃ citakaṃ āropetvā usīrakalāpakehi ālimpesuṃ. Āḷāhane sabbarattiṃ dhammassavanaṃ pavatti. Anuruddhatthero sabbagandhodakena therassa citakaṃ nibbāpesi. Cundatthero dhātuyo parissāvane pakkhipitvā – “na dāni mayā idheva sakkā ṭhātuṃ, mayhaṃ jeṭṭhabhātikassa dhammasenāpatisāriputtattherassa parinibbutabhāvaṃ sammāsambuddhassa ārocessāmī”ti dhātuparissāvanaṃ therassa ca pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā sāvatthiṃ agamāsi. Ekaṭṭhānepi ca dve rattiyo avasitvā sabbattha ekarattivāseneva sāvatthiṃ pāpuṇi. Tamatthaṃ dassetuṃ atha kho cundo samaṇuddesotiādi vuttaṃ.

The great crowd also, having celebrated the festival of the virtuous for seven days, made a pyre with all kinds of fragrant substances; the pyre was one hundred cubits less one. Having placed the Elder’s body on the pyre, they set it alight with bundles of usīra grass. At the cremation ground, the hearing of the Dhamma continued throughout the night. The Elder Anuruddha extinguished the Elder’s pyre with water scented with all fragrances. The Elder Cunda, having placed the relics in a water strainer, thought, 'It is not possible for me to stay here now. I will announce to the Perfectly Enlightened One the fact of the parinibbāna of my elder brother, the General of the Dhamma, the Elder Sāriputta.' Taking the relic strainer and the Elder’s bowl and robe, he went to Sāvatthī. Not staying for two nights in any one place, he reached Sāvatthī by staying only one night in each place. To show this matter, the passage beginning 'Then the novice Cunda...' was said.

Tattha yenāyasmā ānandoti yena attano upajjhāyo dhammabhaṇḍāgāriko āyasmā ānando, tenupasaṅkami. Kasmā panesa ujukaṃ [M 3.0254] satthu santikaṃ agantvā therassa santikaṃ agamāsīti? Satthari ca there ca gāravena. Jetavanamahāvihāre pokkharaṇiyaṃ kirassa nhatvā paccuttaritvā sunivatthasupārutassa etadahosi – “buddhā nāma mahāpāsāṇacchattaṃ viya garuno, phaṇakatasappa sīhabyagghamattavaravāraṇādayo viya ca durāsadā, na sakkā mayā ujukameva satthu santikaṃ gantvā kathetuṃ, kassa nu kho santikaṃ gantabba”nti. Tato cintesi – “upajjhāyo me dhammabhaṇḍāgāriko jeṭṭhabhātikattherassa uttamasahāyo, tassa santikaṃ gantvā taṃ ādāya satthārā saddhiṃ kathessāmī”ti satthari ceva there ca gāravena upasaṅkami.

Therein, regarding the phrase 'where the Venerable Ānanda was', it means he approached the place where his own preceptor, the Treasurer of the Dhamma, the Venerable Ānanda, was. Why, then, did he not go directly to the Teacher's presence, but instead go to the Elder's presence? It was out of respect for both the Teacher and the Elder. It is said that after bathing in the pond in the Jetavana Great Monastery and emerging, while he was properly dressed and covered, this thought occurred to him: 'Buddhas are weighty, like a great stone parasol, and difficult to approach, like a snake with expanded hood, a lion, a tiger, a mighty elephant in must, and so on. It is not possible for me to go directly into the Teacher's presence and speak. To whose presence, I wonder, should I go?' Then he thought: 'My preceptor is the Treasurer of the Dhamma and the best companion of the Elder, my elder brother. I will go to his presence, and taking him with me, I will speak with the Teacher.' Thus, out of respect for both the Teacher and the Elder, he approached.

Idamassa pattacīvaranti “ayamassa paribhogapatto, idaṃ dhātuparissāvana”nti evaṃ ekekaṃ ācikkhi. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “idamassa pattacīvara”nti ettakameva vuttaṃ. Kathāpābhatanti kathāmūlaṃ. Mūlañhi pābhatanti vuccati. Yathāha –

Regarding the phrase 'This is his bowl and robe,' he announced each item individually, saying, 'This is his bowl for personal use, and this is the relic strainer.' In the Pāli text, however, only this much is said: 'This is his bowl and robe.' The term 'kathāpābhata' means the basis for a talk. Indeed, a basis is called a 'pābhata', as it is said:

“Appakenapi [P 3.0222] medhāvī, pābhatena vicakkhaṇo;

Samuṭṭhāpeti attānaṃ, aṇuṃ aggiṃva sandhama”nti. (jā. 1.1.4);

'Even with a small basis, a wise and discerning person establishes themself, just as one fans a tiny fire.'

Bhagavantaṃ [V 3.0250] dassanāyāti bhagavantaṃ dassanatthāya. Kiṃ paniminā bhagavā na diṭṭhapubboti? No na diṭṭhapubbo. Ayañhi āyasmā divā nava vāre, rattiṃ nava vāreti ekāhaṃ aṭṭhārasa vāre upaṭṭhānameva gacchati. Divasassa pana satavāraṃ vā sahassavāraṃ vā gantukāmo samānopi na akāraṇā gacchati, ekaṃ pañhadvāraṃ gahetvāva gacchati. So taṃdivasaṃ tena kathāpābhatena gantukāmo evamāha. Idamassa pattacīvaranti theropi – “idaṃ tassa pattacīvaraṃ, idañca dhātuparissāvana”nti pāṭiyekkaṃyeva dassetvā ācikkhi.

The phrase 'for seeing the Blessed One' means for the purpose of seeing the Blessed One. Now, had the Blessed One not been seen by him before? No, it is not that he had not been seen before. Indeed, this venerable one goes to attend upon him eighteen times in a single day: nine times during the day and nine times at night. However, even if he wished to go a hundred or a thousand times a day, he would not go without a reason; he goes only after taking up some opportunity for a question. So on that day, wishing to go with that basis for a talk, he spoke thus. The Elder also, regarding the phrase 'This is his bowl and robe,' showed each item separately and announced: 'This is his bowl and robe, and this is the relic strainer.'

Satthā hatthaṃ pasāretvā dhātuparissāvanaṃ gahetvā hatthatale ṭhapetvā bhikkhū āmantesi – “yo so, bhikkhave, bhikkhu purimadivase anekāni pāṭihāriyasatāni katvā parinibbānaṃ anujānāpesi, tassa idāni imā saṅkhavaṇṇasannibhā dhātuyova paññāyanti, kappasatasahassādhikaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ pūritapāramī esa, bhikkhave, bhikkhu, mayā pavattitaṃ dhammacakkaṃ [M 3.0255] anupavattako esa bhikkhu, paṭiladdhadutiyaāsano esa bhikkhu, pūritasāvakasannipāto esa bhikkhu, ṭhapetvā maṃ dasasu cakkavāḷasahassesu paññāya asadiso esa bhikkhu, mahāpañño esa bhikkhu, puthupañño hāsapañño javanapañño tikkhapañño nibbedhikapañño esa bhikkhu, appiccho esa bhikkhu, santuṭṭho pavivitto asaṃsaṭṭho āraddhavīriyo codako pāpagarahī esa bhikkhu, pañca jātisatāni paṭiladdhamahāsampattiyo pahāya pabbajito esa bhikkhu, mama sāsane pathavīsamakhantiko esa bhikkhu, chinnavisāṇausabhasadiso esa bhikkhu, caṇḍālaputtasadisanīcacitto esa bhikkhu. Passatha, bhikkhave, mahāpaññassa dhātuyo, passatha, bhikkhave, puthupaññassa hāsapaññassa javanapaññassa tikkhapaññassa nibbedhikapaññassa appicchassa santuṭṭhassa pavivittassa asaṃsaṭṭhassa āraddhavīriyassa[P 3.0223], codakassa, passatha, bhikkhave, pāpagarahissa dhātuyoti.

The Teacher stretched out His hand, took the relic-cloth, placed it on the palm of His hand, and addressed the bhikkhus: 'Bhikkhus, that bhikkhu who on the previous day performed many hundreds of miracles and for whose Parinibbāna I gave permission—of him, now only these relics, resembling the color of a conch shell, are apparent. This bhikkhu, bhikkhus, is one who has fulfilled his perfections for an incalculable aeon and over one hundred thousand kappas. This bhikkhu is one who turns the Wheel of Dhamma in succession to me, who set it in motion. This bhikkhu is one who has obtained the second seat. This bhikkhu is one who has fulfilled the great assembly of disciples. Setting me aside, this bhikkhu is without equal in wisdom in the ten thousand world-systems. This bhikkhu is of great wisdom. This bhikkhu is of extensive wisdom, joyful wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, and penetrative wisdom. This bhikkhu has few wants. This bhikkhu is content, secluded, unassociated, with energy aroused, an admonisher, and a reprover of evil. This bhikkhu is one who went forth, having abandoned great fortunes obtained over five hundred births. This bhikkhu has patience like the earth in my Dispensation. This bhikkhu is like a bull with severed horns. This bhikkhu has a humble mind like the son of an outcaste. Behold, bhikkhus, the relics of one of great wisdom! Behold, bhikkhus, the relics of one of extensive wisdom, joyful wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, penetrative wisdom, of few wants, content, secluded, unassociated, with energy aroused, an admonisher! Behold, bhikkhus, the relics of one who reproves evil!'

“Yo pabbajī jātisatāni pañca,

Pahāya kāmāni manoramāni;

Taṃ vītarāgaṃ susamāhitindriyaṃ,

Parinibbutaṃ vandatha sāriputtaṃ.

He who went forth over five hundred births, having abandoned delightful sensual pleasures; him, Sāriputta, free from lust, with faculties well-composed, who has attained Parinibbāna—do you venerate.

“Khantibalo [V 3.0251] pathavisamo na kuppati,

Na cāpi cittassa vasena vattati;

Anukampako kāruṇiko ca nibbuto,

Parinibbutaṃ vandatha sāriputtaṃ.

Strong in patience, like the earth he is not angered, nor does he act under the sway of his mind; sympathetic, compassionate, and extinguished—him, Sāriputta, who has attained Parinibbāna, do you venerate.

“Caṇḍālaputto yathā nagaraṃ paviṭṭho,

Nīcamano carati kaḷopihattho;

Tathā ayaṃ viharati sāriputto,

Parinibbutaṃ vandatha sāriputtaṃ.

Just as the son of an outcaste, having entered a city, wanders with a humble mind and a basket-bowl in hand; so does this Sāriputta dwell. Him, Sāriputta, who has attained Parinibbāna, do you venerate.

“Usabho yathā chinnavisāṇako,

Aheṭhayanto carati purantare vane;

Tathā ayaṃ viharati sāriputto,

Parinibbutaṃ vandatha sāriputta”nti.

Just as a bull with severed horns wanders, not harming anyone, within the city or in the forest; so does this Sāriputta dwell. Him, Sāriputta, who has attained Parinibbāna, do you venerate.

Iti [M 3.0256] bhagavā pañcahi gāthāsatehi therassa vaṇṇaṃ kathesi. Yathā yathā bhagavā therassa vaṇṇaṃ kathesi, tathā tathā ānandatthero sandhāretuṃ na sakkoti, biḷāramukhe pakkhantakukkuṭo viya pavedhati. Tenāha apica me, bhante, madhurakajāto viya kāyoti sabbaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Tattha madhurakajātotiādīnaṃ attho vuttoyeva. Idha pana dhammāti uddesaparipucchādhammā adhippetā. Tassa hi uddesaparipucchādhamme agahite vā gahetuṃ, gahite vā sajjhāyaṃ kātuṃ cittaṃ na pavattati. Atha satthā pañcapasādavicitrāni akkhīni ummīletvā theraṃ olokento “assāsessāmi na”nti assāsento kiṃ nu kho te, ānanda, sāriputtotiādimāha.

Thus the Blessed One spoke five hundred verses in praise of the elder. As the Blessed One praised the elder, Venerable Ānanda was unable to remain steady, trembling like a young chicken that has fallen into a cat’s mouth. Therefore he said, 'Moreover, venerable sir, my body feels as if it has become weak.' All this should be elaborated. Here, however, by 'Dhamma' is meant the Dhamma of recitation and inquiry. For his mind was not inclined to learn the Dhamma of recitation and inquiry that was not yet learned, or to rehearse what had been learned. Then the Teacher, opening His eyes, which were wonderful with five kinds of clarity, looking at the elder, and comforting him, thinking, 'I shall comfort him,' said, 'What then, Ānanda? Has Sāriputta...?' and so on.

Tattha sīlakkhandhanti lokiyalokuttarasīlaṃ. Samādhipaññāsupi eseva nayo. Vimutti pana lokuttarāva. Vimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ [P 3.0224] paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ, taṃ lokiyameva. Ovādakoti ovādadāyako. Otiṇṇoti otiṇṇesu vatthūsu nānappakārena otaraṇasīlo. Viññāpakoti dhammakathākāle atthañca kāraṇañca viññāpetā. Sandassakoti khandhadhātuāyatanavasena tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ [V 3.0252] dassetā. Samādapakoti “idañcidañca gaṇhathā”ti evaṃ gaṇhāpako. Samuttejakoti abbhussāhako. Sampahaṃsakoti paṭiladdhaguṇehi modāpako jotāpako.

Therein, 'the aggregate of virtue' refers to both mundane and supramundane virtue. The same principle applies to concentration and wisdom. Liberation, however, is solely supramundane. The knowledge and vision of liberation is the reviewing knowledge, and that is only mundane. An 'advisor' is one who gives advice. One who is 'adept' is one who has the habit of entering into various topics in diverse ways. An 'expounder' is one who clarifies both the meaning and the reason when teaching the Dhamma. A 'revealer' is one who demonstrates various phenomena by way of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases. A 'promoter' is one who causes others to take up by saying, 'Take up this and that.' An 'inspirer' is one who encourages. A 'gladdener' is one who makes others rejoice and illuminates them with acquired virtues.

Akilāsu dhammadesanāyāti dhammadesanaṃ ārabhitvā “sīsaṃ vā me rujjati, hadayaṃ vā kucchi vā piṭṭhi vā”ti evaṃ osakkanākāravirahito nikkilāsu visārado ekassāpi dvinnampi sīhavegeneva pakkhandati. Anuggāhako sabrahmacārīnanti padassa attho khandhakavagge vitthāritova. Dhammojaṃ dhammabhoganti ubhayenapi dhammaparibhogova kathito. Dhammānuggahanti dhammena anuggahaṇaṃ.

'Not weary in teaching the Dhamma' means that having begun the Dhamma teaching, he is without any sign of reluctance, such as saying, 'My head aches, or my heart, or my stomach, or my back,' but is unwearied and confident, plunging in with the energy of a lion even for one or two people. The meaning of the phrase 'a helper of his fellow monks' has been explained in detail in the Khandhaka section. 'Nourished by Dhamma' and 'enjoying Dhamma'—by both is meant the partaking of the Dhamma. 'Support through the Dhamma' means support by means of the Dhamma.

Satthā “ativiya ayaṃ bhikkhu kilamatī”ti puna taṃ assāsento nanu taṃ, ānanda, mayātiādimāha. Tattha piyehi manāpehīti mātāpitābhātābhaginīādikehi jātiyā nānābhāvo, maraṇena vinābhāvo, bhavena aññathābhāvo. Taṃ kutettha, ānanda, labbhāti tanti [M 3.0257] tasmā. Yasmā sabbehi piyehi manāpehi nānābhāvo, tasmā dasa pāramiyo pūretvāpi sambodhiṃ patvāpi dhammacakkaṃ pavattetvāpi yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ dassetvāpi devorohanaṃ katvāpi yaṃ taṃ jātaṃ bhūtaṃ saṅkhataṃ palokadhammaṃ, taṃ tathāgatassāpi sarīraṃ mā palujjīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati, rodantenapi kandantenapi na sakkā taṃ kāraṇaṃ laddhunti. So palujjeyyāti so bhijjeyya.

The Teacher, thinking, 'This bhikkhu is extremely weary,' again comforted him, saying, 'Is it not, Ānanda, that by me...?' and so on. Therein, 'from those dear and beloved' means being different from mother, father, brother, sister, and so on, by birth; being separated by death; and being otherwise by existence. In the phrase 'How, Ānanda, could that be obtained here?,' 'that' means 'therefore.' Since there is separation from all that is dear and beloved, therefore, even after fulfilling the ten perfections, attaining full enlightenment, setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, displaying the Twin Miracle, and descending from the deva realm—that this body of the Tathāgata, which is born, has come into being, is conditioned, and is of a nature to break up, should not break up—this state of affairs is impossible. That condition cannot be obtained by weeping or lamenting. 'May that break apart' means 'May that great branch be broken.'

Evameva khoti ettha yojanasatubbedho mahājamburukkho viya bhikkhusaṅgho tassa dakkhiṇadisaṃ gato paññāsayojaniko mahākhandho viya dhammasenāpati. Tasmiṃ mahākhandhe bhinne tato paṭṭhāya anupubbena vaḍḍhitvā pupphaphalādīhi taṃ ṭhānaṃ pūretuṃ samatthassa aññassa khandhassa abhāvo viya there parinibbute soḷasannaṃ paññānaṃ matthakaṃ pattassa aññassa dakkhiṇāsane nisīdanasamatthassa sāriputtasadisassa bhikkhuno abhāvo. Tāya paribhinnāya so rukkho viya [P 3.0225] bhikkhusaṅgho khandhotveva jātoti veditabbo. Tasmāti yasmā sabbaṃ saṅkhataṃ palokadhammaṃ, taṃ mā palujjīti na sakkā laddhuṃ, tasmā.

Herein, in the text `Evameva kho`, the community of bhikkhus should be regarded as like a great Jambu tree one hundred yojanas high, and its great branch, fifty yojanas long, extending to the south, as like the General of the Dhamma. When that great branch was broken, just as there was no other branch capable of gradually growing from that point and filling that place with flowers and fruits, so too, after the Elder attained parinibbāna, there was no other bhikkhu like Sāriputta—who had reached the pinnacle of the sixteen kinds of wisdom—capable of sitting in the seat at the Buddha's right hand. When that great branch was broken, the community of bhikkhus should be understood to have become like that tree, merely a trunk. As for `tasmā`: because all conditioned things have the nature of perishing, it is not possible to obtain the wish, 'May it not perish!'; therefore...

4-5. Ukkacelasuttādivaṇṇanā

4-5. Commentary on the Ukkacela Sutta and the Like

380-381. Catutthe [V 3.0253] aciraparinibbutesu sāriputtamoggallānesūti naciraparinibbutesu dvīsu aggasāvakesu. Tesañhi dhammasenāpati kattikamāsapuṇṇamāya parinibbuto, mahāmoggallāno tato aḍḍhamāsaṃ atikkamma amāvasuposathe. Satthā dvīsu aggasāvakesu parinibbutesu mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivāro mahāmaṇḍale cārikaṃ caramāno anupubbena ukkacelanagaraṃ patvā tattha piṇḍāya caritvā gaṅgāpiṭṭhe rajatapaṭṭavaṇṇavālikāpuline vihāsi. Tena vuttaṃ “aciraparinibbutesu sāriputtamoggallānesū”ti. Ye mahantatarā khandhā te palujjeyyunti idhāpi yojanasatubbedho mahājamburukkho viya bhikkhusaṅgho, tassa dakkhiṇato ca uttarato ca gatā paṇṇāsayojanikā dve mahākhandhā viya dve aggasāvakāti. Sesaṃ purimanayeneva yojetabbaṃ. Pañcame diṭṭhīti kammassakadiṭṭhi.

In the fourth, 'soon after the parinibbāna of Sāriputta and Moggallāna' means when the two chief disciples had attained parinibbāna not long ago. For among them, the General of the Dhamma attained parinibbāna on the full moon day of the month of Kattika, and Mahāmoggallāna half a month later, on the new moon uposatha day. After the Teacher's two chief disciples had attained parinibbāna, while surrounded by the great community of bhikkhus, he was journeying on tour in a great circuit and gradually reached the city of Ukkācela. There, after going for alms, he stayed on a sandbank on the bank of the Ganges, which had the color of a silver plate. Hence it is said, 'soon after the parinibbāna of Sāriputta and Moggallāna.' As for the text, 'The greater branches have broken off': here too, the community of bhikkhus is like a great Jambu tree one hundred yojanas high; its two great branches, each fifty yojanas long, extending to the south and north, are like the two chief disciples. The rest should be understood in the same way as before. In the fifth, 'view' is the view of kamma as one's own property.

6. Uttiyasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Uttiya Sutta

382. Chaṭṭhe [M 3.0258] maccudheyyassa pāranti tebhūmakavaṭṭassa pārabhūtaṃ, nibbānaṃ.

In the sixth, 'the far shore of Death's realm' means Nibbāna, which is the far shore of the round of existence in the three planes.

8. Brahmasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Brahma Sutta

384. Aṭṭhame kāye vā bhikkhūti tasmiṃ kāle bhikkhuyeva natthi, evaṃ santepi yo satipaṭṭhāne bhāveti, so kilesabhindanena bhikkhuyevāti dassento evamāha. Ekāyananti [P 3.0226] ekamaggaṃ. Jātikkhayantadassīti jātiyā khayoti ca antoti ca nibbānaṃ, taṃ passatīti attho. Maggaṃ pajānātīti ekāyanasaṅkhātaṃ ekamaggabhūtaṃ maggaṃ pajānāti. Ekāyanamaggo vuccati pubbabhāgasatipaṭṭhānamaggo, taṃ pajānātīti attho.

6. In the eighth, regarding 'or a bhikkhu in the body': at that time there was no bhikkhu at all. Even so, the Buddha spoke as he did to show that one who cultivates the foundations of mindfulness is indeed a bhikkhu by means of destroying the defilements. 'The one way' means the one path. 'Seeing the destruction and end of birth' means one sees Nibbāna, which is called both the destruction and the end of birth. 'Knows the path' means one knows distinctly the path called the 'one way,' which is the one path. The path of the foundations of mindfulness in the preliminary stage is called the one-way path; the meaning is that one knows this distinctly.

9. Sedakasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Sedaka Sutta

385. Navame sumbhesūti evaṃnāmake janapade. Medakathālikāti evaṃ itthiliṅgavasena laddhanāmaṃ. Mamaṃ rakkha, ahaṃ taṃ rakkhissāmīti ettha ayaṃ tassa laddhi – ācariyo ukkhittavaṃsaṃ [V 3.0254] suggahitaṃ agaṇhanto, antevāsikena pakkhantapakkhantadisaṃ agacchanto, sabbakālañca vaṃsaggaṃ anullokento antevāsikaṃ na rakkhati nāma, evaṃ arakkhito antevāsiko patitvā cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ hoti. Vaṃsaṃ pana suggahitaṃ gaṇhanto, tena pakkhantapakkhantadisaṃ gacchanto, sabbakālañca vaṃsaggaṃ ullokento taṃ rakkhati nāma. Antevāsikopi ito cito ca pakkhanditvā migo viya kīḷanto ācariyaṃ na rakkhati nāma. Evañhi sati tikhiṇavaṃsakoṭi ācariyassa galavāṭake vā nalāṭe vā ṭhapitā ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ bhinditvā gaccheyya. Ācārasampannatāya pana yato vaṃso namati, tato anāmento taṃ ākaḍḍhento viya ekatobhāgiyaṃ katvā vātūpathambhaṃ gāhāpetvā satiṃ sūpaṭṭhitaṃ katvā niccalova nisīdanto ācariyaṃ rakkhati nāmāti.

382. In the ninth, 'in Sumbha' means in a country of that name. 'Medakathālikā' is a name obtained by way of the feminine gender. Regarding 'Protect me, I will protect you,' this is the teacher's view: a teacher who does not grasp the raised bamboo pole well, who does not follow in the direction the pupil leaps, and who at all times does not look up at the tip of the pole, is said not to protect the pupil. An unprotected pupil falls and is crushed to powder. But, by grasping the bamboo pole firmly, going in the direction that pupil leaps, and at all times looking up at the tip of the pole, one is said to protect him. The pupil, too, by leaping here and there and playing like a frolicking deer, is said not to protect the teacher. For if this were to happen, the sharp tip of the pole, placed at the teacher’s throat or forehead, could pierce the place where it stands and go through. But, through accomplishment in conduct, wherever the pole bends, by not yielding towards that direction, but as if pulling his body away, making it incline to one side, causing it to be braced against the wind, having established mindfulness well, and sitting perfectly still—in this way, he is said to protect the teacher.

Tvaṃ ācariya attānaṃ rakkha, ahaṃ attānaṃ rakkhissāmīti ettha ayamadhippāyo – ācariyo vaṃsaṃ suggahitaṃ gaṇhanto, antevāsikena pakkhantapakkhantadisaṃgacchanto[M 3.0259], sabbakālañca vaṃsaggaṃ ullokento, attānameva rakkhati, na antevāsikaṃ. Antevāsikopi kāyampi ekatobhāgiyaṃ katvā vātūpathambhaṃ gāhāpetvā satiṃ sūpaṭṭhitaṃ katvā niccalova nisīdamāno attānaṃyeva rakkhati nāma, na ācariyaṃ.

8. 'You, teacher, protect yourself; I will protect myself'—herein, this is the intention: the teacher, by grasping the bamboo pole well, following in the direction the pupil leaps, and at all times looking up at the tip of the pole, protects only himself, not the pupil. The pupil, too, by making his body incline to one side, causing it to be braced against the wind, having established mindfulness well, and sitting perfectly still, is said to protect only himself, not the teacher.

So tattha ñāyoti yaṃ medakathālikā āha. So tattha ñāyo, so upāyo, taṃ kāraṇanti attho. Satipaṭṭhānaṃ [P 3.0227] sevitabbanti catubbidhaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ sevitabbaṃ. Āsevanāyāti kammaṭṭhānāsevanāya. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, attānaṃ rakkhanto paraṃ rakkhatīti yo bhikkhu kammārāmatādīni pahāya rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānesu mūlakammaṭṭhānaṃ āsevanto bhāvento arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, atha naṃ paro disvā – “bhaddako vatāyaṃ, bhikkhu, sammāpaṭipanno”ti tasmiṃ cittaṃ pasādetvā saggaparāyaṇo hoti. Ayaṃ attānaṃ rakkhanto paraṃ rakkhati nāma.

384. 'That is the rationale here' refers to what Medakathālikā said. The meaning is: 'That is the rationale here, that is the means, that is the reason.' 'The foundations of mindfulness should be cultivated' means the fourfold foundation of mindfulness should be cultivated. 'For the sake of cultivation' means for the sake of cultivating the meditation subject. 'Thus, monks, by protecting oneself, one protects others' means: a monk who, having abandoned delight in work and so on, cultivating and developing the root meditation subject in places for the night and places for the day, attains Arahantship. Then another person, seeing him and thinking, 'Indeed, this monk is excellent, one of right practice,' makes their mind serene towards him and becomes bound for heaven. This is called 'protecting oneself, one protects others.'

Khantiyāti adhivāsanakhantiyā. Avihiṃsāyāti sapubbabhāgāya karuṇāya. Mettacittatāyāti sapubbabhāgāya mettāya. Anudayatāyāti anuvaḍḍhiyā, sapubbabhāgāya muditāyāti attho. Paraṃ rakkhanto attānaṃ rakkhatīti ettha yo bhikkhu rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānaṃ gato tīsu brahmavihāresu tikacatukkajjhānāni nibbattetvā jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā saṅkhāre sammasanto vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Ayaṃ paraṃ rakkhanto attānaṃ rakkhati nāmāti veditabbo.

'With patience' means with the patience of endurance. 'With non-harming' means with compassion that has its preliminary part. 'With a mind of loving-kindness' means with loving-kindness that has its preliminary part. 'With sympathy' means with progressive development, that is, with sympathetic joy that has its preliminary part. This is the meaning. Regarding 'Protecting others, one protects oneself,' herein, a certain monk, having gone to a place for the night and a place for the day, having produced in three divine abodes the jhānas of the threefold and fourfold classifications, and having made jhāna the basis, attains Arahantship by contemplating formations and developing insight. This is to be understood as 'protecting others, one protects oneself.'

10. Janapadakalyāṇīsuttavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Discourse on the Most Beautiful Woman in the Country

386. Dasame [V 3.0255] janapadakalyāṇīti janapadamhi kalyāṇī uttamā chasarīradosarahitā pañcakalyāṇasamannāgatā. Sā hi yasmā nātidīghā nātirassā, nātikisā nātithūlā, nātikāḷā nāccodātā, atikkantā, mānusavaṇṇaṃ appattā dibbavaṇṇaṃ, tasmā chasarīradosarahitā. Chavikalyāṇaṃ, maṃsakalyāṇaṃ, nhārukalyāṇaṃ, aṭṭhikalyāṇaṃ, vayakalyāṇanti imehi pana kalyāṇehi samannāgatattā pañcakalyāṇehi samannāgatā nāma. Tassā hi āgantukobhāsakiccaṃ natthi, attano sarīrobhāseneva dvādasahatthaṭṭhāne ālokaṃ karoti, piyaṅgusāmā vā hoti, suvaṇṇasāmā vā, ayamassā chavikalyāṇatā. Cattāro panassā hatthapādā [M 3.0260] mukhapariyosānañca lākhārasaparikammakataṃ viya rattapavāḷarattakambalasadisaṃ hoti, ayamassā maṃsakalyāṇatā. Vīsati pana nakhapattāni maṃsato amuttaṭṭhāne lākhārasapūritāni viya, muttaṭṭhāne khīradhārāsadisāni, honti ayamassā nhārukalyāṇakatā. Dvattiṃsa dantā suphusitā [P 3.0228] sudhotavajirapanti viya khāyanti, ayamassā aṭṭhikalyāṇatā. Vīsativassasatikāpi pana samānā soḷasavassuddesikā viya hoti nippalitā, ayamassā vayakalyāṇatā.

386. In the tenth discourse, 'janapadakalyāṇī' refers to the supreme beauty in the country, free from the six bodily defects and endowed with the five beauties. For she is neither too tall nor too short, neither too thin nor too fat, neither too dark nor too fair; having surpassed the human complexion, she has not yet reached the divine complexion. Therefore, she is free from the six bodily defects. She is called 'endowed with the five beauties' because she is endowed with these beauties: beauty of skin, beauty of flesh, beauty of sinews, beauty of bones, and beauty of youth. Indeed, she has no need for adventitious radiance, for with the radiance of her own body she illuminates a space of twelve cubits. She has a golden complexion like a ripe priyangu flower or a complexion like that of gold—this is her beauty of skin. Furthermore, her four palms and soles and the edges of her lips are as if perfectly prepared with lac-dye, resembling bright red coral or a red blanket—this is her beauty of flesh. Furthermore, her twenty finger- and toenails, in the place where they are attached to the flesh, are as if filled with lac-dye, and in the place where they are separated, they are like a stream of milk—this is her beauty of sinews. Her thirty-two teeth are well-set and appear like a row of well-polished diamonds—this is her beauty of bones. Furthermore, even when she is one hundred and twenty years old, she appears like one of sixteen years, without gray hair—this is her beauty of youth.

Paramapāsāvinīti ettha pasavanaṃ pasāvo, pavattīti attho. Pasāvo eva pāsāvo. Paramo pāsāvo paramapāsāvo, so assā atthīti paramapāsāvinī. Nacce ca gīte ca uttamapavatti seṭṭhakiriyā, uttamameva naccaṃ naccati, gītaṃ vā gāyatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthameva. Imesu pana dvīsu suttesu pubbabhāgavipassanāva kathitāti.

Herein, regarding 'paramapāsāvinī': `pasavanaṃ` is `pasāvo`, meaning 'action' (`pavatti`). `Pasāvo` is the same as `pāsāvo`. A supreme `pāsāvo` is a `paramapāsāvo`. She possesses this, hence she is `paramapāsāvinī`. This means it is said that she dances a supreme dance or sings a song. The rest has a clear meaning everywhere. However, in these two discourses, only insight that is the preliminary part is taught.

Nālandavaggo dutiyo.

The Second Chapter: Nālanda.

3. Sīlaṭṭhitivaggo

3. The Chapter on the Establishment of Virtue

1-2. Sīlasuttādivaṇṇanā

1–2. Commentary on the Sīla Sutta and so forth.

387-388. Tatiyavaggassa [V 3.0256] paṭhame sīlānīti catupārisuddhisīlāni. Dutiye ummaṅgoti pañhamaggo pañhagavesanaṃ.

In the first discourse of the third chapter, 'sīlāni' means the four kinds of purification virtue. In the second, 'ummaṅgo' means the path of questions, the investigation of questions.

3-5. Parihānasuttādivaṇṇanā

3–5. Commentary on the Parihānasutta and so forth.

389-391. Tatiye parihānaṃ hotīti puggalavasena parihānaṃ hoti. Yo hi buddhesu dharantesupi cattāro satipaṭṭhāne na bhāveti, tassa saddhammo antarahito nāma hoti devadattādīnaṃ viya. Iti imasmiṃ sutte tassa puggalasseva dhammantaradhānaṃ kathitaṃ. Catutthapañcamesu sabbaṃ uttānameva.

In the third discourse, 'parihānaṃ hoti' (there is decline) means there is decline by way of the individual. For if a person does not cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness even while the Buddhas are present, for them the true Dhamma is said to have disappeared, as it did for Devadatta and so forth. Thus, in this discourse, the disappearance of the Dhamma is taught only for that very individual. In the fourth and fifth discourses, everything is clear.

6. Padesasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Discourse on a Part

392. Chaṭṭhe [M 3.0261] padesaṃ bhāvitattāti padesato bhāvitattā. Cattāro hi magge tīṇi ca phalāni nibbattentena satipaṭṭhānā padesaṃ bhāvitā nāma honti.

392. In the sixth discourse, 'padesaṃ bhāvitattā' (because of being cultivated in part) means 'because of being cultivated in part.' Indeed, by one who brings into being the four paths and the three fruits, the foundations of mindfulness are said to be cultivated in part.

7. Samattasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Discourse on Completeness

393. Sattame [P 3.0229] samattaṃ bhāvitattāti samattā bhāvitattā. Arahattaphalaṃ uppādentena hi satipaṭṭhānā samattaṃ bhāvitā nāma honti.

393. In the seventh discourse, 'samattaṃ bhāvitattā' (because of being cultivated completely) means 'because of being cultivated completely.' Indeed, by one who causes the fruit of arahantship to arise, the foundations of mindfulness are said to be cultivated completely.

8-10. Lokasuttādivaṇṇanā

8–10. Commentary on the Lokasutta and so forth.

394-396. Aṭṭhame mahābhiññatanti channaṃ abhiññānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ. Sahassaṃ lokaṃ abhijānāmīti [V 3.0257] satatavihāravaseneva vuttaṃ. Thero kira pātova uṭṭhāya mukhaṃ dhovitvā senāsane nisinno atīte kappasahassaṃ, anāgate kappasahassaṃ anussarati, paccuppannepi sahassaṃ cakkavāḷānaṃ tassāvajjanassa gatiṃ anubandhati. Iti so dibbena cakkhunā sahassaṃ lokaṃ abhijānāti, ayamassa satatavihāro. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

In the eighth discourse, 'great direct knowledge' is spoken of by way of the six direct knowledges. The phrase 'I directly know a thousand worlds' is spoken only by way of constant abiding. It is said that the Elder, having risen early, washed his face, and sat in his dwelling, recollects a thousand aeons in the past and a thousand aeons in the future; and in the present, he follows the course of his advertence to a thousand world-systems. Thus, with the divine eye, he directly knows a thousand worlds. This is his constant abiding. The rest is clear in meaning everywhere.

Sīlaṭṭhitivaggo tatiyo.

The Third Chapter on the Establishment of Virtue.

4. Ananussutavaggavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Ananussuta Chapter

401-406. Catutthavaggassa pañcame viditā vedanāti yā vedanā sammasitvā arahattaṃ patto tāvassa viditā uppajjanti, viditā upaṭṭhahanti, viditā abbhatthaṃ gacchanti nāma. Yā ca pana pariggahitesu vatthārammaṇesu pavattā vedanā, tāpi viditā uppajjanti, viditā upaṭṭhahanti, viditā abbhatthaṃ gacchanti nāma. Vitakkādīsupi eseva nayo. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

In the fifth discourse of the fourth chapter, as to 'feelings are known': whatever feelings one contemplated to attain Arahantship, for that person they arise as known, they are present as known, and they go to cessation as known. Furthermore, whatever feelings occur in regard to comprehended bases and objects, they too arise as known, are present as known, and go to cessation as known. This same method is to be understood also in regard to thoughts and so forth. The rest is clear everywhere.

Ananussutavaggo catuttho.

The Fourth Ananussuta Chapter.

5. Amatavaggo

5. The Chapter on the Deathless

2. Samudayasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Samudaya Sutta

408. Pañcamavaggassa [M 3.0262] dutiye āhārasamudayā kāyassa samudayoti āhārasamudayena kāyasamudayo. Eseva nayo sesesu. Manasikārasamudayāti ettha pana yonisomanasikārasamudayā bojjhaṅgadhammānaṃ samudayo, ayonisomanasikārasamudayā nīvaraṇadhammānaṃ. Iti imasmiṃ sutte sārammaṇasatipaṭṭhānā kathitā.

408. In the second sutta of the fifth chapter, the phrase 'from the arising of nutriment, the arising of the body' means that due to the arising of nutriment, the arising of the physical body occurs. This same method should be understood in the remaining instances. However, in the phrase 'from the arising of attention,' due to the arising of appropriate attention, the arising of the enlightenment-factor states occurs, and due to the arising of inappropriate attention, the arising of the hindrance-states occurs. Thus, in this sutta, the foundations of mindfulness together with their objects are taught.

4. Satisuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Sati Sutta

410. Catutthaṃ [V 3.0258][P 3.0230] suddhikaṃ katvā samudaye kathite bujjhanakānaṃ ajjhāsayena vuttaṃ.

410. When arising was taught, the fourth discourse was presented in a simple form, spoken in accordance with the inclination of those who were to understand.

6. Pātimokkhasaṃvarasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Pātimokkha-restraint Sutta

412. Chaṭṭhe pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutoti catunnaṃ sīlānaṃ jeṭṭhakasīlaṃ dassento evamāha. Tipiṭakacūḷanāgatthero panāha – “pātimokkhasaṃvarova sīlaṃ, itarāni tīṇi sīlanti vuttaṭṭhānaṃ nāma natthī”ti. Vatvā taṃ anujānanto āha – “indriyasaṃvaro nāma chadvārarakkhaṇamattameva, ājīvapārisuddhi dhammeneva samena paccayuppattimattakaṃ, paccayasannissitaṃ paṭiladdhapaccaye idamatthanti paccavekkhitvā paribhuñjanamattakaṃ. Nippariyāyena pātimokkhasaṃvarova sīlaṃ. Yassa so bhinno, ayaṃ chinnasīso viya puriso hatthapāde, sesāni rakkhissatīti na vattabbo. Yassa pana so arogo, ayaṃ acchinnasīso viya puriso jīvitaṃ, sesāni puna pākatikāni katvā rakkhitumpi sakkotī”ti. Tasmā pātimokkhasaṃvarova sīlaṃ, tena pātimokkhasaṃvarena saṃvutoti pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto, upeto samannāgatoti attho.

412. In the sixth sutta, in order to show the chief virtue among the four virtues, He said this: 'restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint.' However, the Elder Tipiṭakacūḷanāga said: 'Only the Pātimokkha restraint is virtue; there is no place where the other three are called "virtue".' Having said this, and approving of that statement, he said: 'The restraint of the faculties is merely the guarding of the six sense doors. Purity of livelihood is merely the arising of requisites righteously and equitably. Virtue dependent on requisites is merely consuming after reflecting on the requisites obtained that "this is for such a purpose." Unequivocally, only the Pātimokkha restraint is virtue. For whom that is broken, it cannot be said that this person will guard the remaining virtues, just as it cannot be said of a man with his head cut off that he will guard his hands and feet. But for whom that is unimpaired, this person is able to guard the remaining virtues, making them natural again, just as a man whose head is not cut off is able to guard his life.' Therefore, only the Pātimokkha restraint is virtue. He is restrained by that Pātimokkha restraint, thus he is called 'pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto'; the meaning is 'endowed with' and 'possessed of'.

Ācāragocarasampannoti ācārena ca gocarena ca sampanno. Aṇumattesūti appamattakesu. Vajjesūti akusaladhammesu. Bhayadassāvīti bhayadassī. Samādāyāti sammā ādiyitvā.
