Sikkhassu sikkhāpadesūti sikkhāpadesu taṃ taṃ sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyitvā sikkha, yaṃ [M 3.0263] yaṃ pana kiñci sikkhāpadesu sikkhākoṭṭhāsesu sikkhitabbaṃ kāyikaṃ vā vācasikaṃ vā, taṃ taṃ sabbaṃ sammā ādāya sikkhassūti ayamettha saṅkhepattho. Vitthāro pana visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.14) vutto. Iti imasmiṃ sutte pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlameva kathitaṃ.

'Endowed with conduct and resort' means endowed with both conduct and resort. 'In minute matters' means in trifling things. 'In faults' means in unwholesome states. 'Seeing danger' means one who sees danger. 'Having undertaken' means having properly undertaken. 'You should train in the training rules' means: among the training rules, having undertaken that particular training rule, you should train. Or alternatively: whatever is to be trained in among the portions of the training, whether it be bodily or verbal, having properly and completely undertaken all of that, you should train. This is the concise meaning here. The detailed explanation, however, is stated in the Visuddhimagga. Thus, in this sutta, only the virtue of the Pātimokkha restraint is taught.

7. Duccaritasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Discourse on Misconduct

413. Sattame kāyasucaritavacīsucaritāni pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ, manosucaritaṃ itarāni tīṇi sīlānīti catupārisuddhisīlaṃ kathitaṃ hoti. Iminā nayena pañcasattanavadasasu kusalakammapathesu [V 3.0259][P 3.0231] pacchimāpi tayo sīlaṃ hotīti veditabbā. Sesaṃ uttānamevāti. Chaṭṭhasattamesu heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo.

413. In the seventh sutta, good bodily conduct and good verbal conduct are the virtue of Pātimokkha restraint; good mental conduct is the other three virtues. Thus, the fourfold purification virtue is taught. By this method, it should be understood that among the ten wholesome courses of action, the last three are also virtue. The rest is simply clear. In the sixth and seventh suttas, the meaning should be understood by the method stated previously.

Amatavaggo pañcamo.

The Deathless Chapter is the fifth.

Satipaṭṭhānasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Satipaṭṭhāna Saṃyutta is concluded.

4. Indriyasaṃyuttaṃ

4. The Connected Discourses on the Faculties

1. Suddhikavaggo

1. The Purity Chapter

1. Suddhikasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Suddhika Discourse

471. Indriyasaṃyuttassa [V 3.0260][M 3.0264][P 3.0232] paṭhame saddhindriyaṃ satindriyaṃ paññindriyanti imāni tīṇi catubhūmakakusalavipākesu ceva kiriyāsu ca labbhanti. Vīriyindriyasamādhindriyāni catubhūmakakusale akusale vipāke kiriyāyāti sabbattha labbhanti. Iti idaṃ suttaṃ catubhūmakasabbasaṅgāhakadhammaparicchedavasena vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

471. In the first sutta of the Indriya Saṃyutta, the faculties of faith, mindfulness, and wisdom—these three—are found in the wholesome and resultant states of the four planes, and in the functional states. The faculties of energy and concentration are found everywhere: in the wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional states of the four planes. Thus, this discourse should be understood as being stated by way of a classification of all-encompassing phenomena of the four planes.

7. Dutiyasamaṇabrāhmaṇasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Second Samaṇabrāhmaṇa Discourse

477. Sattame saddhindriyaṃ nappajānantīti dukkhasaccavasena na pajānanti. Saddhindriyasamudayaṃ nappajānantīti samudayasaccavasena na pajānanti. Evaṃ nirodhaṃ nirodhasaccavasena, paṭipadaṃ maggasaccavasenāti. Sesesupi eseva nayo.

477. In the seventh sutta, 'they do not understand the faculty of faith' means they do not understand it in terms of the truth of suffering. 'They do not understand the origin of the faculty of faith' means they do not understand it in terms of the truth of origin. Similarly, they do not understand cessation in terms of the truth of cessation, and the path in terms of the truth of the path. This same method applies to the remaining faculties as well.

Sukkapakkhe pana adhimokkhavasena āvajjanasamudayā saddhindriyasamudayo hoti, paggahavasena āvajjanasamudayā vīriyindriyasamudayo, upaṭṭhānavasena āvajjanasamudayā satindriyasamudayo, avikkhepavasena āvajjanasamudayā samādhindriyasamudayo, dassanavasena āvajjanasamudayā paññindriyasamudayo hoti. Tathā chandavasena āvajjanasamudayā saddhindriyasamudayo hoti, chandavasena āvajjanasamudayā vīriyasatisamādhipaññindriyasamudayo hoti. Manasikāravasena āvajjanasamudayā saddhindriyasamudayo hoti. Manasikāravasena āvajjanasamudayā vīriyasatisamādhipaññindriyasamudayo [V 3.0261] hotīti evampi attho veditabbo. Imesu paṭipāṭiyā chasu suttesu catusaccameva kathitaṃ.

Furthermore, in the bright section, through resolution, from the arising of advertence there is the arising of the faculty of faith. Through exertion, from the arising of advertence there is the arising of the faculty of energy. Through establishing, from the arising of advertence there is the arising of the faculty of mindfulness. Through non-distraction, from the arising of advertence there is the arising of the faculty of concentration. Through seeing, from the arising of advertence there is the arising of the faculty of wisdom. Likewise, through desire, from the arising of advertence there is the arising of the faculty of faith. Through desire, from the arising of advertence there is the arising of the faculties of energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. Through attention, from the arising of advertence there is the arising of the faculty of faith. Through attention, from the arising of advertence there is the arising of the faculties of energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. The meaning should also be understood in this way. In these six discourses in sequence, only the Four Noble Truths have been taught.

8. Daṭṭhabbasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Daṭṭhabba Discourse

478. Aṭṭhame [P 3.0233] kattha ca, bhikkhave, saddhindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, catūsu sotāpattiyaṅgesūtiādi imesaṃ indriyānaṃ savisaye jeṭṭhakabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Yathā hi cattāro seṭṭhiputtā rājāti rājapañcamesu sahāyesu “nakkhattaṃ [M 3.0265] kīḷissāmā”ti vīthiṃ otiṇṇesu ekassa seṭṭhiputtassa gehaṃ gatakāle itare cattāro tuṇhī nisīdanti, gehasāmikova – “imesaṃ khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ detha, gandhamālālaṅkārādīni dethā”ti gehe vicāreti. Dutiyassa, tatiyassa, catutthassa gehaṃ gatakāle itare cattāro tuṇhī nisīdanti, gehasāmikova – “imesaṃ khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ detha, gandhamālālaṅkārādīni dethā”ti gehe vicāreti. Atha sabbapacchā rañño gehaṃ gatakāle kiñcāpi rājā sabbattha issaro, imasmiṃ pana kāle attano geheyeva – “imesaṃ khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ detha, gandhamālālaṅkārādīni dethā”ti gehe vicāreti. Evameva saddhāpañcamakesu indriyesu tesu sahāyesu ekato vīthiṃ otarantesu viya ekārammaṇe uppajjamānesupi yathā paṭhamassa gehe itare cattāro tuṇhī nisīdanti, gehasāmikova vicāreti, evaṃ sotāpattiyaṅgāni patvā adhimokkhalakkhaṇaṃ saddhindriyameva jeṭṭhakaṃ hoti pubbaṅgamaṃ, sesāni tadanvayāni honti. Yathā dutiyassa gehe itare cattāro tuṇhī nisīdanti, gehasāmikova vicāreti, evaṃ sammappadhānāni patvā paggahalakkhaṇaṃ vīriyindriyameva jeṭṭhakaṃ hoti pubbaṅgamaṃ, sesāni tadanvayāni honti. Yathā tatiyassa gehe itare cattāro tuṇhī nisīdanti, gehasāmikova vicāreti, evaṃ satipaṭṭhānāni patvā upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇaṃ satindriyameva jeṭṭhakaṃ hoti pubbaṅgamaṃ, sesāni tadanvayāni honti. Yathā catutthassa gehe itare cattāro tuṇhī nisīdanti, gehasāmikova vicāreti, evaṃ jhānavimokkhe patvā avikkhepalakkhaṇaṃ samādhindriyameva jeṭṭhakaṃ hoti pubbaṅgamaṃ, sesāni tadanvayāni honti. Sabbapacchā rañño gehaṃ gatakāle pana yathā itare cattāro tuṇhī nisīdanti, rājāva gehe vicāreti, evameva ariyasaccāni patvā pajānanalakkhaṇaṃ paññindriyameva jeṭṭhakaṃ hoti pubbaṅgamaṃ, sesāni tadanvayāni hontīti.

478. In the eighth discourse, the passage beginning, “And where, monks, is the faculty of faith to be seen? In the four factors of stream-entry,” is stated to show the preeminence of these faculties in their respective domains. For it is like when four treasurer’s sons and a king, five companions in all, go out onto the street saying, “We will enjoy the festival.” When they arrive at the home of the first treasurer’s son, the other four sit silently while the householder himself arranges things, saying, “Give them food, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments.” When they arrive at the home of the second, the third, and the fourth treasurer's son, the other four sit silently while the householder himself arranges things, saying, “Give them food, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments.” Then, finally, when they arrive at the king's home, although the king is sovereign everywhere, at this time in his own home he arranges things, saying, “Give them food, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments.” In the same way, among the five faculties including faith, though they arise together on the same object, just as at the house of the first treasurer’s son the other four sit silently while the householder arranges things, so when the factors of stream-entry are attained, the faculty of faith, characterized by conviction, becomes the chief and forerunner, and the others become its followers. Just as at the house of the second treasurer’s son the other four sit silently while the householder arranges things, so when the right strivings are attained, the faculty of energy, characterized by exertion, becomes the chief and forerunner, and the others become its followers. Just as at the house of the third treasurer’s son the other four sit silently while the householder arranges things, so when the foundations of mindfulness are attained, the faculty of mindfulness, characterized by presence, becomes the chief and forerunner, and the others become its followers. Just as at the house of the fourth treasurer’s son the other four sit silently while the householder arranges things, so when the jhānas and liberations are attained, the faculty of concentration, characterized by non-distraction, becomes the chief and forerunner, and the others become its followers. Finally, just as when they arrive at the king's home the other four sit silently while the king himself arranges things, so when the noble truths are attained, the faculty of wisdom, characterized by understanding, becomes the chief and forerunner, and the others become its followers.

9-10. Paṭhamavibhaṅgasuttādivaṇṇanā

9-10. Commentary on the First Analysis Discourse and Others

479-480. Navame [V 3.0262][P 3.0234] satinepakkenāti ettha nipakassa bhāvo nepakkaṃ, paññāyetaṃ nāmaṃ. Kasmā pana satibhājane paññā vuttāti? Satiyā balavabhāvadassanatthaṃ. Balavasati hi idha adhippetā. Sā ca paññāsampayuttāva balavatī hoti, na vippayuttāti paññāsampayuttasatiṃ dassento [M 3.0266] evamāha. Cirakatanti cirakālaṃ kataṃ dānaṃ vā sīlaṃ vā uposathakammaṃ vā. Cirabhāsitanti “asukasmiṃ ṭhāne asukaṃ nāma bhāsita”nti evaṃ cirakāle bhāsitaṃ. Vossaggārammaṇaṃ katvāti nibbānārammaṇaṃ katvā. Udayatthagāminiyāti udayañca atthañca gacchantiyā, udayabbayapariggahikāyāti attho. Imasmiṃ sutte saddhāsatipaññindriyāni pubbabhāgāni, vīriyindriyaṃ missakaṃ, samādhindriyaṃ nibbattitalokuttarameva kathitaṃ. Dasamepi ayameva dhammaparicchedoti.

In the ninth discourse, regarding 'with sagacious mindfulness': here, the state of being sagacious is sagacity; this is a name for wisdom. But why is wisdom mentioned in the section on mindfulness? To show the strength of mindfulness. For strong mindfulness is intended here. And that mindfulness becomes strong only when associated with wisdom, not when dissociated—thus, wishing to show mindfulness associated with wisdom, he spoke thus. 'Done for a long time' means a gift, virtue, or observance day act performed a long time ago. 'Spoken for a long time' means what was spoken a long time ago, as in 'in such-and-such a place, such-and-such was spoken.' 'Making relinquishment the object' means making Nibbāna the object. 'Leading to arising and passing away' means going to arising and passing away; the meaning is 'comprehending rise and fall.' In this discourse, the faculties of faith, mindfulness, and wisdom are preliminary factors, the faculty of energy is mixed, and the faculty of concentration is spoken of as solely the supramundane that has arisen. In the tenth also, this same delineation of phenomena is to be understood.

Suddhikavaggo paṭhamo.

The First Chapter on Purity is concluded.

2. Mudutaravaggo

2. The Chapter on the More Tender

1. Paṭilābhasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Sutta on Attainment

481. Dutiyavaggassa paṭhame sammappadhāne ārabbhāti sammappadhāne paṭicca, sammappadhāne bhāventoti attho. Satindriyepi eseva nayo.

481. In the first sutta of the second chapter, regarding `sammappadhāne ārabbha`: it means depending on the right strivings, by way of developing the right strivings. This is the meaning. This same method should also be known for the faculty of mindfulness.

2. Paṭhamasaṃkhittasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the First Concise Sutta

482. Dutiye tatoti vipassanāmaggaphalavasena nissakkaṃ veditabbaṃ. Samattāni hi paripuṇṇāni pañcindriyāni arahattamaggassa vipassanindriyāni nāma honti. Tato mudutarehīti tehi arahattamaggassa vipassanindriyehi mudutarāni anāgāmimaggassa vipassanindriyāni nāma honti, tato mudutarāni sakadāgāmimaggassa, tato mudutarāni sotāpattimaggassa vipassanindriyāni [V 3.0263] nāma honti, tato mudutarāni dhammānusārimaggassa, tato mudutarāni saddhānusārimaggassa vipassanindriyāni nāma honti.

482. In the second sutta, regarding the word `tato`, the ablative case should be understood by way of insight, path, and fruition. Indeed, the five faculties that are complete and fully complete are called the insight faculties of the path of Arahantship. Softer than those insight faculties of the path of Arahantship are what are called the insight faculties of the path of the non-returner; softer than those are the insight faculties of the path of the once-returner; softer than those are the insight faculties of the path of the stream-enterer; softer than those are the insight faculties of the path of the Dhamma-follower; and softer than those are the insight faculties of the path of the faith-follower.

Tathā [P 3.0235] samattāni paripuṇṇāni pañcindriyāni arahattamaggindriyāni nāma honti, tato mudutarāni anāgāmimaggindriyāni nāma honti, tato mudutarāni sakadāgāmimaggindriyāni nāma honti, tato mudutarāni sotāpattimaggindriyāni nāma honti, tato mudutarāni dhammānusārimaggindriyāni, tato mudutarāni saddhānusārimaggindriyāni nāma honti.

Similarly, the five faculties, being complete and fully complete, are called the path-faculties of Arahantship. Softer than those are the path-faculties of the non-returner; softer than those are the path-faculties of the once-returner; softer than those are the path-faculties of the stream-enterer; softer than those are the path-faculties of the Dhamma-follower; and softer than those are the path-faculties of the faith-follower.

Samattāni [M 3.0267] paripuṇṇāni pañcindriyāni arahattaphalindriyāni nāma honti, tato mudutarāni anāgāmiphalindriyāni, tato mudutarāni sakadāgāmiphalindriyāni, tato mudutarāni sotāpattiphalindriyāni nāma honti. Dhammānusārisaddhānusārino pana dvepi sotāpattimaggaṭṭhapuggalā, maggaṭṭhapuggalavasena nesaṃ nānattaṃ jātanti āgamanenapi maggenapi. Saddhānusārī puggalo hi uddisāpento paripucchanto anupubbena maggaṃ pāpuṇāti, dhammānusārī ekena vā dvīhi vā savanehi. Evaṃ tāva nesaṃ āgamanena nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

The five faculties that are proficient and fully complete are called the faculties of the fruit of Arahantship. Softer than those are the faculties of the fruit of the non-returner; softer than those, the faculties of the fruit of the once-returner; and softer than those are what are called the faculties of the fruit of the stream-enterer. Furthermore, both the Dhamma-follower and the faith-follower are persons established in the path of stream-entry. Their difference arises by way of their approach and by way of their path. Indeed, the faith-follower person, by having the texts recited and by inquiring, gradually attains the path. The Dhamma-follower attains the path with one or two hearings. Thus, firstly, their difference should be known by way of their approach.

Dhammānusārissa pana maggo tikkho hoti, sūraṃ ñāṇaṃ vahati, asaṅkhārena appayogena kilese chindati kadalikkhandhaṃ viya tikhiṇā asidhārā. Saddhānusārissa na tassa viya maggo tikkho hoti, na sūraṃ ñāṇaṃ vahati, sasaṅkhārena sappayogena kilese chindati kadalikkhandhaṃ viya atikhiṇā asidhārā. Kilesakkhaye pana tesaṃ nānattaṃ natthi. Avasesā ca kilesā khīyanti.

Furthermore, for the Dhamma-follower, the path is sharp; the brave knowledge is capable. Without exertion and without effort, it severs the defilements like a sharp sword's edge cutting a banana trunk. For the faith-follower, the path is not sharp like that one's; the brave knowledge is not capable. With exertion and with effort, it cuts the defilements like an unsharp sword's edge cutting a banana trunk. However, in the destruction of the defilements, there is no difference between them. And the remaining defilements are destroyed.

3. Dutiyasaṃkhittasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Second Concise Sutta

483. Tatiye tatoti phalavasena nissakkaṃ veditabbaṃ. Samattāni hi paripuṇṇāni pañcindriyāni arahattaphalindriyāni nāma honti, arahattaphalena samannāgato puggalo arahā nāma hoti. Arahattaphalato mudutarāni anāgāmiphalindriyāni nāma honti, tato mudutarāni sakadāgāmiphalindriyāni, tato mudutarāni sotāpattiphalindriyāni, sotāpattiphalena samannāgato [V 3.0264] puggalo sotāpanno nāma hoti. Indriyavemattatā phalavemattatā hotīti indriyanānattena phalanānattaṃ, phalanānattena puggalanānattanti.

483. In the third [sutta], 'from that' should be understood in the ablative sense by way of fruit. Indeed, the five faculties, when proficient and fully complete, are called the faculties pertaining to the fruit of Arahantship. A person endowed with the fruit of Arahantship is called an Arahant. Faculties milder than those of the fruit of Arahantship are called the faculties pertaining to the fruit of non-returning; faculties milder than those, the faculties of once-returning; faculties milder than those, the faculties of stream-entry. A person endowed with the fruit of stream-entry is called a stream-enterer. As for 'The difference in faculties is the difference in fruit,' this means: through the difference in faculties, there is a difference in fruit; through the difference in fruit, there is a difference in persons.

4. Tatiyasaṃkhittasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Third Concise Sutta

484. Catutthe paripūraṃ paripūrakārī ārādhetīti paripūraṃ arahattamaggaṃ karonto arahattaphalaṃ ārādheti. Padesaṃ padesakārīti [P 3.0236] avasese tayo padesamagge karonto padesaṃ phalattayamattameva ārādheti. Iti imesu catūsupi suttesu missakāneva indriyāni kathitāni.

484. In the fourth [sutta], as for 'one who fulfills completely, the complete-doer, attains,' this means that one who develops the complete path of Arahantship attains the fruit of Arahantship. As for 'a part, the part-doer,' this means that one who develops the remaining three partial paths attains only the partial, threefold fruit. Thus, in all these four suttas, the faculties are taught as mixed.

5-7. Paṭhamavitthārasuttādivaṇṇanā

5-7. Commentary on the First Detailed Sutta, etc.

485-487. Pañcame [M 3.0268] tato mudutarehīti vipassanāvasena nissakkaṃ veditabbaṃ. Paripuṇṇāni hi pañcindriyāni arahattamaggassa vipassanindriyāni honti, tato mudutarāni antarāparinibbāyissa vipassanindriyāni, tato mudutarāni upahaccaparinibbāyissa, tato mudutarāni asaṅkhāraparinibbāyissa, tato mudutarāni sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyissa, tato mudutarāni uddhaṃsotaakaniṭṭhagāmissa vipassanindriyāni nāma honti.

485-487. In the fifth [sutta], 'by those milder than that' should be understood in the ablative sense by way of insight. Indeed, the five faculties, when fully complete, are the insight faculties of the path of Arahantship. Milder than these are the insight faculties of one who attains final Nibbāna in the interval; milder than those, of one who attains final Nibbāna upon landing; milder than those, of one who attains final Nibbāna without exertion; milder than those, of one who attains final Nibbāna with exertion; and milder than those are what are called the insight faculties of one who is bound upstream, heading for the Akaniṭṭha realm.

Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne arahattamaggeyeva ṭhatvā pañca nissakkāni nīharitabbāni. Arahattamaggassa hi vipassanindriyehi mudutarāni paṭhamaantarāparinibbāyissa vipassanindriyāni, tato mudutarāni dutiyaantarāparinibbāyissa, tato mudutarāni tatiyaantarāparinibbāyissa, tato mudutarāni upahaccaparinibbāyissa, tato mudutarāni uddhaṃsotaakaniṭṭhagāmissa vipassanindriyāni. Asaṅkhāraparinibbāyissa sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyinopi eteva pañca janā.

However, in this place, standing only on the path of Arahantship, five ablative cases should be drawn out. Indeed, the insight faculties of the first [type of] one who attains final Nibbāna in the interval are milder than the insight faculties of the path of Arahantship; milder than those are the insight faculties of the second [type of] one who attains final Nibbāna in the interval; milder than those are the insight faculties of the third [type of] one who attains final Nibbāna in the interval; milder than those are the insight faculties of one who attains final Nibbāna upon landing; and milder than those are the insight faculties of one who is bound upstream, heading for the Akaniṭṭha realm. Those who attain final Nibbāna without exertion and with exertion are also these same five individuals.

Idāni tīṇi nissakkāni. Sakadāgāmimaggassa hi indriyehi mudutarāni sotāpattimaggindriyāni, sotāpattimaggeyeva indriyehi mudutarāni dhammānusārimaggindriyāni. Tehipi mudutarāni saddhānusārimaggindriyāni. Chaṭṭhasattamāni vuttanayāneva. Imesu pana tīsupi suttesu pubbabhāgavipassanindriyāneva kathitāni.

Now, three ablative cases are to be brought out. Indeed, the faculties of the path of stream-entry are milder than the faculties of the path of the once-returner. The faculties of the path of a Dhamma-follower are milder than the faculties of the path of stream-entry itself. And milder than those are the faculties of the path of a faith-follower. The sixth and seventh [suttas] follow the method already stated. However, in these three suttas, only the insight faculties of the preliminary stage are taught.

8. Paṭipannasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Paṭipanna Sutta

488. Aṭṭhame [V 3.0265] tato mudutarehīti maggaphalavasena nissakkaṃ veditabbaṃ. Taṃ pāḷiyaṃ vuttameva. Bāhiroti [P 3.0237] imehi aṭṭhahi puggalehi bahibhūto. Puthujjanapakkhe ṭhitoti puthujjanakoṭṭhāse ṭhito. Imasmiṃ sutte lokuttarāneva indriyāni kathitāni.

488. In the eighth [sutta], 'by those milder than that' should be understood in the ablative sense by way of path and fruit. That method is already stated in the Pāḷi text. 'External' means being outside of these eight individuals. 'Standing in the faction of the worldling' means one who stands in the group of worldlings. In this sutta, only the supramundane faculties are taught.

9-10. Sampannasuttādivaṇṇanā

9-10. Commentary on the Sampanna Sutta, etc.

489-490. Navame [M 3.0269] indriyasampannoti paripuṇṇindriyo. Dasamaṃ uttānameva. Imasmiṃ suttadvaye missakāni indriyāni kathitānīti.

489-490. In the ninth [sutta], 'endowed with faculties' means one with complete faculties. The tenth is self-evident. In this pair of suttas, mixed faculties are taught.

Mudutaravaggo dutiyo.

The Second Chapter: On Milder [Faculties]

3. Chaḷindriyavaggo

3. The Chapter on the Six Faculties

2. Jīvitindriyasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Jīvitindriya Sutta

492. Tatiyavaggassa dutiye itthindriyantiādīsu itthibhāve indaṭṭhaṃ karotīti itthindriyaṃ. Purisabhāve indaṭṭhaṃ karotīti purisindriyaṃ. Jīvite indaṭṭhaṃ karotīti jīvitindriyaṃ. Atthuppattikaṃ kiretaṃ suttaṃ. Saṅghamajjhasmiñhi “kati nu kho vaṭṭindriyānī”ti kathā udapādi, atha bhagavā vaṭṭindriyāni dassento tīṇimāni bhikkhavetiādimāha.

492. In the second sutta of the third chapter, regarding the text beginning with 'the female faculty': because it exercises sovereignty in the state of being female, it is the female faculty. Because it exercises sovereignty in the state of being male, it is the male faculty. Because it exercises sovereignty in life, it is the life faculty. This sutta, it is said, arose from a specific occasion. For in the midst of the Saṅgha, a discussion arose: 'How many faculties pertaining to the round of existence are there?' Then the Blessed One, wishing to show the faculties pertaining to the round of existence, said, 'These three, O monks...' and so on.

3. Aññindriyasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Aññindriya Sutta

493. Tatiye anaññātaññassāmītindriyanti “anamatagge saṃsāre ajānitapubbaṃ dhammaṃ jānissāmī”ti paṭipannassa sotāpattimaggakkhaṇe uppannaṃ indriyaṃ. Aññindriyanti tesaṃyeva ñātadhammānaṃ ājānanākārena sotāpattiphalādīsu chasu ṭhānesu uppannaṃ indriyaṃ. Aññātāvindriyanti [V 3.0266] aññātāvīsu arahattaphaladhammesu uppannaṃ indriyaṃ. Tattha tattha tena tenākārena uppannassa ñāṇassevetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Idampi suttaṃ atthuppattikameva. Saṅghamajjhasmiñhi “kati nu kho lokuttarindriyānī”ti kathā udapādi, atha bhagavā tāni dassento tīṇimāni, bhikkhave, indriyānītiādimāha.

493. In the third, the faculty of 'I will come to know the unknown' is the faculty that arises at the moment of the stream-entry path for one practicing with the thought, 'I will know the Dhamma not previously known in beginningless saṃsāra.' The faculty of final knowledge is the faculty that arises in the six instances, beginning with the fruit of stream-entry, in the mode of knowing those very same dhammas that have been known. The faculty of one who has final knowledge is the faculty that arises in the dhammas of the fruit of Arahantship, which have been fully known. In each case, this is a designation for the knowledge that has arisen in that particular mode. This sutta also arose from a specific occasion. For in the midst of the Saṅgha, a discussion arose: 'How many supramundane faculties are there?' Then the Blessed One, wishing to show them, said, 'These three, O monks, are the faculties...' and so on.

4. Ekabījīsuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Ekabījī Sutta

494. Catutthe tato mudutarehīti vipassanato nissakkaṃ veditabbaṃ. Samattāni hi pañcindriyāni arahattamaggassa vipassanindriyāni nāma honti, tato mudutarāni [M 3.0270] antarāparinibbāyissa [P 3.0238] vipassanindriyāni, tato mudutarāni upahaccaparinibbāyissa, tato mudutarāni asaṅkhāraparinibbāyissa, tato mudutarāni sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyissa, tato mudutarāni uddhaṃsotaakaniṭṭhagāmissa vipassanindriyāni nāma. Idhāpi purimanayeneva arahattamagge ṭhatvā pañca nissakkāni nīharitabbāni.

494. In the fourth, 'by those milder than that' should be understood as an ablative with respect to insight. For the five complete faculties are called the insight faculties of the path of Arahantship. Milder than those are the insight faculties of one who attains parinibbāna in the interval; milder than those, of one who attains parinibbāna upon landing; milder than those, of one who attains parinibbāna without exertion; milder than those, of one who attains parinibbāna with exertion; and milder than those, of one who is heading upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm. Here too, following the previous method, by taking the path of Arahantship as the standard, five ablatives are to be drawn out.

Yathā pana purimanaye sakadāgāmimagge ṭhatvā tīṇi nissakkāni, evamidha pañca nīharitabbāni. Sakadāgāmimaggassa hi vipassanindriyehi mudutarāni sotāpattimaggassa vipassanindriyāni, sotāpattimaggassa ca tehi vipassanindriyehi mudutarāni ekabījiādīnaṃ maggassa vipassanindriyāni.

However, just as in the previous method three ablatives were drawn out by taking the once-returner path as the standard, so here five are to be drawn out. For the insight faculties of the stream-entry path are milder than the insight faculties of the once-returner path; and milder than those insight faculties of the stream-entry path are the insight faculties of the path of the one-seeder and so on.

Ettha ca ekabījītiādīsu yo sotāpanno hutvā ekameva attabhāvaṃ janetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, ayaṃ ekabījī nāma. Yathāha “katamo ca puggalo ekabījī, idhekacco puggalo tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā sotāpanno hoti avinipātadhammo niyato sambodhiparāyaṇo, so ekaññeva mānusakaṃ bhavaṃ sandhāvitvā saṃsaritvā dukkhassantaṃ karoti. Ayaṃ vuccati puggalo ekabījī”ti (pu. pa. 33).

Here, among terms such as 'one-seeder,' one who, having become a stream-enterer, attains Arahantship after generating only one more existence, is called a 'one-seeder.' As it is said: 'And what person is a one-seeder? Here, a certain person, with the destruction of the three fetters, is a stream-enterer, not subject to falling into the states of woe, assured, destined for full enlightenment. After running on and transmigrating through only one human existence, they make an end of suffering. This person is called a one-seeder.'

Yo pana dve tayo bhave saṃsaritvā dukkhassantaṃ karoti, ayaṃ kolaṃkolo nāma. Yathāha “katamo ca puggalo kolaṃkolo. Idhekacco puggalo tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā sotāpanno hoti avinipātadhammo niyato sambodhiparāyaṇo, so dve vā tīṇi vā kulāni [V 3.0267] sandhāvitvā saṃsaritvā dukkhassantaṃ karoti. Ayaṃ vuccati puggalo kolaṃkolo”ti (pu. pa. 32). Tattha kulānīti bhavā veditabbā. “Dve vā tīṇi vā”ti idaṃ desanāmattameva, yāva chaṭṭhabhavā saṃsaranto pana kolaṃkolova hoti.

But one who makes an end of suffering after transmigrating through two or three existences is called a 'family-to-family.' As it is said: 'And what person is a family-to-family? Here, a certain person, with the destruction of the three fetters, is a stream-enterer, not subject to falling into the states of woe, assured, destined for full enlightenment. After running on and transmigrating through two or three families, they make an end of suffering. This person is called a family-to-family.' Here, 'families' should be understood as existences. 'Two or three' is merely a mode of teaching; in fact, one who transmigrates for up to six existences is still a 'family-to-family.'

Yassa sattakkhattuṃ paramā upapatti, aṭṭhamaṃ bhavaṃ nādiyati, ayaṃ sattakkhattuparamo nāma. Yathāha “katamo ca puggalo sattakkhattuparamo. Idhekacco puggalo tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā sotāpanno hoti avinipātadhammo niyato sambodhiparāyaṇo, so sattakkhattuṃ deve ca manusse ca sandhāvitvā saṃsaritvā dukkhassantaṃ karoti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo sattakkhattuparamo”ti (pu. pa. 31).

One for whom there is rebirth at most seven times, who does not take up an eighth existence, is called a 'seven-times-at-most.' As it is said: 'And what person is a seven-times-at-most? Here, a certain person, with the destruction of the three fetters, is a stream-enterer, not subject to falling into the states of woe, assured, destined for full enlightenment. After running on and transmigrating among devas and humans seven times, they make an end of suffering. This person is called a seven-times-at-most.'

Bhagavatā [M 3.0271] gahitanāmavaseneva cetāni tesaṃ nāmāni. “Ettakañhi ṭhānaṃ gato ekabījī nāma hoti, ettakaṃ kolaṃkolo, ettakaṃ sattakkhattuparamo”ti bhagavatā etesaṃ nāmaṃ gahitaṃ. Niyamato pana “ayaṃ ekabījī, ayaṃ kolaṃkolo, ayaṃ sattakkhattuparamo”ti natthi.

And these names of theirs are simply by way of the names adopted by the Blessed One. 'Having reached a certain stage, one is called a one-seeder; having reached a certain stage, a family-to-family; having reached a certain stage, a seven-times-at-most'—thus the Blessed One adopted these names for them. However, there is no fixed rule that 'this one is a one-seeder, this one a family-to-family, this one a seven-times-at-most.'

Ko pana nesaṃ etaṃ pabhedaṃ niyametīti? Keci pana therā “pubbahetu niyametī”ti vadanti, keci “paṭhamamaggo”, keci “uparima tayo maggā”, keci “tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ vipassanā”ti. Tattha “pubbahetu niyametī”ti vāde paṭhamamaggassa upanissayo [P 3.0239] kato nāma hoti, upari tayo maggā anupanissayā uppannāti vacanaṃ āpajjati. “Paṭhamamaggo niyametī”ti vāde upari tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ niratthakatā āpajjati. “Upari tayo maggā niyamentī”ti vāde paṭhamamagge anuppanneva upari tayo maggā uppannāti āpajjati. “Tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ vipassanā niyametī”ti vādo pana yujjati. Sace hi upari tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ vipassanā balavatī hoti, ekabījī nāma hoti, tato mandatarāya kolaṃkolo, tato mandatarāya sattakkhattuparamoti.

But what determines this distinction among them? Some elders say, 'A prior cause determines it'; some, 'the first path'; some, 'the three higher paths'; and some, 'the insight of the three paths.' Therein, in the view that 'a prior cause determines it,' a strong basis is said to be made for the first path, which entails that the three higher paths arise without a strong basis. In the view that 'the first path determines it,' the uselessness of the three higher paths is entailed. In the view that 'the three higher paths determine it,' it is entailed that the three higher paths arise even without the first path having arisen. However, the view that 'the insight of the three paths determines it' is reasonable. For if the insight of the three higher paths is strong, one is called a one-seeder; with insight weaker than that, a family-to-family; and with insight weaker than that, a seven-times-at-most.

Ekacco hi sotāpanno vaṭṭajjhāsayo hoti vaṭṭābhirato punappunaṃ vaṭṭasmiṃyeva vicarati sandissati. Anāthapiṇḍiko seṭṭhi, visākhā upāsikā, cūḷarathamahārathā devaputtā, anekavaṇṇo devaputto, sakko devarājā, nāgadatto devaputtoti ime hi ettakā janā vaṭṭajjhāsayā vaṭṭābhiratā ādito paṭṭhāya cha devaloke sodhetvā akaniṭṭhe ṭhatvā parinibbāyissanti[V 3.0268], ime idha na gahitā. Na kevalañcime, yopi manussesuyeva sattakkhattuṃ saṃsaritvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, yopi devaloke nibbatto devesuyeva sattakkhattuṃ aparāparaṃ saṃsaritvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, imepi idha na gahitā. Kālena deve, kālena manusse saṃsaritvā pana arahattaṃ pāpuṇantova idha gahito. Tasmā sattakkhattuparamoti idaṃ idhaṭṭhakavokiṇṇasukkhavipassakassa nāmaṃ kathitanti veditabbaṃ.

Indeed, a certain stream-enterer has an inclination for the round of existence, delights in the round, and repeatedly wanders and is seen within the round itself. The merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, the female lay-disciple Visākhā, the devaputtas Cūḷaratha and Mahāratha, the devaputta Anekavaṇṇa, Sakka, king of the devas, and the devaputta Nāgadatta—these persons, having an inclination for the round and delighting in the round, starting from the beginning, will purify the six deva realms and, having established themselves in the Akaniṭṭha realm, will attain Parinibbāna. These are not included here. And not only these, but also one who, having wandered only among humans for seven rebirths, attains Arahantship; and one who, having been reborn in a deva realm, wanders only among devas for seven consecutive rebirths and attains Arahantship—these too are not included here. However, only one who attains Arahantship after wandering at times among devas and at times among humans is included here. Therefore, it should be understood that this name, 'seven-times-at-most,' was spoken with reference to a dry-insight practitioner established in this sense-sphere existence, whose rebirths are interspersed between the human and deva realms.

Dhammānusārī saddhānusārīti ettha pana imasmiṃ sāsane lokuttaradhammaṃ nibbattentassa dve dhurāni, dve sīsāni, dve abhinivesā – saddhādhuraṃ, paññādhuraṃ[M 3.0272], saddhāsīsaṃ, paññāsīsaṃ, saddhābhiniveso, paññābhinivesoti. Tattha yo bhikkhu “sace saddhāya sakkā nibbattetuṃ, nibbattessāmi lokuttaramagga”nti saddhaṃ dhuraṃ katvā sotāpattimaggaṃ nibbatteti, so maggakkhaṇe saddhānusārī nāma hoti. Phalakkhaṇe pana saddhāvimutto nāma hutvā ekabījī kolaṃkolo sattakkhattuparamoti tividho hoti. Tattha [P 3.0240] ekeko dukkhāpaṭipadādivasena catubbidhabhāvaṃ āpajjatīti saddhādhurena dvādasa janā honti.

As for 'one who follows the Dhamma' and 'one who follows faith'—in this Dispensation, for one bringing about the supramundane Dhamma, there are two yokes, two heads, and two resolves: the yoke of faith and the yoke of wisdom; the head of faith and the head of wisdom; the resolve of faith and the resolve of wisdom. Here, the bhikkhu who, thinking, "If it is possible to bring about the supramundane path through faith, I will bring it about," and making faith his yoke, brings about the path of stream-entry, is called 'one who follows faith' at the moment of the path. But at the moment of fruition, he becomes 'one liberated by faith' and is of three kinds: the one-seeder, the family-to-family, and the one who takes seven more births at most. Here, each one attains a fourfold state according to the mode of practice, such as painful progress. Thus, by the yoke of faith, there are twelve persons.

Yo pana “sace paññāya sakkā nibbattetuṃ, nibbattessāmi lokuttaramagga”nti paññaṃ dhuraṃ katvā sotāpattimaggaṃ nibbatteti, so maggakkhaṇe dhammānusārī nāma hoti. Phalakkhaṇe pana paññāvimutto nāma hutvā ekabījiādibhedena dvādasabhedova hoti. Evaṃ dve maggaṭṭhā phalakkhaṇe catuvīsati sotāpannā hontīti.

But one who, thinking "If it is possible to bring about the supramundane path through wisdom, I will bring it about," and making wisdom his yoke, brings about the path of stream-entry, is called 'one who follows the Dhamma' at the moment of the path. At the moment of fruition, however, he becomes 'one liberated by wisdom' and is of twelve kinds, differentiated as one-seeder, etc. Thus, the two persons established on the path, at the moment of fruition, become twenty-four stream-enterers.

Tipiṭakatissatthero kira “tīṇi piṭakāni sodhessāmī”ti paratīraṃ gato. Taṃ eko kuṭumbiko catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhāsi, thero āgamanakāle “gacchāmi upāsakā”ti āha. “Kahaṃ bhante”ti? “Amhākaṃ ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ santika”nti. “Na sakkā, bhante, mayā gantuṃ, bhaddantaṃ pana nissāya mayā sāsanassa guṇo ñāto, tumhākaṃ parammukhā kīdisaṃ bhikkhuṃ upasaṅkamāmī”ti? Atha naṃ thero āha – “yo bhikkhu catuvīsati sotāpanne dvādasa sakadāgāmī aṭṭhacattālīsa anāgāmī dvādasa arahante dassetvā dhammakathaṃ kathetuṃ sakkoti, evarūpaṃ bhikkhuṃ upaṭṭhātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Imasmiṃ sutte vipassanā kathitāti.

It is said that the Elder Tipiṭaka Tissa, intending, 'I will revise the three Piṭakas,' went to the other shore. A certain householder attended to him with the four requisites. When the Elder was about to depart, he said, "I am going, lay supporter." "Where, venerable sir?" "To the presence of our teachers and preceptors." "I am unable to go, venerable sir, but by relying on the venerable one, the quality of the Dispensation has become known to me. In your absence, what sort of bhikkhu should I approach?" Then the Elder said to him, "A bhikkhu who can explain the twenty-four stream-enterers, twelve once-returners, forty-eight non-returners, and twelve arahants, and is able to give a Dhamma talk—it is proper to attend upon such a bhikkhu." In this sutta, insight is taught.

5-10. Suddhakasuttādivaṇṇanā

5-10. Commentary on the Suddhaka Sutta and so on.

495-500. Pañcame [V 3.0269] cakkhu ca taṃ cakkhudvāre nibbattānaṃ dhammānaṃ ādhipateyyasaṅkhātena indaṭṭhena indriyañcāti cakkhundriyaṃ. Sotindriyādīsupi eseva nayo. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānameva. Imasmiṃ vagge paṭhamasuttañceva chaṭṭhādīni ca pañcāti cha suttāni catusaccavasena kathitānīti.

In the fifth sutta, it is the eye, and it is also a faculty (indriya) in the sense of sovereignty (indaṭṭhena)—which is described as dominance (ādhipateyya)—over the phenomena that arise at the eye-door; therefore, it is the eye-faculty (cakkhundriya). This same method should be understood for the ear-faculty and so on. The remainder is clear everywhere. In this chapter, the first sutta and the five beginning with the sixth—thus six suttas—are taught by means of the four truths.

Chaḷindriyavaggo tatiyo.

The Third Chapter on the Six Faculties.

4. Sukhindriyavaggo

4. The Chapter on the Faculty of Pleasant Feeling

1-5. Suddhikasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-5. Commentary on the Suddhika Sutta and so on.

501-505. Catutthavaggassa [M 3.0273] paṭhame sukhañca taṃ sahajātānaṃ ādhipateyyasaṅkhātena indaṭṭhena indriyañcāti sukhindriyaṃ. Dukkhindriyādīsupi eseva nayo. Ettha [P 3.0241] ca sukhindriyadukkhindriyadomanassindriyāni kāmāvacarāneva, somanassindriyaṃ ṭhapetvā arūpāvacaraṃ sesaṃ tebhūmakaṃ, upekkhindriyaṃ catubhūmakaṃ. Dutiyādīni cattāri catusaccavaseneva kathitāni.

In the first sutta of the fourth chapter, that phenomenon is pleasure, and it is also a faculty (indriya) in the sense of sovereignty (indaṭṭhena)—which is described as dominance (ādhipateyya)—over co-arisen phenomena; therefore, it is the pleasure-faculty (sukhindriya). This same method should be understood for the pain-faculty and so on. Here, the pleasure-faculty, pain-faculty, and displeasure-faculty are only of the sense-sphere. The joy-faculty, excluding the formless-sphere, belongs to the remaining three planes. The equanimity-faculty belongs to all four planes. The four suttas beginning with the second are taught only by means of the four truths.

6. Paṭhamavibhaṅgasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the First Analysis Sutta

506. Chaṭṭhe kāyikanti kāyapasādavatthukaṃ. Sukhanti ayamassa sarūpaniddeso. Sātanti tasseva vevacanaṃ, madhuranti vuttaṃ hoti. Kāyasamphassajanti kāyasamphassato jātaṃ. Sukhaṃ sātanti vuttanayameva. Vedayitanti ayamassa sabbavedanāsādhāraṇo aññadhammavisiṭṭho sabhāvaniddeso. Iminā nayena sesesupi attho veditabbo. Kāyikaṃ vā cetasikaṃ vāti ettha pana cakkhādayo cattāro pasādakāye vatthuṃ katvā uppattivasena kāyikanti vuttaṃ. Kāyapasādavatthukaṃ pana adukkhamasukhaṃ nāma natthi.

506. In the sixth sutta, ‘bodily’ (kāyikaṃ) means having the body-sensitivity as its physical basis. ‘Pleasure’ (sukhaṃ) is the term indicating its own nature. ‘Agreeable’ (sātaṃ) is a synonym for that; it is said to mean ‘sweet’. ‘Born of body-contact’ (kāyasamphassajaṃ) means born from body-contact. ‘Pleasant and agreeable’ (sukhaṃ sātaṃ) is just as has been explained. ‘Felt’ (vedayitaṃ) is the term indicating its intrinsic nature, which is common to all feelings and distinct from other phenomena. By this method, the meaning should be understood in the remaining instances as well. But here, in ‘bodily or mental’ (kāyikaṃ vā cetasikaṃ vā), ‘bodily’ is said in the sense of arising by taking the four sensitive bodies (pasādakāya), beginning with the eye, as a basis. However, there is no so-called neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that has the body-sensitivity as its basis.

9. Kaṭṭhopamasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Sutta on the Simile of the Fire Stick

509. Navame [V 3.0270] dvinnaṃ kaṭṭhānanti dvinnaṃ araṇīnaṃ. Saṅghaṭṭanasamodhānāti saṅghaṭṭanena ceva samodhānena ca. Usmāti usumākāro. Tejoti aggidhūmo. Ettha ca adharāraṇī viya vatthārammaṇaṃ, uttarāraṇī viya phasso, saṅghaṭṭo viya phassasaṅghaṭṭanaṃ, aggi viya vedanā daṭṭhabbā. Vatthārammaṇaṃ vā uttarāraṇī viya, phasso adharāraṇī viya daṭṭhabbo.

509. In the ninth sutta, ‘of two pieces of wood’ (dvinnaṃ kaṭṭhānaṃ) means of two fire-sticks (araṇīnaṃ). The phrase `saṅghaṭṭanasamodhāna` means 'by rubbing and by combining.' ‘Heat’ (usmā) is the state of being hot. ‘Fire’ (tejo) is fire-smoke. Here, the object-basis should be seen as the lower fire-stick, contact as the upper fire-stick, the striking of contact as the rubbing, and feeling as the fire. Alternatively, the object-basis should be seen as the upper fire-stick, and contact as the lower fire-stick.

10. Uppaṭipāṭikasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Uppaṭipāṭika Sutta

510. Dasamaṃ yathādhammarasena paṭipāṭiyā vuttampi imasmiṃ indriyavibhaṅge sesasuttāni viya adesitattā uppaṭipāṭikasuttaṃ nāmāti veditabbaṃ. Tattha nimittantiādīni sabbāni paccayavevacanāneva. Dukkhindriyañca pajānātīti dukkhasaccavaseneva pajānāti. Dukkhindriyasamudayanti kaṇṭakena vā viddhassa maṅkulena [M 3.0274] vā daṭṭhassa paccattharaṇe vā valiyā phuṭṭhassa [P 3.0242] dukkhasahagataṃ kāyaviññāṇaṃ uppajjati, taṃ etassa samudayoti pajānāti.

510. The tenth discourse, though stated in sequence according to the natural order, should be understood as ‘The Discourse Out of Order’ because, in this Analysis of the Faculties, it is not taught in the same way as the other suttas. Therein, ‘sign’ and so forth are all synonyms for 'condition'. ‘And he understands the faculty of pain’ means he understands it in terms of the truth of suffering. ‘The origin of the faculty of pain’: when one is pierced by a thorn, or bitten by a bedbug, or touched by a wrinkle in the bed-covering, body-consciousness accompanied by pain arises; he understands that this is its origin.

Parato domanassindriyasamudayantiādīsupi tesaṃ tesaṃ kāraṇavaseneva samudayo veditabbo. Pattacīvarādīnaṃ vā hi saṅkhārānaṃ saddhivihārikādīnaṃ vā sattānaṃ vināsena domanassindriyaṃ uppajjatīti tesaṃ vināsaṃ tassa samudayoti pajānāti. Subhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā varasayane nipannassa hatthapādasambāhanatālavaṇṭavātādisamphassena sukhindriyaṃ uppajjati, taṃ phassaṃ tassa samudayoti pajānāti. Vuttappakārānaṃ pana sattasaṅkhārānaṃ manāpānaṃ paṭilābhavasena somanassindriyaṃ uppajjati, taṃ paṭilābhaṃ tassa samudayoti pajānāti. Majjhattākārena pana upekkhindriyaṃ uppajjati, taṃ sattasaṅkhāresu majjhattākāraṃ tassa samudayoti pajānāti.

Further, in the cases of ‘the origin of the faculty of displeasure’ and so on, the origin should be understood according to the respective cause of each. For instance, the faculty of displeasure arises with the destruction of conditioned things such as bowls and robes, or with the destruction of beings such as co-residents; he understands their destruction as its origin. When one eats delicious food and lies on an excellent bed, the faculty of pleasure arises due to contact such as the massaging of hands and feet or a breeze from a palm-leaf fan; he understands that contact as its origin. Moreover, the faculty of joy arises through the acquisition of agreeable beings or conditioned things of the aforementioned kind; he understands that acquisition as its origin. The faculty of equanimity arises in a neutral manner; he understands that neutral attitude toward beings or conditioned things as its origin.

Kattha cuppannaṃ dukkhindriyaṃ aparisesaṃ nirujjhati, idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehītiādīsu pana ayaṃ ekatova vinicchayakathā – dukkhindriyañhi paṭhamajjhānassa upacārakkhaṇeyeva nirujjhati pahīnaṃ hoti, domanassādīni dutiyajjhānādīnaṃ. Evaṃ santepi tesaṃ atisayanirodhattā ayaṃ jhānesuyeva nirodho vutto. Atisayanirodho hi tesaṃ paṭhamajjhānādīsu, na nirodhoyeva, nirodhoyeva pana upacārakkhaṇe, nātisayanirodho. Tathā hi nānāvajjane [V 3.0271] paṭhamajjhānupacāre niruddhassāpi dukkhindriyassa ḍaṃsamakasādisamphassena vā visamāsanupatāpena vā siyā uppatti, na tveva antoappanāyaṃ. Upacāre vā niruddhampetaṃ na suṭṭhu niruddhaṃ hoti paṭipakkhena avihatattā. Antoappanāyaṃ pana pītipharaṇena sabbo kāyo sukhokkanto hoti, sukhokkantakāyassa ca suṭṭhu niruddhaṃ hoti dukkhindriyaṃ paṭipakkhena [P 3.0243] vihatattā. Nānāvajjaneyeva ca dutiyajjhānupacāre pahīnassa domanassindriyassa yasmā etaṃ vitakkavicārapaccayepi kāyakilamathe cittupaghāte ca sati uppajjati, vitakkavicārābhāve neva uppajjati. Yattha pana uppajjati, tattha vitakkavicārabhāve, appahīnā eva ca dutiyajjhānupacāre vitakkavicārāti tatthassa siyā uppatti. Na tveva dutiyajjhāne pahīnapaccayattā. Tathā tatiyajjhānupacāre pahīnassāpi sukhindriyassa pītisamuṭṭhānapaṇītarūpaphuṭṭhakāyassa siyā uppatti, na tveva tatiyajjhāne. Tatiyajjhāne hi sukhassa paccayabhūtā [M 3.0275] pīti sabbaso niruddhā. Tathā catutthajjhānupacāre pahīnassāpi somanassindriyassa āsannattā appanāppattāya upekkhāya abhāvena sammā anatikkantattā ca siyā uppatti, na tveva catutthajjhāne. Tasmā “ettha cuppannaṃ dukkhindriyaṃ aparisesaṃ nirujjhatī”ti tattha tattha aparisesaggahaṇaṃ kataṃ.

Where does the arisen pain faculty cease without remainder? In the passage beginning ‘Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, secluded from sensual pleasures…’, this is a single, decisive explanation. For the pain faculty ceases and is abandoned only at the moment of access concentration of the first jhāna, while displeasure and the others cease at the access of the second jhāna and so on. Even so, because their cessation is a surpassing one, this cessation is spoken of as occurring only in the jhānas themselves. For their surpassing cessation occurs in the first jhāna and beyond, not mere cessation. Mere cessation, however, occurs at the moment of access concentration, not surpassing cessation. Indeed, in the access of the first jhāna with its various advertings, even though the pain faculty has ceased, it may still arise due to contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, and so forth, or due to the discomfort of an uneven position—but not within absorption itself. Or, though ceased in access, it is not thoroughly ceased because the opposing factor has not been overcome. But within absorption, through the pervasion of rapture, the whole body becomes steeped in pleasure; and for one whose body is steeped in pleasure, the pain faculty is thoroughly ceased because the opposing factor has been overcome. And in the access of the second jhāna with its various advertings, although the faculty of displeasure has been abandoned, it may still arise when there is bodily fatigue or mental distress, which are conditioned by initial and sustained thought; but it does not arise in the absence of initial and sustained thought. Where it does arise, it is due to the presence of initial and sustained thought; and since initial and sustained thought are not yet abandoned in the access of the second jhāna, it may arise there. But it cannot arise in the second jhāna itself, because its condition has been abandoned. Likewise, in the access of the third jhāna, although the faculty of pleasure has been abandoned, it may still arise for one whose body is pervaded by refined form produced by rapture; but it cannot arise in the third jhāna itself. For in the third jhāna, rapture, which is the condition for pleasure, has completely ceased. Likewise, in the access of the fourth jhāna, although the faculty of joy has been abandoned, it may still arise due to its nearness, due to the absence of absorption-level equanimity, and because it has not been fully transcended; but it cannot arise in the fourth jhāna itself. Therefore, in the phrase ‘here the arisen pain faculty ceases without remainder,’ the term ‘without remainder’ is included in each case.

Yaṃ panettha tadatthāya cittaṃ upasaṃharatīti vuttaṃ, tattha alābhī samāno uppādanatthāya cittaṃ upasaṃharati, lābhī samāno samāpajjanatthāyāti evamattho veditabbo. Imesu dvīsupi suttesu sammasanavārova kathitoti.

Regarding the statement made here, ‘one directs the mind for that purpose,’ the meaning should be understood thus: one who has not yet attained directs the mind for the purpose of producing it, while one who has attained directs it for the purpose of entering into the attainment. In both these suttas, only the section on comprehension has been taught.

Sukhindriyavaggo catuttho.

The Fourth Chapter: The Faculty of Pleasure.

5. Jarāvaggo

5. The Chapter on Aging

1. Jarādhammasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Jarādhammasutta

511. Pañcamavaggassa paṭhame pacchātapeti pāsādacchāyāya puratthimadisaṃ paṭicchannattā pāsādassa pacchimadisābhāge ātapo hoti, tasmiṃ ṭhāne paññattavarabuddhāsane nisinnoti attho[V 3.0272]. Piṭṭhiṃ otāpayamānoti yasmā sammāsambuddhassapi upādinnakasarīre uṇhakāle uṇhaṃ hoti, sītakāle sītaṃ, ayañca himapātasītasamayo. Tasmā mahācīvaraṃ otāretvā sūriyarasmīhi piṭṭhiṃ otāpayamāno nisīdi.

511. In the first sutta of the fifth chapter, `pacchātapeti` means that because the eastern direction was covered by the shadow of the palace, there was sunlight in the western part of the palace. In that place, he was seated on the excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared; this is the meaning. As for `piṭṭhiṃ otāpayamāno`: because even in the appropriated body of the Perfectly Enlightened One, it is hot in the hot season and cold in the cold season, and this was the cold season when dew falls. Therefore, having let the great robe slip down, he sat warming his back with the sun's rays.

Kiṃ pana buddharasmiyo madditvā sūriyarasmi anto pavisituṃ sakkotīti? Na sakkoti. Evaṃ sante kiṃ tāpetīti? Rasmitejaṃ. Yatheva hi ṭhitamajjhanhike parimaṇḍalāya [P 3.0244] chāyāya rukkhamūle nisinnassa kiñcāpi sūriyarasmiyo sarīraṃ na phusanti, sabbadisāsu pana tejo pharati, aggijālāhi parikkhitto viya hoti, evaṃ sūriyarasmīsu buddharasmiyo madditvā anto pavisituṃ asakkuṇantīsupi satthā tejaṃ tāpento nisinnoti veditabbo.

Can the sun's rays, having overcome the Buddha's rays, enter inside? They cannot. This being so, what does he warm himself with? The heat of the rays. For, just as for one sitting at the foot of a tree at high noon when the shade is perfectly round, although the sun's rays do not touch the body, the heat spreads in all directions, as if one were surrounded by flames; so too, it should be understood that even though the sun's rays cannot overcome the Buddha's rays and enter inside, the Teacher sat warming himself with the heat.

Anomajjantoti piṭṭhiparikammakaraṇavasena anumajjanto. Acchariyaṃ bhanteti thero bhagavato piṭṭhito mahācīvaraṃ otāretvā nisinnassa dvinnaṃ [M 3.0276] aṃsakūṭānaṃ antare suvaṇṇāvaṭṭaṃ viya kesaggappamāṇaṃ valiyāvaṭṭaṃ disvā – “evarūpepi nāma sarīre jarā paññāyatī”ti sañjātasaṃvego jaraṃ garahanto evamāha. Garahanacchariyaṃ nāma kiretaṃ.

`Anomajjanto` means massaging by way of tending to the back. As for `Acchariyaṃ bhante`: the Elder, having taken the great robe from the back of the Blessed One who was seated, saw between the two shoulder blades a shining line the size of a hair's tip, like a line on a golden plate. Filled with a sense of spiritual urgency, and wishing to censure aging, he said: 'Even in such a body as this, the nature of aging is apparent!' This, it is said, is called the wonder of censure.

Na cevaṃ dāni, bhante, bhagavato tāva parisuddhoti yathā pakatiyā chavivaṇṇo parisuddho, na evametarahīti dīpento evamāha. Tathāgatassa hi daharakāle saṅkusatasamabbhāhataṃ usabhacammaṃ viya vihatavaliko kāyo hoti, tasmiṃ ṭhapito hattho bhassateva, na santiṭṭhati, telapuñchanākārappatto viya hoti. Mahallakakāle pana sirājālā milāyanti, sandhipabbāni sithilāni honti, maṃsaṃ aṭṭhito muccitvā sithilabhāvaṃ āpajjitvā tattha tattha olambati. Buddhānaṃ pana evarūpaṃ na hoti. Aññesaṃ apākaṭaṃ, santikāvacarattā ānandattherasseva pākaṭaṃ hoti, tasmā evamāha.

As for `Na cevaṃ dāni, bhante, bhagavato tāva parisuddho`, wishing to show that the Blessed One's skin-complexion was not now as pure as it was by nature, he spoke thus. Indeed, in his youth, the Tathāgata's body was without wrinkles, like the hide of a prime bull stretched taut with a hundred pegs. A hand placed on it would just slip off; it would not stay, as if it had attained the state of being polished with oil. In old age, however, for other ordinary beings, the network of veins withers, the joints become loose, and the flesh, separating from the bone, becomes slack and hangs down here and there. But for the Buddhas, such a thing does not happen. For other people, it is not apparent; only for the Elder Ānanda, due to his constant close attendance, was it apparent. Therefore, he spoke thus.

Sithilāni ca gattānīti aññesaṃ mukhe aṃsakūṭantarehi tesu tesu ṭhānesu valiyo santiṭṭhanti, satthu panetaṃ natthi, thero ca dvinnaṃ aṃsakūṭānaṃ antare valiyāvaṭṭakaṃ disvā evamāha. Sabbāni valiyajātānīti idampi attano pākaṭavasena evamāha – satthu pana aññesaṃ viya valiyo nāma natthi. Purato pabbhāro ca kāyoti satthā brahmujugatto, devanagare samussitasuvaṇṇatoraṇaṃ viyassa kāyo ujukameva uggato. Mahallakakāle pana kāyo purato vaṅko [V 3.0273] hoti, svāyaṃ aññesaṃ apākaṭo, santikāvacarattā pana therasseva pākaṭo, tasmā evamāha. Dissati ca indriyānaṃ aññathattanti indriyāni nāma na cakkhuviññeyyāni. Yato pana pakatiyā parisuddho chavivaṇṇo, idāni na tathā parisuddho, aṃsakūṭantare vali paññāyati[P 3.0245], brahmujukāyo purato vaṅko, imināva kāraṇena cakkhādīnañca indriyānaṃ aññathattena bhavitabbanti nayaggāhato evamāha. Dhī taṃ jammi jare atthūti lāmake jare dhī taṃ tuyhaṃ hotu, dhikkāro taṃ phusatu. Bimbanti attabhāvo.

As for `Sithilāni ca gattāni`: for other beings, wrinkles are clearly present on the face, between the shoulder blades, and in various other places, but for the Teacher, this is not so. However, the Elder, having seen a slight wrinkle-line between the two shoulder blades, spoke thus. As for `Sabbāni valiyajātāni`: this too he spoke according to what was apparent to himself. However, for the Teacher, there are no such things as wrinkles that are obvious like those of others. As for `Purato pabbhāro ca kāyo`: the Teacher has a body as straight as Brahmā's; his body rises up perfectly straight, like a golden archway erected in the city of the devas. However, in old age, the body is slightly bent forward. This is not apparent to other people, but due to his constant close attendance, it was apparent only to the Elder; therefore, he spoke thus. As for `Dissati ca indriyānaṃ aññathattaṃ`: the faculties are not cognizable by the eye. But because the skin-complexion, which was naturally pure, is now not so pure, a slight wrinkle is apparent between the shoulder blades, and the body, once straight as Brahmā's, is now slightly bent forward—for this very reason, by way of inference, he spoke thus: 'There must be an alteration in the faculties of the eye and so on.' As for `Dhī taṃ jammi jare atthu`: 'Fie on you, wretched aging! May disgrace befall you.' `Bimbaṃ` means the personal existence.

2. Uṇṇābhabrāhmaṇasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Uṇṇābha Brahmin Sutta

512. Dutiye [M 3.0277] gocaravisayanti gocarabhūtaṃ visayaṃ. Aññamaññassāti cakkhu sotassa, sotaṃ vā cakkhussāti evaṃ ekaṃ ekassa gocaravisayaṃ na paccanubhoti. Sace hi nīlādibhedaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ samodhānetvā sotindriyassa upaneyya – “iṅgha tvaṃ tāva naṃ vavatthapehi vibhāvehi ‘kinnāmetaṃ ārammaṇa’”nti. Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ vināpi mukhena attano dhammatāya evaṃ vadeyya – “are, andhabāla, vassasatampi vassasahassampi vassasatasahassampi paridhāvamāno aññatra mayā kuhiṃ etassa jānanakaṃ labhissasi, taṃ āhara, cakkhupasāde upanehi, ahametaṃ ārammaṇaṃ jānissāmi – yadi vā nīlaṃ, yadi vā pītakaṃ. Na hi eso aññassa visayo, mayhameveso visayo”ti. Sesadvāresupi eseva nayo. Evametāni aññamaññassa gocaravisayaṃ na paccanubhonti nāma.

512. In the second sutta, `gocaravisayaṃ` means the object that is a pasture-ground. `Aññamaññassa` means that the eye does not experience the pasture-ground-object of the ear, or the ear that of the eye; thus one faculty does not experience the pasture-ground-object of another. Indeed, if one were to gather a form-object with distinctions such as blue and bring it near to the ear faculty, saying, 'Come now, you first determine and clarify it, what is this object?'—eye-consciousness, even without a mouth, would by its own nature speak thus: 'O, you blind fool! Even if you were to run around for a hundred years, a thousand years, or a hundred thousand years, where apart from me would you find one who can know this? Bring it, bring it near to the eye-sensitivity. I will know this object—whether it is blue or yellow. Indeed, this is not the domain of another; this is my domain alone.' This same method should be understood for the remaining sense doors as well. Thus, these are said to not experience the pasture-ground-object of one another.

Kiṃ paṭisaraṇanti etesaṃ kiṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ, kiṃ etāni paṭisarantīti pucchati. Mano paṭisaraṇanti javanamano paṭisaraṇaṃ. Manova nesanti manodvārikajavanamanova etesaṃ gocaravisayaṃ rajjanādivasena anubhoti. Cakkhuviññāṇañhi rūpadassanamattameva, ettha rajjanaṃ vā dussanaṃ vā muyhanaṃ vā natthi. Ekasmiṃ pana dvāre javanaṃ rajjati vā dussati vā muyhati vā. Sotaviññāṇādīsupi eseva nayo.

As for `Kiṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ`, he asks: 'What is the refuge of these? What do these resort to?' As for `Mano paṭisaraṇaṃ`, the impulsion-mind is their refuge. As for `Manova nesaṃ`, it is only the mind-consciousness which is the impulsion arising in the mind-door that experiences their pasture-ground-object by way of lusting, etc. Indeed, eye-consciousness is merely the seeing of a form-object; therein there is no lusting, hating, or delusion. However, in that one door, the impulsion lusts, or hates, or is deluded. This same method should be understood for ear-consciousness and so on.

Tatrāyaṃ upamā – pañca kira dubbalabhojakā rājānaṃ sevitvā kicchena kasirena ekasmiṃ pañcakulike gāme parittakaṃ āyaṃ labhiṃsu. Tesaṃ tattha macchabhāgo maṃsabhāgo, addukahāpaṇo vā yottakahāpaṇo vā māsakahāpaṇo [P 3.0246] vā aṭṭhakahāpaṇo vā soḷasakahāpaṇo vā [V 3.0274] catusaṭṭhikahāpaṇo vā daṇḍoti ettakamattameva pāpuṇāti, satavatthukaṃ pañcasatavatthukaṃ sahassavatthukaṃ mahābaliṃ rājāva gaṇhāti.

In this regard, this is the simile: It is said that five village headmen of little power, having served the king with trouble and hardship, obtained a small revenue in a village of only five households. For them, a share of fish, a share of meat, a half-kahāpaṇa, or a yottaka-kahāpaṇa, or a māsaka-kahāpaṇa, or eight kahāpaṇas, or sixteen kahāpaṇas, or sixty-four kahāpaṇas as a fine—only this small amount reaches them. But the great tax—worth a hundred, five hundred, or a thousand—only the king takes.

Tattha pañcakulikagāmā viya pañcapasādā daṭṭhabbā, pañca dubbalabhojakā viya pañcaviññāṇāni; rājā viya javanaṃ, dubbalabhojakānaṃ parittakaāyapāpuṇanaṃ viya cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ rūpadassanādimattaṃ, rajjanādi pana etesu natthi[M 3.0278]. Rañño mahābaliggahaṇaṃ viya tesu dvāresu javanassa rajjanādīni veditabbāni. Evamettha manoti kusalākusalajavanaṃ vuttaṃ.

Therein, the five sensitivities should be understood as like the villages of five households; the five consciousnesses as like the five village headmen of little power; impulsion as like the king. The mere seeing of a form-object, etc., by the eye-consciousness, etc., should be understood as like the village headmen of little power obtaining a small revenue; however, lusting, etc., is not in these. The lusting, etc., of impulsion in those doors should be known as like the king's taking of the great tax. Thus, herein, `mano` refers to wholesome and unwholesome impulsion.

Sati paṭisaraṇanti maggasati paṭisaraṇaṃ. Javanamano hi maggasatiṃ paṭisarati. Vimuttīti phalavimutti. Paṭisaraṇanti phalavimuttiyā nibbānaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ. Tañhi sā paṭisarati. Nāsakkhi pañhassa pariyantaṃ gahetunti pañhassa paricchedaṃ pamāṇaṃ gahetuṃ nāsakkhi, appaṭisaraṇaṃ dhammaṃ “sappaṭisaraṇa”nti pucchi. Nibbānaṃ nāmetaṃ appaṭisaraṇaṃ, na kiñci paṭisarati. Nibbānogadhanti nibbānabbhantaraṃ nibbānaṃ anupaviṭṭhaṃ. Brahmacariyanti maggabrahmacariyaṃ. Nibbānaparāyaṇanti nibbānaṃ paraṃ ayanamassa parā gati, na tato paraṃ gacchatīti attho. Nibbānaṃ pariyosānaṃ avasānaṃ assāti nibbānapariyosānaṃ.

As for 'Mindfulness is the refuge', noble path-mindfulness is the refuge. Indeed, the mind-consciousness which is the impulsion of development resorts to noble path-mindfulness. 'Liberation' means fruition-liberation. As for 'refuge', Nibbāna is the refuge of fruition-liberation. Indeed, it resorts to that. As for 'He was not able to grasp the end of the question', he was not able to grasp the limit and measure of the question; he asked about a Dhamma without refuge as if it had a refuge. This so-called Nibbāna is without refuge; it does not resort to anything. As for 'plunged into Nibbāna', it means gone inside Nibbāna, having entered Nibbāna. As for 'the holy life', it means the holy life of the path. As for 'having Nibbāna as its final goal', for this holy life, the supreme resort, the supreme destination, is Nibbāna; it does not go beyond that—this is the meaning. For this holy life, the end is Nibbāna; therefore it is called 'having Nibbāna as its culmination'.

Mūlajātā patiṭṭhitāti maggena āgatasaddhā vuccati. Imamhi ce, bhikkhave, samayeti kiṃ sandhāyāha? Jhānaanāgāmitaṃ. Tasmiñhi samaye brāhmaṇassa paṭhamamaggena pañca akusalacittāni pahīnāni, paṭhamajjhānena pañca nīvaraṇānīti jhānaanāgāmiṭṭhāne ṭhito. So aparihīnajjhāno kālaṃ katvā tattheva parinibbāyeyya. Sace panassa puttadāraṃ anusāsantassa kammante vicārentassa jhānaṃ nassati, naṭṭhe jhāne gati anibaddhā hoti, anaṭṭhe pana nibaddhāti imaṃ jhānaanāgāmitaṃ sandhāya evamāha.

By 'Rooted, originated, and established', faith that has come by way of the path is meant. As for 'If, monks, at this time...', with reference to what did he say this? With reference to the state of being a 'jhāna-anāgāmī' (one similar to a non-returner by means of jhāna). Indeed, at that time, for the brahmin, five unwholesome consciousnesses were abandoned by the first path, and the five hindrances were abandoned by the first jhāna; therefore, he stood in the position of a 'jhāna-anāgāmī'. He, with his jhāna not having declined, upon passing away, would attain parinibbāna right there in that brahma-world. However, if for him, while instructing his son and wife or while managing his work, the jhāna should be lost, then with the jhāna lost, his destination becomes unfixed. But with it not lost, it is fixed. Therefore, referring to this state of being a 'jhāna-anāgāmī', he spoke thus.

3. Sāketasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Exposition of the Sāketa Sutta

513. Tatiye [P 3.0247] añjanavaneti añjanavaṇṇapupphānaṃ rukkhānaṃ ropitavane. Yaṃ, bhikkhave, saddhindriyaṃ, taṃ saddhābalanti tañhi adhimokkhalakkhaṇe indaṭṭhena saddhindriyaṃ, assaddhiye akampanena [V 3.0275] saddhābalaṃ. Itaresaṃ paggahaupaṭṭhānaavikkhepapajānanalakkhaṇesu indaṭṭhena indriyabhāvo, kosajjamuṭṭhasaccavikkhepāvijjāsu akampanena balabhāvo veditabbo. Evameva khoti tassā nadiyā ekasotaṃ viya saddhāvīriyasatisamādhipaññāvasena etesaṃ ninnānākaraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ, dve sotāni viya indaṭṭhaakampanaṭṭhehi indriyabalavasena nānākaraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ.

513. In the third, 'añjanavane' means in a grove planted with trees bearing añjana-colored flowers. 'That which, bhikkhus, is the faculty of faith, that is the power of faith': for it is the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) in the sense of mastery due to its characteristic of resolution, and it is the power of faith (saddhābala) because it is unshaken by lack of faith. For the others, their nature as faculties should be understood in the sense of mastery in their respective characteristics of exertion, establishment, non-distraction, and discernment; their nature as powers should be understood as being unshaken by laziness, forgetfulness, distraction, and ignorance. 'Thus indeed': just as that river has a single current, so their non-differentiation should be understood by way of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; and just as there are two currents, their differentiation should be understood by way of faculties and powers, due to the meaning of mastery and the meaning of being unshaken.

4. Pubbakoṭṭhakasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Exposition of the Pubbakoṭṭhaka Sutta

514. Catutthe [M 3.0279] amatogadhanti amatabbhantaraṃ. Amataparāyaṇanti amatanibbattikaṃ. Amatapariyosānanti amataniṭṭhaṃ. Sādhu sādhūti therassa byākaraṇaṃ pasaṃsanto sādhukāraṃ deti.

514. In the fourth, 'immersed in the deathless' means the interior of the deathless. 'Having the deathless as the ultimate goal' means resulting in the deathless. 'With the deathless as the final end' means culminating in the deathless. 'Good, good!'—praising the elder's explanation, he gives approval.

5. Paṭhamapubbārāmasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Exposition of the First Pubbārāma Sutta

515. Pañcame tadanvayāti taṃ anugacchamānā, anuvattamānāti attho. Pubbakoṭṭhakaṃ ādiṃ katvā paṭipāṭiyā chasu suttesu phalindriyāneva kathitāni.

515. In the fifth, 'tadanvayā' means following that, conforming to it—this is the meaning. Taking the Pubbakoṭṭhaka Sutta as the starting point, in the sequence of the six discourses, only the faculties that are also powers have been taught.

10. Āpaṇasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Exposition of the Āpaṇa Sutta

520. Dasame ime kho te dhammāti upari saha vipassanāya tayo maggā. Ye me pubbe sutāva ahesunti ye dhammā mayā pubbe “arahattaphalindriyaṃ nāma atthī”ti kathentānaṃyeva sutā ahesuṃ. Kāyena ca phusitvāti nāmakāyena ca phusitvā paṭilabhitvā. Paññāya ca ativijjha passāmīti paccavekkhaṇapaññāya ca ativijjhitvā passāmi. Yā hissa, bhante, saddhāti ayaṃ katarasaddhā? Catūhi indriyehi sampayuttā [P 3.0248] saddhā heṭṭhā kathitāva, ayaṃ pana paccavekkhaṇasaddhā. Sampayuttasaddhā hi missakā, paccavekkhaṇasaddhā lokiyāva. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

520. In the tenth, 'these are the qualities' refers to the three paths above, together with insight. The phrase 'which I had formerly only heard of' means: those teachings which I had previously heard from those who were just saying, 'There is indeed the faculty of the fruit of arahantship.' 'And having touched it with the body' means: having touched and attained it with the mental body. 'And having penetrated it with wisdom, I see' means: having penetrated and seen with the wisdom of reviewing. 'That faith, venerable sir'—what kind of faith is this? The faith associated with the four faculties has been explained below; this, however, is the faith of reviewing. For the associated faith is mixed, while the faith of reviewing is purely mundane. The rest is clear everywhere.

Jarāvaggo pañcamo.

The Chapter on Old Age is the fifth.

6. Sūkarakhatavaggo

6. The Sūkarakhata Chapter

1. Sālasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Sāla Sutta

521. Chaṭṭhavaggassa [V 3.0276] paṭhame sūrenāti sūrabhāvena. Bodhāyāti bujjhanatthāya.

521. In the first sutta of the sixth chapter: 'sūrena' means due to the state of being courageous. 'Bodhāya' means for the purpose of penetrating the Four Truths.

2. Mallikasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Mallika Sutta

522. Dutiye [M 3.0280] mallesūti evaṃnāmake janapade. Imasmiṃ sutte cattāri indriyāni missakāni, ariyañāṇaṃ lokuttaraṃ. Tampi pana catukkindriyanissitaṃ katvā missakanti bhājetuṃ vaṭṭati.

522. In the second sutta: 'mallesu' means in the country of that name. In this sutta, the four faculties [other than wisdom] are a mixture [of worldly and supramundane]; the noble knowledge is supramundane. However, having made that [faculty of wisdom] also dependent on the four faculties, it is proper to classify it as mixed.

3. Sekhasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Sutta on the Learner

523. Tatiye na heva kho kāyena phusitvā viharatīti na nāmakāyena phusitvā paṭilabhitvā viharati, phusituṃ paṭilabhituṃ na sakkoti. Paññāya ca ativijjha passatīti paccavekkhaṇapaññāya pana “upari arahattaphalindriyaṃ nāma atthī”ti pajānāti. Asekhabhūmiyaṃ phusitvā viharatīti paṭilabhitvā viharati. Paññāyāti paccavekkhaṇapaññāya “arahattaphalindriyaṃ nāma atthī”ti pajānāti. Na kuhiñci kismiñcīti dvepi aññamaññavevacanāneva, kismiñci bhave na uppajjissantīti attho. Imasmiṃ sutte pañcindriyāni lokuttarāni, cha lokikāni vaṭṭanissitāneva kathitāni.

523. In the third sutta: 'na heva kho kāyena phusitvā viharati' means one does not dwell having touched and attained with the mental body; one is unable to touch and attain because the faculties are not yet mature. 'Paññāya ca ativijjha passati' means, however, with the wisdom of reviewing, one knows thus: 'Above, there is what is called the faculty of the fruit of Arahantship.' 'Asekhabhūmiyaṃ phusitvā viharati' means one dwells having attained it. 'Paññāya' means with the wisdom of reviewing one knows distinctly thus: 'There is what is called the faculty of the fruit of Arahantship.' 'Na kuhiñci kismiñci': both are just synonyms for each other; the meaning is that they will not arise in any existence whatsoever. In this sutta, the five faculties are supramundane; the six sense faculties are worldly and are taught as being dependent on the round of existence.

4-5. Padasuttādivaṇṇanā

4-5. Commentary on the Padasutta, etc.

524-525. Catutthe yāni kānici padāni bodhāya saṃvattantīti yāni kānici dhammapadāni, ye keci dhammakoṭṭhāsā, bujjhanatthāya saṃvattanti. Pañcamaṃ uttānameva.

In the fourth sutta: 'yāni kānici padāni bodhāya saṃvattanti' means whatever portions of the Dhamma conduce to the understanding of the Four Truths. The fifth sutta is self-evident.

6-7. Patiṭṭhitasuttādivaṇṇanā

6-7. Commentary on the Patiṭṭhita Sutta, etc.

526-527. Chaṭṭhe [V 3.0277][P 3.0249] cittaṃ rakkhati āsavesu ca sāsavesu ca dhammesūti tebhūmakadhamme ārabbha āsavuppattiṃ vārento āsavesu ca sāsavesu ca dhammesu cittaṃ rakkhati nāma. Sattamaṃ uttānameva.

In the sixth sutta: 'cittaṃ rakkhati āsavesu ca sāsavesu ca dhammesu' means that, by taking the phenomena of the three planes as an object and preventing the arising of the taints, one is said to guard the mind on account of both the phenomena that are taints and the phenomena that are objects for the taints. The seventh sutta is self-evident.

8. Sūkarakhatasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Sūkarakhata Sutta

528. Aṭṭhame sūkarakhatāyanti sūkarakhataleṇe. Kassapabuddhakāle kira taṃ leṇaṃ ekasmiṃ buddhantare pathaviyā vaḍḍhamānāya antobhūmigataṃ jātaṃ. Athekadivasaṃ eko sūkaro tassa chadanapariyantasamīpe paṃsuṃ khaṇi. Deve vuṭṭhe paṃsu dhotā, chadanapariyanto pākaṭo [M 3.0281] ahosi. Eko vanacarako disvā “pubbe sīlavantehi paribhuttaṭṭhānena bhavitabbaṃ, paṭijaggissāmi na”nti samantato paṃsuṃ apanetvā leṇaṃ sodhetvā kuṭiparikkhepaṃ katvā dvāravātapānaṃ yojetvā supariniṭṭhitasudhākammacittakammaṃ rajatapaṭṭasadisāya vālikāya santharitaṃ pariveṇaṃ katvā mañcapīṭhaṃ paññāpetvā bhagavato vasanatthāya adāsi, leṇaṃ gambhīraṃ ahosi otaritvā āruhitabbaṃ. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Paramanipaccakāranti bhāvanapuṃsakaṃ, paramanipaccakārī hutvā pavattamāno pavattatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Anuttaraṃ yogakkhemanti arahattaṃ. Sappatissoti sajeṭṭhako. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

528. In the eighth sutta: `sūkarakhatāyaṃ` means in the Sūkarakhata cave. It is said that during the time of Kassapa Buddha, in one Buddha-interval, as the earth was rising, that cave became submerged underground. Then one day, a boar dug the earth near the edge of its roof. When it rained, the loose earth was washed away, and the edge of the roof became visible. A forest-dweller saw it and thought, 'This must have been a place used by virtuous ones in the past. I will restore it.' Having cleared away the earth from all around, cleaned the cave, made an enclosure for the hut, fitted a door and window-frame, and having made a precinct with well-finished plasterwork and painting, strewn with sand like a silver sheet, he prepared a couch and seat and gave it to the Blessed One for his dwelling. The cave was deep; one had to descend into it and climb out of it. This was said in reference to that. `Paramanipaccakāraṃ` is a neuter noun expressing an action; it means that it is said, 'he proceeds, acting with the utmost deference.' `Anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ` means Arahantship. `Sappatisso` means with an elder. The rest has a clear meaning everywhere.

Sūkarakhatavaggo chaṭṭho.

The Sūkarakhata Chapter, the Sixth.

7. Bodhipakkhiyavaggo

7. The Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment

531-650. Sattamavagge satta phalāni pubbabhāgāni, tesaṃ heṭṭhā dve phalāni ādiṃ katvā missakāni. Sesamettha ito parañca sabbaṃ uttānamevāti.

In the seventh chapter, seven fruits are preliminary. Below them, the two fruits, to begin with, are mixed. The rest here, and from here on, is all clear in meaning.

Indriyasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Connected Discourses on the Faculties is concluded.

5. Sammappadhānasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Connected Discourses on Right Exertion

651-704. Sammappadhānasaṃyutte [V 3.0278][P 3.0250] sakalepi pubbabhāgavipassanāva kathitāti.

In the entire Sammappadhāna Saṃyutta, only insight belonging to the preliminary part is taught.

Sammappadhānasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Connected Discourses on Right Exertion is concluded.

6. Balasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Connected Discourses on the Powers

705-812. Balasaṃyutte [V 3.0279] balāni missakāneva kathitāni. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

In the Bala Saṃyutta, the powers are described as mixed. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.

Balasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Connected Discourses on the Powers is concluded.

7. Iddhipādasaṃyuttaṃ

7. The Connected Discourses on the Bases of Spiritual Power

1. Cāpālavaggo

1. The Chapter on Cāpāla

1. Apārasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Apāra Sutta

813. Iddhipādasaṃyuttassa [V 3.0280][M 3.0282] paṭhame chandaṃ nissāya pavatto samādhi chandasamādhi. Padhānabhūtā saṅkhārā padhānasaṅkhārā. Samannāgatanti tehi dhammehi upetaṃ. Iddhiyā pādaṃ, iddhibhūtaṃ vā pādanti iddhipādaṃ. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana iddhipādavibhaṅge (vibha. 431 ādayo) āgatova. Visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.3.69 ādayo) panassa attho dīpito. Tathā maggabojjhaṅgasatipaṭṭhānasaṃyuttesu ceva idha ca ekaparicchedova.

813. In the first discourse of the Iddhipāda Saṃyutta, concentration that arises dependent on desire is desire-concentration. The formations that constitute the main striving are the striving-formations. ‘Endowed’ means furnished with those states. A basis of spiritual power, or a power that is a basis, is called a basis of spiritual power. The same method applies to the rest. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation is already found in the Iddhipādavibhaṅga. Its meaning is also explained in the Visuddhimagga. Likewise, in the Saṃyuttas on the path, the enlightenment factors, and the foundations of mindfulness, as well as here, the treatment is the same.

5. Iddhipadesasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Iddhipadesa Sutta

817. Pañcame [P 3.0251] iddhipadesanti tayo ca magge tīṇi ca phalāni.

817. In the fifth discourse, 'a portion of spiritual power' refers to the three paths and the three fruits.

6. Samattasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Samatta Sutta

818. Chaṭṭhe samattaṃ iddhinti arahattaphalameva. Ādito paṭṭhāya pana navasupi suttesu vivaṭṭapādakā eva iddhipādā kathitā.

818. In the sixth discourse, 'accomplished spiritual power' means the fruit of arahantship itself. From the beginning, however, in all nine suttas, the bases of spiritual power that are a basis for turning away from the round of rebirths are taught.

10. Cetiyasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Cetiya Sutta

822. Dasame nisīdananti cammakhaṇḍaṃ adhippetaṃ. Udenaṃ cetiyanti udenayakkhassa cetiyaṭṭhāne [V 3.0281] katavihāro vuccati. Gotamakādīsupi eseva nayo. Bhāvitāti vaḍḍhitā. Bahulīkatāti punappunaṃ katā. Yānīkatāti yuttayānaṃ viya katā. Vatthukatāti patiṭṭhānaṭṭhena vatthu viya katā. Anuṭṭhitāti adhiṭṭhitā. Paricitāti samantato citā suvaḍḍhitā. Susamāraddhāti suṭṭhu samāraddhā.

822. In the tenth discourse, 'a seat' is intended to mean a piece of hide. 'The Udena Cetiya' is said of a monastery built at the shrine-place of the yakkha Udena. The same method applies to Gotamaka and the others. 'Developed' means increased. 'Made much of' means done again and again. 'Made a vehicle' means made like a yoked vehicle. 'Made a foundation' means made like a base in the sense of a foundation. 'Established' means firmly established. 'Familiarized' means developed all around, well-developed. 'Well undertaken' means properly undertaken.

Iti aniyamena kathetvā puna niyametvā dassento tathāgatassa khotiādimāha. Ettha ca kappanti āyukappaṃ, tasmiṃ tasmiṃ kāle yaṃ manussānaṃ [M 3.0283] āyuppamāṇaṃ, taṃ paripuṇṇaṃ karonto tiṭṭheyya. Kappāvasesaṃ vāti “appaṃ vā bhiyyo”ti vuttavassasatato atirekaṃ vā. Mahāsīvatthero panāha “buddhānaṃ aṭṭhāne gajjitaṃ nāma natthi. Yatheva hi veḷuvagāmake uppannaṃ māraṇantikavedanaṃ dasa māse vikkhambhesi, evaṃ punappunaṃ taṃ samāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā dasa dasa māsepi vikkhambhento imaṃ bhaddakappameva tiṭṭheyyā”ti.
