Having spoken thus in general terms, then wishing to show by specifying, he spoke the words beginning with 'The Tathāgata...'. And here, 'aeon' means the life-aeon; he could remain, completing whatever is the full measure of the human life-span at that particular time. 'Or for the remainder of the aeon' means for more than the aforementioned hundred years, as in the phrase 'a little more'. The Elder Mahāsīva, however, said: 'For the Buddhas, there is no such thing as a roar in the wrong place. For just as in the village of Veḷuva he suppressed for ten months the pain that was approaching death, so too, by repeatedly entering that attainment and suppressing it for ten months at a time, he could remain for this entire fortunate aeon.'

Kasmā pana na ṭhitoti? Upādiṇṇakasarīraṃ nāma khaṇḍiccādīhi abhibhuyyati, buddhā nāma khaṇḍiccādibhāvaṃ apatvāva pañcame āyukoṭṭhāse bahujanassa piyamanāpakāleyeva parinibbāyanti. Buddhānubuddhesu ca mahāsāvakesu parinibbutesu ekakena khāṇukena viya ṭhātabbaṃ hoti, daharasāmaṇeraparivāritena [P 3.0252] vā, tato – “aho buddhānaṃ parisā”ti hīḷetabbataṃ āpajjeyya, tasmā na ṭhitoti. Evaṃ vuttepi so pana na ruccati, “āyukappo”ti idameva aṭṭhakathāyaṃ niyamitaṃ.

But why did he not remain? The body produced by clinging is overcome by such things as broken teeth, but Buddhas, without reaching such a state, attain parinibbāna in the fifth portion of life, at a time when they are dear and agreeable to many people. And when the great disciples who are enlightened after the Buddha have attained parinibbāna, one would have to stand alone like a tree stump, or surrounded by young novices, and thus one would incur reproach—'Alas, the assembly of the Buddhas!' Therefore, he did not remain. Even though this was said, that view is not accepted. 'The life-aeon'—this alone is specified in the commentary.

Yathā taṃ mārena pariyuṭṭhitacittoti ettha tanti nipātamattaṃ. Yathā mārena pariyuṭṭhitacitto ajjhotthaṭacitto aññopi koci puthujjano paṭivijjhituṃ na sakkuṇeyya, evameva nāsakkhi paṭivijjhitunti attho. Māro hi yassa sabbena sabbaṃ dvādasa vipallāsā appahīnā, tassa cittaṃ pariyuṭṭhāti. Therassa ca cattāro vipallāsā appahīnā, tenassa māro cittaṃ pariyuṭṭhāsi. So pana cittapariyuṭṭhānaṃ karonto kiṃ karotīti? Bheravaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ vā dasseti, saddārammaṇaṃ vā sāveti, tato sattā taṃ disvā vā sutvā vā satiṃ vissajjetvā vivaṭamukhā honti, tesaṃ mukhena hatthaṃ pavesetvā hadayaṃ maddati, te visaññī hutvā tiṭṭhanti. Therassa panesa mukhe hatthaṃ pavesetuṃ kiṃ sakkhissati? Bheravārammaṇaṃ pana dasseti, taṃ disvā thero nimittobhāsaṃ na paṭivijjhi. Jānantoyeva bhagavā kimatthaṃ yāvatatiyakaṃ āmantesīti. Parato [V 3.0282] “tiṭṭhatu, bhante, bhagavā”ti yācite “tuyhevetaṃ dukkaṭaṃ, tuyhevetaṃ aparaddha”nti dosāropanena sokatanukaraṇatthaṃ.

Here, in 'as his mind was obsessed by Māra,' the word 'taṃ' is merely a particle. The meaning is: just as any other ordinary person whose mind is obsessed and overwhelmed by Māra would not be able to comprehend, so too was he unable to comprehend. For Māra obsesses the mind of one for whom the twelve distortions have not been entirely abandoned. In the Elder’s case, four distortions remained unabandoned, and for that reason Māra obsessed his mind. Now, what does Māra do when obsessing the mind? He shows a terrifying visual object or makes one hear a frightening sound. Then, beings who see or hear it lose mindfulness, their mouths gape open, and he thrusts his hand into their mouths and crushes their hearts. They stand there senseless. But how could he thrust his hand into the Elder’s mouth? Instead, he shows a terrifying object. Seeing it, the Elder did not comprehend the hint and the suggestion. The Blessed One, knowing this, addressed him up to a third time for what purpose? So that later, when requested with the words, 'May the Blessed One remain, venerable sir,' he could lessen his sorrow by placing the blame on him, saying, 'This wrongdoing is yours, this offense is yours.'

Māro pāpimāti ettha satte anatthe niyojento māretīti māro. Pāpimāti tasseva vevacanaṃ. So hi pāpadhammasamannāgatattā “pāpimā”ti [M 3.0284] vuccati. Kaṇho, antako, namuci, pamattabandhūtipi tasseva nāmāni. Bhāsitā kho panesāti ayañhi bhagavato sambodhipattiyā aṭṭhame sattāhe bodhimaṇḍaṃyeva āgantvā – “bhagavā yadatthaṃ tumhehi pāramiyo pūritā, so vo attho anuppatto, paṭividdhaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ, kiṃ vo lokavicaraṇenā”ti vatvā yathā ajja, evameva – “parinibbātu dāni, bhante, bhagavā, parinibbātu, sugato,”ti yāci. Bhagavā cassa “na tāvāha”ntiādīni vatvā paṭikkhipi. Taṃ sandhāya “bhāsitā kho panesā, bhante,”tiādimāha.

Here, in the text 'Māra the Evil One': because he urges beings toward what is not their welfare and kills them, he is called 'Māra.' 'The Evil One' is a synonym for that very one. Indeed, because he is endowed with evil qualities, he is called 'the Evil One.' 'Kaṇha,' 'Antaka,' 'Namuci,' and 'Kinsman of the Negligent' are also his names. As for 'Moreover, it has been spoken of': indeed, in the eighth week after the Blessed One’s attainment of enlightenment, this Māra came to the very Bodhimaṇḍa and, having said, 'Blessed One, the purpose for which you fulfilled the perfections has been attained by you; omniscience has been penetrated. What use is wandering the world to you?' he entreated just as he did today: 'Now, Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One attain final Nibbāna; may the Sugata attain final Nibbāna!' And the Blessed One rejected his entreaty, saying, 'Not yet…' and so on. With reference to that, he said, 'Moreover, it has been spoken of, Venerable Sir,' and so forth.

Tattha viyattāti maggavasena byattā. Tatheva vinītā. Tathā visāradā. Bahussutāti tepiṭakavasena bahu sutametesanti [P 3.0253] bahussutā. Tadeva dhammaṃ dhārentīti dhammadharā. Atha vā pariyattibahussutā ceva paṭivedhabahussutā ca, pariyattipaṭivedhadhammānaṃyeva dhāraṇato dhammadharāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Dhammānudhammappaṭipannāti ariyadhammassa anudhammabhūtaṃ vipassanādhammaṃ paṭipannā. Sāmīcippaṭipannāti anucchavikapaṭipadaṃ paṭipannā. Anudhammacārinoti anudhammacaraṇasīlā. Sakaṃ ācariyakanti attano ācariyavādaṃ. Ācikkhissantītiādīni sabbāni aññamaññasseva vevacanāni. Sahadhammenāti sahetukena sakāraṇena vacanena. Sappāṭihāriyanti yāva niyyānikaṃ katvā dhammaṃ desessanti.

Therein, 'accomplished' (viyattā) means skilled by way of the path. Similarly, 'disciplined' (vinītā). Likewise, 'confident' (visāradā). 'Very learned' (bahussutā) means: because they have heard much by way of the Tipiṭaka, they are 'very learned.' Because they bear that very Dhamma, they are 'bearers of the Dhamma' (dhammadharā). Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood thus: they are learned in scripture (pariyatti) and learned in penetration (paṭivedha), and because they bear the Dhamma of both scripture and penetration, they are 'bearers of the Dhamma.' 'Practicing in accordance with the Dhamma' (dhammānudhammappaṭipannā) means they practice the insight-Dhamma, which is the practice in conformity with the noble Dhamma. 'Practicing the proper way' (sāmīcippaṭipannā) means they practice the suitable path. 'Living in accordance with the Dhamma' (anudhammacārino) means they are of the nature of practicing in conformity with the Dhamma. 'Their own teacher's teaching' (sakaṃ ācariyakaṃ) means their own teacher's doctrine. 'They will explain' (ācikkhissanti) and so on are all synonyms for one another. 'With the Dhamma' (sahadhammena) means with speech that has a cause and a reason. 'With its wonders' (sappāṭihāriyaṃ) means they will teach the Dhamma having made it lead to escape.

Brahmacariyanti sikkhattayasaṅgahitaṃ sakalaṃ sāsanabrahmacariyaṃ. Iddhanti samiddhaṃ jhānassādavasena. Phītanti vuḍḍhipattaṃ sabbapāliphullaṃ viya abhiññāsampattivasena. Vitthārikanti vitthataṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ disābhāge patiṭṭhitavasena. Bāhujaññanti bahūhi ñātaṃ paṭividdhaṃ mahājanābhisamayavasena. Puthubhūtanti sabbākārena puthulabhāvapattaṃ. Kathaṃ? Yāva devamanussehi suppakāsitaṃ, yattakā viññujātikā devā ceva manussā ca atthi, sabbehi suṭṭhu pakāsitanti attho.

'The holy life' means the entire holy life of the Dispensation, which is comprised of the three trainings. 'Prosperous' (iddhaṃ) means flourishing by way of delight in jhāna. 'Thriving' (phītaṃ) means having attained growth, like a fully blossomed sal tree, by way of the attainment of the higher knowledges. 'Widespread' (vitthārikaṃ) means it has become extensive by way of being firmly established in various regions. 'Well-known among many' (bāhujaññaṃ) means known and penetrated by many by way of the realization of the great populace. 'Expansive' (puthubhūtaṃ) means it has reached a state of being widespread in all aspects. How so? Insofar as it is well-proclaimed by gods and humans; that is to say, the meaning is that it is well-proclaimed by all existing intelligent beings, both gods and humans.

Appossukkoti [V 3.0283] nirālayo. Tvañhi pāpima aṭṭhamasattāhato paṭṭhāya “parinibbātu dāni, bhante, bhagavā, parinibbātu sugato”ti viravanto āhiṇḍittha, ajja dāni paṭṭhāya vigatussāho hohi, mā mayhaṃ parinibbānatthaṃ vāyāmaṃ karohīti vadati.

'Be untroubled' (appossukko) means be without attachment. Indeed, Evil One, you, starting from the eighth week, have been wandering about, crying out, 'Now, Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One attain final Nibbāna; may the Sugata attain final Nibbāna!' Now, starting from today, be without zeal; do not make an effort for my final Nibbāna,' he says.

Sato [M 3.0285] sampajāno āyusaṅkhāraṃ ossajīti satiṃ sūpaṭṭhitaṃ katvā ñāṇena paricchinditvā āyusaṅkhāraṃ vissaji pajahi. Tattha na bhagavā hatthena leḍḍuṃ viya āyusaṅkhāraṃ ossaji, temāsamattameva pana phalasamāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā tato paraṃ na samāpajjissāmīti cittaṃ uppādesi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “ossajī”ti. Ussajītipi pāṭho. Mahābhūmicāloti mahanto pathavikampo. Tadā kira dasasahassilokadhātu akampittha. Bhiṃsanakoti bhayajanako[P 3.0254]. Devadundubhiyo ca phaliṃsūti devabheriyo phaliṃsu, devo sukkhagajjitaṃ gajji, akālavijjulatā nicchariṃsu, khaṇikavassaṃ vassīti vuttaṃ hoti.

'Mindful and clearly comprehending, he relinquished the life-formation' means: having made mindfulness well-established and having determined with knowledge, he released and abandoned the life-formation. Therein, the Blessed One did not cast off the life-formation with his hand like a clod of earth. Rather, having entered the fruition attainment for just three months, he produced the thought, 'Hereafter, beyond those three months, I will not enter it.' With reference to this, it is said, 'he relinquished.' There is also the reading 'he will relinquish' (ossajjissati). 'A great earthquake occurred' means a great trembling of the earth happened. At that time, it is said, the ten-thousandfold world-system shook. 'Terrifying' (bhiṃsanako) means fear-inducing. 'And the celestial drums resounded' means the celestial drums sounded, the sky thundered a dry thunder, untimely flashes of lightning appeared, and a momentary rain fell—this is what is said.

Udānaṃ udānesīti kasmā udānesi? Koci nāma vadeyya “bhagavā pacchato pacchato anubandhitvā – ‘parinibbāyatha, bhante, parinibbāyatha, bhante’ti upadduto bhayena āyusaṅkhāraṃ vissajjesī”ti. Tassokāso mā hotūti. Bhītassa hi udānaṃ nāma natthīti pītivegavissaṭṭhaṃ udānesi.

As for 'he uttered an inspired utterance,' why did he utter it? So that there would be no opportunity for someone to say: 'The Blessed One, being harassed by Māra following closely behind with the words, "Attain final Nibbāna, Venerable Sir; attain final Nibbāna, Venerable Sir!", relinquished the life-formation out of fear.' For one who is afraid, there is no such thing as an inspired utterance. Therefore, he uttered the inspired utterance, which was released by the force of joy at the thought, 'Soon I will be able to lay down this great burden of the aggregates of existence, which has been carried for a long time!'

Tattha sabbesaṃ soṇasiṅgālādīnampi paccakkhabhāvato tulitaṃ paricchinnanti tulaṃ. Kiṃ taṃ? Kāmāvacarakammaṃ. Na tulaṃ, na vā tulaṃ sadisamassa aññaṃ lokiyakammaṃ atthīti atulaṃ. Kiṃ taṃ? Mahaggatakammaṃ. Atha vā kāmāvacaraṃ rūpāvacarañca tulaṃ, arūpāvacaraṃ atulaṃ. Appavipākaṃ tulaṃ, bahuvipākaṃ atulaṃ. Sambhavanti sambhavahetubhūtaṃ, piṇḍakārakaṃ rāsikārakanti attho. Bhavasaṅkhāranti punabbhavassa saṅkhāraṃ. Avassajīti vissajjesi. Munīti buddhamuni. Ajjhattaratoti niyakajjhattarato. Samāhitoti upacārappanāsamādhivasena samāhito. Abhindi kavacamivāti kavacaṃ viya abhindi. Attasambhavanti attani jātakilesaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – savipākaṭṭhena sambhavaṃ bhavābhisaṅkhaṇaṭṭhena bhavasaṅkhāranti ca laddhanāmaṃ tulātulasaṅkhātaṃ lokiyakammañca ossaji, saṅgāmasīse mahāyodho kavacaṃ viya attasambhavaṃ kilesañca ajjhattarato samāhito hutvā abhindīti.

Herein, 'measure' (tulaṃ) is so called because it is weighed and determined, being directly experienced by all, even dogs and jackals. What is that? Sense-sphere kamma. 'Immeasurable' (atulaṃ) is so called because it is not a measure, or because there is no other worldly kamma similar to it. What is that? Exalted-sphere kamma. Alternatively, sense-sphere and form-sphere kamma are 'measurable', while formless-sphere kamma is 'immeasurable'. Kamma with small results is 'measurable'; kamma with great results is 'immeasurable'. 'Arising' (sambhavaṃ) means that which is a cause for arising; the meaning is that which produces aggregates and heaps. 'Formation of existence' (bhavasaṅkhāraṃ) means the formation for renewed existence. 'He cast off' (avassaji) means he relinquished. 'Sage' (muni) means the Buddha-sage. 'Inwardly delighted' (ajjhattarato) means delighted in his own inner self. 'Composed' (samāhito) means composed by way of access and attainment concentration. 'He shattered as if armor' (abhindi kavacamiva) means he shattered it like armor. 'Self-arisen' (attasambhavaṃ) means the defilement born in oneself. This is what is said: He cast off worldly kamma—designated as 'measurable' and 'immeasurable', and named 'arising' because it yields results and 'formation of existence' because it conditions future becoming—and, like a great warrior at the head of a battle shattering his armor, being inwardly delighted and composed, he shattered the self-arisen defilement.

Atha [V 3.0284] vā tulanti tulento tīrento. Atulañca sambhavanti nibbānañceva bhavañca. Bhavasaṅkhāranti bhavagāmikammaṃ. Avassaji munīti “pañcakkhandhā aniccā, pañcannaṃ [M 3.0286] khandhānaṃ nirodho nibbānaṃ nicca”ntiādinā nayena tulayanto buddhamuni bhave ādīnavaṃ nibbāne cānisaṃsaṃ disvā taṃ khandhānaṃ mūlabhūtaṃ bhavasaṅkhāraṃ “kammakkhayāya saṃvattatī”ti evaṃ vuttena [P 3.0255] kammakkhayakarena ariyamaggena avassaji. Kathaṃ? Ajjhattarato samāhito abhindi kavacamivattasambhavaṃ. So hi vipassanāvasena ajjhattarato, samathavasena samāhitoti evaṃ pubbabhāgato paṭṭhāya samathavipassanābalena kavacamiva attabhāvaṃ pariyonandhitvā ṭhitaṃ, attani sambhavattā attasambhavanti laddhanāmaṃ sabbaṃ kilesajātaṃ abhindi. Kilesābhāvena ca kammaṃ appaṭisandhikattā avassaṭṭhaṃ nāma hotīti evaṃ kilesappahānena kammaṃ jahi. Pahīnakilesassa bhayaṃ nāma natthi. Tasmā abhītova āyusaṅkhāraṃ ossaji. Abhītabhāvañāpanatthañca udānaṃ udānesīti veditabbo.

Alternatively, 'weighing' (tulanto) means weighing and distinguishing. And 'the immeasurable' (atulaṃ) and 'that which arises' (sambhavaṃ) refer to Nibbāna and existence respectively. 'Formations of existence' (bhavasaṅkhāraṃ) refers to kamma leading to existence. 'The sage cast off' (avassaji muni): The Buddha-sage, weighing the dangers in existence and the benefits in Nibbāna by such methods as, 'The five aggregates are impermanent; the cessation of the five aggregates, Nibbāna, is permanent,' and seeing that formation of existence which is the root of those aggregates, cast it off by the noble path that destroys kamma, as stated: 'It leads to the destruction of kamma.' How? Inwardly delighted, composed, he shattered the self-arisen like armor. For by way of insight he was inwardly delighted, and by way of serenity he was composed. Thus, from the preliminary stage onwards, with the strength of serenity and insight, he shattered the entire mass of defilements—named 'self-arisen' because it arises in oneself—which stood enveloping his individual existence like armor. And due to the absence of defilements, kamma, being unable to produce a new connection, is called 'cast off'. Thus, he abandoned kamma by the relinquishing of defilements. For one whose defilements are abandoned, there is no such thing as fear. Therefore, fearless, he cast off the life-formation. And it should be understood that he uttered an exclamation to make known his fearless state.

Cāpālavaggo paṭhamo.

The First Chapter: Cāpāla.

2. Pāsādakampanavaggo

2. The Chapter on the Quaking of the Mansion

1-2. Pubbasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-2. Explanation of the Previous Suttas, etc.

823-824. Dutiyavaggassa paṭhame na ca atilīnotiādīni parato āvi bhavissanti. Imasmiṃ sutte chaabhiññāpādakā iddhipādā kathitā, tathā dutiye ca.

823-824. In the first sutta of the second chapter, the passage beginning 'not too lax' will become clear later. In this sutta, the bases of spiritual power that are the foundation for the six super-knowledges are discussed, and likewise in the second.

3. Chandasamādhisuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Discourse on Concentration of Desire

825. Tatiye chandanti kattukamyatāchandaṃ. Nissāyāti nissayaṃ katvā, adhipatiṃ katvāti attho. Padhānasaṅkhārāti padhānabhūtā saṅkhārā, catukiccasādhakasammappadhānavīriyassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Iti ayañca chandotiādīsu chando chandasamādhinā ceva padhānasaṅkhārehi ca, chandasamādhi chandena ceva padhānasaṅkhārehi ca, padhānasaṅkhārāpi chandena ceva chandasamādhinā ca samannāgatā[V 3.0285]. Tasmā sabbe te dhamme ekato katvā ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, chandasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgato iddhipādoti vuttaṃ. Iddhipādavibhaṅge (vibha. 437) pana “yo tathābhūtassa vedanākkhandho tiādinā nayena [M 3.0287] imehi dhammehi samannāgatā sesaarūpino dhammā iddhipādāti vuttā.

825. In the third sutta, 'desire' (chanda) means the desire to act (kattukamyatāchanda). 'Relying on' (nissāya) means having made it a basis, having made it a dominant factor—that is the meaning. 'Effortful formations' (padhānasaṅkhārā) refers to formations that are primary; this is a designation for the energy of right effort that accomplishes the four tasks. Thus, in phrases such as 'this desire' (ayañca chando), desire is endowed with concentration of desire and effortful formations; concentration of desire is endowed with desire and effortful formations; and effortful formations are also endowed with desire and concentration of desire. Therefore, having combined all those phenomena into one, it is said: 'Monks, this is called a basis for spiritual power endowed with concentration of desire and effortful formations.' However, in the Analysis of the Bases of Spiritual Power (Vibh. 437), it is said: 'Whatever feeling aggregate of such a one,' etc.—in that manner, the remaining immaterial phenomena endowed with these phenomena are called a basis for spiritual power.

Apica imepi tayo dhammā iddhīpi honti iddhipādāpi. Kathaṃ? Chandañhi bhāvayato chando iddhi nāma hoti, samādhippadhānasaṅkhārā chandiddhipādo nāma. Samādhiṃ bhāventassa samādhi iddhi nāma hoti, chandappadhānasaṅkhārā [P 3.0256] samādhiddhiyā pādo nāma. Padhānasaṅkhāre bhāventassa padhānasaṅkhārā iddhi nāma hoti, chandasamādhi padhānasaṅkhāriddhiyā pādo nāma, sampayuttadhammesu hi ekasmiṃ ijjhamāne sesāpi ijjhantiyeva.

Moreover, these three phenomena are both spiritual powers (iddhi) and bases for spiritual power (iddhipāda). How? For one who develops desire, desire is called a spiritual power; concentration and effortful formations are called the basis for the spiritual power of desire. For one who develops concentration, concentration is called a spiritual power; desire and effortful formations are called the basis for the spiritual power of concentration. For one who develops effortful formations, effortful formations are called a spiritual power; desire and concentration are called the basis for the spiritual power of effortful formations. For when one associated phenomenon succeeds, the others also succeed.

Apica tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ pubbabhāgavasenāpi etesaṃ iddhipādatā veditabbā. Paṭhamajjhānañhi iddhi nāma, paṭhamajjhānassa pubbabhāgaparikammasampayuttā chandādayo iddhipādo nāma. Etenupāyena yāva nevasaññānāsaññāyatanā, iddhividhaṃ ādiṃ katvā yāva dibbacakkhuabhiññā, sotāpattimaggaṃ ādiṃ katvā yāva arahattamaggā nayo netabbo. Sesiddhipādesupi eseva nayo.

Moreover, their nature as bases for spiritual power should be understood also by way of their being the preliminary part of those respective phenomena. For the first jhāna is called a spiritual power (iddhi), and desire (chanda) and other factors associated with the preliminary practice that is its preparatory part are called a basis for spiritual power (iddhipāda). By this method, the principle should be extended up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; from the varieties of spiritual power (iddhividha) up to the direct knowledge of the divine eye (dibbacakkhu-abhiññā); and from the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga) up to the path of arahantship (arahattamagga). The same principle applies to the remaining bases for spiritual power as well.

Keci pana “anibbatto chando iddhipādo”ti vadanti. Idha tesaṃ vādamaddanatthāya abhidhamme uttaracūḷavāro nāma āgato –

Some, however, say: 'Unarisen desire is a basis for spiritual power.' Here, to refute their assertion, a section called the Uttara Cūḷavāra has been presented from the Abhidhamma:

“Cattāro iddhipādā – chandiddhipādo, vīriyiddhipādo, cittiddhipādo, vīmaṃsiddhipādo. Tattha katamo chandiddhipādo? Idha, bhikkhu, yasmiṃ samaye lokuttaraṃ jhānaṃ bhāveti niyyānikaṃ apacayagāmiṃ diṭṭhigatānaṃ pahānāya paṭhamāya bhūmiyā pattiyā vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati dukkhāpaṭipadaṃ dandhābhiññaṃ, yo tasmiṃ samaye chando chandikatā kattukamyatā kusalo dhammacchando, ayaṃ vuccati chandiddhipādo. Avasesā dhammā chandiddhipādasampayuttā”ti (vibha. 457-458).

'There are these four bases for spiritual power: the basis for spiritual power of desire, the basis for spiritual power of energy, the basis for spiritual power of mind, the basis for spiritual power of investigation. And what is the basis for spiritual power of desire? Here, a bhikkhu, at the time when he develops supramundane jhāna that leads to liberation, leading to the waning away of defilements, for the abandoning of wrong views, for the attainment of the first ground, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is of painful practice and slow in direct knowledge. At that time, whatever desire, wish to do, will to do, wholesome desire for the Dhamma there is, this is called the basis for spiritual power of desire. The remaining phenomena are associated with the basis for spiritual power of desire.' (Vibh. 457-458).

Ime [V 3.0286] pana lokuttaravaseneva āgatā.

These, however, have been presented solely by way of the supramundane.

Tattha raṭṭhapālatthero chandaṃ dhuraṃ katvā lokuttaradhammaṃ nibbattesi. Soṇatthero vīriyaṃ dhuraṃ katvā; sambhutatthero cittaṃ dhuraṃ katvā, āyasmā mogharājā vīmaṃsaṃ dhuraṃ katvāti. Tattha yathā catūsu amaccaputtesu [M 3.0288] ṭhānantaraṃ patthetvā rājānaṃ upanissāya viharantesu eko upaṭṭhāne chandajāto rañño ajjhāsayañca ruciñca ñatvā divā ca ratto ca upaṭṭhahanto rājānaṃ ārādhetvā ṭhānantaraṃ pāpuṇi. Evaṃ chandadhurena lokuttaradhammanibbattako veditabbo.

Among these, the Elder Raṭṭhapāla, making desire his guiding principle, brought forth the supramundane Dhamma. The Elder Soṇa, making energy his guiding principle; the Elder Sambhūta, making mind his guiding principle; and the Venerable Mogharājā, making investigation his guiding principle. Herein, just as among four sons of ministers who, desiring a higher position, lived in dependence on the king, one, having arisen with desire for service, knowing the king's intentions and likings, and attending diligently day and night, pleased the king and attained a higher position, so too should one be understood who brings forth the supramundane Dhamma with desire as the guiding principle.

Eko pana – “divase divase upaṭṭhātuṃ na sakkomi, uppanne kicce parakkamena ārādhessāmī”ti kupite paccante raññā [P 3.0257] pahito parakkamena sattumaddanaṃ katvā pāpuṇi. Yathā so, evaṃ vīriyadhurena lokuttaradhammanibbattako veditabbo. Eko “divase divase upaṭṭhānampi urena sattisarasampaṭicchanampi bhāroyeva, mantabalena ārādhessāmī”ti khattavijjāya kataparicayattā mantasaṃvidhānena rājānaṃ ārādhetvā pāpuṇi. Yathā so, evaṃ cittadhurena lokuttaradhammanibbattako veditabbo.

Another, however, thought: 'I cannot attend every day, but when a task arises, I will strive and please him.' Sent by the king to a rebellious border, he exerted himself, crushed the enemy, and succeeded. Just as he did, so too should one understand the one who brings forth the supramundane Dhamma with energy as the guiding principle. Another thought: 'Attending every day, even enduring the thrust of a spear with my chest, is a burden. I will please him through the power of counsel.' Being skilled in the art of strategy, he arranged his advice and pleased the king, thus succeeding. Just as he did, so too should one understand the one who brings forth the supramundane Dhamma with mind as the guiding principle.

Aparo – “kiṃ imehi upaṭṭhānādīhi, rājāno nāma jātisampannassa ṭhānantaraṃ denti, tādisassa dento mayhaṃ dassatī”ti jātisampattimeva nissāya ṭhānantaraṃ pāpuṇi. Yathā so, evaṃ suparisuddhaṃ vīmaṃsaṃ nissāya vīmaṃsadhurena lokuttaradhammanibbattako veditabboti. Imasmiṃ sutte vivaṭṭapādakaiddhi kathitā.

Yet another thought: 'What need is there for these services and so forth? Kings, it is said, grant positions to those accomplished in birth. If they give to such a person, they will give to me.' Relying solely on his accomplishment in birth, he attained a position. Just as he did, so too should one understand the one who brings forth the supramundane Dhamma by relying on thoroughly purified investigation, with investigation as the guiding principle. In this discourse, the spiritual power that has the turning away (from saṃsāra) as its basis is explained.

4. Moggallānasuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Moggallāna Sutta

826. Catutthe uddhatāti uddhaccapakatikā vipphandamānacittā. Uddhaccena hi ekārammaṇe cittaṃ vipphandati dhajayaṭṭhiyaṃ vātena pahatadhajo viya. Unnaḷāti uggatanaḷā, uṭṭhitatucchamānāti vuttaṃ hoti. Capalāti pattacīvaramaṇḍanādicāpallena yuttā. Mukharāti mukhakharā, kharavacanāti vuttaṃ hoti. Vikiṇṇavācāti asaṃyatavacanā divasampi niratthakavacanappalāpino. Muṭṭhassatīti naṭṭhassatino. Asampajānāti paññārahitā. Asamāhitāti upacārappanāsamādhivirahitā. Bhantacittāti ubbhantacittā samādhivirahena laddhokāsena uddhaccena[V 3.0287]. Pākatindriyāti asaṃvutindriyā. Iddhābhisaṅkhāranti āpokasiṇaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya pāsādapatiṭṭhitaṃ pathavibhāgaṃ “udaka”nti adhiṭṭhāya, udakapiṭṭhe ṭhitapāsādaṃ vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā aṅguṭṭhakena pahari. Gambhīranemoti [P 3.0258] gambhīraāvāṭo, gambhīrabhūmibhāgaṃ anupaviṭṭhoti attho[M 3.0289]. Sunikhātoti suṭṭhu nikhāto, koṭṭetvā suṭṭhu ṭhapito. Idha abhiññāpādakiddhi kathitā.

826. In the fourth [discourse], 'the restless' (uddhatā) refers to those whose minds are naturally restless, floundering. For due to restlessness, the mind flounders on a single object, like a banner on a flagpole struck by the wind. 'The puffed up' (unnaḷā) means those with arisen conceit; it is said to mean those with arisen empty pride. 'The fickle' (capalā) means those endowed with fickleness such as adorning the bowl and robe. 'The garrulous' (mukharā) means harsh-mouthed; it is said to mean harsh in speech. 'Those with scattered speech' (vikiṇṇavācā) means those with unrestrained speech, chattering meaninglessly even all day. 'Those lacking mindfulness' (muṭṭhassatī) means those with lost mindfulness. 'Those lacking clear comprehension' (asampajānā) means those devoid of wisdom. 'The unconcentrated' (asamāhitā) means those devoid of access and absorption concentration. 'Those with a wandering mind' (bhantacittā) means those with a bewildered mind, due to restlessness having gained an opportunity through the absence of concentration. 'Those with unrestrained faculties' (pākatindriyā) means those with unrestrained faculties. 'Manifesting psychic powers' (iddhābhisaṅkhāraṃ) means having attained the water-kasiṇa, emerged, and resolved the portion of earth where a palace stands as 'water,' then, having risen into the sky with the palace standing on the water's surface, struck it with a big toe. 'Deep-rooted' (gambhīranemo) means a deep hollow; the meaning is 'having entered a deep part of the ground.' 'Well-planted' (sunikhāto) means well-dug, thoroughly placed by hammering. Here, the psychic power that is the basis for direct knowledge is explained.

5. Uṇṇābhabrāhmaṇasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Uṇṇābha the Brahmin Sutta

827. Pañcame chandappahānatthanti taṇhāchandassa pahānatthaṃ. Idhāpi vivaṭṭapādakiddhi kathitā.

827. In the fifth [sutta], 'for the purpose of abandoning desire' means for the purpose of abandoning the desire that is craving. Here too, the spiritual power that has the turning away (from saṃsāra) as its basis is taught.

9. Iddhādidesanāsuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Discourse on Spiritual Powers and So Forth

831. Navame yo so bhikkhave maggoti abhiññāpādakaṃ catutthajjhānaṃ adhippetaṃ.

831. In the ninth [sutta], 'that path, monks,' is intended to mean the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for direct knowledge.

10. Vibhaṅgasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Vibhaṅga Sutta

832. Dasame kosajjasahagatoti idha bhikkhu chandaṃ uppādetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikaronto nisīdati. Athassa citte līnākāro okkamati, so “līnākāro me okkanto”ti ñatvā apāyabhayena cittaṃ tajjetvā puna chandaṃ uppādetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karoti. Athassa puna līnākāro okkamati. So puna apāyabhayena cittaṃ tajjetvā chandaṃ uppādetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karotīti evamassa kosajjena vokiṇṇattā chando kosajjasahagato nāma hoti. Kosajjasampayuttoti tasseva vevacanaṃ.

832. In the tenth [sutta], 'accompanied by laziness' is as follows. Here, a monk, having generated a desire for meditation, sits attending to the meditation subject. Then a state of sluggishness descends upon his mind. Knowing, 'A state of sluggishness has descended upon me,' he threatens his mind with the fear of the planes of misery, and having again generated a desire for meditation, he attends to the meditation subject. Then a state of sluggishness descends upon him again. Again, he threatens his mind with the fear of the planes of misery, and having generated a desire for meditation, he attends to the meditation subject. In this way, because his desire for meditation is mixed with laziness, it is called 'desire accompanied by laziness.' The term 'conjoined with laziness' is a synonym for that very term.

Uddhaccasahagatoti idha bhikkhu chandaṃ uppādetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikaronto nisīdati. Athassa cittaṃ uddhacce patati. So buddhadhammasaṅghaguṇe āvajjetvā cittaṃ hāsetvā tosetvā kammaniyaṃ katvā puna chandaṃ uppādetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karoti. Athassa puna cittaṃ uddhacce patati. So puna buddhadhammasaṅghaguṇe āvajjetvā cittaṃ hāsetvā tosetvā kammaniyaṃ katvā chandaṃ [V 3.0288] uppādetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karotīti evamassa uddhaccena vokiṇṇattā chando uddhaccasahagato nāma hoti.

'Accompanied by restlessness' is as follows. Here, a monk, having generated a desire for meditation, sits attending to the meditation subject. Then his mind falls into restlessness. He reflects on the qualities of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha, makes his mind joyful and pleased, makes it workable, and having again generated a desire for meditation, he attends to the meditation subject. Then his mind falls into restlessness again. Again, he reflects on the qualities of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha, makes his mind joyful and pleased, makes it workable, and having generated a desire for meditation, he attends to the meditation subject. In this way, because his desire for meditation is mixed with restlessness, it is called 'desire accompanied by restlessness.'

Thinamiddhasahagatoti idha bhikkhu chandaṃ uppādetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikaronto nisīdati. Athassa thinamiddhaṃ uppajjati. So “uppannaṃ me thinamiddha”nti ñatvā udakena mukhaṃ puñchitvā, kaṇṇe ākaḍḍhitvā paguṇaṃ [P 3.0259] dhammaṃ sajjhāyitvā divā gahitaṃ vā ālokasaññaṃ manasikaritvā thinamiddhaṃ vinodetvā [M 3.0290] puna chandaṃ uppādetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karoti. Athassa puna thinamiddhaṃ uppajjati. So vuttanayeneva puna thinamiddhaṃ vinodetvā chandaṃ uppādetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karotīti evamassa thinamiddhena vokiṇṇattā chando thinamiddhasahagato nāma hoti.

'Accompanied by sloth and torpor' is as follows. Here, a monk, having generated desire, sits attending to his meditation subject. Then sloth and torpor arise in him. Knowing, 'Sloth and torpor have arisen in me,' he washes his face with water, pulls his ears, recites a familiar teaching, or attends to the perception of light grasped during the day, and having dispelled sloth and torpor, he again generates desire and attends to his meditation subject. Then sloth and torpor arise in him again. In the way already stated, he again dispels sloth and torpor, generates desire, and attends to his meditation subject. In this way, because his desire is mixed with sloth and torpor, it is called 'desire accompanied by sloth and torpor.'

Anuvikkhittoti idha bhikkhu chandaṃ uppādetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikaronto nisīdati. Athassa kāmaguṇārammaṇe cittaṃ vikkhipati. So “bahiddhā vikkhittaṃ me citta”nti ñatvā anamatagga (saṃ. ni. 2.124-125) devadūta- (ma. ni. 3.261) celopama (saṃ. ni. 5.1104) anāgatabhayasuttādīni (a. ni. 5.77) āvajjento suttadaṇḍena cittaṃ tajjetvā kammaniyaṃ katvā puna chandaṃ uppādetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karoti. Athassa puna cittaṃ vikkhipati. So puna suttadaṇḍena cittaṃ kammaniyaṃ katvā chandaṃ uppādetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karotīti evamassa kāmavitakkavokiṇṇattā chando bahiddhā pañca kāmaguṇe ārabbha anuvikkhitto anuvisaṭo hoti.

'Repeatedly distracted' is as follows. Here, a monk, having generated desire, sits attending to his meditation subject. Then his mind is distracted towards objects of sensual pleasure. Knowing, 'My mind is distracted outwardly,' he reflects on the Anamatagga Sutta, Devadūta Sutta, Selopama Sutta, Anāgatabhaya Sutta, and so on, and with the staff that is the suttas, he threatens his mind, makes it workable, and having again generated desire, he attends to his meditation subject. Then his mind is distracted again. He again makes his mind workable with the staff of the suttas, generates desire, and attends to his meditation subject. Thus, because his desire is mixed with sensual thoughts, his desire, with respect to the five strands of sensual pleasure, becomes repeatedly distracted and repeatedly scattered outwardly.

Yathā pure tathā pacchāti kammaṭṭhānavasenapi desanāvasenapi purimapacchimatā veditabbā. Kathaṃ? Kammaṭṭhāne tāva kammaṭṭhānassa abhiniveso pure nāma, arahattaṃ pacchā nāma. Tattha yo bhikkhu mūlakammaṭṭhāne abhinivisitvā atilīnādīsu catūsu ṭhānesu cittassa okkamanaṃ paṭisedhetvā, duṭṭhagoṇe yojetvā sārento viya caturassaghaṭikaṃ otārento viya catunnaṃ ṭhānānaṃ ekaṭṭhānepi asajjanto saṅkhāre sammasitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Ayampi yathā pure tathā pacchā viharati nāma. Ayaṃ kammaṭṭhānavasena purimapacchimatā. Desanāvasena pana kesā pure nāma, matthaluṅgaṃ pacchā nāma. Tattha yo bhikkhu kesesu abhinivisitvā vaṇṇasaṇṭhānādivasena kesādayo pariggaṇhanto catūsu ṭhānesu asajjanto yāva matthaluṅgā bhāvanaṃ pāpeti, ayampi yathā [V 3.0289] pure tathā [P 3.0260] pacchā viharati nāma. Evaṃ desanāvasena purimapacchimatā veditabbā. Yathā pacchā tathā pureti idaṃ purimasseva vevacanaṃ.

'As before, so after': the state of being before and after should be understood by way of the meditation subject and by way of the teaching. How? First, regarding the meditation subject: application to the meditation subject is called 'before'; the fruit of Arahantship is called 'after.' In this regard, a monk who, having applied himself to his fundamental meditation subject, prevents the mind's descent into the four states, such as being too sluggish, and, like a charioteer yoking and driving stubborn oxen, or like someone lowering a four-cornered block, without getting stuck in any of the four states, he contemplates the formations and attains the fruit of Arahantship. This one, too, is said to dwell 'as before, so after.' This is the state of being before and after by way of the meditation subject. By way of the teaching: the hairs of the head are called 'before'; the brain is called 'after.' In this regard, a monk who, having applied himself to the hairs of the head, comprehends the hairs of the head and so on by way of their color, shape, etc., and without getting stuck in the four states, brings the meditation to fulfillment as far as the brain. This one, too, is said to dwell 'as before, so after.' In this way, the state of being before and after should be understood by way of the teaching. 'As after, so before' is a synonym for the former.

Yathā adho tathā uddhanti idaṃ sarīravasena veditabbaṃ. Tenevāha “uddhaṃ pādatalā adho kesamatthakā”ti. Tattha yo bhikkhu pādatalato paṭṭhāya yāva kesamatthakā dvattiṃsākāravasena vā pādaṅguliaggapabbaṭṭhito yāva sīsakaṭāhaṃ, sīsakaṭāhato yāva pādaṅgulīnaṃ aggapabbaṭṭhīni[M 3.0291], tāva aṭṭhivasena vā bhāvanaṃ pāpeti catūsu ṭhānesu ekaṭṭhānepi asajjanto. Ayaṃ yathā uddhaṃ tathā adho, yathā adho tathā uddhaṃ viharati nāma.

'As below, so above': this should be understood by way of the body. For that reason, it was said: 'Upwards from the soles of the feet, downwards from the tips of the hair.' In this regard, a monk brings the meditation to fulfillment either by way of the thirty-two parts, starting from the soles of the feet up to the tips of the hair; or by way of the bones, starting from the bones in the tips of the toes up to the skull, and from the skull down to the bones in the tips of the toes, without getting stuck in even one of the four states. This is called dwelling 'as above, so below; as below, so above.'

Yehi ākārehīti yehi koṭṭhāsehi. Yehi liṅgehīti yehi saṇṭhānehi. Yehi nimittehīti yehi upaṭṭhānehi. Ālokasaññā suggahitā hotīti yo bhikkhu aṅgaṇe nisīditvā ālokasaññaṃ manasi karoti, kālena nimīleti, kālena ummīleti. Athassa yadā nimīlentassāpi ummīletvā olokentassa viya ekasadisameva upaṭṭhāti, tadā ālokasaññā jātā nāma hoti. “Divāsaññā”tipi tasseva nāmaṃ. Sā ca pana rattiṃ uppajjamānā suggahitā nāma hoti. Svādhiṭṭhitātipi tasseva vevacanaṃ. Suṭṭhu adhiṭṭhitā suṭṭhu ṭhapitā svādhiṭṭhitā nāma vuccati. Sā atthato suggahitāyeva. Yo vā ālokena thinamiddhaṃ vinodetvā chandaṃ uppādetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karoti, tassa divāpi ālokasaññā suggahitā svādhiṭṭhitā nāma. Ratti vā hotu divā vā yena ālokena thinamiddhaṃ vinodetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karoti, tasmiṃ thinamiddhavinodane āloke uppannā saññā suggahitāyeva nāma. Vīriyādīsupi eseva nayo. Imasmiṃ sutte channaṃ abhiññānaṃ pādakiddhi kathitā.

“By what characteristics?” means “by what aspects.” “By what signs?” means “by what forms.” “By what indications?” means “by what manifestations.” “The perception of light is well grasped” means: When a bhikkhu, sitting in an open space, attends to the perception of light, sometimes closing his eyes, sometimes opening them. Then, when, even to one closing the eyes, it appears exactly the same as to one who has opened them and is looking, at that time the perception of light is said to have arisen. “Perception of day” is also a name for it. And when that perception arises at night, it is called well grasped. “Well established” is also a synonym for it. Well determined, well placed, is called “well established.” In meaning, it is just “well grasped.” Alternatively, for a bhikkhu who, by means of light, dispels sloth and torpor, generates desire, and attends to the meditation subject, the perception of light is well grasped and well established even during the day. Alternatively, whether it be night or day, by whatever light one dispels sloth and torpor and attends to the meditation subject, the perception that has arisen in that light which is the cause for dispelling sloth and torpor is indeed called “well grasped.” This same method should be applied to energy and so on. In this discourse, the psychic power that is the basis for the six higher knowledges is taught.

Pāsādakampanavaggo dutiyo.

The Second Chapter on the Shaking of the Palace.

3. Ayoguḷavaggo

3. The Chapter on the Iron Ball.

2. Ayoguḷasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Discourse on the Iron Ball.

834. Tatiyavaggassa [V 3.0290] dutiye iminā cātumahābhūtikenāti iminā catumahābhūtamayena evaṃ bhārikena garukena samānenāpi. Omātīti pahoti sakkoti, idaṃ tepiṭake buddhavacane asambhinnapadaṃ. Kāyampi [P 3.0261] citte samodahatīti kāyaṃ gahetvā citte āropeti, cittasannissitaṃ karoti, cittagatiyā peseti. Cittaṃ nāma mahaggatacittaṃ, cittagatigamanaṃ lahukaṃ hoti. Cittampi kāye samodahatīti cittaṃ gahetvā [M 3.0292] kāye āropeti, kāyasannissitaṃ karoti, kāyagatiyā peseti, kāyo nāma karajakāyo, kāyagatigamanaṃ dandhaṃ hoti. Sukhasaññañca lahusaññañcāti abhiññācittasahajātasaññā. Sā hi santasukhasamannāgatattā sukhasaññā nāma hoti, kilesadandhāyitattassa ca abhāvā lahusaññā nāma.

834. In the second discourse of the third chapter: “With this consisting of the four great elements” means: with this body, which is composed of the four great elements, and which is thus heavy and weighty, even so. `Omāti` means: he is able, he is capable; this is a distinct term in the Buddha’s words in the Tipiṭaka, as it does not occur elsewhere. “He places the body in the mind” means: taking the body, he places it in the mind, makes it dependent on the mind, and directs it with the speed of the mind's movement. The mind here refers to the sublime mind, and the movement of the mind is swift. “He places the mind in the body” means: taking the mind, he places it in the body, makes it dependent on the body, and directs it with the speed of the body's movement. The body here refers to the physical body, and the movement of the physical body is slow. “The perception of pleasure and the perception of lightness” refers to the perception that is co-arisen with the mind of higher knowledge. For, because it is endowed with tranquil happiness, it is called the perception of pleasure; and because of the absence of sluggishness from defilements, it is called the perception of lightness.

Ayoguḷo divasaṃ santatto lahutaro ceva hotīti so hi dvīhi tīhi janehi ukkhipitvā kammāruddhane pakkhittopi divasaṃ paccamāno vivarānupaviṭṭhena tejena ceva vāyena ca vāyosahagato ca usmāsahagato ca tejosahagato ca hutvā evaṃ lahuko hoti, yathā naṃ kammāro mahāsaṇḍāsena gahetvā ekato parivatteti ukkhipati bahi nīharati. Evaṃ pana mudu ca hoti kammaniyo ca. Yathā naṃ so khaṇḍaṃ khaṇḍaṃ vicchindati, kūṭena hananto dīghacaturassādibhedaṃ karoti. Imasmiṃ sutte vikubbaniddhi kathitā.

“An iron ball heated all day becomes even lighter” means that even when lifted by two or three people and placed in the blacksmith’s furnace, being heated all day, and penetrated by the fire element and the air element that have entered through the vents, having become associated with the air element, associated with heat, and associated with the fire element, it becomes so light that the blacksmith, grasping it with large tongs, can turn it over, lift it, and take it out. Furthermore, it becomes both soft and workable, so that the blacksmith can cut it into pieces and, striking it with a hammer, make it into various shapes such as long, square, and so on. In this discourse, the psychic power of transformation is taught.

3-10. Bhikkhusuttādivaṇṇanā

3–10. Commentary on the Bhikkhu Suttas, and so on.

835-842. Tatiye vivaṭṭapādakiddhi kathitā, tathā catutthe. Apica dve phalāni ādiṃ katvā heṭṭhā missakiddhipādā kathitā, sattasu phalesu pubbabhāgā. Sattamādīni cattāri heṭṭhā kathitanayāneva.

In the third [sutta], the basis of psychic power for unveiling is explained, and likewise in the fourth. Furthermore, beginning with the two fruits [suttas], the mixed bases of psychic power are explained below; in the seven fruits [suttas], the preliminary parts are explained. The four [suttas] beginning with the seventh are in the same manner as previously explained.

11-12. Moggallānasuttādivaṇṇanā

11–12. Commentary on the Moggallāna Suttas, and so on.

843-844. Ekādasamadvādasamesu [V 3.0291] cha abhiññā kathitā. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

In the eleventh and twelfth [suttas], the six higher knowledges are explained. The rest is straightforward in meaning everywhere.

Iddhipādasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Connected Discourses on the Bases of Psychic Power is concluded.

8. Anuruddhasaṃyuttaṃ

8. The Connected Discourses on Anuruddha

1. Rahogatavaggo

1. The Chapter on Solitude

1-2. Paṭhamarahogatasuttādivaṇṇanā

1–2. Commentary on the First Sutta on Solitude, and so on.

899-900. Anuruddhasaṃyuttassa [V 3.0292][P 3.0262][M 3.0293] paṭhame āraddhāti paripuṇṇā. Saṅkhepato panettha chattiṃsāya ṭhānesu arahattaṃ pāpetvā vipassanā kathitā, dutiye dvādasasu ṭhānesu arahattaṃ pāpetvā vipassanā kathitā.

In the first [sutta] of the Connected Discourses on Anuruddha, āraddhā means complete. Here, in brief, insight is explained in thirty-six instances leading to arahantship. In the second, insight is explained in twelve instances leading to arahantship.

3. Sutanusuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Sutanu Sutta

901. Tatiye mahābhiññatanti chaabhiññābhāvaṃ. Hīnaṃ dhammantiādīsu imāya pāḷiyā attho veditabbo –

901. In the third [sutta], mahābhiññatā means the state of having the six higher knowledges. The meaning of the passage beginning hīnaṃ dhammanti, and so on, is to be understood according to this Pali text as follows:

“Katame dhammā hīnā? Dvādasa akusalacittuppādā, ime dhammā hīnā. Katame dhammā majjhimā? Tīsu bhūmīsu kusalaṃ, tīsu bhūmīsu vipāko, tīsu bhūmīsu kiriyābyākataṃ sabbañca rūpaṃ, ime dhammā majjhimā. Katame dhammā paṇītā? Cattāro maggā apariyāpannā, cattāri ca sāmaññaphalāni nibbānañca, ime dhammā paṇītā”ti (dha. sa. 1423-1425).

"What states are inferior? The twelve unwholesome states of consciousness; these states are inferior. What states are middling? Wholesome [states] in the three planes, resultant [states] in the three planes, functional-indeterminate [states] in the three planes, and all form; these states are middling. What states are sublime? The four paths that are not included [in the planes], the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna; these states are sublime."

4-7. Paṭhamakaṇḍakīsuttādivaṇṇanā

4–7. Commentary on the First Kaṇḍakī Sutta, and so on.

902-905. Catutthe kaṇḍakīvaneti mahākaramandavane. Chaṭṭhe sahassaṃ lokanti iminā therassa [V 3.0293] satata vihāro dassito. Thero hi pātova mukhaṃ dhovitvā atītānāgate kappasahassaṃ anussarati. Paccuppanne pana dasacakkavāḷasahassaṃ ekāvajjanassa āpāthamāgacchati. Sattamaṃ uttānameva.

In the fourth [sutta], kaṇḍakīvane means in the great Karamanda grove. In the sixth [sutta], sahassaṃ lokaṃ indicates the Elder’s constant dwelling. For the Elder, after washing his face in the morning, recollects a thousand aeons of past and future. In the present, however, ten thousand world-systems come into the range of a single advertence. The seventh [sutta] is straightforward in meaning.

8. Salaḷāgārasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Salaḷāgāra Sutta

906. Aṭṭhame [P 3.0263] salaḷāgāreti salaḷarukkhamayāya paṇṇasālāya, salaḷarukkhassa vā dvāre ṭhitattā evaṃnāmake agāre. Imasmiṃ sutte vipassanāya saddhiṃ vipassakapuggalo kathito.

906. In the eighth [sutta], salaḷāgāre means a leaf-hut made of salaḷa wood, or a house so named because it stands at the entrance to a salaḷa tree. In this sutta, a person practicing insight, together with insight, is explained.

9. Ambapālivanasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Ambapālīvana Sutta

907. Navame [M 3.0294] āsabhiṃ vācanti attano arahattabhāvadīpakaṃ uttamavācaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

907. In the ninth [sutta], āsabhiṃ vācaṃ means the supreme speech proclaiming one's own state of Arahantship. The rest is straightforward in meaning everywhere.

Rahogatavaggo paṭhamo.

The Chapter on Solitude, the First.

2. Dutiyavaggavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Second Chapter

909-922. Dutiyavagge ṭhānañca ṭhānatotiādīhi thero dasabalañāṇaṃ paṭijānāti. Kimpanetaṃ sāvakānaṃ hotīti? Ekadesena hoti, sabbaññubuddhānaṃ panetaṃ nippadesaṃ sabbākāraparipūranti.

In the second chapter, with phrases beginning 'ṭhānañca ṭhānatoti,' the Elder professes the knowledge of the ten powers. But does this exist for disciples? It exists in part, but for the omniscient Buddhas, it is complete and perfect in every way.

Anuruddhasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Connected Discourses on Anuruddha is concluded.

9. Jhānasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Connected Discourses on Jhāna

923. Jhānasaṃyuttaṃ [V 3.0294] uttānatthameva.

923. The Connected Discourses on Jhāna is straightforward in meaning.

Jhānasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Connected Discourses on Jhāna is concluded.

10. Ānāpānasaṃyuttaṃ

10. The Connected Discourses on Mindfulness of Breathing

1. Ekadhammavaggo

1. The Chapter on One Thing

1. Ekadhammasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Sutta on One Thing

977. Ānāpānasaṃyuttassa [V 3.0295][M 3.0295] paṭhame ekadhammoti eko dhammo. Sesamettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ sabbaṃ sabbākārena visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.215) ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhānaniddese vuttameva.

977. In the first [sutta] of the Connected Discourses on Mindfulness of Breathing, 'ekadhammo' means one dhamma. Whatever else should be said here, all of that has already been stated in every way in the Visuddhimagga in the exposition of the Ānāpānassati meditation subject.

6. Ariṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Ariṭṭha Sutta

982. Chaṭṭhe bhāvetha noti bhāvetha nu. Kāmacchandoti pañcakāmaguṇikarāgo. Ajjhattaṃ bahiddhā ca dhammesūti ajjhattikabāhiresu dvādasasu āyatanadhammesu[P 3.0264]. Paṭighasaññā suppaṭivinītāti paṭighasampayuttasaññā suṭṭhu paṭivinītā, samucchinnāti attho. Iminā attano anāgāmimaggaṃ katheti. Idāni arahattamaggassa vipassanaṃ dassento so satova assasissāmītiādimāha.

982. In the sixth [sutta], 'bhāvetha no' means 'bhāvetha nu.' 'Kāmacchando' is lust related to the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'Ajjhattaṃ bahiddhā ca dhammesu' means in the internal and external twelve sense-base dhammas. 'Paṭighasaññā suppaṭivinītā' means the perception associated with aversion is well-subdued, meaning it is utterly eradicated. By this, he speaks of his own path of non-returning. Now, wishing to show the insight for the path of Arahantship, he says, 'Mindful, I will breathe in,' and so on.

7. Mahākappinasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Mahākappina Sutta

983. Sattame iñjitattaṃ vā phanditattaṃ vāti ubhayenapi calanameva kathitaṃ.

983. In the seventh [sutta], with 'iñjitattaṃ vā phanditattaṃ vā', by both terms only movement is described.

8. Padīpopamasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Sutta with the Simile of the Lamp

984. Aṭṭhame [V 3.0296] neva kāyopi kilamati na cakkhūnīti aññesu hi kammaṭṭhānesu kammaṃ karontassa kāyopi kilamati, cakkhūnipi vihaññanti. Dhātukammaṭṭhānasmiñhi kammaṃ karontassa kāyo kilamati, yante pakkhipitvā pīḷanākārappatto viya hoti. Kasiṇakammaṭṭhāne kammaṃ karontassa cakkhūni phandanti kilamanti, nikkhamitvā patanākārappattāni viya honti. Imasmiṃ pana kammaṭṭhāne kammaṃ karontassa neva kāyo kilamati, na akkhīni vihaññanti. Tasmā evamāha.

984. In the eighth sutta, regarding the words 'neither does the body tire, nor the eyes': for in other meditation subjects, when undertaking the practice, the body tires and the eyes are afflicted. Indeed, when undertaking the practice in the element meditation subject, the body tires; it is as if it has been placed in a press and reached a state of being squeezed. When undertaking the practice in a kasiṇa meditation subject, the eyes flicker and tire; it is as if they are bulging out and have reached a state of being about to fall. But in this meditation subject, when undertaking the practice, neither does the body tire, nor are the eyes afflicted. Therefore, He spoke thus.

Sabbaso [M 3.0296] rūpasaññānantiādi kasmā vuttaṃ, kiṃ ānāpāne kasiṇugghāṭanaṃ labbhatīti? Tipiṭakacūḷābhayatthero panāha – “yasmā ānāpānanimittaṃ tārakarūpamuttāvalikādisadisaṃ hutvā paññāyati, tasmā tattha kasiṇugghāṭanaṃ labbhatī”ti. Tipiṭakacūḷanāgatthero “na labbhatevā”ti āha. Alabbhante ayaṃ ariyiddhiādiko pabhedo kasmā gahitoti? Ānisaṃsadassanatthaṃ. Ariyaṃ vā hi iddhiṃ cattāri vā rūpāvacarajjhānāni catasso vā arūpasamāpattiyo nirodhasamāpattiṃ vā patthayamānena bhikkhunā ayaṃ ānāpānassatisamādhi sādhukaṃ manasikātabbo. Yathā hi nagare laddhe yaṃ catūsu disāsu uṭṭhānakabhaṇḍaṃ, taṃ catūhi dvārehi nagarameva pavisatīti, janapado laddho ca hoti. Nagarasseva heso ānisaṃso. Evaṃ ānāpānassatisamādhibhāvanāya ānisaṃso esa ariyiddhiādiko pabhedo, sabbākārena [P 3.0265] bhāvite ānāpānassatisamādhismiṃ sabbametaṃ yogino nipphajjatīti ānisaṃsadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Sukhañceti ettha soti kasmā na vuttaṃ? Yasmā bhikkhūti imasmiṃ vāre nāgataṃ.

Why was the passage beginning 'With the complete surmounting of perceptions of form...' stated? Is the removal of the kasiṇa sign attainable in mindfulness of breathing? The Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya, however, said: 'Because the sign of mindfulness of breathing appears similar to a cluster of stars, a string of pearls, and so on, the removal of the kasiṇa sign is attainable therein.' The Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga said: 'It is not attainable at all.' If it is unattainable, why is this distinction, such as the noble psychic powers and so on, mentioned? For the purpose of showing the benefit. For a monk who aspires to noble psychic power, or the four form-sphere jhānas, or the four formless attainments, or the attainment of cessation, this concentration of mindfulness of breathing should be well attended to. Just as when a city is obtained, the revenue that arises in the four directions enters the city itself through the four gates, and thus the country is also obtained—this is a benefit of the city itself. Similarly, this distinction of noble psychic power and so on is a benefit of the development of the concentration of mindfulness of breathing. When the concentration of mindfulness of breathing is developed in every way, all this is accomplished for the yogi. Thus, it was stated for the purpose of showing the benefit. In the phrase 'sukhañca,' why was 'so' not stated? Because 'bhikkhu' does not occur in this passage.

9. Vesālīsuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Vesālī Sutta

985. Navame vesāliyanti evaṃnāmake itthiliṅgavasena pavattavohāre nagare. Tañhi nagaraṃ tikkhattuṃ pākāraparikkhepavaḍḍhanena visālībhūtattā vesālīti vuccati. Idampi ca nagaraṃ sabbaññutaṃ patteyeva sammāsambuddhe sabbākāravepullataṃ pattanti veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ gocaragāmaṃ dassetvā nivāsaṭṭhānamāha mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāyanti. Tattha mahāvanaṃ nāma sayaṃjātaṃ aropimaṃ saparicchedaṃ mahantaṃ vanaṃ. Kapilavatthusāmantā pana mahāvanaṃ himavantena saha ekābaddhaṃ aparicchedaṃ [V 3.0297] hutvā mahāsamuddaṃ āhacca ṭhitaṃ. Idaṃ tādisaṃ na hoti, saparicchedaṃ mahantaṃ vananti mahāvanaṃ. Kūṭāgārasālā pana mahāvanaṃ nissāya kate ārāme kūṭāgāraṃ antokatvā haṃsavaṭṭakacchannena katā sabbākārasampannā buddhassa bhagavato gandhakuṭīti veditabbā.

985. In the ninth sutta, 'at Vesālī' means: in the city of this name, a designation used in the feminine gender. For that city is called Vesālī because it had become extensive through the expansion of its walled enclosure three times. And it should be understood that this city, too, attained its full prosperity in every way only after the Sammāsambuddha had attained omniscience. Thus, having indicated the alms-resort village, He stated the dwelling place: 'in the Great Wood, at the Hall with the Gabled Roof.' Therein, the 'Great Wood' is a large, self-grown, unplanted forest with defined boundaries. The Great Wood near Kapilavatthu, however, was a single continuous expanse with the Himālaya and, being without boundaries, stood reaching the great ocean. This one is not like that; it is a large forest with defined boundaries, hence 'Great Wood.' As for the 'Hall with the Gabled Roof,' it should be known as the fragrant chamber of the Blessed One, the Buddha, which was complete in all aspects, built in a monastery established in dependence on the Great Wood, incorporating a gabled structure, and covered with a roof in the shape of a goose's wing.

Anekapariyāyena asubhakathaṃ kathetīti anekehi kāraṇehi asubhākārasandassanappavattaṃ kāyavicchandanīyakathaṃ katheti. Seyyathidaṃ – atthi [M 3.0297] imasmiṃ kāye kesā lomā nakhā dantā…pe… muttanti. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Bhikkhave, imasmiṃ byāmamatte kaḷevare sabbākārenapi vicinanto na koci kiñci muttaṃ vā maṇiṃ vā veḷuriyaṃ vā agaruṃ vā candanaṃ vā kuṅkumaṃ vā kappuraṃ vā vāsacuṇṇādiṃ vā aṇumattampi sucibhāvaṃ passati, atha kho paramaduggandhaṃ jegucchaassirikadassanaṃ kesalomādinānappakāraṃ asucimeva passati, tasmā na ettha chando vā rāgo vā karaṇīyo. Yepi uttamaṅge sirasi jātā kesā nāma, tepi asubhā ceva asucino [P 3.0266] ca paṭikūlā ca. So ca nesaṃ asubhāsucipaṭikūlabhāvo vaṇṇatopi saṇṭhānatopi gandhatopi āsayatopi okāsatopīti pañcahākārehi veditabbo. Evaṃ lomādīnampīti ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.307) vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Iti bhagavā ekamekasmiṃ koṭṭhāse pañcapañcappabhedena anekapariyāyena asubhakathaṃ katheti.

'He speaks the discourse on the unattractive in many ways' means: for many reasons, He speaks a discourse that proceeds by showing the aspects of the unattractive, a talk that leads to the analytical dissection of the body. It is as follows: 'In this body there are head hairs, body hairs, nails, teeth… and so on… urine.' What is meant by this? 'Monks, in this fathom-long carcass, one who searches in every way does not see even a minute amount of any pure substance, be it a pearl, a gem, a beryl, aloe wood, sandalwood, saffron, camphor, or scented powders and the like. Rather, one sees only what is extremely foul-smelling, disgusting, unsightly, and of various kinds of impurity, such as head hairs and body hairs. Therefore, neither desire nor lust should be formed in this regard. Even the so-called head hairs that grow on the head, the highest limb, are unattractive, impure, and repulsive. And their state of being unattractive, impure, and repulsive should be understood in five aspects: in terms of color, shape, smell, origin, and location. The same applies to body hairs and so on.' This is the summary here; the detail, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the Visuddhimagga. Thus, the Blessed One speaks the discourse on the unattractive in many ways, with five divisions for each and every constituent part.

Asubhāya vaṇṇaṃ bhāsatīti uddhumātakādivasena asubhamātikaṃ nikkhipitvā padabhājanīyena taṃ vibhajanto vaṇṇento asubhāya vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati. Asubhabhāvanāya vaṇṇaṃ bhāsatīti yā ayaṃ kesādīsu vā uddhumātakādīsu vā ajjhattabahiddhāvatthūsu asubhākāraṃ gahetvā pavattassa cittassa bhāvanā vaḍḍhanā phātikammaṃ, tassā asubhabhāvanāya ānisaṃsaṃ dassento vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati, guṇaṃ parikitteti. Seyyathidaṃ – “asubhabhāvanābhiyutto, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kesādīsu vā vatthūsu uddhumātakādīsu vā pañcaṅgavippahīnaṃ pañcaṅgasamannāgataṃ tividhakalyāṇaṃ dasalakkhaṇasampannaṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ paṭilabhati. So taṃ paṭhamajjhānasaṅkhātaṃ cittamañjūsaṃ nissāya vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā uttamatthaṃ arahattaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti.

'He speaks in praise of the unattractive' means: having laid down the matrix of the unattractive by way of a bloated corpse and so on, He speaks in praise of the unattractive by analyzing and explaining that matrix with the analysis of terms. 'He speaks in praise of the cultivation of the unattractive' means: with regard to the development, strengthening, and repeated practice of the mind that proceeds by grasping the aspect of unattractiveness in internal and external objects—such as head hairs and so on, or bloated corpses and so on—He speaks in praise by showing the benefits of that cultivation of the unattractive; He extols its virtues. It is as follows: 'Monks, a monk who is devoted to the cultivation of the unattractive—in regard to objects such as head hairs and so on, or bloated corpses and so on—obtains the first jhāna, which has five factors abandoned, is endowed with five factors, is threefold virtuous, and is complete with ten characteristics. Relying on that first jhāna, which is known as a casket for the mind, he develops insight and attains the supreme goal, Arahantship.'

Icchāmahaṃ, bhikkhave, aḍḍhamāsaṃ paṭisallīyitunti ahaṃ, bhikkhave, ekaṃ aḍḍhamāsaṃ paṭisallīyituṃ nilīyituṃ ekakova hutvā viharituṃ icchāmīti attho. Nāmhi kenaci upasaṅkamitabbo [V 3.0298] aññatra ekena piṇḍapātanīhārakenāti yo attanā payuttavācaṃ akatvā mamatthāya saddhesu kulesu paṭiyattapiṇḍapātaṃ nīharitvā mayhaṃ upanāmeti, taṃ piṇḍapātanīhārakaṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ ṭhapetvā nāmhi aññena kenaci bhikkhunā vā gahaṭṭhena vā upasaṅkamitabboti.

'I wish, monks, to go into seclusion for half a month' means: 'Monks, I wish to dwell for one half-month in seclusion, in hiding, being all alone.' 'I am not to be approached by anyone except for one who brings the alms-food' means: 'Setting aside that one monk who brings the alms-food—he who, without making a verbal request himself, brings prepared alms-food from faithful families and offers it to me for my sake—I am not to be approached by any other monk or householder.'

Kasmā [M 3.0298] pana evamāhāti? Atīte kira pañcasatā migaluddakā mahatīhi daṇḍavāgurādīhi araññaṃ parikkhipitvā haṭṭhatuṭṭhā ekatoyeva yāvajīvaṃ migapakkhighātakammena [P 3.0267] jīvikaṃ kappetvā niraye uppannā. Te tattha paccitvā pubbe katena kenacideva kusalakammena manussesu uppannā kalyāṇūpanissayavasena sabbepi bhagavato santike pabbajjañca upasampadañca labhiṃsu. Tesaṃ tato mūlākusalakammato avipakkavipākā aparāparacetanā tasmiṃ aḍḍhamāsabbhantare attūpakkamena ca parūpakkamena ca jīvitūpacchedāya okāsamakāsi. Taṃ bhagavā addasa. Kammavipāko ca nāma na sakkā kenaci paṭibāhituṃ. Tesu ca bhikkhūsu puthujjanāpi atthi, sotāpannasakadāgāmianāgāmikhīṇāsavāpi. Tattha khīṇāsavā appaṭisandhikā, itare ariyasāvakā niyatagatikā sugatiparāyaṇā, puthujjanānaṃ gati aniyatā.

But why did he speak thus? It is said that in the past, five hundred deer-hunters, having encircled a forest with large sticks, nets, and so on, joyfully and delightedly, all together, made their living for their entire lives by the act of killing deer and birds, and were reborn in hell. Having been tormented there, due to some wholesome kamma done previously, they were reborn among humans. By the power of a good supporting condition, they all received the going forth and full ordination in the presence of the Blessed One. From that root unwholesome kamma of theirs, a subsequent volition whose result had not yet ripened created an opportunity within that half-month for the cutting off of their life faculty through their own actions or the actions of others. The Blessed One saw that. And the result of kamma cannot be prevented by anyone. Among those monks there were worldlings, as well as stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arahants whose cankers were destroyed. Therein, those whose cankers were destroyed were without relinking; the other noble disciples were of fixed destiny, bound for a good destination; but the destiny of the worldlings was unfixed.

Atha bhagavā cintesi – “ime attabhāve chandarāgena maraṇabhayabhītā na sakkhissanti gatiṃ visodhetuṃ, handa nesaṃ chandarāgappahānāya asubhakathaṃ kathemi. Taṃ sutvā attabhāve vigatacchandarāgatāya gativisodhanaṃ katvā sagge paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhissanti, evaṃ tesaṃ mama santike pabbajjā sātthikā bhavissatī”ti. Tato tesaṃ anuggahāya asubhakathaṃ kathesi kammaṭṭhānasīsena, no maraṇavaṇṇasaṃvaṇṇanādhippāyena. Kathetvā ca panassa etadahosi – “sace imaṃ aḍḍhamāsaṃ maṃ bhikkhū passissanti, ‘ajja eko bhikkhu mato, ajja dve…pe… ajja dasā’ti āgantvā ārocessanti, ayañca kammavipāko na sakkā mayā vā aññena vā paṭibāhituṃ, svāhaṃ taṃ sutvāpi kiṃ karissāmi, kiṃ me anatthakena anayabyasanena sutena, handāhaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ adassanaṃ upagacchāmī”ti. Tasmā evamāha – “icchāmahaṃ, bhikkhave, aḍḍhamāsaṃ paṭisallīyituṃ, nāmhi kenaci upasaṅkamitabbo aññatra ekena piṇḍapātanīhārakenā”ti.

Then the Blessed One considered: 'These monks, being worldlings, fearing death because of sensual passion for this individual existence, will not be able to purify their destiny. Come, let me teach them a discourse on foulness for the abandoning of sensual passion. Having heard it, and being without sensual passion for this individual existence, they will purify their destiny and take rebirth in heaven. Thus, their ordination in my presence will be fruitful.' Then, for their benefit, he taught a discourse on foulness with a meditation subject as its basis, not with the intention of praising the virtues of death. And after teaching, this thought occurred to him: 'If the monks see me during this half-month, they will come and report, "Today one monk has died, today two... today ten." And this result of kamma cannot be averted by me or by another. What shall I do, even having heard that? What use to me is hearing of this unbeneficial misfortune and calamity? Come, I shall withdraw from the sight of the monks.' Therefore, he said: 'Monks, I desire to go into seclusion for half a month. I am not to be approached by anyone except the one who brings alms-food.'

Apare panāhu – “parūpavādavivajjanatthaṃ evaṃ vatvā paṭisallīno”ti. Pare kira bhagavantaṃ [V 3.0299] upavadissanti – “ayaṃ ‘sabbaññū ahaṃ saddhammavaracakkavattī’ti [P 3.0268] paṭijānamāno attanopi sāvake aññamaññaṃ ghātente nivāretuṃ na sakkoti, kiṃ aññaṃ sakkhissatī”ti? Tatra paṇḍitā vakkhanti – “bhagavā paṭisallānamanuyutto na imaṃ pavattiṃ jānāti, kocissa ārocayitāpi natthi[M 3.0299], sace jāneyya addhā nivāreyyā”ti. Idaṃ pana icchāmattaṃ, paṭhamamevettha kāraṇaṃ. Nāssudhāti ettha assudhāti padapūraṇamatte avadhāraṇatthe vā nipāto, neva koci bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamīti attho.

But other teachers say: 'Having spoken thus, he went into seclusion for the sake of avoiding the criticism of others.' It is said that others will criticize the Blessed One: 'This one, while claiming, "I am all-knowing, the supreme wheel-turner of the True Dhamma," cannot prevent his own disciples from killing one another—what else will he be able to do?' Therein, the wise will say: 'The Blessed One is devoted to seclusion and does not know of this occurrence, nor is there anyone to inform him. If he knew, he would surely prevent it.' But this is merely their wish; the first reason mentioned is the cause here. In 'nāssudhā,' the word 'assudhā' is a particle merely for filling out the line or for emphasis; the meaning is that no one at all approached the Blessed One.

Anekehi vaṇṇasaṇṭhānādīhi kāraṇehi vokāro assāti anekākāravokāro. Anekākāravokiṇṇo anekākārena sammissoti vuttaṃ hoti. Ko so? Asubhabhāvanānuyogo, taṃ anekākāravokāraṃ. Asubhabhāvanānuyogamanuyuttā viharantīti yuttappayuttā viharanti. Aṭṭīyamānāti tena kāyena aṭṭā dukkhitā honti. Harāyamānāti lajjamānā. Jigucchamānāti jigucchaṃ uppādayamānā. Satthahārakaṃ pariyesantīti jīvitaharaṇakasatthaṃ pariyesanti. Na kevalañca te satthaṃ pariyesitvā attanā vā attānaṃ jīvitā voropenti, migalaṇḍikampi pana samaṇakuttakaṃ upasaṅkamitvā, “sādhu no, āvuso, jīvitā voropehī”ti vadanti. Ettha ca ariyā neva pāṇātipātaṃ kariṃsu, na samādapesuṃ, na samanuññā ahesuṃ. Puthujjanā pana sabbamakaṃsu.

Because it is mixed with many causes such as color, shape, and so on, it is called 'anekākāravokāro' (of many kinds and varieties). 'Anekākāravokiṇṇo' means mixed with many kinds. What is that? The practice of meditation on foulness; that is 'anekākāravokāraṃ.' 'They dwell devoted to the practice of meditation on foulness' means they dwell diligently engaged. 'Being distressed' means they are afflicted by that body and become miserable. 'Being ashamed' means feeling shame. 'Being repulsed' means giving rise to revulsion. 'They seek a weapon-bringer' means they search for a life-taking weapon. And not only did they seek a weapon and deprive themselves of life, but they also approached a sham ascetic named Migalaṇḍika and said, 'Friend, please deprive us of life.' Herein, the noble ones neither committed the destruction of life, nor caused others to do so, nor consented to it. But the worldlings did all of these things.

Paṭisallānā vuṭṭhitoti tesaṃ pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ jīvitakkhayappattabhāvaṃ ñatvā tato ekībhāvato vuṭṭhito jānantopi ajānanto viya kathāsamuṭṭhāpanatthaṃ āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ āmantesi. Kiṃ nu kho, ānanda, tanubhūto viya bhikkhusaṅghoti ito, ānanda, pubbe bahū bhikkhū ekato upaṭṭhānaṃ āgacchanti, uddesaṃ paripucchaṃ gaṇhanti, sajjhāyanti, ekapajjoto viya ārāmo dissati. Idāni pana aḍḍhamāsamattassa accayena tanubhūto viya tanuko mando appako viraḷo viya jāto bhikkhusaṅgho. Kiṃ nu kho kāraṇaṃ? Kiṃ disāsu pakkantā bhikkhūti?

Having arisen from seclusion: knowing that those five hundred monks had reached the end of their life-faculty, he arose from that state of solitude. Though knowing, as if not knowing, for the purpose of starting a conversation, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda. 'What is this, Ānanda? The Saṅgha of monks seems diminished.' This means: 'Ānanda, formerly, many monks would come together to the attendance hall, they would take up recitation and questioning, and they would chant. The monastery appeared as if lit by a single lamp. But now, after the passing of half a month, the Saṅgha of monks has become diminished, as if thin, few, small, and scattered. What, I wonder, is the reason? Have the monks departed to the various directions?'

Athāyasmā ānando kammavipākena tesaṃ jīvitakkhayappattiṃ asallakkhento asubhakammaṭṭhānānuyogapaccayā [P 3.0269] pana sallakkhento tathā hi pana, bhante bhagavātiādiṃ vatvā bhikkhūnaṃ arahattappattiyā aññaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ yācanto, sādhu, bhante, bhagavātiādimāha. Tassattho [V 3.0300] – sādhu, bhante, bhagavā aññaṃ kāraṇaṃ ācikkhatu, yena bhikkhusaṅgho arahatte patiṭṭhaheyya[M 3.0300]. Mahāsamuddaṃ orohaṇatitthāni viya aññānipi dasānussati, dasakasiṇa, catudhātuvavatthāna, brahmavihāra, ānāpānassatipabhedāni bahūni nibbānorohaṇakammaṭṭhānāni santi, tesu bhagavā bhikkhū samassāsetvā aññataraṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhatūti adhippāyo.

Then the Venerable Ānanda, not perceiving that their attainment of the end of life was due to the result of kamma, but perceiving that it was due to the practice of the meditation subject of foulness, spoke the words beginning, 'Indeed, venerable sir, Blessed One,' and, requesting another meditation subject for the monks' attainment of Arahantship, said, 'It would be good, venerable sir, Blessed One,' and so on. The meaning of this is: 'It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would declare another cause by which the Saṅgha of monks might be established in Arahantship. Just as there are fords for descending into the great ocean, there are many other meditation subjects that are means for descending into Nibbāna, such as the ten recollections, the ten kasiṇas, the analysis of the four elements, the divine abidings, and the various kinds of mindfulness of breathing. Among these, may the Blessed One, having comforted the monks, declare one of the meditation subjects.' This is the intention.

Atha bhagavā tathā kātukāmo theraṃ uyyojento tenahānandātiādimāha. Tattha vesāliṃ upanissāyāti vesāliyaṃ upanissāya samantā gāvutepi aḍḍhayojanepi yāvatikā viharanti, te sabbe sannipātehīti attho. Sabbe upaṭṭhānasālāyaṃ sannipātetvāti attanā gantuṃ yuttaṭṭhānaṃ sayaṃ gantvā aññattha daharabhikkhū pahiṇitvā muhutteneva anavasese bhikkhū upaṭṭhānasālāyaṃ samūhaṃ katvā. Yassadāni, bhante, bhagavā kālaṃ maññatīti ettha ayamadhippāyo – bhagavā bhikkhusaṅgho sannipatito, esa kālo bhikkhūnaṃ dhammakathaṃ kātuṃ, anusāsaniṃ dātuṃ, idāni yassa tumhe kālaṃ jānātha, taṃ kātabbanti.

Then the Blessed One, wishing to do so and urging the Elder, said, 'Well then, Ānanda,' and so on. Therein, 'dwelling in dependence on Vesālī' means: 'However many monks dwell all around, within a gāvuta or half a yojana, assemble all of them'—this is the meaning. 'Having assembled all in the attendance hall' means: having gone himself to the places it was suitable for him to go, and having sent junior monks to other places, in just a moment he gathered the monks without remainder in the attendance hall. Regarding the phrase, 'Now, venerable sir, the Blessed One knows the time,' this is the intended meaning: 'Venerable sir, the Saṅgha of monks is assembled. This is the time to give a Dhamma talk to the monks, to give instruction. Now, for whatever you know the time to be, that should be done.'

Atha kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi, ayampi kho, bhikkhaveti. Āmantetvā ca pana bhikkhūnaṃ arahattappattiyā pubbe ācikkhitaasubhakammaṭṭhānato aññaṃ pariyāyaṃ ācikkhanto ānāpānassatisamādhītiādimāha. Tattha ānāpānassatisamādhīti ānāpānapariggāhikāya satiyā saddhiṃ sampayutto samādhi, ānāpānassatiyaṃ vā samādhi, ānāpānassatisamādhi. Bhāvitoti uppādito vaḍḍhito vā. Bahulīkatoti punappunaṃ kato. Santo ceva paṇīto cāti santo ceva paṇīto ceva. Ubhayattha evasaddena niyamo veditabbo. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Ayañhi yathā asubhakammaṭṭhānaṃ kevalaṃ paṭivedhavasena santañca paṇītañca, oḷārikārammaṇattā pana paṭikūlārammaṇattā ca ārammaṇavasena neva santaṃ na paṇītaṃ, na evaṃ kenaci pariyāyena [P 3.0270] asanto vā appaṇīto vā, apica kho ārammaṇasantatāyapi santo vūpasanto nibbuto, paṭivedhasaṅkhātāya aṅgasantatāyapi, ārammaṇapaṇītatāya paṇīto atittikaro, aṅgapaṇītatāyapīti. Tena vuttaṃ “santo ceva paṇīto cā”ti.

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'This too, monks...' Having addressed them, and wishing to explain another method for the attainment of Arahantship different from the meditation on foulness previously taught, he spoke the words beginning with 'concentration through mindfulness of breathing.' Therein, 'concentration through mindfulness of breathing' is the concentration associated with the mindfulness that grasps the in-and-out breaths, or the concentration based on mindfulness of breathing. 'Developed' means produced or increased. 'Cultivated' means done again and again. 'Peaceful and sublime' means it is both peaceful and sublime. In both terms, the emphasis should be understood by the word 'eva'. What is meant? For, just as the meditation on foulness is peaceful and sublime solely by way of penetration, but on account of having a gross object and a repulsive object, it is, by way of the object, neither peaceful nor sublime; this concentration is not so. It is not unpeaceful or unsublime in any way. Rather, on account of the peacefulness of its object, it is peaceful, calmed, and extinguished; and also on account of the peacefulness of its factors, which is called penetration. On account of the sublimity of its object, it is sublime and does not cause satiety; and also on account of the sublimity of its factors. Therefore it is said, 'peaceful and sublime.'

Asecanako [M 3.0301] ca sukho ca vihāroti ettha pana nāssa secananti asecanako, anāsittako abbokiṇṇo pāṭiyekko āveṇiko, natthi ettha parikammena vā upacārena vā santatā, ādisamannāhārato pabhuti attano sabhāveneva santo ca paṇīto cāti attho. Keci [V 3.0301] “asecanako”ti anāsittako ojavanto, sabhāveneva madhuro”ti vadanti. Evamayaṃ asecanako ca appitappitakkhaṇe kāyikacetasikasukhappaṭilābhāya saṃvattanato sukho ca vihāroti veditabbo.

'And a dwelling that is unadulterated and pleasant.' Herein, 'asecanaka' (unadulterated) means there is no sprinkling for it. It is not poured upon, unmixed, individual, and unique. In this concentration, peacefulness does not come about by means of preliminary work or access concentration; from the very first application of mind, it is peaceful and sublime by its own intrinsic nature. This is the meaning. Some say: '"asecanaka" means not needing anything poured on it, yet full of essence; sweet by its own nature.' Thus, this should be understood as a dwelling that is both 'unadulterated' and 'pleasant' because it leads to the attainment of bodily and mental pleasure at each moment of absorption.

Uppannuppanneti avikkhambhite. Pāpaketi lāmake. Akusale dhammeti akosallasambhūte dhamme. Ṭhānaso antaradhāpetīti khaṇeneva antaradhāpeti vikkhambheti. Vūpasametīti suṭṭhu upasameti, nibbedhabhāgiyattā anupubbena ariyamaggavuddhippatto samucchindati, paṭippassambhetīti vuttaṃ hoti. Gimhānaṃ pacchime māseti āsāḷhamāse. Ūhataṃ rajojallanti aṭṭha māse vātātapasukkhāya gomahiṃsādipādappahārasambhinnāya pathaviyā uddhaṃ hataṃ ūhataṃ ākāse samuṭṭhitaṃ rajañca reṇuñca. Mahā akālameghoti sabbaṃ nabhaṃ ajjhottharitvā uṭṭhito āsāḷhajuṇhapakkhe sakalaṃ aḍḍhamāsaṃ vassanakamegho. So hi asampatte vassakāle uppannattā akālameghoti idha adhippeto. Ṭhānaso antarādhāpeti vūpasametīti khaṇeneva adassanaṃ neti pathaviyaṃ sannisīdāpeti. Evameva khoti opammanidassanametaṃ. Tato paraṃ vuttanayameva.

'Arisen, arisen' refers to those states that are unsuppressed. 'Evil' means lowly. 'Unwholesome states' means states born of unskillfulness. 'Instantly dispels' means it makes them disappear and suppresses them in that very moment. 'Pacifies' means it thoroughly pacifies; because it partakes of penetration, having gradually reached the growth of the Noble Path, it eradicates and calms. This is what is meant. 'In the last month of the hot season' means in the month of Āsāḷha. 'The dust and dirt stirred up' means the fine dust and coarse dust which, from the earth that for eight months was dried by wind and sun and broken up by the trampling of the feet of cattle, buffaloes, and so on, is thrown up, raised up, and has arisen in the sky. 'A great out-of-season cloud' is a great rain cloud that, having arisen and covered the entire sky, rains for the whole fortnight in the waxing moon of Āsāḷha. Since it arises before the rainy season has arrived, it is intended here as an 'out-of-season cloud.' 'Instantly dispels and pacifies' means it leads them to disappearance in a moment and makes them settle on the ground. 'Just so' is a term indicating the simile. What follows is in the way already stated.

10. Kimilasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Kimila Sutta.

986. Dasame kimilāyanti evaṃnāmake nagare. Etadavocāti thero kira cintesi – “ayaṃ desanā na yathānusandhikā katā, yathānusandhiṃ gamessāmī”ti desanānusandhiṃ ghaṭento etaṃ avoca. Kāyaññataranti pathavīādīsu kāyesu aññataraṃ vadāmi [P 3.0271] vāyokāyaṃ vadāmīti attho. Atha vā cakkhāyatanaṃ…pe… kabaḷīkāro āhāroti pañcavīsati rūpakoṭṭhāsā rūpakāyo nāma, tesu ānāpānaṃ phoṭṭhabbāyatane [M 3.0302] saṅgahitattā kāyaññataraṃ hoti, tasmāpi evamāha. Tasmātihāti yasmā catūsu kāyesu aññataraṃ vāyokāyaṃ, pañcavīsati koṭṭhāse vā rūpakāye aññataraṃ ānāpānaṃ anupassati, tasmā kāye kāyānupassīti attho. Evaṃ sabbattha attho veditabbo. Vedanāññataranti tīsu vedanāsu aññataraṃ, sukhavedanaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

986. In the tenth sutta, 'in Kimilā' means in the city of that name. 'He said this': It is said the Elder reflected, 'This teaching was not given with its proper connection; I will establish its proper connection.' Connecting the teaching's sequence, he spoke this. 'One among the bodies' means: 'I say it is one among the bodies such as the earth element; I say it is the wind-body.' This is the meaning.
