Alternatively, the eye-base... up to... physical nutriment—these twenty-five material parts are called the material body. Among them, the in-and-out breath, because it is included in the tangible base, is one among the bodies. Therefore, he also spoke thus. 'Therefore': Because one contemplates the in-and-out breath, which is one among the four bodies (the wind-body), or one among the twenty-five parts of the material body, therefore one is a 'contemplator of the body in the body.' This is the meaning. The meaning should be understood in this way everywhere. 'One among the feelings': This is said with reference to pleasant feeling among the three feelings.

Sādhukaṃ manasikāranti pītipaṭisaṃveditādivasena uppannaṃ sundaraṃ manasikāraṃ. Kiṃ pana manasikāro sukhā vedanā hotīti? Na hoti, desanāsīsaṃ panetaṃ. Yatheva hi “aniccasaññābhāvanānuyogamanuyuttā”ti (ma. ni. 3.147) ettha saññānāmena paññā vuttā, evamidhāpi [V 3.0302] manasikāranāmena jhānavedanā vuttāti veditabbā. Etasmiñhi catukke paṭhamapade pītisīsena vedanā vuttā, dutiyapade sukhanti sarūpeneva vuttā. Cittasaṅkhārapadadvaye “saññā ca vedanā ca cetasikā ete dhammā cittappaṭibaddhā cittasaṅkhārā”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.174) vacanato “vitakkavicāre ṭhapetvā sabbepi cittasampayuttakā dhammā cittasaṅkhāre saṅgahitā”ti vacanato cittasaṅkhāranāmena vedanā vuttā. Taṃ sabbaṃ manasikāranāmena saṅgahetvā idha “sādhukaṃ manasikāra”nti āha.

“Careful attention” means the excellent attention that arises by way of experiencing rapture and so forth. But is attention a pleasant feeling? It is not; however, this is a heading in the teaching. For just as in the phrase “devoted to the practice of developing the perception of impermanence,” wisdom is spoken of by the name “perception,” so too here, it should be understood that the feeling of jhāna is spoken of by the name “attention.” In this tetrad, in the first phrase, feeling is spoken of with rapture as its head; in the second phrase, it is spoken of directly by its own nature as “pleasure.” In the two phrases on mental formations, because of the statement, “Perception and feeling are mental factors, these phenomena are bound to the mind, these are mental formations,” and because of the statement, “Except for initial and sustained thought, all phenomena associated with the mind are included in mental formations,” feeling is spoken of by the name “mental formation.” Having collected all of that under the name “attention,” here it is said, “careful attention.”

Evaṃ santepi yasmā esā vedanā ārammaṇaṃ na hoti, tasmā vedanānupassanā na yujjatīti. No na yujjati, mahāsatipaṭṭhānādīsupi hi taṃ taṃ sukhādīnaṃ vatthuṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā vedanā vedayati, taṃ pana vedanāpavattiṃ upādāya “ahaṃ vedayāmī”ti vohāramattaṃ hoti, taṃ sandhāya “sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Apica “pītippaṭisaṃvedī”tiādīnaṃ atthavaṇṇanāyametassa parihāro vuttoyeva. Vuttañhetaṃ visuddhimagge –

Even so, it is argued, because this feeling is not an object, the contemplation of feeling is not appropriate. The reply is: No, it is not that it is inappropriate. For in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta and others, one feels feeling by taking as object the respective bases of pleasure and so on. However, depending on that occurrence of feeling, there is merely the conventional expression, “I feel.” It is with reference to that conventional expression that it is said, “Feeling a pleasant feeling, I know I feel a pleasant feeling,” and so on. Moreover, in the explanation of the meaning of “experiencing rapture,” etc., this response has already been given. For this is stated in the Visuddhimagga:

“Dvīhākārehi pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti – ārammaṇato ca asammohato ca. Kathaṃ ārammaṇato pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti? Sappītike dve jhāne samāpajjati, tassa samāpattikkhaṇe jhānapaṭilābhena ārammaṇato pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti ārammaṇassa [P 3.0272] paṭisaṃviditattā. Kathaṃ asammohato pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti? Sappītike dve jhāne samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya jhānasampayuttapītiṃ khayato vayato sammasati, tassa vipassanākkhaṇe lakkhaṇappaṭivedhena asammohato [M 3.0303] pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 1.172) “‘dīghaṃ assāsavasena cittassa ekaggataṃ avikkhepaṃ pajānato sati upaṭṭhitā hoti, tāya satiyā tena ñāṇena sā pīti paṭisaṃviditā hotī’ti. Eteneva nayena avasesapadānipi atthato veditabbānī”ti.

“Rapture is experienced in two ways: by way of the object and by way of non-delusion. How is rapture experienced by way of the object? One enters into the two jhānas accompanied by rapture. For him, at the moment of attainment, through the attainment of jhāna, rapture is experienced by way of the object, because the object is experienced. How is rapture experienced by way of non-delusion? Having entered into the two jhānas accompanied by rapture and emerged, one contemplates the rapture associated with jhāna as perishing and vanishing. For him, at the moment of insight, rapture is experienced by way of non-delusion through the penetration of its characteristics. And this was stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: ‘For one who knows the unification and non-distraction of the mind by means of the long in-breath, mindfulness is established. By that mindfulness and by that knowledge, that rapture is experienced.’ In this very way, the remaining terms should also be understood according to their meaning.”

Iti yatheva jhānapaṭilābhena ārammaṇato pītisukhacittasaṅkhārā paṭisaṃviditā honti, evaṃ imināpi jhānasampayuttena vedanāsaṅkhātamanasikārapaṭilābhena ārammaṇato vedanā paṭisaṃviditā [V 3.0303] hoti. Tasmā suvuttametaṃ “vedanāsu vedanānupassī bhikkhu tasmiṃ samaye viharatī”ti.

Thus, just as rapture, pleasure, and mental formations are experienced by way of the object through the attainment of jhāna, so too, for this yogi, feeling is experienced by way of the object through the attainment of attention associated with jhāna and designated as feeling. Therefore, it is well said: “A monk dwells contemplating feelings in feelings at that time.”

Nāhaṃ, ānanda, muṭṭhassatissa asampajānassāti ettha ayamadhippāyo – yasmā “cittapaṭisaṃvedī assāsissāmī”tiādinā nayena pavatto bhikkhu kiñcāpi assāsapassāsanimittamārammaṇaṃ karoti, tassa pana cittassa ārammaṇe satiñca sampajaññañca upaṭṭhāpetvā pavattanato citte cittānupassīyeva nāmesa hoti. Na hi muṭṭhassatissa asampajānassa ānāpānassatisamādhibhāvanā atthi, tasmā ārammaṇato cittapaṭisaṃviditavasena “citte cittānupassī bhikkhu tasmiṃ samaye viharatī”ti.

“Ānanda, I do not speak of this for one with lapsed mindfulness, for one without clear comprehension.” Here, this is the intended meaning: because, although a monk who proceeds in the manner of “I will breathe in experiencing the mind,” etc., makes the counterpart sign of the in-and-out breath his object, yet because he proceeds having established mindfulness and clear comprehension on the object of the mind, he is indeed named one who contemplates mind in mind. For there is no development of the concentration of mindfulness of breathing for one with lapsed mindfulness and without clear comprehension. Therefore, by means of experiencing the mind by way of the object, it is said: “a monk dwells contemplating mind in mind at that time.”

So yaṃ taṃ hoti abhijjhādomanassānaṃ pahānaṃ, taṃ paññāya disvā sādhukaṃ ajjhupekkhitā hotīti ettha abhijjhā kāmacchandanīvaraṇameva, domanassavasena byāpādanīvaraṇaṃ dassitaṃ. Idañhi catukkaṃ vipassanāvaseneva vuttaṃ, dhammānupassanā ca nīvaraṇapabbādivasena pañcavidhā hoti, tassā nīvaraṇapabbaṃ ādi, tassāpi idaṃ nīvaraṇadvayaṃ ādi. Iti dhammānupassanāya ādiṃ dassetuṃ abhijjhādomanassānanti āha. Pahānanti aniccānupassanāya niccasaññaṃ pajahatīti evaṃ pahānakarañāṇaṃ adhippetaṃ. Taṃ paññāya disvāti taṃ aniccavirāganirodhapaṭinissaggañāṇasaṅkhātaṃ pahānañāṇaṃ aparāya vipassanāpaññāya, tampi aparāyāti evaṃ vipassanāparamparaṃ dasseti[M 3.0304]. Ajjhupekkhitā hotīti yañcassa pathapaṭipannaṃ [P 3.0273] ajjhupekkhati, yañca ekato upaṭṭhānaṃ ajjhupekkhatīti dvidhā ajjhupekkhati nāma. Tattha sahajātānampiajjhupekkhanā hoti ārammaṇassāpi ajjhupekkhanā. Idha ārammaṇa ajjhupekkhanā adhippetā. Tasmātihānandāti yasmā “aniccānupassī assāsissāmī”tiādinā nayena pavatto na kevalaṃ nīvaraṇādidhamme, abhijjhādomanassasīsena pana vuttānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānakarañāṇampi paññāya disvā ajjhupekkhitā hoti, tasmā dhammesu dhammānupassī bhikkhu tasmiṃ samaye viharatīti veditabbo.

“So, that which is the abandoning of covetousness and displeasure, having seen it with wisdom, one looks on it well with equanimity.” Here, covetousness is just the hindrance of sensual desire; by means of displeasure, the hindrance of ill will is shown. For this tetrad is spoken of only by way of insight. And the contemplation of phenomena is sixfold, by way of the section on the hindrances, etc. Of that, the section on the hindrances is the beginning; and of that too, this pair of hindrances is the beginning. Thus, to show the beginning of the contemplation of phenomena, he said, “of covetousness and displeasure.” By “abandoning,” the knowledge that accomplishes abandonment is intended, as when one abandons the perception of permanence by means of the contemplation of impermanence. By “having seen that with wisdom,” it shows the succession of insight, in this way: having seen that knowledge of abandonment—characterized as the knowledge of impermanence, dispassion, cessation, and relinquishment—with a subsequent insight-wisdom, and that too with a subsequent one. By “one looks on with equanimity,” it is meant that one looks on with equanimity in two ways: one looks on with equanimity at the meditation mind that has entered the path, and one looks on with equanimity at the manifestation as a single whole. Therein, there is equanimity towards co-arisen states and also equanimity towards the object. Here, equanimity towards the object is intended. Therefore, Ānanda, because one who proceeds in the manner of “contemplating impermanence, I will breathe in,” etc., does not merely look on with equanimity at the hindrances and other states, but rather, having also seen with wisdom the knowledge that accomplishes the abandonment of the phenomena spoken of under the heading of covetousness and displeasure, one looks on with equanimity, therefore it should be understood that at that time the monk dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena.

Evameva khoti ettha catumahāpatho viya cha āyatanāni daṭṭhabbāni. Tasmiṃ paṃsupuñjo viya chasu āyatanesu kilesā. Catūhi disāhi āgacchantā sakaṭarathā viya catūsu ārammaṇesu [V 3.0304] pavattā cattāro satipaṭṭhānā. Ekena sakaṭena vā rathena vā paṃsupuñjassa upahananaṃ viya kāyānupassanādīhi pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ upaghāto veditabboti.

‘Just so...’ Here, the six sense bases should be seen as like a crossroads. The defilements in the six sense bases are like a heap of dust on it. The four establishments of mindfulness, proceeding in their four objects, are like carts and chariots coming from the four directions. Just as the heap of dust is crushed by a cart or a chariot, so the destruction of evil, unwholesome states by the contemplation of the body and so forth should be understood.

Ekadhammavaggo paṭhamo.

The First Chapter on a Single Thing.

2. Dutiyavaggo

2. The Second Chapter

1-2. Icchānaṅgalasuttādivaṇṇanā

1–2. Commentary on the Icchānaṅgala Sutta and so forth.

987-988. Dutiyavaggassa paṭhame evaṃ byākareyyāthāti kasmā attano vihārasamāpattiṃ ācikkhati? Upārambhamocanatthaṃ. Sace hi te “na jānāmā”ti vadeyyuṃ, atha nesaṃ titthiyā “tumhe ‘asukasamāpattiyā nāma no satthā temāsaṃ vihāsī’tipi na jānātha, atha kasmā naṃ upaṭṭhahantā viharathā”ti upārambhaṃ āropeyyuṃ, tato mocanatthaṃ evamāha.

2. In the first sutta of the second section, why does he declare his own attainment of dwelling? To free them from reproach. For if they were to say, “We do not know,” then the sectarians might level a reproach against them, saying, “You do not even know that ‘Our teacher dwelt in such-and-such an attainment for the three months of the rains retreat,’ so why do you dwell attending upon him?” To free them from that, he spoke thus.

Atha kasmā yathā aññattha “satova assasati, dīghaṃ vā assasanto”ti (dī. ni. 2.374; ma. ni. 1.107; saṃ. ni. 5.977) eva-vākāro vutto. Evaṃ idha na vuttoti? Ekantasantattā. Aññesañhi [M 3.0305] assāso vā pākaṭo hoti passāso vā, bhagavato ubhayampetaṃ pākaṭameva niccaṃ upaṭṭhitassatitāyāti ekantasantattā na vutto. Atha “sikkhāmī”ti avatvā kasmā “assasāmī”ti ettakameva vuttanti? Sikkhitabbābhāvā. Satta hi sekhā sikkhitabbabhāvā [P 3.0274] sekhā nāma, khīṇāsavā sikkhitabbābhāvā asekhā nāma, tathāgatā asikkhitabbā asekkhā nāma natthi tesaṃ sikkhitabbakiccanti sikkhitabbābhāvā na vuttaṃ. Dutiyaṃ uttānameva.

Then why is it that, just as elsewhere the words `eva` or `vā` are used, as in “mindful he breathes in, or breathing in long…,” it is not stated so here? Because of absolute tranquility. For others, either the in-breath or the out-breath is evident, but for the Blessed One, both are always evident due to his constantly present mindfulness; thus, because of absolute tranquility, it is not stated. Then, without saying “I train,” why is only “I will breathe in” stated? Because there is nothing to be trained in. Indeed, the seven trainees are called ‘trainees’ because they have something to be trained in. Those whose cankers are destroyed are called ‘non-trainees’ because they have nothing to be trained in. For the Tathāgatas, there is nothing to be trained in, they are called non-trainees; for them there is no task of training. Therefore, because there is nothing to be trained in, it is not stated. The second sutta is self-evident.

3-10. Paṭhamaānandasuttādivaṇṇanā

3–10. Commentary on the First Ānanda Sutta, and so forth.

989-996. Tatiye pavicinatīti aniccādivasena pavicinati. Itaraṃ padadvayaṃ etasseva vevacanaṃ. Nirāmisāti nikkilesā kāyikacetasikadarathapaṭipassaddhiyā kāyopi cittampi [V 3.0305] passambhati. Samādhiyatīti sammā ṭhapiyati, appanācittaṃ viya hoti. Ajjhupekkhitā hotīti sahajātaajjhupekkhanāya ajjhupekkhitā hoti.

In the third sutta, `pavicinati` means one investigates by way of impermanence and so forth. The other two words are synonyms of this. `Nirāmisā` means free from defilements; through the calming of bodily and mental distress, both body and mind become tranquil. `Samādhiyati` means it is well established, becoming like a mind in absorption. `Ajjhupekkhitā hoti` means one is equanimous with co-arisen equanimity.

Evaṃ cuddasavidhena kāyapariggāhakassa bhikkhuno tasmiṃ kāye sati satisambojjhaṅgo, tāya satiyā sampayuttañāṇaṃ dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgo, taṃsampayuttameva kāyikacetasikavīriyaṃ vīriyasambojjhaṅgo, pītipassaddhicittekaggatā pītipassaddhisamādhisambojjhaṅgā, imesaṃ channaṃ bojjhaṅgānaṃ anosakkanaanativattanasaṅkhāto majjhattākāro upekkhāsambojjhaṅgo. Yatheva hi samappavattesu assesu sārathino “ayaṃ olīyatī”ti tudanaṃ vā, “ayaṃ atidhāvatī”ti ākaḍḍhanaṃ vā natthi, kevalaṃ evaṃ passamānassa ṭhitākārova hoti, evameva imesaṃ channaṃ bojjhaṅgānaṃ anosakkanaanativattanasaṅkhāto majjhattākāro upekkhāsambojjhaṅgo nāma hoti. Ettāvatā kiṃ kathitaṃ? Ekacittakkhaṇikā nānāsarasalakkhaṇā vipassanābojjhaṅgā nāma kathitā.

Thus, for a monk who comprehends the body in these fourteen ways, mindfulness regarding that body is the enlightenment factor of mindfulness. The knowledge associated with that mindfulness is the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena. The bodily and mental energy associated with that is the enlightenment factor of energy. Joy, tranquility, and one-pointedness of mind are the enlightenment factors of joy, tranquility, and concentration. The neutral state regarding these six enlightenment factors, which is described as neither falling short nor overshooting, is the enlightenment factor of equanimity. For just as with horses moving evenly, the charioteer has no need to prod one, thinking, “This one is lagging,” nor to pull back another, thinking, “This one is running too fast,” but simply remains watching with a stable posture; even so, the neutral state regarding these six enlightenment factors, which is described as neither falling short nor overshooting, is called the enlightenment factor of equanimity. What has been taught by this? The insight enlightenment factors, which are of a single mind-moment and have various essential characteristics, have been taught.

Vivekanissitantiādīni vuttatthāneva. Ettha pana soḷasakkhattukā ānāpānassati missakā kathitā, ānāpānamūlakā satipaṭṭhānā pubbabhāgā[M 3.0306], tesaṃ mūlabhūtā ānāpānassati [P 3.0275] pubbabhāgā. Bojjhaṅgamūlakā satipaṭṭhānā pubbabhāgā, tepi bojjhaṅgā pubbabhāgāva. Vijjāvimuttipūrakā pana bojjhaṅgā nibbattitalokuttarā, vijjāvimuttiyo ariyaphalasampayuttā. Vijjā vā catutthamaggasampayuttā, vimutti phalasampayuttāti. Catutthapañcamachaṭṭhānipi imināva samānaparicchedāni. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

The words beginning with `vivekanissitaṃ` have the meaning already explained. Here, however, mindfulness of breathing with its sixteen instances is taught as mixed. The foundations of mindfulness that have mindfulness of breathing as their root are the preliminary part, and mindfulness of breathing, which is the root-cause for them, is the preliminary part. The foundations of mindfulness that have the enlightenment factors as their root are the preliminary part, and those enlightenment factors are also the preliminary part. However, the enlightenment factors that fulfill knowledge and liberation are purely supramundane. Knowledge and liberation are associated with the noble fruit. Alternatively, knowledge is associated with the fourth path, and liberation is associated with the fruit. The fourth, fifth, and sixth suttas also have the same sections as this one. The rest is clear everywhere.

Ānāpānasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Connected Discourses on Mindfulness of Breathing is Concluded.

11. Sotāpattisaṃyuttaṃ

The Connected Discourses on Stream-Entry

1. Veḷudvāravaggo

1. The Bamboo Gate Section

1. Cakkavattirājasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Exposition on the Discourse of the Wheel-turning Monarch

997. Sotāpattisaṃyuttassa [V 3.0306][M 3.0307][P 3.0276] paṭhame kiñcāpīti anuggahagarahaṇesu nipāto. Catunnañhi mahādīpānaṃ issariyādhipaccaṃ rajjaṃ anuggaṇhanto catunnañca apāyānaṃ appahīnabhāvaṃ garahanto satthā “kiñcāpi, bhikkhave, rājā cakkavattī”tiādimāha. Tattha catunnaṃ dīpānanti dvisahassadīpaparivārānaṃ catunnaṃ mahādīpānaṃ. Issariyādhipaccanti issarabhāvo issariyaṃ, adhipatibhāvo ādhipaccaṃ, issariyaṃ ādhipaccaṃ etasmiṃ rajje, na chedanabhedananti issariyādhipaccaṃ. Kāretvāti evarūpaṃ rajjaṃ pavattāpetvā. Kiñcāpi, bhikkhave, ariyasāvakoti ettha anuggahapasaṃsāsu nipāto. Piṇḍiyālopena hi yāpanaṃ anuggahanto catunnañca apāyānaṃ pahīnabhāvaṃ pasaṃsanto satthā “kiñcāpi, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako”tiādimāha. Tattha nantakānīti anantakāni. Terasahatthopi hi vatthasāṭako dasacchedanato paṭṭhāya nantakanteva saṅkhaṃ gacchati.

In the first sutta of the Sotāpattisaṃyutta, the particle 'kiñcāpi' is a particle in the meanings of favoring and censuring. For, desiring to favor the kingship of sovereignty and dominion over the four great continents, and desiring to censure the state of not having abandoned the four states of deprivation, the Teacher said, “Even if, monks, a wheel-turning king…” and so on. Therein, 'of the four continents' means of the four great continents with their retinue of two thousand minor islands. 'Sovereignty and dominion' means: the state of being a ruler is sovereignty; the state of being a master is dominion. In this kingship there is sovereignty and dominion, but not cutting and destroying; therefore, it is called 'sovereignty and dominion'. 'Having caused to be' means having established such a kingship. In the passage, “Even if, monks, a noble disciple…”, the particle is used in the meanings of favoring and praising. For, desiring to favor sustenance by morsels of almsfood, and desiring to praise the state of having abandoned the four states of deprivation, the Teacher said, “Even if, monks, a noble disciple…” and so on. Therein, 'nantakāni' means without fringes. For even a cloth garment of thirteen cubits, from the moment its fringe is cut off, is reckoned as 'without a fringe'.

Aveccappasādenāti acalappasādena. So panāyaṃ pasādo kiṃ eko, anekoti? Ekova, so maggena āgatappasādo. Yesu pana vatthūsu apubbaṃ acarimaṃ ruhati, tesaṃ vasena “buddhe aveccappasādenā”tiādinā nayena tidhā vutto. Yasmā ca eko, tasmāva ninnānākaraṇo hoti. Ariyasāvakassa hi buddheyeva pasādo ca pemañca gāravañca mahantaṃ, na dhamme vā saṅghe vā, dhammeyeva vā mahantaṃ[P 3.0277], na buddhe vā saṅghe vā, saṅgheyeva vā mahantaṃ, na buddhe vā dhamme vāti etaṃ natthi. Itipi so bhagavātiādīni visuddhimagge vitthāritāneva.

‘With unwavering confidence’ means with unshakable confidence. Now, is this confidence one or many? It is just one; it is the confidence that has come by way of the path. However, with respect to the objects in which it arises neither previously nor subsequently but all at once, it is spoken of in three parts by the method beginning, “with unwavering confidence in the Buddha,” and so on. And because it is one, it therefore makes no distinctions. For it is not the case for a noble disciple that confidence, affection, and respect are great only towards the Buddha, and not towards the Dhamma or the Saṅgha; or great only towards the Dhamma, and not towards the Buddha or the Saṅgha; or great only towards the Saṅgha, and not towards the Buddha or the Dhamma. The passages beginning with, “Indeed, that Blessed One…” have already been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga.

Ariyakantehīti [V 3.0307] ariyānaṃ kantehi piyehi manāpehi. Pañca hi sīlāni bhavantaragatāpi ariyā na kopenti, evaṃ tesaṃ piyāni. Tāni sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Akhaṇḍehītiādi sadisavasena vuttaṃ. Mukhavaṭṭiyañhi chinnekadesā pāti khaṇḍāti vuccati, majjhe bhinnā chiddāti, ekasmiṃ padese visabhāgavaṇṇā gāvī sabalāti, nānābinducittā kammāsāti, evameva paṭipāṭiyā [M 3.0308] ādimhi vā ante vā bhinnaṃ sīlaṃ khaṇḍaṃ nāma, majjhe bhinnaṃ chiddaṃ, yattha katthaci dvinnaṃ vā tiṇṇaṃ vā paṭipāṭiyā bhinnattā sabalaṃ, ekantaraṃ bhinnaṃ kammāsaṃ. Tesaṃ dosānaṃ abhāvena akhaṇḍāditā veditabbā. Bhujissehīti bhujissabhāvakarehi. Viññuppasatthehīti buddhādīhi viññūhi pasaṃsitehi. Aparāmaṭṭhehīti “idaṃ nāma tayā kataṃ, idaṃ vītikkanta”nti evaṃ parāmasituṃ asakkuṇeyyehi. Samādhisaṃvattanikehīti appanāsamādhiṃ upacārasamādhiṃ vā saṃvattetuṃ samatthehi.

‘Pleasing to the noble ones’ means pleasing, dear, and agreeable to the noble ones. For the noble ones do not violate the five precepts even when they have gone to another existence; in this way, they are dear to them. This was said in reference to those precepts. ‘Unbroken,’ etc., is said by way of simile. For a bowl with a piece of its rim broken is called ‘broken’; when broken in the middle, it is called ‘pierced’; a cow with a dissimilar color in one spot is called ‘spotted’; and one variegated with various spots is called ‘mottled’. In the very same way, virtue broken in sequence at the beginning or at the end is called ‘broken’; broken in the middle, it is ‘pierced’; because of being broken in sequence in two or three places anywhere, it is ‘spotted’; broken with an interval, it is ‘mottled’. Due to the absence of these faults, the state of being unbroken, etc., should be understood. ‘Liberating’ means bringing about a state of freedom. ‘Praised by the wise’ means praised by the wise, such as the Buddhas and others. ‘Untouched’ means unable to be touched upon thus: ‘This was done by you; this was transgressed.’ ‘Conducive to concentration’ means capable of bringing about absorption concentration or access concentration.

2. Brahmacariyogadhasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Brahmacariyogadhasutta

998. Dutiye yesaṃ saddhāti padena buddhe pasādo gahito. Sīlanti padena ariyakantāni sīlāni gahitāni. Pasādoti padena saṅghe pasādo gahito. Dhammadassananti padena dhamme pasādo gahitoti evaṃ cattāri sotāpattiyaṅgāni vuttāni. Kālena paccentīti kālena pāpuṇanti. Brahmacariyogadhaṃ sukhanti brahmacariyaṃ ogāhitvā ṭhitaṃ uparimaggattayasampayuttaṃ sukhaṃ. Yo panesa gāthāya āgato pasādo, so katarapasādo hotīti. Tipiṭakacūḷābhayatthero tāva “maggapasādo”ti āha, tipiṭakacūḷanāgatthero “āgatamaggassa paccavekkhaṇappasādo”ti. Ubhopi therā paṇḍitā bahussutā, ubhinnaṃ subhāsitaṃ. Missakappasādo esoti.

998. In the second sutta, by the phrase ‘whose faith’ (yesaṃ saddhā), confidence in the Buddha is taken. By the word ‘virtue’ (sīlaṃ), the virtues cherished by the noble ones are taken. By the word ‘confidence’ (pasādo), confidence in the Saṅgha is taken. By the phrase ‘seeing of the Dhamma’ (dhammadassanaṃ), confidence in the Dhamma is taken. In this way, the four factors of stream-entry are stated. ‘They attain in time’ (kālena paccenti) means they attain in due course. ‘The happiness immersed in the holy life’ (brahmacariyogadhaṃ sukhaṃ) is the happiness associated with the three higher paths, established by immersing in the noble practice. Now, as for this confidence that appears in the verse, what kind of confidence is it? The Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya said, ‘It is confidence associated with the path.’ The Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga said, ‘It is the confidence in reviewing of one who has attained the path.’ Both elders are wise and learned; the speech of both is well-spoken. It should be understood that this is a mixed confidence.

3. Dīghāvuupāsakasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Dīghāvu-upāsaka Sutta

999. Tatiye [P 3.0278] tasmāti yasmā catūsu sotāpattiyaṅgesu sandissasi, tasmā. Vijjābhāgiyeti vijjākoṭṭhāsike. Sabbasaṅkhāresūti sabbesu tebhūmakasaṅkhāresu. Evamassa upari tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ vipassanā kathitā. Vighātanti dukkhaṃ.

999. In the third sutta, ‘therefore’ (tasmā) means ‘because you appear in the four factors of stream-entry, therefore.’ ‘Pertaining to knowledge’ (vijjābhāgiye) means being a part of knowledge. ‘In all conditioned phenomena’ (sabbasaṅkhāresu) means in all conditioned phenomena of the three planes. Thus, for him, insight into the three higher paths was taught. ‘Vighātaṃ’ means suffering.

4-5. Paṭhamasāriputtasuttādivaṇṇanā

4-5. Commentary on the First Sāriputta Sutta, etc.

1000-1001. Catuttha [V 3.0308] uttānameva. Pañcame sotāpattiyaṅganti sotāpattiyā pubbabhāgapaṭilābhaṅgaṃ. Buddhe aveccappasādādayo pana paṭiladdhaguṇā [M 3.0309] sotāpannassa aṅgā nāma, tepi pana sotāpattiyaṅganti āgatā. Tatrāyaṃ dvinnampi vacanattho – sappurise sevanto bhajanto payirupāsanto dhammaṃ suṇanto yoniso manasikaronto dhammānudhammaṃ pubbabhāgapaṭipadaṃ paṭipajjanto sotāpattiṃ paṭilabhatīti sappurisasaṃsevādayo sotāpattiatthāya aṅganti sotāpattiyaṅgaṃ nāma, itare paṭhamamaggasaṅkhātāya sotāpattiyā aṅgantipi sotāpattiyaṅgaṃ, paṭividdhasotāpattimaggassa sotāpattimaggo aṅgantipi sotāpattiyaṅgaṃ.

The fourth sutta is self-evident. In the fifth sutta, ‘a factor of stream-entry’ (sotāpattiyaṅga) means a factor for attaining the preliminary stage of stream-entry. Furthermore, the acquired qualities such as unwavering confidence in the Buddha are called factors of a stream-enterer, yet these too are referred to as ‘factors of stream-entry’. Herein is the meaning of both: ‘By associating with, attending on, and waiting upon good people, listening to the Dhamma, wisely considering, and undertaking the preliminary practice in accordance with the Dhamma, one attains stream-entry.’ Therefore, associating with good people and so on are a cause for the sake of stream-entry, and are thus called ‘a factor of stream-entry’. The other qualities are a factor that is a sign of stream-entry—designated as the first path—and are thus also called ‘a factor of stream-entry’. The stream-entry path is a factor of the penetrated stream-entry path, and is thus also called ‘a factor of stream-entry’.

6. Thapatisuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Thapati Sutta

1002. Chaṭṭhe sādhuke paṭivasantīti sādhukanāmake attano bhogagāmake vasanti. Tesu isidatto sakadāgāmī, purāṇo sotāpanno sadārasantuṭṭho. Magge purisaṃ ṭhapesunti tesaṃ kira gāmadvārena bhagavato gamanamaggo. Tasmā “bhagavā kāle vā akāle vā amhākaṃ suttānaṃ vā pamattānaṃ vā gaccheyya, atha passituṃ na labheyyāmā”ti maggamajjhe purisaṃ ṭhapesuṃ.

1002. In the sixth sutta, ‘sādhuke paṭivasanti’ means: they dwell in their own revenue-village named Sādhuka. Among them, Isidatta is a once-returner and Purāṇa is a stream-enterer; both are content with their own wives. ‘Magge purisaṃ ṭhapesuṃ’ means: it is said that the Blessed One's path of travel was through their village gate. Therefore, thinking, ‘The Blessed One might pass by at a timely or untimely hour, while we are asleep or heedless, and then we would not get to see him,’ they stationed a man in the middle of the path.

Anubandhiṃsūti na dūratova piṭṭhito piṭṭhito anubandhiṃsu, bhagavā pana sakaṭamaggassa majjhe jaṅghamaggena agamāsi, itare ubhosu passesu anugacchantā agamaṃsu. Maggā okkammāti buddhānañhi kenaci saddhiṃ gacchantānaṃyeva paṭisanthāraṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati kenaci saddhiṃ ṭhitakānaṃ[P 3.0279], kenaci saddhiṃ divasabhāgaṃ nisinnānaṃ. Tasmā bhagavā cintesi – “imehi me saddhiṃ gacchantassa paṭisanthāraṃ kātuṃ ayuttaṃ, ṭhitakenapi kātuṃ na yuttaṃ, ime hi mayhaṃ sāsane sāmino āgataphalā. Imehi saddhiṃ nisīditvāva divasabhāgaṃ paṭisanthāraṃ karissāmī”ti maggā okkamma yena aññataraṃ rukkhamūlaṃ tenupasaṅkami.

‘Anubandhiṃsu’ means: they followed closely behind, not from afar. The Blessed One, however, proceeded along the footpath in the middle of the cart track, while the others went along following on both sides. ‘Maggā okkamma’ means: for Buddhas, it is proper to exchange friendly greetings with someone only while walking, or while standing with someone, or while sitting with someone for part of the day. Therefore, the Blessed One thought: ‘It is not proper for me to exchange friendly greetings with them while walking, nor is it proper to do so while standing. For these are masters in my Dispensation, who have attained the fruit. I will exchange friendly greetings with them for part of the day only after sitting down.’ Having stepped aside from the path, he approached the foot of a certain tree.

Paññatte āsane nisīdīti te kira chattupāhanaṃ kattaradaṇḍaṃ pādabbhañjanatelādīni ceva aṭṭhavidhañca pānakaṃ sarabhapādapallaṅkañca gāhāpetvā agamaṃsu, ābhataṃ pallaṅkampi paññāpetvā adaṃsu[V 3.0309], satthā tasmiṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsūti sesāni chattupāhanādīni bhikkhusaṅghassa dethāti vatvā sayampi bhagavantaṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu.

Paññatte āsane nisīdi means: it is said that they had someone bring an umbrella and sandals, a walking stick, foot-anointing oil and so on, eight kinds of beverages, and a couch with legs of a Sarabha deer, and then they came. Having prepared the couch they had brought, they offered it, and the Teacher sat on it. Ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu means: after saying, 'Give the remaining things—the umbrella, sandals, and so on—to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus,' they themselves, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side.

Sāvatthiyā [M 3.0310] kosalesu cārikaṃ pakkamissatītiādi sabbaṃ majjhimapadesavasenava vuttaṃ. Kasmā? Niyatattā. Bhagavato hi cārikācaraṇampi aruṇuṭṭhāpanampi niyataṃ, majjhimapadeseyeva cārikaṃ carati, majjhimadese aruṇaṃ uṭṭhapetīti niyatattā majjhimadesavasena vuttaṃ. Āsanne no bhagavā bhavissatīti ettha na kevalaṃ āsannattāyeva tesaṃ somanassaṃ hoti, atha kho “idāni dānaṃ dātuṃ gandhamālādīhi pūjaṃ kātuṃ dhammaṃ sotuṃ pañhaṃ pucchituṃ labhissāmā”ti tesaṃ somanassaṃ hoti.

The statement beginning Sāvatthiyā kosalesu cārikaṃ pakkamissati is all spoken with reference to the Middle Country. Why? Because it is fixed. For the Blessed One's wandering and his bringing about the dawn are fixed: he wanders only in the Middle Country and brings about the dawn only in the Middle Country. Thus, it is spoken with reference to the Middle Country because it is fixed. Here, regarding Āsanne no bhagavā bhavissati, their gladness does not arise merely because of his proximity. Rather, their gladness arises because they think: 'Now we will get to give alms, to make offerings with perfumes, garlands, and so on, to listen to the Dhamma, and to ask questions.'

Tasmātiha thapatayo sambādho gharāvāsoti thapatayo yasmā tumhākaṃ mayi dūrībhūte anappakaṃ domanassaṃ, āsanne anappakaṃ somanassaṃ hoti, tasmāpi veditabbametaṃ “sambādho gharāvāso”ti. Gharāvāsassa hi dosena tumhākaṃ evaṃ hoti. Sace pana gharāvāsaṃ pahāya pabbajitā, atha evaṃ vo mayā saddhiṃyeva gacchantānañca āgacchantānañca taṃ na bhaveyyāti imamatthaṃ dīpento evamāha. Tattha sakiñcanasapalibodhaṭṭhena sambādhatā veditabbā. Mahāvāse vasantassapi hi sakiñcanasapalibodhaṭṭhena gharāvāso sambādhova. Rajāpathoti rāgadosamoharajānaṃ āpatho, āgamanaṭṭhānanti attho. Abbhokāso [P 3.0280] pabbajjāti pabbajjā pana akiñcanaapalibodhaṭṭhena abbhokāso. Caturatanikepi hi gabbhe dvinnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pallaṅkena pallaṅkaṃ ghaṭetvā nisinnānampi akiñcanaapalibodhaṭṭhena pabbajjā abbhokāso nāma hoti. Alañca pana vo thapatayo appamādāyāti evaṃ sambādhe gharāvāse vasantānaṃ tumhākaṃ appamādameva kātuṃ yuttanti attho.

Tasmātiha thapatayo sambādho gharāvāso means: O householders, because for you, when I am far away, much displeasure arises, and when I am near, much gladness arises, for that reason too it should be known that 'the household life is confining.' Indeed, it is due to the fault of the household life that this happens to you. But if, having abandoned the household life, you had gone forth, then that would not happen to you who would be coming and going together with me. Illuminating this meaning, he spoke thus. Therein, its confining nature should be understood in the sense of being with hindrances and obstacles. For even for one dwelling in a great mansion, the household life is still confining in the sense of being with hindrances and obstacles. Rajāpatho means it is the path for the dust of greed, hatred, and delusion; it is the place of their coming. Abbhokāso pabbajjā means: but the going forth is an open space in the sense of being without hindrances and without obstacles. For even if two bhikkhus are sitting in a small chamber of four cubits with their couches touching, the going forth is called an 'open space' because of the meaning of being without hindrances and without obstacles. Alañca pana vo thapatayo appamādāya means: for you who are living in such a confining household life, it is proper only to be heedful.

Ekaṃ purato ekaṃ pacchato nisīdāpemāti te kira dvepi janā sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitesu dvīsu nāgesu tā itthiyo evaṃ nisīdāpetvā rañño nāgaṃ majjhe katvā ubhosu passesu gacchanti, tasmā evamāhaṃsu. Nāgopi rakkhitabboti yathā kiñci visevitaṃ na karoti, evaṃ rakkhitabbo hoti. Tāpi bhaginiyoti yathā pamādaṃ nāpajjanti, evaṃ rakkhitabbā honti. Attāpīti sitahasitakathitavipekkhitādīni akarontehi [M 3.0311] attāpi rakkhitabbo hoti. (Tehi tathā karontehi na attāpi rakkhitabbo hoti). Tathā karonto hi “sāmidubbho eso”ti niggahetabbo hoti. Tasmātiha thapatayoti yasmā tumhe rājā niccaṃ rājabhaṇḍaṃ paṭicchāpeti, tasmāpi [V 3.0310] sambādho gharāvāso rajāpatho. Yasmā pana paṃsukūlikabhikkhuṃ evaṃ paṭicchāpento natthi, tasmā abbhokāso pabbajjā. Evaṃ sabbatthāpi alañca pana vo thapatayo appamādāya appamādameva karothāti dasseti.

Ekaṃ purato ekaṃ pacchato nisīdāpema means: it is said that both persons, having had those women sit thus on two elephants that were fully adorned with all ornaments, and having placed the king's elephant in the middle, proceeded on both sides. Therefore they spoke thus. Nāgopi rakkhitabbo means: the elephant too must be guarded so that it does not do anything contrary. Tāpi bhaginiyo means: those ladies too must be guarded so that they do not become heedless. Attāpi means: oneself too must be guarded by not smiling, laughing, talking, looking around, and so on. For one who acts in such a way should be suppressed, with the thought, 'This is one who is treacherous to his master.' Tasmātiha thapatayo means: because the king constantly entrusts you with the royal property, for that reason too the household life is confining, a path of dust. But because there is no one who thus entrusts things to a bhikkhu who wears rag-robes, the going forth is an open space. Thus in all cases, it shows: 'It is indeed enough for you, O householders, to be heedful; you should practice only heedfulness.'

Muttacāgoti vissaṭṭhacāgo. Payatapāṇīti āgatāgatānaṃ dānatthāya dhotahattho. Vossaggaratoti vossaggasaṅkhāte cāge rato. Yācayogoti yācitabbakayutto. Dānasaṃvibhāgaratoti dānena ceva appamattakampi kiñci laddhā tatopi saṃvibhāge rato. Appaṭivibhattanti “idaṃ amhākaṃ bhavissati, idaṃ bhikkhūna”nti evaṃ akatavibhāgaṃ, sabbaṃ dātabbameva hutvā ṭhitanti attho.

Muttacāgo means one with liberal generosity. Payatapāṇī means one with hands washed for the purpose of giving to whoever comes. Vossaggarato means one who delights in giving, which is known as relinquishment. Yācayogo means fit to be requested from. Dānasaṃvibhāgarato means one who delights in giving and in sharing with others even some small thing that has been obtained. Appaṭivibhattaṃ means that no division has been made, such as, 'This will be for us, this will be for the bhikkhus'; everything stands as something to be given.

7. Veḷudvāreyyasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Veḷudvāreyya Sutta

1003. Sattame veḷudvāranti gāmadvāre paveṇiāgatassa veḷugacchassa atthitāya evaṃladdhanāmo gāmo. Attupanāyikanti [P 3.0281] attani upanetabbaṃ. Samphabhāsenāti amantabhāsena. Samphappalāpabhāsenāti samphappalāpasambhāsena niratthakena aññāṇavacanenāti attho.

1003. In the seventh sutta, Veḷudvāra is the name given to a village because of the existence of a bamboo grove, which had come down through generations, at the village gate. Attupanāyika means what should be applied to oneself. Samphappalāpabhāsa means frivolous talk; that is, useless, unwise speech—this is the meaning.

8-9. Paṭhamagiñjakāvasathasuttādivaṇṇanā

8-9. Commentary on the First Giñjakāvasatha Sutta, etc.

1004-5. Aṭṭhame ñātiketi ekaṃ taḷākaṃ nissāya dvinnaṃ cūḷapitimahāpitiputtānaṃ dve gāmā, tesu ekasmiṃ gāmake. Giñjakāvasatheti iṭṭhakāmaye āvasathe. Orambhāgiyānanti heṭṭhābhāgiyānaṃ, kāmabhaveyeva paṭisandhiggāhāpakānanti attho. Oranti laddhanāmehi vā tīhi maggehi pahātabbānītipi orambhāgiyāni. Tattha kāmacchando byāpādoti imāni dve samāpattiyā vā avikkhambhitāni maggena vā asamucchinnāni nibbattivasena uddhaṃ bhāgaṃ rūpabhavaṃ arūpabhavaṃ vā gantuṃ na denti. Sakkāyadiṭṭhiādīni [M 3.0312] tīṇi tattha nibbattampi ānetvā puna idheva nibbattāpentīti sabbānipi orambhāgiyāneva. Anāvattidhammoti paṭisandhivasena anāgamanasabhāvo.

In the eighth sutta, regarding Ñātika: near a single reservoir, there were two villages belonging to the sons of a younger and an elder paternal uncle. Because these were the villages of two sets of kinsmen (ñāti), they received the name Ñātika. In one of those villages, Giñjakāvasatha means in a dwelling made of bricks. Orambhāgiyāni (lower fetters) means those belonging to the lower part; the meaning is that they cause one to take rebirth only in the sensual realm. Alternatively, they are called orambhāgiyāni because they are to be abandoned by the three paths which are named 'lower' (ora). Among these, sensual desire and ill will, if not suppressed by meditative attainments or eradicated by the path, do not allow one to proceed to a higher state—the form realm or the formless realm—by way of rebirth. The three fetters beginning with identity view, even for one who has arisen there, bring them back and cause them to be reborn right here. Thus, all five are indeed lower fetters. Anāvattidhamma (one not subject to return) means having the nature of not returning, by way of rebirth.

Rāgadosamohānaṃ [V 3.0311] tanuttāti ettha kadāci uppattiyā ca pariyuṭṭhānamandatāya cāti dvedhāpi tanubhāvo veditabbo. Sakadāgāmissa hi puthujjanānaṃ viya abhiṇhaṃ rāgādayo na uppajjanti, kadāci karahaci uppajjanti. Uppajjamānā ca na puthujjanānaṃ viya bahalabahalā uppajjanti, makkhipattaṃ viya tanukā uppajjanti. Dīghabhāṇakatipiṭakamahāsīvatthero panāha – “yasmā sakadāgāmissa puttadhītaro honti, orodhā ca honti, tasmā bahalā kilesā. Idaṃ pana bhavatanukavasena kathita”nti. Taṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “sotāpannassa satta bhave ṭhapetvā aṭṭhame bhave bhavatanukaṃ natthi, sakadāgāmissa dve bhave ṭhapetvā pañcasu bhavesu bhavatanukaṃ natthi, anāgāmissa rūpārūpabhavaṃ ṭhapetvā kāmabhave bhavatanukaṃ natthi, khīṇāsavassa kismiñci bhave bhavatanukaṃ natthī”ti vuttattā paṭikkhittaṃ hoti.

Here, in the phrase 'the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion,' the state of being attenuated should be understood in two ways: by their occasional arising and by the weakness of their obsession. For a once-returner, lust and so forth do not arise as frequently as for worldlings; they arise only now and then. And when they do arise, they do not arise as intensely as for worldlings, but are attenuated, like a fly's wing. However, the Elder Mahāsīva, a Tipiṭaka master and Dīgha-reciter, said: 'Because a once-returner has sons and daughters, and has a harem, their defilements are strong. This statement, however, was made in terms of the reduction of existences.' That statement is refuted in the Great Commentary because it is said: 'For a stream-enterer, setting aside seven existences, there is no reduction of existence in the eighth existence; for a once-returner, setting aside two existences, there is no reduction of existence in five existences; for a non-returner, setting aside the form and formless realms, there is no reduction of existence in the sensual realm; for an arahant, there is no reduction of existence in any existence whatsoever.'

Imaṃ [P 3.0282] lokanti imaṃ kāmāvacaralokaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – sace hi manussesu sakadāgāmiphalaṃ patto devesu nibbattitvā arahattaṃ sacchikaroti, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. Asakkonto pana avassaṃ manussalokaṃ āgantvā sacchikaroti. Devesu sakadāgāmiphalaṃ pattopi sace manussesu nibbattitvā arahattaṃ sacchikaroti, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. Asakkonto pana avassaṃ devalokaṃ gantvā sacchikarotīti.

'This world' is said with reference to this sense-sphere world. The meaning here is this: If one who has attained the fruit of once-returning among humans is reborn among the devas and realizes arahantship, that is good. But if unable to do so, they must inevitably return to the human world and realize it. If one who has attained the fruit of once-returning among the devas is reborn among humans and realizes arahantship, that is good. But if unable to do so, they must inevitably go to the deva world and realize it.

Vinipatanaṃ vinipāto, nāssa vinipāto dhammoti avinipātadhammo, catūsu apāyesu avinipātanasabhāvoti attho. Niyatoti dhammaniyāmena niyato. Sambodhiparāyaṇoti uparimaggattayasaṅkhātā sambodhi paraṃ ayanaṃ assa gati paṭisaraṇaṃ avassaṃ pattabbāti sambodhiparāyaṇo. Vihesāvesāti tesaṃ tesaṃ ñāṇagatiṃ ñāṇūpapattiṃ ñāṇābhisamparāyaṃ olokentassa kāyakilamathova esa, ānanda, tathāgatassāti dīpeti. Cittavihesā pana buddhānaṃ natthi.

'Falling down' is 'downfall.' 'Not subject to downfall' means one for whom downfall is not their nature; the meaning is one who has the nature of not falling into the four states of deprivation. 'Fixed' means fixed by the principle of the Dhamma. 'Destined for enlightenment' means that for such a one, the enlightenment designated as the three higher paths is the ultimate resort, destination, and refuge, to be inevitably attained. 'This is a vexation' shows: 'Ānanda, for the Tathāgata, observing the destination, the rebirth, and the future life of those various individuals is only a bodily fatigue.' However, there is no mental vexation for the Buddhas.

Dhammādāsanti [M 3.0313] dhammamayaṃ ādāsaṃ. Yenāti yena dhammādāsena samannāgato. Khīṇāpāyaduggativinipātoti idaṃ nirayādīnaṃyeva vevacanavaseneva vuttaṃ. Nirayādayo hi vaḍḍhisaṅkhātato ayato apetattā apāyo, dukkhassa gati paṭisaraṇanti. Duggati, dukkaṭakārino ettha vivasā nipatantīti vinipāto. Navamaṃ uttānameva.

'Mirror of Dhamma' means a mirror made of Dhamma. 'By which' means by which mirror of Dhamma one is endowed. 'One for whom states of loss, bad bourns, and downfall are destroyed' is said merely by way of synonyms for hell and the like. For hells and the like are called 'states of loss' (apāya) because they are devoid of profit (āya), which is designated as growth; 'bad bourn' (duggati) because they are a destination and resort of suffering; and 'downfall' (vinipāta) because those who perform evil deeds fall helplessly therein. The ninth sutta is simply clear.

10. Tatiyagiñjakāvasathasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Third Discourse at the Brick Hall

1006. Dasame [V 3.0312] paropaññāsāti atirekapaññāsa. Sādhikanavutīti atirekanavuti. Chātirekānīti chahi adhikāni. So kira gāmo kiñcāpi nātimahā ahosi, ariyasāvakā panettha bahū. Tattha tattha ahivātarogena ekappahāreneva catuvīsati pāṇasatasahassāni kālamakaṃsu, tesu ariyasāvakā ettakā nāma ahesuṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

1006. In the tenth, 'more than fifty' means in excess of fifty. 'With more than ninety' means in excess of ninety. 'Exceeding by six' means more by six. It is said that although that village was not very large, there were many noble disciples there. In that place, due to a pestilence, two million four hundred thousand beings died in a single onslaught, and among them there were this many noble disciples. The rest is clear everywhere.

Veḷudvāravaggo paṭhamo.

The First Chapter on Veḷudvāra.

2. Rājakārāmavaggo

2. The Chapter on the King's Monastery

1. Sahassabhikkhunisaṅghasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Community of a Thousand Nuns

1007. Dutiyassa [P 3.0283] paṭhame rājakārāmeti raññā kāritattā evaṃ laddhanāme ārāme, taṃ raññā pasenadikosalena kataṃ. Paṭhamabodhiyaṃ kira lābhaggayasaggapattaṃ satthāraṃ disvā titthiyā cintayiṃsu – “samaṇo gotamo lābhaggayasaggapatto, na kho panesa aññaṃ kiñci sīlaṃ vā samādhiṃ vā nissāya evaṃ lābhaggayasaggapatto. Bhūmisīsaṃ pana tena gahitaṃ, sace mayampi jetavanasamīpe ārāmaṃ kārāpetuṃ sakkuṇeyyāma, lābhaggayasaggapattā bhaveyyāmā”ti. Te attano attano upaṭṭhāke samādapetvā satasahassamatte kahāpaṇe labhitvā te ādāya rañño santikaṃ agamaṃsu. Rājā “kiṃ eta”nti? Pucchi. Mayaṃ jetavanasamīpe titthiyārāmaṃ karoma, sace samaṇo gotamo vā samaṇassa gotamassa sāvakā vā āgantvā vāressanti, vāretuṃ mā adatthāti lañjaṃ adaṃsu. Rājā lañjaṃ gahetvā “gacchatha kārethā”ti āha.

1007. In the first of the second chapter, regarding Rājakārāma: in the monastery that obtained this name because it was built by the king; it was built by King Pasenadi of Kosala. It is said that at the time of the first enlightenment, seeing the Teacher who had attained the peak of gain and reputation, the heretics thought: 'The ascetic Gotama has attained the peak of gain and reputation. But it is not by relying on any other virtue or concentration that he has attained such a peak of gain and reputation. Rather, the most auspicious place in the land has been taken by him. If we too could have a monastery built near Jetavana, we would also attain the peak of gain and reputation.' Having persuaded their own supporters, they obtained about one hundred thousand kahāpaṇas, and taking them, they went to the king's presence. The king asked, 'What is this?' They gave a bribe, saying, 'We are building a monastery for heretics near Jetavana. If the ascetic Gotama or the disciples of the ascetic Gotama come and try to prevent it, do not allow them to prevent it.' The king, having taken the bribe, said, 'Go and do it.'

Te [M 3.0314] gantvā, attano upaṭṭhākehi dabbasambhāre āharāpetvā, thambhussāpanādīni karontā, uccāsaddā mahāsaddā ekakolāhalaṃ akaṃsu. Satthā gandhakuṭito nikkhamma pamukhe ṭhatvā “ke pana te, ānanda, uccāsaddā mahāsaddā kevaṭṭā maññe macchavilope”ti?, Pucchi. Titthiyā, bhante[V 3.0313], jetavanasamīpe titthiyārāmaṃ karontīti. Ānanda, ime sāsanena paṭiviruddhā bhikkhusaṅghassa aphāsuvihāraṃ karissanti, rañño ārocetvā vārāpehīti.

They went, had materials brought by their supporters, and while doing things like erecting pillars, they made loud noises, great noises, a single uproar. The Teacher, emerging from the Fragrant Abode and standing at the entrance, asked, 'Ānanda, who are these making loud noises, great noises? They seem like fishermen, I think, scrambling for fish.' 'Venerable sir, the heretics are building a monastery for heretics near Jetavana.' 'Ānanda, these opponents of the Teaching will cause an uncomfortable dwelling for the community of monks. Inform the king and have them stopped.'

Thero bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ gantvā rājadvāre aṭṭhāsi. Rañño “therā, deva, āgatā”ti nivedayiṃsu. Rājā lañjassa gahitattā na nikkhami. Therā gantvā satthu ārocayiṃsu. Satthā sāriputtamoggallāne pesesi. Rājā tesampi dassanaṃ na adāsi. Te āgantvā satthu ārocayiṃsu “na, bhante, rājā nikkhanto”ti. Satthā taṅkhaṇaṃyeva byākāsi – “attano rajje ṭhatvā kālaṃ kātuṃ na labhissatī”ti.

The elder, together with the community of monks, went and stood at the king's gate. They informed the king, 'Your Majesty, the elders have come.' The king, because he had taken the bribe, did not come out. The elders went and informed the Teacher. The Teacher sent Sāriputta and Moggallāna. The king did not grant an audience even to them. They came and informed the Teacher, 'Venerable sir, the king did not come out.' At that very moment, the Teacher declared: 'Remaining in his own kingdom, he will not get to pass away.'

Dutiyadivase ca sāmaṃyeva bhikkhusaṅghaparivāro gantvā [P 3.0284] rājadvāre aṭṭhāsi. Rājā “satthā āgato”ti sutvā nikkhamitvā, nivesanaṃ pavesetvā, sārapallaṅke nisīdāpetvā, yāgukhajjakaṃ adāsi. Satthā paribhuttayāgukhādanīyo “yāva bhattaṃ niṭṭhāti, tāva satthu santike nisīdissāmī”ti āgantvā nisinnaṃ rājānaṃ “tayā, mahārāja, idaṃ nāma kata”nti avatvā, “kāraṇeneva naṃ saññāpessāmī”ti idaṃ atītakāraṇaṃ āhari – mahārāja, pabbajite nāma aññamaññaṃ yujjhāpetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Atītepi isayo aññamaññaṃ yujjhāpetvā saha raṭṭhena rājā samuddaṃ paviṭṭhoti. Kadā bhagavāti?

On the second day, he himself, surrounded by the community of monks, went and stood at the king's gate. Hearing, 'The Teacher has come,' the king came out, led him into the residence, seated him on a splendid couch, and offered him gruel and solid food. After the Teacher had consumed the gruel and food, to the king who had come and sat down thinking, 'I will sit in the Teacher's presence until the meal is finished,' he did not say, 'Great king, this deed was done by you.' Instead, thinking, 'I will make him understand by means of a reason,' he brought up this past incident: 'Great king, it is not proper to make those who have gone forth quarrel with one another. In the past, a king, having made sages quarrel with one another, entered the ocean along with his kingdom.' 'When was this, Blessed One?'

Atīte, mahārāja, bharuraṭṭhe bharurājā nāma rajjaṃ kāreti. Pañcasatā pañcasatā dve isigaṇā pabbatapādato loṇambilasevanatthāya bharunagaraṃ gantvā nagarassa avidūre dve rukkhā atthi, paṭhamaṃ āgato isigaṇo ekassa rukkhassa mūle nisīdi, pacchāgatopi ekassāti. Te yathābhirantaṃ viharitvā pabbatapādaṃ eva agamaṃsu. Te puna āgacchantāpi attano rukkhamūleyeva nisīdanti. Addhāne gacchante eko rukkho sukkhi, tasmiṃ sukkhe āgatā tāpasā “ayaṃ rukkho mahā, amhākampi tesampi [M 3.0315] pahossatī”ti itaresaṃ rukkhamūlassa ekapadese nisīdiṃsu. Te pacchā āgacchantā rukkhamūlaṃ apavisitvā bahi ṭhitāva “kasmā tumhe ettha nisīdathā”ti āhaṃsu. Ācariyā amhākaṃ rukkho sukkho, ayaṃ rukkho mahā, tumhepi pavisatha, tumhākampi amhākampi pahossatīti. Te “na mayaṃ pavisāma, nikkhamatha tumhe”ti kathaṃ vaḍḍhetvā “na tumhe attanova manena nikkhamissathā”ti hatthādīsu gahetvā nikkaḍḍhiṃsu. Te “hotu sikkhāpessāma ne”ti iddhiyā sovaṇṇamayāni dve cakkāni rajatamayañca [V 3.0314] akkhaṃ māpetvā pavaṭṭentā rājadvāraṃ agamiṃsu. Rañño “evarūpaṃ, deva, tāpasā paṇṇākāraṃ gahetvā ṭhitā”ti nivedayiṃsu. Rājā tuṭṭho “pakkosathā”ti te pakkosāpetvā “mahākammaṃ tumhehi kataṃ, atthi vo kiñci mayā kattabba”nti āha. Āma, mahārāja, amhākaṃ nisinnaṭṭhānaṃ ekarukkhamūlaṃ atthi, taṃ aññehi isīhi gahitaṃ, taṃ no dāpehīti. Rājā [P 3.0285] purise pesetvā tāpase nikkaḍḍhāpesi.

In the past, great king, in the Bharu country, a king named Bharu ruled. Two groups of five hundred sages each went from the Himalayan foothills to the city of Bharu for the purpose of partaking of salt and sour flavors. Not far from the city there were two trees. The group of sages that arrived first sat at the base of one tree, and the group that arrived later sat at the base of the other. Having dwelt there as long as they pleased, they returned to the Himalayan foothills. When they came again, they would sit at the base of their own respective trees. As time went on, one tree withered. When it withered, the ascetics who arrived thought, 'This tree is large; it will be enough for us and for them,' and they sat down in one part of the base of the other sages' tree. When those sages arrived later, they did not enter the base of the tree but stood outside and said, 'Why are you sitting here?' The others replied, 'Teachers, our tree has withered. This tree is large; you too should enter, it will be enough for you and for us.' They said, 'We will not enter. You get out!' Having escalated the argument, they said, 'You will not leave of your own accord,' and grabbing them by their hands and so on, they dragged them out. The others thought, 'So be it. We shall teach them a lesson.' By means of psychic power, they created two golden wheels and a silver axle and, rolling them, went to the king's gate. They announced to the king, 'Your Majesty, ascetics are standing here holding such a gift.' The king was pleased and said, 'Summon them.' Having had them summoned, he said, 'A great deed has been done by you. Is there anything that should be done for you by me?' 'Yes, great king. There is the base of a tree where we used to sit. It has been taken by other sages. Have it given to us.' The king, sending his men, had those ascetics dragged out.

Te bahi ṭhitā “kiṃ nu kho datvā labhiṃsū”ti olokayamānā “idaṃ nāmā”ti disvā “mayampi lañjaṃ datvā puna gaṇhissāmā”ti iddhiyā sovaṇṇamayaṃ rathapañjaraṃ māpetvā ādāya agamaṃsu. Rājā disvā tuṭṭho – “kiṃ, bhante, kātabba”nti?, Āha. Mahārāja amhākaṃ rukkhamūle añño isigaṇo nisinno, taṃ no rukkhamūlaṃ dāpehīti. Rājā purise pesetvā te nikkaḍḍhāpesi. Tāpasā aññamaññaṃ kalahaṃ katvā, “ananucchavikaṃ amhehi kata”nti vippaṭisārino hutvā pabbatapādameva agamaṃsu. Tato devatā “ayaṃ rājā dvinnaṃ isigaṇānaṃ hatthato lañjaṃ gahetvā aññamaññaṃ kalahaṃ kārāpesī”ti kujjhitvā mahāsamuddaṃ ubbaṭṭetvā tassa rañño vijitaṃ yojanasahassamattaṭṭhānaṃ samuddameva akaṃsūti.

Standing outside, they looked on, thinking, 'What indeed did they give to obtain it?' Seeing that it was by giving a certain thing, they thought, 'We too shall give a bribe and take it back.' By their supernatural power, they created a golden chariot-cage, and taking it, they went. The king, seeing it, was delighted and asked, 'Venerable sirs, what is to be done?' They said, 'Great king, another group of ascetics is seated at the foot of our tree; have the foot of our tree given to us.' The king sent his men and had those ascetics driven out. The ascetics, having quarreled with one another, became remorseful, thinking, 'An unsuitable thing has been done by us,' and went back to the foot of the mountain. Then the deities became angry, thinking, 'This king, having taken a bribe from the hands of two groups of ascetics, caused them to quarrel with each other.' They caused the great ocean to surge up and made that king's territory, an area of a thousand yojanas, into an ocean itself.

“Isīnamantaraṃ katvā, bharurājāti me sutaṃ;

Ucchinno saha raṭṭhehi, sa rājā vibhavaṅgato”ti. (jā. 1.2.125) –

Having created a division among the ascetics, King Bharu—so I have heard—was annihilated along with his kingdom; that king went to destruction.

Evaṃ bhagavatā imasmiṃ atīte dassite yasmā buddhānaṃ nāma kathā okappaniyā hoti, “tasmā rājā attano kiriyaṃ sallakkhetvā anupadhāretvā [M 3.0316] mayā akattabbaṃ kammaṃ kata”nti “gacchatha, bhaṇe, titthiye nikkaḍḍhathā”ti nikkaḍḍhāpetvā cintesi – “mayā kārito vihāro nāma natthi, tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne vihāraṃ kāressāmī”ti tesaṃ dabbasambhārepi adatvā vihāraṃ kāresi. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

Thus, when this past event was pointed out by the Blessed One, because the speech of the Buddhas is indeed trustworthy, the king, having reflected on his own action, thought, 'Without proper consideration, a deed that should not be done has been done by me.' Having had the sectarians driven out with the words, 'Go, sirs, drive out the sectarians!', he then thought, 'There is no monastery that I have had built; I shall have a monastery built in that very place.' Without giving them back their building materials, he had the monastery built. In reference to that, this was said.

2-3. Brāhmaṇasuttādivaṇṇanā

2-3. Commentary on the Brāhmaṇa Sutta and so forth.

1008-9. Dutiye udayagāmininti attano samaye vaḍḍhigāminiṃ. Maraṇaṃ āgameyyāsīti maraṇaṃ iccheyyāsi, pattheyyāsi vā. Tatiyaṃ uttānameva.

In the second sutta, `udayagāminiṃ` means leading to growth in one’s own doctrine. `Maraṇaṃ āgameyyāsi` means: would you desire death, or would you long for it? The third sutta is self-evident.

4. Duggatibhayasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Duggatibhaya Sutta

1010. Catutthe [V 3.0315] sabbaduggatibhayaṃ samatikkantoti manussadobhaggaṃ paṭikkhittaṃ.

In the fourth sutta, by the phrase 'having overcome all fear of bad destinations,' human misfortune is rejected.

5. Duggativinipātabhayasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Duggativinipātabhaya Sutta

1011. Pañcame [P 3.0286] sabbaduggativinipātabhayaṃ samatikkantoti manussadobhaggena saddhiṃ cattāro apāyā paṭikkhittā.

4. In the fifth sutta, by the phrase 'having overcome all fear of bad destinations and ruin,' the four lower realms are rejected along with human misfortune.

6. Paṭhamamittāmaccasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Paṭhamamittāmaccasutta

1012. Chaṭṭhe mittāti aññamaññassa gehe āmisaparibhogavasena vohāramittā. Amaccāti āmantanapaṭimantanairiyāpathādīsu ekato pavattakiccā. Ñātīti sassusasurapakkhikā. Sālohitāti samānalohitā bhātibhaginimātulādayo.

1010. In the sixth, 'friends' means friends by transaction, through the partaking of material goods in each other's houses. 'Companions' are those who have shared duties in matters such as conversation, friendly talk, deportment, and so on. 'Relatives' are those on the side of the father-in-law and mother-in-law. 'Blood-kin' are those of the same blood, such as brothers, sisters, maternal uncles, and so on.

7. Dutiyamittāmaccasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Dutiyamittāmaccasutta

1013. Sattame aññathattaṃ nāma pasādaññathattaṃ bhāvaññathattaṃ gatiaññathattaṃ lakkhaṇaññathattaṃ vipariṇāmaññathattanti anekavidhaṃ. Tattha mahābhūtesu bhāvaññathattaṃ adhippetaṃ. Suvaṇṇādibhāvena hi ghanasaṇṭhitāya pathavidhātuyā vilīyitvā udakabhāvaṃ āpajjamānāya purimabhāvo vigacchati, bhāvaññathattaṃ paññāyati. Lakkhaṇaṃ pana na vigacchati, kakkhaḷalakkhaṇāva hoti. Ucchurasādibhāvena ca yūsākārasaṇṭhitāya āpodhātuyā [M 3.0317] sussitvā ghanapathavibhāvaṃ āpajjamānāya purimabhāvo vigacchati, bhāvaññathattaṃ paññāyati. Lakkhaṇaṃ pana na vigacchati, ābandhanalakkhaṇāva hoti. Tatridaṃ aññathattanti ettha pana gatiaññathattaṃ adhippetaṃ, tañhi ariyasāvakassa natthi. Pasādaññathattampi natthiyeva, idha pana pasādaphalaṃ pakāsetuṃ gatiaññathattameva dassitaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

1013. In the seventh, 'alteration' is of many kinds: alteration of confidence, alteration of state, alteration of destination, alteration of characteristic, and alteration by transformation. Among these, alteration of state is intended with regard to the great elements. For when the earth element, which is solid and compact in the form of gold and so on, melts and reaches the state of water, its former state ceases, and an alteration of state is discerned. But its characteristic does not cease; it is still of the characteristic of hardness. And when the water element, which has reached a liquid state in the form of sugarcane juice and so on, is cooked and reaches the state of the solid earth element as lump sugar, its former state ceases, and an alteration of state is discerned. But its characteristic does not cease; it is still of the characteristic of cohesion. Here, however, in the phrase 'this is alteration', alteration of destination is intended, for that does not exist for a noble disciple. Alteration of confidence also does not exist, but here, to show the fruit of confidence, only alteration of destination is shown. The rest is clear everywhere.

Rājakārāmavaggo dutiyo.

The Rājakārāma Vagga is the second.

3. Saraṇānivaggo

3. The Saraṇāni Vagga.

1-2. Paṭhamamahānāmasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-2. Commentary on the Paṭhamamahānāma Sutta and so forth.

1017-18. Tatiyassa [V 3.0316][P 3.0287] paṭhame iddhanti telamadhuphāṇitādīhi samiddhaṃ. Phītanti hatthūpagasīsūpagagīvūpagādialaṅkāravasena supupphitaṃ. Ākiṇṇamanussanti nirantaramanussaṃ. Sambādhabyūhanti byūhā vuccanti avinibbiddharacchāyo, yā paviṭṭhamaggeneva niggacchanti, tā sambādhā byūhā bahukā etthāti sambādhabyūhaṃ. Imināpi nagarassa ghanavāsameva dīpeti. Bhantenāti ito cito ca paribbhamantena uddhatacārinā. Dutiyaṃ uttānameva.

In the first of the third, 'prosperous' means endowed with oil, honey, molasses, and so on. 'Flourishing' means like a well-blossomed flower, by way of ornaments for the hands, head, neck, and so on. 'Crowded with people' means filled with people without interval. 'With congested thoroughfares': 'thoroughfares' are said to be streets that are not through-ways, from which one must exit by the same way one entered. There are many such congested thoroughfares here, thus it is 'with congested thoroughfares'. By this too, it shows that the city is densely inhabited. 'Wandering' means by one wandering restlessly here and there, behaving with agitation. The second is clear.

3. Godhasakkasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Godhasakka Sutta.

1019. Tatiye bhagavāva etaṃ jāneyya etehi dhammehi samannāgataṃ vā asamannāgataṃ vāti idaṃ so sakko tīhi dhammehi samannāgatassa puggalassa sotāpannabhāvaṃ, catūhi vā dhammehi samannāgatassa sotāpannabhāvaṃ bhagavāva jānātīti adhippāyena āha.

1019. In the third sutta: This statement, 'Only the Blessed One would know whether one is endowed with these qualities or not endowed,' that Sakyan, Godha, spoke with the intention that only the Blessed One knows the state of being a stream-enterer for a person endowed with three qualities, or the state of being a stream-enterer for a person endowed with four qualities.

Kocideva dhammasamuppādo uppajjeyyāti kiñcideva kāraṇaṃ uppajjeyya. Ekato assa bhagavā, ekato bhikkhusaṅghoti yasmiṃ kāraṇe uppanne bhagavā bhikkhusaṅghena nānāladdhiko hutvā ekaṃ vādaṃ vadanto ekato assa, bhikkhusaṅghopi ekaṃ vadanto ekatoti [M 3.0318] attho. Tenevāhanti yaṃ vādaṃ tumhe vadetha, tamevāhaṃ gaṇheyyanti. Nanu ca ariyasāvakassa ratanattaye pasādanānattaṃ natthi, atha kasmā esa evamāhāti? Bhagavato sabbaññutāya. Evañhissa hoti “bhikkhusaṅgho attano asabbaññutāya ajānitvāpi katheyya, satthu pana aññāṇaṃ nāma natthī”ti. Tasmā evamāha. Aññatra kalyāṇā aññatra kusalāti kalyāṇameva kusalameva vadāmi, na kalyāṇakusalavimuttanti. Apicassa anavajjanadoso esoti.

‘If some arising of a matter were to arise’ means if some cause whatsoever were to arise. ‘On one side would be the Blessed One, on the other the Saṅgha of monks’ means: when some cause arises, the Blessed One, having a different view from the Saṅgha of monks and speaking one doctrine, would be on one side, and the Saṅgha of monks, also speaking one doctrine, would be on the other side; this is the meaning. ‘Therefore I...’ means: ‘Whatever view you speak, that very one I would accept.’ Is it not so that for a noble disciple there is no difference in confidence in the Three Jewels? Why then does he speak thus? Because of the Blessed One’s omniscience. For it occurs to him thus: ‘The Saṅgha of monks, due to their not being omniscient, might speak even without knowing, but for the Teacher, there is nothing called the unknown.’ Therefore, he speaks thus. ‘Except for the good, except for the wholesome’ means: ‘I speak only of the good, only of the wholesome; I do not speak of what is devoid of the good and wholesome.’ Moreover, this is his blameless fault.

4. Paṭhamasaraṇānisakkasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the First Sutta about Saraṇāni the Sakyan.

1020. Catutthe [V 3.0317][P 3.0288] idha mahānāma ekacco puggaloti idaṃ na kevalaṃ saraṇāni eva apāyato mutto, imepi puggalā muttāti dassetuṃ āraddhaṃ. Mattaso nijjhānaṃ khamantīti pamāṇena ca olokanaṃ khamanti. Iminā dhammānusārimaggaṭṭhapuggalaṃ dasseti. Agantā nirayanti maggaṭṭhapuggalo hi apāyato parimuttoti vā parimuccissatīti vā vattuṃ na vaṭṭati, parimuccatīti pana vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Yasmā ca parimuccati, tasmā gantā nāma na hotīti, “agantā”ti vutto, na gacchatīti attho. Saddhāmattaṃ pemamattanti iminā saddhānusārimaggaṭṭhapuggalaṃ dasseti. Mahāsālāti samīpe ṭhiteva cattāro mahāsārarukkhe dassento āha. Maraṇakāle sikkhaṃ samādiyīti maraṇasamaye tīsu sikkhāsu paripūrakārī ahosīti dasseti.

1020. In the fourth sutta, this phrase, 'Here, Mahānāma, a certain person...' was introduced to show that not only was Saraṇāni the Sakyan freed from the plane of misery, but these persons too are freed. 'They tolerate reflection to a degree' means they endure contemplation to a certain measure. By this, it indicates the person established in the path as a Dhamma-follower. As for 'not a goer to hell': indeed, for a person established in the path, it is not proper to say that they 'are freed' from the plane of misery or 'will be freed,' but it is proper to say that they 'are being freed.' And because one is being freed, one is not called a 'goer'; for that reason, it is said 'not a goer' (agantā), meaning one is not going. By this phrase, 'mere faith, mere affection,' it indicates the person established in the path as a faith-follower. As for 'great sāl trees,' he said this while pointing out four great sāl trees full of heartwood that were standing nearby. 'At the time of death, he undertook the training' shows that at the time of death, he became a fulfiller of the three trainings.

5. Dutiyasaraṇānisakkasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Second Sutta about Saraṇāni the Sakyan.

1021. Pañcame dukkhettanti visamakhettaṃ. Dubbhūmanti ūsarabhūmiṃ loṇūpahataṃ. Khaṇḍānīti paribhinnāni. Pūtīnīti udakena temetvā pūtibhāvaṃ āpannāni. Vātātapahatānīti vātātapena hatattā nirojabhāvaṃ gatāni. Asārādānīti anādinnasārāni agahitasārāni. Asukhasayitānīti na koṭṭhādīsu pakkhipitvā suṭṭhu ṭhapitāni. Sukhasayitānīti ṭhapitaṭṭhānato cattāro māse acalitāni.

1021. In the fifth [discourse]: 'an uneven field' means an uneven field. 'Barren land' means alkaline soil damaged by salt. 'Broken' means split or fragmented. 'Rotten' means soaked with water and become putrid. 'Scorched by wind and sun' means destroyed by wind and sun, having lost their vigor. 'Without essence' means their essence has not been taken. 'Not well laid' means not properly placed in storage. 'Well laid' means undisturbed for four months from where they were placed.

6. Paṭhamaanāthapiṇḍikasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the First Anāthapiṇḍika Discourse.

1022. Chaṭṭhe [M 3.0319] ṭhānaso vedanā paṭippassambheyyāti khaṇena vedanā paṭippassambheyya. Micchāñāṇenāti [P 3.0289] micchāpaccavekkhaṇena micchāvimuttiyāti aniyyānikavimuttiyā. Tasmā saddhañca sīlañcāti gāthā vuttatthā eva. Yatra hi nāmāti yo nāma.

1022. In the sixth [discourse]: 'the feeling should be allayed as it arises' means the feeling should be allayed in a moment. 'With wrong knowledge' means with wrong reflection. 'With wrong liberation' means with non-leading-out liberation. Therefore, 'faith and virtue'—the verse is of stated meaning. 'Wherever indeed' means that which indeed.

7. Dutiyaanāthapiṇḍikasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Second Anāthapiṇḍika Discourse.

1023. Sattame [V 3.0318] samparāyikaṃ maraṇabhayanti samparāyahetukaṃ maraṇabhayaṃ gihisāmīcikānīti gihīnaṃ anucchavikāni. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

1023. In the seventh [discourse]: 'fear of death concerning the next world' means fear of death that has the next world as its cause. 'Householders’ customary practices' means suitable for householders. The rest is clear throughout.

Saraṇānivaggo tatiyo.

The Saraṇāni Vagga is the third.

4. Puññābhisandavaggo

4. The Chapter on Streams of Merit.

1. Paṭhamapuññābhisandasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the First Discourse on Streams of Merit.

1027. Catutthassa paṭhame puññābhisandā kusalābhisandāti puññanadiyo kusalanadiyo. Sukhassāhārāti sukhassa paccayā.

1027. In the first [discourse] of the fourth [chapter]: 'streams of merit, streams of the wholesome' means rivers of merit, rivers of the wholesome. 'Providers of happiness' means conditions for happiness.

4. Paṭhamadevapadasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the First Discourse on Deva-Footprints.

1030. Catutthe devapadānīti devānaṃ ñāṇena, devassa vā ñāṇena akkantapadāni. Visuddhiyāti visujjhanatthāya. Pariyodapanāyāti puriyodapanatthāya jotanatthāya. Imasmiṃ sutte cattāropi phalaṭṭhapuggalā visuddhaṭṭhena devā nāma jātā.

1030. In the fourth [discourse]: ‘divine states’ means states trodden by the knowledge of the devas or by the knowledge of a deva. ‘For purification’ means for the purpose of being purified. ‘For cleansing’ means for the purpose of being cleansed all around. In this discourse, the four persons established in fruition are called ‘devas’ in the sense of being purified.

8. Vassasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Rainy Season Discourse

1034. Aṭṭhame pāraṃgantvāti pāraṃ vuccati nibbānaṃ, taṃ patvāti attho. Āsavānaṃ khayāya saṃvattantīti na paṭhamaṃ nibbānaṃ gantvā pacchā saṃvattanti, gacchamānā eva saṃvattanti. Desanā pana evaṃ katā.

1034. In the eighth [discourse]: ‘having gone to the far shore’ means the far shore is called Nibbāna; the meaning is having attained it. ‘They conduce to the destruction of the taints’ means they do not first go to Nibbāna and then conduce to it; they conduce to it while in the process of going. The teaching, however, is presented thus.

10. Nandiyasakkasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Nandiya the Sakyan Discourse

1036. Dasame [M 3.0320] divā pavivekāya rattiṃ paṭisallānāyāti divā pavivekatthāya rattiṃ paṭisallānatthāya[V 3.0319]. Dhammā na pātubhavantīti samathavipassanā dhammā na uppajjanti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

1036. In the tenth [discourse]: ‘for seclusion by day, for retreat by night’ means for the purpose of seclusion by day, for the purpose of retreat by night. ‘The dhammas do not appear’ means the dhammas of serenity and insight do not arise. The rest is clear throughout.

Puññābhisandavaggo catuttho.

The Fourth Chapter on Streams of Merit.

5. Sagāthakapuññābhisandavaggo

5. The Chapter on Streams of Merit with Verses

1. Paṭhamaabhiasandasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the First Sutta on Streams of Merit

1037. Pañcamassa [P 3.0290] paṭhame asaṅkhyeyyoti āḷhakagaṇanāya asaṅkhyeyyo, yojanavasena panassa saṅkhyā atthi. Bahubheravanti saviññāṇakaaviññāṇakānaṃ bheravārammaṇānaṃ vasena bahubheravaṃ. Puthūti bahu. Savantīti sandamānā. Upayantīti upagacchanti.

1037. In the first [sutta] of the fifth [chapter]: ‘innumerable’ means immeasurable by the āḷhaka measure, but its quantity exists in terms of yojanas. ‘Very fearful’ means having many fearful objects by way of fearful objects, both sentient and non-sentient. ‘Many’ means abundant. ‘Flowing’ means streaming. ‘Approaching’ means drawing near.

2. Dutiyaabhisandasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Second Sutta on Streams of Merit

1038. Dutiye yatthimā mahānadiyo saṃsandanti samentīti yasmiṃ saṃbhajje etā mahānadiyo ekībhavanti, nirantarā bhavantīti attho.

1038. In the second [sutta]: ‘where these great rivers meet and converge’ means that at that confluence these great rivers become one, becoming uninterrupted—this is the meaning.

3. Tatiyaabhisandasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Third Sutta on Streams of Merit

1039. Tatiye puññakāmoti puññatthiko. Kusale patiṭṭhitoti maggakusale patiṭṭhito. Bhāveti maggaṃ amatassa pattiyāti nibbānassa pāpuṇanatthaṃ arahattamaggaṃ bhāveti. Dhammasārādhigamoti dhammasāro vuccati ariyaphalaṃ dhammasāro, adhigamo assāti dhammasārādhigamo, adhigataphaloti attho. Khaye ratoti kilesakkhaye rato.

1039. In the third [sutta]: ‘desiring merit’ means one who seeks merit. ‘Established in the wholesome’ means established in the wholesome [state] of the path. ‘He develops the path for the attainment of the deathless’ means he develops the path to Arahantship for the purpose of reaching Nibbāna. ‘Attainment of the essence of the Dhamma’: the noble fruit is called the essence of the Dhamma; one for whom there is attainment of this essence of the Dhamma is a ‘dhammasārādhigamo’; the meaning is one who has attained the fruit. ‘Delighting in destruction’ means delighting in the destruction of defilements.

4. Paṭhamamahaddhanasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the First Sutta on Great Wealth

1040. Catutthe [V 3.0320][M 3.0321] aḍḍho mahaddhanoti sattavidhena ariyadhanena aḍḍho ceva mahaddhano ca. Teneva bhogena mahābhogo. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

1040. In the fourth [sutta]: ‘rich and greatly wealthy’ means rich and greatly wealthy with the sevenfold noble wealth. By that same possession, one has great possessions. The rest is clear everywhere.

Sagāthakapuññābhisandavaggo pañcamo.

The Fifth Chapter on Streams of Merit with Verses.

6. Sappaññavaggo

6. The Chapter on the Wise

2. Vassaṃvuttasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Sutta on Residing for the Rains

1048. Chaṭṭhassa dutiye ayamadhippāyo – sotāpanno bhikkhu ettakena vosānaṃ anāpajjitvā tāneva indriyabalabojjhaṅgāni samodhānetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā sakadāgāmimaggaṃ pāpuṇissati, sakadāgāmī anāgāmimaggaṃ, anāgāmī arahattamagganti imamatthaṃ sandhāya bhagavatā imasmiṃ sutte sāsane tanti paveṇī kathitāti.

1048. In the second [sutta] of the sixth [chapter], this is the intended meaning: a monk who is a stream-enterer, not arriving at a slackening of effort with just this much, having unified those same faculties, powers, and enlightenment factors, and having developed insight, will reach the path of the once-returner; a once-returner, the path of the non-returner; a non-returner, the path of Arahantship. With reference to this meaning, the Blessed One, in this sutta, set forth the textual lineage of the Dispensation.

3. Dhammadinnasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Dhammadinna Sutta

1049. Tatiye [P 3.0291] dhammadinnoti sattasu janesu eko. Buddhakālasmiñhi dhammadinno upāsako, visākho upāsako, uggo gahapati, citto gahapati, hatthako āḷavako, cūḷaanāthapiṇḍiko, mahāanāthapiṇḍikoti ime satta janā pañcasataupāsakaparivārā ahesuṃ. Etesu esa aññataro.

1049. In the third [sutta]: Dhammadinna is one of seven people. For, during the Buddha's time, the lay follower Dhammadinna, the lay follower Visākha, the householder Ugga, the householder Citta, Hatthaka of Āḷavī, Cūḷa Anāthapiṇḍika, and Mahā Anāthapiṇḍika—these seven people had retinues of five hundred lay followers each. Among these, this one was one.

Gambhīrāti dhammagambhīrā sallasuttādayo. Gambhīratthāti atthagambhīrā cetanāsuttantādayo. Lokuttarāti lokuttaratthadīpakā asaṅkhatasaṃyuttādayo. Suññatappaṭisaṃyuttāti sattasuññatādīpakā khajjanikasuttantādayo. Upasampajja viharissāmāti paṭilabhitvā viharissāma. Evañhi vo, dhammadinna, sikkhitabbanti evaṃ tumhehi candopamapaṭipadaṃ rathavinītapaṭipadaṃ moneyyapaṭipadaṃ mahāariyavaṃsapaṭipadaṃ [V 3.0321] pūrentehi sikkhitabbaṃ. Iti satthā imesaṃ upāsakānaṃ asayhabhāraṃ āropesi. Kasmā[M 3.0322]? Ete kira na attano bhūmiyaṃ ṭhatvā ovādaṃ yāciṃsu, avisesena pana sabbabhāraṃ ukkhipituṃ samatthā viya “ovadatu no, bhante, bhagavā”ti yāciṃsu. Tena tesaṃ satthā asayhabhāraṃ āropento evamāha. Na kho netanti na kho etaṃ. Nakāro panettha byañjanasandhimattamevāti veditabbo. Tasmāti yasmā idāni attano bhūmiyaṃ ṭhatvā ovādaṃ yācatha, tasmā.

‘Profound’ means profound in Dhamma, such as the Sallasutta and others. ‘Profound in meaning’ means profound in exegesis, such as the Cetanāsuttanta and others. ‘Supramundane’ means expositors of the supramundane, such as the Asaṅkhatasaṃyutta and others. ‘Connected with emptiness’ means expositors of the emptiness of a being, such as the Khajjanikasuttanta and others. ‘Having attained, we will dwell’ means having attained, we will dwell. ‘Thus, Dhammadinna, you should train’ means: in this way you must train by fulfilling the practice like the moon, the practice of the relay chariots, the practice of sageliness, and the practice of the great noble traditions. Thus, the Teacher placed upon these lay followers an unbearable burden. Why? It is said that they did not request advice while standing on their own ground, but as if they were capable of lifting the entire burden, they requested indiscriminately, saying, ‘Venerable sir, may the Blessed One advise us.’ Therefore, the Teacher, placing upon them an unbearable burden, spoke thus. ‘Na kho netaṃ’ should be parsed as ‘na kho etaṃ’. Here, the letter ‘n’ should be understood as being merely for euphonic conjunction. ‘Therefore’ means: because now you request advice while standing on your own ground, therefore…

4. Gilānasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Discourse on the Sick

1050. Catutthe na kho panetanti na kho amhehi etaṃ. Sappañño upāsakoti sotāpanno adhippeto. Assāsanīyehi dhammehīti assāsakarehi dhammehi. Assāsatāyasmāti assāsatu āyasmā. Mārisoti maraṇapaṭibaddho. Maraṇadhammoti maraṇasabhāvo. Adhimocehīti ṭhapehi. Adhimocitanti ṭhapitaṃ. Evaṃ [P 3.0292] vimuttacittassāti evaṃ arahattaphalavimuttiyā vimuttacittassa. Yadidaṃ vimuttiyā vimuttanti yaṃ idaṃ vimuttiṃ ārabbha vimuttiyā nānākaraṇaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, na taṃ vadāmi. Bhikkhusaṅghassa hi cetiyaṅgaṇabodhiyaṅgaṇavattesu ceva asītikkhandhakavattesu cāti āgamanīyaguṇesu pamāṇaṃ nāma natthi, paṭividdhe pana magge vā phale vā upāsakānañca bhikkhūnañca nānākaraṇaṃ natthi.

1050. In the fourth [sutta]: ‘na kho panetaṃ’ means ‘we have not heard this.’ ‘A wise lay follower’ means a stream-enterer is intended. ‘With comforting qualities’ means with qualities that bring solace. ‘Assāsatāyasmā’ means: may the venerable one be comforted. ‘Mārisa’ means one connected with death. ‘Subject to death’ means having the nature of death. ‘Resolve’ means ‘establish.’ ‘Resolved’ means ‘established.’ ‘Thus, with a liberated mind’ means thus, with a mind liberated by the liberation that is the fruit of Arahantship. ‘That is, liberated by liberation’ means whatever distinguishing factor of liberation could be spoken of in relation to liberation, that I do not speak of. For the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, indeed, in the preliminary virtues of the path, such as the duties of the stupa grounds, the Bodhi-tree grounds, and the eighty Khandhaka duties, there is no measure. However, when the path or the fruit has been penetrated, there is no distinguishing factor between lay followers and bhikkhus.

9. Paññāpaṭilābhasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Discourse on Gaining Wisdom

1055. Navame paññāpaṭilābhāya saṃvattantīti ettha satta sekkhā paññaṃ paṭilabhanti nāma, khīṇāsavo paṭiladdhapañño nāmāti veditabbo. Parato paññābuddhiyātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

1055. In the ninth [sutta], regarding the phrase ‘it leads to the acquisition of wisdom,’ here the seven trainees are said to be gaining wisdom, whereas the one whose taints are destroyed is called one who has gained wisdom; thus it should be understood.
