Hereafter, in such phrases as ‘wisdom, understanding,’ and so on, this is the same method. The remainder is clear everywhere.

Sappaññavaggo chaṭṭho.

The Sappañña Chapter, the Sixth.

7. Mahāpaññavaggo

7. The Chapter on Great Wisdom

1. Mahāpaññāsuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Sutta on Great Wisdom

1058. Sattame [V 3.0322][M 3.0323] mahāpaññatāya saṃvattantītiādīsu “mahante atthe pariggaṇhātīti mahāpaññā”tiādinā paṭisambhidāyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 2.4) vuttanayeneva sabbattha sabbapadesu attho veditabbo. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

1058. In the seventh, in 'it leads to great wisdom' and so on, the meaning should be understood everywhere in all passages according to the method stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: 'It comprehends great meanings, therefore it is “great wisdom.”' The remainder is clear everywhere.

Sotāpattisaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Connected Discourses on Stream-Entry is concluded.

12. Saccasaṃyuttaṃ

12. The Connected Discourses on the Truths

1. Samādhivaggo

1. The Chapter on Concentration

1. Samādhisuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Sutta on Concentration

1071. Saccasaṃyuttassa [V 3.0323][P 3.0293][M 3.0324] paṭhame samādhiṃ, bhikkhaveti te kira bhikkhū cittekaggatāya parihāyanti, atha nesaṃ satthā – “evamete cittekaggataṃ labhitvā, kammaṭṭhānaṃ vaḍḍhetvā, visesaṃ pāpuṇissantī”ti imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, “idaṃ dukkha”nti yogo karaṇīyoti ettha yathābhūtādivasena kāraṇacchedo veditabbo. Idañhi vuttaṃ hoti – bhikkhave, yasmā samāhito bhikkhu cattāri saccāni yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, tasmā tumhehi ca samāhitehi catunnaṃ saccānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānanatthāya “idaṃ dukkha”nti yogo karaṇīyo. Tathā yasmā cattāri saccāni tathāgatasseva pātubhāvā pākaṭāni honti, yasmā ca tathāgatena suvibhattāni, yasmā ca tesu aparimāṇā vaṇṇā aparimāṇāni padabyañjanāni, yasmā ca tesaṃ appaṭividdhattā vaṭṭaṃ vaḍḍhati, tesaṃ paṭividdhakālato paṭṭhāya na vaḍḍhati, tasmā “evaṃ no vaṭṭaṃ na vaḍḍhissatī”ti tumhehi “idaṃ dukkha”nti yogo karaṇīyo.

1071. In the first sutta of the Connected Discourses on the Truths, regarding 'concentration, monks': it seems those monks were declining in one-pointedness of mind. Then the Teacher, thinking, 'Thus, having attained one-pointedness of mind and having developed the meditation subject, they will reach distinction,' began this teaching for them. Therefore, in the passage, 'Therefore, monks, an effort should be made: “This is suffering,”' the division of the reason should be understood by way of 'as it really is,' and so on. For this is what is said: Monks, because a concentrated monk understands the four truths as they really are, therefore you too, having become concentrated, for the sake of understanding the four truths as they really are, should make the effort: 'This is suffering.' Furthermore, because the four truths become manifest only with the appearance of the Tathāgata, and because they are well-analyzed by the Tathāgata, and because in them there are immeasurable letters and immeasurable phrases and expressions, and because from not having penetrated them the round of existence increases, but from the time of penetrating them onwards it does not increase; therefore, thinking, 'Thus our round of existence will not increase,' you should make the effort: 'This is suffering.'

2. Paṭisallānasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Sutta on Seclusion

1072. Dutiyaṃ kāyavivekavikalānaṃ kāyavivekapaṭilābhatthāya vuttaṃ.

1072. The second sutta was spoken for the sake of attaining bodily seclusion for those deficient in bodily seclusion.

3. Paṭhamakulaputtasuttādivaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Suttas beginning with the First on the Clan Son

1073-75. Tatiye abhisamayāyāti abhisamayatthāya. Samaṇabrāhmaṇāti cettha sāsanāvacarā [V 3.0324] adhippetā. Tathā catutthapañcamesu, tena tena abhilāpena bujjhanakānaṃ pana ajjhāsayenetāni vuttāni.

In the third sutta, 'for realization' (abhisamayāya) means for the purpose of realization. Here, 'ascetics and brahmins' (samaṇabrāhmaṇā) is intended to mean those who are followers of the Dispensation. The meaning is to be understood similarly in the fourth and fifth suttas; however, these were spoken according to the inclination of those who are to awaken, by means of this or that particular expression.

6. Dutiyasamaṇabrāhmaṇasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Explanation of the Second Sutta on Ascetics and Brahmins

1076. Chaṭṭhe [M 3.0325] abhisambuddhaṃ pakāsesunti abhisambuddho ahanti evaṃ attānaṃ abhisambuddhaṃ pakāsayiṃsu. Imasmiñhi sutte sabbaññubuddhā ca samaṇagahaṇena gahitā.

1076. In the sixth sutta, 'they would declare themselves fully enlightened' (abhisambuddhaṃ pakāsesuṃ) means they would declare, 'I am fully enlightened,' thus proclaiming themselves as fully enlightened. For in this sutta, the Omniscient Buddhas are also included under the term 'ascetics'.

10. Tiracchānakathāsuttavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Sutta on Animal-Level Talk

1080. Dasame [P 3.0294] anekavihitanti anekavidhaṃ. Tiracchānakathanti aniyyānikattā saggamokkhamaggānaṃ tiracchānabhūtaṃ kathaṃ. Rājakathantiādīsu rājānaṃ ārabbha “mahāsammato mandhātā dhammāsoko evaṃ mahānubhāvo”tiādinā nayena pavattakathā rājakathā. Esa nayo corakathādīsu. Tesu “asuko rājā abhirūpo dassanīyo”tiādinā nayena gehasitakathāva tiracchānakathā hoti. “Sopi nāma evaṃ mahānubhāvo khayaṃ gato”ti evaṃ pavattā pana kammaṭṭhānabhāve tiṭṭhati. Coresupi “mūladevo evaṃ mahānubhāvo meghamālo evaṃ mahānubhāvo”ti tesaṃ kammaṃ paṭicca “aho sūrā”ti gehasitakathāva tiracchānakathā. Yuddhepi bhāratayuddhādīsu “asukena asuko evaṃ mārito evaṃ viddho”ti kāmassādavaseneva kathā tiracchānakathā, “tepi nāma khayaṃ gatā”ti evaṃ pavattā pana sabbattha kammaṭṭhānameva hoti. Apica annādīsu “evaṃ vaṇṇavantaṃ gandhavantaṃ rasavantaṃ phassasampannaṃ khādimha bhuñjimha pivimha paribhuñjimhā”ti kāmassādavasena kathetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Sātthakaṃ pana katvā “pubbe evaṃ vaṇṇādisampannaṃ annaṃ pānaṃ vatthaṃ sayanaṃ mālaṃ gandhaṃ vilepanaṃ sīlavantānaṃ adamha, cetiye pūjaṃ akarimhā”ti kathetuṃ vaṭṭati.

1080. In the tenth sutta, 'of various kinds' (anekavihitaṃ) means of diverse kinds (anekavidhaṃ). 'Animal-level talk' (tiracchānakathā) refers to talk that is obstructive to the paths to heaven and liberation because it is not a means of escape. In 'talk about kings' (rājakathā), and so on, talk that proceeds by referring to kings, such as, 'Mahāsammata, Mandhātā, and Dhammāsoka were of such great power,' is 'talk about kings.' This method also applies to 'talk about thieves,' and so on. Among these, worldly talk, such as, 'Such and such a king is handsome and pleasing to see,' is animal-level talk. However, when the talk proceeds as, 'Even he, of such great power, came to ruin,' it stands as a meditation subject. Regarding thieves, too, worldly talk such as, 'Mūladeva was of such great power; Meghamāla was of such great power,' and then, based on their deeds, 'Oh, how brave!' is animal-level talk. In talk about war, too, such as the Bhārata war, to say, 'So-and-so was killed in this way; so-and-so was struck down in that way,' out of sensual delight, is animal-level talk. But when it proceeds as, 'They too, indeed, came to ruin,' it becomes a meditation subject in every case. Furthermore, regarding food and so on, it is not proper to speak out of sensual delight, saying, 'We ate, consumed, drank, and enjoyed food so endowed with color, fragrance, taste, and texture.' It is proper, however, to make it meaningful and say, 'In the past, we gave food, drink, clothing, bedding, garlands, perfumes, and ointments endowed with such qualities as color to the virtuous; we made offerings at a cetiya.'

Ñātikathādīsupi “amhākaṃ ñātakā sūrā samatthā”ti vā, “pubbe mayaṃ evaṃ vicitrehi yānehi vicarimhā”ti vā assādavasena vattuṃ na vaṭṭati. Sātthakaṃ pana katvā “tepi no ñātakā khayaṃ gatā”ti vā, “pubbe mayaṃ evarūpā upāhanā saṅghassa adamhā”ti vā kathetabbā. Gāmakathādīsupi suniviṭṭhadunniviṭṭhasubhikkhadubbhikkhādivasena vā “asukagāmavāsino [V 3.0325] sūrā samatthā”ti vā evaṃ assādavasena vattuṃ na vaṭṭati, sātthakaṃ pana katvā “saddhā pasannā”ti vā, “khayaṃ gatā”ti vā vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Nigamanagarajanapadakathāsupi eseva nayo.

In 'talk about relatives' (ñātikathā), and so on, it is not proper to speak with delight, saying, 'Our relatives are brave and capable,' or 'In the past, we traveled in such splendid vehicles.' Instead, one should speak meaningfully, saying, 'Even those relatives of ours have passed away,' or 'In the past, we gave such sandals to the Saṅgha.' In 'talk about villages' (gāmakathā), and so on, it is not proper to speak with delight, describing whether a village is well-established or poorly established, prosperous or experiencing famine, or saying, 'The residents of such-and-such a village are brave and capable.' Instead, one should speak meaningfully, saying, 'They are faithful and devout,' or 'They have passed away.' The same principle applies to 'talk about towns, cities, and districts' (nigamanagarajanapadakathā).

Itthikathāpi [M 3.0326][P 3.0295] vaṇṇasaṇṭhānādīni paṭicca assādavasena vattuṃ na vaṭṭati, “saddhā pasannā khayaṃ gatā”ti evameva vaṭṭati. Sūrakathāpi “nandimitto nāma yodho sūro ahosī”ti assādavasena vattuṃ na vaṭṭati, “saddho pasanno ahosi, khayaṃ gato”ti evameva vaṭṭati. Surākathātipi pāṭho. Sāpi cesā surākathā “evarūpā nāma surā pītā ratijananī hotī”ti assādavaseneva na vaṭṭati, ādīnavavasena pana “ummattakasaṃvattanikā”tiādinā nayena vaṭṭati. Visikhākathāpi “asukavisikhā suniviṭṭhā dunniviṭṭhā”ti vā, “asukavisikhāya vāsino sūrā samatthā”ti vā assādavaseneva vattuṃ na vaṭṭati, “saddhā pasannā khayaṃ gatā”ti eccevaṃ vaṭṭati. Kumbhaṭṭhānakathāti udakatitthakathā vuccati, kumbhadāsikathā vā. Sāpi “pāsādikā naccituṃ gāyituṃ chekā”ti assādavasena na vaṭṭati, “saddhā pasannā”tiādinā nayeneva vaṭṭati.

Similarly, in 'talk about women' (itthikathā), it is not proper to speak with delight regarding their beauty or form; it is only proper to say, 'She was faithful, serene, and has passed away.' Likewise, in 'talk about heroes' (sūrakathā), it is not proper to speak with delight, saying, 'There was a brave warrior named Nandimitta'; it is only proper to say, 'He was faithful, serene, and has passed away.' There is also the reading 'talk about liquor' (surākathā). Even this 'talk about liquor' is not proper to speak of in terms of pleasure, saying, 'Such and such liquor, when drunk, brings about delight'; rather, it is proper to speak of it in terms of its dangers, in the manner of, 'It leads to madness,' and so on. Similarly, in 'talk about streets' (visikhākathā), it is not proper to speak with delight, saying, 'Such and such a street is well-laid-out or poorly laid-out,' or 'The residents of such and such a street are brave and capable'; it is only proper to say, 'They were faithful, serene, and have passed away.' 'Talk about water-pot places' (kumbhaṭṭhānakathā) is said to be talk about watering places (udakatitthakathā), or talk about water-pot maidservants (kumbhadāsikathā). Even here, it is not proper to speak with delight, saying, 'She is charming and skilled in dancing and singing'; rather, it is proper to speak in the manner of, 'She was faithful, serene,' and so on.

Pubbapetakathāti atītañātikathā. Tattha vattamānañātikathāsadisova vinicchayo. Nānattakathāti purimapacchimakathāhi vimuttā avasesā nānāsabhāvā niratthakakathā. Lokakkhāyikāti “ayaṃ loko kena nimmito, asukena nāma nimmito, kāko seto aṭṭhīnaṃ setattā, balākā rattā lohitassa rattattā”ti evamādikā lokāyatavitaṇḍasallāpakathā. Samuddakkhāyikā nāma “kasmā samuddo sāgaro, sāgaradevena khanitattā sāgaro, khato meti hatthamuddāya niveditattā samuddo”ti evamādikā niratthakasamuddakkhāyikakathā. Iti bhavo iti abhavoti yaṃ vā taṃ vā niratthakakāraṇaṃ vatvā pavattitakathā itibhavābhavakathā. Ettha ca bhavoti sassataṃ, abhavoti ucchedaṃ. Bhavoti vuddhi, abhavoti [P 3.0296] hāni. Bhavoti kāmasukhaṃ, abhavoti attakilamatho. Iti imāya chabbidhāya itibhavābhavakathāya saddhiṃ bāttiṃsa tiracchānakathā nāma honti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

'Talk about former departed ones' (pubbapetakathā) is talk about past relatives. The determination here is the same as for talk about present relatives. 'Talk of diversity' (nānattakathā) refers to the remaining useless talk of various natures, distinct from the preceding and succeeding talks. 'Talk about the world' (lokakkhāyikā) is worldly, contentious, and frivolous discussion, such as: 'By whom was this world created? It was created by so-and-so. A crow is white because its bones are white; a heron is red because its blood is red.' 'Talk about the ocean' (samuddakkhāyikā) refers to useless talk about the ocean, such as: 'Why is the ocean called 'sāgara'? Because it was dug by the deva Sāgara. It is called 'samudda' because it was announced with a hand gesture, saying, 'It has been dug by me.'' 'Talk of existence and non-existence' (itibhavābhavakathā) is talk that proceeds by stating some pointless reason, such as 'existence is thus' or 'non-existence is thus.' Here, 'existence' (bhava) means eternalism, and 'non-existence' (abhava) means annihilationism. 'Existence' means growth, and 'non-existence' means decline. 'Existence' means sensual pleasure, and 'non-existence' means self-mortification. Thus, along with these six types of 'talk of existence and non-existence,' there are thirty-two kinds of animal-like talk. The rest is clear in meaning everywhere.

Paṭhamo vaggo.

The First Chapter.

2. Dhammacakkappavattanavaggo

2. The Chapter on Setting in Motion the Wheel of Dhamma

1. Dhammacakkappavattanasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta

1081. Dutiyassa [V 3.0326][M 3.0327] paṭhame bārāṇasiyanti evaṃnāmake nagare. Isipatane migadāyeti isīnaṃ patanuppatanavasena evaṃladdhanāme migānaṃ abhayadānavasena dinnattā migadāyasaṅkhāte ārāme. Ettha hi uppannuppannā sabbaññuisayo patanti, dhammacakkappavattanatthaṃ nisīdantīti attho. Nandamūlakapabbhārato sattāhaccayena nirodhasamāpattito vuṭṭhitā anotattadahe katamukhadhovanādikiccā ākāsena āgantvā paccekabuddhaisayopettha otaraṇavasena patanti, uposathatthañca anuposathatthañca sannipatanti, gandhamādanaṃ paṭigacchantāpi tatova uppatantīti iminā isīnaṃ patanuppatanavasena taṃ “isipatana”nti vuccati.

1081. In the first sutta of the second chapter: 'In Bārāṇasī' means in the city so named. 'At Isipatana in the Migadāya' means in the park called Migadāya, which received the name Isipatana because it is the place of the descending and ascending of seers, and which is called Migadāya because it was given as a sanctuary for deer. For here, all-knowing seers, whenever they arise, descend and sit down for the purpose of setting in motion the Wheel of Dhamma—this is the meaning. Also, Paccekabuddha seers—having emerged from the attainment of cessation at the Nandamūlaka cave after seven days, having performed the duty of washing the face and so on at Lake Anotatta, and having come through the sky—descend here by way of alighting. They also assemble for the purpose of the Uposatha and the Anuposatha. And when returning to Mount Gandhamādana, they fly up from there. Thus, because of this descending and ascending of seers, it is called 'Isipatana'.

Āmantesīti dīpaṅkarapādamūle katābhinīhārato paṭṭhāya pāramiyo pūrento anupubbena pacchimabhave katābhinikkhamano anupubbena bodhimaṇḍaṃ patvā tattha aparājitapallaṅke nisinno mārabalaṃ bhinditvā paṭhamayāme pubbenivāsaṃ anussaritvā majjhimayāme dibbacakkhuṃ visodhetvā pacchimayāmāvasāne dasasahassilokadhātuṃ unnādento sabbaññutaṃ patvā satta sattāhāni bodhimaṇḍe vītināmetvā mahābrahmunā āyācitadhammadesano buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ voloketvā lokānuggahena bārāṇasiṃ gantvā pañcavaggiye saññāpetvā dhammacakkaṃ pavattetukāmo āmantesi.

'He addressed them' means: Starting from when he made his aspiration at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, fulfilling the perfections in due course, he reached his final existence. In that final existence, having made the great renunciation, he gradually reached the Bodhi-maṇḍa. There, seated on the unconquered throne, having vanquished the forces of Māra, in the first watch of the night he recollected his past lives; in the middle watch, he purified the divine eye; and at the end of the last watch, causing the ten-thousandfold world system to resound, he attained omniscience. Having spent seven weeks at the Bodhi-maṇḍa, being one whose teaching of the Dhamma was requested by the great Brahmā, he surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye out of compassion for the world. Having gone to Bārāṇasī and convinced the group of five monks, desiring to set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, he addressed them.

Dveme, bhikkhave, antāti dve ime, bhikkhave, koṭṭhāsā. Imassa pana padassa saha samudāhārena samudāhāranigghoso heṭṭhā avīciṃ upari bhavaggaṃ patvā dasasahassilokadhātuṃ pattharitvā [P 3.0297] aṭṭhāsi. Tasmiṃyeva samaye aṭṭhārasakoṭisaṅkhā brahmāno samāgacchiṃsu, pacchimadisāya sūriyo atthameti, pācīnadisāya āsāḷhanakkhattena yutto puṇṇacando uggacchati. Tasmiṃ samaye bhagavā imaṃ dhammacakkappavattanasuttaṃ ārabhanto “dveme, bhikkhave, antā”tiādimāha.

'These two extremes, O monks' means: these two portions, O monks. Simultaneously with this utterance, its reverberation, having reached Avīci below and the peak of existence above, spread throughout the ten-thousandfold world system and remained. At that very moment, eighteen crores of Brahmās assembled. In the western direction, the sun was setting; in the eastern direction, the full moon, conjoined with the Āsāḷha constellation, was rising. At that time, the Blessed One, beginning this Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, spoke the words beginning with, 'These two extremes, O monks...'

Tattha [M 3.0328] pabbajitenāti gihisaṃyojanaṃ chinditvā pabbajjupagatena. Na sevitabbāti na vaḷañjetabbā[V 3.0327]. Yo cāyaṃ kāmesu kāmasukhallikānuyogoti yo ca ayaṃ vatthukāmesu kilesakāmasukhassa anuyogo. Hīnoti lāmako. Gammoti gāmavāsīnaṃ santako. Pothujjanikoti andhabālajanena āciṇṇo. Anariyoti na ariyo na visuddho na uttamo na vā ariyānaṃ santako. Anatthasaṃhitoti na atthasaṃhito, hitasukhāvahakāraṇaṃ anissitoti attho. Attakilamathānuyogoti attano kilamathassa anuyogo, attano dukkhakaraṇanti attho. Dukkhoti kaṇṭakāpassayaseyyādīhi attamāraṇehi dukkhāvaho.

Therein, 'by one who has gone forth' means by one who has gone forth after cutting the fetters of a householder. 'Not to be pursued' means not to be practiced. 'And this devotion to indulgence in sensual pleasure' means this devotion to the pleasure associated with defilements in regard to sensual objects. 'Base' means inferior. 'Of the villagers' means belonging to village-dwellers. 'Of the common person' means practiced by blind, foolish common people. 'Ignoble' means not noble, not pure, not excellent, nor belonging to the noble ones. 'Unconnected with benefit' means not connected with benefit; the meaning is that it is not based on a cause that brings welfare and happiness. 'The devotion to self-mortification' means the devotion to afflicting oneself; the meaning is the causing of suffering to oneself. 'Painful' means bringing suffering through self-torments such as lying on a bed of thorns.

Paññācakkhuṃ karotīti cakkhukaraṇī. Dutiyapadaṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Upasamāyāti kilesūpasamatthāya. Abhiññāyāti catunnaṃ saccānaṃ abhijānanatthāya. Sambodhāyāti tesaṃyeva sambujjhanatthāya. Nibbānāyāti nibbānasacchikiriyāya. Sesamettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ heṭṭhā tattha tattha vuttameva. Saccakathāpi sabbākāreneva visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.529) vitthāritā.

'Vision-creating' (cakkhukaraṇī) is so called because it creates the eye of wisdom. The second term is a synonym for that very one. 'For calming' means for the purpose of calming the defilements. 'For direct knowledge' means for the purpose of directly knowing the four truths. 'For enlightenment' means for the purpose of fully awakening to those very truths. 'For Nibbāna' means for the purpose of realizing Nibbāna. Whatever else should be said here has already been said below in the respective places. The discourse on the truths has also been explained in detail in every way in the Visuddhimagga.

Tiparivaṭṭanti saccañāṇakiccañāṇakatañāṇasaṅkhātānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ parivaṭṭānaṃ vasena tiparivaṭṭaṃ. Ettha hi “idaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ, idaṃ dukkhasamudaya”nti evaṃ catūsu saccesu yathābhūtaṃ ñāṇaṃ saccañāṇaṃ nāma. Tesuyeva “pariññeyyaṃ pahātabba”nti evaṃ kattabbakiccajānanañāṇaṃ kiccañāṇaṃ nāma. “Pariññātaṃ pahīna”nti evaṃ tassa tassa kiccassa katabhāvajānanañāṇaṃ katañāṇaṃ nāma. Dvādasākāranti tesaṃyeva ekekasmiṃ sacce tiṇṇaṃ tiṇṇaṃ ākārānaṃ vasena dvādasākāraṃ. Ñāṇadassananti etesaṃ tiparivaṭṭānaṃ dvādasannaṃ ākārānaṃ vasena uppannañāṇasaṅkhātaṃ dassanaṃ. Dhammacakkhunti aññattha [P 3.0298] tayo maggā tīṇi ca phalāni dhammacakkhu nāma honti, idha paṭhamamaggova.

'Having three turnings' means having three turnings by way of the three turnings designated as the knowledge of the truth, the knowledge of the function, and the knowledge of the accomplishment. Herein, the knowledge of the four truths as they really are—such as 'This is the noble truth of suffering,' 'This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering'—is called the knowledge of the truth. Regarding these same truths, the knowledge of the function to be performed—such as 'This should be fully understood,' 'This should be abandoned'—is called the knowledge of the function. The knowledge of the fact that each respective function has been accomplished—such as 'This has been fully understood,' 'This has been abandoned'—is called the knowledge of the accomplishment. 'Having twelve aspects' means having twelve aspects by way of three aspects for each of the truths. 'The knowledge and vision' is the vision, designated as knowledge, that arises by way of these three turnings and twelve aspects. 'The Dhamma-eye': elsewhere, the three lower paths and the three lower fruits are called the Dhamma-eye, but here only the first path is meant.

Dhammacakketi paṭivedhañāṇe ceva desanāñāṇe ca. Bodhipallaṅke nisinnassa hi catūsu saccesu uppannaṃ dvādasākāraṃ paṭivedhañāṇampi, isipatane nisinnassa dvādasākārāya saccadesanāya pavattitaṃ desanāñāṇampi dhammacakkaṃ nāma. Ubhayampi hetaṃ dasabalassa ure pavattañāṇameva. Imāya [M 3.0329] desanāya pakāsentena bhagavatā dhammacakkaṃ pavattitaṃ nāma. Taṃ panetaṃ dhammacakkaṃ yāva aññāsikoṇḍaññatthero aṭṭhārasahi brahmakoṭīhi saddhiṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāti[V 3.0328], tāva naṃ bhagavā pavatteti nāma, patiṭṭhite ca pavattitaṃ nāma. Taṃ sandhāya pavattite ca pana bhagavatā dhammacakke bhummā devā saddamanussāvesuntiādi vuttaṃ.

'In the Wheel of Dhamma' refers to both the knowledge of penetration and the knowledge of teaching. For the one seated on the throne of enlightenment, the twelve-aspected knowledge of penetration that arose regarding the four truths is called the Wheel of Dhamma; and for the one seated at Isipatana, the knowledge of teaching set in motion through the teaching of the truths in twelve aspects is also called the Wheel of Dhamma. Both of these are indeed the knowledge that arose in the breast of the Ten-Powered One. By the Blessed One proclaiming this teaching, the Wheel of Dhamma is said to be set in motion. However, this Wheel of Dhamma is said to be being set in motion by the Blessed One only for as long as the Elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña, together with eighteen crores of Brahmās, is not yet established in the fruit of stream-entry; and when he is established, it is said to have been set in motion. With reference to this, it was said: 'And when the Wheel of Dhamma had been set in motion by the Blessed One, the earth-dwelling devas raised a cry...'

Tattha bhummāti bhūmaṭṭhakadevatā. Saddamanussāvesunti ekappahāreneva sādhukāraṃ datvā – “etaṃ bhagavatā”tiādīni vadantā anusāvayiṃsu. Obhāsoti sabbaññutaññāṇobhāso. So hi tadā devānaṃ devānubhāvaṃ atikkamitvā virocittha. Aññāsi vata, bho, koṇḍaññoti imassapi udānassa udāhāranigghoso dasasahassilokadhātuṃ pharitvā aṭṭhāsi.

Herein, 'earth-dwelling' means the deities established on the earth. 'They raised a cry' means that, with a single utterance, they gave their approval and, saying, 'This by the Blessed One,' and so on, they caused it to be heard successively. 'Radiance' means the radiance of the knowledge of omniscience. For at that time, it surpassed the divine radiance of the devas and shone forth. The resounding echo of this inspired utterance, 'Indeed, Koṇḍañña has understood!' also pervaded the ten-thousandfold world-system and stood fast.

9. Saṅkāsanasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Saṅkāsana Sutta

1089. Navame aparimāṇā vaṇṇāti appamāṇāni akkharāni. Byañjanāti tesaṃyeva vevacanaṃ, vaṇṇānaṃ vā ekadesā yadidaṃ byañjanā nāma. Saṅkāsanāti vibhattiyo. Ekamekasmiñhi sacce sabbākārena vitthāriyamāne vaṇṇādīnaṃ anto nāma natthi. Tasmā evamāha.

1089. In the ninth sutta, 'immeasurable letters' means countless syllables. 'Consonants' is a synonym for these, or what are called consonants are a part of the letters. 'Elucidations' means the analyses. For when each single truth is expounded in every way, there is no end to the letters, and so on. Therefore, He spoke thus.

10. Tathasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Tathā Sutta

1090. Dasame sabhāvāvijahanaṭṭhena tathaṃ. Dukkhañhi dukkhameva vuttaṃ. Sabhāvassa amoghatāya avitathaṃ. Na hi dukkhaṃ adukkhaṃ nāma hoti. Aññabhāvānupagamena anaññathaṃ. Na hi dukkhaṃ samudayādibhāvaṃ upagacchati. Samudayādīsupi eseva nayoti.

1090. In the tenth sutta, 'real' (tatha) is meant in the sense of not abandoning its own nature. For suffering is spoken of as just suffering. 'Not false' (avitatha) is meant because of the infallibility of its own nature. For suffering is not called non-suffering. 'Not otherwise' (anaññatha) is meant by not taking on another nature. For suffering does not take on the nature of origination, etc. This same method should be understood for origination and so forth.

Dhammacakkappavattanavaggo dutiyo.

The Dhammacakkappavattana Vagga, the second chapter.

3. Koṭigāmavaggo

3. The Koṭigāma Chapter

1. Koṭigāmasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Koṭigāma Sutta

1091. Tatiyassa [V 3.0329][P 3.0299] paṭhame ananubodhāti ananubujjhanena. Appaṭivedhāti appaṭivijjhanena.

1091. In the first sutta of the third chapter, 'from not awakening' (ananubodhā) means through not properly awakening. 'From not penetrating' (appaṭivedhā) means through not penetrating.

2. Dutiyakoṭigāmasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Second Koṭigāma Sutta

1092. Dutiye [M 3.0330] cetovimutti paññāvimuttīti phalasamāpattiphalapaññānaṃ nāmaṃ.

1092. In the second sutta, 'liberation of mind' and 'liberation by wisdom' are names for the attainment of fruition and the wisdom of fruition.

7. Tathasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Tathā Sutta

1097. Sattame tasmā ariyasaccānīti yasmā tathāni avitathāni anaññathāni, tasmā ariyānaṃ saccānīti vuccanti. Na hi vitathāni ariyā ariyasaccato paṭivijjhanti.

1097. In the seventh sutta, regarding 'therefore, they are noble truths': because they are real, not false, and not otherwise, they are therefore called the truths of the noble ones. For the noble ones do not penetrate what is false as a noble truth.

8. Lokasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Loka Sutta

1098. Aṭṭhame tathāgato ariyo, tasmā “ariyasaccānī”ti yasmā ariyena tathāgatena paṭividdhattā desitattā ca tāni ariyasantakāni honti, tasmā ariyassa saccattā ariyasaccānīti attho.

1098. In the eighth sutta: the Tathāgata is noble; therefore, they are called 'Noble Truths'. The meaning is this: because they have been penetrated and taught by the noble Tathāgata, they are the property of the noble one. Therefore, because they are truths belonging to the noble one, they are called 'Noble Truths'.

10. Gavampatisuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Gavampati Sutta

1100. Dasame sahañcaniketi sahañcaniyanagare. Yo, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ passati, dukkhasamudayampi [V 3.0330] so passatītiādi ekapaṭivedhavasena vuttaṃ, imasmiñhi sutte ekapaṭivedhova kathito.

1100. In the tenth sutta, 'at Sahañcanika' means in the city of Sahañcaniya. 'Bhikkhus, one who sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering,' and so on, was spoken by way of a single penetration, for in this sutta, only a single penetration is taught.

Koṭigāmavaggo tatiyo.

The Koṭigāma Vagga, the third chapter.

4. Sīsapāvanavaggo

4. The Sīsapā Forest Chapter

1. Sīsapāvanasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Sīsapā Forest Sutta

1101. Catutthassa paṭhame yadidaṃ uparīti yāni imāni upari. Sīsapāvaneti sīsapārukkhe.

1101. In the first sutta of the fourth chapter, 'these above' (yadidaṃ upari) refers to those which are above. 'In the sīsapā forest' (sīsapāvane) means in the sīsapā tree.

2. Khadirapattasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Khadirapatta Sutta

1102. Dutiye [P 3.0300] anabhisameccāti ñāṇena anabhisamāgantvā, appaṭivijjhitvāti attho.

1102. In the second sutta, 'not having realized' (anabhisamecca) means not having properly approached through knowledge, not having penetrated; this is the meaning.

3. Daṇḍasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Daṇḍa Sutta

1103. Tatiye [M 3.0331] asmā lokā paraṃ lokanti imamhā manussalokā paraṃ nirayampi, tiracchānayonimpi, pettivisayampi, manussalokampi, devalokampi, gacchanti, punappunaṃ vaṭṭasmiṃyeva nibbattantīti attho.

1103. In the third sutta, 'from this world to another world' means: from this human world they go to another world—to hell, to the animal realm, to the ghost realm, to the human world, or to the deva world. They are reborn again and again only in the cycle of existence; this is the meaning.

5. Sattisatasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Sattisata Sutta

1105. Pañcame evañcetaṃ, bhikkhave, assāti, bhikkhave, evaṃ ce etaṃ bhaveyya, nirantaraṃ [V 3.0331] sattisatehi haññamānassa dukkhadomanassehi sahevesa saccābhisamayo bhaveyya ceti attho.

1105. In the fifth sutta, 'Monks, if it were so' means: Monks, if it were so, for a person being incessantly struck by a hundred spears, this penetration of the truths would occur together with that very suffering and displeasure; this is the meaning.

9. Indakhīlasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Indakhīla Sutta

1109. Navame mukhaṃ olokentīti ajjhāsayaṃ olokenti. Ajjhāsayo idha mukhanti adhippeto.

1109. In the ninth sutta, 'they look at the face' (mukhaṃ olokenti) means they observe the inclination. Here, by 'face' (mukha), inclination is intended.

10. Vādatthikasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Exposition on the Vādatthika Sutta

1110. Dasame silāyūpoti silāthambho. Soḷasakukkukoti soḷasahattho. Soḷasakukkūtipi pāṭho. Heṭṭhā nemaṅgamāti heṭṭhā āvāṭaṃ paviṭṭhā. Aṭṭha kukku uparinemassāti aṭṭha hatthā āvāṭassa upari uggantvā ṭhitā bhaveyyuṃ. Bhusāti balavatī. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

1110. In the tenth sutta, 'silāyūpo' means a stone pillar. 'Soḷasakukkuko' means sixteen cubits. There is also the reading 'soḷasakukkū'. 'Aṭṭha kukku heṭṭhā nemaṅgamā' means eight cubits would be established, having entered the lower part of the pit. 'Aṭṭha kukku upari nemassa' means eight cubits would be standing, having risen above the pit. 'Bhusā' means powerful. The rest is clear everywhere.

Sīsapāvanavaggo catuttho.

The Sīsapāvana Chapter is the fourth.

5. Papātavaggo

5. The Precipice Chapter

1. Lokacintāsuttavaṇṇanā

1. Exposition on the Lokacintā Sutta

1111. Pañcamassa paṭhame sumāgadhāya pokkharaṇiyāti evaṃnāmikāya pokkharaṇiyā. Lokacintaṃ cintentoti, “kena nu kho candimasūriyā katā, kena mahāpathavī, kena mahāsamuddo, kena sattā uppāditā, kena pabbatā, kena ambatālanāḷikerādayo”ti evarūpaṃ lokacintaṃ cintento nisīdi.

1111. In the first sutta of the fifth chapter, 'by the Sumāgadhā lotus pond' means by a pond so named. 'Pondering about the world' means he sat down thinking, 'By whom, I wonder, were the moon and sun made? By whom was the great earth made? By whom was the great ocean made? By whom were beings produced? By whom were the mountains produced? By whom were mangoes, palmyra fruits, coconuts, and so on produced?'—pondering such thoughts concerning the world.

Vicetoti [V 3.0332][P 3.0301][M 3.0332] vigatacitto vikkhittacitto vā. Bhūtaṃyeva addasāti te kira asurā sambarimāyaṃ samparivattetvā yathā ne so puriso hatthiassādīsu āruhante ukkhipitvā, bhisamuḷālacchiddehi pavisante passati, evaṃ adhiṭṭhahiṃsu. Taṃ sandhāya satthā “bhūtaṃyeva addasā”ti āha. Devānaṃyeva mohayamānāti devānaṃ cittaṃ mohayantā. Tasmāti yasmā lokacintaṃ cintento ummattakopi hoti, tasmā.

'Viceto' means having a mind devoid of one's own and others' welfare, or a scattered mind. As for 'bhūtaṃyeva addasā' (he saw what was real): It is said that those asuras, having employed Sambari's magic, resolved in such a way that the man would see them riding on elephants, horses, and so on, lifting up a lotus bud, and entering through the holes of the lotus stalks and roots. Referring to this, the Teacher said, 'bhūtaṃyeva addasā'. 'Devānaṃyeva mohayamānā' means bewildering the minds of the gods. 'Tasmā' (therefore) means: because one who ponders about the world can even become mad, therefore.

2-3. Papātasuttādivaṇṇanā

2-3. Exposition on the Papāta Sutta, etc.

1112-13. Dutiye paṭibhānakūṭoti eko mahanto pabbatasadiso mariyādapāsāṇo. Tatiye aniṭṭharūpanti aniṭṭhasabhāvaṃ.

In the second sutta, Paṭibhānakūṭa is a single, great, mountain-like boundary stone. In the third sutta, 'aniṭṭharūpaṃ' means of an unpleasant nature.

4. Kūṭāgārasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Exposition on the Kūṭāgāra Sutta

1114. Catutthe heṭṭhimaṃ gharaṃ akaritvāti thambhabhittipādussāpanādinā gharassa heṭṭhimabhāgaṃ akatvā.

1114. In the fourth sutta, 'not constructing the lower part of the house' means not making the lower portion of the house, such as by setting up pillars, the base of walls, and so on.

5. Vālasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Exposition on the Vāla Sutta

1115. Pañcame santhāgāreti sippuggaṇhanasālāyaṃ. Upāsanaṃ karonteti kaṇḍakhipanasippaṃ karonte. Asanaṃ atipātenteti kaṇḍaṃ atikkamente. Poṅkhānupoṅkhanti ekaṃ kaṇḍaṃ khipitvā yathā assa sarassa poṅkhaṃ vijjhati, aparaṃ anupoṅkhaṃ nāma dutiyassa poṅkhaṃ, puna aparaṃ tassa poṅkhanti evaṃ atipātente addasa. Yatra hi nāmāti ye nāma. Durabhisambhavataranti dukkarataraṃ. Sattadhā bhinnassa vālassa koṭiyā koṭiṃ paṭivijjheyyāti ekaṃ vālaṃ sattadhā bhinditvā, tassa ekaṃ bhedaṃ gahetvā, vātiṅgaṇamajjhe bandhitvā, aparaṃ bhedaṃ kaṇḍassa aggakoṭiyaṃ bandhitvā, [P 3.0302] usabhamatte ṭhito kaṇḍabaddhāya koṭiyā taṃ vātiṅgaṇabaddhakoṭiṃ paṭivijjheyyāti attho. Tasmāti yasmā evaṃ duppaṭivijjhāni cattāri saccāni, tasmā.

1115. In the fifth sutta, 'santhāgāra' means in the hall for learning crafts. 'Upāsanaṃ karonte' means those practicing the skill of shooting arrows. 'Asanaṃ atipātente' means those shooting arrows. 'Poṅkhānupoṅkhaṃ' means he saw them shooting in such a way that, having shot one arrow, another pierces its nock; a subsequent arrow, called anupoṅkha, pierces the nock of the second; and again another pierces the nock of that one. 'Yatra hi nāma' means 'ye nāma' (those who). 'Durabhisambhavataraṃ' means more difficult. 'Sattadhā bhinnassa vālassa koṭiyā koṭiṃ paṭivijjheyya' means: having split one hair into seven strands, having taken one strand, having tied it in the middle of an eggplant, and having tied another strand to the very tip of an arrow; standing at a distance of an usabha, he could pierce that tip tied to the eggplant with the tip bound to the arrow—this is the meaning. 'Tasmā' means: because the Four Noble Truths are so difficult to penetrate, therefore.

7. Paṭhamachiggaḷayugasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Exposition on the First Sutta on the Yoke with a Hole

1117. Sattame [V 3.0333][M 3.0333] aññamaññakhādikāti aññamaññaṃ khādanaṃ. Dubbalakhādikāti balavantehi macchādīhi dubbalānaṃ macchādīnaṃ khādanaṃ.

1117. In the seventh sutta, 'aññamaññakhādikā' means the mutual devouring of one another. 'Dubbalakhādikā' means the devouring of the weak fish and other creatures by the strong fish and other creatures.

8. Dutiyachiggaḷayugasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Exposition on the Second Sutta on the Yoke with a Hole

1118. Aṭṭhame mahāpathavīti cakkavāḷagabbhantarā mahāpathavī. Adhiccamidaṃ, bhanteti idaṃ adhiccuppattikaṃ sace taṃ yugaṃ na pūti bhaveyya, samudde udakaṃ na susseyya, so ca kacchapo na mareyya, api nāma yadicchāvasena siyāti attho.

1118. In the eighth sutta, 'the great earth' means the great earth inside the world-sphere. 'This is by chance, venerable sir' means this is a chance occurrence; if that yoke were not to decay, the water in the ocean were not to dry up, and that tortoise were not to die, then perhaps it might happen by some chance—such is the meaning.

Evaṃ adhiccamidaṃ, bhikkhaveti ettha mahāsīvatthero cattāri yugāni dasseti – puratthimacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ ṭhitena purisena pakkhittayugassa hi chiggaḷena tassa andhakacchapassa gīvāya pavesanaṃ viya manussapaṭilābho adhiccapaṭilābhī. Dakkhiṇacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ ṭhitena pakkhittassa pana paribbhamantassa purimayugaṃ patvā chiggaḷena chiggaḷupari āruḷhassa chiggaḷena gīvappavesanaṃ viya tathāgatuppādo adhiccatarasambhavo. Pacchimacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ ṭhitena pakkhittassa pana paribbhamantassa purimayugadvayaṃ patvā chiggaḷena chiggaḷupari āruḷhassa chiggaḷena gīvappavesanaṃ viya tathāgatappaveditassa dhammavinayassa dīpanaṃ adhiccatarasambhavaṃ. Uttaracakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ ṭhitena pakkhittassa pana paribbhamantassa purimayugattayaṃ patvā chiggaḷena chiggaḷupari āruḷhassa chiggaḷena gīvappavesanaṃ viya catusaccapaṭivedho ativiya adhiccatarasambhavo veditabbo. Navamādīni abhisamayasaṃyutte vuttanayānevāti.

In reference to “Thus, monks, this is by chance,” the great elder Mahāsīva illustrates four yokes: For a man standing at the eastern edge of the world-circle, the entry of a yoke thrown by him through its hole into the neck of that blind turtle is like the attainment of human birth, a chance attainment. For one standing at the southern edge of the world-circle, the entry of the neck through the hole of a yoke that has mounted upon the hole of the first yoke, having reached it while spinning, is like the arising of a Tathāgata, a rarer chance occurrence. For one standing at the western edge of the world-circle, the entry of the neck through the hole of a yoke that has mounted upon the holes of the first two yokes, having reached them while spinning, is like the illumination of the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, a rarer chance occurrence. For one standing at the northern edge of the world-circle, the entry of the neck through the hole of a yoke that has mounted upon the holes of the first three yokes, having reached them while spinning, is to be understood as like the penetration of the Four Noble Truths, an exceedingly rare chance occurrence. The ninth and subsequent suttas are to be understood by the method stated in the Abhisamaya Saṃyutta.

Papātavaggo pañcamo.

The Precipice Chapter is the fifth.

6. Abhisamayavaggavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Chapter on Penetration

1121. Abhisamayavaggo [V 3.0334][P 3.0303] nidānavagge abhisamayasaṃyutte vitthāritova.

1121. The Chapter on Penetration has already been elaborated in the Connected Discourses on Penetration, in the Chapter on Causation.

7. Paṭhamaāmakadhaññapeyyālavaggo

7. The First Chapter on the Repetition Series concerning Raw Grain

3. Paññāsuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Discourse on Wisdom

1133. Āmakadhaññapeyyāle [M 3.0334] ariyena paññācakkhunāti vipassanaṃ ādiṃ katvā lokiyalokuttarena ñāṇacakkhunā.

1133. In the repetition series concerning raw grain, 'with the noble eye of wisdom' means with the eye of knowledge, which is mundane and supramundane, beginning with insight.

4. Surāmerayasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Discourse on Liquor and Spirits

1134. Surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhānā paṭiviratāti ettha surā nāma piṭṭhasurā, odanasurā, pūvasurā, kiṇṇapakkhittā, sambhārasaṃyuttāti pañcavidhā. Merayaṃ nāma pupphāsavo, phalāsavoti, evaṃ vutto yo koci āsavo. Majjanti tadeva ubhayaṃ, yaṃ vā panaññampi surāsavavinimuttaṃ madanīyaṃ. Yāya cetanāya taṃ pivanti, sā pamādassa kāraṇattā pamādaṭṭhānaṃ nāma, tato paṭiviratāti attho.

1134. In the passage 'abstained from liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are a basis for heedlessness': Here, 'surā' is of five kinds: liquor made from flour, liquor made from cooked rice, liquor made from cakes, liquor to which yeast is added, and liquor combined with other ingredients. 'Meraya' refers to spirits made from flowers and spirits made from fruit—any such spirit spoken of. 'Majja' refers to both of these, or any other intoxicating substance apart from liquor and spirits. The volition with which one drinks it is called a 'pamādaṭṭhāna', a basis for heedlessness, because it is a cause of heedlessness. 'Paṭiviratā' means one has abstained from that. This is the meaning.

6-7. Matteyyasuttādivaṇṇanā

6-7. Commentary on the Discourse on Respect for One's Mother, etc.

1136-37. Matteyyāti mātuhitā, mātari sammāpaṭipannāti attho. Petteyyādīsu pituhitā petteyyā.

`Matteyyā` means those who act for the welfare of their mother; that is, those who practice rightly towards their mother. This is the meaning. In `petteyyā`, etc., `petteyyā` are those who act for the welfare of their father.

8-9. Sāmaññasuttādivaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on Respect for Ascetics, etc.

1138-39. Samaṇānaṃ [V 3.0335] hitā sāmaññā. Brāhmaṇānaṃ hitā brahmaññā. Tesu tesu sammā paṭipannānaṃyevetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

`Sāmaññā` are those who act for the welfare of ascetics. `Brahmaññā` are those who act for the welfare of brahmins. This is a designation only for those who practice rightly towards these respective persons.

10. Pacāyikasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Discourse on Respect

1140. Kule jeṭṭhāpacāyinoti kule jeṭṭhānaṃ apacāyino, nīcavuttinoti attho.

1140. 'Honoring the elders in the family' means being respectful to the elders in the family; that is, being of humble conduct. This is the meaning.

8. Dutiyaāmakadhaññapeyyālavaggo

8. The Second Chapter on the Repetition Series concerning Raw Grain

8. Bījagāmasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Discourse on Seed-Growth

1148. Bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambhāti [M 3.0335] mūlabījaṃ, khandhabījaṃ, phaḷubījaṃ, aggabījaṃ, bījabījanti pañcavidhassa bījagāmassa ceva yassa kassaci nīlatiṇarukkhādikassa bhūtagāmassa ca samārambhā, chedanapacanādibhāvena vikopanā paṭiviratāti attho.

1148. ‘Abstaining from the destruction of seed-growth and plant-growth’ means abstaining from destroying—by way of cutting, cooking, and so on—the five kinds of seed-growth (root-seed, stem-seed, joint-seed, shoot-seed, and seed-seed) and any kind of plant-growth, such as green grass, trees, and the like. This is the meaning.

9. Vikālabhojanasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Discourse on Eating at the Wrong Time

1149. Vikālabhojanāti kālātikkantabhojanā, majjhanhikātikkamato paṭṭhāya yāvakālikaparibhogāti attho.

1149. ‘Eating at the wrong time’ means eating past the proper time; that is, the consumption of food permissible only in the forenoon, starting from when midday has passed. This is the meaning.

10. Gandhavilepanasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Discourse on Scents and Ointments

1150. Mālādīsu mālāti yaṃ kiñci pupphaṃ. Gandhanti yaṃ kiñci [P 3.0304] gandhajātaṃ. Vilepananti chavirāgakaraṇaṃ. Tattha piḷandhantā dhārenti nāma, ūnaṭṭhānaṃ pūrentā maṇḍenti nāma, gandhavasena [V 3.0336] chavirāgavasena ca sādiyantā vibhūsenti nāma. Ṭhānaṃ vuccati kāraṇaṃ. Tasmā yāya dussīlyacetanāya tāni mālādhāraṇādīni mahājano karoti, tato paṭiviratāti attho.

1150. Regarding ‘garlands, etc.’: ‘Garland’ means any kind of flower. ‘Scent’ means any kind of fragrant substance. ‘Ointment’ means that which colors the skin. Therein, those who wear them are said to be ‘wearing’; those who fill deficient spots are said to be ‘embellishing’; and those who enjoy them by means of fragrance and skin-coloring are said to be ‘adorning’. The word `ṭhāna` (basis) is said to mean `kāraṇa` (cause). Therefore, the meaning is that one abstains from that unwholesome volition with which the populace undertakes those acts of wearing garlands and so forth.

9. Tatiyaāmakadhaññapeyyālavaggo

9. The Third Chapter on the Repetition Series concerning Raw Grain

1. Naccagītasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Discourse on Dancing and Singing

1151. Sāsanassa ananulomattā visūkaṃ paṭāṇībhūtaṃ dassananti visūkadassanaṃ. Attanā naccananaccāpanādivasena naccā ca gītā ca vāditā ca antamaso mayūranaccādivasenāpi pavattānaṃ naccādīnaṃ visūkabhūtā dassanā cāti naccagītavāditavisūkadassanā. Naccādīni hi attanā payojetuṃ vā parehi payojāpetuṃ vā payuttāni passituṃ vā neva bhikkhūnaṃ, na bhikkhunīnaṃ vaṭṭanti.

1151. `Visūkadassanaṃ` means seeing that is like a thorn-trap (paṭāṇībhūtaṃ) and unsuitable (visūkaṃ) because it is not in conformity with (ananulomattā) the Teaching (sāsanassa). `Naccagītavāditavisūkadassanā` means [abstaining] from dancing, singing, and playing music—which occur by means of one's own dancing or causing others to dance, etc., down to at least peacock dancing and the like—and from seeing such dancing, etc., which is unsuitable. Indeed, dancing and so forth, whether one performs them oneself, causes others to perform them, or watches them being performed, are not allowable for monks or for nuns.

2. Uccāsayanasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Discourse on High and Great Beds

1152. Uccāsayanaṃ [M 3.0336] vuccati pamāṇātikkantaṃ. Mahāsayanaṃ akappiyattharaṇaṃ, tato paṭiviratāti attho.

1152. A 'high bed' (uccāsayana) is said to be that which exceeds the proper measure. A 'great bed' (mahāsayana) is one with an unallowable covering. Abstaining from that is the meaning.

3. Jātarūpasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Discourse on Gold and Silver

1153. Jātarūpanti suvaṇṇaṃ. Rajatanti kahāpaṇo – lohamāsako, jatumāsako, dārumāsakoti ye vohāraṃ gacchanti, tassa ubhayassāpi paṭiggahaṇā paṭiviratā. Neva naṃ uggaṇhanti na uggaṇhāpenti, na upanikkhittaṃ sādiyantīti attho.

1153. 'Jātarūpa' means gold. 'Rajata' means a kahāpaṇa—or a lohamāsaka, jatumāsaka, or dārumāsaka—anything that is used in trade. [The precept means] abstaining from accepting both of these. They neither accept it themselves, nor have it accepted by others, nor do they consent to what has been placed nearby. This is the meaning.

4. Āmakadhaññasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Discourse on Uncooked Grain

1154. Āmakadhaññapaṭiggahaṇāti [V 3.0337] sāli-vīhi-yava-godhuma-kaṅgu-varaka-kudrūsakasaṅkhātassa sattavidhassāpi āmakadhaññassa paṭiggahaṇā. Na kevalañca etesaṃ paṭiggahaṇameva, āmasanampi bhikkhūnaṃ na vaṭṭatiyeva.

1154. 'Accepting uncooked grain' means [abstaining] from accepting the seven kinds of uncooked grain, namely: fine rice (sāli), paddy (vīhi), barley (yava), wheat (godhuma), millet (kaṅgu), panic grass (varaka), and kodo millet (kudrūsaka). Not only is accepting them unallowable for monks, but even touching them is not allowable.

5. Āmakamaṃsasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Discourse on Uncooked Meat

1155. Āmakamaṃsapaṭiggahaṇāti ettha aññatra uddissa anuññātā āmakamaṃsamacchānaṃ paṭiggahaṇameva bhikkhūnaṃ na vaṭṭati, no āmasanaṃ.

1155. Regarding 'the acceptance of uncooked meat': Here, apart from what is specifically permitted, only the acceptance of uncooked meat and fish is not allowable for monks; touching them is not unallowable.

6. Kumārikasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Discourse on Young Girls

1156. Itthikumārikapaṭiggahaṇāti ettha itthīti purisantaragatā, itarā kumārikā nāma. Tāsaṃ paṭiggahaṇampi āmasanampi akappiyameva.

1156. Regarding 'the acceptance of women and young girls': Here, a 'woman' (itthī) is one who has gone to another man; the other is called a 'young girl' (kumārikā). Their acceptance and even touching are indeed unallowable.

7. Dāsidāsasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Discourse on Female and Male Slaves

1157. Dāsidāsapaṭiggahaṇāti ettha dāsidāsavaseneva tesaṃ paṭiggahaṇaṃ na vaṭṭati, “kappiyakārakaṃ dammi, ārāmikaṃ dammī”ti evaṃ vutte pana vaṭṭati.

1157. Regarding 'the acceptance of female and male slaves': Here, their acceptance as female and male slaves is not allowable. However, if it is said, 'I give a suitable attendant (kappiyakāraka),' or 'I give a monastery attendant (ārāmika),' then it is allowable.

10. Catutthaāmakadhaññapeyyālavaggo

10. The Fourth Chapter on the Repetition Series concerning Raw Grain

1. Khettavatthusuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Discourse on Fields and Sites

1161. Ajeḷakādīsu [M 3.0337][P 3.0305] khettavatthupariyosānesu kappiyākappiyanayo vinayavasena upaparikkhitabbo[V 3.0338]. Tattha khettaṃ nāma yasmiṃ pubbaṇṇaṃ ruhati. Vatthu nāma yasmiṃ aparaṇṇaṃ ruhati. Yattha vā ubhayaṃ ruhati, taṃ khettaṃ. Tadatthāya akatabhūmibhāgo vatthu. Khettavatthusīsena cettha vāpitaḷākādīnipi saṅgahitāneva.

1161. In cases beginning with goats and sheep and ending with fields and sites, the principle of what is allowable and unallowable should be investigated according to the Vinaya. Therein, a 'field' (khetta) is that in which early grain grows. A 'site' (vatthu) is that in which later grain grows. Or, where both grow, that is a 'field'. A portion of land not yet prepared for that purpose is a 'site'. And here, under the heading of 'fields and sites', even reservoirs, lakes, and so forth are included.

2-3. Kayavikkayasuttādivaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Kayavikkayasutta and so forth.

1162-63. Kayavikkayāti kayā ca vikkayā ca. Dūteyyaṃ vuccati dūtakammaṃ, gihīnaṃ paṇṇaṃ vā sāsanaṃ vā gahetvā tattha tattha gamanaṃ. Pahiṇagamanaṃ vuccati gharā gharaṃ pesitassa khuddakagamanaṃ. Anuyogo nāma tadubhayakaraṇaṃ. Tasmā dūteyyapahiṇagamanānuyogāti evamettha attho veditabbo.

'Buying and selling' means from buying and from selling. 'Messengership' is called the work of a messenger: taking a letter or message of householders and going here and there. 'Going when sent' is called the minor going of one sent from house to house. 'Application' is the name for doing both of these. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: from the application to messengership and going when sent.

4. Tulākūṭasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Tulākūṭa Sutta.

1164. Tulākūṭādīsu kūṭanti vañcanaṃ. Tattha tulākūṭaṃ tāva rūpakūṭaṃ, aṅgakūṭaṃ, gahaṇakūṭaṃ, paṭicchannakūṭanti catubbidhaṃ hoti. Tattha rūpakūṭaṃ nāma dve tulā samarūpā katvā gaṇhanto mahatiyā gaṇhāti, dadanto khuddikāya deti. Aṅgakūṭaṃ nāma gaṇhanto pacchābhāge hatthena tulaṃ akkamati, dadanto pubbabhāge. Gahaṇakūṭaṃ nāma gaṇhanto mūle rajjuṃ gaṇhāti, dadanto agge. Paṭicchannakūṭaṃ nāma tulaṃ susiraṃ katvā anto ayacuṇṇaṃ pakkhipitvā gaṇhanto taṃ pacchābhāge karoti, dadanto aggabhāge.

1164. In the context of fraudulent scales and so forth, 'kūṭa' means deception. Therein, fraudulent scales are of four kinds: deception by appearance, deception by parts, deception by handling, and concealed deception. Herein, deception by appearance is making two scales of the same appearance, and when taking, one takes with the large one, and when giving, one gives with the small one. Deception by parts is, when taking, one presses down on the scale with the hand on the back part, and when giving, on the front part. Deception by handling is, when taking, one holds the rope at the base, and when giving, at the tip. Concealed deception is making the scale hollow, putting iron powder inside, and when taking, one causes that powder to be in the back part, and when giving, in the front part.

Kaṃso vuccati suvaṇṇapāti, tāya vañcanaṃ kaṃsakūṭaṃ. Kathaṃ? Ekaṃ suvaṇṇapātiṃ katvā aññā dve tisso lohapātiyo suvaṇṇavaṇṇā karonti. Tato janapadaṃ gantvā, kiñcideva aḍḍhakulaṃ pavisitvā, “suvaṇṇabhājanāni kiṇathā”ti vatvā, agghe pucchite samagghataraṃ dātukāmā honti, tato tehi “kathaṃ imesaṃ suvaṇṇabhāvo jānitabbo”ti [M 3.0338] vutte “vīmaṃsitvā gaṇhathā”ti suvaṇṇapātiṃ pāsāṇe ghaṃsitvā sabbapātiyo datvā gacchanti.

A golden bowl is called 'kaṃsa,' and deception with it is called 'kaṃsakūṭa.' How? Having made one golden bowl, they make two or three other copper bowls to have the color of gold. Then, having gone to a district and entered some affluent family, they say, 'Buy golden vessels.' When the price is asked, they are willing to give them for a very fair price. Then, when they are asked by them, 'How is the genuine gold nature of these to be known?' they say, 'Test and take them.' They rub the golden bowl on a touchstone, give all the bowls, and depart.

Mānakūṭaṃ hadayabheda-sikhābheda-rajjubhedavasena tividhaṃ hoti. Tattha hadayabhedo sappitelādiminanakāle labbhati[P 3.0306]. Tāni hi gaṇhanto heṭṭhāchiddena mānena “saṇikaṃ āsiñcā”ti vatvā antobhājane [V 3.0339] bahuṃ paggharāpetvā gaṇhāti, dadanto chiddaṃ pidhāya sīghaṃ pūretvā deti. Sikhābhedo tilataṇḍulādiminanakāle labbhati. Tāni hi gaṇhanto saṇikaṃ sikhaṃ ussāpetvā gaṇhāti, dadanto vegena sikhaṃ bhindanto deti. Rajjubhedo khettavatthuminanakāle labbhati. Lañjaṃ alabhantā hi khettaṃ amahantaṃ mahantaṃ katvā minanti.

Deception in measuring is of three kinds: by way of piercing the measure, breaking the peak, and breaking the rope. Herein, piercing the measure is found when measuring things like ghee and oil. For when taking them, using a measure with a hole at the bottom, one says, 'Pour slowly,' and having caused much to flow out into a container underneath, one takes it. When giving, one covers the hole, fills it quickly, and gives. Breaking the peak is found when measuring things like sesame and rice. For when taking them, one slowly raises up the peak and takes. When giving, one fills it quickly and gives while breaking the peak. Breaking the rope is found at the time of measuring fields and sites. For, not receiving a bribe, they measure a field that is not large, making it seem large.

5. Ukkoṭanasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Ukkoṭana Sutta

1165. Ukkoṭanādīsu ukkoṭananti sāmike assāmike kātuṃ lañjaggahaṇaṃ. Vañcananti tehi tehi upāyehi paresaṃ vañcanaṃ. Tatridamekaṃvatthu – eko kira luddako migañca migapotakañca gahetvā āgacchati. Tameko dhutto “kiṃ, bho, migo agghati, kiṃ migapotako”ti?, Āha. “Migo dve kahāpaṇe, migapotako eka”nti ca vutte kahāpaṇaṃ datvā, migapotakaṃ gahetvā thokaṃ gantvā nivatto “na me, bho, migapotakena attho, migaṃ me dehī”ti āha. Tena hi dve kahāpaṇe dehīti. Nanu, bho, mayā paṭhamaṃ eko kahāpaṇo dinnoti. Āma dinnoti. Imampi migapotakaṃ gaṇha, evaṃ so ca kahāpaṇo, ayañca kahāpaṇagghanako migapotakoti dve kahāpaṇā bhavissantīti. So “kāraṇaṃ vadatī”ti sallakkhetvā migapotakaṃ gahetvā migaṃ adāsīti.

1165. Among the terms ukkoṭana, etc., ukkoṭana is the taking of a bribe to make a rightful owner a non-owner. Vañcana is the deceiving of others by various stratagems. In this regard, there is this one story: It is said that a certain hunter, having caught a deer and a fawn, was coming along. A certain rogue asked him, 'Sir, what is the price of the deer? What is the price of the fawn?' When he replied, 'The deer is two kahāpaṇas, the fawn is one,' the rogue gave him one kahāpaṇa, took the fawn, and after going a short distance, returned and said, 'Sir, I have no use for the fawn; give me the deer.' The hunter said, 'In that case, give me two kahāpaṇas.' The rogue replied, 'But sir, did I not already give you one kahāpaṇa?' The hunter said, 'Yes, you did.' The rogue then said, 'Take this fawn also. Thus, that kahāpaṇa and this fawn worth one kahāpaṇa will become two kahāpaṇas.' The hunter, perceiving, 'He speaks with reason,' took the fawn and gave him the deer.

Nikatīti yogavasena vā māyāvasena vā apāmaṅgaṃ pāmaṅganti amaṇiṃ maṇinti, asuvaṇṇaṃ suvaṇṇanti katvā patirūpakena vañcanaṃ. Sāciyogoti kuṭilayogo. Etesaṃyeva ukkoṭanādīnametaṃ nāmaṃ. Tasmā ukkoṭanasāciyogā vañcanasāciyogā nikatisāciyogāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Keci aññaṃ dassetvā aññassa parivattanaṃ sāciyogoti vadanti. Taṃ pana vañcaneneva saṅgahitaṃ.

Nikati is deception by means of contrivance or illusion, making what is not an ornament into an ornament, what is not a gem into a gem, what is not gold into gold, thus deceiving with a counterfeit. Sāciyoga is a crooked contrivance. This is just another name for these very things: ukkoṭana, and so on. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as ukkoṭana-sāciyoga, vañcana-sāciyoga, and nikati-sāciyoga. Some say that sāciyoga is showing one thing and exchanging it for another, but that is included under vañcana.

6-11. Chedanasuttādivaṇṇanā

6-11. Commentary on the Chedana Sutta and so forth

1166-71. Chedanādīsu [M 3.0339] chedananti hatthacchedanādi. Vadhoti maraṇaṃ. Bandhoti rajjubandhanādīhi bandhanaṃ. Viparāmosoti himaviparāmoso, gumbaviparāmosoti duvidho. Yaṃ himapātasamaye himena paṭicchannā hutvā maggapaṭipannaṃ janaṃ musanti, ayaṃ himaviparāmoso. Yaṃ gumbādipaṭicchannā musanti, ayaṃ gumbaviparāmoso.

1166-71. Among the terms chedana, etc., chedana is the cutting off of hands and so forth. Vadha is killing. Bandha is binding with ropes and so forth. Viparāmosa is of two kinds: robbery by snow (himaviparāmosa) and robbery by thickets (gumbaviparāmosa). When, at a time of snowfall, they rob a person proceeding on the path while being concealed by snow, this is robbery by snow. When they rob while being concealed by thickets and so forth, this is robbery by thickets.

Ālopo [V 3.0340][P 3.0307] vuccati gāmanigamādīnaṃ vilopakaraṇaṃ. Sahasākāroti sāhasakiriyā, gehaṃ pavisitvā, manussānaṃ ure satthaṃ ṭhapetvā, icchitabhaṇḍaggahaṇaṃ. Evametasmā chedanavadhabandhanaviparāmosaālopasahasākārā paṭiviratā. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

Ālopa is said to be the plundering of villages, towns, and so forth. Sahasākāra is a violent action, such as entering a house, placing a weapon against people's chests, and taking desired goods. Thus, one abstains from cutting, killing, binding, robbery, plundering, and violent action. The rest is everywhere of clear meaning.

Āmakadhaññapeyyālavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Āmakadhañña-peyyāla is concluded.

Iti sāratthappakāsiniyā saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

Thus in the Sāratthappakāsinī, the Commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya,

Mahāvaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Mahāvagga is concluded.

Nigamanakathā

The Conclusion

Ettāvatā [M 3.0340] hi –

Thus far indeed:

“Bahukārassa [P 3.0308] yatīnaṃ vipassanācāranipuṇabuddhīnaṃ,

Saṃyuttavaranikāyassa atthasaṃvaṇṇanaṃ kātuṃ.

To compose an explanation of the meaning of the excellent Saṃyutta Nikāya, which is of great benefit to monks skilled in the practice of insight and possessing subtle wisdom,

“Saddhammassa ciraṭṭhitimāsisamānena yā mayā;

Nipuṇā aṭṭhakathā āraddhā sāratthapakāsinī nāma.

this subtle commentary named Sāratthappakāsinī was begun by me, wishing for the long-lasting duration of the True Dhamma.

“Sā hi mahāaṭṭhakathāya sāramādāya niṭṭhitā esā;

Aṭṭhasattatimattāya pāḷiyā bhāṇavārehi.

For this has been completed, having extracted the essence from the Great Commentary, the Pāli of which measures seventy-eight recitation sections.

“Ekūnasaṭṭhimatto visuddhimaggopi bhāṇavārehi;

Atthappakāsanatthāya āgamānaṃ kato yasmā.

Since the Visuddhimagga, amounting to fifty-nine recitation sections, was also composed by me for the purpose of clarifying the meaning of the Āgamas,

“Tasmā tena sahāyaṃ aṭṭhakathā bhāṇavāragaṇanāya;

Thokena aparipūraṃ sattatiṃsasataṃ hoti.

therefore, together with that, this commentary, by the reckoning of recitation sections, amounts to one hundred and thirty-seven, lacking a little.

“Sattatiṃsādhikasata-parimāṇaṃ bhāṇavārato evaṃ;

Samayaṃ pakāsayantiṃ mahāvihārādhivāsīnaṃ.

Amounting thus to over one hundred and thirty-seven recitation sections, and declaring the doctrine of the residents of the Great Monastery,

“Mūlaṭṭhakathāya [V 3.0341] sāramādāya mayā imaṃ karontena;

Yaṃ puññamupacitaṃ tena hotu sabbo sukhī loko.

by me, composing this by extracting the essence from the root commentary, whatever merit has been accumulated—by that merit may the whole world be happy.

“Etissā karaṇatthaṃ therena bhadantajotipālena;

Sucisīlena subhāsitassa pakāsayantañāṇena.

For the sake of composing this, by the Elder, the venerable Jotipāla, of pure virtue, with wisdom that clarifies the well-spoken word,

“Sāsanavibhūtikāmena yācamānena maṃ subhaguṇena;

Yaṃ samadhigataṃ puññaṃ tenāpi jano sukhī bhavatū”ti.

who, desiring the flourishing of the Dispensation and being of excellent virtue, requested me—by whatever merit has been acquired, through that also may the people be happy.

Paramavisuddhasaddhābuddhivīriyappaṭimaṇḍitena sīlācārajjavamaddavādiguṇasamudayasamuditena sakasamayasamayantaragahanajjhogāhaṇasamatthena paññāveyyattiyasamannāgatena tipiṭakapariyattippabhede sāṭṭhakathe satthusāsane appaṭihatañāṇappabhāvena mahāveyyākaraṇena karaṇasampattijanitasukhaviniggatamadhurodāravacanalāvaṇṇayuttena yuttamuttavādinā vādīvarena mahākavinā pabhinnapaṭisambhidāparivāre chaḷabhiññādippabhedaguṇappaṭimaṇḍite uttarimanussadhamme [M 3.0341] suppatiṭṭhitabuddhīnaṃ theravaṃsappadīpānaṃ therānaṃ mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ [P 3.0309] vaṃsālaṅkārabhūtena vipulavisuddhabuddhinā buddhaghosoti garūhi gahitanāmadheyyena therena katā ayaṃ sāratthappakāsinī nāma saṃyuttanikāyaṭṭhakathā.

This commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya, called Sāratthappakāsinī, was made by the Elder named Buddhaghosa—a name given by his revered teachers—who was an ornament to the lineage of the Elders residing in the Great Monastery, who were lamps to their lineage, their wisdom well-established in the superhuman states; he was of vast and pure intellect; adorned with qualities such as the sixfold direct knowledge; surrounded by the retinue of the analytical knowledges; a great poet; a supreme debater; a speaker of what is reasoned and well-said; possessing the beauty of sweet and lofty speech born of accomplished means; a great grammarian whose unhindered knowledge shines in the Teacher’s Dispensation with its Tipiṭaka and commentaries; skilled in fathoming the depths of his own and others' traditions; endowed with sharp wisdom; adorned with supremely pure faith, wisdom, and energy; and replete with an assemblage of virtues such as morality, conduct, integrity, and gentleness.

“Tāva tiṭṭhatu lokasmiṃ, lokanittharaṇesinaṃ;

Dassentī kulaputtānaṃ, nayaṃ sīlavisuddhiyā.

May it remain in the world for those seeking to escape from the world, showing sons of good family the way to purity of virtue,

“Yāva buddhoti nāmampi, suddhacittassa tādino;

Lokamhi lokajeṭṭhassa, pavattati mahesino”ti.

for as long as even the name 'Buddha'—of the great seer, the pure-minded, the steadfast, the chief of the world—endures in the world.

Sāratthappakāsinī nāma

Named the Sāratthappakāsinī,

Saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathā sabbākārena niṭṭhitā.

the commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya is concluded in every respect.
